The most virulent antisemites tended to hate Jews from below, blaming them for their own failures and disappointments. Now, however, anti-Jewish bigotry, or at least tacit approval of anti-Jewish bigotry, is coming from people with serious power: the leader of a major political party, a famous pop star, and the world’s richest man. Goldberg is not wrong and is not alone in sounding this alarm. Antisemitism is on the rise. Locally, nationally, and globally it threatens the lives of many, and threatens the very well-being of our society. This reality must call the church to action. BACKGROUND For nearly 20 years, Piedmont Community Service Crew, a coed Venturing unit with Piedmont Scouts, has been providing an opportunity for local teens to develop life skills while in pursuit of helping others and our environment. The crew is led by a team of member leaders who practice organizing and planning service projects. PCSC seeks activities where the teen members learn practical skills while making a tangible impact. One of its most visible activities is the Piedmont 4th of July Pancake Breakfast every year from 8 to 10 a.m. on July 4th in the Veterans Hall. The Crew took it over from the Recreation Department in 2015 and has seen it grow steadily. Other popular activities include planning menus and cooking meals for the food insecure, building tiny homes for the houseless, and constructing planter boxes for seniors. The crew has even created a homework club at an East Oakland elementary school where they tutor kids to improve morale and attendance at school. Unlike many service clubs that only provide volunteer effort, PCSC has a fundraising component that allows the crew to cover the cost in addition to planning and working. Each year crew’s VPs of Fundraising start planning for the pancake breakfast in May. They typically have more than 400 breakfast diners who range from old-timers who have been attending the event for decades, to new families with kids in tow. Proceeds from the pancake breakfast and other fundraising events allow the crew to fund many major service projects, most notably to plan and execute the renovation of a low income or disabled Oakland person’s home each year, in collaboration with Rebuilding Together Oakland with a budget of thousands of dollars. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council approved Piedmont’s participation in a Priority Development Area (PDA) program at its meeting on Tuesday, June 20. The program is overseen by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission and the Association of Bay Area Governments. The council nominated two city sites, Moraga Canyon and parts of Grand Avenue near Linda Avenue. Nominating the sites doesn’t commit the city to developing housing there, but renders the city eligible to receive competitive state grant funds for opportunities to develop them, or study and plan for development. In nominating the two sites, “We’re just queuing up potential access to funds, and those funds can be used for soft costs for planning for studies … that we may do anyway, as part of the unfunded mandate from the state,” said Councilmember Tom Ramsey, a former member of the Planning Commission. He was referring to Piedmont’s ongoing Housing Element state certification process, for which $1.3 million is allocated in the city budget for the coming fiscal year. In a presentation to the Council, City Associate Planner Gopika Nair said that PDA status applies to “areas for future housing growth that are near transit or within ‘high resource areas’ that offer abundant amenities” such as well-resourced schools and wide access to jobs. The Council also nominated Moraga Canyon, where 132 potential homes are planned as part of the city’s Housing Element, as a “priority site” under the MTA and ABAG program. As distinguished from PDA sites, Nair said that priority status applies to sites which can accommodate a high number of housing units for a wide range of incomes, transit options, green space, and facilities, such as Moraga Canyon, which alongside the Corporation Yard, also features a sports field and skate park. A staff report for the meeting states that MTC has approved “$6.7 million in planning grants to local governments” as part of its PDA funding, while $28 million is allocated “to provide predevelopment financing for affordable housing” through the Priority Site program. Nair added that Grand and Linda Avenues are not eligible for priority status, as the Housing Element envisions this site only as a “mixed multi-family residential [and] commercial zone.” To be eligible for state grants under this program, Piedmont must have its Housing Element certified by the state by December 31, 2023. “I’m fairly confident that we’ll be certified by the end of the year, Planning Director Kevin Jackson told the Council.
articles.title: City Council nominates sites for state housing grants

articles.text: Every year on the Fourth of July, Piedmont residents and parade goers can look forward to juicy hamburgers brought to you by Scouts from Piedmont’s Troop 1. The famous juicy burgers, cheeseburgers, and Impossible burgers – made possible through the donation of Dave Larson and Piedmont Grocery – will be available for purchase for $8, with water and watermelon for an additional $2. Buying burgers not only supports the Troop, but also the individual Scouts, who plan and prepare for the stand in the spring and learn important skills such as communication, time management, and safety. Running the stand on the Fourth is a complete Troop effort. The older, more experienced Scouts cook and flip the burgers, while the younger Scouts carefully wrap them to keep them warm. Look for the Troop 1 burger stand near the Exedra this July 4th! The Troop 1 burger stand will be near the Exedra this July 4th
articles.title: Troop 1 Burgers a staple on 4th of July

articles.text: Come join the Piedmont Community Band, the city’s only musical organization that has only one rehearsal during the year. The band is a past winner of the Highland Cup, the highest award given at the July 4th Parade. The band is comprised of amateur and professional musicians – all volunteers – most who live in town and can’t resist the challenge of playing music while marching in formation. Dressed in blue pants, white shirts and a red kerchief, they are led by Ken Kawaichi, who, dressed as Emperor Norton, has the distinction of walking the length of the parade route backwards. It’s time to get out your instruments – trumpets, trombones, tubas, clarinets and drums – and help celebrate Independence Day in Piedmont. If you are new in town, it’s an ideal way to meet people, To sign up, contact Greg Slatoff at goslatoff@ yahoo.com, or call Jane Reed at 654-2670. articles.text: Big Bang Beat, a 12-piece band featuring songs of the 60’s Motown sound, the fabulous funk of the 70’s, and dance hits from the 80’s and 90’s, returns to Piedmont as the featured band on the main stage in Piedmont Park following the city’s 2023 Fourth of July Parade. The band is led by four dazzling female singers decked out in sequined mini dresses, plus a horn section and a choreographed stage show. Its zany, non-stop energy has made Big Bang Beat a fixture at clubs, conventions, fund-raisers and corporate and private parties throughout the U.S. Nine of the band members are veterans of the Zasu Pitts Memorial Orchestra. Big Bang Beat is a frequent headline band at clubs throughout California and Nevada, and has performed in Switzerland, Hawaii, Malaysia, Canary Islands, Istanbul, Acapulco, and the Caribbean.

pages.text: Wednesday, June 28, 2023 5 Calling all musicians for July 4th Parade Come join the Piedmont Community Band, the city’s only musical organization that has only one rehearsal during the year. The band is a past winner of the Highland Cup, the highest award given at the July 4th Parade. The band is comprised of amateur and professional musicians – all volunteers – most who live in town and can’t resist the challenge of playing music while marching in formation. Dressed in blue pants, white shirts and a red kerchief, they are led by Ken Kawaichi, who, dressed as Emperor Norton, has the distinction of walking the length of the parade route backwards. It’s time to get out your instruments – trumpets, trombones, tubas, clarinets and drums – and help celebrate Independence Day in Piedmont. If you are new in town, it’s an ideal way to meet people, To sign up, contact Greg Slatoff at goslatoff@ yahoo.com, or call Jane Reed at 654-2670. articles.text: At its May 24 meeting, the Piedmont School Board adopted a phonics-based reading curriculum to supplement its current “balanced literacy” program for grades K-3. T he bala nced literacy approach prioritizes “whole language” reading, which teaches children to focus on whole words by guessing their meaning through context, as opposed to the “structured literacy” approach, which teaches children to focus on sounding the parts of words out phonetically. An example of this difference is provided on the publisher’s blog of Lucy Calkins, a balanced literacy proponent whose “Units of Study” curriculum was implemented by the Piedmont School District in 2019. She has since rewritten her own system to more fully embrace phonics, in accordance with the criticisms of parents and educators who espouse the phonetic “science of reading.” Describing this revision, Calkins writes, “When a child is reading a sentence such as, ‘It was cold, so I put on my jacket,’ and the child gets stuck on jacket, we now suggest the teacher nudge by saying, ‘Look at the letters, have a go with that word,’ rather than saying, ‘Think about what’s happening. articles.text: I am an ADHD Focus Coach located in Piedmont. I work with students and people with ADHD to help them overcome obstacles and achieve their goals. I am certified in Applied Positive Psychology and use my education and my personal experience with ADHD to coach my clients. This week, I am going to talk about habit formation and how a 30-day challenge might be just what you need to start your next habit. Habits are defined as “a settled or regular tendency or practice, especially one that is hard to give up.” We tend to think about habits in the context of things that are bad for our health and also in the context of things that are good for our health. Learning how to use the science behind habit formation to your advantage can make it easier to achieve the goals you set for yourself. Once something is put into a regular practice, it takes a lot of the effort out of getting that thing done for the day. You’ve already decided that you’re going to do whatever it is every day so there’s no longer that activation energy required each day to complete the task. The decision has been made and the only thing left to do is to get that thing accomplished since it’s part of your daily checklist. I recommend 30-day challenges as a way to try out habits that you want to implement without committing to doing them as a habit for the rest of your life. A 30-day challenge is when you commit to doing your new habit every day for 30 days and then decide at the end of that trial period whether or not you will continue that habit and for what amount of time. There are countless habits you could implement using this method but a few that my clients have seen success with are meditation, yoga, trying a new hobby, journaling, and going for a daily walk. Forming habits can be especially difficult with ADHD because people with ADHD tend to struggle with daily routines and organization. Incorporating something into your daily routine can make it easier to remember and accomplish the things you want to get done for the day, especially things like fitness and things that benefit mental health which can be harder to make time for. Using the 30-day challenge methodology is especially useful for people with ADHD because it does not have to be the same habit every time which allows for novelty. At the end of the 30 days, you can decide whether or not you want to implement the new hobby or try something else. 30-day challenges are a great way for people with ADHD to make positive lifestyle changes and stay focused on the goals they set. What can you do every day for the next 30 days? Erica Monical is the founder and focus coach at MindsGlowing. She can be reached at 415- 680-6990 or mindsglowing@ gmail.com.

articles.text: The Piedmont School Board will hold its final meeting tonight, Wednesday, June 28, before new Superintendent Jennifer Hawn takes over on July 1. The school board plans to ratify the appointment of a new Piedmont High School Assistant Principal to take the place of Irma Muñez. Asst. Principal Erin Igoe remains on staff, as does PHS Principal Sukanya Goswami. Finance officer Ruth Alahydoian will announce the adoption of the 2023-24 District General Fund Budget. An updated Coaches Stipend will be revealed which will include the addition of Girls Beach Volleyball, Girls Flag Football and a Frosh Girls Lacrosse team in an effort to balance the number of male and female roster spots. The Citizens’ Bond Oversight Committee will give its annual report on the Measure H! Bond program which paid for a $30 million classroom building, and a $25 million theater building. Board members are expected to discuss how they can close a funding gap of $1,800,000. An agreement will be announced between CalStateTEACH and the district to provide student teacher placements. The meeting is open to the public and will take place in Piedmont City Council Chambers at 120 Vista Avenue. Participation in public comment may be made remotely on Zoom. us/j/82420401914.

10 Wednesday, June 28, 2023 Postcards from Camp Postcards from Camp Letters to home by kids at Camp Augusta Throughout the summer the Post prints a sampling of letters written by kids attending Camp Augusta, Piedmont’s residential camp at Lake Vera outside Nevada City in the Sierra foothills. Founded in 1931, the camp remains a vital part of the life of hundreds of children each summer. Chilly weather didn’t dampen spirits as campers got up to all kinds of creative activities, which was the focus in the second week of camp. The ropes courses and high-energy activities were more popular, which was a nice side effect. For more information, see campaugusta.org. An Oak cabin creates an obstacle course on the Tiny Field as a team building activity. Campers making sourdough bread, a classic staple of the summer A cabin builds and then burns a cardboard town. Manzi 2 constructs a car out of a mountain board and cardboard big enough to fit camp baby. Manzi 3 sprays water guns at a cabin mate on Giant Swing. Campers are taught how to build cardboard boats.

articles.text: With the new school year quickly approaching, the Class of 2024 looks past the summer break to what could be a defining year of their athletic careers as a senior. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them when they return. PETER KRUMINS Water Polo & Baseball Peter Krumins is an influential member of Piedmont High’s water polo team in the fall and baseball team in the spring. He’s already won three WACC championships in his time at the school with two consecutive titles with water polo and was a member of PHS’ 2022 Shoreline championship in baseball. In water polo, Krumins helped lead the Highlanders to a 20-7 record and win its second WACC title by scoring six goals in their 13-4 win over Alameda on October 29. He was also a key player in Piedmont’s 2021 WACC Title, which was the first in school history, where he scored twice in a 12-8 win over Berkeley. On the baseball team, Krumins spent most of his time at third base but also appeared as a pitcher in 2023. articles.text: With making mention of the current athletic accomplishments of student-athletes at Piedmont High, it can get easy to lose track of those who have continued their careers after moving on from the small town in the hills. In this week’s issue, we take a look at Andy Melian (football), Kai Johnson (basketball), and Gavin Horne (track and field). Kai Johnson Weber State Kai Johnson, PHS Class of 2021, was a four-year starter at Piedmont High and was named the Post’s Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year as a senior. She’s entering her junior year at Weber State. Lat year she appeared in 29 games and had 38 points, 18 rebounds, seven assists, seven steals, and two blocks. As a freshman, she played in 26 games with 19 points, 14 steals, 16 rebounds, three assists, and one blocked shot. For Piedmont, she was the team’s captain for her final two years at the school. Johnson was a major part of a strong fouryear run for the girls’ basketball program, finishing with records of 23-7 in 2017/2018, 20-11 in 2018/2019, 21-7 in 2019/2020, and 15-3 in 2021’s shortened pandemic season. Andy Melian, PHS Class of 2021, finished his sophomore year after appearing in 10 games for Kenyon College. Andy Melian Kenyon College Andy Melian, PHS Class of 2021, just finished his sophomore year at Kenyon College and earned regular playing time for the Owls. In 2022, Melian appeared in 10 games and recorded 19 total tackles and 3.5 tackles for loss. During his senior year at Piedmont, Melian was a key in the school’s perfect 5-0 season in 2021. He had the most productive season of any defensive lineman on the team, recording seven sacks and 16 tackles for loss in the shortened season. He wreaked havoc with 11 total tackles, two sacks, seven tackles for loss, and a block extra point in the season-opener against the Castro Valley Trojans, put down three tackles for loss against Mt Eden, a sack and two tackles for loss on Berkeley, seven tackles, two sacks, and four tackles for loss on Washington, and two sacks and three tackles for loss in the season-finale against Kennedy on April 16. Gavin Horne, PHS Class of 2021, is making a name for himself in the jumping events with PomonaPitzer. Gavin Horne Pomona-Pitzer Gavin Horne, PHS Class of 2021, recently completed his sophomore year on Pomona-Pitzer’s track and field team, primarily competing in jumping events. Competing in the long jump and triple jump, he reached the SCIAC Track and Field Championships on April 29-30. In the long jump, Horne was 15th of 24 with a distance of 5.78 meters. In the triple jump, Gavin finished 14th with a distance of 11.34 meters. His long jump at the SCIAC Championship marked a personal record for him, while also reaching a distance of 11.42 meters in the triple jump at the PLNU Invitational on March 25. Kai Johnson (34), PHS Class of 2021, completed her sophomore year at Weber State.

Wednesday, June 28, 2023 13 Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 16th year. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmont-post.com. AUDREY LAM Soccer Piedmont High Class of 2023 Brown University Class of 2027 Audrey Lam helped lead the girls’ soccer team to a 13-1-6 (W-T-L) record and winning its first North Coast Section championship in 20 years. She was the WACC Player of the Year and received a first-team All-League selection for the second time. Lam brought flair that’s rarely seen at Witter Field, with an array of skills with back heel flicks, shots from distance, long passing with pin-point accuracy, and technical footwork to weave around and between defenders. She’s perhaps the most decorated soccer prospect in PHS history as a three-time invite to the United States’ Youth National Team. She was invited to train with the U18/U19 team in April, was invited to Kansas City in 2019, and played for the U-17 Women’s National Team in friendlies against Spain and Germany in August last year. She signed a Letter of Intent to continue her soccer career at Brown University in Rhode Island. What is your workout program this summer? I have an app with my Brown University Soccer Team, which uploads new workouts each day for us to follow. This program ensures that we come into Brown fit and ready to start preseason. What are your fitness goals for this summer? My fitness goals for this summer are to become as fast and strong as possible while also developing and fine tuning my technical skills. How are you measuring your development? Through the app, we can mark our PR which gives us an idea of how much harder we need to work. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’m working on my own, as well as continuing to go to my WPSL practices, games, and tournaments. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? A recent milestone was being called up to the U-20 Women’s National Team for camp in North Carolina. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? Remember that you are a student first and an athlete second. If your goal is to compete in college and beyond, it’s important to maintain good grades while pursuing your dreams as an athlete. Additionally, you have to understand that to achieve your goals, there will be things you’ll have to sacrifice. Staff Photo William Daniel, PHS Class of 2023, scored the game-winning goal in Piedmont’s NCS title game. He’s off to Leeds Beckett University in England. WILLIAM DANIEL Soccer Staff Photo Audrey Lam, PHS Class of 2023, was the Post’s Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year and will continue her soccer career at Brown University. Piedmont High Class of 2023 Leeds Beckett University Class of 2027 William Daniel graduates from Piedmont High after helping lead the soccer team to a second consecutive Division 4 North Coast Section championship. He scored the game-winning goal in a 1-0 win over University. Daniel appeared as a midfielder in Todd Sullivan’s system, but also had the height and strength to move into the forward role. He was a three-year varsity letterman, but missed much of his first two years due to injuries. Daniel highlights his summer schedule while rehabbing from extensive hip surgery. What is your workout program this summer? Since I am recovering from hip surgery on both sides, my program right now is strictly physical therapy exercises. They consist of things like balancing on one leg, light squats, and many hip stretches. Further into the summer I will slowly bring up the intensity and work on strength training. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My fitness goals are to get back to being fully healthy so that I will be able to play soccer. I will be starting college ball in England in September, so it is crucial for me to get better by then. How are you measuring your development? I measure development by looking at what I could do with my body a week before. For example, I’ll be tracking how long I can walk, how far my hips could bend, etc. I’m confident using weekly increments is the best way to go. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? Most of the time I am working on my own, but I see a physical therapist twice a week and he checks out my progress each visit. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? My recent milestone is being able to walk normally. Since my left hip had surgery three weeks after the right, it was hard to walk without a limp, but now I can move like I used to. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Follow your passions and turn them into a career. If there is a sport you love with all of your heart, not only work hard to be a professional at it, but also study a degree that will get you a job working in that same sport--even if it isn’t on the field. EMILY FITZGERALD Soccer Piedmont High Class of 2023 UC San Diego Class of 2027 Emily Fitzgerald graduates from Piedmont High as one of the best playoff performers in school history. She helped Piedmont win the Div. 4 North Coast Section championship with goals in all five postseason matches, including the Div. 3 CIF NorCal Tournament against No. 1 Sequoia. As a four-year starter, she scored 11 goals in nine post-season playoff games, and logged Piedmont’s first goal in State postseason history. She scored the opening goal in the 35th minute of the finals against University, and in the Norcal playoffs forced overtime with Sequoia with a goal. In 2022, Fitzgerald scored four times in an opening round 4-0 win over College Prep. As a freshman in 2020, she scored once in an opening-round 2-1 win over Urban. Her 2021 season did not feature an NCS postseason due to the global pandemic. She earned first-team AllLeague honors as a senior and is set to continue playing at UC San Diego. Fitzgerald also recently appeared with Pleasanton RAGE in its USL W League season, which is a pre-professional development league. What is your workout program this summer? I have a fitness packet from UC San Diego. It includes three lifts a week and then daily fitness. Each day’s fitness and weightlifting is written out with detail. Along with the fitness packet, I am playing on semi-pro team Pleasanton RAGE to improve my soccer specific skills. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My fitness goals for this summer are to become game-fit for college soccer. I want to be ready to play a 90 minute game at the Division 1 level. How are you measuring your development? To measure my development, I’m doing a weekly 300-yard (25-yard shuttle) test. This test involves sprinting to the 25-yard line and back six times in under one minute. The goal of this test is to see how many 300-yard shuttles you can do in under one minute with just a two-minute rest in between. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am currently working on my own for fitness. From a soccer standpoint, I work with trainer and former Piedmont great, Nikolai Littleton. Also, I am playing for Pleasanton RAGE’s USL W League semi-pro team. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone was scoring in my first USL game versus Olympic Club. Also, I played against high-level teams like Oakland Soul, SF Glens, and California Storm. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Work hard and push yourself, but also don’t forget to live the sport as much as possible. Having an intense internal drive and love for the game is necessary for success. articles.text: 4th in double scull, 9th in quadruple Piedmont High junior Anna Lavin (left) and teammate Isabella Warner of Carondolet placed fourth in the U-17 double scull at the 2023 Youth National Championship. Piedmont High School junior Anna Lavin, competing with Artemis Rowing Club, reached the 2023 U.S. Rowing Youth National Championship in Sarasota, Florida earlier this month, June 8-11. She raced in two events, finishing as the country’s fourth fastest boat in the women’s U-17 double scull, while also finishing ninth in the women’s youth quadruple scull. “It definitely took a lot to get there. Originally, we weren’t planning on bringing two boats. We qualified in our double and we thought that would be the only boat we were going to take. But we wound up qualifying in the quad, so we thought why not bring two,” said Lavin. In the U-17 double scull, Lavin paired with Isabella Warner of Carondolet, finishing the A Final in fourth of eight boats with a time of 7:57.502. To get there, Lavin and Warner finished the semifinals with a time of 8:02.565 in a field of eight and placed sixth of 26 in the time trials in 7:48.422. Lavin and Warner qualified for National Championships by placing second in California’s unofficial state meet, the Southwest Regional Championship at Lake Natoma in Sacramento on May 8. “When we were going into regionals, we were against some really competitive boats. Our goal was to reach the Grand Final A at Nationals, which we ended up doing. Going into time trials, we just knew we wanted to be in the top-12, we wound up placing sixth. We were both nervous, but super dedicated to that boat. Isabella and I are really good friends, so it was a really good experience,” said Lavin. This year marked Lavin’s first time competing in the double scull with Warner. “Last year, I was in U-16 (my age group) and they don’t take any doubles. We didn’t want to race up an age group and instead raced in the coxed quad. This year was our first season in our doubles. We have a small club at Artemis, so I’m super lucky Isabella rowed there also because we’re a good match. Going into fall season, we wanted to try out our doubles, so we did a few races. We placed second in our last race of the fall, so we were super excited going into the spring. We did a lot of racing and knew we wanted to try and get to Nationals. We were just dedicated to it,” said Lavin. Lavin’s boat won the B Final in. the quadruple scull in a field of eight to finish as the ninth fastest quadruple boat in the country. She paired with Warner, Oakland Tech’s Amalia Campbell, and Head-Royce’s Josie Landreth In the semifinals for sixth place. “We weren’t really sure where that boat was going to go. It was a youth event and Isabella and I race U17, while it was the first year for the other girls racing at the youth level. It’s good to get that experience so we can come back in future years,” said Lavin. It marked her second appearance at the Youth National Championship with the quadruple scull’ He boat placed 14th in the 2022 Nationals in Florida. Anna Lavin’s youth quadruple boat finished ninth at Nationals. Pictured are Oakland Tech’s Amalia Campbell (left), Lavin, HeadRoyce’s Josie Landreth, and Isabella Warner of Carondolet.
articles.title: PHS junior Anna Lavin competes in two events at Youth National Championship

articles.text: Faces Saint Kitts and Nevis today, Trinidad and Tobago Sunday The CONCACAF Gold Cup is rolling through its first of three Group Stage matches. The United States Men’s National Soccer Team opened with a narrow 1-1 draw against Jamaica on Saturday, June 24 at Soldier Field in Chicago. They are now set to face small Caribbean nation of Saints Kitts and Nevis today, June 28, and close against lowly ranked Trinidad and Tobago on July 2. Getting by Jamaica with a 1-1 draw was the minimum needed by the United States to have a chance at winning Group A. Jamaica is considered the strongest of the other three teams in Group A. The U.S. dominated possession against the Reggae Boyz with 68 percent possession and 13 shots on goal, with four on target. However, Jamaica did great work on the counter attack and arguably should’ have won. Jamaica struck first in the 13th minute when Everton winger Demarai Gray sent a long pass in from a free kick, connecting with Philadelphia Union center back Damion Lowe for the header goal. The Reggae Boyz could have gone up 2-nil after drawing a penalty kick in the 27th minute, but U.S. keeper Matthew Turner read Leon Bailey’s shot to the right post perfectly for a deflection, and Bailey’s rebound opportunity went far left. But it took 88 minutes of the 90-minute game fort the U.S. to find the equalizer. Jesus Ferriera sent in a cross in front of net, making contact with a defender Photo courtesy of FrontRowSoccer.com U.S. Men’s Soccer Team goalkeeper Matthew Turner came up huge by stopping a penalty kick by Jamaica’s Leon Bailey.
articles.title: USMNT ties Jamaica 1-1

pages.text: Wednesday, June 28, 2023 15 HIKING WITH JON Walking Angel Island State Park’s perimeter trail By Jonathan Comeaux It’s hard to think of a better location to take in the beauty of the Bay Area and acknowledge its history than Angel Island, now a state park. It’s a true gem resting right on the Marin County shore, where hikers, campers, bikers, and families can take in its gorgeous surroundings and learn about the area’s past. The perimeter loop of Angel Island is approximately 6.2 miles with 495 feet of elevation gain, but added detours to the Immigration Station, Fort McDowell, Quarry Point and Beach, or other beaches will easily equate to a hike of over eight miles with nearly 1,000 feet of elevation gain. Starting your hike walking past the Angel Island Visitor Center, turning left once you hit the paved Perimeter Road, you’ll walk slightly under two miles to the Immigration Station. The area was constructed in 1905 and controlled the entry of approximately one million Chinese citizens into the country. The area provides a look into the culture of AmeriThe Post Exchange at Fort McDowell, with the Golden Gate Bridge in the distance. The lush captain’s quarters on Angel Island. The western side of the island provides a view of Alcatraz. The view from Quarry Beach, a great place to rest for a snack. A view of the Angel Island Immigration Station. can under the Chinese Exclusion Act and the harsh reality of Asian immigrants. Outside the Detention Center reads phrases that reflected the reality for the vast amount of Chinese immigrants; “Bravery, Loneliness, Frustration, Anger, Segregation, Confinement, Courage, Sacrifice.” There is a $5 admittance cost to enter. The hospital is free to the public. Along the shore is “The Wharf,” where immigrants took their first steps into the country. You can picture how it may have looked while gazing out to the Bay’s water. Although it’s a beautiful place to rest, it’s a harsh reminder of what immigrants endured the very second they entered the United States. Just a half of a mile past the Immigration Station is the abandoned buildings of Fort McDowell, a former barracks for soldiers, the plush captain’s quarters, and a decrepit building where the mess hall was located. Nearby is the former officer’s building, which is now a museum. Although it was closed on our visit, a park ranger allowed me inside to take photos. Inside are old relics from World War I and Staff Photos There is a great view of the Bay from the Wharf, but a harsh reminder of the experience for Asian Immigrants entering the country in the early 1900s. A view of the abandoned soldier barracks at Fort McDowell. World War II. Including cannon balls, and a section of jail cells. The area is typically open in the busy season around the 4th of July, so be sure to visit now. Continuing for nearly three miles along the western side of the Island, you’ll have a continues view of San Francisco, Alcatraz, and the Golden Gate Bridge until reaching the Camp Reynolds Hospital. If you continue off trail past the hospital, a short walk takes you to Point Stuart, which provides a secluded view of the Golden Gate, Sausalito, and Belvedere Island of Marin County. From Point Stuart, it’s just one mile back to the starting point where you can wait for the ferry. Catch a bite and a drink at the Angel Island Café, which often has live music on the weekends. If you want to save your leg and foot strength, bike rentals are available for $26 per hour or $99 for the entire day. Reprinted from Piedmont Post, June 2022. Point Stuart provides a secluded view of the Golden Gate.

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) is partnering with the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) to offer free admission to both museums for OMCA members July 14 through 16. Visit SFMOMA to view its newest exhibition, Frank Bowling: The New York Years 1966– 1975, the first major exhibit of the artist’s work in North America in forty years. The exhibition features 45 vibrant and largescale paintings, and a selection of archival materials such as recorded interviews of the artist in New York and London, film footage and photographs from Bowling’s 1968 visit to Guyana. Also on display is Kinship: Photography and Connection, which features six contemporary photographers who exhibit portraiture photographs and share a relationship with their subjects: whether they are familial, platonic, romantic, cultural, or geographic in nature. There are plenty of exhibitions to enjoy now at the Oakland Museum. Its newest exhibition Into the Brightness: Artists from Creativity Explored, Creative Growth & NIAD is the first-ever full exhibition at a major art museum that features art by individuals with learning disabilities, including artists from Creativity Explored in San Francisco, Creative Growth in Oakland, and NIAD (Nurturing Independence Through Artistic Development) Art Center in Richmond. Also visit Oakland Museum on Fridays after 5 p.m. for “Friday Nights” events, with rotating musicians and bands, outdoor family-friendly activities and after-hours admission to the museum. Present your OMCA membership card and a photo ID at the SFMOMA check-in desk and enjoy free admission Friday, July 14 through Sunday, July 16. For more information, visit https:// museumca.org/event/bonus-reciprocity-weekend-at-sfmoma/. Photo of front of Oakland Museum > edwardjones.com | Member SIPC
articles.title: Oakland Museum members to receive free admission to SFMOMA July 14-16

articles.text: The Legion of Honor, of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, welcomed the pubic last weekend to view the opening an exhibit of The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England this Saturday, June 24. This is the first major exhibition in the United States of portraiture and decorative arts of the Tudor courts. It will include works from the museum’s collection, including a late 16th century panel painting, as well as tapestries commissioned or acquired by Henry VII and Henry VIII. “Few may be aware of the distinctive art and visual propaganda that was central to the splendor and drama of the Tudor court,” said Thomas Campbell, Director of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Now, in the first exhibition of its kind in the US, The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England reunites scores of sumptuous paintings, precious jewels, rich tapestries and rare artifacts from collections around the world to bring the Tudor dynasty vividly to life–from the bloody founding of the dynasty in 1485 by Henry VII on the fields of Bosworth, to the final moments of Queen Elizabeth in 1603.” The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England will be on view from June 24 through September 24. For tickets and more information, visit https://www.famsf.org.
articles.title: The Tudors exhibit opens at Legion of Honor

articles.text: Exhibition on view through July 10 San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum’s exhibit Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in Art, currently at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco, ends soon. The exhibition features more than 120 artworks borrowed from 20 of the finest museums and private collections in the world, with a focus on the arts of the Indian cultural sphere. Beyond Bollywood includes artwork from India, Pakistan, Nepal, Tibet, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, and Indonesia. “We hope visitors will come away with a transformed notion of the importance and power of dance,” said exhibition co-curator Forrest McGill. “[Both] what it has meant in the past, and what it can mean in their own lives today.” “Dance dialogues,”events that include asian folk dance with expert speaker panels, take place June 22 and July 9. These popups will include 30-minute dance performances and demonstrations in the museum gallery, followed by a question and answer session, recurring monthly on selected Photo courtesy of charyaburt.com Cambodian dance company Charya Burt will perform during “Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in Art,” at the Asian Art Museum. Sundays and Thursdays. Admission is included with your ticket to Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in Art. Space is limited; reservations are recommended. For a full list of featured dancers and speakers, visit https://asianart. org/beyond-bollywood-events/. Beyond Bollywood will be on display through July 10. For more information, and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://exhibitions.asianart. org/exhibitions/beyond-bollywood-2000-years-of-dance-inart/.
articles.title: Asian Art Museum’s Beyond Bollywood ends soon

pages.text: 16 Wednesday, June 28, 2023 Arts & Entertainment Oakland Museum members to receive free admission to SFMOMA July 14-16 By Allyson Aleksey Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) is partnering with the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) to offer free admission to both museums for OMCA members July 14 through 16. Visit SFMOMA to view its newest exhibition, Frank Bowling: The New York Years 1966– 1975, the first major exhibit of the artist’s work in North America in forty years. The exhibition features 45 vibrant and largescale paintings, and a selection of archival materials such as recorded interviews of the artist in New York and London, film footage and photographs from Bowling’s 1968 visit to Guyana. Also on display is Kinship: Photography and Connection, which features six contemporary photographers who exhibit portraiture photographs and share a relationship with their subjects: whether they are familial, platonic, romantic, cultural, or geographic in nature. There are plenty of exhibitions to enjoy now at the Oakland Museum. Its newest exhibition Into the Brightness: Artists from Creativity Explored, Creative Growth & NIAD is the first-ever full exhibition at a major art museum that features art by individuals with learning disabilities, including artists from Creativity Explored in San Francisco, Creative Growth in Oakland, and NIAD (Nurturing Independence Through Artistic Development) Art Center in Richmond. Also visit Oakland Museum on Fridays after 5 p.m. for “Friday Nights” events, with rotating musicians and bands, outdoor family-friendly activities and after-hours admission to the museum. Present your OMCA membership card and a photo ID at the SFMOMA check-in desk and enjoy free admission Friday, July 14 through Sunday, July 16. For more information, visit https:// museumca.org/event/bonus-reciprocity-weekend-at-sfmoma/. The Tudors exhibit opens at Legion of Honor By Allyson Aleksey The Legion of Honor, of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, welcomed the pubic last weekend to view the opening an exhibit of The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England this Saturday, June 24. This is the first major exhibition in the United States of portraiture and decorative arts of the Tudor courts. It will include works from the museum’s collection, including a late 16th century panel painting, as well as tapestries commissioned or acquired by Henry VII and Henry VIII. “Few may be aware of the distinctive art and visual propaganda that was central to the splendor and drama of the Tudor court,” said Thomas Campbell, Director of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Now, in the first exhibition of its kind in the US, The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England reunites scores of sumptuous paintings, precious jewels, rich tapestries and rare artifacts from collections around the world to bring the Tudor dynasty vividly to life–from the bloody founding of the dynasty in 1485 by Henry VII on the fields of Bosworth, to the final moments of Queen Elizabeth in 1603.” The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England will be on view from June 24 through September 24. For tickets and more information, visit https://www.famsf.org. Asian Art Museum’s Beyond Bollywood ends soon Exhibition on view through July 10 Photo of front of Oakland Museum By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum’s exhibit Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in Art, currently at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco, ends soon. articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s production Out of Character is playing onstage now through July 30. Tony Award-winner Ari’el Stachel, director for Out of Character, is an Israeli-American of Yemeni Jewish descent living in Berkeley. This new single-character show follows Stachel’s attempts to hide his Middle Eastern background after 9/11 as a young adult. Covering his identity and culture led the artist to experience years of anxiety, prompting him to eventually explore it as a play theme. Stachel joins former Berkeley Rep artistic director Tony Taccone to tell his story in a solo show. Out of Character looks at the intersections of race, mental health and survival. Post-show discussions led by Berkeley Rep staff members take place on July 7, 13 and 18. To purchase tickets and learn more, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/shows/out-of-character/. Director Ari’el Stachel.

articles.text: Valley of the Moon Music Festival in Sonoma County will take place July 15 through 30 and tickets are now available. This year’s festival, now in its ninth season, will highlight works originally written for large orchestras in chamber music ensembles. The festival is widely enjoyed in part due to its mix of alfresco and indoor concerts, as well as livestream events. The festival opens on July 15 with “The Symphony as a Trio,” featuring Mozart’s Piano Quartets as written like concertos. The piano is featured, accompanied by a “mini orchestra” of three string players featuring Axel Trolese as soloist. For a full lineup, and to purchase tickets, visit https://valleyofthemoonmusicfestival.org/ event/the-symphony-as-a-triomozart-beethoven/. articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is currently performing the musical A Chorus Line through September 9. Directed by Bill English and based on the book by James Kirkwood Jr. and Nicholas Dante, A Chorus Line follows 17 Broadway dancers who are auditioning for eight openings in a chorus line. The play explores the inner lives, desires and ambitions of the performers, while capturing the spirit, tension and hope that comes with auditions. A Chorus Line is Broadway’s longest running musical and the winner of the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 1976, and winner of nine Tony Awards, four Drama Desk awards, and three Obie Awards. The play was conceived and originally directed and choreographed by Michael Bennett with music by Marvin Hamlisch and lyrics by Edward Kleban. Music direction at SF Playhouse is by Dave Dobrusky with choreography by Nicole Helfer. The cast features Dalton Bertolone, Samatha Cardenas, Danielle Cheiken, Gabi Chun, Tony Conaty, Maggie Connard, Chachi Delgado, Zeke Edmonds, Alison Ewing and Elihu Guerrero. To purchase tickets and learn more. Visit: https://www.sfplayhouse.org/sfph/2022-2023-season/a-chorus-line/ Cast members of San Francisco Playhouse’s current production of A Chorus Line.
articles.title: SF Playhouse presents “A Chorus Line” now through September

articles.text: Remarkably, a short story by the science fiction writer Philip K. Dick, adapted for the screen as The Adjustment Bureau, turns out to be the best romance of the year. A different love story to be sure, crafted from an unusual premise; however, because Hollywood has served up an endless string of trivial nonsense, this film comes as a welcome surprise. It begins with Elise Sellas (Emily Blunt), a ballet dancer, and David Norris (Matt Damon), a hotshot politician running for the state senate, meeting cute in the men’s room of the Waldorf Astoria. David is preparing to deliver a very difficult speech. Certain that he’s alone, he begins rehearsing. Suddenly, Elise steps out of one of the stalls. They begin a gentle, smart badinage and their mutual attraction is quickly evident – to them and the audience. But here’s the rub: all that has happened to them is part of a greater plan. If either deviates from the plan, well, a small adjustment will be necessary. Enter stage left, the Adjustment Bureau: men in snap-brim hats, dark suits, and narrow ties, who warn David that he cannot pursue a relationship with Elise, for reasons that will not be disclosed. David, impulsive and a bit reckless, is not inclined to cooperate, sensing that in Elise he has met someone unlike anyone before. Perhaps you have to suspend your disbelief to be fully engaged by The Adjustment Bureau. You must be willing to give the story sufficient latitude, all in the interest of being intrigued and perhaps even surprised. It helps that the fantasy/sci fi aspects of the film are handled so seamlessly that it never seems contrived or in any way jarring. It all fits nicely together. Regarding the story: as David grows more intent on pursuing a relationship with Elise, the story delves into the existential question of free will. Do we design our own lives or are there forces greater than ourselves that guides us? Should David be allowed to choose? Are any of truly free to choose? In the world of Philip K. Dick, the ability to make choices is an illusion. During those periods in history when the Bureau stepped back and let mankind truly choose, the result was the 20th century, one of the most violent in history. Hence, the Bureau concluded that it was time to provide some guidance. So David falls down the rabbit hole (where would sci-fi/fantasy be without it?), and sets in motion a test of wills between himself the Bureau, who insist that Elise cannot be part of his destiny. Act two and three involve an escalation of tension, some well choreographed chase scenes, while pieces of the puzzle begin to fall into place. If your threshold for such storytelling is high, if your imagination is captured by such a premise, then you will find The Adjustment Bureau a solidly entertaining film, a perfect blend of romance and the improbable, nicely imagined and well acted. If storytelling must mirror life, well, this movie, not so much. The Adjustment Bureau. Written and directed by George Nolfi. Starring Matt Damon, Emily Blunt, John Slattery, Anthony Mackie and Terrance Stamp. 1 hr. 45 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. Matt Damon and Emily Blunt star in The Adjustment Bureau
articles.title: The Adjustment Bureau – when sci-fi and romance converge

articles.text: What is always compelling about post-apocalyptic films is the freedom writers have to take the remnants of civilization and construct their own view of how the world might be found. Often they tap into that latent feeling that if the constraints and demands of modern society, along with the intrusive overlay of technology, were swept away, along with most people (say a worldwide pandemic), leaving everything else in tact, then life for those who survive, while desperately lonely, might just be a magnificent shopping spree. The supplies and equipment and clothing and cars are endless and should last several generations. Okay, no hospitals, likely no doctors, but lots of drug stores, hardware stores and Safeways. This particular vision is closer to utopian than not, and such scenarios have an almost 60s texture: those left behind return to their roots, find fulfillment in a simpler, agrarian life, establish embracing communities, band together to confront those who don’t share their values. A fine example is The Postman, one of the better post-apocalyptic films to come out of the 90s. And then there is the vision of a world that is far more dystopian. In these films an event has altered the landscape, leaving the environment all but stripped of foliage, the forests gray-brown stumps, the sky raining ash and covered by a perpetual gray mist. All is barren, as are the souls of men. This is the vision of the film The Book of Eli. A solitary man (Denzel Washington) is walking west. It proves to be a harrowing journey. The patina of restraint, of law and order, has been supplanted by a simmering, lethal violence. Predators are everywhere, the strong victimizing the weak. With its desolate, sepia tones, The Book of Eli is an engaging film. Briefly, Eli on his way to the Pacific Ocean, arrives at a bleak-looking town where, he discovers, they have water, the hard currency of this brave new world. A ruthless leader, Carnegie (Gary Oldman), surrounded by a brigade of thugs, is looking for a particular book, believing that it will give him the words to expand his powers well beyond his small fiefdom. He is convinced that Eli, who has disclosed that he reads a book every day, might have the last remaining copy. There are moments of stylized violence that never feel gratuitous and certainly add to the mystery of this singular man called Eli. Who is he? And how has he survived some 30 years of wandering through the detritus of a ruined civilization, a man on a mission that transcends simply heading west, a mission from which he will not be deterred. There is a religious overlay to the narrative, but the film never feels preachy. And there is a wonderful twist at the end of the film that is unexpected. Post apocalyptic films have the potential to be far more interesting than catastrophic disaster films – examples being The Day After Tomorrow and 2012. Post films can dwell on the fragility of civilization. They can make the point that without a modicum of harmony and order and restraint, society can quickly devolve into chaos, framed by an endless desolation. In these films, human nature can be examined in its most brutal and its most heroic form. Such possibilities are what make this genre so potentially powerful and certainly entertaining. The Book of Eli. Directed by Allen Hughes. Starring Denzel Washington, Gary Oldman, Mila Kunis. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated R. Released in 2010, Now streaming on Hulu/Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: The Book of Eli a post-dystopian story

articles.text: Song of the Sea is a spare but ethereal Irish mythical tale that will captivate young audiences. It blends Celtic legend with a wonderful hand-drawn design and intelligent storytelling. The film has at its center, two children, 10-year-old Ben (David Rawle) and his 6-year-old sister, Saoirse. They live with their grieving father (Brendan Frasera), a ;ight house keeper, on a remote island off the coast of Ireland. They lost their mother when Saoirse was born, and as we soon learn, this strange little girl, who is in touch with the faeries, is a Selkie, half seal and half human and is inextricably drawn to the sea. The children’s granny, Macha, (Fionna Eleanagan) lives on the mainland and convinces the father that the kids should be living with her in Dublin where they will be safe. He relents; however soon Ben and Saoirse long for their father and the island, and the sea, and so set out on a long, cross-country journey back to what they consider home. It proves to be an adventure where they encounter curious beings in surprising places. Song of the Sea is a gentle tale that as times can feel like a soft hug. The artwork is ravishing, painterly, and creates a compelling Irish fantasy, mixed with a bit of melancholy, accompanied with a lyrical musical score. Readers who recall the many Japanese films reviewed in this space, created by the extraordinary Studio Ghibli, will see the influence of their work in every highly imaginative frame. Song of the Sea. Directed by Tomm Moore. Animated. Starring Brendan Fraser, Fionna Flanagan, David Rawle. 1 hr., 34 min. Rated PG. Released n 2015. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv. A scene from Song of the Sea
articles.title: Song of the Sea a lovely Irish tale

articles.text: A scene from Rango Just when you thought computer-generated imagery (CGI) had peaked, the folks at Industrial Light and Magic (ILM), under the direction of Gore Verbinksi (“Pirates of the Carribean”), create Rango, an animated feature film that is a showstopper. It’s a marvel, done brilliantly in 2D, no less, with attention to detail that is unlike anything created thus far. The essential story is classic, a familiar western trope. It begins with a thespian lizard in his terrarium (a small pool, a palm tree, and a plastic fish), riding in the back of a car. The family is driving across the Mojave Desert when they hit a bump in the road and the terrarium cum lizard is bounced out, landing in the road, while the car continues out of sight. And so the lizard – a chameleon of sorts, blue-skinned, bugeyed, wearing an aloha shirt – stands on the side of the road as the sizzling sun leaches moisture out of everything. Parched, he makes his way across the desert to a town called Dirt, inhabited by an array of critters – rodents, lizards, Gila monsters – all desperate for water. Dirt, according to the mayor (Ned Beatty), is having a small drought. The remaining water, so precious, is in a bank vault. Our aloha lizard walks into a saloon where, when challenged, creates a persona and a story that is so authentic that he is quickly viewed as a savior and as the next sheriff. The stranger calls himself Rango (Johnny Depp) and soon swaps his aloha shirt for western duds. Unbeknownst to the townsfolk, Rango is a tenderfoot, a true dude, about to go up against the meanest, gnarliest, most conniving set of desert critters imaginable, all involved with something nefarious. And all the dude is packing is his faux story (he killed a mess of outlaws with one shot, he says) and a rusty six-gun with only one bullet in the chamber. Wearing his newly issued tin star, his spurs jingling, Rango has to ride hard, shoot straight, and eventually face down hombres like Bad Bill (Ray Winstone) or Rattlesnake Jake (Bill Nighy), while trying not to flinch. His life is further complicated when he meets Beans (Isla Fisher), a sweet little thing, also a lizard, who is fighting with the shifty, underhanded, no’count Mayor (Ned Beatty) over selling her pappy’s ranch. Close your eyes and you can hear a spaghetti-western soundtrack. Keep the faith, buckaroos. and you will, in the end, meet the Spirit of the West, a leathery, tough-as-nails cowboy ridin’ his golf cart across some pretty mean territory, a lean question mark of a man who gives Rango some darned good advice. Are ya feeling lucky? Well, are ya? This is a great movie. But the writing is so adult, the jokes and vocabulary at times so dang highfalutin, that a lot of what is said will sail right over the heads of the peanut gallery. But no worries. There’s enough adventure packed into Rango for both audiences. Which is a good thing. Rango. Directed by Gore Verbinski. Animated. With voices of Johnny Depp, Bill Nighy, Alfred Molina. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG. Released in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/HBO Max.
articles.title: Rango a kids’ film parents will love

The artwork is ravishing, painterly, and creates a compelling Irish fantasy, mixed with a bit of melancholy, accompanied with a lyrical musical score. Readers who recall the many Japanese films reviewed in this space, created by the extraordinary Studio Ghibli, will see the influence of their work in every highly imaginative frame. Song of the Sea. Directed by Tomm Moore. Animated. Starring Brendan Fraser, Fionna Flanagan, David Rawle. 1 hr., 34 min. Rated PG. Released n 2015. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv. A scene from Rango By Chris Honoré Just when you thought computer-generated imagery (CGI) had peaked, the folks at Industrial Light and Magic (ILM), under the direction of Gore Verbinksi (“Pirates of the Carribean”), create Rango, an animated feature film that is a showstopper. It’s a marvel, done brilliantly in 2D, no less, with attention to detail that is unlike anything created thus far. The essential story is classic, a familiar western trope. It begins with a thespian lizard in his terrarium (a small pool, a palm tree, and a plastic fish), riding in the back of a car. The family is driving across the Mojave Desert when they hit a bump in the road and the terrarium cum lizard is bounced out, landing in the road, while the car continues out of sight. And so the lizard – a chameleon of sorts, blue-skinned, bugeyed, wearing an aloha shirt – stands on the side of the road as the sizzling sun leaches moisture out of everything. Parched, he makes his way across the desert to a town called Dirt, inhabited by an array of critters – rodents, lizards, Gila monsters – all desperate for water. Dirt, according to the mayor (Ned Beatty), is having a small drought. The remaining water, so precious, is in a bank vault. Our aloha lizard walks into a saloon where, when challenged, creates a persona and a story that is so authentic that he is quickly viewed as a savior and as the next sheriff. The stranger calls himself Rango (Johnny Depp) and soon swaps his aloha shirt for western duds. Unbeknownst to the townsfolk, Rango is a tenderfoot, a true dude, about to go up against the meanest, gnarliest, most conniving set of desert critters imaginable, all involved with something nefarious. And all the dude is packing is his faux story (he killed a mess of outlaws with one shot, he says) and a rusty six-gun with only one bullet in the chamber. Wearing his newly issued tin star, his spurs jingling, Rango has to ride hard, shoot straight, and eventually face down hombres like Bad Bill (Ray Winstone) or Rattlesnake Jake (Bill Nighy), while trying not to flinch. His life is further complicated when he meets Beans (Isla Fisher), a sweet little thing, also a lizard, who is fighting with the shifty, underhanded, no’count Mayor (Ned Beatty) over selling her pappy’s ranch. Close your eyes and you can hear a spaghetti-western soundtrack. Keep the faith, buckaroos. and you will, in the end, meet the Spirit of the West, a leathery, tough-as-nails cowboy ridin’ his golf cart across some pretty mean territory, a lean question mark of a man who gives Rango some darned good advice. Are ya feeling lucky? Well, are ya? This is a great movie. But the writing is so adult, the jokes and vocabulary at times so dang highfalutin, that a lot of what is said will sail right over the heads of the peanut gallery. But no worries. There’s enough adventure packed into Rango for both audiences. Which is a good thing. Rango. Directed by Gore Verbinski. Animated. With voices of Johnny Depp, Bill Nighy, Alfred Molina. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG. Released in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/HBO Max. articles.text: The public is invited at a summer recital by the Diluvian String Quartet on Sunday, July 16, at Piedmont Center for the Arts. The program will include: The Lyric Quartet by William Grant Still, Quartettsatz by Franz Schubert, and String Quartet No.2 in A Minor, Op.13 by Felix Mendelssohn. Doors open at 6:30 and the concerts begins at 7:00 p.m. A dessert reception and drinks will follow the concert. Tickets are available at: https://www. eventbrite.com/e/656199669877. Music Notes Schubert’s Quartettsatz is a brilliant un-finished work in one movement. Like his famous “Unfinished Symphony,” this piece could easily be titled “The Unfinished Quartet.” It is at once stirring and moving, sweet and innocent, all tied together with the composer’s magic ability to spin a gorgeous melody. Written at the age of 18, Mendelssohn’s quartet in A minor, Opus 13, was composed seven years after Schubert’s Quartettsatz, and only a few months after Beethoven’s death. If you remember what being 18 years old was like, but still have not found the words to describe it, come hear Mendelssohn paint a sonic image of the passion, the brooding, the mirth and the agility of youth. It is an absolute gem. William Grant Still is one of the greatest composers in American history, and has lately been getting the recognition he deserves. In the Lyric Quartet, he writes music describing three of his close friends and their defining character traits: Sentimental, Quiet, and Jovial. Yet he also captures the complexities of each friend within each movement. This piece, rarely performed, is musical poetry unlike any other, still fresh after nearly 50 years. wine grapes. articles.text: Part 64 in a biweekly series Each building in our built environment contains any number of design components: roofs, walls, windows, doors, details, and so on. How these pieces of the building are treated by the architect and then assembled together determines not only a building’s architectural style and character, but also its overall quality. These components can be derived from many sources, including historical models, or from common usage, or simply by aesthetic fashion (which is quite common). And like all of architecture, there is a melding of use and appearance. There is a function for most all components to accommodate as well as an aesthetic to express. Architectural design evaluation requires ultimately a review of the totality of the components all put together—the coordination of and synergy between all of the parts. But just as the entire building can’t be envisioned and designed all at once, it is helpful in the design process and in judging quality to evaluate the separate design components themselves—to work with the more manageable separate parts, as we often do in this column. One design component I have always liked is the through-building passageway with living space above. This can assume different forms and uses such as the auto entry on relatively new attached townhomes here in Piedmont, or on an historic public walkway shown in Croatia. It is difficult to articulate why these are so appealing, Maybe the associated sense of interest or mystery which makes you want to go see what is on the other side of the arch. Always an important building component is the entry. This simple Piedmont craftsman bungalow with a clear, distinct, well-proportioned entry creates a wonderful welcoming feeling. Notice the subordinate car parking space to the left. By way of contrast, it is hard to imagine a worse entry than the one hidden behind the parked car on the poorly designed and badly landscaped house to the right above. 12-MONTH FINANCING *some restrictions apply CL#788850

articles.text: It was the first day of summer and the weather was wonderful for 43 walkers and two K-9 best friends for last week’s excursion by the Walking on Wednesdays group. The group had taken long walks the two weeks before. They thought a walk around the center of town, revisiting some Piedmont history, would be a relaxing way to start the summer. School was out so the walkers could visit the high school and Havens Elementary School. The group took the first sidewalk into the high school campus. They went past the new auditorium and came to the STEM building with its semiopen, gated Robotics classroom work area. As they were peeking into the space, Kevin Clark, leader of the prize-winning Highland Robotics, came out with his daughter and able assistant, Elle. He invited everyone in and explained information on the team and its successes. Each year the robotics teams work on a different national project, with the aim of reaching the finals, held this year in Houston. Kevin and Elle showed the group its current robot, “Paddo the Frog, and posed for a group photo. The walkers went to the Wetmore House at the corner of Vista and Bonita. It is the oldest house in Piedmont and was built without plans in 1878 by Jess Wetmore and his brother. Next was a walk through the Havens School playground and some more history. The City of Piedmont was incorporated in 1907, and since its population was growing dramatically after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire, city leaders decided to build two schools to serve the community. The first school was built in 1910 and opened in 1911. It was originally named “The Bonita Avenue School,” but was later renamed “Frank C. Havens Elementary School” after the land’s donor. pages.text: Wednesday, June 28, 2023 23 Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers celebrate first day of summer It was the first day of summer and the weather was wonderful for 43 walkers and two K-9 best friends for last week’s excursion by the Walking on Wednesdays group. The group had taken long walks the two weeks before. They thought a walk around the center of town, revisiting some Piedmont history, would be a relaxing way to start the summer. School was out so the walkers could visit the high school and Havens Elementary School. The group took the first sidewalk into the high school campus. They went past the new auditorium and came to the STEM building with its semiopen, gated Robotics classroom work area. As they were peeking into the space, Kevin Clark, leader of the prize-winning Highland Robotics, came out with his daughter and able assistant, Elle. He invited everyone in and explained information on the team and its successes. Each year the robotics teams work on a different national project, with the aim of reaching the finals, held this year in Houston. Kevin and Elle showed the group its current robot, “Paddo the Frog, and posed for a group photo. The walkers went to the Wetmore House at the corner of Vista and Bonita. It is the oldest house in Piedmont and was built without plans in 1878 by Jess Wetmore and his brother. Next was a walk through the Havens School playground and some more history. The City of Piedmont was incorporated in 1907, and since its population was growing dramatically after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire, city leaders decided to build two schools to serve the community. The first school was built in 1910 and opened in 1911. It was originally named “The Bonita Avenue School,” but was later renamed “Frank C. Havens Elementary School” after the land’s donor. Leaving Havens through Oakland Avenue gate, they crossed the street to Craig Avenue and at the end of the block saw the original home of Piedmont’s first mayor, Hugh Craig. Drawing on Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s research, the group learned of the City of Piedmont’s founding, and the role Craig played in it. He was born in Sydney, Australia in 1841 to Scottish parents, and grew up in New Zealand before moving to Oakland in 1874. He married Inez Gilcrest in 1875 and bought five acres on Vernal Avenue (now named Highland). The Craigs built a house in the middle of the land, a beautiful Italian Victorian, built in 1883, and the second oldest home in Piedmont. It is surprisingly large with 4,359 square feet. Craig was elected mayor by the Piedmont Board of Trustees in 1907 and served until 1914. To fund the new city, Mayor Craig instituted a new property tax. Prior to incorporation, all residents paid the same, small tax to the County. However, the new Piedmont tax was based on the size of the home’s parcel. Craig’s tax was not popular with residents, and was also an issue for Craig. In 1912 Highland Avenue was being expanded, and he had his home put on log rollers and pulled by horses to the corner of his property where it is now at 55 Craig Avenue. He subdivided his land and created Craig Avenue with lots on both sides of the street. Perhaps not surprisingly, he was not re-elected mayor in 1914. There had been a lot of history and talking this morning, so it was time to do some walking. The group went up Mountain, down Caperton Avenue to Richardson Way, up it to Lakeview Avenue, down it to Caperton and Highland again. A swing around Gilford Avenue to the top of Piedmont Park got the walkers back to their starting point. It had been a fun, back to the future and Piedmont history kind of morning. articles.text: Forrest Yeh, a 2012 Piedmont High graduate, has received two patents for his first invention, a battery-less otoscope, a device that sees into the ear. Yeh, now in his second year of a residency in Internal Medicine at Highland Hospital, created the medical device to operate on ambient light so it can function inside a hyperbaric chamber or MRI machine. Yeh identified the need for the device when he learned that 2% of people that go in a hyperbaric chamber for any treatment have a risk of blowing out their earForrest Yeh demonstrates his invention with Piedmont friend Matteo Scanu. Forrest Yeh’s battery-free otoscope Forrest Yeh with his invention and the patent drums. Yeh’s otoscope can operate safely in the high pressure and oxygen level environment of the chamber to monitor a patient’s ear while receiving treatment. Hyperbaric chambers are commonly used in wound care, and to treat scuba divers with the bends. The chambers can also be used to treat carbon monoxide poisoning and bites from brown recluse spiders. “A lot of the time, patients aren’t necessarily conscious if they’re in there,” explained Yeh. “If there’s an emergency, you can’t ask them if their ears are hurting. You just need to take a look in their ears,” he added. Without a battery, Yeh’s otoscope does not have any components that could explode in a high flammability environment. Yeh’s otoscope collects ambient light in the chamber and can be pointed towards a window or other light source. “It funnels [light] through a fiber-optic cable and focuses the light into the ear,” Yeh explained. Yeh attended Wildwood Elementary and Piedmont High School before enrolling at the University of California in Merced for Bio Engineering and Cognitive Science. Upon graduation he went to medical school at St. George’s University, Grenada, West Indies. Yeh created a startup company in college focused on LED lighting. “I’m taking engineering concepts I’ve learned about and am trying to apply them to medicine,” he said. Yeh received the Design patent in March of 2023, which protects the shape of the object, or how it looks. He did the 3-D imaging and machining on his own, to have a physical prototype before filing for the patents in 2020. In June he received the Utility patent which protects its function, which is harder to obtain and provides an inventor with more protection. Filing for the Utility patent costs $5,000 and once received, is good for 20 years. With two patents in-hand, one option for Yeh is to start his own company and seek FDA approval to produce it. Another option is to license the device to an existing company, such as Welch Allyn which already produces otoscopes. “This is my first step as a professional inventor, I have books full of other inventions. One of the main reasons I practice medicine is to continue to be exposed to all the problems in healthcare and try to come up with new solutions,” he said. articles.text: It is sometimes difficult to articulate why we like or dislike certain design components –why they are considered good or bad. This is certainly in part because our tastes are all somewhat different, formed by our experiences, education, and personal philosophy. And too probably because we prioritize our assessments differently: we may personally like something for example because it is so innovative, or so aesthetically sensitive, or simply because it functions so well. The interesting thing is that this individual, somewhat mysterious process of forming an opinion on most art and architecture seems to most often result in a general consensus on the design quality and/or worth of a particular work. The design concept of building massing, including window size and placement (fenestration) can vary considerably. Contrast these two-story multifamily apartment buildings. In the Piedmont building a rational functional approach to the forms created by entry placement and window sizes results in interest and character. The dull, uninteresting flat walled example of the other building looks as if the prominent, confusing arched elements needed to be bricked up for some reason. There is no street appeal nor urban design contribution.

articles.text: On Friday evening, June 23, a water main broke under St. James Drive on the 100 block resulting in a house being flooded and the street being closed from 7:30 p.m. on Friday through early Sunday morning. The water was shut off by EBMUD for 8 hours on Friday from 9 p.m. onward. The break resulted in the home of David Duong and Jennifer Ho being flooded. “As our home was below street level, the water came in through our garage, flooded through the floor down to the ceiling of a floor below, and then intruded down through that floor and through the ceiling of a floor below that, ultimately flooding into three vertical rooms. We’ve had dehumidifiers and fans going in them since Friday night,” said Duong. As the damaged areas dry, the couple expects to spend three to four weeks demolishing the ceiling and walls, and then repairing and painting them. Phil Witte, a St. James Drive neighbor, said that when the main broke on Friday, “water and silt was flowing for roughly two hours. It didn’t overflow too many curbs.” “None of the neighbors knew that night whether we’d have water again when we woke up in the morning, but thankfully we did,” Witte added. The Police Department closed St. James Drive from 7:30 p.m. on Friday through Saturday. The affected road was open again by 6:00 a.m. on Sunday. Photos by Phil Witte Water and silt pour down St. James Drive. A broken water main flooded St. James Drive on the evening of Friday, June 23, prompting a road closure. This message that God is helping Jew and Gentile to find common ground receives very clear expression in Paul’s letter to the Galatians: There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus. In other writings Paul refers to this assertion that the well-being of both the Jew and Gentile are intertwined as a mystery, a grand and good surprise. He asserts that the proclamation of this mystery is central to his apostolic calling. Long before e pluribus unum (out of many, one) became the motto of the United States of America, visionaries like Paul and writer of Matthew honored the hope it expresses. It is distressing that antisemitism is on the rise. Those of us who identify ourselves as followers of Jesus do well to counter it with the message of Epiphany. Rev.
