articles.text: The Benefits of Proposition 19 Did you know that if you are 55+years old you can transfer your property tax basis to a home anywhere in the state of California? Have you been dreaming about San Diego sunshine or golf courses in Palm Springs? If so, this newsletter may be relevant for you. Change in Average Sales Price Year over Year Fun Facts 52% of CA homeowners age 55+ haven’t moved since 1999. That’s 2.2 million homeowners. 77% of CA homeowners age 55+ haven’t moved since 2009. That’s 3.2 million homeowners. 57% of owner-occupied homes in CA were owned by people age 55+ in 2019. All of these homeowners qualified for Prop. 19 tax portability benefits. (Source: California Association of Realtors) Individuals who are 55+ years old, severely disabled, or victims of wildfires and natural disasters may transfer the taxable value of their property to a replacement property anywhere in the state, up to three times. The purchase of the new property must be made within two years of the sale of the original property. And, you can buy a new home that is worth more than your old home. In this case, there will be an upward adjustment in the tax basis — however, taxes will still be lower than they would have been without the Prop. 19 benefit. What’s more, Prop. 19, protects the right of parents and grandparents to pass on their family home to their children and grandchildren for continued use as their primary residence by limiting property tax increases on these family homes. For more information on Prop. 19 go to: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov Change in Number of Properties Sold by City Year over Year Dedicated to clients, culture, and community, Calia Homes is a team of exceptional real estate professionals who work together with the common goal of providing unparalleled client services in a supportive and collaborative environment. Our mission is to create smooth, successful – and even enjoyable – transactions in any market. caliahomes.com Our local market saw a notable decrease in the number of sold properties, year over year. However, despite this decrease in sales, our average prices remained relatively stable. The average home price fell by 2.2% in Oakland, 5.5% in Piedmont, and 8% in Berkeley. Looking at the recent Piedmont sales on the back page of this newsletter, we found that homes appear to be staying on the market longer. Properties sold in May were on the market for an average of 18 days. However, currently pending properties were on the market for an average of 32 days. Active properties on the market have already been on the market more than 29 days. This may point to a slowing market.

articles.text: The Piedmont School Board announced on June 14 that Ariel Dolowich will take over as the district’s new Curriculum Director and Assistant Superintendent as of July 1. He most recently was with Newark Unified School District as its Director of Teaching and Learning for the past four years. The job included leading professional development for principals and staff, providing district-wide communication for certificated and classified staff, designing and presenting Town Hall meetings, and partnering with during labor negotiations. “The Assistant Superintendent position will be a promotion for him, with increased responsibility that includes the duties that are typical in a curriculum director position,” explained incoming Piedmont Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. “Dr. Hawn was participating in the [hiring] process, which I think is very appropriate. [Hawn and Dolowich] will be working so closely together and [they] look like a good team already,” said board member Cory Smegal. The school board has agreed to a three-year contract at $180,000 per year. Dolowich replaces Cheryl Wozniak. Dolowich is an active leadership coach of principals with Alameda County Office of Education. His resume also includes nine years as the Principal of Ochoa Middle School in Hayward. “I was really impressed by the breadth of Ariel’s experience and the recognition that he has received from his peers in education and just his thoughtfulness in responding to our questions,” said School Board President Veronica Anderson-Thigpen. Ariel Dolowich, Piedmont School District’s new Curriculum Director, lives in the East Bay with his wife and three children.
articles.title: Ariel Dolowich named as new Curriculum Director

articles.text: A fuel tank estimated to be at least 100 years old was removed by Alameda County workers on Tuesday, June 20. Meanwhile, contractors are over halfway done hauling soil off-site. The buried tank was found by excavators at the pool site in late May. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said the tank, which measures about five feet by 36 inches, “was used to fuel the home of private residents about 100 years ago, before the advent of natural gas lines.” On Monday, June 19, one day before the tank was removed, an Alameda County fire marshal, an environmental inspector, and a crew of four to five contractors pumped out the fuel that was in the tank, according to Gonzales. Because the tank still contained gasoline, it was considered a toxic substance, and the city was required to submit a work plan to the county for its removal. Public Works staff submitted this plan to the Alameda County Department of Environmental Health in early June. As part of this plan, the subcontractor GEOCON tested the soil around the tank, which was discovered five feet underground just outside the Carriage House, by Bonita Avenue. “After the initial soil testing,” Gonzales said, “we found no evidence of the tank in the soil samples we took. articles.text: The removal of the artificial turf at Witter Field has begun. “No Parking” signs line Palm Drive. Over the course of the next three months an estimated 400 truckloads of material will be brought back and forth along the narrow street. The project to renovate the field’s turf and irrigation system, which began on June 6, is expected to continue until December 1. Piedmont School District Facilities Director Pete Palmer, the point of contact for the project, did not respond to requests for a timeline of field turf demolition. The district has not yet announced where the high school and club sports programs will be located this fall. The sports involved include: football (two teams), cross-country, and Piedmont Soccer Club teams (est. 1,000 players). Replacement of the field surface in prior years was done during summer vacation and completed prior to the start of classes and fall sports. articles.text: Editor: In a letter published on May 24, I expressed the opinion that the City should not (as proposed in the U.C. Berkeley graduate students’ development concept) hand over land with a value of $7 million for 103 affordable-housing apartments, given that we soon will need to spend tens of millions of dollars to upgrade the City’s civic center. (In contrast, land for 30 market-rate townhomes would be purchased from the City for $5.3 million.) A letter by Jerry Kennelly published on May 31 explained why the apartment development concept is not financially realistic under any circumstances, thus giving me hope that this particular land grab will not take place. However, Piedmonters should be aware that City staff (and, apparently, the City Council) have been ready to give away City land for quite some time. Quoting portions of answers to Frequently Asked Questions set forth at https://www.piedmontishome.org/faqs: • “The City could choose to sell land at fair market value, or could sell or lease its land for low cost to an affordable housing developer in exchange for the provision of affordable housing.” • “[D]ue to the high cost of land in Piedmont, it is generally understood that a multi-family affordable housing development in Piedmont will only be economically feasible if the land is provided at little or no cost.” • “The City is not obligated to enter into any agreement and is able to pursue a process in its own best interest.” I urge Piedmonters to let the City Council and City staff know that giving away City land, whether for a period of years or in perpetuity, is not in our best interest: • Providing land at little or no cost may help a few hundred new residents, but it will constitute an inappropriate taking of property, or proceeds thereof, from more than 10,000 existing residents. • Nothing in the Housing Element or applicable State law requires such a taking. • Those who are eager to see affordable-housing apartments built should look for a way to pay for the land, such as via philanthropic organizations. –Dana H. articles.text: Piedmont Police Chief Nationally, 1 in 3 children live in a home with at least one firearm. Despite various safe storage laws regarding children, 4.6 million kids live in a home with an unlocked, loaded gun. This tragically results in 8 kids a day who are unintentionally killed or injured by family guns that were accessed by a child. With the prevalence of firearms in our society, asking about their presence and how they’re stored should be as common as our inquiries about swimming pools, animals, and allergies. Starting the conversation can be awkward for several reasons. For one, it’s not common for this topic to be brought up. Even though I was asked in the past, it was the one and only time. Like many things, increased familiarity and frequency will lead to increased comfort. That’s the premise behind the ASK (“Asking Saves Kids”) campaign, an initiative developed by Brady United Against Gun Violence in partnership with the American Academy of Pediatrics. On June 21st – the first day of summer – each year, Brady reminds parents to ask whether there is an unlocked gun in homes where their child goes to play. articles.text: As summer arrives, Piedmont adults and youth have a wealth of opportunities to explore local volunteer work. There are several volunteer opportunities this summer at the Oakland Zoo for those who love working with animals. You can work alongside a zookeeper assisting with daily animal care, as a conservation volunteer interpreting the Zoo’s conservation initiatives to guests, or as a docent sharing your passion for wildlife and conservation with Zoo visitors. There are also a variety of internships available to teens and adults in seasonal (fall, winter, and summer) sessions. To learn more about volunteer programs at the Zoo, visit oaklandzoo.org/ volunteer-and-internship-opportunities. Piedmont Center for the Arts Throughout the year, the all-volunteer-run, nonprofit Piedmont Center for the Arts hosts theater shows, visual arts exhibits, music performances, literary events, and more. Volunteers do everything — from production, carpentry, and painting to hosting receptions for events, handling box office duties, set design, and costuming. The PCA particularly needs volunteers to staff the galleries and to assist at other events. To learn more and get involved, email the PCA at info@piedmontcenterforthearts.org. Museum of Children’s Art (MOCHA) Students who have a love of art and are interested in the education field would enjoy volunteering at the Museum of Children’s Art (MOCHA) in Oakland this summer. Tasks include everything from preparing art materials, to aiding youth art workshops and afterschool library events, to assisting with special events at the museum. Email info@mocha. org for volunteer inquiries. Visit mocha.org to learn more about summer events at the museum. Alameda County Community Food Bank The Alameda County Community Food Bank needs volunteers to prepare food in the ACCFB Oakland warehouse, and to help distribute food at neighborhood distribution sites throughout the county. For a full list of volunteer needs at local pantries and other organizations, email volunteer@ accfd.org, or visit accfb.org/get-involved/volunteer. A calendar of all volunteer opportunities for adults and youth 10 years old and up is available at accfb.org/get-involved/volunteer-calendar. Donations are also welcome. Is there a volunteer effort or organization that you would like to highlight? Interested in expanding this list? articles.text: Block party street closure applications due June 28 This year’s 4th of July Parade, with a theme of “Paint the Town Red, White, and Blue,” will begin on Tuesday, July 4, at 11 a.m. on Highland Avenue. One of Piedmont’s oldest and most beloved traditions, the parade, now in its 56th year, features floats from neighborhoods and community organizations, a rich array of antique and classic cars, and several bagpipe bands in keeping with Piedmont’s Scottish traditions. Pancake breakfast An all-you-can eat pancake breakfast will take place before the parade from 8 to 10 a.m. at the Veterans Hall. The breakfast is operated each year by the Piedmont Community Service Crew, a coed venturing unit with the Piedmont Scouts. Sausages are provided by Piedmont Grocery and fresh fruit is provided by Village Market. Tickets for the breakfast are $15 for age 15 and up, $10 for youth age three to 14, and free for children under three. Tickets are available at the door or may be purchased in advance online at bit.ly/3CDO3Zu. Community picnic Following the parade, festivities will continue in Piedmont Park with a community picnic and music by the group Big Bang Beat, from 12 noon to 3 p.m. Block party applications due June 28 Neighborhoods planning a 4th of July block party need to complete an application for street closure online at bit.ly/3JnJDd7, or in person at City Hall,, 120 Vista Avenue. . Applications are due by 5 p.m. on Wednesday, June 28. The city will confirm approval of applicants by Friday, June 30, and the Public Works Department will deliver barricades to streets on Monday, July 3.

articles.text: Big Bang Beat, a 12-piece band featuring songs of the 60’s Motown sound, the fabulous funk of the 70’s, and dance hits from the 80’s and 90’s, returns to Piedmont as the featured band on the main stage in Piedmont Park following the city’s 2023 Fourth of July Parade. The band is led by four dazzling female singers decked out in sequined mini dresses, plus a horn section and a choreographed stage show. Its zany, non-stop energy has made Big Bang Beat a fixture at clubs, conventions, fund-raisers and corporate and private parties throughout the U.S. Nine of the band members are veterans of the Zasu Pitts Memorial Orchestra. Big Bang Beat is a frequent headline band at clubs throughout California and Nevada, and has performed in Switzerland, Hawaii, Malaysia, Canary Islands, Istanbul, Acapulco, and the Caribbean. articles.text: David Hopkins, a longtime Supervisor of the before-school and after-school Schoolmates program, will be Grand Marshal of this year’s 4th of July parade, the 56th annual. Hopkins will be retiring after this summer and 34 years with the Recreation Department. “I love this community,” he said. “This is above and beyond – that people want me to be part of this. I’ve always been in the parade. It’s such a huge honor. I can’t begin to tell you.” This year the Parade Committee has a new chair for the first time in over two decades. Kathy Kelleher, the daughter of parade founder Dick Johnson, and a member of the committee for many years, will take over the duties of Carla Betts who served as chair for 20 years. On selecting Hopkins, Kelleher said, “It was an easy decision. He’s the right guy. He is retiring and we appreciate all that he’s done for our community,” said Kelleher. “He sort of transcends through generations. He has made me smile, he made my kids smile, and he is a good guy.” Asked to describe the duties of a Grand Marshal, Kelleher said, “It’s about honoring them all day. They ride in the parade, and they get to judge the parade entries and decide the awards. Then there’s an area blocked off for them in the park for the music afterwards.” Hopkins is known for wearing a tank top regardless of the weather. His smile, booming Staff photo Schoolmate Supervisor David Hopkins is Grand Marshal of this year’s 4th of July Parade. voice, and infectious enthusiasm have captivated kids for three decades. He has a special gift in working with children. The Parade Committee has announced that the theme of this year’s parade will be “Paint the Town Red, White and Blue,” which seems especially fitting in the year when the mirthful Hopkins brings his own brand of good cheer to the entire community.
articles.title: David Hopkins named Grand Marshal of 2023 parade

articles.text: Be part of Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade Come join the Piedmont Community Band, the city’s only musical organization that has only one rehearsal during the year. The band is a past winner of the Highland Cup, the highest award given at the July 4th Parade. The band is comprised of amateur and professional musicians – all volunteers – most who live in town and can’t resist the challenge of playing music while marching in formation. Dressed in blue pants, white shirts and a red kerchief, they are led by Ken Kawaichi, who, dressed as Emperor Norton, has the distinction of walking the length of the parade route backwards. It’s time to get out your instruments – trumpets, trombones, tubas, clarinets and drums – and help celebrate Independence Day in Piedmont. If you are new in town, it’s an ideal way to meet people, To sign up, contact Greg Slatoff at goslatoff@yahoo.com, or call Jane Reed at 654-2670. 4th of July Parade
articles.title: Come join the Band

articles.text: Bagpipes in Piedmont have been a tradition since 1932 when football coach Glen “Brick” Johnson started the Kiltie Band at Piedmont High School. Today, the Piedmont Highlanders Drums and Pipes is a community band performing in parades and at special events throughout the Bay Area. Band members wear a traditional Scottish military style uniform of the Seaforth Highlanders which wore MacKenzie tartan kilts. The band officers include Pipe Major Ellison Dunlap, Jr.; Drum Sergeant Nancy Dunlap amd Band Manager Fred Rutledge. The band regularly performs at the Scottish Highland Games at the Dunsmuir Estate in Oakland, on John Muir Day at the Muir Estate in Martinez, and in the St. Patrick Day Parade in Dublin. It has performed at the Tartan Day Games at Ardenwood Historic Farm in Fremont and in the Celtic Festival in Fremont. It is the opening band at the Alameda County Fair Parade in Pleasanton. The Piedmont Highlanders have played at Grace Cathedral on Armistice Day and at the San Francisco Giants ballpark at the opening game of the baseball playoffs. The band has won ribbons as best band in the Newark parade, at the Walnut Festival in Walnut Creek, and in the Annual Piedmont 4th of July Parade. For additional information, contact Ellison Dunlap at 465- 3699. Photo of Highlander bagpipe band
articles.title: Piedmont Highlanders continue tradition since 1932

articles.text: Tammy Medress has retired from the classroom after a 29-year teaching career, 25 of which were as a fifth grade teacher at Beach School. Medress sat down with the Post for a chat about school, her career, the teaching profession and what’s next in her life. In doing the math, she estimates that 700 students went through her Piedmont classroom over the years. “I kind of wanted to be a teacher when I was younger. I was a writing tutor and a big sister when I was at Cal. A bunch of things led me towards teaching,” she said. Medress got her bachelor’s degree in English Literature at UC Berkeley in 1989, then earned a Masters in Education and a teaching credential also from Cal in 1993. “When I was first looking for a job, Nancy McHugh, who was the principal, offered me a job at Beach. articles.text: An excited, energetic group of 40 recent eighth grade graduates from Piedmont Middle School met before dawn on June 3 to embark on a tour of Washington, D.C. with organizers and parent chaperones Stacy Morgan, Kim Hunter, and Sabrina Smith. They spent five jam-packed days touring sites in the nation’s capital including the Lincoln Memorial, Jefferson Memorial, Arlington Cemetery, the National Archives, the Holocaust Museum, the Martin Luther King, Jr. Memorial, the World War II, Vietnam, and Korean War Memorials, the National Museum of African American History, the White House Visitor Center, a number of Smithsonian museums, and George Washington’s home in Mount Vernon. “Although 14-year-olds are often famously hard to get a read on and they all like different things,” said Morgan, “the students were really intrigued by the Changing of the Guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Arlington Cemetery. The military ceremony was unlike anything they had seen.” She added that the eighth graders also enjoyed using a digital flight simulator and viewing the hangar and space shuttle at the Smithsonian Air and Space Museum, on their way back to the airport. “The kids all got a lot out of this unique experience flying across the country. For some, it was the first time they had traveled alone without their parents,” she said. The students stayed in a hotel in Maryland just outside Washington D.C. Two to four kids were assigned to respective suites, which each contained a kitchen, living room area, and sleeping areas. Along with the numerous sights, one highlight of the trip was a special tour of the Capitol arranged by Hunter and culminating in a meeting with Congressman Eric Swalwell of Dublin, with whom Hunter had worked in the DA’s office. Swalwell spoke with students for 20 minutes about his background and work in Congress, and his experience as a candidate for U.S. President. Morgan, who organized the trip, said, “It was the first year we’ve done something like this. I realized that many other middle schools have officially sanctioned D.C. trips, so I reached out to the PMS principal in late fall last year. When she said that the school couldn’t organize a trip like that due to ‘policy regulations,’ the other parents and I worked with an educational travel company, WorldStrides, to put it together.” Interested parents joined a Zoom call about the trip with a WorldStrides account representative last January. As students began signing up, Morgan, Hunter, and Smith began developing a detailed itinerary. “Given that there were only about 130 total students in the eighth grade class, it’s amazing that 40 enrolled in our first year holding this trip,” said Morgan. The trip remains a parent-run program. This year’s three chaperones are looking for next year’s organizers. “It was such a well-organized and positive experience. We’re looking for parents of rising eighth graders interested in taking it on for next year,” said Morgan. “It would be wonderful if this trip could continue to be a Piedmont Middle School tradition.” Interested parents are encouraged to contact Stacy Morgan at Stacy.Morgan94@gmail.com. articles.text: Recent discoveries unveil an astonishing 146 moons How many moons does Saturn have? In May, we would have said 83. Now, we’d say 146, nearly double what we had previously discovered. Dozens of small moons orbiting the planet Saturn were recently discovered by a team of astronomers led by Edward Ashton, using the Canadian-France-Hawaiian Telescope during a survey between 2019 and 2021. After analyzing data from the survey, the team identified about 80 previously unknown objects orbiting Saturn. These irregular moons are different from the bright object we see in the night sky and are shaped like potatoes. They may be leftovers of bigger moons that could have shattered in orbit. Moons can be fragmented by asteroids, comets and collisions between moons. Some moons orbit in retrograde, meaning the opposite way of other moons. It’s thought that they may orbit strangely because they were products of a more recent collision. The International Astronomical Union’s Minor Planet Center (MPC) is now reviewing the survey team’s data and confirming Photo courtesy of NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute their discoveries. Since May 3rd, the MPC formally recognized 60 new moons. This brings the total confirmed moon count for Saturn to more than 140. You may be aware of Saturn’s largest moon, Titan. The only moon in the solar system with a similar atmosphere nitrogen-rich atmosphere as Earth, Titan is home to clouds, lakes, seas, and rain of liquid hydrocarbons. There is a whole ocean underneath a thick layer of icy crust. There could be an entire world of life brewing beneath the surface, or the planet could be lifeless. These new discoveries mean Saturn has regained its title as the planet with the most moons. The planet Jupiter, with its stronger magnetic field, likely has more moons, but so far astronomers have only confirmed 92 moons around Jupiter. Saturn now has more moons than the rest of the planets combined. of coastal redwoods in the East Bay. articles.text: With only so many of our end-of-year awards to go around, some of the major contributions made throughout the year tend to get lost. In this article, we reflect on three athletes who were either entering their first year as a starter or getting time in a featured role for the first time in their PHS athletic career. Three who made a huge impact in the largest role of their time at Piedmont included Eva Levingston in basketball, threesport athlete Sam Shelby, and Albert Bellingrath in football and volleyball. Staff Photo Eva Levingston, PHS Class of 2023, was forced to miss her junior year due to transfer rules and became a main scorer, rebounder, and defender for the Highlanders as a senior. EVA LEVINGSTON Basketball Eva Levingston was perhaps the largest breakout performer at the school in 2022-23. After sitting out her junior year due to CIF transfer rules following her time at Alameda High, Levingston stepped into the Purple and White with a mission to prove that she was a major player. . She did just that, earning firstteam All-League honors in her only year at the school, continuously reeling in double-doubles for points and rebounds. She had 10 points and 14 rebounds in a 62-47 win over O’Dowd, 17 points and 10 rebounds in a 69-62 win over O’Dowd, and 21 points and over 10 rebounds in a 69-63 win over Salesian. Levingston will continue playing basketball at Cal State Fullerton. ALBERT BELLINGRATH Volleyball, Football SAM SHELBY Football, Soccer, Track Sam Shelby, a sophomore, is among the few three-sport athletes at the school. Even rarer is he’s a key player in each of the football, soccer and track teams. Shelby did it all on the football team, contributing as a receiver, running back, defensive back, return specialist, and he can pass—lining up at quarterback on occasion. He scored five Staff Photo Sam Shelby was a key three-sport athlete in football, soccer, and track as a sophomore. touchdowns on the varsity team before cancelation of its season. On the soccer team, Shelby appeared as a winger, using his speed to bomb down the flank. He earned starting minutes as a sophomore in Todd Sullivan’s system, contributing towards the team’s Division 4 North Coast Section title. With track in the recent spring season, Sam was a member of the squad’s 4x400 relay team which reached the CIF State Championship meet on May 26 alongside Christian Taylor, Parker Long, and Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai. They finished in 3:23.84, 21st of 24 teams. To get there, they second out of eight teams at the NCS Meet of Champions on May 20 with a time of 3:24.58. Albert Bellingrath was a standout freshman on the volleyball team last spring and the JV football team back in the fall. On the volleyball team, Bellingrath earned starting time as a middle hitter, making a difference as a defensive and offensive threat. He’ll be expected to make a big jump in the lineup as a sophomore. Bellingrath also received praise as a tight end and defensive lineman on the junior varsity football team back in the fall. He scored once in a 34-0 win over Tennyson. Staff Photos Albert Bellingrath was a key player on the volleyball team and junior varsity football team.

Wednesday, June 21, 2023 13 Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 16th year. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmont-post.com. PARKER LONG Cross Country, Track & Field Piedmont High Class of 2023 Cal Poly Class of 2027 Parker Long was our 2023 Athlete of the Year after finishing his career at Piedmont High among the best half milers. He was the third fastest runner in school history at 1:53.25, set at the Dublin Distance Fiesta on March 18. His time put him just back of the Post’s 2018 Athlete of the Year Reece Proctor (1:52.64), and Piedmont Sports Hall of Famer, Gordon Johnson (1:51.10), He was .15 ahead of teammate Cooper Downing (1:53.4). Long won the NCS Meet of Champions’ 800 meter run with a time of 1:53.80 in a field of 12 finalists. He was also a member of Piedmont’s 4x400 relay team that qualified for the CIF State Championship, where they clocked a time of 3:23.84 in the preliminary round. He helped the team hit a season-best of 3:22.93 at the NCS Meet of Champions on May 20, which was until then the third fastest time in school history. It placed them narrowly behind last year’s record-setting time of 3:21.77, set by Parker Terrill, Luke Alban, Cooper Downing, and Long as the second leg. Piedmont High’s second-fastest time in the 4x400 was set in 1989 by a group led by Johnson. In the fall, Long finished sixth of 71 at the WACC Championship in 15:59.1. The previous year, he helped the 2021 program qualify for the CIF State Meet. What is your workout program this summer? Until I receive my workout regimen from my coaches at Cal Poly, my goal is to get miles in and build a strong base. I’ll continue ramping up my workouts through the summer. What are your fitness goals for this summer? I’d like to feel comfortable running higher mileage. One of the biggest differences between high school and collegiate running is the amount of miles you run. How are you measuring your development? Every runner does this differently. Many people log their miles and paces for each run with a watch. I just focus on how I feel during each run; if I feel comfortable doing certain runs or workouts, or if I am having difficulty completing it. I don’t record my runs or use a watch anymore; I’ve found it to be distracting. Running is pretty simple at the end of the day, it is just about feel. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? Right now, I’m training on my own. But I’ll be getting my training plan from my coach at Cal Poly, Ryan Vanhoy. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? A recent achievement was winning the NCS Meet of Champions’ 800-meter event. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? Just run. Don’t worry too much about the intricate details of what you are doing. Don’t over-train during off-season, which is common. Don’t stress. As long as you’re having fun with training, you are headed in the right direction. Staff Photo Eleanor Lavin, PHS Class of 2023, will continue her lacrosse career at Occidental College. teammates. It has been really fun to complete this workout plan with my new team this summer. We have a group chat where we all motivate each other. It’s a very positive community. MICHAEL AIKAWA Baseball ELEANOR LAVIN Lacrosse Staff Photo Parker Long, PHS Class of 2023, was The Post’s Athlete of the Year and will continue running at Cal Poly in San Luis Obispo Piedmont High Class of 2023 Oberlin College Class of 2027 Eleanor Lavin just concluded her High School career as a leader on Piedmont’s lacrosse team, helping them receive a berth in the Division 2 North Coast Section postseason playoffs and earning a NorCal All-Star Team selection by Team USA as a midfielder. Piedmont went 8-8 in 2023, including a 4-1 league record and second-place finish in the Western Alameda County Conference Championship tournament. PHS narrowly lost 11-9 to Bishop O’Dowd in the finals. She details her plans ahead of attending Oberlin College in Ohio. What is your workout program this summer? I am doing a summer workout program provided by my coaches at Oberlin College. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My fitness goals are to have a faster 300-meter sprint time and to strengthen my arms and core. How are you measuring your development? Our program has testing days, where we have a spreadsheet to log our data to measure our progress. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? Our team is training together with a program designed by the coaches. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Graduating from high school and being selected for the NorCal All-Star game. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Build relationships with your Piedmont High Class of 2023 Lewis & Clark College Class of 2027 Michael Aikawa was a fouryear starter at Piedmont High. He earned second-team All-League honors as a senior and was firstteam in 2022. We named him the Post’s 2021 Sophomore of the Year. Aikawa contributed both as a shortstop and pitcher in 2023, closing the year as Piedmont’s leading hitter with a .357 average, 25 hits, 12 doubles, one home run, 13 RBIs and 22 runs scored. As a pitcher, he led the way with 37 innings, a 4-2 record, 44 strikeouts and a sterling 1.324 ERA, despite being the first year he ever appeared on the mound for the Highlanders. He details his workout plans ahead of the start of his collegiate career at Lewis & Clark in Portland. What is your workout program this summer? I’m following the Lewis & Clark baseball team’s workout program provided by the trainer on an phone app. Additionally, I have added in plyometrics, sprinting, and other baseball related exercises. What are your fitness goals for the summer? Consistently throwing over 100 yards in long toss, along with gaining quickness, speed, and strength in the weight room. How are you measuring your development? I’m measuring how far I am throwing and the increase in my throwing velocity. For quickness, speed, and strength, I’m seeing how quickly I can move the weight, increasing the weight, and decreasing my 60 yard dash time. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am mainly working on my own thus far this summer, following what the Lewis & Clark trainer suggests for me to do. In addition, I’m working with my summer coaches from my club team. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Graduating from high school. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Recently, I realized the amount of sacrifice it takes to be a student-athlete, especially a student-athlete working to reach the next level. If becoming a student-athlete is what you have a passion for and if it is what you want to become, then there is no sacrifice too big to make. Staff Photo Michael Aikawa, PHS Class of 2023, just concluded his baseball career at the school as a four-year varsity starter. He’s off to Lewis & Clark to continue playing.

articles.text: CONCACAF Gold Cup starts Saturday International soccer is back for the United States Soccer Federation. The men’s team won the CONCACAF Nations League on Sunday, June 18 with a 2-0 victory over Canada, after bashing rival Mexico 3-0 in the semifinals on Thursday, June 15. Both games were played at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas. Their Nations League victory marked the United States’ fifth-consecutive victory of a major CONCACAF tournament. The U.S. won the Nations League in 2020, the Gold Cup in 2021, and now the Nations League in 2023. It was a heated semifinal game with Mexico. Midfielder Weston McKennie got a red card and had his jersey ripped. Sergino Dest nearly was red carded as well after getting in an altercation. He was subsequently pelted with beer cups. The baton for being the best team in CONCACAF seems to have passed from Mexico to the U.S.; the men’s team is undefeated through its six matches against El Tri at 4-2-0. The match with Mexico was marred by a brawl that resulted in the ejection of Mexico’s Cesar Miramontes and McKennie in the 69th and 71st minutes. Dest and Gerardo Arteaga’s skirmish in the 85th minute led to trash raining down on the players. Following the brawl, the match was halted twice due to Mexico fans chanting homophobic slurs. In the eighth minute of second-half stoppage time, referees called the match after the chant rang onto the broadcast. In the Finals versus Canada, the United States scored early in the 12th minute on a perfect cross from Gio Reyna, locating defender Chris Richard for a leaping header goal. Photo courtesy of CONCACAF Gold Cup The U.S. Men’s Soccer team now prepares for the 2023 Gold Cup with a very different roster than Nations League. The U.S. struck again in the 34th minute when newcomer Folarin Balogun scored on a right-footed rocket you love to see out of a striker. Balogun has dual citizenship with England and the U.S., and recently decided to play for the United States. He’s a product of Arsenal’s youth academy of the Premier League and came up through England’s youth system. Balogun has spent 2022-2023 on loan from Arsenal with Reims in France’s Ligue 1 and could become the answer the U.S. has been seeking at striker Gold Cup starts Saturday The United States Men’s National Team is set to take part in this year’s Gold Cup, stretching from June 24 through July 16. This year’s Gold Cup roster will look vastly different from what appeared in Nations League with a majority of players coming America’s major League. Soccer League. Instead of Christian Pulisic and Balogun leading the attack, the front line will likely include Earthquakes’ Cade Cowell and FC Dallas’ Jesús Ferreira. Goalkeeper Matt Turner is the only holdover player from the Nations League’s starting lineup. The Gold Cup features four groups of three teams with the top-two from each group advancing o the Quarterfinals. The United States plays in Group A Photos courtesy of 90Min.com Weston McKennie kisses his jersey after it was ripped during a heated game against Mexico in the Nations League semifinals. Photos courtesy of 90Min.com Falorin Balogun scored a terrific goal in his debut with the U.S. Soccer team.

articles.text: For Bay Area residents, the welcome sight of Horsetail Falls’ gushing waters off in the distance as you drive on U.S. 50 means you’ve nearly arrived at South Lake Tahoe. In Twin Bridges between Strawberry and the Sierra at Tahoe Resort along the El Dorado Freeway is a magnificent 500-foot waterfall cascading down Pyramid Creek. It’s just 30 minutes from Stateline, Nevada. Horsetail Falls requires just two miles of legwork, four miles round trip, while hiking beside the beautiful flowing Pyramid Creek and the trail gets steeper as you ascend toward the falls. The two mile mark puts you at around 750 feet in elevation gain while walking at over 6,100 feet. The majority of legwork comes in the final half mile over steep boulders and rocks, and proper footwear is required. Although our day ended at two-miles, the trail continues up the mountain towards backpacking areas for another mile to the mouth of the falls, the venture point to reach countless alpine lakes. Avalanche Lake is at the top of the falls. The entire trail is largely unmaintained, but keeping your eyes on the beaten path was simple enough. In Twin Bridges between Strawberry and the Sierra at Tahoe Resort along the El Dorado Freeway is a magnificent 500-foot waterfall cascading down Pyramid Creek. It’s just 30 minutes from Stateline, Nevada. Horsetail Falls requires just two miles of legwork, four miles round trip, while hiking beside the beautiful flowing Pyramid Creek and the trail gets steeper as you ascend toward the falls. The two mile mark puts you at around 750 feet in elevation gain while walking at over 6,100 feet. The majority of legwork comes in the final half mile over steep boulders and rocks, and proper footwear is required. Although our day ended at two-miles, the trail continues up the mountain towards backpacking areas for another mile to the mouth of the falls, the venture point to reach countless alpine lakes. There are also small The trail continues over a vast rockface into the Desolation Wilderness towards Horsetail Falls. Your view of the Desolation Wilderness continues as you ascend the trail. Hikers can find countless areas for resting by Pyramid Creek. The Pyramid Creek Trailhead where the day starts Staff Photos Horsetail Falls in Desolation Wilderness is a 500-foot cascade on Pyramid Creek. It takes just two miles of hiking, 750 feet in elevation gain while at over 6,100 feet. The hike along Pyramid Creek is just as majestic as the reward of reaching Horsetail Falls. blue-spray painted markings to keep hikers on the trail. Should hikers opt against making it all the way to the falls, there are countless areas to jump into the creek or sunbathe on the rocks. Beneath the falls is a popular swimming hole with ample space to jump, swim, or just wade. On a hot summer day, a dip into the cold freshwater was the perfect refresher before the hike down. “The locals may be upset that you’re sharing this, it is really a treasured spot,” said Chad from Sacramento, who put on a display of dives into the swimming hole. Punch in “Pyramid Creek Trailhead” to access this hike’s parking lot, which is $10 for all day and overnight. Reprinted from Piedmont Post in August 2021 A visitor from Sacramento dives into the swimming hole beneath Horsetail Falls. Keep your eyes peeled for blue spray-painted markings on rocks, stumps, or the ground as you continue on the unmaintained trail.

articles.text: Colorful exhibition on view through July 10 San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum’s exhibit Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in Art ends soon. The exhibition features more than 120 artworks borrowed from 20 of the finest museums and private collections in the world, with a focus on the arts of the Indian cultural sphere. Beyond Bollywood includes artwork from India, Pakistan, Nepal, Tibet, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, and Indonesia. “We hope visitors will come away with a transformed notion of the importance and power of dance,” said exhibition co-curator Forrest McGill. “[Both] what it has meant in the past, and what it can mean in their own lives today.” “Dance dialogues,” that include Asian folk dances with expert speaker panels, take place June 22 and July 9. These pop-ups will include 30-minute dance performances and demonstrations in the museum gallery, followed by a question and answer session. These recur monthly on selected Sundays and Thursdays. Admission is included with your ticket to Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in Art. Space is limited and reservations are recommended. For a full list of featured dancers and speakers, visit https:// asia na r t.org / beyond-bollywood-events/. Beyond Bollywood will be on display through July 10. For more information, and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://exhibitions.asianart. org/exhibitions/beyond-bollywood-2000-years-of-dance-inart/. Cambodian dance company Charya Burt will perform during “Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in Art,” at the Asian Art Museum. articles.text: The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England opens Saturday The Legion of Honor, of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, opens to the public this weekend an exhibit of historic significance. The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England opens this Saturday, June 24. This is the first major exhibition in the United States of portraiture and decorative arts of the Tudor courts. It will include works from the museum’s collection, including a late 16th century panel painting, as well as tapestries commissioned or acquired by Henry VII and Henry VIII. “Few may be aware of the distinctive art and visual propaganda that was central to the splendor and drama of the Tudor court,” said Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Now, in the first exhibition of its kind in the US, The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England reunites scores of sumptuous paintings, precious jewels, rich tapestries and rare artifacts from collections around the world to bring the Tudor dynasty vividly to life–from the bloody founding of the dynasty in 1485 by Henry VII on the fields of Bosworth, to the final moments of Queen Elizabeth in 1603.” The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England will be on view from June 24 through September 24. For tickets and more information visit https://www.famsf.org. Karah Son sings the title role of Cio-Cio-San in San Francisco Opera’s production of Puccini’s Madame Butterfly
articles.title: Historic Tudors exhibit now at Legion of Honor

articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s production of Madame Butterfly will be performed through July 1. Giacomo Puccini’s spectacular and heartbreaking drama is conducted by Music Director Eun Sun Kim with all-new staging by director Amon Miyamoto. The cast is headed by Karah Son as Cio-Cio-San, Michael Fabiano as Lt. Pinkerton, and Lucas Meachem as Sharpless. Also appearing are Hyona Kim, Lucas Meachem, and Julius Ahn. Costume designs are by the late fashion icon Kenzō Takada The drama centers around a young Japanese woman, Cio-CioSan, who wholeheartedly devotes herself to her absent American husband, naval officer Pinkerton, only to discover that he is married to another woman. It is a tragic tale and considered one of opera’s most enduring stories of unrequited love. The opera is sung in Italian with English supertitles. Performances take place June 9, 18, 21, 24, 27; and July 1. Tickets are available online at https://www.sfopera.com/operas/ madame-butterfly/#performances or by calling the box office at (415) 864-3330.

pages.text: 16 Wednesday, June 21, 2023 Arts & Entertainment Beyond Bollywood ends soon at Asian Art Museum Colorful exhibition on view through July 10 By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum’s exhibit Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in Art ends soon. The exhibition features more than 120 artworks borrowed from 20 of the finest museums and private collections in the world, with a focus on the arts of the Indian cultural sphere. Beyond Bollywood includes artwork from India, Pakistan, Nepal, Tibet, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, and Indonesia. “We hope visitors will come away with a transformed notion of the importance and power of dance,” said exhibition co-curator Forrest McGill. “[Both] what it has meant in the past, and what it can mean in their own lives today.” “Dance dialogues,” that include Asian folk dances with expert speaker panels, take place June 22 and July 9. These pop-ups will include 30-minute dance performances and demonstrations in the museum gallery, followed by a question and answer session. These recur monthly on selected Sundays and Thursdays. Admission is included with your ticket to Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in Art. Space is limited and reservations are recommended. For a full list of featured dancers and speakers, visit https:// asia na r t.org / beyond-bollywood-events/. Beyond Bollywood will be on display through July 10. For more information, and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://exhibitions.asianart. org/exhibitions/beyond-bollywood-2000-years-of-dance-inart/. articles.text: Celebrate Independence Day with the San Francisco Symphony at the Shoreline Amphitheatre in Mountain View. Edwin Outwater will conduct the symphony for this outdoor concert featuring actress and vocalist Capathia Jenkins. The performance celebrates America’s independence with traditional fanfare and the music of “Queen of Soul” Aretha Franklin. The evening will conclude with an exuberant fireworks display, Outwater was resident conductor of the San Francisco Symphony from 2001 to 2006; and in September 2019, he led the San Francisco Symphony orchestra with rock band Metallica to open the new Chase Center. Outwater also conducted alongside former symphony conductor Michael Tilson Thomas. Jenkins is best known for her performances on Broadway, especially for her roles in Newsies and Fame Becomes Me. She has appeared with numerous orchestras in the country including the Houston Symphony, Cleveland Orchestra and Pittsburgh Symphony, as well as the San Francisco Symphony. The program includes Liberty Fanfare by John Williams, Fantasy and Variations on Carnival of Venice (arr. Jean-Baptiste Arban), Hoedown from Four Dance Episodes from Rodeo by Aaron Copland, Orange Blossom Special by Ervin T. Rouse (arr. Gabe Witcher), Armed Forces Salute, and a special tribute to the great soul singer Aretha Franklin. Visit https://www.sfsymphony. org/Buy-Tickets/2022-23/Shoreline-4th-of-July to purchase tickets, or call the box office at (415) 864-6000. Capathia Jenkins

articles.text: Matthew McConaughey and Ryan Phillippe in The Lincoln Lawyer If you are a fan of writer Michael Connelly, then it’s possible you’ve read “The Lincoln Lawyer.” Connelly, once a Los Angeles crime reporter turned fiction writer, has created a memorable series of L.A.-based crime novels, many featuring detective Hieronymous Bosch. All are engaging reads. The Lincoln Lawyer is one of those bestselling novels, adapted to the screen by scriptwriter Joe Romano. Mickey Haller, the lead character, is a Los Angeles defense attorney, denizen of a chauffeured Lincoln Continental that he uses as his mobile office. He is the half-brother of Harry Bosch, and, like Harry, he’s flawed, street smart, resilient and guided by his own moral gyroscope. He can be a hard case when the need arises; but then working the gritty back streets of L.A. isn’t for the faint of heart. Matthew McConaughey, thankfully having moved beyond the sugarcoated, flash the six pack rom-coms of the last several years, chews up the L.A. scenery in this compelling whodunit. The corner-cutting Haller is his best role since A Time to Kill, a remarkable legal thriller based on John Grisham’s debut novel that was only picked up after he hit it big with The Firm. Haller takes his clients where he can find them, defending bikers and hookers, and, as is revealed, Louis Roulet (Ryan Phillippe), a rich kid from a prominent family, who is accused of raping and beating a prostitute who was working one of the downtown bars. While guilt or innocence is not relevant to providing a solid defense, and Mickey’s mantra is, ala Jerry McGuire, “show me the money,” he does acknowledge that the most terrifying client a lawyer can have is one who is innocent. And so Haller begins to peal the onion, building the defense, using his lead investigator, Frank Levin (William H. Macy). Levin’s no rookie, his face deeply lined, his eyes tired, his hair touching his shoulders. What’s the adage? It’s not your age, it’s the mileage. Like Mick, he’s intuitive, knows the streets, and is bulldog tenacious. Macy, one of the best character actors in films today, is exceptional, as are all of the actors in The Lincoln Lawyer, especially Marisa Tomei. Her face is now lined and even more attractive as her strength and character shine through. Maturing, accomplished actresses like Tomei are a trea-

articles.text: The Big Short is a muckraking blur of a movie. It’s filled with financial jargon – “credit-default swaps,” “collateralized debt,” “ninja loans,” “subprime mortgages,” “debt repackaging”. In the collective, it is arcane and delivered in dialogue that is manic and almost surreal. It also breaks the fourth-wall, that unspoken agreement between the audience and the characters in which they will not turn to the camera and speak directly to the moviegoer. It is a film of endless conversations, in boardrooms, offices, and hotel foyers that even those listening, the financial insiders, seem unable to fully grasp what they are being told. Having said that, The Big Short is one heck of a fine movie, riveting at times, because just enough of what is discussed makes sense While the film is intended to be a tragicomedy it is, ultimately, far more tragic than comedic. What is argued and explained and then bet on - big time – is that the housing bubble of 2007-2009 will pop like a carnival balloon and those who sell short will walk away with millions. I think it’s like betting that all of the liar loans made during the real estate boom, when prices were endlessly soaring, will collapse and millions of folks will find themselves and their mortgages underwater. The film follows a crew from different sectors of the financial world debating whether the housing bubble is going to burst. Or not. There’s Dr. Michael Burry (Christian Bale), a fund manager, who runs the numbers and says that the best position for his clients is to wager that the housing market will collapse. An over-caffeinated Mark Baum (Steve Carell), also a Wall Street guy, and his crew, is slowly convinced by another inside guy, Jared Vennett (Ryan Gosling), that Burry could be right. Ditto Ben Rickert (Brad Pitt), a semi-retired banker-trader who also is reading the same tea leaves. All are beginning to bet against the market, which is bullish on real estate, sensing that a financial Armageddon is about to take place. And when it does they will be, unlike most banks and investment houses, positioned to cash in. The only moral voice in the film is that of Ben Rickert, who points out that if their prediction is accurate, and so it seems, the outcome will be a train wreck of major proportions and people will face ruin unlike anything experienced since the Great Depression of 1929. articles.text: While The Stepfather is neither subtle nor shy, it does ratchet up serious tension as the film moves toward its predictable and harrowing conclusion. The story is familiar (it’s actually a remake of the 1987 movie of the same name) and aims at that primordial fear that we don’t really know the people we’re close to until it may be too late. David Harris (Dylan Walsh), charming and smooth, inserts himself into the lives of a mother, Susan Harding (Sela Ward), and her three children. Susan is just coming out of a divorce and is vulnerable. The kids are teens and adjusting to a split family and weekends with dad. Suddenly they have a supportive guy around, someone who often insists that all he values in life is family. He tells them, his wife and daughter were killed in a car accident more than a year ago. The screenwriters do an interesting thing at the outset. They make it clear to the audience that Harris is a psychopath and pure evil in the guise of a wonderful guy. In other words, the first shoe is immediately dropped. What gives the film an unrelenting tension is that the audience is waiting for the second shoe to drop. The test of the film is how effective the filmmakers are in revealing to the unsuspecting family that Harris is a stone-cold killer who is moving placidly among his victims with a wide smile and a loving, helpful persona. But all the while small chinks – ever so subtle, ever so easily explained – in his behavior begin to appear. It’s chilling to watch. Walsh, as an actor, does a superb job in transforming his face from barely controlled rage to wide smiles in mere seconds. Susan is oblivious. She’s in love. Her oldest son, Michael (Penn Bradley), however, begins to suspect that something is deeply wrong; however, his girlfriend (Amber Heard) insists that it is all in his imagination. The audience, of course, knows he’s right. The second shoe is about to fall. It’s only a matter of time. And it’s those minutes that make all the difference. As psych-horror films go, The Stepfather is well done. It’s a B-movie to be sure, one targeted at teens who unabashedly enjoy the genre and will surely turn out for this one. The Stepfather. Directed by Nelson McCormick. Starring Dylan Walsh, Sela Ward, Penn Badgley and Amber Heard. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2009. Streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv. articles.text: Max Records in a scene from Where the Wild Things Are In an article in the New York Times Magazine, director Spike Jonze, when discussing his latest film, Where the Wild Things Are, said, “Everything we did, all the decisions that we made, were to try to capture the feeling of what it is to be 9.” While it is true that a movie targeting young filmgoers must engage their imaginations and emotions, it shouldn’t necessarily mirror what it feels like to be 9-years-old. At least not completely. There must also be magic and surprise. In other words, a film of this ilk will find more success if it’s a fable that asks young audiences to suspend their disbelief and climb on board – which, of course, they are fully prepared to do. Say, at the drop of a hat. But first, consider the book. Written by Maurice Sendak and published in 1963, it has sold 19 million copies worldwide, 10 million in the U.S. alone. Its success begs the question, Why? What is there about this story that young readers so completely embrace? The story, after all, comprises only 338 words; 41 lines of text; and is only 37 pages long. Perhaps it’s the fact that story is a seamless melding of reality and fantasy. Max, dressed in his wolf costume, consumed with a riptide of emotion, rebels, causing mischief, and is sent to his room. And that’s when the magic begins. His room grows into a forest and he finds a boat and sails to a distant shore where he discovers a band of feral monsters – large, furry, exotic, all strange hybrid animals. He becomes the king of the monsters, wears a crown, carries a scepter, and is empowered. It’s an overwhelming feeling for Max. He stands and yells to the monsters that it’s time to howl and experience their inner wildness. Eventually, however, he decides to return to his family, to those who love him most. Max (Max Records) is coping with the divorce of his parents, and with a sense of isolation so complete that he talks to fences as if they could talk back. But if he deviates too far from the fable template (and from Sendak’s book), he does so at his peril. pages.text: Wednesday, June 21, 2023 19 MOVIES FOR KIDS Where the Wild Things Are Max Records in a scene from Where the Wild Things Are By Chris Honoré In an article in the New York Times Magazine, director Spike Jonze, when discussing his latest film, Where the Wild Things Are, said, “Everything we did, all the decisions that we made, were to try to capture the feeling of what it is to be 9.” While it is true that a movie targeting young filmgoers must engage their imaginations and emotions, it shouldn’t necessarily mirror what it feels like to be 9-years-old. At least not completely. There must also be magic and surprise. In other words, a film of this ilk will find more success if it’s a fable that asks young audiences to suspend their disbelief and climb on board – which, of course, they are fully prepared to do. Say, at the drop of a hat. But first, consider the book. Written by Maurice Sendak and published in 1963, it has sold 19 million copies worldwide, 10 million in the U.S. alone. Its success begs the question, Why? What is there about this story that young readers so completely embrace? The story, after all, comprises only 338 words; 41 lines of text; and is only 37 pages long. Perhaps it’s the fact that story is a seamless melding of reality and fantasy. Max, dressed in his wolf costume, consumed with a riptide of emotion, rebels, causing mischief, and is sent to his room. And that’s when the magic begins. His room grows into a forest and he finds a boat and sails to a distant shore where he discovers a band of feral monsters – large, furry, exotic, all strange hybrid animals. He becomes the king of the monsters, wears a crown, carries a scepter, and is empowered. It’s an overwhelming feeling for Max. He stands and yells to the monsters that it’s time to howl and experience their inner wildness. Eventually, however, he decides to return to his family, to those who love him most. Where the Wild Things Are is an elegant and simple story, wonderfully illustrated by Sendak, and one that would appeal to any youngster who feels conflicted and perhaps frustrated at being buffeted by the whims of family, school and siblings, who wishes only for a magic place where he or she can be king. The story is familiar (it’s actually a remake of the 1987 movie of the same name) and aims at that primordial fear that we don’t really know the people we’re close to until it may be too late. David Harris (Dylan Walsh), charming and smooth, inserts himself into the lives of a mother, Susan Harding (Sela Ward), and her three children. Susan is just coming out of a divorce and is vulnerable. The kids are teens and adjusting to a split family and weekends with dad. Suddenly they have a supportive guy around, someone who often insists that all he values in life is family. He tells them, his wife and daughter were killed in a car accident more than a year ago. The screenwriters do an interesting thing at the outset. They make it clear to the audience that Harris is a psychopath and pure evil in the guise of a wonderful guy. In other words, the first shoe is immediately dropped. What gives the film an unrelenting tension is that the audience is waiting for the second shoe to drop. The test of the film is how effective the filmmakers are in revealing to the unsuspecting family that Harris is a stone-cold killer who is moving placidly among his victims with a wide smile and a loving, helpful persona. But all the while small chinks – ever so subtle, ever so easily explained – in his behavior begin to appear. It’s chilling to watch. Walsh, as an actor, does a superb job in transforming his face from barely controlled rage to wide smiles in mere seconds. Susan is oblivious. She’s in love. Her oldest son, Michael (Penn Bradley), however, begins to suspect that something is deeply wrong; however, his girlfriend (Amber Heard) insists that it is all in his imagination. The audience, of course, knows he’s right. The second shoe is about to fall. It’s only a matter of time. And it’s those minutes that make all the difference. As psych-horror films go, The Stepfather is well done. It’s a B-movie to be sure, one targeted at teens who unabashedly enjoy the genre and will surely turn out for this one. The Stepfather. articles.text: Come enjoy the music, art and special events at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Summer. Weekends to July 2, 11 a.m.–2 p.m. In Search of Beauty Fine Art Exhibition LAST TWO WEEKENDS! Elena Doronkina has mounted a fine art exhibition showing her own work as well as that of two friends, also well-known artists, Alexander Zimin and Galina Filimonova, which will be open Saturdays and Sundays through July 2 at the hours above. In addition to showcasing their work, primarily still lifes and landscapes in watercolors and oils, they will use this event to express support for Ukraine. One-Half of all sale proceeds from the exhibit will be donated to support children in Ukraine, specifically those in South Village in the Kharkiv Region. Sunday, June 25, 2023, 4:00 p.m. Ro Sham Bo Jazz Vocal Sextet Ro Sham Bo is a dynamic sextet singing original arrangements of jazz, latin, bossa nova, R&B, and pop music, from timeless standards to recent releases, all a cappella. This award-winning group has been entertaining the Bay Area for two decades. This afternoon concert, opened by special guests from Pitch, Please! will be followed by an evening reception. In 2013 and 2018, Ro Sham Bo took home the firstplace championship at the SF Bay Area Regional Harmony Sweepstakes and was also awarded audience favorite at the National Harmony Sweepstakes in 2018. Ro Sham Bo has performed to sold-out audiences at Anna’s Jazz Island and the historic La Peña Cultural Center. You can also find them serenading listeners at the personality-filled and eclectic Omega Salvage, the quirky Van Kleef bar in Uptown Oakland, and the family-friendly Montclair Farmers Market. For tickets go to https://www.brownpapertickets.com/event/6032176. Sunday, July 16, 7:00 p.m. Diluvian String Quartet Concert For their summer recital, Musical Portraits, Diluvian will include quartets by Franz Schubert, William Grant Still, and Felix Mendelssohn. Elizabeth Castro Abrams and Jessica Scrimale, violins; Raphael Gold, viola; and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello; will perform these delightful pieces dating from 1820 to 1960 before offering a simple dessert reception with beverages. Advance tickets are recommended and available from Eventbrite at https://www. eventbrite.com/e/656199669877. articles.text: Havens’ Avenue of Palms was for sale in 1922. They hired Houghton Sawyer, Albert Farr and Engineer Robert E. Carney to design a model city center. Continuing Farr’s Spanish Mission design at City Hall, their Master Plan called for an elaborate Exedra at the entrance to Piedmont Park, a grand threestory City Hall, additions to the current City Hall, a library, museum and municipal garages. They planned to re-route the streetcar line into a tunnel where passengers could enter and exit streetcars at an elegant plaza with a fountain at the park level. Passengers would not have to cross the streetcar tracks. The Master Plan was to be completed in phases, with each building to be approved by voters before construction. The grand three-story City Hall was scaled down to the present onestory Community Hall. Voters approved the first phase in 1924 which included funds to build the Exedra and the Community Hall. Later units of the Master Plan were never realized. School construction took precedence. The Junior High School and Wildwood School were built in 1923. Later bond issues failed to pass, and the Depression ended all thoughts of grand new construction. Piedmont’s new Community Hall and Exedra opened on April 3, 1925. Civic leaders and residents entered the newly landscaped Piedmont Park through the Exedra, which reporters compared to the “Arch of Triumph.” Guests admired Howard Gilkey’s new landscape design, with its rose garden behind the Exedra, extensive lawns and flowering shrubs along the path to the hall. The Community Hall was dedicated as a meeting place and social hall for all Piedmont residents. The lower level of the hall became the new armory for Piedmont’s Battery D of the 143rd Field Artillery. Piedmont Park had been saved The original Piedmont High School designed by William Weeks in 1921. from development. Only two small parts of the original park were sold to real estate developers. The land that became Guilford Road was sold as “Guilford Place” in 1921, and the land that became Palm Drive was sold as the Lower Piedmont Park Tract in 1922. Today, a few palm trees survive on Palm Drive from Havens’ “Avenue of Palms.” The new Community Hall and Exedra in 1925. The 1922 Master Plan for the Community Center featured a tunnel for the streetcars.
articles.title: The History of Piedmont

articles.text: Frank C. Havens opened Piedmont Park in 1898 with a new Clubhouse, the mineral springs, a rustic teahouse, and the beauty of the ravine, waterfalls and meandering paths through bucolic Bushy Dell Canyon. Havens added “The Maze” (1904), an “Avenue of Palms” to the Maze from Grand Avenue, a Japanese Tea House (1907) and the Piedmont Art Gallery (1907). He added a bandstand for Sunday concerts, rustic park benches the upper park and exotic plants including Queen palm trees, Canary Island date palms, cordyline and banana trees, orchids and roses. Piedmont Park thrived until 1916. Visitors enjoyed an afternoon in the park, ate lunch in the Clubhouse or enjoyed tea in one of two teahouses, listened to Sunday concerts at the bandstand, marveled at Havens’ collection in the Piedmont Art Gallery, got lost in the Maze and wandered the paths throughout the ravine. reported that lawsuits totaling $90,000 were filed against Frank C. Havens. The Anglo-California Trust Company held the mortgage on the park for $172,000, and neither the interest nor the principal had been paid. The park was to be sold at a foreclosure auction in 1917. Havens had auctioned off his art collection, and now he was selling Piedmont Park to raise funds. In 1916, Piedmont Park was for sale. The School Board voted to purchase some of the park land for a new high school and athletic field. They wanted to buy 13 acres, but Havens would not sell less than 27 acres. The city of Piedmont wanted to save the park from development, but did not have the funds to purchase the remaining parkland. In November of 1916, Piedmont voters defeated a measure to raise funds to purchase the parkland. Piedmont Park land was still available in 1921 when Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander and others offered to purchase 14 acres of the park if the city would reimburse them. This plan allowed the entire 27-acre parcel to be sold. The School District could buy the 13 acres they wanted, and the city would have its park. Alexander purchased the land for the city in 1921 and one year later voters passed a bond issue, and the city reimbursed Wallace Alexander and his partners in full. Piedmont High School In 1921, construction began immediately on the high school. Architect William Weeks designed a reinforced concrete school with terra cotta trim for 500 students. The auditorium spanned the front of the school with two stories of classrooms behind. Two wings held more classrooms. The cooking and science labs were to be set away from the main building in these wings, removing any odors and fire risk. (The history of Piedmont High School will be explored in a later column.) New Municipal Park In 1922 the City Trustees went to work on a new civic center. The Oakland Tribune announced the sale of Piedmont Park in 1917. Development to develop the park into residential home sites. He sent his art to San Francisco to be auctioned where paintings went to the new deYoung Museum, the Oakland Art Gallery (the predecessor of today’s Oakland Museum of California), and private collectors. (Havens’ art collection was described in my previous column published on December 5.) But Havens was in financial trouble. The Oakland Tribune ❏ New Membership

They planned to re-route the streetcar line into a tunnel where passengers could enter and exit streetcars at an elegant plaza with a fountain at the park level. Passengers would not have to cross the streetcar tracks. The Master Plan was to be completed in phases, with each building to be approved by voters before construction. The grand three-story City Hall was scaled down to the present onestory Community Hall. Voters approved the first phase in 1924 which included funds to build the Exedra and the Community Hall. Later units of the Master Plan were never realized. School construction took precedence. The Junior High School and Wildwood School were built in 1923. Later bond issues failed to pass, and the Depression ended all thoughts of grand new construction. Piedmont’s new Community Hall and Exedra opened on April 3, 1925. Civic leaders and residents entered the newly landscaped Piedmont Park through the Exedra, which reporters compared to the “Arch of Triumph.” Guests admired Howard Gilkey’s new landscape design, with its rose garden behind the Exedra, extensive lawns and flowering shrubs along the path to the hall. The Community Hall was dedicated as a meeting place and social hall for all Piedmont residents. The lower level of the hall became the new armory for Piedmont’s Battery D of the 143rd Field Artillery. Piedmont Park had been saved The original Piedmont High School designed by William Weeks in 1921. from development. Only two small parts of the original park were sold to real estate developers. The land that became Guilford Road was sold as “Guilford Place” in 1921, and the land that became Palm Drive was sold as the Lower Piedmont Park Tract in 1922. Today, a few palm trees survive on Palm Drive from Havens’ “Avenue of Palms.” If you enjoy reading these history columns, please consider becoming a member of the Piedmont Historical Society and receiving our annual newsletter. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, June 21, 2023 Features Spanish-Inspired Chopped Salad with Shrimp By Deborah Quok Now that we are in for warmer weather (hopefully!), it’s time to feature salads on our menus. I started making versions of this salad dressing years ago and hope it will appeal to you too. Spanish sherry vinegar and a generous pinch of sweet, smoked paprika, Pimentón de La Vera dulce, are key here. Authentic pimentón comes from western Spain, which I also feature in my Spanish-Style Garlic Bread Soup recipe. A few advance notes: As with most salads, this recipe is highly flexible and scalable. Use salad ingredients you enjoy/have available. Radishes, cauliflower, carrots will work, just be ready for more crunch. I used raw, but using barely steamed, such as asparagus, work too. The dressing recipe makes about 1/4 cup, potentially a bit more than you need for the salad. Use your judgement. You can store any remainder in the refrigerator, just bring to room temperature so the olive oil comes back to a liquid form. Spanish-Inspired Chopped Salad with Shrimp Makes about 4 cups INGREDIENTS For the shrimp: • 4 large shrimp, 10-15 count • 1 large clove garlic, minced • 1 tablespoon Spanish olive oil, extra-virgin For the dressing: • 1 teaspoon Dijon mustard • 1 tablespoon sherry vinegar • 1-1/2 tablespoon Spanish olive oil, extra-virgin • 1 teaspoon fresh marjoram leaves, minced • 1/2 teaspoon Pimentón de La Vera dulce, aka smoked paprika • • 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground 1/4 teaspoon sea salt, to taste For the salad: • 1 cup Persian cucumber, sliced into bite-sized chunks (substitute English cucumber) • 1 cup cherry tomatoes, halved • 1 cup firm, ripe avocado, about 1 medium, sliced into bite-sized chunks • 1/2 cup red bell pepper, about one-half of a medium pepper, diced • 1/2 cup red onion, about onehalf of a medium onion, diced • 1/4 cup f lat leaf parsley, coarsely chopped INSTRUCTIONS For the shrimp: If frozen, thaw in cold water, remove the shells and devein by slicing about 1/8-inch across the back of the shrimp and removing the “vein”. Heat the olive oil in a small frying pan over medium heat and add the garlic. When the garlic just barely begins to sizzle, add the shrimp. Cook until the first side becomes translucent, only takes 2-3 minutes. Turn the shrimp and move them about the pan to keep the garlic moving too. Cook another few minutes until the shrimp are no longer translucent. They will cook quickly, and if the garlic looks like it’s getting too browned, reduce the heat to low. The shrimp will continue cooking just fine. Remove the shrimp, garlic, and oil to a plate to cool. For the dressing: Measure the sherry vinegar into a large bowl. Add mustard, marjoram, pimentón de La Vera, salt and pepper. Stir to mix. Slowly drizzle in the olive oil, whisking continuously to maximize emulsification. Season to taste, set aside. Finish the salad: Add the prepared, chopped vegetables to the dressing and toss gently. Place the shrimp atop and serve. pages.text: Wednesday, June 21, 2023 23 Walking on Wednesday Walking on Wednesdays group takes on St. James Drive By Dick Carter The Walking on Wednesdays group walked the entire length of Grand Avenue in Piedmont two weeks ago. Last week they thought it would be interesting to see the length of another important street in Piedmont. St. James Drive is seven tenths of a mile long, ending at Park Boulevard. It is flat, and easy to walk. Walking its length provided the opportunity to go to one of the least visited streets with Piedmont homes, Cavendish Lane. There was a strong turnout of 42 walkers and three K-9 best friends at the Exedra on another cloudy, mild, spring morning. Before beginning, the walkers saw the newly completed Highland-Guildford steps at the edge of Piedmont Park. This was a $155,000 renovation project approved by the City Council in September 2021. The previous wooden railroad tie steps were replaced with colored concrete, and landings, metal handrails, landscaping, six benches, and a small plaza were also added. The group went up Highland to Sheridan Avenue and paused to see the construction of a garage on Crocker. It will provide a 1906 Albert Farr designed, previously garage-less home with three new parking spaces. The walkers went past Crocker Park to Hampton’s intersection with St. James Drive, where the street starts. This first St. James block may have been an extension of St. James Drive because one block further down at La Salle Avenue are two large columns that marked one of the entrances to St. James Woods, an early, large Piedmont neighborhood. It was noted that the columns are missing lanterns on their tops. Mike Henn told the story from his days on the City Planning Commission that the neighborhood once wanted the City to put replicas of the originals on the columns. However, neither the residents nor the City wanted to pay for them, so it never happened. There is still electricity in the columns if anyone wants to install them. The walkers also noted the distinctive four brown tiles that are inlayed in each section of the concrete sidewalks that were part of the original St. James residential development. At the end of St. James at Park Blvd., some walkers needed to head back, but one block down Park, just past Trestle Glen Road, is Cavendish Lane. Some walkers wanted to see it. This is a narrow street that looks like an alley. It is in Oakland, but there are four homes with Piedmont addresses at its end. The street was damaged in February 2017 after it was undermined by heavy rains and a faulty construction project on a Trestle Glen home below. The hillside and road slipped away, and the Piedmont families were unable to access their homes by car for six weeks. The City of Piedmont made temporary fixes, but permanent repairs by Oakland were not begun until two years later. After walking a few hundred feet the group saw the previously damaged roadway with a very large blue tarp covering the hillside below a retaining wall. A Piedmont Public Works notice, dated August 2021, was a taped on it and said all construction work was to be stopped because of violations of City ordinances. It was time for the group to retrace their steps to the Exedra. It was a four-mile walk, longer than usual. However, the walkers had seen some interesting construction projects, and the entirety of not one, but two interesting streets. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. This layer tends to thin with age which can make it difficult for an older person to feel warm. Additionally, when someone is cold, the blood vessels in their skin constrict in an effort to retain heat. However, aging can reduce the elasticity of blood vessel walls in the skin, making it even more challenging to remain warm in fluctuating temperatures. • Medication Side Effects. For example, the chance of having high blood pressure increases with age, and many seniors need to take medicine to regulate their blood pressure levels.
