By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: My husband who is a Windows user always complains that my computer is running software that is too old. My Mac is a 2019 iMac, and I am still running the software that came on it, which is I think Mojave. Is it really a bad idea not to keep it up to date? And can my Mac even run the latest? –Leena P., Oakland Dear Leena: Although I never like to get in the middle of a computer marriage squabble, in this case I must side with your hubby. Of course, I understand that it takes quite a while to get used to a new machine as well as a new operating system (OS) like Mojave and software. And in some cases, especially when there are big changes, waiting a bit to upgrade for a few months won’t hurt. But Mojave is 4 operating systems (and this doesn’t even count the supplemental updates) behind the current one, which is Ventura. And a new one is coming out in October. And your machine can definitely run the current OS, assuming you have enough space on your hard drive. There have been some big changes in the user experience with the newer operating systems. Basically, one of the main changes, is that each of the operating systems make all of your devices work together better. Here are some reasons to keep your computer’s OS up to date. By the way, the OS is the software that manages your experience on the computer, including supporting applications like Safari, Mail, Pages, etc. 1. The longer you wait, the more extreme the changes will be. So, for example if you wait for 3-4 years to upgrade, the way Mac Mail and Safari works will take longer to get used to. Also, for example System Preferences has been changed to System Settings. It’s a very different interface and takes a bit to get used to. When you upgrade regularly, the changes seem more gradual. 2. Many of the updates are bug fixes. So, if an application has been found to be unstable, often the update fixes it. 3. Drivers for your printers, scanners and other devices may become out of date. And some of the newer printers will need new updated drivers, which the newer OS versions will have, but the older ones may not. 4. The older your Mac’s OS is, the less secure it is. Even though Macs generally are less vulnerable to viruses and hackers, malware is designed to exploit loopholes in an operating system’s security design infrastructure. Apple often releases software patches to ensure your Mac is as secure as possible. In some cases, some websites will not open with older browsers (Safari, Chrome and Firefox are browsers), as they are not considered secure. And browsers like Safari get updates often, as hackers and malware get more invasive. 5. New OS versions always come with new features. One of the best features in the current OS (Ventura) is Continuity Camera, which allows you to use your iPhone as a webcam. I found this to be a game changer for me, as the iPhone 14 has a fantastic camera. 6. New versions of some software won’t work on older operating systems, or at least are not supported. For example, most of the games on the App store will not work on anything before OS Monterey, which is 3 versions newer than yours. Of course, there are some reasons not to upgrade. If you depend on software that is no longer being updated (like early versions of Photoshop, ProTools, iWeb, MuseScore and even early versions Microsoft Office), you may want to stick to your older OS to be able to continue using those applications. And the newer operating systems break the compatibility with some of the older software. I know several people who keep an older machine around for that very reason. And if you want to make sure that your Mac download updates automatically, here’s how you do it on Mojave (also Monterey, Big Sur and Catalina). Open System Preferences, click on Software Update, check the box beside Automatically keep my Mac up to date (or Download new updates when available). Then select the box Install macOS updates. It is prudent to keep things as up to date as possible, if for no other reason than safety and security. This castle seems to be a virtual undiscovered treasure to most of those living in the Bay Area. It is just off the coast of Highway 1. The Mccloskey family, who was so traumatized by the horrific earthquake and fire in 1906, they moved from San Francisco to Pacifica to build their “safe” house. They built a concrete fortress that would be impenetrable Sam’s Castle is a colossal 22-room medieval-style masterpiece. Since the early 20th century it has served as an architectural oddity and a place used as a gambler’s “party house” during Prohibition, and a recuperative building for “ladies who elected not to become mothers”. Its colorful history involves rum-runners, ghosts and more. The castle even hosted events for the Red Cross and eventually leased it to the Two docents, who portrayed Mr. and Mrs. McCloskey in costume, gave the Piedmont Seniors a private tour of the amazing castle. They were told that there were very few closets in the castle, as closets were taxed as if they were full rooms. The last owner, Sam Mazza, was an eccentric gentleman who purchased the castle in 1929 for $29,000, as a place to store the thousands of antiques he had collected over the years. Some of his artifacts, like a Clark Gable ceremonial robe, were items he purchased from the movie studios at auction. During the tour, the Seniors had the opportunity to marvel at the sheer quantity of ornate pieces from the Mazza collection, including swords, coats of arms, Oriental collectibles, a plethora of brass hangings, statues, and paintings. After the tour, the group was treated to a special spread of teas, coffees, and a smorgasbord of cheeses, crackers and delicious cookies served by the attentive staff on the lanai overlooking the Pacific Ocean. Today the Mazza Castle serves as headquarters for the Sam Mazza Foundation, a 501(c)3 charitable organization that supports the arts and arts education. This 22-room medieval castle is a hidden gem not to be missed. On to Taco Bell After the castle tour the Seniors’ next stop was to the “infamous” Taco Bell in Pacifica. This is not your usual fast-food joint. It is located directly above the Pacific Ocean with a spectacular view and many surfers. It also serves alcohol, which makes it unique. The group returned home via scenic Highway 1 overlooking the Coast and through Half Moon Bay. It was a glorious day many will long remember. articles.text: Dear Jim: We are about to start a remodel and are debating about whether to hire a designer and then a contractor, or whether we should do design-build with a single firm. Your thoughts? –Austin H. Know yourself A decision about how you want the design aspects of your project to occur should be made and stuck to. Will you be hands-on, making the bulk of the selections and design decisions? Or will you want the contractor or designer to make choices and provide you with selections to choose from? This may seem simple, but in our experience the matter of how you want to work is decided early on to avoid mistakes. Know your designer Finding and sourcing compatible fixtures, cabinets, tile, flooring, paint colors, etc. are all skills that most designers possess. However, some lack the construction knowledge needed to integrate their choices into architectural drawings and construction work. In a recent project, our client’s designer didn’t read our architect’s drawing properly and ordered a vanity that was too wide, had to be returned, and reordered, causing project delays Recessing appliances and closets into the crawlspace of this basement second unit created much needed working space. and high return shipping and restocking fees. Get to know your project First, decide on your level of involvement. Often clients tell us they are hands-off, then change their minds and want to be more involved later in the game. Understand that any changes in the design-build process, including increasing your involvement can significantly affect timelines, budget and choices. Next, make sure your contractor or design-builder has clear expectations on the decision-making process for items being selected and ordered, and the time frames for delivery and budget. Keep in mind that the current supply chains are erratic. Having to return and reorder supplies may sideline a project. Finally, in addition to your designer and contractor being a good fit for you, be sure your selections properly fit the space and are reviewed by the contractor, designer and you before being ordered. Measure twice and cut once applies to the design process, too. Conversations with Your Local Contractor is a feature by Jim Gardner of Jim Gardner Construction Inc., who is a long-time Piedmont resident and has been doing structural repair and basement renovation in your neighborhood since 1983. The letter also stated that, for the duration of the renovation project, updates on construction activity and parking restrictions would be provided on the district website monthly, “no later than the 24th of each month for the following month.” Accordingly, community members should expect details on July parking restrictions by June 24. This information, which restricts parking from the first day of the project, seems to contradict what residents were told in a community meeting held by the district on May 22. At that time Palmer said there would be eight days of truck activity (and parking restrictions) in June for removal of the turf; few in July for the installation of drainage systems; nine days in August for the installation of drain rock; and 10 days in September. At that meeting, Palm Drive residents were also told that they would be surveyed as to their preferred morning start time for the project, As of June 20 they have not been asked for their preferences. The school district has not scheduled any future community meetings. Project background The Witter Field renovation project was approved by the Piedmont School Board on January 25, 2023. The current turf is well beyond its eight-year life span. In 2007, when it was installed, the new turf cost $219,000; installation took two weeks. Similar to the many years when the field was grass, the field has flooded and been unplayable for periods of time each winter due to rain and insufficient drainage. A $4,156,933 contract for the renovation was awarded to Robert Bothman Construction. Speaking on the project’s total cost, Palmer has said that “All in all, we’re expecting it to be right around $5 million.” Bothman was also the low bidder in 2019 with a bid of $3.5 million, but under former School Superintendent Randy Booker, the project stalled and work was never begun. PUSD plans to use State Modernization Funds to pay for the project. This funding is tied to the H1 bond, which paid for the new Alan Harvey Theater and the STEAM building. The district’s General Fund will not be used for the project. Current information about the Witter Field project is available on the district website at bit.ly/ WitterField. She scored the game-winning goal in Piedmont’s sudden-death 2-1 win over No. 1 seed University— where PHS was the No. 3 seed. With the lacrosse team, Marshburn was a midfielder and was often tasked to move the ball up field using her speed and elusiveness. She was among Piedmont’s leaders in ground ball recoveries. articles.text: Nothing signals the start of summer in Piedmont quite like the sight of Cub Scouts taking over Dracena Park. The annual, week-long Cub Scout Day Camp kicked off on Monday, June 12, and will run through late Friday afternoon when the celebrated Egg Drop signals the conclusion of summer camp at Dracena Park. articles.text: Hillsides to be cleared by goats starting next week Piedmont has retained the services of approximately 200 goats for its annual summer cleanup of the hillsides surrounding the Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue. The goats, which reduce fire hazards by eating dry vegetation on city property, are a popular sight each year at the beginning of summer. Fire Chief Dave Brannigan said that although the date of their arrival has not been set, the goats ­ – coming from Ecosystem Concepts Inc. – are expected to arrive in Piedmont sometime next week after they complete their current shrub-eating job at Oak Knoll, near the Oakland Zoo. The four-legged grazers will begin their work on the large slope behind the Corporation Yard, and will later be moved across Moraga Avenue to Blair Park. Their vegetation-eating is crucial in light of the impending fire season, as it is a natural way to prevent ladder fuel from forming. Brannigan has said that a good rule of thumb to prevent ladder fuel — a firefighting term for vegetation which carries a fire from the landscape upward to tree or shrub canopies — is to leave three times the amount of space above. articles.text: Editor: I play pickleball regularly at Linda Beach and enjoy the friendly community vibe. This type of feel and activity helps hold communities together. Recently I have noticed more families and kids playing. It is not just a game for seniors. We play with reduced noise balls and make every effort to be respectful of the neighbors’ issues. The main noise I hear is the joyful noise of kids playing at the soccer field and school adjacent to the courts. I believe pickleball is the highest and best use of this space and hope the Piedmont Recreation Commissioners vote to make it permanent at Linda Beach. –Dan Gayton REVIEWERS

articles.text: Editor: As this school year ends, we are feeling hopeful again for the future of PUSD in ways we couldn’t have imagined a few years ago. A big part of that hopefulness is due to the leadership of our interim superintendent, Donald Evans, over the last year. From the start, Dr. Evans approached his new job with curiosity and openness – rather than the defensiveness and lack of transparency we had grown used to. He showed an eagerness to engage with and listen to *all* stakeholders in the district, rather than sowing division, which only undermines kids’ educations. He brought a positive energy and lightness to School Board meetings that had been missing. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department has announced the beginning of its “Cop on the Block” program, a yearlong series of community outreach events. It is “designed to bring officers out of cars and into neighborhoods,” according to the department. Neighbors are invited to bring their questions, comments and concerns to officers as they patrol the city’s blocks on foot at selected locations and times. It will be the city’s first scheduled walking patrol. “We rolled out Cop on the Block as a way to encourage more non-enforcement contact with the community. It’s very casual. We plan it each week; a randomly selected member of the department will walk up and down the block for a minimum of half an hour and for as long as people want to chat – about baseball, tree-trimming, parking, crime, anything,” said Police Captain Chris Monahan. “We plan to keep going with the program until we cover the whole city; if it goes well, we’ll speed it up a bit,” he added. “I’m about 25 percent through amassing my list of every block in Piedmont, and I’m at 300 blocks already. articles.text: The most popular entry in Piedmont’s 4th of July parade year after year is the lovable Balloon Platoon from Pleasanton. 50 years ago, KNBR disc jockeys Mike Cleary of Piedmont and Frank Dill challenged their Bay Area listeners to put on a parade, and Pleasanton was selected. It became the KNBR Good Times Parade, and anyone with a little red wagon could A Mariners group at the Pleasanton Presbyterian Church entered with a Viking ship the first year, then came up with the idea of the tubby sailors carrying The group quickly became a comic marching group. Though many of the men were veterans of various branches of the military, there was a belief that slavish obedience to commands was counterproductive, so the Balloon Platoon was born. Invitations soon came to participate in other communities’ parades. In 20 years, the group has trooped in several bowl games, appeared at the Indianapolis 500, marched in the Christmas parade in London. Though not bearing bagpipes, the Platoon went to Edinburgh in 2000 to participate in the Millennium Pipe Festival. One spring the Balloon Platoon appeared in the National Cherry Blossom Festival parade in Washington, D.C. The group meets rarely, only to decide which parade invites to accept. “We usually reject offers that are strict forward motion parades,” explained leader Hal Strunk. “The Marine Corps band does that really well – we do not.” The age of Platoon members ranges from 21 to 80, and all are associated with the church in Pleasanton. As the Balloon Platoon passes by on Highland Avenue on July 4th, look for its special routines: Shake-n-Bake, pirouettes, carousels, big pinwheels, the Manual of Mops – and even a 21-Mop Salute. articles.text: For the 20th year, the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band will take a lead position in Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade, with its parasol-toting, shuffle-stepping Grand Marshal leading the way. Zenith, a Berkeley-based group, lays claim to being the most authentic brass band playing the music of old New Orleans from the formative years of 100 years ago to the present. Parade bands in New Orleans are still part of the musical tradition in the Crescent City, playing for funerals, parades, picnics and dances. All members of the Zenith band have been playing in similar jazz bands in the Bay Area for many years. Its Grand Marshal leads the way, proudly holding a fringed parasol, wearing a colorful sash, and doing a shuffle step down the length of Highland Avenue. People dancing behind the band, sometimes swirling parasols, are known as the second line. Everyone is invited to join the second line. The Zenith New Orleans Parade Band has been a major attraction for many years at Photo by Raymond Holbert Alan Carr has assumed the role of Grand Marshal of the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band for his late father, Hollis Carr. the New Orleans By the Bay production at Shoreline Amphitheater. It has been part of the Traditional Jazz portion of the Concord Jazz Festival for 17 years, and for the past seven years it has appeared at the Bodega Bay Fisherman’s Festival. The band plays each year at the Sacramento Jazz Jubilee in Old Town during June.
articles.title: The return of Piedmont’s New Orleans tradition

articles.text: Come join the Piedmont Community Band, the city’s only musical organization that has only one rehearsal during the year. The band is a past winner of the Highland Cup, the highest award given at the July 4th Parade. The band is comprised of amateur and professional musicians – all volunteers – most who live in town and can’t resist the challenge of playing music while marching in formation. Dressed in blue pants, white shirts and a red kerchief, they are led by Ken Kawaichi, who, dressed as Emperor Norton, has the distinction of walking the length of the parade route backwards. It’s time to get out your instruments – trumpets, trombones, tubas, clarinets and drums – and help celebrate Independence Day in Piedmont. If you are new in town, it’s an ideal way to meet people, To sign up, contact Greg Slatoff at goslatoff@ yahoo.com, or call Jane Reed at 654-2670.

articles.text: On the last moment of the 2023 school year, Friday, June 2, at 11:59 a.m. and 50 seconds, Principal Carol Cramer started a 10 second countdown with Wildwood School 5th graders. The annual countdown for elementary school students, known as “the ruckus,” took on an additional meaning this year as it signaled the final seconds of Cramer’s career. At zero, students shouted and banged hand-held noise makers, while the flash of parents’ cameras captured the moment. Cramer’s career, which started in the classroom in 1984, culminated as the clock struck noon. Her 35 years in Piedmont School district began at Beach School in 1988, one block from her home, as a 2nd grade teacher. It ended on the lunch patio in the front of Wildwood School where 5th graders were cheerfully celebrating their advancement to middle school. Carol quietly picked up a bell given to her in her first year as Principal in 2000. The bell, now 5th grade teacher Lydia Tang (left), Principal Carol Cramer, Counselor Colleen Stormer, and 5th grade teacher Hannah Swernoff Carol Cramer counts down the final seconds of her career with Wildwood 5th graders on June 2, 2023. Principal Carol Cramer with Wildwood 5th graders on the last day of school, June 2 broken, sat on her desk for 23 years. For Cramer, the silence of the bell was welcome, as will be the absence of the bells designating lunch, recess and dismissal every day on the Wildwood campus. Cramer retires to a quieter life in her Piedmont home, with husband Jim and son Jack who will be entering his senior year at the high school.
articles.title: Wildwood Principal Carol Cramer’s last day of school

articles.text: Common Sense, a national nonprofit organization dedicated to helping kids and families thrive in a world of media and technology, has recognized Piedmont Middle School (PMS) as a Common Sense School. The recognition acknowledges the school’s commitment to creating a culture of “digital citizenship.” Common Sense began making entertainment and technology recommendations for families and schools in 2003. Being named a common sense school acknowledges the schools commitment to taking a whole-community approach to preparing its students to think critically and use technology responsibly to learn, create, and participate while preparing them for the perils that exist in the online realm, such as plagiarism, loss of privacy, and cyberbullying. “We’re honored to be recognized as a Common Sense School,” said Principal Karyn Shipp. “By preparing our students to use technology safely and responsibly, we are providing them an opportunity to build lifelong habits to help them succeed in a tech-driven world,” she added. “Piedmont Middle School deserves high praise for giving its students the foundational skills they need to compete and succeed in the 21st-century workplace and participate ethically in society at large,” said Kelly Mendoza, vice president of education programs at Common Sense Education. To learn more about the criteria Piedmont Middle School met to become recognized as a Common Sense School and the organization’s efforts, visit Commonsense.org/education/recognition-schools.
articles.title: Piedmont Middle School recognized as “Common Sense School”

The recognition acknowledges the school’s commitment to creating a culture of “digital citizenship.” Common Sense began making entertainment and technology recommendations for families and schools in 2003. Being named a common sense school acknowledges the schools commitment to taking a whole-community approach to preparing its students to think critically and use technology responsibly to learn, create, and participate while preparing them for the perils that exist in the online realm, such as plagiarism, loss of privacy, and cyberbullying. “We’re honored to be recognized as a Common Sense School,” said Principal Karyn Shipp. “By preparing our students to use technology safely and responsibly, we are providing them an opportunity to build lifelong habits to help them succeed in a tech-driven world,” she added. “Piedmont Middle School deserves high praise for giving its students the foundational skills they need to compete and succeed in the 21st-century workplace and participate ethically in society at large,” said Kelly Mendoza, vice president of education programs at Common Sense Education. articles.text: I think it’s time we face the truth. Curiosity did not, in fact, kill the cat. Actually, studies will say that staying curious for as long as possible can actually have positive effects on your long-term health and well-being. If you want to cultivate a creative mind, your first job is to cultivate a curious mind. A curious mind is looking at the world through a lens of “not knowing.” There is always the opportunity to have a beginner’s mindset with something new to learn around every corner. And that experience of discovery and seeing possibilities is an opportunity for creativity. A creative act brings something new into the world, but if you aren’t curious, you will never ask yourself, “What wants to be discovered here?” Even if you have done the same task over and over again, what is different about this particular moment in time? The Broadway actor does the same show over and over again, eight times per week, sometimes for years, but the performance has to feel new and fresh for every audience or the magic just won’t be there. How do those actors keep it fresh? They cultivate presence, moment to moment, noticing what How can we cultivate creativity in our daily routines? is unique and special about this particular show. They listen with intensity to their fellow actors, hearing the words from their mouths as if it is the first time they have ever heard them. They find ways to make things novel and fun. And, above all, they are curious, ready to see what the moment will deliver and open to receiving it. In essence, they continue to find opportunities for creativity, even within repetition. In our daily lives, we have so many tasks we perform by rote. What if we chose to bring our curious mind to cultivate the creative experience in the most mundane of tasks. What if today, we get curious about washing dishes? • • What sounds do I hear? What does the water feel like on my hands? • Does the viscosity of the soap remind me of anything? • How could I do this faster? What happens if I go slower? All of a sudden, something totally boring might become more interesting. And, you never know, maybe you will invent something that will revolutionize dish washing and we will never have to do it again. More time to spend with the cat! pages.text: Wednesday, June 14, 2023 9 Summer Thoughts Curiosity: the most powerful tool for a creative mind By Nina Meehan I think it’s time we face the truth. Curiosity did not, in fact, kill the cat. Actually, studies will say that staying curious for as long as possible can actually have positive effects on your long-term health and well-being. If you want to cultivate a creative mind, your first job is to cultivate a curious mind. A curious mind is looking at the world through a lens of “not knowing.” There is always the opportunity to have a beginner’s mindset with something new to learn around every corner. And that experience of discovery and seeing possibilities is an opportunity for creativity. A creative act brings something new into the world, but if you aren’t curious, you will never ask yourself, “What wants to be discovered here?” Even if you have done the same task over and over again, what is different about this particular moment in time? The Broadway actor does the same show over and over again, eight times per week, sometimes for years, but the performance has to feel new and fresh for every audience or the magic just won’t be there. How do those actors keep it fresh? They cultivate presence, moment to moment, noticing what How can we cultivate creativity in our daily routines? is unique and special about this particular show. They listen with intensity to their fellow actors, hearing the words from their mouths as if it is the first time they have ever heard them. They find ways to make things novel and fun. And, above all, they are curious, ready to see what the moment will deliver and open to receiving it. In essence, they continue to find opportunities for creativity, even within repetition. In our daily lives, we have so many tasks we perform by rote. What if we chose to bring our curious mind to cultivate the creative experience in the most mundane of tasks. What if today, we get curious about washing dishes? • • What sounds do I hear? What does the water feel like on my hands? • Does the viscosity of the soap remind me of anything? • How could I do this faster? What happens if I go slower? All of a sudden, something totally boring might become more interesting. And, you never know, maybe you will invent something that will revolutionize dish washing and we will never have to do it again. More time to spend with the cat! articles.text: Piedmont resident Guy Avagliano did what many have dreamed of doing. In the span of 59 days, he took an all-American trip this spring, visiting all 30 Major League baseball stadiums. Avagliano took the long way. Leaving Oakland on April 2, he arrived in San Francisco at Oracle Park 16,000 miles later on May 30. After retiring as an actuary at the start of the year, Avagliano realized he might have time to tackle the two-month trip. “I’ve always been a baseball fan, but the appeal to me was to do this in one long road trip,” said Avagliano. “It kind of started out as a fun math puzzle from a logistical standpoint, to be able to get to all those stadiums on days when there were games.” Guy Avagliano (left) at Chase Field in Phoenix, Arizona on April 9 with childhood friend Greg McIntyre. Along the way Avagliano visited seven new state, incresing his tally to a complete 50 by taking detours to reach Arkansas and Maine. He also visited six baseball museums and 15 minor league baseball stadiums. Avagliano said the mystique and antiquity of Wrigley Field made it his favorite stadium. The St. Louis Cardinals had the best crowd, while Atlanta had the nicest new stadium. A beignet in New Orleans was the best food he ate, and the Tampa Bay Rays are his pick to win the World Series later this fall. The adventures before each first pitch and after the ninth inning gave the trip true meaning. After a Facebook post announcing his intention to take the trip, he got a call from a longlost childhood friend, Greg McIntyre, inviting him to stay in Arizona when he visited the stadium in Phoenix. Guy’s wife, Alison, confirmed the pair had not seen each other in 50 years. “Yeah, well he was pretty cool when he was 10,” noted Guy. Avagliano took the family SUV, a 2013 Infiniti with 180,000 miles on it. He had three unexpected auto repairs, including one near the Arizona–New Mexico border, but none of them caused a change of plans. Avagliano, who has lived in Piedmont since 2000, is originally from Maplewood, NJ so he scheduled some extra days on the East Coast part of the trip. In addition to seeing his only living aunt and uncle in New Jersey, he also saw 13 first cousin and five second cousins. “I saw my grandparents’ houses, my kindergarten, my first little league field, my first church. That was that just the best day, and there wasn’t even any baseball that day,” he said. Guy credits Alison, who joined him for part of the trip, for her support in making it a successful journey. “Alison was a real trooper throughout this. We even spent our 25th anniversary on the road, We had brunch in her hometown, Asheville, NC, then spent 500 miles driving to my cousin’s house to stay with people she’s never met,” he said. Sometimes the best parts of a journey happen when you least expect it. After leaving a minor league game in the ninth inning, a foul ball left the stadium and bounced a few feet away for him to pick up. Foul balls, road trips and life, are sometimes all about being in the right place at the right time. Upon returning home on May 30 from his epic tour of Major League ballparks, the big screen in Oracle Park in San Francisco honors the completion of Guy Avagliano’s journey. Guy Avagliano kicks of his cross-country tour of visiting 30 major League ballparks in 59 days. He is pictured at the first game in Oakland on April 2, with Piedmonter Frank Helm. Guy with daughter Paige Avagliano in Pittsburgh’s PNC Park on May 6. Guy Avagliano’s stamp collection from every Major League ballpark. Guy Avagliano visited Wrigley Field to see the Cubs play the St. Louis Cardinals on May 9. He doubled back to Chicago to see the White Sox five days later. Wife Alison (left), daughter Laine and Guy Avagliano in Kauffman Stadium, home of the Kansas City Royals, on May 22.

articles.text: Sports, games & crafts offered to pre-teens and young teens Summer is officially underway in Piedmont when the popular Scherman Summer Camp fires up some fun for kids in grades 5-10. The camp began this week on Monday, June 12, run by Julian and Quincy Scherman at the Havens School blacktop. Julian Scherman, PHS class of 2021, and brother Quincy, an incoming senior, are the sons of Piedmont Middle School teacher Ted Scherman. They are returning for their third year of running the day camp. In less than an hour on Monday, campers cycled through many schoolyard games, including ball tag, wall ball, basketball, knockout, four square, handball and card games before going to lunch at Mulberry’s Market. “I’m having fun, camp sure is a lot better than staying at home where I might just be on the computer,” said Emilio Roberts, an incoming 7th grader. articles.text: Photo by Todd Marshburn Piedmont’s boys’ and girls’ soccer teams celebrate winning the North Coast Section championship at the same time – at Beach Chalet Soccer Field in San Francisco on February 25. The 2022-23 school year has officially concluded at Piedmont High with teams turning the page on another sports calendar. In this article, the Post reflects on our favorite five moments from the past year. 1. February 25 an historic day Saturday, February 25 marked an historic day for Piedmont High. The boys’ soccer team, girls’ soccer team, and girls’ basketball team won the North Coast Section championship – and all on the same day. All four of Piedmont’s winter sports teams reached the NCS semifinals – a feat rarely accomplished. The boys’ soccer team, the No. 8 seed, started the legendary day with a 1-0 upset victory over No. 2 University, winning backto-back Div. 4 NCS championships. William Daniel scored the game-winner with 10 minutes left in regulation. The Highlanders did not allow any goals in the postseason, winning 2-0 over No. 9 St. Helena in the first round, devastating No. 1 Cardinal Newman 1-0 in the quarterfinals, beat No. 5 Healdsburg 1-0 in the semifinals, and then upending the University Red Devils at Beach Chalet Field in Golden Gate Park. The girls’ soccer team, seeded No. 3, then took home the NCS banner with a 2-1 upset victory in overtime against No. 1 University, also at Beach Chalet Field. In the 86th minute of sudden-death overtime, Hailey Marshburn scored the game-winner after making a long run from her defensive left back spot. It was her only goal of the season. It was the first championship in coach Dan Chubbock’s 20 years with Piedmont, and his third finals appearance. articles.text: Golden State Rowing Club sent three athletes to the US Rowing Youth National Championships in Sarasota, Florid, an event that lasted from Thursday through Sunday, June 8-11. Piedmont High junior Daniel Grasman, Orinda Academy senior and Piedmont resident Aaron Feldhammer, and PHS senior Chris Fung all qualified for the event. All three progressed to the semifinals on Friday, June 9, placing them among the top 16 rowers in the country in their respective categories. Grasman raced the U17 single scull, winning the B Final on Saturday, and finishing the year as the country’s No. 9 overall rower in his event. He clocked a time of 7:45.148, beating second-place Oscar Spencer of Cambridge by two seconds. The US Rowing broadcast commentators were impressed with Daniel’s performance. “What a mature race there by Daniel Grasman of Golden State to make sure that the pressure that was applied by four boats were attempting to cut down that lead, and he was able to make a Daniel Grasman won the U-17 single scull B Final with a time of 7:45.148. Chris Fung (left) and Aaron Feldhammer placed fifth in the youth double scull B Final in 6:54.435. Golden State Rowing Club sent three Piedmont rowers to the Youth National Championship in Sarasota, Florida. Pictured are coach James Kwan (left), Daniel Grasman, Aaron Feldhammer, and Chris Fung. difference right there with that last 500,” said lead announcer and Olympic gold medalist Lindsay Shoop. The second commentator, Grace Latz, agreed: “Calm and composed; he trusted his training and the work that he put in, and that paid off.” To get there, Grasman was 12th of 29 in the opening time trial. The following day, he placed fifth of eight rowers in the semifinals. In the Youth Men’s double scull Feldhammer and Fung were fifth of eight entries with a time of 6:54.435 in the B Final on June 11, placing them as the No. 13 boat in the country. To get there, the duo was ninth of 30 in Thursday’s time trial with a time of 6:31.496. The next day, the two were sixth of eight in the semifinals in 7:06.264. Golden State Rowing Club was created by Piedmont High alum James Kwan (PHS 2009) in 2022. Since then, the program has quickly grown. articles.text: Piedmont hosts 7th and 8th Grade Championship meet on May 25 Piedmont Middle School’s track and field team participated in five meets through the spring season, including the 6th grade championship at Albany Middle School on May 23, and the 7th and 8th grade Championship hosted at Witter Field on May 25. The girls’ teams won both the varsity and JV events at the 7th and 8th grade level, and the boys’ 8th grade team won the varsity and JV levels. In the 6th Grade Championship, the JV boys brought back the first place trophy to the school, and the varsity Boys took second place. The JV Girls finished third and the Varsity Girls were second-place. “The Piedmont team once again showed what happens when each and every single athlete works together not as individuals but as one team,” said veteran PMS coach Minori Tsuge, “Each and every one of our athletes contributed to this year’s success. It it isn’t just about winning but repEric Anderssel Venner helped the 8th grade 4x400 relay team win. He also was undefeated in the individual 100 and 200 meter events. Piedmont Middle School’s track team wrapped up a successful season at the 7th and 8th grade Championship on May 25. resenting [the school] with pride. I could not be more proud of our young athletes who really peaked at the perfect moment.” “It is so important to show that no matter what your ability is, you can thrive in sports and represent your team and school,” added coach Christine Chapon. 7th/8th Grade Championships Dresden Schulte- Sasse was second in the 7th grade varsity championship in 5:26.13, which also was a new school record. 8th grade varsity athlete Eric Anderssell Venner won both the 100 and 200 meter races and set a school record in the 100 with a time of 12.21 seconds. Sebastien Swain won the 800 in 2:17.56 and placed second in the 1600 in 5:05.71. Thomas Ero came in second in the 800 in 2:21.06 and third in the 1600 in 5:22.31, Colin Amen was fourth in 5:35.01. Aiden Morgan was 2nd in the 400 meters in 59:37. The 4x100 and 4x400 relay teams of Sebastian Swain, Aiden Claire Aubrecht went undefeated in the 100 meter dash this season. Seventh grader Dresden SchulteSasse placed second in the 1600 meters in 5:26.13, and set a school record. Morgan, Thomas Ero, and Eric Andersell Venner won both events with school records of 50.70 and 4:07.13. Girls Results For the varsity girls team, 7th grade Lucy Dorsey was second in High jump with a height of 4 feet, 8 inches, tying a school record . 7th grade Viviane Oesterer was second in the 800 (2:46.69), 1600 (5:58.21) and Long Jump in 11 feet, 1 inch. The 4x400 relay team of Dorsey, Oesterer, Mia Bechtel and Olivia Bailey won their event. 8th grader Claire Aubrecht won the 100 to finish an undefeated season; she was second in the 200. 8th grader Elsa Wallway won the 1600 in 5:43.93 and won the shot put with a throw of 23 feet, 10 inches. She was 2nd in the 800 with a time of 2:30.30.

articles.text: Finnish operatic composer Kaija Saariaho The San Francisco Symphony made its once-a-year venture into theater with the semi-staged opera Adriana Mater (2006) by Kaija Saariaho, displaying a brilliant cast with dramatic singing and evocative acting on the confined makeshift stages. The performance of the rabidly antiwar tragedy Adriana Mater about the heroine’s travails in a brutal conflict could hardly have been timelier, echoing the on-going Ukraine campaign’s bloodshed. It also serves as a heartfelt memorial to composer Saariaho, who had passed away at age 70 one week earlier. She had ranked among the world’s foremost active creators of music for the voice. Musical complexity and sophistication like Saariaho’s is no guarantee of successful opera, as we learned with the 20th century Polish School. The ensemble is a multi-dimensional undercurrent beneath the voices, more severe than attractive, coming strong to the fore only in a couple of instrumental interludes. Wading through this drama was a difficult ordeal for an audience that concluded with respectful but restrained applause at the end. This is an opus that warrants a stage-play adaptation, taking advantage of the Lebanese Amin Maalouf’s trenchant libretto, whose French was rarely discernible given the hyper-dramatic voices and orchestra. Fortunately, English translations were projected throughout. Maalouf’s tragedy recalled antiwar dramas of Brecht, Remorque, Borchert and Hasek. The S.F. Symphony’s semistaged performance was especially challenging for fellow Finn Esa-Pekka Salonen, conducting while extensively cueing the forces in every direction about ing the nature and name of the rapist-father. Most of act two consists of Yonas threatening to kill his dad Tsargo (bass-baritone Christopher Purves), by then a pathetic derelict shadow of his old warrior self. Soprano Axelle Fanyo played Adriana’s sister Refka, the contrasting figure of peaceful moderation. The opening night’s success was shared also by the mercurial stage director (and frequent John Adams collaborator) Peter Sellars, guiding the singers while separated on four 15-foot-square platforms wiping out part of the front row. The singers were much challenged by carrying small tablets of the tricky score throughout. The wonder was that the drama still shone through. articles.text: Hurricane Diane, presented by Berkeley’s Aurora Theatre, will premiere this Friday, June 16. Written by Madeleine George, the play follows protagonist Carol, a seemingly ordinary if not materialistic woman. who resides on a cul-de-sac in New Jersey. One day, she is visited by the Greek god Dionysus, under the guise of a lesbian gardener named Diane. Diane is determined to reverse climate change and restore earthly order by seducing a band of mortal followers. She sets out to woo Carol from her picture-perfect suburban life. George, a Pulitzer Prize finalist, calls it a “hilarious evisceration of the blind eye we all turn to climate change and the bacchanalian catharsis that awaits us, even in our own backyards.” Hurricane Diane is directed by Jennifer King. Post show discussions will be held on June 23, June 27, July 5 and July 13. Purchase tickets at www. auroratheatre.org, at by calling the box office at (510) 843 - 4822.
articles.title: Hurricane Diane premieres this Friday at Aurora Theatre

articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre’s (ACT) production of the beloved classic Wizard of Oz is playing onstage in San Francisco now through June 25. The classic tale by L. Frank Baum is transformed for the ACT stage by Tony Award–nominated director and choreographer Sam Pinkleton and Tony Award-winning designer David Zinn. “The myth of Dorothy and her friends, and their big adventure, means something different to every single person you ask – whether it’s childhood nostalgia, queer survival, or an unhealthy obsession with flying monkeys,” said Pinkleton. “I’m giddy and honored to enlist the brains, heart, and courage of the Bay Area, in collaboration with mega-genius David Zinn, to create an intimate, intergenerational, human-powered Wizard of Oz that is bursting with contradictions and big beating hearts – just like San Francisco itself.” The play is a family-friendly and appropriate for young audiences. The cast includes El Beh, Keiko Shimosato, Darryl Jones, Katrina McGraw, Kunal Prasad, Ezra Reaves, Cathleen Riddley and Travis Rowland. For more infor mation, and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/202223-season/wizard-of-oz/. ACT is currently performing The Wizard of Oz, based on the book by L. Frank Baum.
articles.title: Wizard of Oz at ACT through June 25

articles.text: Soprano Julia Bullock joins San Francisco Symphony Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen and the symphony orchestra for a program inspired by the music of George Gershwin and Margaret Bonds. Bullock is an American classical singer, originally from St. Louis, who has regularly shared the stage with Salonen. The performance will include the San Francisco Symphony premieres of Reena Esmail’s Black Iris, George Gershwin’s “Somebody from Somewhere” and “Soon,” and Margaret Bonds’ “Winter Moon” and “The Negro Speaks of Rivers.” Also on the program is Gershwin’s “Summertime” and Maurice Ravel’s Daphnis et Chloe. Performances are June 29 through July 1. Tickets are available at https://www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2022-23/ Esa-Pekka-Salonen-Julia-Bullock, or by calling the box office at (415) 864-6000. articles.text: Among the cornucopia of flowers which the de Young Museum’s annual Bouquets de Art brought to San Francisco last week, the floral design by Valerie Lee’s team bloomed for the gazing crowds. The annual event ended on Sunday, June 11, marking its 39th year of being the most widely-attended event at the museum. Veteran designers exhibiting at the show are allowed to choose their favorite art pieces in the museum’s collection and then are given their muse, based on a lottery, to emulate with a flower design. Now in her 24th consecutive year as an exhibitor, Lee chose Alexander Pope’s “The Wild Swan” painting from 1900 for its “stark drama and contrast of dark and light,” as well as for the painting’s vivid gold frame. “I love the idea of inviting the community at large to view and enjoy flowers, creativity and art at the de Young Museum,” said Lee. “There is such a local following with this show, which makes it very exciting and engaging for me. Many of our J. Miller customers, friends from Piedmont, and Piedmont Garden Club friends look forward to this annual show.” Over 100 floral designers hailing from throughout the Bay Area participated in Bouquets to Art this year. “I especially love how all ages and generations can enjoy The floral display by J. Miller Flowers at the annual Bouquets to Art exhibit at the deYoung Museum in San Francisco is a tribute to Alexander Pope’s 1900 painting, “The Wild Swan”. the f lower-filled galleries,” Lee added. “My children have attended the show for 24 years, and now they bring their friends, attend the gala, and even assist with my exhibit.” For her display, she chose to use phalaenopsis orchids, peonies, calla lilies, parrot tulips, lilacs, smokebush and succulents – a unique yet faithful textural interpretation of the stark whites and subtly shaded greens and yellows in Pope’s painting. Pictures of Lee’s exhibit will join the series of 31 greeting cards from earlier Bouquets to Arts that she unveiled last month, available at J. Miller flowers. “So many of our customers and Garden Club friends attend Bouquets to Art every year. They love these images and cards,” Lee said. “The sense of community this show builds has been remarkable. Bouquets to Art is a magnet bringing together nature, art, flowers and friends.”
articles.title: J. Miller Flowers honors art of Alexander Pope at Bouquets to Art

articles.text: Annual event featuring local artists is June 17 to August 13 The 19th annual Sculpture in the Garden show opens at Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery on Saturday, June 17, with a special opening night event from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. Sculpture in the Garden, held this year from June 17 to August 13, is an annual art show and sale that combines sculptural art with the natural beauty of the Garden. All sculptures in the Garden are for sale. Admission to the event is free with regular garden admission. Opening night gives visitors a first-look at the pieces for sale and on display during the year’s exhibit. Food will be provided, and each ticket includes a complimentary beverage. Sculpture “sip a strolls” will be held July 7 and August 4, where attendees may stroll through the Garden after hours with wine or cocktail in hand. To learn more, and to see this year’s featured artists, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org/sculpture-in-the-garden/. Briggita in the Garden square is among a dozen local artists. ®

articles.text: Visit the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art to view its newest exhibition, Frank Bowling: The New York Years 1966–1975, the first major exhibit of the artist’s work in North America in 40 years. Sir Richard Sheridan Patrick Michael Aloysius Franklin Bowling, known as Frank Bowling, was born in British Guiana, now Guyana, and moved from London to New York. He is best known for his large-scale, abstract and colorful paintings, color field painting and lyrical abstraction; sometimes referred to as ‘abstract expressionism.’ SF MOMA’s exhibition features 45 vibrant and largescale paintings, and a selection of archival materials such as recorded interviews of the artist in New York and London, film footage and photographs from Bowling’s 1968 visit to Guyana. “We are looking forward to engaging our communities with the exceptional work of Frank Bowling and to offering an in-depth exploration of the enduring influence of his time in New York, both on his own work and on the development of art more broadly,” said Christopher Bedford, the Helen and Charles Schwab Director at SFMOMA. “In particular, the presentation of the 5+1 exhibition provides an opportunity to experience Bowling as a scholar and teacher committed to elevating the voices of Black artists and expanding the understanding of art history as it unfolded. This very much aligns with our institutional vision to share significant, if perhaps lesser-known, facets of artists’ careers and to explore artistic achievement through a spectrum of lenses and perspectives.” The New York Years opened May 20, and will be on display through September 10. The exhibition is co-organized with the Museum of Fine Arts Boston. For more information, and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit www.sfmoma.org. Frank Bowling, Elder Sun Benjamin, 2018
articles.title: Frank Bowling exhibit at SF MOMA through September

articles.text: Martin Scorsese, director extraordinaire, once commented that before becoming enamored with filmmaking he considered the priesthood. Filmgoers and critics have noted that the brittle tension between faith and the human condition haunts many of his films. Silence, made in 2016, may be his most overt and obscure film to date, one in which he examines the extraordinary lengths men and women have been willing to go to sustain their beliefs, even when confronted with what can only be characterized as profound silence. The film is set in Japan. The year is 1640. It was a time when Catholic priests journeyed throughout Europe and Asia, proselytizing their faith, searching with more than a hint of fanaticism for converts. Silence opens with Father Cristovao Ferreira, sinking to his knees, his face a mask of pain and agony, as he watches several crucified priests splashed with boiling water from a hot spring, by Japanese soldiers, to the point of being scalded to death. The film then cuts to two young Jesuit priests seated before their superior, Father Valignano (Claran Hinds), who reads to them a letter from Father Ferreira in which he admits that he has forsaken his religion and now lives as a Japanese resdent. The two Portuguese priests, Father Sebastio Rodriques (Andrew Garfield) and Father Francisco Garupe (Adam Driver), listen in disbelief. They were mentored by Father Ferreira (Liam Neeson) and refuse to believe that he would apostatize. They plead with Father Valignano to permit them to travel to Japan in the hopes of finding their teacher. Liam Neeson stars in Silence Father Valignano understands the danger that Japan represents – it was a country that resisted most harshly the presence of what it considered arrogant European priests who would attempt to convert the people, At first he says no. But hearing the pleas of the two priests he finally relents, reminding them that they will be the last priests ever go to Japan. And so the journey of the two profoundly naïve, yet deeply religious young priests begins. It was a pilgrimage they never could have imagined, filled with unintended consequences. At first protected by a small Christian cult, they hide in caves and a shack, fearful that they will be discovered, always asking if anyone has heard of Father Ferreira. No one has. They also fear being discovered by a man known as The Inquisitor (Issei Ogata) whose mission it is to extirpate this incompatible religion and its adherents from his country. He gives each convert the opportunity to step on what is called the fumi-e, a small plaque bearing a resemblance of Christ or Mary. If they refuse they are tortured: drowned, beheaded or crucified. Father Rodrigues is ultimately captured and forced to bear witness to the horror the Japanese Christians must endure. It is almost more than he can bear and at one point he says, “I pray but I am lost. Am I praying to silence?” This is a dark and painful film to watch. But it is also profound in its construction. Some in the audience may feel it’s a long, difficult slog, for what Father Rodrigues is compelled to watch is oft repeated. He knows he can put a stop to the torment, his own and the Japanese Christians, if he will only yield his faith and become an apostate. What is remarkable throughout the film is the presence of the question that Father Rodrigues asks: “Am I praying to silence?” It is a fundamental interrogatory, embedded in all religion. Are those who prostrate themselves and declare their belief and inviolable devotion truly heard? Or is faith a revetment against a reality that can be overwhelming in its starkness and finality? articles.text: The antecedents of today’s noir films – the name is taken from the French “black film” – originated in the 40s and 50s. Those early films (The Big Sleep, D.O.A.) were moody, stylized, shot in black and white and derivative of the period’s gritty, hardboiled crime novels, also known as pulp fiction. A contemporary example is Drive. At first blush this film may seem like just another car chase film, similar to the Transporter franchise. Drive, however, is far more than gleaming muscle cars racing along the dark streets of L.A. with the cops or bad guys in hot pursuit. Rather, it is in the best tradition of the noir genre and pulp cinema. It is economical in plot and dialogue, with a central character – a man with no name, called simply Driver (Ryan Gosling), He is laconic to a fault, possessing no history other than now. He is a Hollywood stunt driver who moonlights as a getaway driver for robbers, and as a mechanic for an old friend, Shannon (Bryan Cranston), who owns a garage in a frayed part of town. As a character, Driver follows Eastwood and McQueen, two consummate actors who turned detachment and isolation into an art form. And yet, this iconic individual, a Hollywood archetype, often finds himself touched by others. Pulled back to humanity. In the case of Drive it’s Irene (Carey Mulligan) and her young son who live just down the hall. What unravels is an intense narrative, much of it having little to do with driving. Very bad people are involved with Irene’s husband, Standard (Oscar Isaac), who is newly released from prison and owes money to a crew who are determined to collect. They have a job for him that will cancel the debt and protect his family. Gosling gives a nuanced yet powerful performance, conveyed solely through his unflappable presence. He’s a superb actor, with a solid resume, appearing over the last decade in small indie films such as Half-Nelson, Blue Valentine, Lars and the Real Girl and The Notebook, a commercially successful movie based on the Nicholas Sparks’ novel. Albert Brooks and Ron Perlman are perfectly cast as Bernie and Nino, two lethal, ruthless scammers who inhabit a world of greed and violence that knows no fealty or forgiveness. Their portrayals, like Gosling’s, are exceptional, both character actors at the top of their game. Again, this film is not what is often referred to as action-packed. Ultimately, it is not about adrenalin for the sake of adrenalin. It is about something far more subtle. Be warned, however, Drive is also punctuated by bursts of violence that can be unexpected, though never gratuitous. Danish director Nicolas Winding Refn, along with his cinematographer, Newton Thomas Sigel, have managed to create a film far more engaging and complex than expected. If you love movies of this ilk and if you loved the noir films of some 60 years ago, don’t miss Drive. Drive. Starring Ryan Gosling, Carey Mulligan, Bryan Cranston, Ron Perlman and Albert Brooks. Directed by Nicolas Winding Refin. 1 hr., 40 min. Rated R. Released 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/Apple tv/Prime. Ryan Gosling in Drive

pages.text: 18 Wednesday, June 14, 2023 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Silence – Scorcese’s examination of faith By Chris Honoré Martin Scorsese, director extraordinaire, once commented that before becoming enamored with filmmaking he considered the priesthood. Filmgoers and critics have noted that the brittle tension between faith and the human condition haunts many of his films. Silence, made in 2016, may be his most overt and obscure film to date, one in which he examines the extraordinary lengths men and women have been willing to go to sustain their beliefs, even when confronted with what can only be characterized as profound silence. The film is set in Japan. The year is 1640. It was a time when Catholic priests journeyed throughout Europe and Asia, proselytizing their faith, searching with more than a hint of fanaticism for converts. Silence opens with Father Cristovao Ferreira, sinking to his knees, his face a mask of pain and agony, as he watches several crucified priests splashed with boiling water from a hot spring, by Japanese soldiers, to the point of being scalded to death. The film then cuts to two young Jesuit priests seated before their superior, Father Valignano (Claran Hinds), who reads to them a letter from Father Ferreira in which he admits that he has forsaken his religion and now lives as a Japanese resdent. The two Portuguese priests, Father Sebastio Rodriques (Andrew Garfield) and Father Francisco Garupe (Adam Driver), listen in disbelief. They were mentored by Father Ferreira (Liam Neeson) and refuse to believe that he would apostatize. They plead with Father Valignano to permit them to travel to Japan in the hopes of finding their teacher. Liam Neeson stars in Silence Father Valignano understands the danger that Japan represents – it was a country that resisted most harshly the presence of what it considered arrogant European priests who would attempt to convert the people, At first he says no. But hearing the pleas of the two priests he finally relents, reminding them that they will be the last priests ever go to Japan. And so the journey of the two profoundly naïve, yet deeply religious young priests begins. It was a pilgrimage they never could have imagined, filled with unintended consequences. At first protected by a small Christian cult, they hide in caves and a shack, fearful that they will be discovered, always asking if anyone has heard of Father Ferreira. No one has. They also fear being discovered by a man known as The Inquisitor (Issei Ogata) whose mission it is to extirpate this incompatible religion and its adherents from his country. He gives each convert the opportunity to step on what is called the fumi-e, a small plaque bearing a resemblance of Christ or Mary. If they refuse they are tortured: drowned, beheaded or crucified. Father Rodrigues is ultimately captured and forced to bear witness to the horror the Japanese Christians must endure. It is almost more than he can bear and at one point he says, “I pray but I am lost. Am I praying to silence?” This is a dark and painful film to watch. But it is also profound in its construction. Some in the audience may feel it’s a long, difficult slog, for what Father Rodrigues is compelled to watch is oft repeated. He knows he can put a stop to the torment, his own and the Japanese Christians, if he will only yield his faith and become an apostate. What is remarkable throughout the film is the presence of the question that Father Rodrigues asks: “Am I praying to silence?” It is a fundamental interrogatory, embedded in all religion. Are those who prostrate themselves and declare their belief and inviolable devotion truly heard? Or is faith a revetment against a reality that can be overwhelming in its starkness and finality? Silence doesn’t begin to answer those questions. But it is indeed one that Scorsese asks – to his credit. Silence. Directed by Martin Scorsese. Starring Andrew Garfield, Claran Hinds, Adam Driver, Liam Neeson. 2 hrs., 40 min. Rated R. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. She reads them a story she has written, envelopes each of them with a caring embrace and asks them if they want a small nightlight on or off and the door left open or closed. It’s an endearing ritual. Because Henry is so vigilant and insightful, he begins to notice that the girl next door, Christina (Maddie Ziegler), a classmate at school, seems withdrawn and troubled. At its center The Book of Henry is magical and allows the emotions that fill every scene to sweep the audience along. I loved the ambience, the characters, the warm glow, and I believed without hesitation that though Henry is wise beyond his years and stunningly bright, he is still a kid and a kind kid. There are and will continue to be an abundance of movies that are shallow and meaningless, except for CGI’s ability to create harrowing, seamless action. Marvel and DC studios are drawing endless buckets from this well. Henry’s legacy is about the people in his life and what they mean to him. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honore’ The Transformers film franchise made its debut in 2007, followed by four sequels, each directed by Michael Bay and each, incrementally, shredding the original charm and solid story telling. Bay seemed content to indulge his predilection for CGI chaos, over-the-top histrionics, explosions, and bot slams. In every way the recently released Bumblebee (a prequel) is not only redemptive, but resurrects that sweet spot mined by Shia LaBeof, as Sam Witwicky, in the first Transformers when he negotiates with his dad for a car. He finds a hard-used, yellow Camaro on a lot and convinces his dad that this rusty ride works for him. And so his adventure begins. Ditto Charlie Watson (Hailee Steinfeld), who is on the cusp of turning 18 and declares that, like Sam, all she wants is a car. Any After a brief lead-in segment where the Autobots/Optimus Prime and the Decepticons/Megatron are locked in a destructive battle on Cybertron, their home planet, the narrative shifts to 1987. The place is the San Francisco Bay Area. Charlie is grieving for her father who died two years before of a heart attack while they were restoring a vintage Corvette that still sits in the garage. As it turns out, she’s an appealing but rebellious gear head who works on old cars at a local garage when she’s not going to school. She also feels unheard and alienated at home. Her mom (Pamela Adion) has remarried, her stepdad is okay, and her younger brother is doing just fine. It’s Charlie who feels adrift. Nosing around the junk-laden garage where she hangs out daily, Charlie discovers a vintage yellow VW Beetle hidden under a tarp. She is immediately smitten and pleadingly negotiates with the owner of the garage for this clearly abandoned ride. As it turns out, the key is in the ignition, the engine works and, with the owners blessing (Happy Birthday, he tells her), she’s soon driving off toward home and that empty spot next to her dad’s Corvette. With the Beetle safely in the garage, she walks around its exterior and decides to check its undercarriage. It’s at his moment that there is a classic and wondrous reveal. As she is shinning a light under the rusty chassis, she sees two large aqua blue eyes looking back at her. Abruptly, unexpectedly, the benign-looking VW transforms and there standing before her is a huge banana yellow bot. It’s a meet cute scene that ends with a startled, at-first-disbelieving Charlie naming the Transformer Bumblebee. As she learns, he proves to be a gentle, even timid, giant. And after catching her breath, she and B.B. tentatively bond. Actually, as it turns out, both, in a way, are hiding out – though for B.B. the stakes are much higher. They begin what proves to be a touching friendship. It’s at this point in the story that Charlie’s adventure begins. This is a relationship story. Even when the Decepticons locate Bumblebee (who we learn from the initial set up that he is on a mission for Optimus Prime), the film doesn’t drop off a cliff into vacuous violence that became the brand for the five sequels. Bumblebee is a genuinely good movie that engages and entertains. It’s perfect for those tweens and newbie teens who likely don’t have a clue what life was like in 1987, but understand what it feels like to discover a bot in their home garage. The film comes along at Christmas time, and beckons to parents and kids alike to spend two hours with this Hasbro endorsed tale that has the iconic E.T. embedded in scene after scene. It is distinctly a user-friendly family film. Bumblebee. Directed by Travis Knight. Starring Hailee Steinfeld, John Cena and Pamela Adion. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Bumblebee a sweet family film

articles.text: Part 63 in a biweekly series What impressed me most during a recent trip to Portugal was the incredible Urban Design found there! As many readers of this column know by now, this field of environmental design is my favorite and something I feel very strongly about. Urban Design can at its core be defined as the responsive siting of buildings and the design of the spaces between them. It involves the coordination of the associated design fields of Planning, Architecture, and Landscape Architecture all working together to produce (hopefully) interesting, active, community enhancing public and civic spaces. This concept is vitally important in our built environment and yet has been little understood and often neglected during much of the last century, a time when our focus has been, often exclusively, on individual buildings. A way for us to re-learn this area of critical design is to look around and study examples in other parts of the state, country and world. Both good and bad examples are valuable as things to emulate or avoid. It is also important to understand that we can never really Excellent Urban Design exists in all scales in Portugal. At the largest size, the Avenida de Liberdade in Lisbon, is a wonderful tree-lined grand boulevard and view corridor connecting the newer city on high ground to the Tejo River below. It is a linear park filled with every manner of monument, shop and seating place. At a much smaller scale, the Proaca Luis square, also in Lisbon, is one of many such community gathering places, with adjacent bus stops, taxi stands, historical monuments, food kiosks, and places for street musicians. Bryan Keane

Walkers cover Grand Avenue By Dick Carter The Walking on Wednesdays group hadn’t walked the length of Grand Avenue in Piedmont in over a year, so they planned to walk it on June 7. There was a strong, first week of summer vacation turnout of 42 walkers and two K-9 best friend on hand at the Exedra. The walkers headed off down Magnolia Avenue past the quiet high school, and the not so quiet construction site for the CommuGrand Ave Church Oakland from the Tribune, Sun, Mar 22, 1953. Piedmont - 12 train - Grand Avenue. Piedmont - Grand Ave 1908 Photo nity Pool. The group continue to San Carlos Avenue, which might also be called Rose Avenue for all the beautiful flowers in the front yards. They crossed Oakland at Latham, the only road named Street in Piedmont. They went to a traffic island at the bottom of Lower Grand Avenue where they stopped for a group photo in front of the original entrance to the Piedmont Manor real estate neighborhood whose first home was sold in 1906. At Arroyo Avenue the history of Grand Avenue from Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s past Post articles was shared. Back in the 1870s, today’s Grand Avenue was known as Pleasant Valley Road. It ran from Lake Merritt to the Piedmont hills. Today, the street in Piedmont is Grand Avenue until it crosses the Oakland city line where it becomes Pleasant Valley again. At what is now Grand and Linda Avenues a restaurant named “A Mon Chateau” (My Castle) was built in 1892. Over time it had a number of owners and a troubled history with the police because of owner and patron behaviors, which included having no liquor licenses and gambling. In 1914 the building became the Grand Avenue Grocery Company and the Del Monte Market in 1922. In 1929 the Piedmont City Council adopted an ordinance that allowed businesses from the city line to Linda Avenue on the west side of Grand Avenue, and to Fairview Avenue on the east side. Seven months later voters rejected another zoning ordinance to extend the business district to Oakland Avenue. Today, the business district on Grand Avenue remains the same as it was in 1929. In the 1930’s Piggly Wiggly, a division of Safeway, opened a second grocery store up the street at the corner of Sunnyside and Grand. The competition was stiff for the Del Monte Market. It floundered and closed, and the A Mon Chateau building was torn down. A series of gas stations later occupied the site. Finally, in 1987 the block-long, current Piedmont Financial Center was built. Further down the street was a not very successful “Big T” grocery store, which eventually became today’s Ace Hardware. At Linda Avenue the walkers noted the site of the former A Mon Chateau restaurant. They continued to Ace Hardware, then made the long, uphill walk back to the Exedra via Wildwood and Magnolia Avenues, completing a three-mile walk. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. A turnout of 42 walkers and two K-9 best friends participated in a walk on Grand Avenue on June 7. Pictured are: Nancy DeRoche, Alicia Rivera, Jim Kuo, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mike Henn, Judy Love, Peggy Schultz, Jim Kellogg, Lois Price, Phil Witte, Elizabeth Richter, Edith Lee, Rob Smith, Sarah Johnson, Melba Yee, Lilly Guardia-Labar, Allie Pembleton, Dave DeRoche, Nancy Olsen, Charlene Louie, Karen Palmer, Sherry Jacobs, Kat Lang, Larry Olsen, Stella Houston, Tina Shum, Mike Gallant, Nava Shahan, Bob Wong, Karen Fetherston, Kathy Rolefson, Adrienne Hamlin, Joyce Bailey, Brenda Ferrero, Jasmine Cai, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Sharona Fischrup, Sharon Anderson and Kay Kewley as first-time walkers. The walkers were also happy that Tatum Boyle brought her third grade daughter, Lucia Maggio.

articles.text: When California winemakers started to get serious about making world class wine in the 1960s they looked to two regions of France for guidance. From Bordeaux they imported Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauvignon Blanc and from Burgundy they imported Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. These two wine regions have been the dominant influences ever since. But in the last two decades another area of France has become a major influence on California wine production -- the Rhone Valley. About 30 years ago wine writer Robert Parker began touting the Rhone area as the up-and-coming alternative to overpriced Burgundies and Bordeaux. Parker’s influence was pervasive and today, Cote Roties, Hermitages, and Chateauneuf du Papes from the Rhone, are among the most sought after of France’s wines. In the last three decades the production of Rhone style wines in California has increased dramatically. A Rhone style wine is defined as one made from any of the following official Rhone grapes (or combinations thereof) Syrah, Mouvedre, Grenache, Cinsault, Carignane, and Petite Sirah for the red wines, and Viognier, Grenache Blanc Marsanne, and Roussanne for white. There are now hundreds of wineries making this style of wine from southern California up to Washington state. But the capital seems to be Paso Robles in central California, now home to America’s finest producer of Rhone wines – Tablas Creek. In 1989 The Perrin family, owners of the famous Chateauneuf du Pape winery Chateau Beaucastel, and Robert Haas, an American wine importer, bought property on a limestone ridge near Paso Robles with a desire to make Rhone style wines in America. They brought over grafts of the vines that made the great Beaucastel and began propagating them in a nursery near the winery. Today Tablas Creek is producing America’s finest Rhone style wines. The winery makes a large number of wines but many sell out quickly. For availability, see www.vineyardbrands. com or www.tablascreek.com. Tablas Creek is an interesting winery to visit and they welcome visitors with admirable hospitality. Always best to call ahead, it is about a four-hour drive from Piedmont. Much of the Tablas Creek range of wines is also available at Wine.com. The following wines were selected from their current releases and are worth searching out. • 2022 Patelin de Tablas Rose This light-colored Provencal-styled Rose is made from Grenache, Mourvedre, Counoise and Vermentino. It is utterly charming with a nose of fresh strawberries that jumps out of the glass. In the mouth it is fresh and lively with notes of cherries. The finish is smooth and clean and leaves you wanting another sip. Great as an aperitif or as a porch pounder on a hot afternoon. • 2022 Patelin de Tablas Blanc This wine is made from seven different grapes – the majority being Grenache Blanc and Viognier. The Viognier provides a lovely, perfumed nose of honeysuckle and apricots. On the palate it is round and soft with terrific acidity and good structure. The perfect wine to serve with fish or seafood. • 2021 Esprit Blanc de Tablas This is a step up in intensity from the Patelin Blanc. Made from Roussanne, Picpoul, Grenache Blanc Bourboulenc and Clairette Blanche the wine has loads of tropical fruit, pineapple, and floral notes in its medium-bodied, pure, crisp and lengthy personality. It has good weight in the mouth and voluptuous fruit. It has beautifully integrated acidity and will be versatile on the dinner table. articles.text: Piedmont Flix Fest flexes with musical The first sound movie – The first so-called “talkie” – was a musical. Called The Jazz Singer, and starring Al Jolson, it came out in 1927. By 1930 people were not only sound-move crazy, they were movie-musical crazy as well. In fact for 30 years, until the 1960s, musicals were a movie staple. Piedmont’s 2nd Thursdays Flix Fest paid homage to them last week with one of the best: MGM’s The Band Wagon. The movie was presented to the audience by Piedmont resident Bob Hall, a theater reviewer with the Piedmont Post for 24 years. Starting with 1939’s The Wizard of Oz, the MGM studio, with its big budgets and big stars, became the leading Hollywood producer of lush technicolor musicals – Meet Me in St. Louis, An American in Paris, Singin’ in the Rain. The latter is an affectionate satire of the movies, while The Band Wagon, which came out a year later in 1953, is an affectionate satire of Broadway, in both its pretensions and its frivolity. Written by Betty Comden and Adolf Greene, and directed by Vincente Minnelli (who was married to MGM star Judy Garland long enough to produce a famous daughter), The Band Wagon zeros in on once-successful movie song-and-dance-man, Tony Hunter, played by Fred Astaire. Hoping to revive his career, Tony heads to Broadway, where he gets entangled in a pretentious, doomed musical version of Faust. His luck isn’t all bad, though. He also gets entangled with Gabrielle Girard, played by the stunning Cyd Charisse, who had perhaps the most spectacular legs in all movie history. And he gets to reunite with old pals, Lily and Lester Marton, played amusingly by Nanette Fabray and Oscar Levant. The story heads in a positive direction when the Faust cast decides to drop its pompous project in favor of a bright, cheerful show. That leads to lively numbers, particularly one featuring three quarreling babies, and the movie’s most famous sequence, the “Girl Hunt” ballet, a spoof of Mickey Spillane. Astaire and Charisse have another fine moment swaying to “Dancing in the Dark” in Central Park. The movie concludes with a rousing “That’s Entertainment.” Next month’s 2nd Thursdays Flix Fest, on July 13, will screen Stanley Kubrick’s noir classic, The Killing. Sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, the Flix Fest takes place in the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with a show time at 10:30. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration with the PRD is required and can be done at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. You’re welcome to bring snacks or lunch.

The following wines were selected from their current releases and are worth searching out. • 2021 Grenache This opens to a straightforward nose of red-fruited essences that offer fresh, ripe expressions. Medium-bodied, the wine displays a balanced mid-palate with an easy-drinking frame before ending with an uncomplicated finish that shines with freshness. Drink over the next three or four years. • 2020 Esprit de Tablas This is Tablas Creek’s effort to go head to head with a fine Chateauneuf du Pape and it is an admirable showing. Mostly Mourvedre, Grenache and Syrah it is loaded with gamy and meaty characteristics, as well as blackcurrants, raspberries, olive tapenade and loads of peppery spice. The nose shows traces of vanilla and baking spices with seductive cherries and toasted almonds. Medium bodied, it’s silky in feel with a prolonged, softly dusty finish. Delicious now the wine should last for another 5 to 6 years. • 2020 Le Complice This was a new Tablas Creek wine to me. It is designed to celebrate the kinship of Syrah and an obscure Rhone grape called Terret Noir. The kinship works. It shows full-bodied and decadent aromas and flavors of blackberries, chocolate, and spice. It is a big wine, but it stays fresh and lively on the palate with impeccable balance and fine tannin. • 2020 En Goblet Another new wine to mem En Goblet is the French term for a head pruned vine which is what this wine is made from. The wine offers big, ripe and voluptuously styled notes of plums, leather, herbs and pepper on the nose. These give way to a full-bodied red that has tons of sweet fruit, a rich, mouth-filling texture, and a big finish.
