articles.text: On a beautiful Saturday morning, April 15, An energetic group of 16 members of the Piedmont Seniors ventured to San Rafael for a delicious lunch, followed by a wonderful visit to the Guide Dogs for the Blind graduation ceremony. They first were treated to a scrumptious brunch/lunch at San Rafael Joe’s, which is a throwback Italian restaurant with “down home” fare. After lunch the group headed to the Guide Dogs for the Blind’s beautiful, spacious facility near downtown. The grounds are so serene that it is easy to picture trainers working their magic with the dogs. Guide Dogs was founded in 1942 to provide guide dogs to World War II veterans who lost their sight from injuries sustained in the war. The organization has grown to become the largest guide dog school in North America. To date, Guide Dogs have partnered nearly 16,000 people of all ages, and from all walks of life, with guide dogs. It is a rigorous selection process, and many dogs fail to qualify. They need to learn to obey only their owner and cannot run up to other people or animals. Dogs learn to guide their owner through public transportation sites, airport terminals, and public streets. All of the services for their clients are provided free of charge, including personalized training and extensive post-graduation support, plus financial assistance for veterinary care, if needed. Their work is made possible by the generous support of donors and volunteers. They receive no government funding. The dogs that do not qualify are put up for adoption. Television icon Betty White was one of the fortunate recipients. She adopted a golden retriever, Pontiac, from Guide Dogs. Betty also advocated for those with disabilities, notably blindness. The president of Guide Dogs stated, “Betty’s legacy of compassion, activism, and love of the human-animal bond will live on for years to come”. Having a guide dog has allowed so many people to become independent and live a more meaningful life. For those wanting to observe a Guide Dogs ceremony, be prepared to bring Kleenex. It is a very moving and emotional time to watch the dogs go from their trainers to their new owners. For more information about Piedmont Seniors’ activities, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@ piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: A photo of the audience at a May 24 public meeting on community safety. The Piedmont Seniors hosted a Community Safety Meeting at the Piedmont Community Hall on May 24 with more than 100 on hand to hear Police Chief Jeremy Bowers address issues of concern. With recent nefarious events, including a couple of brazen attacks on seniors, it was no surprise there was so much concern. Chief Bowers covered several topics, focusing especially on community safety and crime concerns. He explained that the City of Piedmont Police will be implementing foot patrols starting this month so that officers can become more familiar with Piedmont neighborhoods. He offered several tips: don’t walk after dark and walk with a friend when at all possible. He said that the police will come to any house to take a report of a crime, and the importance of having an accurate accounting of incidents. The Chief also mentioned that the police department is using social media, including Facebook, Instagram and Next Door, to inform the public. Lisa Douglas, the department’s Support Services Coordinator, reminded audience members that it is the “behavior “of the suspicious person that needs to be reported; not how he/she appears. Douglas explained in detail what “suspicious behavior” is, i.e.: if one believes a specific crime may be occurring; if someone appears to be in physical danger; or if someone is peering into cars or yards. Douglas also said that Piedmont has at least one dispatcher on duty at all times. It was a very informative and useful presentation. If you have any questions, please feel free to contact the City of Piedmont Police at its non-emergency number: 420-3000.
articles.title: Big turnout for police public safety meeting

He explained that the City of Piedmont Police will be implementing foot patrols starting this month so that officers can become more familiar with Piedmont neighborhoods. He offered several tips: don’t walk after dark and walk with a friend when at all possible. He said that the police will come to any house to take a report of a crime, and the importance of having an accurate accounting of incidents. The Chief also mentioned that the police department is using social media, including Facebook, Instagram and Next Door, to inform the public. Lisa Douglas, the department’s Support Services Coordinator, reminded audience members that it is the “behavior “of the suspicious person that needs to be reported; not how he/she appears. Douglas explained in detail what “suspicious behavior” is, i.e.: if one believes a specific crime may be occurring; if someone appears to be in physical danger; or if someone is peering into cars or yards. Douglas also said that Piedmont has at least one dispatcher on duty at all times. It was a very informative and useful presentation. If you have any questions, please feel free to contact the City of Piedmont Police at its non-emergency number: 420-3000. Democracy is not a spectator sport! Although they have moved on to Piedmont Middle School, the Girl Scouts of Troop 33943 continue to give back to Beach School. This spring they painted murals for the Beach School Garden. In April, the Scouts helped the annual Beach Revue by selling raffle tickets, operating concession stands, selling apparel, and handing out programs. They also helped the show’s producers, Dana Murray, Heidianne Pillsbury and Rebecca Ackerman, where needed. articles.text: On May 31, a robust group of 36 Wednesday Walkers were ready for some exercise and camaraderie on a cool and cloudy morning, perfect for a long walk. It had been some time since the group had walked on Crest Road, which is off Hampton Road and parallels La Salle Avenue past Hampton Park. Crest is a long, slow climb. It is not easy, and anyone who wanted a shorter walk could return to the city center. The group went up Highland, Sheridan, and Wildwood Avenues, through the Hall Fenway to Crocker Avenue, to Hampton Road and Hampton Park. The walkers regrouped at the park where they stopped for a group photo. Drawing on information from Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s research, the group was told that the park was part of 50 acres that were purchased in 1911 by Louis Titus, a Berkeley real estate developer. He intended to build a mansion, but the new City of Piedmont raised property taxes dramatically in 1912, and Titus dropped his plans. In 1914 James Tyson, a lumber and shipping businessman bought 30 acres of the land for his home. He was a strong supporter of Piedmont Boy Scouts, which was founded in 1910, and in 1921 he made the land t(now Hampton Park) available to the scouts for an outdoor camp. During the Great Depression in 1938 the Tysons also made the land available to Piedmont schools. A WPA project leveled the land, which was intended to be the site of a future East Piedmont school, which was never built. In the 1950s and 60s the area was a dusty, sometimes muddy youth baseball field. Later, youth soccer was played there often on a soggy field, as underground water was an ongoing problem. In 2000 the Piedmont Play School building was constructed at the back of the park. Dramatic improvements were made during 2017 in a $2 million public-private partnership. Drainage and artificial turf were installed that made the field much more serviceable during the year. Some walkers headed back to the Exedra while the majority crossed La Salle Avenue, passed through the two white columns that marked the main entrance to the 1920s St. James Woods real estate development. The group walked a steep block on the development’s brown tile inlay sidewalk to the foot of Crest Road. The neighborhood is governed by the St. James Wood Homes Association that was founded in 1926 and represents 185 homes in Piedmont and Oakland. The CC&R’s require board approval of changes to homes’ color scheme changes and when owners want to remove trees. They must also seek approval to changes in the location or height of structures, including walls and fences. It was then time to start the accent of Crest. The group continued their climb on Crest to Somerset Road, and looked for a hidden path to Huntleigh Road. The path seems to have been swallowed up by a yard, and no longer exists. The walkers crossed the Oakland/Piedmont city line twice before emerging on Estates Drive with a view of San Francisco in the distance. Going down Estates to the top of Hampton Road started the group’s decent return to the Exedra. It was a nearly four-mile walk, longer than usual. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Book-loving children and parents headed to Children’s Fairyland for its annual Children’s Book Festival last Saturday, June 3. Now in its sixth year, it attracted an estimated 1,400 people who enjoyed the work of 32 local book authors and illustrators. This year’s headline speakers included Angela Dalton, Christian Robinson, Mac Barnett, Nidhi Chanani, Danielle Anderson-Craig, and Shawn Harris. Oakland public school teacher and local “Story Time” web show reader Peter Limata served as the guest host. Highlights of the festival included read-aloud sessions by the authors, a book sale, and an autograph booth by The Collective, an Oakland bookstore. It also included a mindfulness space by Oakland Public Library, and an arts and crafts space by the Museum of Children’s Art. The Children’s Book Festival, previously known as “Turn the Page,” was created in 2016 by five people: Angela Moffett (librarian at Children’s Fairyland), Margaret Rodriguez (librarian at the Oakland Public Library), Shana Barcus (formerly the Education Director at Fairyland from 2013 to 2017), Nina Lindsey (Associate Director at Oakland Public Library), and Luan Stauss (former owner of Laurel Bookstore Children’s book author Serena Allen at a story and craft booth at the annual Children’s Book Festival. Photos by Morgan Rothenbaum Children’s authors and illustrators Mac Barnett (left), Christian Robinson, and Shawn Harris speak at the Children’s Book Festival. in Oakland). Moffett, who still heads the festival, said “The first year felt just as good as last weekend. Every kid deserves the opportunity to develop a lifelong love of reading, and it was wonderful seeing children’s faces light up when they saw an author or illustrator just like them, in their community.” Moffett said that after a meetand-greet and book signing by illustrator Christian Robinson and her own godson, both of whom are African-American, the young boy told her, “It was awesome to see someone that looked like him and that it made him excited to return to writing and drawing. What was originally a hobby opened up to be a real career option for the boy.” Most authors at the festival, like Robinson, donated their time. Many, like the headlining author Mac Barnett – who used to play Peter Pan in theater productions twice a day as a boy at Children’s Fairyland – frequented the amusement park during their own childhoods. “Those who received the magic of this place as kids now want to pass that on and be the giver of magic, telling stories that resonate with children from all walks of life, all across the Bay,” said Moffett. Another highlight of the festival was the read-aloud presentation of contributors to the anthology published at the end of the annual, two-month Youth Writers Workshop at Children’s Fairyland. Held in January and February and headed this year by local children’s author and educator Leticia Hernandez, the program gave 25 young writers and illustrators, aged 8-12, the opportunity to present their work to parents and other children attending the Book Festival. “It was wonderful seeing the diverse backgrounds, ages, and income levels of people attending the readings and other exhibitions,” said Moffett. “The magic of it for us this year was in seeing people – both children and young authors or illustrators very early in their professional career – getting to meet their idols and getting inspired to contribute to the children’s literary world.” Children’s book author Danielle Anderson-Craig (right), looks at a drawing by a young fan. Children’s book author Susan Gal signs a book for a young reader at the annual Children’s Book Festival. Author, illustrator, and art teacher Tiffany Golden (right), shares her work at the Children’s Book Festival. Controversy continues An email to affected neighborhood residents circulated by Palm Drive resident Jason Alderman on May 31 noted that the notice of “no parking” restrictions released on June 5, one day before the Witter Field project was to begin, contradicted what neighbors were told at the community meeting on May 22. At that meeting, Palmer told the approximately 30 attendees that the major portions of the project will be completed in June, August and September. Residents were told that there would be eight days of truck activity (and parking restrictions) in June for the existing turf to be hauled out; “not a lot” in July when a new irrigation system would be installed, nine days in August for the installation of drain rock, and 10 days in September. Residents were also told that, over the course of these four months, 400 truckloads would be brought back and forth on Palm Drive. Since the May 22 meeting, wrote Alderman, the school district seems to “have made several unilateral changes of note. articles.text: It was then time for every graduate’s 15 seconds of fame, to hear their name announced, shake the hand of Superintendent Donald Evans and then greet Principal Goswami who awaited with their diploma. From Ava Adarkar to Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai, the crowd roared and students beamed for each graduate. After moving the tassels from right to left on their graduation caps, the graduates were saluted musically with “March de Triomphe.” The newly minted graduates then raced to the far side of the field to toss their caps skyward – and then hug one another one last time before heading out into the world. After looking back on the repetitive days, logging onto our computers, constantly pulling up our masks, and anxiously waiting for a negative; so much has changed. We have all come back. We are new people, so much smarter and stronger than before. I am so grateful for the teachers and amazing Piedmont staff that have guided, not just me, but all of us through our high school journey. We couldn’t have done it without you. Sure, we may have complained about homework, tests, and putting our phones in the phone prison, but deep down we know you had our best interests at heart. To my fellow graduates: We did it! I am so, so proud of us. Since that Friday the 13th we have worked hard, grown together, and overcome challenges to get here today. As we move on, I want to remind you that we are not alone. We have each other, and we have the support of everyone around us. And because of that, we will make a difference in this world. One thing we’ve learned in high school is that no matter what, we will always be okay.

articles.text: Renovation to start June 6; 400 truckloads on Palm Drive The long-delayed renovation of Witter Field’s irrigation system and turf is scheduled to begin on June 6. Work won’t be completed until approximately December 1, meaning a six month relocation of all summer and fall sports. The School District held a community meeting on Monday, May 22, with neighbors, and attended by the city’s Public Works Director. A follow-up meeting with Public Works staff on May 26 produced a construction schedule for the project. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said, “officially, the approved working hours for PUSD’s contractors during this project are 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. However, the contractors won’t be working past 4 p.m. We’ve been in discussions with the district about altering those hours to be a little earlier, while preventing significant parking burdens on local residents. We’ve also been reaching out to them about clarifying these details on their website and answering community questions in future meetings.” There will be “no parking” restrictions through the month of June, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., on Palm Drive, El Cerrito Avenue, and Winsor Avenue. According to PUSD Facilities Director Pete Palmer, the major work will be done “in June, August and September.” Witter Field at Piedmont High School.

articles.text: After a four-year interruption due to the COVID pandemic, Mountain View Cemetery held its 99th annual Memorial Day ceremony on the morning of Monday, May 29, honoring U.S. men and women who have died in military service. Approximately 200 people attended the event seated before a grandstand draped in American flags. After a musical opening by the David Hardiman Trio, the ceremony began led by the Piedmont Highlanders Drum and Pipes Trio led by Pipe Major Ellison Dunlap, Jr. Members of Piedmont Boy Scout Troop 6 from Corpus Christi Church, a fixture at the ceremony for many years, presented the colors and led the attendees with a Pledge of Allegiance. Following the singing of the National Anthem by the singing group Tosca, a traditional release of doves, and then a gun salute by members of the Sons of the American Legion. The Rev. John Sutton, a U.S. Navy Reserves veteran and a Mountain View Cemetery Trustee, provided an invocation that included a history of Mountain View Cemetery. “We mourn the fallen men and women who gave their lives for this country. We gather today to honor names too many to count: those who have died in service, are dying in service, and those who will die in service to their country,” he stated. Sutton then introduced this year’s guest speaker, Lt. Col. Austin Street of the U.S. Air Force 21st Airlift Squadron. Street gave a moving account of the history of Memorial Day, “the holiday which began from the tradition of laying flowers, wreaths, and flags on the graves of the fallen and which was first celebrated on May 30, 1868 to commemorate the sacrifices of Civil War soldiers.” “We honor our brothers and sisters in arms, who returned home draped in the flag we hold as a symbol of freedom,” Street continued. “This day allows

articles.text: The city of Piedmont received additional comments on its Housing Element from the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) on May 23, as the State’s 60-day review period concluded. However, as more revisions were requested by the state, the Element is not yet state-compliant. HCD reviewers requested that the city provide additional analysis regarding housing mobility, affordability, and the likelihood of development on certain sites, along with additional details as to the timeline of implementing the Element. Planning Department staff expect to complete the requested additions and submit a revised Housing Element to HCD by mid-summer, after which another 60-day state review period will begin. If the Element is compliant by May 31, Piedmont will have three years to implement a substantial number of its programs (by January 31, 2026). But because the Element will not be compliant by May 31, the city will have less than one year to implement programs – by January 31, 2024. articles.text: Editor: The UC student presentation to the City Council on building affordable apartments in Blair Park (which is a great idea!) was good until they got to their estimate of $985,000 per unit. At that price, no apartments will ever be built, whether the land is free or paid for. Luxury apartment buildings all over the country are built for between $300,000 and $400,000 per unit and include swimming pools, spas, dog washing rooms, exercise gyms, lounges and other amenities. That $400k construction price includes land, development costs and profits of the builder and developer and all those amenities. To make a 4% return on a $400,000 unit, rent has to be at least $2,000 per month to cover property taxes, insurance and maintenance. And 4% is less than you now make in a risk-free money market fund. The student projected price of $985,000 per apartment for Blair Park shows the difference between the university world and the real world. The City Council should solicit some presentations from a few actual developers to get real world expectations for this important project. –Jerry Kennelly For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. Of this decision BJC’s General Counsel, Holly Holman, writes, “Viewed upon the facts alone, the decision may be explained as simply upholding a line between individual prayer that is protected by the First Amendment and government-sponsored prayer that is prohibited by the same amendment. It provides no support for official school-sponsored religious practices. Nor does it support religious exercises by school officials that expressly coerce student participation.” Still, there is reason for concern about the way this ruling will be understood and implemented by school districts across the country and concern for the direction the court seems to be heading in interpreting religious liberty. The BJC insists that two religious clauses of the First Amendment, no establishment and free exercise, need to be held in healthy tension. The current court seems to be dedicated to advancing a doctrine of free exercise that undermines the equally important principle of no establishment. articles.text: Earlier this month the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) launched a matching funds campaign to raise $100,000 in contributions toward landscaping to help make Piedmont’s new community pool a truly beautiful and sustainable space in the City. PBF has offered to match from its own funds all donations up to $100,000 so that $200,000 will be available to assure healthy, environmentally sound landscaping with smart irrigation to assure water conservation. From the outset of the project to build the new community pool, PBF has been a strong supporter. It endorsed Measure UU, urging voters to take the bold step of authorizing 19 million dollars to fund the building of a stateof-the-art aquatic facility. PBF was one of the first contributors to the PRFO-led effort to cover increased construction costs, pledging $25,000 to help kickstart that campaign. This new PBF campaign will support installation of native and drought-tolerant planting as well as other green infrastructure, including a solar trellis with photovoltaic cells and a bioswale for storm water retention. Descriptive brochures were recently mailed to every home in Piedmont to announce the campaign. Early returns are extremely encouraging as more than $30,000 in contributions have been received during the first few weeks. PBF President Karen Sullivan urges Piedmonters to support its effort to see that their new pool and community gathering center will be a model of sustainability, incorporating renewable energy technology, water-conserving design, and beautiful native landscaping. She emphasized that every dollar given will be doubled until together we have reached the combined total of $200,000. Contributions may be mailed to Piedmont Beautification Foundation, Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Ave., Piedmont, CA 94611. Online contributions can be sent to piedmontbeautification.org. PBF (a jointly governed organization with Trustees from the City Council and the Piedmont Garden Club, along with 25 community advisors that include representation from other local garden clubs) has been funding projects to “improve, beautify, and maintain the premises and projects of the City of Piedmont” for almost 60 years. PBF has expanded the scope of its projects to more broadly promote safety and sustainability. A separate endowment was established to help the City pay for the ever-increasing expense of maintaining its many recreational venues. Most recently, an improved entrance to Piedmont Park at the corner of Highland and Guilford will open in time for July 4th festivities. Improved lighting and handrails will enhance the safety and appeal of this access to the park and Community Hall for residents and those attending special events alike. Image courtesy of ELS Architecture and Urban Design the Piedmont Garden Club, while the remaining $100,000 was provided by the City’s Facility Maintenance fund for 2021-2022. The Piedmont Department of Public Works had issued a notice to proceed with the project in early December 2022. The contractor replaced the previous steps – which were wooden railroad ties of varying sizes – with colored concrete steps and landings and added metal handrails on both sides of the steps and landings. Further improvements include trees and flowers, six benches, and a small plaza with a permeable-pavement floor for groundwater runoff. pages.text: Wednesday, May 31, 2023 3 Beautification Foundation leading fundraising for community pool landscaping By Cameron Wolfe, Jr. Earlier this month the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) launched a matching funds campaign to raise $100,000 in contributions toward landscaping to help make Piedmont’s new community pool a truly beautiful and sustainable space in the City. PBF has offered to match from its own funds all donations up to $100,000 so that $200,000 will be available to assure healthy, environmentally sound landscaping with smart irrigation to assure water conservation. From the outset of the project to build the new community pool, PBF has been a strong supporter. It endorsed Measure UU, urging voters to take the bold step of authorizing 19 million dollars to fund the building of a stateof-the-art aquatic facility. PBF was one of the first contributors to the PRFO-led effort to cover increased construction costs, pledging $25,000 to help kickstart that campaign. This new PBF campaign will support installation of native and drought-tolerant planting as well as other green infrastructure, including a solar trellis with photovoltaic cells and a bioswale for storm water retention. Descriptive brochures were recently mailed to every home in Piedmont to announce the campaign. Early returns are extremely encouraging as more than $30,000 in contributions have been received during the first few weeks. PBF President Karen Sullivan urges Piedmonters to support its effort to see that their new pool and community gathering center will be a model of sustainability, incorporating renewable energy technology, water-conserving design, and beautiful native landscaping. She emphasized that every dollar given will be doubled until together we have reached the combined total of $200,000. Contributions may be mailed to Piedmont Beautification Foundation, Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Ave., Piedmont, CA 94611. Online contributions can be sent to piedmontbeautification.org. PBF (a jointly governed organization with Trustees from the City Council and the Piedmont Garden Club, along with 25 community advisors that include representation from other local garden clubs) has been funding projects to “improve, beautify, and maintain the premises and projects of the City of Piedmont” for almost 60 years. PBF has expanded the scope of its projects to more broadly promote safety and sustainability. A separate endowment was established to help the City pay for the ever-increasing expense of maintaining its many recreational venues. Most recently, an improved entrance to Piedmont Park at the corner of Highland and Guilford will open in time for July 4th festivities. Improved lighting and handrails will enhance the safety and appeal of this access to the park and Community Hall for residents and those attending special events alike. articles.text: Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan discusses wildfire safety tips with KTVU anchor Gasia Mikaelian on Monday, May 22. With California wildfire season quickly approaching, Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan appeared on KTVU, Channel 2 on Monday morning, May 22 to offer fire prevention and safety tips for viewers of the program. Brannigan told KTVU anchor Gasia Mikaelian that homeowners’ responsibility for fire prevention “is whatever is on your property. Cities take care of the trees and vegetation in the public rights-of-way and the parks.” Ideally, he said, people should leave at least five feet of room between vegetation and flammable property (like homes, fences and decks), and 10 feet between tree limbs and roofs or chimneys. To prevent ladder fuel – a firefighting term for vegetation which carries a fire from the landscape upward to tree or shrub canopies – Brannigan said “for the height of the fuel, you want three times the amount of space above it, so if you have one foot of grass, try to have three feet between whatever is above it.” Mikaelian suggested that property owners may find their yards in particularly dangerous situations this fire season due to high vegetation growth after last winter’s rainstorms. “We have a saying that every year is going to be the worst fire season, whether its dry and drought or whether it’s wet and a lot of growth,” Brannigan replied, urging owners to clear their yards of dead and excess vegetation ahead of the dryer months of September and October. In Piedmont particularly, he said, “We have a lot of beautiful old homes. Some have wood siding and wood shingles. Having vegetation right up against that presents a particular danger in lieu of regular tree and shrub maintenance.” In the Bay Area more broadly, he continued, “when you look at statewide [fire] guidance, it often involves five feet, thirty feet, a hundred feet, we just don’t have that kind of space, so we’re trying to come up with practical, realistic guidelines to keep your property safe as well as the adjacent properties and prevent fire from spreading.” Just as crucial a point of wildfire safety he continued, is knowledge of evacuation routes: “Know, from where you live, work, go to school, at least two ways out of your neighborhood, but also know multiple ways you can get yourself out, whether by car, by walking, whether you’re in a wheelchair or bicycle … also talk to your neighbors, if you have people around you who might need a little bit of extra help,” Brannigan said. Although some may think that the recent, relatively damp and cool May weather may have delayed this year’s fire season, he explained, “We’re already getting into the dryer seasons. articles.text: Assistant Piedmont High School Principal Irma Muñoz was recently named the new principal of Millennium High School. She succeeds Shannon Fierro, who will continue as Principal of Piedmont Adult School. Speaking to the Piedmont School Board on May 24, she said, “Eight years ago I joined the Piedmont community, and this moment is not only a highlight of my years in Piedmont, but of my career.” “I look forward to working with Millennium students, parents, and staff to continue its culture of support and belonging, of equity and inclusion, of seeing each student and family for the strengths and qualities that they bring to our school,” she added. “I thank you for trusting me with this important task, and I am honored to serve as the next principal of Millennium High School.” Muñoz has served as Assistant Principal at the high school since June 2015. Although The school’s other Assistant Principal, Erin Igoe, remains, and the school plans to fill Muñoz’s vacancy. Muñoz previously served as Assistant Principal at San Leandro High School from 2014 to 2015, and at Mills High School from 2006 to 2014. After graduating from UC Davis with an undergraduate degree in Chicano studies in 1995, she went on to receive master’s degrees in education from Stanford in 1996 and from UC Berkeley in 2005. She will begin doctoral studies this summer through the Leaders for Equity and Democracy program at Berkeley. Superintendent Donald Evans described more of Muñoz’s accomplishments in Piedmont beyond her administrative roles: She has been instrumental in providing mental health support for students while overseeing the PUSD Wellness Center, and has led many of the district’s Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging (DEIB) initiatives including the establishment of the district’s Black, Indigenous, and People of Color Network, support of Ethnic Studies and Affinity Mentorship courses, and participation on the DEIB Council,” he said. Fierro, who was appointed as principal of both MHS and Piedmont Adult School in 2017, said that she is leaving Millennium to pursue a doctoral degree in Education for Social Justice at Hayward State (CSU East Bay). Fierro will remain principal of Piedmont Adult School, and will teach 8th grade Spanish 1 at Piedmont Middle School. “I’m excited to get back into the classroom teaching world language as I did for seven years before going into administration,” she said. Irma Muñoz has been named as the new principal of Millennium High School.
articles.title: Irma Muñoz appointed new Millennium High School principal

articles.text: Photos by Sohrab “Seb” Ford Affinity mentor, senior Julia Banuelos, presents Sidney Dearing’s story. Piedmont High’s Associated Student Body (ASB) offered, along with the affinity mentors, a history of Piedmont presentation to all juniors and seniors in the Alan Harvey Theater on April 28. The presentation was ASB’s first large step into diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) work. The presentation educated students on Piedmont’s past with hate crimes, minstrel shows, the KKK, redlining and exclusionary housing. The story of Sidney Dearing, the first Black man to buy a home in Piedmont and who was forced to leave after numerous threats, shocked many students. While the presentation highlighted the racism of Piedmont’s past, ASB was not afraid to acknowledge the continued segregation between Piedmont and Oakland, asking students, “What is Piedmont doing that continues to create this racial divide?” ASB Junior Sara Broach worked with the class’s community outreach committee to create and present the history of Piedmont lesson. “We think that educating the student body about the history of Piedmont is important because the racist foundations our town was built on still persist today,” said Broach, “We believe that education is the first step in progressing DEI work. ASB hopes to continue integrating DEI work into our school, by supporting affinity groups, celebrating everyone’s culture, and contributing to education,” Broach added, “We know that one presentation isn’t going to fix the centuries-old issues, so we are determined to implement permanent DEI education into the school.” ASB advisor and Ethnic Studies teacher Hayley Adams finds these student assemblies necessary to confront the racism in Piedmont’s history. “This is the first time that the secondary schools have been engaged in the direct conversation of Piedmont’s racist history,” said Adams, “As the teacher of both Ethnic Studies and ASB, Juniors Elena Stevens and Jack Cramer Sara Broach and Audrey La Jeunesse offer a “South vs. Piedmont Pop Quiz.” it’s been really important to have these conversations in a larger school-wide setting.” “Ethnic Studies is much larger than it’s often perceived to be. Ethnic Studies is everything around us, everything we breathe, we do, it’s teenagers, it’s culture, it’s everything,” Adams added, “So it’s really important that ASB, is more engaged in culture.”
articles.title: PHS ASB embarks on DEI work with History of Piedmont

While the presentation highlighted the racism of Piedmont’s past, ASB was not afraid to acknowledge the continued segregation between Piedmont and Oakland, asking students, “What is Piedmont doing that continues to create this racial divide?” ASB Junior Sara Broach worked with the class’s community outreach committee to create and present the history of Piedmont lesson. “We think that educating the student body about the history of Piedmont is important because the racist foundations our town was built on still persist today,” said Broach, “We believe that education is the first step in progressing DEI work. ASB hopes to continue integrating DEI work into our school, by supporting affinity groups, celebrating everyone’s culture, and contributing to education,” Broach added, “We know that one presentation isn’t going to fix the centuries-old issues, so we are determined to implement permanent DEI education into the school.” ASB advisor and Ethnic Studies teacher Hayley Adams finds these student assemblies necessary to confront the racism in Piedmont’s history. “This is the first time that the secondary schools have been engaged in the direct conversation of Piedmont’s racist history,” said Adams, “As the teacher of both Ethnic Studies and ASB, Juniors Elena Stevens and Jack Cramer Sara Broach and Audrey La Jeunesse offer a “South vs. Piedmont Pop Quiz.” it’s been really important to have these conversations in a larger school-wide setting.” “Ethnic Studies is much larger than it’s often perceived to be. Ethnic Studies is everything around us, everything we breathe, we do, it’s teenagers, it’s culture, it’s everything,” Adams added, “So it’s really important that ASB, is more engaged in culture.” MHS selects ASB officers for next year By Jay Russell On Wednesday, May 10, Millennium High School (MHS) students elected their Associated Student Body (ASB) cabinet members of their student government for next school year. “Given the small size of MHS, we often only have a few applicants interested in holding office. Those who expressed interest this year were offered the positions. In the cases where there were two interested candidates, they agreed to each take the role for a semester,” explained Principal Shannon Fierro. MHS Associated Student Body Amiyah Denard, MHS President (Fall and Spring) Shay Ottaviano, Vice President (Fall) Axe Johnson, Vice President (Spring) Grace Rego, Secretary (Fall) Meykeda King-Polk, Secretary (Spring) John Pope, Treasurer The election for the MHS Student Representative to the School Board occurred on an electronic ballot on May 22. The following students were elected: • Orla Cohen (current junior) • Shakila Zuberi (current sophomore) The MHS board members will split the year’s duties. One Piedmont High and one Millennium representative will be at every school board meeting.

articles.text: Senior Aryana Fisher was awarded two perpetual awards and the Outstanding Journalist Award. Founded in 1890, the DAR nonprofit is a lineage-based membership service organization for women who are directly descended from a person involved in America’s fight for independence. Fisher was selected for exemplifying the qualities of being a good citizen: dependability, service, leadership, and patriotism. Fisher served as editor-in-chief of the student publication, The Piedmont Highlander, and president of the Mock Trial team. As editor she managed the student staff and oversaw the production of their monthly newsmagazine. Fisher also volunteered as an intern with the Social Justice Collaborative, a legal nonprofit in Berkeley, working with refugees and asylum seekers. LWV Civics in Action Award – Sohrab Ford Piedmont senior Sohrab (Seb) Ford was named the winner of the 2023 League of Women Voters Civics in Action Award. Ford demonstrated a commitment to improving the community throughout his four years at Piedmont. Teacher Hayley Adams presented Ford with the award saying he was her favorite student, and everyone’s favorite student. Ford was a leader on and off campus with school clubs, extracurricular activities and as an intern with the Piedmont Post. Ford took a leadership role in validating the Affinity Mentorship group. At the Culture of Belonging event this year, Ford gave a speech to the community about supporting trans students by not being sexist. As a representative of the Affinity Mentorship group, he spoke impactfully to Piedmont Middle School students about mental health. Buy tickets in advance. The beautiful year-round public campground has miles of hiking and riding trails. Anthony Chabot Campground sits 1 ½ miles above Lake Chabot in Castro Valley, California. The campground has 12 RV sites with full-hookups, 53 drive-up tent sites, and 10 hike-in tent sites. Start up the campfire and bust out the s’mores while having a quick family getaway. It is also a great place to host a thrilling birthday party. Pacific Pipe has extensive hours of operation M-F: 7:00 a.m.-10:00 p.m. and weekends 10:00 a.m.- 7:00 p.m. Alcatraz Tours Cityexperiences.com/san-francisco/city-cruises/alcatraz/ Pier 33, The Embarcadero, San Francisco Take the kids on an unforgettable tour to Alcatraz Island. Steeped in local history, tours of the former federal penitentiary are also available at night and with a “behind the scenes” option. articles.text: Articulation errors, which affect the accurate production of speech sounds, can vary among children. I often get asked why some children effortlessly produce clear and intelligible speech, while others struggle with articulation errors. Let’s look at some of the reasons children may be difficult to understand. The most common reason for pronunciation errors is developmental. Children follow a general sequence of speech sound development based on age. As development progresses, children may temporarily make errors (usually simplifications) during certain stages. For example, children can correctly produce the “p” sound by the age of 2, whereas children may not be able to correctly produce the “r” sound until 5 or so years of age. If the errors persist beyond the age of expectancy, and/or if the child has a high number of developmental errors, we may find it quite difficult to understand the child’s message. On the other hand, differences in oral structure and function can contribute to articulation errors, instead of developmental issues. Structural abnormalities, such as cleft palate or malocclusion, can affect a child’s ability to produce specific sounds accurately. For instance, a child with a cleft palate may struggle with the production of sounds like “s” and “sh” due to the opening in the roof of their mouth. In contrast, a child without these abnormalities may have clearer speech due to the absence of physical constraints. Hearing plays a vital role in speech development. Children with hearing loss or frequent ear infections may experience difficulties perceiving and imitating Articulation errors in children are complex and influenced by a combination of factors. speech sounds accurately. For example, a child with hearing loss may produce distorted vowels because they are unable to distinguish the subtle auditory differences between vowel sounds without proper auditory input. Another possible reason for speech difficulty in children is phonological, meaning the child is having difficulty applying the rules governing sounds in English, or another language. These language specific patterns of errors affect multiple sounds. For example, by around three years of age children learning English are expected to realize that consonants are important at the end of words, for example the word “tree” vs the word “treat”, and those final consonants should be marked and change meaning. Coordination of muscle movements can also play a part in speech production for some children. For example, perhaps a child can produce all the sounds contained within a multisyllabic word in isolation or within syllables or short words, but when attempting to coordinate the movements required to put them all together in a multisyllabic word precision may be lost. Articulation errors in children are complex and influenced by a combination of factors, including developmental variations, oral structure and function, hearing impairment, and phonological skills, motor planning and coordination. Understanding these factors is essential for parents, educators, and speech-language professionals to provide appropriate support and intervention. By addressing the underlying causes of articulation errors and implementing targeted therapy strategies, children can develop clearer and more accurate speech. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com S P E E C H , I N C .

articles.text: The 3rd annual Day of Solidarity coalesced supportive groups within Piedmont School District for a peaceful demonstration on the third anniversary of the murder of George Floyd, May 25. An estimated 150 students, teachers, and community members met at the Exedra to show support by taking pledges of solidarity, creating signs, and discussing justice. The school event wasn’t specifically about Black Lives Matter, or LGBTQ+ solidarity, but about supporting an environment of welcoming and inclusion. “This started when a group of teachers that really cared about advancing social justice and equity in our district were hearing students say how frustrated they were and how they didn’t feel heard. We wanted to show up in a different way,” said Millennium High teacher Michelle Mazzeo, one of the event planners. One of the goals was to send a collective message about the importance of equity work in the Piedmont 5th grade students hold up their signs of solidarity at the Exedra. schools. Another part of the day was for teachers and staff to take a pledge of solidarity. Tables with pens and name tags allowed students, community members and teachers to write down their commitments on posters or to wear fun name tags on their chest. Teacher pledges this year included: “I pledge to center equity work in our schools,” and “I pledge to center students and their experiences.” One focus included protecting LGBTQ+ rights after three flags on the high school flagpole were burned, including a Pride flag, two weeks earlier. MHS Freshmen Charlotte Silver and Angela Enkh-Amgalan help at the sign-making table. PHS senior Leah Bell and her dad, PHS Campus Security Michael Bell, prepare to raise a new American flag in front of the high school on May 25. MHS Senior Maddy Hill and her family band play at the Exedra Plaza during Piedmont High School’s third annual Day of Solidarity. New American, California and Pride flags were raised after the original flags were burned two weeks earlier. Photo by Simran Titan MHS junior Adia Lee and sophomore Ellie Willats create chalk art at the Day of Solidarity event. For the third year PUSD’s Day of Solidarity has rallied students, teachers, school staff and community members at the Exedra.

articles.text: An Olympic torch, of sorts, made its way into every 6th grade classroom on Monday May 22, signaling the commencement of the annual Greek Olympics at Witter Field. 6th graders put aside their computers and books for one morning and became athletes representing the City States of Olympia, Sparta, Athens, and Rhodes. Singing songs of their citystate, the Olympic brigade paraded from the middle school to Witter Field, where Teacher-God Hera gave a welcoming speech to the eager Piedmont Olympians. The Greek Olympics, a tradition started in 1996 by teacher Jane Hickman, serves as a culmination of the Ancient Greek studies. “Olympians, today we ask, nor, we expect you, to show us that sports unite us. May the Games be held in peace, in the true spirit of the Olympic Truce,” said school counselor Amy Sharp in the role of Hera. After the welcoming speech, each of the eight core classes performed their rehearsed chants honoring a particular God or Goddess. The Games began as groups competed in eight events. Modern changes were made: the javelin was a toilet plunger; the discus a frisbee; the shot in shot put was a softball. Longjump, tug of war, jump rope, the relay race, and the three-legged race were performed without much alteration from the Ancient Greek methods. With brightly decorated shirts representing the city states the Olympians battled for spots on the podium in each event. In lieu of being presented with medals, the top three athletes in each event received stamps on their shirts. After all events were tallied the city-state of Olympia was declared the overall winner. Olympians seeking glory were given the option of running a marathon (4 laps at Witter Field, the equivalent of one mile.) The top finishers were: 1st, Travers Kemp, 5:55 – Olympia 2nd, Olivia Nealon, 5:56 – Rhodes 3rd, Mason Gray, 5:58 – Olympia The top three runners received wreaths for their embodiment of Nike, the Goddess of Victory. An optional mile Marathon was offered after a full day of Olympic games at Witter Field. The top three 1-mile runners with newly adorned wreaths: Olivia Nealon (left), Travers Kemp and Mason Gray. Phoebe Hess soars through the air in the long jump for Sparta. Olivia Lucaccini (left), Sammy Schey, Mackenna Small and Hazel Schaeffer at the 6th grade Greek Olympics. Olympians in a contemporary rendition of the javelin toss with plungers. Cheers of “Sparta!” rang during the tug of war event. Rohan Sietan jumps towards the 14’ mark in the long jump. Teachers serve as the Greek pantheon and announce that Olympia was this year’s winner of the Greek Olympics. One of many relay race iterations – Piggy- back relays.

articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team, seeded No. 8, advanced to the Division 4 North Coast Section Semifinals before losing 11-10 in an exhilarating game to No. 5 Justin Siena in Napa on Wednesday, May 24. It featured the Highlanders responding from a 6-1 deficit at one point and an 11-7 disadvantage entering the top of the seventh inning. PHS was potentially one hit away from the go-ahead run with the bases loaded. “That was a great high school baseball game. They got their great hits and we got ours,” said coach Eric Olson. “I was super Staff Photos Piedmont’s baseball team suffered an 11-10 loss in the NCS Semifinals to Justin-Siena, ending their season. Michael Aikawa pumps up his team after hitting a double. Brandon Dicke after he slid into third base for a triple. proud of how we battled. We gave up a tough inning and then came back to take the lead. Our guys showed heart and grit.” The team turned into a Cinderella story with intense games each step of the way despite having an undersized roster and only limited pitching experience. They upset No. 9 Branson 4-3 in a 12-inning game that stretched over two days on May 17-18. Then they pulled off a major upset, beating No. 1 Fortuna 5-2 on May 20. “Playoffs are just so much more intense, especially being a senior having the season on the line. Everything is played at a higher level. This felt like a championship game and we played our hearts out,” said senior leader Ryan McConathy. “Little things decide games like those. We pushed through and made it closer than it should’ve been for Justin-Siena. We’re a team that doesn’t give up... I think we got hot at the right time, we are definitely playing our best baseball right now, and it’s terrible it has to come to an end. In the middle of the season, we were struggling and picked it up,” added sophomore Markos Lagios. It was a terrific two-game series between the schools this year. Piedmont defeated Justin-Siena 12-8 on March 2, making 41 runs between the two games. “When we played these guys the first time, it was the same thing. We got up big and then they came back, then we went up again and they answered,” said McConathy. The Highlanders will be without the big bats of McConathy and Michael Aikawa, but will return most of the starters. Game Recap Justin-Siena took a 1-0 lead following the bottom of the first, but Piedmont tied it in the second inning thanks to John Olsen drawing a walk with the bases loaded. However, the Braves got out the inning without further damage after drawing back-toback fly outs. Justin-Siena scored five runs in the bottom of the second to go ahead 6-1. In the top of the fourth, PHS went ahead 7-6 with six runs. McConathy led off with a double
articles.title: Piedmont falls short of comeback in 11-10 NCS Semifinals loss to Justin-Siena

articles.text: Pied mont’s t rack team returned to Veteran’s Memorial Stadium at Buchannan High School in Clovis for the 103rd CIF State Championship meet on Friday May 26. Piedmont was represented by Parker Long in the 800 meter, and as a member of the 4x400 relay team with Christian Taylor, Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai, and Sam Shelby. Long finished Friday’s preliminary race in 1:55.83, placing 19th of 27 runners. He entered the race after winning the NCS Meet of Champions in 1:53.80 in his first season competing at the distance. “The top people were going to be around 1:51, so I knew I had my work cut out for me in a really tight field. I feel like I’m learning more about every position in the 800; where’s it’s good to be, where it isn’t good to be, and when to kick and make your move. I feel like I’m understanding the event more,” described Long. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, May 31, 2023 Sports Piedmont falls short of comeback in 11-10 NCS Semifinals loss to Justin-Siena By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s baseball team, seeded No. 8, advanced to the Division 4 North Coast Section Semifinals before losing 11-10 in an exhilarating game to No. 5 Justin Siena in Napa on Wednesday, May 24. It featured the Highlanders responding from a 6-1 deficit at one point and an 11-7 disadvantage entering the top of the seventh inning. PHS was potentially one hit away from the go-ahead run with the bases loaded. “That was a great high school baseball game. They got their great hits and we got ours,” said coach Eric Olson. “I was super Staff Photos Piedmont’s baseball team suffered an 11-10 loss in the NCS Semifinals to Justin-Siena, ending their season. Michael Aikawa pumps up his team after hitting a double. Brandon Dicke after he slid into third base for a triple. proud of how we battled. We gave up a tough inning and then came back to take the lead. Our guys showed heart and grit.” The team turned into a Cinderella story with intense games each step of the way despite having an undersized roster and only limited pitching experience. They upset No. 9 Branson 4-3 in a 12-inning game that stretched over two days on May 17-18. Then they pulled off a major upset, beating No. 1 Fortuna 5-2 on May 20. “Playoffs are just so much more intense, especially being a senior having the season on the line. Everything is played at a higher level. This felt like a championship game and we played our hearts out,” said senior leader Ryan McConathy. “Little things decide games like those. We pushed through and made it closer than it should’ve been for Justin-Siena. We’re a team that doesn’t give up... I think we got hot at the right time, we are definitely playing our best baseball right now, and it’s terrible it has to come to an end. In the middle of the season, we were struggling and picked it up,” added sophomore Markos Lagios. It was a terrific two-game series between the schools this year. Piedmont defeated Justin-Siena 12-8 on March 2, making 41 runs between the two games. “When we played these guys the first time, it was the same thing. We got up big and then they came back, then we went up again and they answered,” said McConathy. The Highlanders will be without the big bats of McConathy and Michael Aikawa, but will return most of the starters. articles.text: Jack Nelson made his biggest impact on the lacrosse field, but also was a starter on soccer and football. Piedmont lacrosse stars Jack Nelson and Molly Ashton were named as the school’s 2023 Outstanding Senior Athletes, an honor that includes academics, student leadership, and citizenship. JACK NELSON lacrosse, soccer, football Jack Nelson was a talented member of the lacrosse, soccer, and football teams. He helped Piedmont win its sixth consecutive Western Alameda County Conference championship in lacrosse and earned back-toback first-team All-League honors. Seeded No. 3, the PHS lacrosse team battled its way to the D2 North Coast Section title game before losing 10-9 in double-overtime to No. 1 Tamalpais. Nelson was also a member of the soccer team in the winter and helped them win a second consecutive NCS Championship. A versatile athlete, he played as a fullback, midfielder, and forward. Jack Nelson was honored as Piedmont’s Outstanding Male Athlete ay the Senior Awards ceremony. On the football team, Nelson was the team’s leading running back and middle linebacker before the varsity season was terminated due to a shortage of players. MOLLY ASHTON lacrosse Lacrosse star Molly Ashton was named the school’s Outstanding Female Athlete at the Senior awards ceremony. Molly Ashton received firstteam All-League honors as the lacrosse team’s leading scorer. It was the second straight year she earned honors from the WACC. She was a three-year varsity player with the Highlanders. The team had an 8-8 record and finished the league tournament with a nail-biting 11-9 loss to Bishop O’Dowd in the championship game. In the game, Ashton scored two goals and won two draws. She had a season-high of six goals scored against Berkeley in the first round of the WACC playoffs on April 25, resulting in a narrow 11-9 win. She also had four goals in a thrilling 11-10 overtime win over Las Lomas on March 28. Molly Ashton was a three-year varsity letter on the lacrosse team.

Terrill competed in the 2023 Pac-12 Championship in the Pole Vault, finishing 10th with a height of 16 feet, 3.5 inches. He departed from Piedmont High as the school’s all-time record holder in the pole vault with a height of 16 feet, 1 inch— Distance runner Ellie Black, also a freshman at Cal, also competed in the Pac-12 Championship. . Ellie Black University of California Ellie Black, PHS Class of 2022, now a freshman at. Cal, is competing in both cross-country and track. In the USF Invitational at Golden Gate Park in September, Black finished the 6,000- meter run (3.72 miles) race with a time of 22:03.8, to help the Golden Bears to place d eighth of 13 teams. She was the top runner for California, ahead of senior Natalie Weiner (41st), senior Lucy Hurt (44th), freshman Emilie Barrett (46th), and freshman Carolina Dawson (53rd). Black also ran in the UCR 41st Annual Cross Country Invitational later in September, where she was 31st of 265 runners in 21:01.2. She went down as one of Piedmont High’s all-time greats on the women’s team. She had PHS’ second-best time ever in the 3200 with a 10:46.09 and was third all-time in the 1600 in 5:07.23. On the cross country team, Black won the WACC Championship in 18:38.6 and was fourth of 105 in the NCS Finals with a time of 18:10.7. As an individual qualifier at the CIF Championship she placed 17th of 207 runners in 18:44. Pitcher Izzy Epstein, PHS Class of 2022, finished her freshman season at Chapman University with a sterling 1.77 ERA.

articles.text: The Spring season of the Piedmont Junior Running Club program for 4th and 5th graders concluded with a mini-track meet on Wednesday, May 24, at Witter Field.. A total of 60 boys and girls from Beach, Havens, and Wildwood Elementary Schools participated, with four running events and one field event. The Junior Running Club, created by Leonard Goldman, provides an introduction to running for kids not yet in middle school, and every season concludes with a track meet. This year’s meet included a 75-yard sprint, 60-yard hurdles Photos by Steve Zirklebach Nicholas Phung, Graham Grippando, Eleanor Chi, and Trina Branneria in the 75-yard sprint Charley Harnett, Finley Muthig, Evan Jahn, Eleanor Hathorn, and Liliane Giguere in the 60-yard hurdles 5th graders Bailey Gregovich, Simone Tornatore, Kenji Holt, and Miles Duran Xuan Tran, Miles Duran, Finley Muthig, Henley Azad, Sofia Faucher, and Teo Wickner in the sprint Runners in the 4x100m Relay 5th grade long jumper Ben Cole Half milers Saya Presley, Ronan Price, Noah Adams, and Kai Synder in the 800-meter run race, 800-meter run, 4x100-meter relay, and long jump. There were eight heats in the sprints with the Graham Grippando, Siena Botero, Theo Thomas, Sammy Laubach, and Eli Song in the 60-yard hurdles Distance runners Kenji Holt and Trina Branneria Kian Ghassemi, Harriet Killion, Sammy Laubach, Solomon Sandrock, and Kai Synder in the 800-meter run Willa Brozowski-Schrader and Teak Hergott in the 800-meter run winners advancing to the finals. The same format applied to the hurdles using three 12-inch hurdles and one 6-inch hurdle in each lane. The winner of both the sprint and hurdles was Henley Azad a 5th grader at Havens. Her time in the sprint was 10.9 seconds and 9.15 seconds in the hurdles. Teams of four runners from each school participated in the relays, with each running a 100- meter leg. There were two heats, and a team from Havens won the first heat in 66.6 seconds, a new record in the event. The winner of heat two and 2nd place overall winner was a team from Beach in a time of 68.8 seconds. The concluding running event was 800 meters (the equivalent of a half mile). Wildwood 5th grader Kenji Holt won the first heat with a time of 2-minutes, 46-seconds. The winner of heat two was Azad in a time of 2:57. The May 24 meet was the last sports event at Witter Field before it is closed for nearly six months for a renovation of the field and track. The Piedmont Junior Running Club is a year-round running program for kids in grades 2-5. It will hold a four-week summer program starting in July, followed by a Fall program that begins when school is back in session. For more information, contact Len Goldman at lgoldman@pacbell.net.
articles.title: Junior Running Club hosts season-ending track meet

articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is currently showing an exhibit by Frank Bowling titled Frank Bowling: The New York Years 1966–1975, It is the first major exhibit of the artist’s work in North America in 40 years. Sir Richard Sheridan Patrick Michael Aloysius Franklin Bowling, known as Frank Bowling, was born in British Guiana, now Guyana, and moved from London to New York. He is best known for his large-scale, abstract and colorful paintings, color field painting and lyrical abstraction; sometimes referred to as ‘abstract expressionism.’ The San Francisco exhibition features 45 vibrant and large-scale paintings, and a selection of archival materials, including recorded interviews of the artist in New York and London, and film footage and photographs from Bowling’s 1968 visit to Guyana. “We are looking forward to engaging our communities with the exceptional work of Frank Elder Sun Benjamin, 2018, by Frank Bowling Bowling and to offering an in-depth exploration of the enduring influence of his time in New York, both on his own work and on the development of art more broadly,” said Christopher Bedford, the Director at SFMOMA. “In particular, the presentation of the exhibition provides an opportunity to experience Bowling as a scholar and teacher committed to elevating the voices of Black artists and expanding the understanding of art history as it unfolded. This very much aligns with our institutional vision to share significant, if perhaps lesser-known, facets of artists’ careers and to explore artistic achievement through a spectrum of lenses and perspectives.” Frank Bowling – The New York Years opened May 20, and will be on display through September 10. The exhibition is co-organized with the Museum of Fine Arts Boston. For more information, and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit www.sfmoma.org.
articles.title: Frank Bowling exhibit opens at SF MOMA

articles.text: The Legion of Honor, of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, will exhibit The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England beginning June 24. This is the first major exhibition in the United States of portraiture and decorative arts of the Tudor courts. It will include works from the museum’s collection, including a late 16th century panel painting, as well as tapestries commissioned or acquired by Henry VII and Henry VIII. “Few may be aware of the distinctive art and visual propaganda that was central to the splendor and drama of the Tudor court,” said Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Now, in the first exhibition of its kind in the US, The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England reunites scores of sumptuous paintings, precious jewels, rich tapestries and rare artifacts from collections around the world to bring the Tudor dynasty vividly to life–from the bloody founding of the dynasty in 1485 by Henry VII on the fields of Bosworth, to the final moments of Queen Elizabeth in 1603.” The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England will be on view from June 24 through September 24. For more information and tickets, visit https://www.famsf.org. Queen Elizabeth I (1533–1603) (detail), Oil on panel, by Nicholas Hilliard (England, circa 1547–1619)
articles.title: The Tudors exhibit opens June 24 at Legion of Honor

articles.text: Tickets for Festival Napa Valley are now on sale. The two-week event (July 8-23), now in its 17th season, will take place in iconic Napa Valley locations and kicks off July 8 with a gourmet chef-inspired dinner and performance by Jennifer Grim. Grim has performed as a flutist with Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center, St. Luke’s Chamber Ensemble, Zéphyros Winds, and the New York Chamber Soloists. She also serves as principal flute of the Mostly Mozart Orchestra of New York. Proceeds from the evening benefit scholarships for women and girls in the arts and arts education. The festival is headlined by Grammy-award winning country singer Carrie Underwood, and includes a variety of soloists and chamber music groups. “Whatever we put on stage, we want to make sure it’s the best of the best,” said Festival Napa Valley co-founder and director of artistic planning Charles Letourneau. “From that, we try to balance (a) variety of genres, artists and programs so that we put together an experience that people will remember forever.” Visit https://festivalnapavalley. org/2023-summer-season/quicklook/ for full programming and to purchase tickets. American composer William Grant Still for String Orchestra, opened the program. The San Francisco Chamber Orchestra is a supremely competent and professional orchestra. They played everything on the program with dogged determination. Conductor Fankuchen was obviously enjoying himself on stage. He flails his arms and shrugs shoulders up and down with every beat. There was another brief lecture, and the orchestra launched into the Concerto for wind instruments, timpani, percussion and string orchestra by the Swiss composer Frank Martin. The primary difference between this piece and the first one was the addition of wind instruments and percussion, which increased the volume. There was no difference in musical demeanor. After intermission, I moved to the balcony from the Orchestra for a different perspective. The conductor informed the audience with some tidbits of information about Mendelssohn and the orchestra played with the same professionalism as in the first half.
articles.title: Festival Napa Valley to open July 8

articles.text: I acknowledge that Kidnap is pulp cinema. A B-movie which has an A-list, Oscar-winning actress handling just about every moment of this unpretentious thriller. It is quite a ride. Here’s the set up: Karla Dyson (Halle Berry) is a waitress and a devoted single mom. Her sweet 6-year-old son is Frankie (Sage Correa), who is sitting at the restaurant counter coloring, waiting for his mom to get off work. Finally they leave and head for an afternoon at the park, replete with lots of fun stuff for kids. Clearly Karla is a committed mom who adores her small boy. While they are sitting trying to decide what to do next, she gets a phone call on her cell from her divorce lawyer. Concerned, she tells Frankie to sit in his chair, not to move, and then turns away, walks several steps up a hill, and has a disconcerting conversation about custody. She breaks the conversation and says, “Marco…” and waits for “Polo.” Hearing Frankie’s response she ends the conversation and returns to her seat; however, when she gets there, Frankie is gone. Missing. Frantic, she begins calling out “Marco” but gets no “Polo” in reply. Hurrying through the park she calls out to the boy. Nothing. And then she sees a large, wild-haired woman pushing Frankie into the backseat of a blue Mustang. Screaming she runs after the car and helplessly watches it speed away. It’s at this point that Kidnap becomes a pure adrenalin-inducing movie. Karla doesn’t wait for the police to arrive; she doesn’t look to others in the park for help, though there are other mothers who are concerned. Sage Correa and Halle Berry in Kidnap Creating Community through the Power of Music. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, May 31, 2023 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Kidnap a peek at pulp cinema By Chris Honoré I acknowledge that Kidnap is pulp cinema. A B-movie which has an A-list, Oscar-winning actress handling just about every moment of this unpretentious thriller. It is quite a ride. Here’s the set up: Karla Dyson (Halle Berry) is a waitress and a devoted single mom. Her sweet 6-year-old son is Frankie (Sage Correa), who is sitting at the restaurant counter coloring, waiting for his mom to get off work. Finally they leave and head for an afternoon at the park, replete with lots of fun stuff for kids. Clearly Karla is a committed mom who adores her small boy. While they are sitting trying to decide what to do next, she gets a phone call on her cell from her divorce lawyer. Concerned, she tells Frankie to sit in his chair, not to move, and then turns away, walks several steps up a hill, and has a disconcerting conversation about custody. She breaks the conversation and says, “Marco…” and waits for “Polo.” Hearing Frankie’s response she ends the conversation and returns to her seat; however, when she gets there, Frankie is gone. Missing. Frantic, she begins calling out “Marco” but gets no “Polo” in reply. Hurrying through the park she calls out to the boy. Nothing. And then she sees a large, wild-haired woman pushing Frankie into the backseat of a blue Mustang. Screaming she runs after the car and helplessly watches it speed away. It’s at this point that Kidnap becomes a pure adrenalin-inducing movie. Karla doesn’t wait for the police to arrive; she doesn’t look to others in the park for help, though there are other mothers who are concerned. articles.text: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2, released in 2011, is the eighth and last film in a series that began the same year that the twin towers fell in New York. It’s been a remarkable ride, these movies and books, in the aggregate a stunning achievement, unequaled in sheer breadth and depth. It was J.K. Rowling who wrote seven volumes totaling some 4200 pages, each book resonating with her fans, all those young Potterheads. From the depths of her imagination, she created a cultural phenomenon that remains thus far unrivaled. Youngsters sat outside of bookstores at midnight, wearing peepers and pointed hats, carrying wands, waiting for the next book, often a tome the size of the New York phone book. Each was quickly devoured and discussed. The eight films, waited for with delicious anticipation, comprise 20 hours of screen time and have generated some $7 billion in box office receipts. All of this begs the question: Why? What is there about an orphaned boy, Harry Potter, sent off to wizard school by his disgruntled Muggle relatives, to a place named, improbably, Hogwarts? Perhaps it’s as simple as Harry possessing a magical power and an abiding fearlessness, something that every young person would delight in having. As the series progresses, as multiple narrative strands are gradually brought together, Harry prepares to confront his nemesis, Lord Voldermot. And so we arrive at part two of the final film. For all those Potterheads who have passed the last fourteen years immersed in the labyrinthine adventures of Harry (Daniel Radcliffe) and Hermione (Emma Watson) and Ron (Rupert Grint), this last film will be bittersweet. The long, rambling narrative could easily have been brought to the screen as a series of B-movies. Instead, each film has been lavishly crafted and richly produced and adapted. Part two of Deathly Hallows may be the best of the eight. It is intense and astonishingly good. As are the English actors who have, at the insistence of Rowling, peopled the franchise from the outset. Of course, when walking in to the theater, it helps to have been immersed in Potter lore. Which is no small thing. You need more than a program to get current; you need a wizard dictionary. For some filmgoers, part two will merely amaze. As for the already initiated, and even the recently ordained, this last installment will be captivating. It dazzles as the climax draws near and as Harry moves ever closer to that moment when he may, indeed, die at the hands (or wand) of He Who Shall Not Be Named. Of course, the outcome is known to those who have read the seventh book; but no matter. It is all wonderful and again wonderful and an appropriately soaring finale. As an aside: In a scene from act three, Dumbledore says to Harry, “Words are our most inexhaustible source of magic.” Indeed. Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2. Directed by David Yates, Starring Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson, Rupert Grint, Alan Rickman and Ralph Fiennes. 2 hrs., 10 min. Rated PG. Released in 2011. articles.text: The Edge of Seventeen is superb, perhaps one of the best movies about adolescent angst and coming of age in the last 25 years. It’s that good. To write and direct a film that captures the essence of being 17, when your life feels unmoored and uncertain, that is no small thing. Director Kelly Fremon Craig gets it just right, avoiding clichés. At the center is Nadine (Hailee Steinfeld), suffering a perfect storm of emotions. Several years ago she lost her father, to whom she was especially close. And now her best friend since childhood, Krista (Haley Lu Richardson), has fallen for her older, eternally perfect and popular brother, Darian (Blake Jenner). Nadine feels abruptly rejected and betrayed and so banishes Krista from her life. Convinced she is utterly alone, she decides to kill herself. During lunch hour she informs her history teacher, Mr. Bruner (played wonderfully by Woody Harrelson) of her intention. While Nadine is a master of histrionics and self-absorbed drama, the laconic and dry Mr. Bruner becomes the perfect counterweight to her mood swings. Their classroom scenes are some of the best in the film. Meanwhile, Nadine fantasizes in a lustful way about Nick (Alexander Calvert), a bad boy, edgy, enigmatic, who works part time at Pet Land. Nadine also finds herself drawn to a classmate, Erwin (Hayden Szeto), a budding filmmaker and gifted illustrator. The Edge of Seventeen is not a collage of adolescent stereotypes; rather, it’s a film about fully formed characters. Nadine is surrounded by a circle of friends and adults, to include her frazzled mom (Kyra Sedgwick), who care about her, despite all of Nadine’s rage and lashing out and expressed self-loathing. At one point she says, “I’ve had the worst thought: I’ve got to spend the rest of my life with myself.” She shares this with Mr. Bruner who merely offers her half of his lunchtime cookie. The narrative gradually morphs into is an attrition of Nadine’s anger and confusion, emotions that have turned her life into a roller coaster ride of hostility and all-consuming Hailee Steinfeld and Haley Lu Richardson in The Edge of Seventeen bewilderment. She loses her manic self-centeredness while she begins to gain small personal insights that come at her unexpectedly like small gifts. Who among us can forget what it was like to be 17? What is there about being an adolescent that feels so real and involving? Will we ever live so intensely again, a time akin to walking on a high wire, framed by a sense of perpetual vertigo? Writer Craig gets all of that just right and so has made an achingly spot-on film that is to be embraced for what it manages to accomplish. The Edge of Seventeen. Directed by Kelly Fremon Craig. Starring Hailee Steinfeld, Woody Harrelson, Kyra Sedgwick. Released in 2016. 104 min. Rated R. Instead, she gets behind the wheel of her Minivan and gives hot pursuit. She is hysterical. Every frame from this point on in the movie is shot within the van, Karla’s face a roadmap of hysterical determination. Halle Berry is perfect as the desperate mom ready to do whatever it takes to not lose her son. This is 82 minutes of disaster and rising dread and she is incredibly effective. Kidnap is a winner, if you enjoy the genre. And Halle Berry is unafraid to look frantic in a white-knuckle, breathtaking way. The kidnapers? You only meet them once, briefly, individually and they are a seedy, remorseless, chilling pair – a man and a woman. Frankie is indeed in harm’s way. Kidnap. Directed by Luis Prieto.
