articles.text: 3 Artists, 3 Styles, 3 Visions Art has always been a powerful tool for social commentary and political expression. This June, Elena Doronkina and two friends, Alexander Zimin and Galina Filimonova are having a fine art exhibit at Piedmont Center for the Arts. In addition to showcasing their work, they are using the exhibit to express support for Ukraine. Half of the sale proceeds from the exhibit will be donated to support children in Ukraine, specifically those in South Village in the Kharkiv Region. The exhibit will showcase three unique styles which blend classical techniques with modern ideas. Their work is renowned for the use of vibrant colors, intricate details, and emotive expressions. Each piece represents the artist’s innermost thoughts and feelings, conveyed through various mediums, including oil and watercolors. An opening reception will be held on Saturday, June 10, from 4:00 to 7:00 p.m. The artists have a loyal following; their work has been exhibited in galleries, private collections, and museums worldwide. The exhibit will be a celebration of creativity, beauty, and the human spirit. After COVID, it will be a muchneeded opportunity for people to come together and appreciate the joys of life. The exhibit will be a reminder of art’s power to inspire, uplift, and connect us with one another. Gallery hours are Saturdays and Sundays from June 10 to July 2 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Elena Doronkina is an award-winning artist and an American Women Artists associate member. For the last five years, she has been a Program Director at the Alamo Danville Artist’s Society (ADAS), and a manager at Blackhawk Gallery in Danville, CA. Point Lobos, Carmel (oil) 11x16 Galina Filimonova is an Internationally known watercolor artist. Her first significant exhibition took place in 1994 in Imatra (Finland). Since then, she has taken part in many exhibitions held in Russia, Germany, Finland, Greece, and Italy. Italy. He was a prizewinner at the landscape art festival in Carmel, CA, in 2001 and 2002. While teaching art since 2008, he participated in the international educational project, Repin Institute in Kotka, (Finland), and has repeatedly held master classes in painting here in California. Alexander Zimin is an internationally known Artist. His first significant exhibition was held in Finland, at the Koscengalleria, in Imatra. articles.text: As you probably know, Napa Valley has specific geographic parameters that are set by U.S. law. Within the Napa AVA (American Viticultural Area) there are 16 separate smaller subAVA’s that give more specificity to where the grapes on the label come from. Many of the names have become famous themselves – Oakville, Rutherford, Stag’s Leap, Mount Veeder, Calistoga, etc. The most recent AVA to be designated was Coombsville, which got its start in 2011. The Coombsville AVA is located east of the city of Napa in the southeastern corner of Napa County. The region was formed millions of years ago when a volcano exploded leaving a “cup and saucer” shaped geographic area. Coombsville is distinguished from other parts of the Napa Valley by its slightly cooler climate and soil conditions which are a mix of well-draining river rock and mineral-rich volcanic ash. The rolling terrain provides various aspects that lend to optimization of many varietals, though Cabernet Sauvignon dominates the abundant hillside vineyards. The area takes its name from Nathan Coombs, who purchased the land from Nicholas Higuera’s Rancho Entre Napa, an 1836 Mexican land grant. It was at this parcel that Coombs created the city of Napa in 1847. Located east of Napa, Coombsville’s agricultural orientation was initially focused on livestock and subsistence farming as opposed to vineyard development. It was only in the mid 20th century that the region began to attract attention from grape growers and vintners. To try to bring this overlooked appellation some notoriety, the region’s wineries have formed the Coombsville Vintners and Growers Association. They have an attractive website which gives the history or the region and profiles of the member wineries and growers. (coombsvillenapa.org). On May 6 they held a tasting of the area’s wines at the Culinary Institute of America (COPIA) in Napa. Over 25 wineries participated, and the quality of the wines poured was very high. The following wines were the standouts and are certainly worth seeking out. • 2019 Napa de Oro Caroline’s Red Blend A Bordeaux style blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc, it offers black cherries, currants and blueberry scents. Very big, concentrated and powerful in the mouth, it coats the palate with black fruits and savory layers, supported by firm, grainy tannins and seamless freshness, finishing with great persistence. • 2011 Marita’s Vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon The Marita’s Cabernet shows expressive plum, blackberry and cigar box notes with hints of bay and eucalyptus leaves. Full-bodied and concentrated in the mouth, the muscular fruit is well supported by firm tannins and ample freshness, finishing long and satisfying. • 2019 Covert Syrah The Covert Syrah unwinds in the glass with notes of cassis, plums, violets and dark chocolate. On the palate the wine is supple, velvety and medium to full-bodied, with lots of peppery fruit and good acidity, as well as excellent concentration and length. articles.text: An early 20th century look at Piedmont Park When Frank C. Havens opened Piedmont Park in 1898, only the Clubhouse, the rustic teahouse, the mineral springs and the beauty of the ravine, waterfalls and wandering paths were there to attract visitors to the park. Havens continued to add more attractions to draw visitors to Piedmont Park and to the city itself. Many visitors enjoyed the weather and views and decided to build their homes here. Frank Havens and his Realty Syndicate was there to sell them a home site. In 1904 he built “The Maze.” Gardeners planted a large circular hedge maze in the natural bowl where Witter Field stands today. This privet maze challenged all who entered to reach the bright red pagoda at the center. Ladders strategically placed throughout the Maze allowed those feeling hopelessly lost to climb a ladder to the top of the hedge and get their bearings. And true to the nature and design of mazes, the Maze in Piedmont was a double challenge; the return trip out of the Maze was just as challenging as that to the center. lower entrance to Piedmont Park. Havens developed a lane from Grand Avenue to the Maze and on to the park paths. He lined it with palm trees, some of which still survive on what is now Palm Drive. The Maze from 1904 is now the location of the high school’s Witter Field. One year after the 1906 earthquake and fire in San Francisco, Havens added more attractions to Piedmont Park. Many refugees from San Francisco fled to the East Bay, and Havens wanted to draw them to Piedmont and sell them property for building homes. In keeping with the Victorian interest in the exotic, Havens added a Japanese Tea House. Built as a replica of the late-fifteenth century Silver Pavilion in Kyoto, Japan, the teahouse opened in 1907 where today’s Japanese Tea House stands. (The current tea house was moved to Piedmont Park in 1976 from an estate where Piedmont Middle School now stands.) A Japanese gate led to a Japanese-style garden with ponds and a moon bridge. Stickwork fences, pillars and benches complemented these Japanese grounds. Also in 1907, Havens built his Piedmont Art Gallery on the site of today’s tennis courts in the park. The spacious art gallery had a large skylight and was built to display Havens’ collection of 375 pieces of art by English, French, Russian, American and other painters. Two additional gallery wings extended beyond the main gallery. Eleven countries in all were represented by this collection. The centerpieces of Havens’ collection were 162 large Russian masterpieces that were exhibited at the 1904 St. Louis Exposition. After the exposition, the paintings were stored in Canada. In order to avoid paying customs This rustic teahouse was built near today’s bus shelter. fees on the paintings, they were unscrupulously appraised far below their value. Havens and his agent then snatched them up at a fraction of their worth. Havens was particularly fond of California impressionists, and his collection also included work by William Keith, Charles Rollo Peters, Gordon Couts, Thomas Hill, Xavier Martinez and others. Xavier Martinez and Gordon Couts lived and painted in Piedmont at this time. Havens’ art collection was said to be one of the finest collections in the country. Havens charged admission to the Art Gallery, and artist Richard Partington, Havens’ sister-in-law Carrie Sterling and son Seyd Havens served successively as curators of the gallery. In 1916, Havens had plans to develop the park into residential home sites. He sent his paintings to San Francisco where they were auctioned off. Some paintings went to private collectors, some to the new Oakland Art Museum, and many went to the de Young Museum in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, May 31, 2023 The History of Piedmont By Gail G. Lombardi When Frank C. Havens opened Piedmont Park in 1898, only the Clubhouse, the rustic teahouse, the mineral springs and the beauty of the ravine, waterfalls and wandering paths were there to attract visitors to the park. Havens continued to add more attractions to draw visitors to Piedmont Park and to the city itself. Many visitors enjoyed the weather and views and decided to build their homes here. Frank Havens and his Realty Syndicate was there to sell them a home site. In 1904 he built “The Maze.” Gardeners planted a large circular hedge maze in the natural bowl where Witter Field stands today. This privet maze challenged all who entered to reach the bright red pagoda at the center. Ladders strategically placed throughout the Maze allowed those feeling hopelessly lost to climb a ladder to the top of the hedge and get their bearings. And true to the nature and design of mazes, the Maze in Piedmont was a double challenge; the return trip out of the Maze was just as challenging as that to the center. By this time, there was a lower entrance to Piedmont Park. Havens developed a lane from Grand Avenue to the Maze and on to the park paths. He lined it with palm trees, some of which still survive on what is now Palm Drive. The Maze from 1904 is now the location of the high school’s Witter Field. An early 20th century look at Piedmont Park One year after the 1906 earthquake and fire in San Francisco, Havens added more attractions to Piedmont Park. Many refugees from San Francisco fled to the East Bay, and Havens wanted to draw them to Piedmont and sell them property for building homes. In keeping with the Victorian interest in the exotic, Havens added a Japanese Tea House. Built as a replica of the late-fifteenth century Silver Pavilion in Kyoto, Japan, the teahouse opened in 1907 where today’s Japanese Tea House stands. (The current tea house was moved to Piedmont Park in 1976 from an estate where Piedmont Middle School now stands.) A Japanese gate led to a Japanese-style garden with ponds and a moon bridge. Stickwork fences, pillars and benches complemented these Japanese grounds. Also in 1907, Havens built his Piedmont Art Gallery on the site of today’s tennis courts in the park. The spacious art gallery had a large skylight and was built to display Havens’ collection of 375 pieces of art by English, French, Russian, American and other painters. Two additional gallery wings extended beyond the main gallery. Eleven countries in all were represented by this collection. The centerpieces of Havens’ collection were 162 large Russian masterpieces that were exhibited at the 1904 St. Louis Exposition. After the exposition, the paintings were stored in Canada. In order to avoid paying customs This rustic teahouse was built near today’s bus shelter. fees on the paintings, they were unscrupulously appraised far below their value. Havens and his agent then snatched them up at a fraction of their worth. Havens was particularly fond of California impressionists, and his collection also included work by William Keith, Charles Rollo Peters, Gordon Couts, Thomas Hill, Xavier Martinez and others. Xavier Martinez and Gordon Couts lived and painted in Piedmont at this time. Havens’ art collection was said to be one of the finest collections in the country. Havens charged admission to the Art Gallery, and artist Richard Partington, Havens’ sister-in-law Carrie Sterling and son Seyd Havens served successively as curators of the gallery. In 1916, Havens had plans to develop the park into residential home sites. He sent his paintings to San Francisco where they were auctioned off. Some paintings went to private collectors, some to the new Oakland Art Museum, and many went to the de Young Museum in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park. If you enjoy reading these history columns twice monthly, consider becoming a member of the Piedmont Historical Society and receiving the annual newsletter. For more information on Piedmont’s history and the Historical Society, see: Piedmonthistorical. org, or contact Gail Lombardi at lombardg@pacbell.net. articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group had two destinations for their weekly walk last on May 24. They were aware of the recent assaults of older adults, and they wanted to attend a public meeting on safety by Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. They decided to take a short walk to Sierra, Caperton, and Guilford Avenues and be back at the Community Hall by 11:15 for Bowers’ talk. Milt Edelin and his wife, Yvonne, who live on Sierra, offered to have the group visit their gardens. The group could also get a peek of a special room in their house based on the design in Marie Antoinette’s Le Petit Trianon outside of Paris, and it was added to their house in the 1920s. As the group made its way on Sierra, the walkers noted the street’s lovely homes, some of which were designed by Julia Morgan in the early 20th Century. Milt and Yvonne took the walkers up their driveway past the front yard garden to more flowers along the house’s side and back. They peeked into the house and saw a room that is a recreation of French history. Marie Antoinette would feel at home in the beautiful sitting room with its amazing ceiling. The walkers then walked Caperton and Guilford Avenues to the Community Hall for the safety presentation. The hall was quickly filling and soon more than 100 people were ready for the safety discussion. Seniors group leader Janet Epstein welcomed everyone and introduced Chief Bowers. He provided information on the recent Piedmont robberies, and described how surveillance cameras and the city’s car license plate readers are powerful tools. He described his officers’ response to the crimes and complimented the Oakland Police Department for their work. He said he and his officers take what happened in the city personally, and he wanted residents to know Piedmont Police will respond to their calls and protect them. He said we cannot let what happened keep us from living our lives, but we can take precautions. People should be aware of the time of day, consider the routes they are taking, and let people know where they are going. If confronted, people should give up possessions and extricate themselves for the situations as quickly as possible. Catalytic converter thieves are a big problem now, and they carry weapons. People should not confront them, but rather call the police. Chief Bowers also said more license plate readers are coming to Piedmont, and he is creating a “Cop on the Block” program with officers, including himself, walking all of Piedmont streets. He also introduced Commander Lisa Douglas, who heads PPD’s dispatch center. She also provided helpful information on how to best call in issues. Many attendee questions were then taken. Everyone agreed it was an excellent, informative discussion. The walkers appreciated Janet Epstein and the Seniors group for scheduling it, and the great work Chief Bowers and his team are doing. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Public safety was clearly on the minds of the Wednesday Walkers and a large turnout of 55 walkers was on hand on May 24. Among those participating were: Albert Chen, Sarah Johnson, Nadine Guffanti, Karin Fetherston, Charlene Louie, Jim Kuo, Alicia Rivera, Larry Olsen, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Gloria DaSilva, Quincy Dong, Martin Levy, Rob Smith, Stella Houston, Tina Shum, Noemi Alvarado, Helen Dong, Edith Lee, Greg Slatoff, Mike Henn, Judy Love, Karen Palmer, Carole Lyons, Harriette Louie, Winston Lee, Brenda Ferrero, Phil Witte, Peggy Schultz, Jane Holland with K-9 best friend Sasha, Tatum Boyle, Adriene Hamlin, Jim Kellogg, Ian Morgan, Nancy Olsen, Milt Edelin, Joanne Larson, Ann Quinby, Judith Lee, Elizabeth Richter, Kathy Rolefson, Helene Farber, Fangfang Lai, Pat Keller, Alissa Quan, Jennifer Peltzer, Ken Moy, Greg Keller, Vincent Fisher, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Helen Goldberg and Nava Shahan who were walking with the group for the first time. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I just upgraded my iPhone to the latest software, and it seems that my battery life has really gone down. The phone is less than a year old, so I don’t understand why it goes down so fast. Do you have any advice? Bradford K., Piedmont Dear Bradford: It’s not unusual for the battery to be drained for a while during an operating system update, just like on your computer, Spotlight on your iPhone has to re-index after an update. And the more things like photos, notes, email you have on your phone, the longer this can take. There are also processes that help the update be completed and this can be a battery drain for a while. It should even out eventually. But it’s wise to make sure that some settings you have aren’t causing unnecessary drain on your iPhone battery. 1. Check which apps are using a high percentage: Go to Settings/Battery/ and scroll down to see which apps are using the most battery. Also, while you are there, check Battery Health & Charging to make sure your battery capacity is still operating well relative to when it was new. If the capacity is less than 80%, it may be time to get a new phone or battery. 2. Go to Settings/ Display & Brightness (or swipe down diagonally from right to left to bring up the control center) and turn your brightness down. Operating at full brightness can really eat up your battery. 3. Turn off Raise to Wake, also in Settings/ Display & Brightness, and make sure the Raise to Wake button is off (gray). While you are there, make sure Auto lock is set to a reasonable time (2 or 3 minutes). Shorter time is best for battery health. 4. Turn on Auto Brightness. This setting adjusts your screen brightness according to the levels of ambient light. To do this go to: Settings/Accessibility/ Display and Text Size and scroll to the bottom, and switch on Auto-Brightness. 5. Turn off Background App Refresh: Go to Settings/General/ Background App Refresh and toggle it off. This means apps will not refresh until you turn them on, and most of the time you won’t even notice a difference, except you will notice better battery performance. 6. Use Low Power Mode. This is useful if you were running out of battery in a place where you don’t have a charging station. It’s suspense background activity and other processes on the phone to help extend battery life. To enable this, go to: Settings/Battery /Low Power Mode. 7. Turn off keyboard haptics. Anything that makes the phone vibrate, including keyboard, haptics, can drain the battery. To disable this, go to Settings/Sounds & Haptics and make sure Keyboard Feedback is set to “None”. Unless you need to have a vibration during ring or silent mode, you can turn those features off here, too. 8. Set your mail to “Fetch” and not “Push”. If you have your mail set to “Push”, your iPhone will automatically retrieve mail as it comes into your mail server. But if you send it to “Fetch”, it will come in when you determine, either every 15, 30, 60 minutes, or manually. Set it less frequently to help with battery performance. This can be done per account, so, for example, if you’re waiting for a very important email from one of your email accounts, you can have a more active setting for that account. 9. Turn off location services for apps that don’t need it (which in reality is most of them). Go to Settings/Privacy and Security/ Location Services. Some things like airline apps can be set to “While Using” and others can be set to “Never”. 10. Turn off some of the System Services. Go to Settings/ Privacy&Security/Location Services/System Services. Scroll to the bottom and turn off iPhone analytics, routing in traffic, and improve maps in product improvement. Also, you can turn off most of the system services except may be emergency calls, and SOS, find my iPhone, and may be setting time zone if you’re traveling. 11. Force restart your phone: sometimes a force restart can help solve battery issues. You can force restart any modern iPhone with Face ID by pressing Volume Up, then pressing Volume Down, then pressing and holding the Side/Power button until you see the Apple logo on screen. If none of these seem to help, it may be time to schedule an appointment with Apple to make sure there is nothing wrong with the actual hardware. Cookie Segelstein is the MacMama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 510-520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com. The Piedmont Seniors group in front of Filoli Home Museum in Redwood City. articles.text: Why it matters as a grandmother, grandfather The term Grandparent conjures up all kinds of images. When you imagine yourself in the role, what do you see? It might surprise you to know that the kind of grandparent you are is likely to reflect the kind of parent you have been over the years. What kind of parent-child relationship have you had with your child? Do you fit into one of these categories? • The Expert You are a guiding light in your child’s life and they seem to forever be turning to you for advice on every single issue that arises. Making decisions on their own is still a work in progress and they always want to run things by you first. • The Tyrant You make all the decisions. It has been difficult for you as your kids have grown into adults and strive for independence. You know they aren’t mature enough to make big decisions, and you wield your power in most matters. • The Old-Timer Your kids have always thought that your opinions and advice are completely outdated and that you’re just not in tune with the world. They think you’re adorable. Every time you open your mouth, your children giggle about your vocabulary, your lack of tech savvy, and your old-fashioned ideas. • The Worrier Your children are constantly reassuring you that Everything is ok, This is normal, We’ve got this. They get exasperated with you because they can’t seem to take a step without your habit of pointing out the (non-existent) dangers that lurk around every corner. • The Playmate Everyone in the family knows you are the fun one. Kids and animals are always drawn to you, yet you don’t know the first thing about child safety, health, discipline, or nutrition, and you don’t care! You’re wonderful, but unreliable. • The Workhorse You do it all–shopping, cooking, cleaning, car-pooling, planning–and you fit everything into your day, no matter what, even though you have always held a full-time job. You never say no to anything your child needs from you or asks you to do. • The Nurturer You see things through your kids’ eyes, and help them be their best self. Your children look to you for guidance, but they know you will always allow them to make their own choices in life. You are an active listener, and gentle and sensitive with your opinions. You are cheering for them at every success and hug them close when they are in distress. These are just a few examples of the many categories of parent-child dynamics that can evolve in a family, and of course there’s lots of overlap. What’s helpful to recognize is that your family’s history of interaction will influence how you relate to each other once your child becomes a parent. What could possibly go wrong? The Expert may find that they are not knowledgeable enough on some topics to be helpful. The Tyrant may find it difficult to be cut out of decision making. The Old-Timer may always feel they are an outsider in a modern family. The Worrier might require an unreasonable amount of reassurance about raising a child today. The Playmate may be useless as a caregiver. The Workhorse could be crushed under responsibilities that they can’t handle and don’t know how to escape. Be The Nurturer. As a nurturing grandparent, you are building upon the relationship of mutual respect that you started when you were a young parent. When your kids were small you taught them good manners, and helped them develop compassion and empathy for others. You asked their opinion often and allowed them to make their own choices as long as they were safe ones. You helped them to understand that they are not the only person in the world, and encouraged them to care about other people’s feelings. You celebrated their successes and were a safety net for them when they needed one. You were, and still are, a role model for them. Take the first step towards self-awareness and think about how your parenting personality may now influence your grandparenting style. If you need to make a few changes, try and do that. Prioritize your relationship with your adult children. When that relationship is strong and mutually respectful, the joyous and loving relationship with your grandchildren can flourish. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Grandparent Meet-Ups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides information and resources for grandparents. Contact her at cynthia@itstheirturn.com. Find us on Facebook.

articles.text: Clive Chandler, 87, passed away at Alta Bates Hospital on May 25, 2023, after a brief illness. Clive grew up on Hunts Point in Bellevue, Washington, the son of Marshall and Helen (Beer) Chandler. He attended Lakeside Academy in Seattle and Phillips Academy in Andover, Massachusetts, graduating from Andover in 1953. He went on to Princeton University, studying international politics and economics at the Woodrow Wilson School, and graduated cum laude four years later. In 1968 he obtained a law degree magna cum laude from Georgetown University School of Law. Clive entered the U.S. Foreign Service after college graduation as the youngest foreign service officer in the history of the American foreign service. He was 21 years, two months old. He served in the Mediterranean area – Naples, Italy; Nice, France; and Algiers, Algeria, interspersed by assignments in Washington, D.C. and with the U.S. Mission to the United Nations. As personal aide to the U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations in 1959-1960, Clive witnessed the chaotic UN session where Nikita Khrushchev, Fidel Castro, Gamal Abdel Nasser, Harold Macmillan and other world leaders delivered their demands and Khrushchev famously banged his shoe. The Algiers stint was marked by the French-Algerian war in which the Arab population rebelled and the indigenous French people of Algeria, led by the Secret Army Organization, fought a terrorist resistance against both the Arab rebels and the French Government, leading to the independence of Algeria in 1962. In Washington, as a sidelight to his normal duties, Clive was a French-English, English-French interpreter for a variety of American personalities, including the U.S. President, Vice President, Secretary of State and Secretary of Defense, and was one of the interpreters on the day of the burial of President Kennedy. In 1968, having earned a law degree through Georgetown University’s four-year night program, Clive left the Foreign Service, and moved to New York City as an associate at the Dewey Ballantine law firm. That year, he and Margaret Ann Eliel married in her hometown, Alexandria, Virginia. Four years later, they and their newly-born daughter, Margaret, moved to Beach Camp on the south coast of Trinidad in the West Indies. They lived there for six years while Clive worked as Administrative Manager and Legal Adviser to Trinidad-Tesoro Petroleum Company Limited, a 51-49 joint venture of Trinidad and Tobago and Tesoro Petroleum. Their son, Ted, was born in 1974. Clive considered the multicultural, multiracial atmosphere of Trinidad an excellent setting for his young family and they all have fond memories of those years. In 1978, Clive was asked to become Vice President and General Counsel of Tesoro in San Antonio, Texas, but he declined in favor of Buttes Gas & Oil Co., a much smaller New York Stock Exchange petroleum company. It was based in Oakland and allowed him to be closer to his family on the West Coast. He helped Buttes reorganize financially, and in 1986 he moved to the legal department of Bechtel Corporation in San Francisco. Clive greatly enjoyed legal and petroleum work and had some notable successes: delivering ground-breaking interpretations of the U. S.-Trinidad and Tobago double-tax treaty, negotiating a favorable outcome of Buttes’s dispute with the National Iranian Oil Company over petroleum deposits in the Strait of Hormuz of the Persian Gulf, and drafting a new petroleum policy, law and regulations for Romania after the fall of the Soviet empire. He continued to work long after normal retirement age. Clive and Ann and their two children moved to Piedmont in 1978 and became members of Clive and Ann Chandler celebrate their honeymoon on Guadeloupe in 1969. Clive Chandler, a member of the U.S. Foreign Service for 20 years and a Piedmont resident since 1978, died on May 25. He was 87. Piedmont Community Church. His community involvement included helping found the Piedmont Choirs (now the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choirs) and volunteering on the board of the Piedmont Swim Club (now the Piedmont Community Pool). He is remembered by many Piedmont parents and children as the host of a summer retreat at Pope Valley where many Piedmont children learned to swim, fish and drive an automobile at a sprawling vineyard property of several thousand acres. He was a caring and supportive husband and father, and was particularly pleased that both his daughter and son graduated from Princeton University, his alma mater. Clive is predeceased by his parents and by his sister, Marcia Johnson. He is survived by his wife of 54 years, Ann; his daughter and son-in-law Margaret and Jeff Hiller of Piedmont, and son and daughter-in-law, Ted and Giselle Chandler of Santa Monica. He is survived by grandchildren Megan and Genevieve Hiller of Piedmont, and Layla and Roya Chandler of Santa Monica. He is also survived by his sister and brother-in-law, Henrietta and Jim Ratcliff of Oakland, and five nieces and nephews and their families. Private graveside services were held recently in Mountain View Cemetery. The family requests that in lieu of flowers, memorial donations be made to the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choirs, the Piedmont Community Church, or a charity of your choice. The Chandler family 50 years after Clive and Ann Chandler were married. Pictured are Genevieve, Megan, Jeff and Margaret Hiller (left), Clive and Ann Chandler, Ted, Giselle and Layla Chandler with infant Roya in 2019.

He is survived by grandchildren Megan and Genevieve Hiller of Piedmont, and Layla and Roya Chandler of Santa Monica. He is also survived by his sister and brother-in-law, Henrietta and Jim Ratcliff of Oakland, and five nieces and nephews and their families. Private graveside services were held recently in Mountain View Cemetery. The family requests that in lieu of flowers, memorial donations be made to the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choirs, the Piedmont Community Church, or a charity of your choice. The Chandler family 50 years after Clive and Ann Chandler were married. Pictured are Genevieve, Megan, Jeff and Margaret Hiller (left), Clive and Ann Chandler, Ted, Giselle and Layla Chandler with infant Roya in 2019.

Also during this period developments in technique sparked a shift from solely repetitious patterns into the creation of artistic murals where the tile was painted on as if it were a canvas. Consequently, much of the tile work began to depict allegorical and mythological portrayals of the lives of saints and scenes from the Bible. Instead of craftsmen creating repetitive patterns with the tiles, artists were painting them as large-scale panels and signing their names to the creations. Another notable architectural element in Portugal is the decorative ironwork seen on numerous doors, gates, windows and balconies. Many are designed in different ways to complement and reinforce the architecture forms of which they abut or are attached. These add especially nice “punctuation points” to many of the different styles of buildings. articles.text: City staff submitted a revised Housing Element to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) on May 9, and comments from the state were due yesterday, May 23. The City Council voted to adopt the Element on March 20. However, the Element is not yet state-compliant. The city released a notice on May 15 that, “based on the experience of cities throughout the Bay Area, it is possible that additional revisions will be requested.” However, none of the revisions in the submitted Element required any significant changes, rather asking the city to “provide additional detail regarding infrastructure, programs to increase housing production, implementation timelines, and program evaluation.” Piedmont’s Housing Element outlines proposed policies and programs that would allow the city to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031. This drafting cycle is repeated every eight years. The revised Element, with tracked changes, is available at bit.ly/43aXR8x. If the Element is compliant by May 31, Piedmont will have three years to implement a substantial number of its programs. If the Element is compliant after May 31, the city will have less than one year to implement programs (January 31, 2024). articles.text: Theme: Remembering, Honoring Our Fallen Heroes After a four-year interruption due to the COVID pandemic, Mountain View Cemetery will again honor U. S. military personnel who have given their lives for the country. The ceremony, which marks the cemetery’s 99th commemoration of our country’s fallen, will take place at 10 a.m., Monday, May 29, at the second fountain on the cemetery’s Main Avenue. Scouts from Piedmont Troop 6 will present the colors. The program will include the traditional placing of a wreath and a 21-gun salute to honor those who have died serving our country. Members of the TOSCA singing group, the Piedmont Highlanders Pipe & Drum Trio, and the Dave Hartman Trio will participate in a musical salute to the fallen. Guest speakers will be announced. Following the program, docent Dennis Evanosky will offer a tour of the cemetery’s Grand Army of the Republic plot. The plot is reserved for soldiers and sailors who served in the Union army during the Civil War (1861-1865), including a Medal of Honor recipient.
articles.title: Memorial Day at Mountain View Cemetery this Monday

Punishing cheating is necessary to maintain the integrity of the learning process and ensure that students are truly mastering the material. Furthermore, evaluating student behavior and participation can provide valuable feedback to both the student and the teacher. It can encourage students to engage in class discussions and contribute to the learning community. While it is important to ensure that these evaluations are fair and not influenced by bias, removing them altogether may not be the best solution. articles.text: Piedmont Fire Chief As summer nears, many of our thoughts turn to barbecues, vacations, and days at the beach. As Piedmont’s Fire Chief, my mind goes to a thornier subject – the approach of fire season, a threat that looms larger each year as wildfires across California become more frequent and severe. The urban forest that makes Piedmont so beautiful also brings vulnerability. The lush greenery brought on by heavy rains this winter will soon turn to thick, dry vegetation. While it’s not possible to extinguish wildfire risk entirely, we can all sprinkle a dose of protection on our community by taking a few simple steps – starting in our own back (and front) yards. I’m talking about vegetation management. Probably not the most glamorous task on your summertime to-do list, but one of the most important. Don’t “leaf” your most significant investment to chance – a well-prepared yard acts as a buffer zone, providing a layer of defense to your home in the event of a wildfire. The first step in weeding out risk is to clear your yard of debris and flammable materials. Do you have leaves, pine needles on the ground or in your gutter? Get rid of them. Dead plants hiding on the property? They need to go. Using the space under your deck to store extra paint or propane containers? Move them elsewhere. Next, you want to create space between plants, structures, and other objects. Trim your vulnerability by removing any branches that hang over your roof or near a chimney. Move patio furniture and wood piles away from vegetation. Prune trees so the lowest branches are at least six feet from the ground, or three times the height of shrubs below. By removing fuel sources that could act as a “ladder,” you make it harder for a fire to move from the ground to the treetops. Finally, keep all vegetation in your yard in good health. People often ask whether a specific type of tree or shrub is safe to plant. Native plants have evolved to adapt to fire conditions in California. But even non-natives, if well maintained and watered, can be fire resistive. Whatever landscaping you’ve chosen, you can stem fire risk by trimming away dead or dying material, including removing shedding bark and leaves from Eucalyptus trees, which are especially flammable. It’s best to not have plants within five feet of your home, but if you do, take extra care to keep them well watered. Taking these simple, but essential steps to prepare your yard at the beginning of every summer will create the peace of mind that comes with knowing you’ve done what you can to protect your property. Even better, your actions will serve as a model for others. The steps we take as individuals have the potential to ignite a ripple effect, spreading awareness and inspiring our neighbors to prepare their own yards. When each of us plants the seeds of safety on our own property, we cultivate a collective defense, increasing the likelihood of slowing or containing spread of a wildfire. Find helpful tools, including a printable yard-maintenance checklist and links to other useful resources on our website at piedmont.ca.gov/vegetation. And remember, your Fire Department is here to help. If you have questions or would like us to come inspect your yard, call us at 420- 3030. Let’s blaze a safer path together. “Dude...do you have an attitude problem?”
articles.title: As wildfire season looms, safety begins in our backyards

articles.text: PG&E workers returned to the Piedmont Community Pool site on Saturday, May 20 to complete disconnecting power from the former Carriage House and pool locker room, work that began in February. With gas and electrical lines fully removed, contractors can continue to excavate without further delays. The one-day job, which PG&E workers were scheduled to perform the week of May 8, involved the pulling of an electrical line which used to service the now-demolished Carriage House on Magnolia Avenue. Although demolition-related utility work is done, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that PG&E “will need to return to provide electrical power to the new pool [facilities] later in the project.” Meanwhile, contractors continue to excavate and trucks continue to haul away soil. An estimated five more weeks of truck activity is expected. The soil is being hauled to different sites depending on whether or not the soil is contaminated. Gonzales explained: “The soil near the [former] Carriage House particularly has diesel fuel in it due to vehicle runoff and old wood preservative sprays, so it’s going to a waste management landfill in Livermore called Altamont. Cleaner soil on the site is being hauled off for what’s called ‘beneficial reuse,’ to be used as cover in future construction projects elsewhere.” A subcontractor, GEOCON, is testing the soil for chemical pollutants and Coastland Civil Engineering is tracking this excavation and testing process to make sure that it conforms to state environmental and building codes. For more information, visit piedmont.ca.gov/newpool. Those with questions about the project may contact Construction Manager George Sanen of Griffin Structures by email at gsanen@ griffinstructures.com. Photo courtesy of Public Works Dept. Piedmont Community Pool contractors on Magnolia Avenue load soil into a truck to be hauled away.
articles.title: PG&E delays over, soil removal continues

articles.text: Piedmont Police were notified by the Oakland Police Department on Tuesday, May 23 that a crew of nine juveniles ranging in age from 12-17 were arrested on May 21. OPD has connected the group to 35 reported robberies in the East Bay. The locations are 14 neighborhoods in Oakland, including Rockridge, Grand Lake, Mosswood, and Temescal, as well as El Cerrito and Piedmont. “In recent weeks, the City of Oakland has been terrorized by violent individuals wreaking havoc and committing robberies upon unassuming community members. The Oakland Police Department (OPD) is investigating several different robbery series citywide, where robbery crews are brazenly victimizing individuals at alarming rates,” a press release from OPD states. Piedmont Police do not yet know if any of the suspects are connected with the mugging and assault of two Piedmont women in their 70s on May 6. The arrest of the nine juvenile suspects occurred when Oakland officers spotted a vehicle wanted in connection with a series of robberies and tracked the vehicle to the 100 block of 14th Street on the westside of Lake Merritt. As officers arrived, multiple occupants exited the vehicle and went into a nearby establishment; the vehicle took off at high speed. An Oakland PD helicopter tracked the vehicle to the area of 6th Avenue and East 15th Street. Four occupants got out of the vehicle and fled on foot. Officers followed the juveniles on foot and quickly detained them. Additionally, five individuals were safely taken into custody at the establishment by Lake Merritt. The investigation is ongoing. Anyone with additional information is asked to contact the Oakland Police Department Robbery Section at 238-3326. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. As Piedmont’s Fire Chief, my mind goes to a thornier subject – the approach of fire season, a threat that looms larger each year as wildfires across California become more frequent and severe. The urban forest that makes Piedmont so beautiful also brings vulnerability. The lush greenery brought on by heavy rains this winter will soon turn to thick, dry vegetation. While it’s not possible to extinguish wildfire risk entirely, we can all sprinkle a dose of protection on our community by taking a few simple steps – starting in our own back (and front) yards. I’m talking about vegetation management. Probably not the most glamorous task on your summertime to-do list, but one of the most important. Don’t “leaf” your most significant investment to chance – a well-prepared yard acts as a buffer zone, providing a layer of defense to your home in the event of a wildfire. The first step in weeding out risk is to clear your yard of debris and flammable materials. Do you have leaves, pine needles on the ground or in your gutter? Get rid of them. Dead plants hiding on the property? They need to go. Using the space under your deck to store extra paint or propane containers? Move them elsewhere. Next, you want to create space between plants, structures, and other objects. Trim your vulnerability by removing any branches that hang over your roof or near a chimney. Move patio furniture and wood piles away from vegetation. Prune trees so the lowest branches are at least six feet from the ground, or three times the height of shrubs below. By removing fuel sources that could act as a “ladder,” you make it harder for a fire to move from the ground to the treetops. Finally, keep all vegetation in your yard in good health. People often ask whether a specific type of tree or shrub is safe to plant. Native plants have evolved to adapt to fire conditions in California. But even non-natives, if well maintained and watered, can be fire resistive. Whatever landscaping you’ve chosen, you can stem fire risk by trimming away dead or dying material, including removing shedding bark and leaves from Eucalyptus trees, which are especially flammable. It’s best to not have plants within five feet of your home, but if you do, take extra care to keep them well watered. Taking these simple, but essential steps to prepare your yard at the beginning of every summer will create the peace of mind that comes with knowing you’ve done what you can to protect your property. Even better, your actions will serve as a model for others. The steps we take as individuals have the potential to ignite a ripple effect, spreading awareness and inspiring our neighbors to prepare their own yards. When each of us plants the seeds of safety on our own property, we cultivate a collective defense, increasing the likelihood of slowing or containing spread of a wildfire. Find helpful tools, including a printable yard-maintenance checklist and links to other useful resources on our website at piedmont.ca.gov/vegetation. And remember, your Fire Department is here to help. If you have questions or would like us to come inspect your yard, call us at 420- 3030. Let’s blaze a safer path together. articles.text: Members of the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWVP) attended the biennial California League of Women Voters Convention this past weekend in San Francisco May 19 to 21. The convention drew over 200 delegates, staff, and League members from across the state. In attendance as delegates from Piedmont were Jennifer Trainor, Lois Corrin, Lorrel Plimier, and Kathleen Quenneville. Plimier, the president of LWVP, was voted in as a member of the Board of Directors for California. In addition to taking care of required League business, the Convention featured speakers and panels on voting and voting rights who drew attention to barriers to voting, what motivates people to vote, and what sources of information voters rely on. Friday and Saturday were full of workshops and caucuses on topics including Homelessness and Affordable Housing, California Water, Community Outreach, Social Justice, and Creating a Culture of Belonging. Trainor and Plimier led the workshop on Community Outreach, which included panelists from the electoral alliance San Francisco Rising, the college student nonprofit CALPIRG Students, and the Council on American-Islamic Relations. A highlight of this year’s Convention was the Drag for Democracy fundraiser on Saturday evening that not only entertained attendees with local drag celebrities, but also gave awards to several local politicians and activists who work for LGBTQ+ people, rights, and equality. articles.text: On Thursday, May 19, the Piedmont School District Wellness Center unveiled its new counseling room in Piedmont Middle School. Dozens of students made their way to the event during their lunch break to check out the new space and learn about Wellness Center offerings. The staff greeted students with a table of healthy snacks and giveaways. The Wellness Center provides counseling services, mental health support, and education to Piedmont High School, Middle School and Millennium students. During the 2022-2023 school year, the Wellness Center logged over 2,000 visits by students at the three schools. The new space at PMS was furnished and decorated thanks to a parent-run Wellness Center Support Committee and funded by community donations. Wellness Center staff will use the space to continue offering counseling by appointment during school hours and drop-in support during lunch breaks. Piedmont’s middle and high schools are very fortunate to have the level of support the Wellness Center offers students. “Our program here is unique,” said PHS Assistant Principal Irma Muñoz, who oversees the Wellness Center. “Not all schools can offer students this depth of mental health support.” Dr. Sari Sanghvi, who co-supervises the Wellness Center with Dr. Alisa Crovetti, said, “It is our priority to put mental health at the forefront, as well as to take a preventative and proactive approach to supporting the mental health of our students.” In a recent survey by the district, parents ranked student mental health as a top priority, second only to academic curriculum. With funding from the district, Alameda County and community donations, the Wellness Center 7th grade students Ethan Block, Quinton Cole, Lukas Toth and Miles Simon show their support for the new Wellness Center counseling room at Piedmont Middle School. Wellness Center and its PMS staff: Dr. Nicholas Saldivar, Counselor Charles Garrett, Dr. Alisa Crovetti, Dr. Sari Sanghvi, PHS Assistant Principal Irma Muñoz, and counselors Linnéa Limón and Lizzie Pfeiffer. 7th graders Olivia Stevens and Hannah Joerger check out the new Wellness Center space. provides two supervisors and seven interns who offer counseling services. The Wellness Center also provides weekly opportunities throughout the school year for the Center’s therapists in training to learn from experts in the field on various topics that are directly applicable to supporting students. Past topics have included solution-focused therapy, suicide and substance abuse prevention, and how to support gender-expansive students. Earlier this month, the Wellness Center obtained American Psychological Association (APA) accreditation, a highly prestigious recognition that involves a rigorous, two-year evaluation process. PUSD’s Wellness Center is also a member of the U.C. Berkeley Psychology Internship Consortium (BPIC). “With our recent APA accreditation and BPIC affiliation, we have access to the highest caliber of predoctoral psychology graduate students to continue providing high-level service to Piedmont students,” said Crovetti. To connect with someone at the Wellness Center or if interested in joining the Wellness Center Support Committee, call Wellness Center Health Clerk Viki Salazar at 594-2803, or e-mail vsalazar@piedmont.k12. ca.us.

articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra, the oldest youth orchestra in California and the oldest independent youth orchestra in the nation, is now accepting new members. Auditions are being conducted for trumpet, trombone, bass trombone, tuba, bassoon, oboe, violin, viola, and double bass. Founded in 1936 in Berkeley, YPSO has been led by conductor and Music Director David Ramadanoff for 35 years, with an orchestra of more than 100 musicians from schools through the greater Bay Area. YPSO will tour and perform in Japan next year, and will perform in the Bay Area Youth Orchestra Festival at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco. Submission of screening videos are due by June 1. For details and registration: www.ypsomusic.org/how-to-join YPSO rehearses most Monday evenings at First Congregational Church of Oakland, 2501 Harrison Street from 6:00-9:30 p.m. There is also an annual weekend retreat in the Fall in Carmel Valley and several Saturday afternoon intensives during the year.
articles.title: YPSO holding auditions for next year’s orchestra

Wellness Center and its PMS staff: Dr. Nicholas Saldivar, Counselor Charles Garrett, Dr. Alisa Crovetti, Dr. Sari Sanghvi, PHS Assistant Principal Irma Muñoz, and counselors Linnéa Limón and Lizzie Pfeiffer. The best quality in all departments 7th graders Olivia Stevens and Hannah Joerger check out the new Wellness Center space. provides two supervisors and seven interns who offer counseling services. The Wellness Center also provides weekly opportunities throughout the school year for the Center’s therapists in training to learn from experts in the field on various topics that are directly applicable to supporting students. Past topics have included solution-focused therapy, suicide and substance abuse prevention, and how to support gender-expansive students. Earlier this month, the Wellness Center obtained American Psychological Association (APA) accreditation, a highly prestigious recognition that involves a rigorous, two-year evaluation process. PUSD’s Wellness Center is also a member of the U.C. Berkeley Psychology Internship Consortium (BPIC). “With our recent APA accreditation and BPIC affiliation, we have access to the highest caliber of predoctoral psychology graduate students to continue providing high-level service to Piedmont students,” said Crovetti. To connect with someone at the Wellness Center or if interested in joining the Wellness Center Support Committee, call Wellness Center Health Clerk Viki Salazar at 594-2803, or e-mail vsalazar@piedmont.k12. ca.us. articles.text: I am an ADHD Focus Coach in Piedmont working with students and people with Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, helping them overcome obstacles and achieve their goals. I am certified in Applied Positive Psychology and use my education and my personal experience with ADHD to coach my clients. This week I am talking about different types of mindfulness besides meditation that people with ADHD can implement to improve their lives. Mindfulness is “a mental state achieved by focusing one’s awareness on the present moment.” This can be particularly difficult for people with ADHD who are often easily distracted. The most well-known method of mindfulness is mindfulness meditation which is where you cultivate more mindfulness through a dedicated meditation practice. This can be very beneficial for people with ADHD and I recommend it to clients with great success. With that being said, not everyone with ADHD has the desire to or the ability to develop a consistent meditation practice especially children with ADHD. I am going to discuss a few ways to be mindful without a meditation practice. The first practice I recommend to my clients is mindful eating. This is a practice where you put away the screens and anything else you might have to distract you for the time that you’re eating. This can help you savor the food more and enjoy the present moment while still having a sensation to focus on. To give this a try, sit down with your favorite meal and enjoy the tastes and smells with less distractions. The second practice I recommend is a sensory check in. This can also be a grounding exercise for people with anxiety. To give this a try, you’re going to want to identify in your mind one thing you can taste, one thing you can touch, one thing you can smell, one thing you can hear and one thing you can see. This is another way to bring yourself back into the present moment and feel a little bit more grounded there. There are lots of ways to experience the present moment without a dedicated meditation practice. These 1are just a few that I’ve seen success with my clients. With ADHD, it can often be difficult to sit for an entire meditation practice but practicing mindfulness can help with ADHD symptoms over time and has benefits for everyone. Erica Monical is the founder and focus coach at MindsGlowing. She can be reached at 415- 680-6990 or mindsglowing@ gmail.com. Practice mindefulness when you eat.

articles.text: Members of Wildwood Dads Club and friends woke up with the sun to hit the links on Friday, May 12, for an all-day golf tournament. The event, in its inaugural year, began with a party bus from Piedmont to Oakmoore Golf Course in Stockton. After a successful year of fundraising for the school, the Dads Club put together the trip as another bonding experience. The off the beaten path location in Stockton was chosen because the entire course is designed to be rented out for small tournaments. Dads Club President Adam Fishman served as the “Drink Cart Guy.” Instead of a companion golfer next to him he teamed up with an industrial Mike Niver (left), Reed Johnson, Paul Kennedy and Greg Wheeler Wildwood Dads Club golfers ready to play at Oakmoore Golf Course sized cooler. Fishman patrolled the course serving drinks to parched golfers on a day with the temperature in the 90s. He also provided them with veggie burritos and chips. The day’s competition was a shotgun start with four groups of four in a best-ball tournament. Trophies were awarded for long drive on hole 18 (Mike Stearns), best golf outfit (Jay Russell), longest putt (Matt Derrigo), and best team (Max Roman’s foursome). “Wildwood dads convened for a day of teambuilding and camaraderie. The event culminated a successful school year of volunteerism and fundraising for Wildwood Elementary School,” confirmed dad Scott Zengel. The golfing ended in the early afternoon just as the Stockton heat kicked into high gear. Wildwood Dads and friends proceeded to fire up the barbeque for spareribs and hot dogs as they shared the day’s bloopers, high notes, and adventures. The success of the first tournament is likely to make it an annual tradition. articles.text: The Piedmont High Associated Student Body (ASB) successfully put on a successful Day on the Green event at Witter Field on Friday, May 19. A cloudy morning gave way to a beautiful sunny day for the school-wide event with music, sports, food trucks and a time to relax before the end of the school year. Classes for all high school students were dismissed at 1:00 p.m. allowing for a full afternoon of fun. Junior Jane Hempeck was the lead ASB organizer of the event, which has been a student and staff favorite since 2012. “I think it’s definitely a good close to the year. Everyone always has a ton of fun and it’s a good stress reliever before finals week. Kids stay for a long time and it has always been a really popular event for us,” said Hempeck. Two food trucks parked near right-field of the baseball field and served free Chinese food and shaved ice. Food options also included hot dogs and pizza. A voting booth was set up on the field, for students to vote for next year’s ASB members and to vote for the student reps to ASB Tech Coordinator Friedie Schickedanz (left) and ASB member Eliza Hammond check the sound system. ASB, Student Body Government, members Jane Hempeck, Gen Hiller, Hailey Marshburn, Lindsay Kottle, Lily Caldwell, Izzy Grimmer, and Sara Broach at the annual Day on the Green festivities at Witter Field. Juniors Lola Bien (left), Charlotte Davies, Elle Ruegg, Kate Meyjes, and Laurel Bentley decorate tote bags. The tropical shaved Kona Ice truck was a perfect remedy for the warm afternoon. The friendship bracelet and tote bag tables brought creativity to the event. Amelia Addington shows her voting preferences on her shirt. the school board. The grass was populated with picnickers on the perimeter of an athletic bonanza of spikeball, corn hole, frisbee, volleyball and soccer. Students enjoyed taro card reading by English teacher Elise Marks, booths for making friendship bracelets and for decorating custom tote bags.

articles.text: Piedmont freshman Lucas Smolko capped off a tremendous debut season on the varsity tennis team by advancing to the finals of the Division 2 North Coast Section Individual Tournament on Tuesday, May 16 at McKinleyville High School in Northern California.. Smolko lost in the finals to freshman Gus Grumet from University High in San Francisco, 6-3, 6-1. It sets up three more years of top-level tennis by both players. “It was really an awesome experience. I wasn’t sure if I was going to get into the tournament when I first started WACC, so I was just happy to get in. I didn’t have any high expectations. I had a lot of fun and got a great result… Gus is a really good player all-around, I knew he was tough going in. Almost any time I hit to his backhand, he gained a point,” said Smolko. Grumet is one of the topranked freshmen in the U.S. “Lucas was seeded second and was able to live up to his seed,” said Piedmont assistant coach Corey Reich. “The No. 1 seed, Gus Grumet, is ranked No. 5 in the U.S. in his age category. The first set was the best tennis I’ve seen Lucas play. He was bombing first serves at a high percentage, ripping forehands and backhands, and keeping Gus as off balance as possible. To get there, Lucas defeated Alexander Steele of International in San Francisco in three-sets after dropping the first set, powering back to a strong 4-6, 6-0, 6-3 victory. “That was an interesting match because we’ve played a lot in tournaments and we’ve become friends. He’s a tough players, it was a little bit of a grudge match. I started the first set a little slow and then the wind started to pick up. I began using that to my advantage because low-slices work really well with the wind. I began implementing that and got into longer rallies,” said Smolko. The previous day, May 15, Smolko beat Bela Randles of Arcata in the first round in straight sets, 6-1, 6-1, then smoked Bishop O’Dowd’s Nea Freshman Lucas Smolko holds the second-place tennis banner he won for Piedmont High School. Chai in straight sets, 6-3, 6-0. Smolko’s finals appearance marked his second trip to a tournament’s championship match after falling to San Leandro’s Elijah Cho in the Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament on April 29. He appeared as Piedmont’s No. 1 singles starter throughout the season. “It was a great experience this season. It was great to be on a team because tennis is such an individual sports. The coaches were great. To have the opportunity to go to NCS and compete with my teammates was really fun,” said Smolko. Also representing Piedmont was Arun Brahma and Monte Imburg, who lost their opening doubles match, 6-3, 6-1, to Lick Wilmerding’s Saahil Mishra and Este Liu. In singles Ethan Pham lost in the first round to Lev Cohen of Stuart Hall, 6-2, 6-3. This officially marks the end of Piedmont High’s tennis season. Seniors Brady Colbert, Xiaowei Elias, Chris Li, and Pham will graduate. Returning players in 2024 will include a strong roster, with Smolko, Ben Breber, Monte Imburg, Graham Alban, Nick King, Will Tenney, and Nate Welch. articles.text: 4x400 relay team punches ticket to State Championship Piedmont High’s track and field returned to toe the line at the 2023 North Coast Section Meet of Champions on Friday and Saturday, May 19-20 at Dublin High School. The Highlanders competed in nine events and were able to qualify in two for the 2023 CIF State Championship in Clovis by way of top-three finishes. Senior Parker Long wound up winning the 800 meter run with a blistering time of 1:53.80, coming just .55 of a second away from matching his record time. He came in .80 of a second ahead of Joaquin Foster of San Domenico and a field of 12 finalists. “I watched all of the runners in the prelims and I got the sense going in that people were going to go out fast at the start and everyone would be aggressive. My strategy was to let that happen, stay in the mix, but not make a big move until late in the race… When people go out faster, that means they’ll have less of a kick at the end of the race. I just tried to stay patient because I knew there would be a time to pass the people who went out fast,” said Piedmont’s 4x400 relay team finished second to qualify for the CIF State Championship. Pictured are assistant coach Steve Zirkelbach (left), Parker Long, Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai, Sam Shelby, and head coach Pouyan Assadi. Long regarding his strategy. At the NCS Bayshore the previous week, Long got boxed into Lane 1 early on, requiring him to sprint from the back up into second-place on the last straightaway. Long, who just started running the event this season, feels he was able to pull some knowledge gained at Bayshore. “In that race I learned that if I went into Lane 1 too early, it’s really easy to get boxed in because everyone is going to be going around you. In Bayshore, people were very aggressive. We were all jostling for position and it resulted in everyone not getting their best time. This meet, I think the field worked better together and we all ran a faster time. I tried to not spend as much time in Lane 1 this time and was in Lane 2 for a lot of the race so that it wouldn’t be possible to get boxed in,” said Long. Long is currently No. 3 in Piedmont High’s all-time list in the 800 after clocking a 1:53.25 run at the Dublin Distance Fiesta to start the season on March 18, which marked his very first time competing in the event. He is narrowly behind The Posts’ 2018 Athlete of the Year, Reece Proctor, and Piedmont Sports Hall of Famer, Gordon Johnson’s 34-year old record. PHS’ all-time top-three times are as follows: 1. articles.text: Could Piedmont’s baseball team be the Cinderella story of the Division 4 North Coast Section playoffs? Seeded No. 8, the Highlanders have made their way to the NCS Semifinals after upsetting No. 1 Fortuna 5-2 on Saturday, May 20. To get there, they defeated No. 9 Branson 4-3 in 12 innings at Humphries Diamond in a game that required two days of play, Wednesday and Thursday, May 17-18. Piedmont will now travel to No. 5 Justin-Siena in Napa today, May 24, for a 5:00 p.m. game. The Highlanders beat the Braves 12-8 on March 2 with home runs by Mike Aikawa and Peter Krumins. Getting the save against Fortuna was senior pitcher Ryan McConathy, who struck out the side in the bottom of the seventh inning. He was also a key part in Piedmont’s 12-inning win over Branson, with four innings of shutout relief. This all comes after McConathy underwent Tommy John surgery on the elbow of his throwing arm at the end of his junior year. He missed out on playing football due to the injury and could only contribute as a designated hitter in 2022. “I just felt great on the mound. I didn’t feel like I lost anything and was in the zone. I didn’t start pitching until halfway through the season and we had tons of physical therapy before the season. Throughout the season, I would pitch more and more in the bullpen to see if I could handle it. I just knew I could go longer,” “I told my coach my arm has been feeling good and I could go however long he needed me. Every inning, I went back into the dugout and said, ‘I got one more if you need me, A lot of it was adrenaline, but this is my senior season and I may not get another chance.” NCS Playoffs In the opening round, Piedmont responded from a 3-2 deficit to tie 3-3 in the bottom of the fifth, and then the two sides traded scoreless innings on Wednesday until the game was called at sunset. The following day, the Highlanders turned a double-play to end the top of the 12th. Krumins then smacked a double to the left field fence and advanced to third on a botched throw. With a 1-2 count, Dimitri Papahadjopulos went opposite field to knock a single through the gap between first- and second-base to bring in Krumins. “I went 3-1 and I knew he was going to challenge me. You never want to walk the leadoff hitter, so I knew he was going to give me the perfect pitch. I was looking up and the guy who was on second-base started moving toward center field, then I saw the ball overthrown and coach Eric telling me to go,” said Krumins. “I just wanted to bring Peter [Krumins] home,and get my job done,” added Papahadjopulos. Papahadjopulos also put Piedmont ahead 2-1 against Fortuna and had a one-run double. Upsetting No. 1 Fortuna The two teams battled 0-0 until Fortuna broke the deadlock in the bottom-fourth with one run. In the top of the fifth, PiedStaff Photo Dimitri Papahadjopulos was instrumental in the two games, recording three RBIs in each game. Photo by Mark Aikawa Piedmont celebrates after defeating Branson in extra innings. The larger accomplishment was upsetting No. 1 Fortuna. mont added two runs with a oneout single by Aikawa, walks by Lagios and Krumins. Papahadjopulos put PHS ahead with a single to score Aikawa and Lagios for a 2-1 lead. Piedmont added three more runs in the top of the seventh with a leadoff double by Lagios and a one-out double by Papahadjopulos to score Lagios, 3-1. With two outs, McConathy slugged a triple to score Papahadjopulos, 4-1. Jack Meyjes then brought in McConathy with a single. Final stats: Aikawa was 2-for-4 with a run scored. Lagios was 1-for-2 with a double and two runs scored. Papahadjopulos was 2-for-4 with three RBIs and one run scored. McConathy was 2-for-4 with a triple, run scored, and an RBI. 4-3 win vs. Branson Piedmont scored twice in the bottom of the first inning with a one-out single by Lagios, a walk by Krumins, and a double to the left-centerfield fence by Papahadjopulos to score Lagios and Krumins. After Branson went ahead 3-2, PHS tied in the bottom of the fifth. Aikawa led off with a double and went to third on a faulty pickoff attempt. A second throwing error allowed Aikawa to score. After back-and-forth baseball postponed the game after the bottom of the 11th inning, Piedmont got the job done with Krumins and Papahadjopulos in the bottom of the 12th. Final stats: Papahadjopulos was 2-for-6 with three RBIs. Krumins was 1-for-5 with two runs scored. Lagios was 1-for-5 with a run scored. Aikawa was 1-for-4 with a run scored. articles.text: Four Piedmont High lacrosse players participated in this year’s Team USA Lacrosse NorCal AllStar Games at Tamalpais High School on Sunday, May 21. articles.text: Photo courtesy of MyScorebookLive.com Piedmont High will introduce Girls’ Flag Football as an official school sport in the fall of 2023. It’s an exciting time for Piedmont High girls’ athletes. In the fall, PHS will introduce girls’ flag football as an official sport, and will compete with eight other schools in the Western Alameda County Conference, The Highlanders are expected to field both Varsity and Junior Varsity rosters. “It looks like we’ll have a varsity and JV team,” said PHS Athletic Director Bradley Smet. “There’s a lot of girls interested and I’m getting questions about it every day. We’ll have athletes from other sports who have been recruiting friends.” The varsity roster will be coached by Piedmont High English teacher Beth Black, with Hayley Adams as manager of the JV team. “We’ve had just one interest meeting and there were girls in that room who were so excited. The intensity about being able to play football was exhilarating. Not one of them has played the game. I’m very excited about the prospect of building this from the ground up,” said Black. “It’s the first-ever flag football team is coming here. This is a nation-wide endeavor. I’m hoping the Rec. Department can start a feeder program for middle school athletes,” added Black. Piedmont will play teams from Alameda, Berkeley, Encinal, Hayward, Mt. Eden, San Leandro, and Tennyson in the WACC and have a season-ending league tournament similar to water polo. The Highlanders will practice and play their games on the outfield of Humphries Diamond. Per league standards, the field of play can range between 50-80 yards in length and 30-50 yards in width, including a 10-yard end zone. “We’ll likely have over 20 games. There will be a league tournament at the end of the season.” Games are played in a 7-on-7 format with all seven players eligible as pass receivers, including the center after snapping the ball. There are no punts, field goals, or extra-point attempts—touchdowns are worth six points, while you can gain one extra point by converting a 5-yard play or twopoints from 10-yards. Punts automatically place the ball deep in the opponent’s half of the field. It’s a fast-paced game with two 22-minute halves, including a running clock for the first 20-minutes of each half. Quarterbacks are only allowed to scramble once every four downs, while defenses are allowed one pass rusher. Defense’s sending two pass rushers enables the quarterback to scramble past the line of scrimmage regardless of whether they’ve already used their running ability within the four downs. It’s not just a passing league as well with handoffs also permitted on offense. “The quarterback can run but only per every series of downs, so we’ll going to be working with that on how we’re going to structure our offense with handoffs to a running back, or even a handoff to our quarterback,” said Black. Staff Photo Piedmont will practice and likely play its games on the outfield of the baseball field.
articles.title: Girls’ flag football a new sport at PHS this Fall

articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team is set to re-enter the Western Alameda County Conference in the Fall after playing last season as an independent with no league affiliation. The Highlanders will compete in the WACC’s Shoreline Division with Alameda, American (Fremont), Arroyo (San Lorenzo), Kennedy (Fremont), Newark Memorial, and San Lorenzo. Shoreline Div. is the lower level of three competitive divisions. The upper divisions are Foothill and Mission. The Highlanders will face previous opponents from the Mission Division, Encinal and Mt. Eden. “We’ll play Mt. Eden and Encinal in our pre-season games,” said athletic director Bradley Smet. “That will be a Staff Photos Varsity football returns to Piedmont High School after a one-year interruption. It will compete in the fall in the Western Alameda County Conference’s Shoreline Division. good test to see if we belong in the Shoreline or if we should push up into the Mission.” PHS athletic director Bradley Smet talks about the school’s football plans for the upcoming fall. He is pictured with Brandon Dicke. Piedmont head football coach Jordan Seiden discusses re-entering the WACC in 2023 and the team’s summer plans. Piedmont last played in the Shoreline Division in 2015 when they won a second consecutive league championship Their reward was to be promoted to the Foothill Division, where they played until 2019. PHS was in the Mission Division in 2020 and 2021. “It’s nice to get back to some normalcy to be a part of a league. It will be nice to play meaningful football again,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “I think it’s going to be good for us.” The team will also play Templeton, Smet’s former team in San Luis Obispo County. Seiden plans to start summer training camp on June 12 and will participate in 7 v. 7 tournaments during the summer. “We’re getting into a couple of tournaments; one at Laney College, one at American High School, and we’ll be taking part in some weekly games at Moreau High School as well. We’re going to be all over the place this summer, getting out to other schools and getting workouts over the summer,” said Seiden. With Witter Field set to undergo renovations starting in June, Piedmont will be forced to practice on other fields and will have summer sessions squeezed onto the outfield of Humphries Diamond. The school is also near finalizing its in-season practice site, with Laney College as the most likely destination. PHS will have no home games due to a $4 million renovation to Witter Field from June to December.
articles.title: PHS football re-enters WACC in Shoreline Division

articles.text: SF Jazz presents the brilliant jazz violinist Mads Tolling this weekend, May 27 and 28. He will be joined by pianist Tammy L. Hall and bassist Marcus Shelby. Tolling is an internationally renowned violinist and composer, a two-time Grammy award-winner, and the 2016 DownBeat Critics Poll Rising Star winner. He is best known for his work with the Turtle Island Quartet, Stanley Clarke, Bob Weir, and local groups including the all-star San Francisco String Trio. Tolling is a regular performer at the SF Jazz Center. He first performed at the center in 2010 in a double bill with Regina Carte and worked with Marcus Shelby’s Orchestra during the Duke Ellington tribute in 2019. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfjazz.org/tickets/ productions/mads-tolling-trio/. Jazz violinist Mads Tolling

articles.text: Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside will begin its “Summer Nights” events on June 1. The historic house is open until 7 p.m. and the Gardens open until 8 p.m. Summer Nights are a tradition at Filoli, and serve as a time to gather with family and friends and enjoy the sunset and summer blooms. Every Thursday night throughout the summer, the Grove Bar is serving wine and beer in the garden, nestled under the shade of the Olive Grove. The Georgian-style terraces around the historic house offer sweeping views of the Santa Cruz Mountains, a contrast to the 16-acre formal English Renaissance-style garden to the south. All admissions, including Summer Nights, require advance reservations. Masks will be required for those who are not vaccinated. Visit https://filoli.org/summer-nights/ for more information.
articles.title: Summer nights events at Filoli begin June 1

articles.text: Visit the Festival Pavilion at Fort Mason Center in San Francisco on June 10 and 11 for the 10th anniversary of the West Coast Craft Fair. articles.text: Show continues in Mill Valley through May 28 Marin Theatre Company in Mill Valley currently is performing the West Coast premiere of Where Did We Sit on the Bus? Written by playwright Brian Quijada, with compositions by Satya Chávez, it will be performed now through Sunday, May 28. The play is a high-octane, tour-de-force theatrical experience that examines what it means to be of Latin heritage in America. The story begins in a third grade classroom, where students are learning about the civil rights movement and Rosa Parks. A young Hispanic girl raises her hand to ask her teacher, legacy and importance of Latin and Hispanic people and culture in the United States, through the inquisitive eyes of a young girl. Where Did We Sit on the Bus? Is a solo exploration infused with Latin rhythms, hip-hop, and live-looping, following that young student into adulthood as she navigates her own history and lineage. Directed by Matt Dickson and performed by Satya Chávez, the play will be performed on stage tomorrow, May 25, and Thursday, May 26. Closing night is Sunday, May 28. Visit https://www.marintheatre.org/productions/where-didwe-sit-on-the-bus to purchase tickets.
