articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre (ACT) will produce Wizard of Oz from June 1-25 at the Toni Rembe Theatre in downtown San Francisco. The classic tale by L. Frank Baum is transformed for the ACT stage by Tony Award–nominated director and choreographer Sam Pinkleton and Tony Award-winning designer David Zinn. “The myth of Dorothy and her friends, and their big adventure, means something different to every single person you ask—whether it’s childhood nostalgia, queer survival, or an unhealthy obsession with flying monkeys,” said Pinkleton. “I’m giddy and honored to enlist the brains, heart, and courage of the Bay Area—in collaboration with mega-genius David Zinn—to create an intimate, intergenerational, human-powered Wizard of Oz that is bursting with contradictions and big beating hearts.” The play is family-friendly and appropriate for young audiences. The cast includes El Beh, Keiko Shimosato, Darryl Jones, Katrina McGraw, Kunal Prasad, Ezra Reaves, Cathleen Riddley and Travis Rowland. For more infor mation, and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/202223-season/wizard-of-oz/. ACT will produce Wizard of Oz starting on June 1.
articles.title: ACT premieres Wizard of Oz June 1

pages.text: Wednesday, May 24, 2023 17 By Allyson Aleksey Marin Theatre Company in Mill Valley currently is performing the West Coast premiere of Where Did We Sit on the Bus? Written by playwright Brian Quijada, with compositions by Satya Chávez, it will be performed now through Sunday, May 28. The play is a high-octane, tour-de-force theatrical experience that examines what it means to be of Latin heritage in America. The story begins in a third grade classroom, where students are learning about the civil rights movement and Rosa Parks. A young Hispanic girl raises her hand to ask her teacher, Marin Theatre currently performing Where Did We Sit on the Bus? Show continues in Mill Valley through May 28 legacy and importance of Latin and Hispanic people and culture in the United States, through the inquisitive eyes of a young girl. Where Did We Sit on the Bus? Is a solo exploration infused with Latin rhythms, hip-hop, and live-looping, following that young student into adulthood as she navigates her own history and lineage. Directed by Matt Dickson and performed by Satya Chávez, the play will be performed on stage tomorrow, May 25, and Thursday, May 26. Closing night is Sunday, May 28. articles.text: Tony Scott, brother of Ridley Scott and director of The Taking of Pelham 123, has a reputation as a shooter, meaning he is a master at creating and sustaining an adrenalin-inducing pace that never gives the audience a moment’s reprieve. Scott floods the screen with a visual disorder that is always on the precipice of becoming serious chaos, a stylized technique that catapults the film ever forward. The story, written by John Godey in 1973, was adapted to the screen in 1974 starring Walter Mathau, Robert Shaw and Martin Balsam. At the time it was considered a gripping, groundbreaking, quasi-documentary urban paranoia film. The new release, scripted by Brian Hegeland (L.A. Confidential, Man on Fire, Mystic River), plays not on old urban fears that were so much in vogue in the mid-70s, but weaves a tight narrative of contemporized, hightech action and graphic violence. Like its antecedent, this updated Pelham offers exceptional performances by Denzel Washington as Walter Garber, a subway train dispatcher, and John Travolta portraying a demonic hijacker, Ryder. Testimony to Travolta’s talent is his ability to transform himself into the quintessential bad guy, replete with jailhouse tattoos, fu Manchu mustache and a rage that is ever convincing. It’s Ryder who contacts central dispatch and when Garber answers the radio call, demands $10 million from the City of Denzel Washington in The Taking of Pelham 123

articles.text: I acknowledge that in my travels I had never heard of the French writer, Sidonie-Gabrielle Colette, famous to millions as Colette, and best known in America for her novella Gigi, brought to the screen as a musical by Lerner and Loewe. She grew up in Burgundy in a middle-class home, surrounded by a bucolic beauty. Her life (1873-1954) was fulsome, encompassing three marriages, a daughter, numerous affairs, as well as living in Paris during the German occupation. The film Colette, while a biopic, is not hagiographic; rather it is a quietly engaging character study of a woman (Keira Knightly doing some of her best work) who lived a very individual life, often libertine in her choices. During her youth she married Henry Gauthier-Villars, a prolific writer using the nom de plume of Willy, some 15 years her senior. They lived in Paris where she reluctantly began to write a scandalous series titled Claudine, each semi-autobiographical, and all published as the work of Willy. The novels proved to be a sensation in Paris. As shown in one scene in the film, Willy, desperate for cash (he spends freely on women and the race track), locks Colette in a room, refusing to let her out until she writes the beginning chapters of another Claudine. If there is tension in the film – if tension is the right word – it Dominic West and Keira Knightley in Colette is how Colette attempts to detach herself from a marriage steeped in inequity. Willy is unrepentantly egotistical. However, it is clear that their relationship is, well, complicated, often driven by frustration, sparked by mutual infidelity as well as dependency, and cushioned by an affection that began as love. Colette also discovers that she is bisexual and at one point she and Willy share an American debutante staying in Paris. Meanwhile, Colette bridles at the fact that her prose, which has only improved, yet continues to be ghostwritten while Willy receives the fraudulent credits and accolades. Finally, Willy crosses a line that allows Colette to sever their marriage and she then enters into a relationship with a cross-dressing woman named Missy (Denise Gough) with whom she travels and performs as part of a theater group. It’s at this point that the film takes on a somber, more deliberate tone. Obviously, Colette is but one act in a life that was lived absent any strict adherence to even French norms. To say that she was unconventional does not begin to capture her willingness to risk all for what she desired as well as her art. Colette. Directed by Wash Westmoreland. articles.text: And so, finally, the popular culture juggernaut known as Harry Potter – meaning the gripping, stand in front of a bookstore at midnight to get the next book because this adventure is just too good – is coming to a close. The penultimate film, Deathly Hallows: Part I, has arrived. It amounts to a long setup, preparing the legions of serious fans for the grand finale that will follow.. Beginning in 1998 with Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone, the books and the films have all defied expectations. Start with the idea that young readers would lug home the equivalent of a phone book, eagerly squirrel themselves away in their rooms and read, and read nonstop. And with each movie, wait in long lines, impatient to see Harry (Daniel Radcliffe), Hermione Granger (Emma Watson) and Ron Wesley (Rupert Grint) survive their days at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry. Legions of young and old readers have all taken the journey with Harry as he has morphed from a young orphan at Hogwarts, filled with uncertainty, into a young man who, along with his friends, now stands alone against his nemesis, the epitome of evil, Lord Voldemort (Ralph Fiennes). If you’re not a Potterhead then this movie will be a complete mystery. Not a thing will make sense. But then, these films are not made for walk-in-cold audiences who wouldn’t know a wizard from a Muggle. What is indisputable is that it’s beautifully shot, made possible by state-ofthe-art CGI, and filled with firstrate performances by endlessly talented English actors. For the fans who are completely plugged-in, then all is wonderfully clear. A footnote: that this story, when taken as a whole, sprang from the imagination of R.K. Rowling represents a stunning achievement in storytelling and is truly remarkable. Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part I. Starring Daniel Radcliffe, Rupert Grint, Emma Watson. Directed by Daniel Yates. 2 hrs., 26 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2010. Now Streaming on Prime/VUDU/ Apple tv. articles.text: Nathan Gamble and Winter the Dolphin in a scene from Dolphin Tale If there are kids somewhere in the house, don’t hesitate to make the case that Dolphin Tale is sweet and moving and worth seeing. The youngsters will relish every minute. The film is based on the true story of Winter, a young dolphin that became entangled in a crab fisherman’s lines and was washed up on the Gulf Coast, near Clearwater, Florida. Seriously injured, she is nursed back to health by the staff at the Clearwater Marine Aquarium (CMA). And so the story begins. Sawyer Nelson (Nathan Gamble), 11-years-old, lonely, who was abandoned by his father some years before, his grades suffering, is resisting spending the summer enrolled in summer school. And it’s on the way to school early one morning, he discovers the bleeding dolphin on the beach and helps the fisherman cut her loose from the entangling net. And it’s then, in that moment, he and the dolphin make a connection, one that will change his life forever. Unbeknownst to his mother, Lorraine (Ashley Judd), he begins visiting the CMA every day (skipping school) and soon discovers a world where people are dedicated to rescuing and caring for marine mammals so they can eventually be released back into the environment. The refuge is run by Dr. Clay Haskett (Harry Connick, Jr.) with the help of his daughter, Hazel (Cozi Zuehlsdorff), also a pre-teen like Sawyer, who gives the dolphin the name Winter. And It’s at the CMA that he soon meets young Hazel; Dr. Clay; and Reed Haskett (Kris Kirstofferson), Clay’s father. But most importantly, he deepens his bonds with Winter, who is now struggling to survive. With regret, Dr. Haskett makes the decision to surgically remove Winter’s tail in order to save her life, and then sets about trying to create a prosthetic tail with the help of Dr. Cameron McCarthy (Morgan Freeman) of the VA Hospital. If there is help for Winter he can find it. How Winter’s life is changed parallels the changes brought about in the life of Sawyer. All are transformed, and in some way rescued in a wonderful, uplifting way. Dophin Tale is a family movie not to be missed. Dolphin Tale. Directed by Charles Martin Smith. Starring Nathan Gamble, Harry Connick, Ashley Judd, Cozi Selldorf, Kris Kristofferson and Morgan Freeman. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated PG. Released in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv supported by a fine cast led by James Gandolfini as New York’s lame duck mayor and John Turturro in the role of a NYC hostage negotiator. The Taking of Pelham 123 is filmed on the streets of New York, in the subway tunnels beneath the city, and within the confines of the Lexington Line car, offering stark contrasts between light and dark, all of which creates a powerful sense of foreboding. If you appreciate the genre, Pelham will be decidedly entertaining. The Taking of Pelham 123. Directed by Tony Scott. Starring Denzel Washington, John Travolta, John Turturo, Michael Rispoli and Luiz Guzman. 1 hr. 26 min. Rated R. Released in 2009. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Netflix.
articles.title: Dolphin Tale a movie to watch with your kids

Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization whose mission is “to make live musical experiences accessible to all.” Since its inception in 1938, the organization has presented the Stern Grove Festival as free concerts in Sigmund Stern Grove, an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. There was music of all kinds, including small chamber ensembles, jazz, folk music and light rock. The only large ensemble was a combination of the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, the Oakland Civic Orchestra, and some members of the former Holy Names Orchestra. The audience had fun on the lawn and dogs were cavorting everywhere. What a pleasure it is to share our music with the public. Happy faces were everywhere. The orchestra played one of its specialties, Tchaikovsky‘s marvelous Serenade for Strings. While we were playing, I was reminded of political satire. As you are reading this satire, think of the events that foment our The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet world. Is anything actually new? “They stole the election,” cried the Democrats in 2016. The Republicans countered four years later accusing the Democrats of fraud. There was no doubt that Russia meddled in American affairs and the election in 2016. The popular vote was close, but the electoral college favored the populist Republican claim. The current news? Iran is causing trouble. Russia denies the nationhood of Ukraine and goes to war. Tariffs, immigration, crime, and national turmoil… accusations are everywhere. Oh, the acrimony. Forget Putin, forget Trump. It is back to 1880. It’s Farmers Market time It was a sparkling weekend. Summer fruits coming into season make shopping a pleasure. That’s the way it was on Sunday at the Montclair Farmers Market. Everyone was in a good mood. Even though I am not a Romanian, I enjoy doing the shopping. While making the rounds, I took a look at Prather Meats. Perry was behind the counter, and the two of us just started to talk. He is a very friendly guy and started to tell me about Prather Meats and how he prepares them. I selected a New York steak, which looked excellent… Beautiful color, and well marbled. His enthusiasm overflowed. Not only that, but his generosity was overwhelming. He included a large package of hamburger meat and another package of sirloin tips. I used a very simple preparation method for the New York steak. A pinch of salt on the steak and a small clove of garlic. I then put the meat into a solar cooker and cooked it for about five hours. The result was fabulous. A simple salad accompanied the steak, together with some roasted vegetables which were cooked in the solar cooker with the steak. articles.text: Dear Jim: I am about to start on a new retaining wall project in my backyard. I’ve received several bids, but they vary dramatically. I’m not sure I need a permit, and the unlicensed landscaper that was recommended to me is about half the price of the licensed contractors. Would it be OK to go for the unlicensed bid if they do good work? –Harry S. It’s Complicated There are a variety of factors to consider when picking the right person or company to do your project, whether they are licensed or not. Some of these are obvious, but there may be other issues to consider that are more subtle, which I will try to briefly outline here. Licenses and Permitting Most jobs require building or trade permits, with some notable exceptions. Different cities or jurisdictions have slightly different rules regarding what projects are permittable or that might require planning and zoning approval that will determine the size or where on the property things can be built. Piedmont tends to be more restrictive, but in many communities work like driveways, walkways, landscape retaining walls (less that 3’), fences 6’ or less, and a variety of interior work such as cabinets, flooring, painting, and wallpapering, etc. are not regulated. Once you check on your specific project with the city, if no permits are required then you are clear to work with an unlicensed vendor if you choose to. Liability and Risk Unlicensed folks are generally uninsured, which makes you liable for any injuries that might occur on the job, damage to your property, improper work, or their failure to complete the project or return afterwards should any issues arise. Since unlicensed workers are often less financially solvent than licensed contractors, they are less likely to stick around should problems arise and may not come back to correct them. Limited knowledge base; scope of work Even if your unlicensed company has good intentions, the fact that their jobs are done without approved plans, design or engineering, or inspections means that it may be difficult to monitor the progress and quality of the work. When jobs are more complex there are more likely to be issues. For example, fence building may be basic, but the details of designing and installing a proper drainage system or the dimensions and rebar placement in a concrete wall, etc. may require knowledge they don’t possess or drawings that aren’t available. These can be critical details that determine if the work stands the test of time. The Bottom Line If the job is simple enough and doesn’t required permits, do your homework. If you have someone unlicensed you want to hire, make sure your homeowner’s insurance covers the project or upgrade it for the work. Check their references and previous projects. Further, have them sketch out what they plan on doing and fact check it with someone licensed or do some online research to validate their approach. Finally, when in doubt, get somebody licensed (preferably with 20-30 years doing your specific type of work) and you will sleep better knowing your bases are covered. Conversations with Your Local Contractor is a feature by Jim Gardner Construction Inc. If you have residential, homeowner questions, or suggestions for an article you’d like Jim to highlight, send an email to jim@ jimgardnerconstruction.com. Jim Gardner is a long-time Piedmont resident and has been doing structural repair and basement renovation in your neighborhood since 1983.

articles.text: Linh Becker, Jane Hammond and Boxcar Flower Farm Longtime friends and tennis partners Linh Becker of Piedmont and Jane Hammond of Berkeley created Boxcar Flower Farm as a pandemic-era passion project. Since taking over the farm in spring 2020, however, business has bloomed beyond all expectations. Jess Myles, the florist from whom the pair purchased the farm, had owned Boxcar since 2016, running many youth farming apprenticeship programs at the historic 16th Street Train Station in West Oakland. “When Jess had to leave for family matters on the East Coast,” said Becker, “we knew it would be an ideal project. As a result, we had a fantastically happy and healthy [time during the] pandemic, being able to bring flowers to our community outdoors.” Hammond met Becker as members of the same team at the Berkeley Tennis Club about seven years ago. “Although we both knew a fair amount about gardening, over the past three years, it’s been a steep learning curve figuring out what grows best and when,” said Hammond. The soil and setting of Boxcar, located in the former parking lot of the landmark station — which has not serviced trains for 30 years — proved perfect for the farm. The land is less than a quarter of an acre, and Becker and Hammond make use of every inch. Since 2020, they have acquired a fertilizer bin with over 100,000 worms, a beehive, a rain collection system, a farm cat, and countless monarch and swallowtail butterflies to pollinate the blooms. Currently, the farm is financially sustained by its Community Supported Agriculture (CSA) shares. On specified days, Berkeley-based subscribers pick up flowers from the farm or from Hammond’s house. On other days, Piedmont- and Oakland-based subscribers pick up flowers from the farm or from Becker’s house. Hammond estimates that 50-60% of Boxcar’s subscribers (now numbering more than 60) have been with the farm since the beginning. The pair has also gained a devoted following at Thornhill Coffee House in Montclair, where Boxcar bouquets are sold. “We’ve grown so much, we donate flowers to just about anybody who asks,” said Becker. Linh Becker (left) and Jane Hammond, owners of Boxcar Flower Farm at the 16th Street Train Station building on Wood Street in West Oakland Buttercup flowers available for sale at Boxcar Sweet peas in bloom at Boxcar Flower Farm

Linh Becker (left) and Jane Hammond, owners of Boxcar Flower Farm at the 16th Street Train Station building on Wood Street in West Oakland Buttercup flowers available for sale at Boxcar Sweet peas in bloom at Boxcar Flower Farm Some of the 90 succulents that Boxcar Flower Farm donated to Piedmont High School for Teacher Appreciation Week, May 1-5 “We’ve donated to the annual Spring Fling fundraiser for Piedmont elementary schools, we gave 90 succulent plants to Piedmont High this month during Teacher Appreciation Week, and in the spring I leave small vases of flowers on my doorstep with a note for people to take them and enjoy.” As flowers have multiplied at Boxcar, so has business. The farm serviced corsages and boutonnieres for the Piedmont High School Senior Prom last April and recently they gained a partnership as florist for the San Francisco Giants. “We’re getting to the point where we may have to start turning people down,” said Hammond. “Although we just keep growing, physical expansion is hard; we’re next to a homeless camp, and the land all around us is owned by developers who would like nothing more than to create condominiums.” But given the historic status of the train station and years of legal permit battles likely to be faced by developers, the duo isn’t worried about being uprooted any time soon. “I quit working in the corporate world shortly after the pandemic, and Jane recently retired from her business,” explained Becker. “We continue to run this farm because we love to contribute to things we’re passionate about. It’s our primary work, but it doesn’t feel like work. It’s supposed to be part-time, but it’s very compelling for us to be at the farm nearly every day.” “Right now we’re drowning in sweet peas, buttercups, roses and poppies,” she added with a smile. “It’s a lovely problem to have,” noted Hammond, “but we still make the reason we met a priority. Even now we’re booking our farming schedule around when we play tennis in Piedmont or Berkeley.” (510) 652-1662 Office (510) 652-1690 Fax info@woodwindowswarehouse.com woodwindowswarehouse.com 1301 66th Street Emeryville, CA 94608 Wood Windows Warehouse Residential & Commercial Custom & Standard CA Contractors License No. 823258 KAPLAN ARCHITECTS

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Oakland Zoo Donna, a 44-year-old elephant at Oakland Zoo since 1989, will be moved to a sanctuary in Tennessee next month. Oakland Zoo announced that it is moving Donna – a 44-yearold, 9,000-pound elephant who has resided at the zoo since 1989 – to a large sanctuary in Tennessee in early June. One of the last African elephants remaining in a Bay Area zoo, Donna bonded for life with Lisa, a 46-year-old elephant. In the wake of Lisa’s death last month, zookeepers felt that Donna would remain healthier among other female African elephants who bond with each other even more closely than with males. Colleen Kinzley, the zoo’s Vice President of Animal Care, said that for over three decades, Donna and Lisa would spend every night sleeping next to each other and almost all of their time in close proximity. “In the week or so following Lisa’s death,” she added, “we definitely noticed a big difference in Donna. She was unsettled, she was calling, vocalizing for Lisa … not having those female relationships is leaving a very big hole in her social opportunity and her overall quality of life.” Since the Oakland Zoo does not breed elephants, it must receive them from other zoos if it is to sustain its population. However, cohabitation with other species, like Indian elephants, was not advisable due to varied habitat, health, and size requirements. After a yearlong nationwide search with the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA), no compatible female African elephants in protected care were available to join Donna. Thus, the zoo decided to move her to the Elephant Sanctuary, a 3,000- acre refuge 85 miles southwest of Nashville. Donna’s peers there will include a 41-year-old named Flora, a 50-year-old named Tange, and a 39-year-old named Sukari. The Sanctuary, which is the only one of its kind certified by the AZA, has 11 elephants total. In contrast to the Oakland Zoo’s 6-acre elephant habitat, the natural refuge boasts 3,060 acres. Gina Kinzley, the Oakland Zoo’s lead elephant keeper, said that Donna would be brought to the Sanctuary in a trailer for a 40-hour journey. Donna’s departure comes as zoos across North America reduce or dissolve their elephant programs. The San Francisco Zoo phased out its elephant program around 2004 and hasn’t had elephants since. According to the AZA, approximately 160 African elephants currently live in U.S. zoos. One African elephant remains at Oakland Zoo: a 29-year-old, 13,500-pound male named Osh. Since he has exhibited no signs of stress given that male elephants are less socially dependent, zoo officials have no current plans to move him. They are hoping to have other males join him in the near future.

pages.text: 24 Wednesday, May 24, 2023 Chocolate Pudding - Oaxacan Style Photo by Deborah Quok Chocolate Pudding, Oaxacan Style is this week’s recipe. By Deborah Quok INGREDIENTS Here’s something that’s perfect for this weekend – but this recipe comes with a warning: May become habit forming! The original is Susana Trilling’s, and is one of her signature recipes, showcasing Oaxaca, Mexico’s famous product – Chocolate. Rich and chocolate-y, with hints of cinnamon, this dessert is creamy but with texture from bread and cherries. Use it for authenticity. Budin de Chocolate Oaxaqueño – Adapted from Susana Trilling, Seasons of My Heart Makes six, 6-ounce ramekins For the pudding: • 1/4 cup dried cherries • 2 tablespoons Cointreau liqueur • 1-3/4 cup sweet baguette, cut into 1/2-inch cubes • 8 ounces Oaxacan chocolate, such as Seasons of My Heart (substitute a Mexican chocolate such as Rancho Gordo’s) • 1/4 cup brewed coffee, strong • 1/8 teaspoon sea salt • 2 large eggs • 1/2 cup crème fraiche • 1/4 cup heavy whipping cream • 1/8 cup granulated sugar • 1/2 teaspoon Mexican vanilla • 1/8 teaspoon Mexican cinnamon For the topping: • 1 cup heavy whipping cream • 1/2 teaspoon Mexican vanilla • 1 ounce Oaxacan chocolate, grated GOOD THROUGH JUNE 2023 GOOD THROUGH JUNE 2023 PREPARATION Preheat oven to 350˚F. Put the dried cherries and Cointreau in a small saucepan and bring to a simmer. Remove from heat and let cherries continue to soak. Spread bread cubes on a baking sheet and bake until lightly toasted, 10-15 minutes. Set aside. Put the chocolate, coffee and salt into a double boiler over barely simmering water. Stir occasionally while the chocolate melts. Whisk until smooth. Allow to cool. Put the eggs, crème fraiche, cream, sugar, vanilla and cinnamon in a medium sized bowl and whisk until blended. Add the melted chocolate and continue stirring until thoroughly blended. Add the soaked cherries, with any remaining liqueur, and toasted bread cubes; stir well. Set aside at room temperature until the bread completely soaks up the mixture, about 2 hours. (This can be made a day ahead; refrigerate the mixture.) When ready to bake, preheat the oven to 350˚F. Bring a kettle of water to a boil. Divide the pudding mixture into six buttered ramekins. Put them in a baking pan large enough to hold them all without touching. Slide out the oven rack, put the pan on the rack; then pour in the boiling water to come halfway up the sides of the ramekins. Avoid getting water into the puddings. Bake until the puddings are set but still moist, 45-50 minutes. Check to see if done by inserting a clean knife into the center of a pudding. If it comes out clean, the pudding is ready. Remove from the oven and place on a rack to cool. After 15 minutes, remove the puddings from the ramekins, if desired. For the topping: whip the cream and vanilla together to desired consistency. Serve puddings with plenty of whipped cream and grated chocolate. For more information and to suggest a dish or food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com. articles.text: Thirty-nine walkers and four K-9 best friends showed up on Wednesday, May 17 for last week’s Walking on Wednesdays sponsored by the Recreation Department. Before the group headed off, it was noted that the Piedmont Seniors group will have a public discussion with the police on community safety on Wednesday, May 24, at 11:15 a.m. at the Community Hall. Sherry Jacobs, a regular walker with the group, had suffered some injuries two weeks earlier, and the group wanted to wish her well and see how she was doing. The group also wanted to go to Dracena Park and see the damage to trees from the most recent storm. The group headed down Magnolia Avenue and were greeted by Sherry and her wheelie-walker. She said it will be a few more weeks before she will be able to rejoin the group. After a good conversation, the group continued down Magnolia to a little-known cul-de-sac, MacKinnon Place, and its lesser known 110-foot, hidden pathway and stairs down to Arbor Drive. Then it was up to Jerome Avenue, across Oakland Avenue, up to Latham Street, up Cambridge Way to Ricardo Avenue and Dracena Park. Near the entrance was an “Appreciation Tree” covered with messages about what Piedmonters are thankful for. The history of the park was shared with the walkers. Dracena Park was the site of the quarry that Walter Blair created in the second half of the 19th Century. Blair was the first European settler in the area and his presence continued with walkers as they emerged from the park onto Blair Avenue. Then it was up to the well-named Bonita Avenue and across it back to Magnolia and the Exedra. Beautiful homes line the well-named, pretty Bonita. One house is a Victorian of the “Jewel Box” style built in 1889 and rebuilt in the 1990s. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. The group was pleased to welcome Lori Austin, Tatum Boyle, and Judy Love who were walking with the group for the first time. articles.text: The city has already begun implementing some of the programs. These include an incentive passed by the City Council late last November to make it easier for Piedmonters to convert existing spaces into ADU housing. The city also issued a Request for Proposals on January 23 to seek a consultant for the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. A major part of the Element, this plan would include 132 new units of housing on 18 acres of city-owned land on both sides of Moraga Canyon, to include Blair Park. Consequences for Piedmont Piedmont is subject to the “Builder’s Remedy,” a clause added to California’s Housing Accountability Act in 1990 by which developers can file an application for a housing development which does not comply with a city’s local zoning laws. Any development applied for under the Builder’s Remedy must have 20% of its units available to lower-income households, or all its units available to middle-income households or transitional or supportive housing. However, state restrictions still hold — significantly the California Environmental Quality Act, a statute passed in 1970 by then-governor Ronald Reagan which limits proposed building projects on the grounds of potentially “significant environmental effects.” Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson has said that the Builder’s Remedy is “generally a tool used by developers in cities where there are available sites or “where somebody has been working on a project for a while and now have their opportunity to push it forward. It’s not really that useful for properties that have no developer interests, because it takes time to figure out what kind of project makes sense.” Under the Remedy, any noncompliant city is also ineligible for state grants and funding for road repair and infrastructure. However, Jackson confirmed that city staff has been “researching the grants we do get and expect to get,” and there are none for which this late adoption period renders Piedmont ineligible. More information about the Housing Element and IS-ND is available at PiedmontisHome.org. For questions about the Element, contact Kevin Jackson by email at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov.

pages.text: 30 Wednesday, May 24, 2023 Witter Field Continued from page 1 completed prior to the start of classes, including fall sports schedules. According to Palmer, work is scheduled to begin on June 6 and should be completed by December 1. Earlier renovations of the field involved converting the grass field to FieldTurf, an artificial grass, to eliminate the field flooding every winter. Most contracts with the FieldTurf company specified that the warranty for the life of its product was approximately eight years. The current field surface was last replaced in 2007, 16 years ago. The renovation is expected to include: • Perforated subsurface drainage; surface perimeter trench drains; a drain mat; perm drain rock; drainage at the top of the bleachers; additional area drains • Storm drain rerouted from its current location under the field, to follow the Wildwood side of the track through to the Bushy Dell Creek manhole • Restored existing track • Erosion control for construction • Removal of existing turf; new synthetic turf and recyclable infill • Hardscape demolition, base material excavation • ADA-compliant concrete paving and ramps on the west side of the Field House • Seismic foundations for football, softball and hardball fields • Goal posts and lacrosse nets • New scoreboards Schedule, impacts Palmer told the Post that the “heavy lifting” of the project will be “in June, August and September.” There will be an estimated eight days of truck activity in June (when turf will be hauled out), “not a lot” in July (when drainage systems including underground piping will be installed), nine in August (when drain rock will be installed), and ten in September. Palmer told the approximately 30 participants at the meeting that, over the course of the project, 400 truckloads would be brought back and forth along Palm Drive. The primary entrance and exit route for trucks navigating Palm will be along Winsor Avenue. Contractor vehicles will also use El Cerrito Avenue and park in the Witter Field parking lot. The path to the dog park will be sectioned off, said Palmer, “along with the bleachers, the track and the synthetic turf field. You’ll still be able to get to the hardball field by walking on the El Cerrito side.” “No parking” signs will be in place on Palm Drive and parts of Wildwood, Park View, and Winsor Avenues through September. Occasional “no parking” restrictions will be in place on El Cerrito and Jerome Avenues near Witter Field. Per the presentation, construction schedule assumes a No Parking start time of 7 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. “When school starts up in August, we could actually get the trucks in there and out before student drop-off,” Palmer said. Palm Drive resident Anastasia Edel, who attended the meeting with her husband, Misha, said “Given that more water will go through an old pipe rerouted into a storm drain, many neighbors are concerned of new flood risks to their basements.” “When we asked why Palm Drive was chosen as the truck route and what the city’s plan was for dealing with noise and safety measures for neighborhood kids or damage to the street after such heavy use,” she added, “we were shut down again: ‘The engineers did their studies, I won’t discuss it here.’” Fliers announcing the Monday night meeting were distributed to affected households on Thursday, May 18, four days in advance. The meeting itself was two weeks prior to the planned start of construction on June 6. Some households received no fliers at all. “Palmer made it sound like a done deal. The discussion wasn’t about why they were using our tax money to do such a drastic project in such an aggressive, last-minute manner, it was people confused about what impacts they would face in the first place. He was repeating ‘We want the voices of our community to be heard,’ but it was so perfunctory,” Misha said. “Evidently they did all of this prior planning, but we were notified only two weeks before the project was supposed to begin. They did such a poor job of explaining the details,” he added. “Coordination between the city and the school wasn’t what it should have been. Given the relatively unpleasant summer we, the neighbors, all expect as a result, the question now is: ‘How can the school cooperate with the city to make neighborhood voices heard going forward?’” Project background Construction to renovate Witter Field’s turf and irrigation system was approved by the Piedmont School Board on January 25. The price tag for this effort to avoid flooding of the community’s principal sports field was $4,156,933, and a contract in that amount was awarded to Robert Bothman Construction. However, Palmer told the Post, “All in all, we’re expecting it to be right around $5 million. We’re hoping we can raise some funds to pay for things like the scoreboards, which are about $360,200 [and] $270,000.” Bothman was also the low bidder in 2019 with a bid of $3.5 million. Under former School Superintendent Randy Booker, the project stalled and work was never begun. The school district plans to use State Modernization Funds to pay for the project. This funding is tied to the H1 bond, which paid for the new Alan Harvey Theater and the STEAM building. The district’s General Fund will not be used for the project. The current turf of the field is well beyond its eight-year life span. In 2007, when it was installed and still under warranty, the new turf cost $219,000, with installation in two weeks. Similar to the many years when the field was grass, the field has flooded and been unplayable for periods of time each winter due to rain and insufficient drainage. For questions contact Facilities Director Pete Palmer at 594- 2877 or by email at ppalmer@ piedmont.k12.ca.us. Witter Field flooded significantly in 2017, following a six-year drought. articles.text: IS YOUR HOUSE IN A LIVING TRUST? Many of us postpone putting our houses in a trust because a) we are busy, b) we do not like to think about death and dying, and c) we do not fully understand the consequences of not having our assets in a living trust. California is a probate state. The probate process is lengthy, expensive, and complex; especially if there are disputes among beneficiaries. By placing our homes in a trust, we can control the distribution of funds from our estate, and ensure that our estate does not unnecessarily spend money on attorneys, court fees, appraisal fees, and other professional fees which can greatly reduce the estate’s overall value. If an estate goes through probate, here is the schedule of attorney fees for “ordinary services:” 1. Four percent on the first $100,000 2. Three percent on the next $100,000 3. Two percent on the next $800,000 4. One percent on the next $9,000,000 5. One-half of one percent on the next $15,000,000 6. Above $25,000,000, a reasonable amount will determined by the court (Source: Probate Code, https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/) We calculated the base amount an estate would likely pay in probate attorney fees if we had a $1,000,000 estate and a $5,000,000 estate: • $1,000,000 estate would pay $23,000 • $5,000,000 estate would pay $63,000 Yet, the cost to the estate goes well beyond the basic probate attorney fees. The cost also includes months of lost time dealing with the probate court system, appraisals, and professional service fees that may be required. Further, an estate may be assigned a real estate agent who is more inclined to turn properties quickly than ensure that heirs receive the maximum sales price. This could lead to a loss of hundreds of thousands of dollars for the estate. The cost of putting property and assets into a revocable trust typically runs $2,000 - $4,000. The process often takes 2 - 4 weeks and includes 2 - 3 attorney meetings. “Death is the ultimate surprise, but it shouldn’t be a surprise that it’s a surprise.” ADDITIONAL TRUST BENEFITS Tax Benefits There may be ways to reduce estate taxes and gift taxes to help minimize the capital gains taxes on property sales. Protection from Creditors A trust may be able to help shield assets from potential lawsuits or other legal actions. Privacy Avoiding Conservatorship Placing a house and assets in a trust can help to keep financial affairs private and out of the public record. With a properly structured trust, a trust-designated trustee can manage assets rather than a court-appointed conservator. Faster Asset Distribution Assets in a trust can typically be distributed to beneficiaries much more quickly than assets that go through probate. Flexibility Trusts offer flexibility in terms of how assets are managed and distributed. Trusts can be updated as needed as long as the trustee is mentally competent. Protection for Blended Families For families with children from previous marriages, a trust can help ensure that assets are distributed amongst beneficiaries as desired. pages.text: Piedmont Estate Update May 2023 IS YOUR HOUSE IN A LIVING TRUST? Many of us postpone putting our houses in a trust because a) we are busy, b) we do not like to think about death and dying, and c) we do not fully understand the consequences of not having our assets in a living trust. California is a probate state. The probate process is lengthy, expensive, and complex; especially if there are disputes among beneficiaries. By placing our homes in a trust, we can control the distribution of funds from our estate, and ensure that our estate does not unnecessarily spend money on attorneys, court fees, appraisal fees, and other professional fees which can greatly reduce the estate’s overall value. If an estate goes through probate, here is the schedule of attorney fees for “ordinary services:” 1. Four percent on the first $100,000 2. Three percent on the next $100,000 3. Two percent on the next $800,000 4. One percent on the next $9,000,000 5. One-half of one percent on the next $15,000,000 6. Above $25,000,000, a reasonable amount will determined by the court (Source: Probate Code, https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/) We calculated the base amount an estate would likely pay in probate attorney fees if we had a $1,000,000 estate and a $5,000,000 estate: • $1,000,000 estate would pay $23,000 • $5,000,000 estate would pay $63,000 Yet, the cost to the estate goes well beyond the basic probate attorney fees. The cost also includes months of lost time dealing with the probate court system, appraisals, and professional service fees that may be required. Further, an estate may be assigned a real estate agent who is more inclined to turn properties quickly than ensure that heirs receive the maximum sales price. This could lead to a loss of hundreds of thousands of dollars for the estate. The cost of putting property and assets into a revocable trust typically runs $2,000 - $4,000. The process often takes 2 - 4 weeks and includes 2 - 3 attorney meetings. “Death is the ultimate surprise, but it shouldn’t be a surprise that it’s a surprise.” - Michael Altshuler ADDITIONAL TRUST BENEFITS Tax Benefits There may be ways to reduce estate taxes and gift taxes to help minimize the capital gains taxes on property sales. Protection from Creditors A trust may be able to help shield assets from potential lawsuits or other legal actions. Privacy Avoiding Conservatorship Placing a house and assets in a trust can help to keep financial affairs private and out of the public record. With a properly structured trust, a trust-designated trustee can manage assets rather than a court-appointed conservator. Faster Asset Distribution Assets in a trust can typically be distributed to beneficiaries much more quickly than assets that go through probate. Flexibility Trusts offer flexibility in terms of how assets are managed and distributed. Trusts can be updated as needed as long as the trustee is mentally competent. Protection for Blended Families For families with children from previous marriages, a trust can help ensure that assets are distributed amongst beneficiaries as desired. Avoiding Ancillary Probate Ancillary probate is required when the estate owns property in a state other than the state of residence, and can be costly and time-consuming. By placing out-of-state property in a trust, ancillary probate can be avoided. “The importance of holding assets, including real property, in a trust, is significant,” says Kenneth Hecht, an attorney with Knox Ricksen, LLP. “In addition to the savings in avoiding the time, expense, and inconvenience of probate proceedings, a revocable estate planning trust allows the trustee to manage, and if needed, sell the trust assets both during the lives of, and upon the death of, the creators (or Grantors) without court involvement.” SALES IN APRIL BY CITY April 2022 vs April 2023 Dedicated to clients, culture, and community, Calia Homes is a team of exceptional real estate professionals who work together with the common goal of providing unparalleled client services in a supportive and collaborative environment. articles.text: Two Piedmont women in their 70s were attacked in separate incidents 11 minutes apart by a group of three male and two female juveniles on Saturday, May 6, at around 6:00 p.m. Both women were knocked to the ground then kicked and beaten by teens 14-18 years old who jumped out of a stolen 2019 black Hyundai Kona. The first victim was walking on Magnolia Avenue just before 6:00 p.m. in front of the high school, when four Black juveniles got out of the car, knocked her over and proceeded to kick and hit her on the ground for around five minutes. She suffered a broken pelvis and multiple contusions and bruises on her legs and arms. Piedmont police responded and she was taken to the hospital by Piedmont paramedics. Roughly 11 minutes later, another report was received by police dispatch of a similar attack – juveniles, both boys and girls, who got out of a black SUV and attacked a woman on El Cerrito Avenue who was in front of her house. The second victim said she was “struck in the head with a closed fist which caused her to fall to the sidewalk.” She suffered several injuries to the face and head and was taken by paramedics to a hospital. Both victims have been released and are back at home. The first victim on Magnolia is a retired Oakland and Berkeley school teacher. She also used to work at Juvenile Hall, so she considers herself knowledgeable about being aware of her surroundings. She considers herself lucky that her injuries were not worse. She gave the following account to the Post: “I was walking up Magnolia and I saw a black SUV pass me and park on the corner of Jerome facing the field. I didn’t think anything of it. Then I got to the middle school, the black SUV passed me again, and pulled over by the high school entrance. Four kids, piled out of the car and walked down as a group towards the middle school. I looked and I made good eye contact with them. And then there was a boy walking after them. He had a look on his face that I call a smirk, one of those ‘look out, I’m tough, I’m big.’ Except for the smirk on his face, he was a pretty nice looking kid,” she said. “Just as I passed him, I heard footsteps running up behind me. At the same moment, I felt my hair grabbed and then I guess they pushed me down. I don’t even remember. The next thing I know is I’m on the ground face down,” she continued. Her glasses fell from her face, cutting her nose, and then the group proceeded to kick her on the ground and hit her with something resembling a plastic bat. Although she covered her head with her arms, a barrette hair clip she wore was kicked hard enough to break. “They did kick me in the head obviously,” she said. “It did not appear to be a robbery. Their motive was to do harm and do some mischief and mayhem,” she said. The fact that the attack lasted minutes indicates that the primary objective of the juveniles was not monetary. “It seemed like hours while I was there, but probably was only maybe five minutes.” At the end of the attack the juveniles took her backpack. When they left, she took out her phone and called 911. The friend she was meeting at the Center for the Arts drove by, saw her and tended to her until the police arrived shortly after. While police and paramedics were attending to the woman in front of the high school, a call came in about boys and girls attacking a woman in front of her home on El Cerrito Avenue. The backpack of the woman on Magnolia was found by the police on El Cerrito Avenue and nothing had been taken. However, the victim on El Cerrito Avenue had her backpack containing an iphone stolen after being attacked. Images of the suspects and their vehicle were captured by surveillance cameras at the school. Detective John Lagios, in conjunction with other law enforcement agencies, was able to decipher the license plate of the vehicle. The car used in the attack was recovered in Oakland at 61st and Stanford Avenues in North Oakland, three days later. The suspects are described as three male and two female Black juveniles 14-18 years old, 5’4”- 5’5”, and 120-130 pounds. The police encourage residents to always be aware of their surroundings.
articles.title: 2 Piedmont women mugged

articles.text: Editor: I would like to express my opinion on healthy free school lunch. I believe that everyone should get healthy free school lunch for 3 reasons: it is easier for families, it has health benefits, and it provides social benefits. First: It is easier for families because it is not as much of a hassle for students to get out of their house for school. Students know they will get a quality lunch at school, and don’t have to worry about remembering their lunch box. Second. It is healthier for kids. Did you know that 1 in 5 Californians struggle with food insecurity? This means that they cannot afford clean and healthy food. If students don’t get clean and healthy food, they are at a higher risk of problems later in life, and not growing properly into adulthood. Third. There are social benefits. Kids get bullied for a lot of things, and one of those things could be the food they bring for lunch. If everyone gets the same lunch, this problem would not exist. Some kids bring homecooked food from different cultures and backgrounds. If we were to have healthy free school lunch, personally I would try to make what we eat diverse every day. Now that you know some of the health benefits, social benefits, and how healthy free school lunch is less work for families, I think it’s important that we make healthy free school lunches available everywhere and get the same benefits that we already have in Piedmont. Everyone can help by making posters, banners, even stage a rally in order to raise 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com
articles.title: In favor of universal healthy free school lunches

articles.text: Editor I’ve spoken at the last two Piedmont Rec Committee meetings but want to add my voice once again to the desire to have permanent pickleball courts at Linda Beach. I know from attending the meetings that some residents have complained about noise but given that I live about as close as you can get, I can attest that you do hear the “pinging” of the ball – but I also hear birthday parties at the tot lot, bells and clamor at Beach School, softball, soccer, little league, men’s soccer games, lacrosse practice, ultimate frisbee, etc. at Beach Field. I can also hear the announcers calling football games at the High School a half mile away. I’ve lived here for more than 25 years. We bought the house fully aware that we were purchasing in an area ripe with kids and adults at play and at work. A community that came together to celebrate, to support one another, and forge new friendships. Those are all the aspects that pickleball provides the community. It’s truly one of the most welcoming to newcomers of any group I’ve been lucky to be a part of. The group has also been so sensitive to complaints…making sure to park their cars away from the school at pickup and drop-off times, to work to get quieter balls and paddles, and to put in hundreds of volunteer hours to teach the sport to kids and adults alike. Come out and try a game. You won’t be disappointed. –Amy Kaminer REVIEWERS
articles.title: Pickleball welcomes newcomers

articles.text: Editor: The trial at Linda Beach is demonstrating the importance and viability of dedicated pickleball courts there. Pickleball demand is surging, but prior to the trial, no courts were open in Piedmont for a majority of weekday hours. In the trial’s first stage approximately 60 players per day used the Linda Beach courts, a large majority Piedmont residents, and wait times were more reasonable. With limited court space in Piedmont, dedicating Linda Beach to pickleball is more than fair to tennis. The tennis courts at Linda are undersized and the least used in the city. Based on Rec. Dept. data, the number of pickleball players using Linda Beach is on par with the number of recreational tennis players using all of Piedmont’s remaining tennis courts, which occupy eight times the space. We are sensitive to neighbor concerns and are working to address them. Fears about parking have not materialized. The park area has always been vibrant, including an elementary school, dog park, sports teams, and buses passing on Linda Ave. and the bridge above. Prior to the trial, in four years of part-time pickleball play, the Rec. Dept. received no noise complaints, including when families were home during the pandemic. A survey found pickleball noise to be a non-issue. For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.
articles.title: Pickleball Courts at Linda Beach

Dept. data, the number of pickleball players using Linda Beach is on par with the number of recreational tennis players using all of Piedmont’s remaining tennis courts, which occupy eight times the space. We are sensitive to neighbor concerns and are working to address them. Fears about parking have not materialized. The park area has always been vibrant, including an elementary school, dog park, sports teams, and buses passing on Linda Ave. and the bridge above. Prior to the trial, in four years of part-time pickleball play, the Rec. Dept. received no noise complaints, including when families were home during the pandemic. A survey found pickleball noise to be a non-issue. articles.text: Police Chief City of Piedmont As I write this, communities throughout our country have been devastated by recent mass shootings. Just weeks ago, we experienced our own fear inducing event here in Piedmont when a student threatened to bring a firearm to school. The epidemic of gun violence is not limited to mass shootings. Thousands are killed by guns every year in suicides, domestic and crime-related shootings, and unintentional shootings. We know this is our reality. The Piedmont City Council and Piedmont Board of Education have both officially recognized the ongoing and exigent need to address gun violence. Meaningful legislative gun reform on a national level is beyond overdue. The current state of affairs leaves many feeling helpless, at a loss, and in fear. But we are not helpless. We can work to control what we have the power to control. As usual with our Piedmont community, concerned residents are taking the lead. Last year, two local representatives of Brady United Against Gun Violence approached former Superintendent Randy Booker and me about working together to address this crisis. As a result, we formed a team of PUSD administration and City staff who have been working with these individuals to identify tangible actions that could make our community safer from gun violence, again thinking about what is in our control. We identified several focus areas, starting with safe gun storage education. Often, individuals who own a gun assume their children aren’t aware and don’t even know where a gun is stored. This is a dangerous assumption. If you own a gun, always assume that your child is aware and take steps to ensure the gun is not accessible to them. Here are some actionable steps you can take now: 1) Always keep guns locked in a gun safe. 2) Use a trigger lock. If you don’t have one, come by the police department and we will give you one. 3) If you don’t want your gun, surrender it to us. We will destroy it free of charge. Juvenile Officer Hugo Diaz has begun this education work at a series of meetings with PHS and PMS Parent Clubs. We will be rolling out additional educational materials in the coming weeks on safe gun storage and other actions you can take, such as having the uncomfortable conversations about the presence of guns in homes where your child may be visiting. When each of us takes steps within our power to improve the safety of our own lived situations, it improves all our safety collectively. Piedmont Police work daily to prevent gun violence – through proactive enforcement that takes guns off the street, through accepting and destroying unwanted firearms, and through other actions within our power as law enforcement. In the case of the recent threat to one of our Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers schools, the students who overheard a concerning comment did the right thing within their own power by telling their teacher. ter, we will have lost many more people to gun violence nationally. As grim as that feels, I know we can find power as a community, one household at a time, to make a difference by securing weapons within our own homes. Finally, we can and must reach out for help if there are safety concerns associated with the presence of firearms in a complex life situation. Piedmont Police are experienced with procuring gun violence restraining orders and may be able to remove the guns from the situation. You can reach us 24 hours a day at 420-3000 for a non-emergency request and 911 for all emergencies. The police will review the Community Safety meeting they held in March, and will be able to provide some updates on the mugging and injury to two older Piedmont residents walking in separate locations on sidewalks on Saturday early evening, May 6. articles.text: On Sunday, June 4, the Piedmont Community Church Chancel Choir will premiere The Image, a newly commissioned piece written by Minister of Music Stephen Main. Scored for choir, soloists and chamber orchestra, and with texts written by Dr. Main, this full-length cantata explores the theological concept of the Imago Dei, (the “Image of God”) in which humankind is made and the role it plays in Western history. With contrasting sections of dark imagery and shimmering ecstasy, this piece is meant to be thought-provoking as well as deeply inspiring. It will be performed one time at the 10 a.m. worship service. For more information, visit PiedmontChurch.org or contact the church at 547-5700. • Expansion of the Police Dispatch Center $1.5 million from the Facilities Capital budget is allocated this year to relocate the center. Dispatcher staffing will be increased at an “estimated cost of $1.5 million over the next five years.” • Upkeep of city buildings The report includes the need to address the city’s aging facilities. While “no funding is currently allocated to substantially address these needs in the immediate future, an ad hoc subcommittee of the City Council has been named to revisit work performed to date and advance the policy topic with the entire governing body.” For questions, contact Finance Director Michael Szczech by phone at 420-3045, or by email at mszczech@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: Excavators pile up soil to be hauled away from site of new community As excavation continues at the site of the new community pool, soil is hauled away and will continue through the end of June, although trucks have only been on-site two to three days a week. Since May 8 the fence on Magnolia Avenue bordering the pool site has been moved to create a separate traffic lane for trucks coming and going. Meanwhile, pool contractors Wickman Development continue to excavate and stockpile soil With concrete piers for approximately 385 feet of a new retaining wall all drilled, workers are now installing wood lagging and caissons to shore the As Wickman installs the piers, the drilling subcontractor, Case Pacific, is installing the caissons Meanwhile, there are more “PG&E is supposed to return to the site for one final job. They contacted us saying they were scheduled [last week] to do so,’ said Gonzales. The job, which is expected to take “a day or two,” involves removing an electrical line that serviced the former Carriage House on Magnolia Avenue. As of Friday, May 12, PG&E workers had not arrived, nor had they responded to requests for a schedule update which were made by pool project manager George Sanen of Griffin Structures. PG&E removed a gas meter from the old pool house during demolition work in late March, and returned on April 19 to perform emergency repairs for a gas leak caused by this removal. For more information on the Piedmont Community Pool project, visit piedmont.ca.gov/newpool. Those with questions about the project can contact Construction Manager George Sanen of Griffin Structures by email at gsanen@griffinstructures.com, or by phone at 415-858-8582.

Events will include: • A music stage with local performers • Children’s games including a Splash Zone for water games and an educational booth from the East Bay Regional Park District (EBRPD) • • • • • this Sunday A Mobile Fish Exhibit from EBRPD, featuring a 1,500-gallon aquarium on wheels which contains the most diverse collection of California freshwater fish A hands-on opportunity to explore EBMUD utility trucks Beer from Drake’s Brewing Co. and wine sourced from EBMUD’s Mokelumne River watershed An H2O Science Hub exhibiting EBMUD’s latest water technology innovations Over 30 community booths from local businesses and organizations like BART, Oaklandish, and Kaiser Per- • • manente Food trucks from local vendors A Water on Wheels station for those with water bottles to fill up on EBMUD water The Temescal Regional Recreation Area is located at 6502 Broadway Terrace. The north parking lot off of Broadway will be closed for the event; parking will be limited to the street and the south Broadway Terrace parking lot. Advance registration for this free event is required. To register for the centennial, visit bit.ly/3W- 69TOs. PIEDMONT 56 th 4th of July Parade Excavators pile up soil to be hauled away from site of new community pool. By Selen Ozturk As excavation continues at the site of the new community pool, soil is hauled away and will continue through the end of June, although trucks have only been on-site two to three days a week. Since May 8 the fence on Magnolia Avenue bordering the pool site has been moved to create a separate traffic lane for trucks coming and going. Meanwhile, pool contractors Wickman Development continue to excavate and stockpile soil on-site. With concrete piers for approximately 385 feet of a new retaining wall all drilled, workers are now installing wood lagging and caissons to shore the piers. As Wickman installs the piers, the drilling subcontractor, Case Pacific, is installing the caissons and lagging. PG&E delays Meanwhile, there are more delays by PG&E. “PG&E is supposed to return to the site for one final job. They contacted us saying they were scheduled [last week] to do so,’ said Gonzales. The job, which is expected to take “a day or two,” involves removing an electrical line that serviced the former Carriage House on Magnolia Avenue. As of Friday, May 12, PG&E workers had not arrived, nor had they responded to requests for a schedule update which were made by pool project manager George Sanen of Griffin Structures. PG&E removed a gas meter from the old pool house during demolition work in late March, and returned on April 19 to perform emergency repairs for a gas leak caused by this removal. For more information on the Piedmont Community Pool project, visit piedmont.ca.gov/newpool. Those with questions about the project can contact Construction Manager George Sanen of Griffin Structures by email at gsanen@griffinstructures.com, or by phone at 415-858-8582. 2023 PARADE ENTRY FORM We hope your group will be a part of this year’s 4th of July Parade in Piedmont. This year’s parade theme is Paint the Town Red White White and Blue The parade will take place on Highland Avenue starting at 11 a.m. on Tuesday, July 4. . As a reminder, candy may be handed out on the parade route but not thrown from vehicles. articles.text: Piedmont High School art students displayed their creative works from throughout the year in an art show on Thursday, May 11 in the Alan Harvey Theater The exhibit will be on view through Thursday, May 18. articles.text: Dave Ragones, was officially honored as winner of the 2023 Arthur Hecht Award at the May 10 school board meeting. The Piedmont School District had announced the award on March 22, but Ragones, the Co-Founder and President of Piedmont Makers, was unable to attend. The May 10 board meeting allowed him to be presented and honored with the award in person. Ragones, a consummate volunteer, handed Piedmont Maker Faire t-shirts to school board members. The Maker Faire is this Sunday, May 21, at Piedmont High School. “My volunteer journey in town [began] with volunteering in the classroom. [I started] in my daughter’s kindergarten classroom and with youth soccer. It was through coaching these sports teams that the idea was hatched to create a similar experience for kids who were excited about STEAM,” said Ragones. Ragones co-founded Piedmont Makers in 2013 with Piedmonter Vince Monical, while also working closely with parents Kurt Fleischer and Dion Lim. Makers began as a movement to capitalize on parent’s involvement with Pixar and similar Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and Math (STEAM) affiliations. In 2014, Ragones and Piedmont Makers partnered with the school district to hold the first K-12 Piedmont School Maker Faire which serves as an annual showcase of STEAM education in Piedmont with student and community projects. Piedmont was the first school district in the nation to host an official K-12 School Maker Faire in partnership with Maker Education. With the vision of creating Dave Ragones accepts the Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award at the May 10 School Board meeting. a place for students to succeed beyond academics and athletics, robotics has expanded from a single high school team in 2015 to 60 teams and over 400 students participating in grades K-12. In 2020, Ragones and Piedmont Makers partnered with the school district on a fundraising campaign for the new Engineering Lab in the STEAM Building. which ultimately raised $420,000 to outfit the lab with laser cutters and engravers, CNC routers, 3D printers and a lab manager to work with teachers and students. The Engineering Lab opened its doors in January 2022, providing a capstone facility for teachers, students, and the world championship qualifying Highlander Robotics team. In addition to Piedmont Makers, Ragones currently serves on the board of the Piedmont Baseball Softball Foundation. He is long-time Piedmont youth coach for baseball, soccer, and softball. He has built a 25-year career in technology working for companies such as Salesforce, NVIDIA, and SAP SuccessFactors. The Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered their efforts over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. Arthur ‘Art’ Hecht was a tireless community volunteer dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1982 and was very active with the Piedmont Continuation High School (now Millennium High School). In 1998, the Volunteer of the Year Award was established by school board member Dewey Watson in Hecht’s memory.
articles.title: Dave Ragones honored with Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award

articles.text: Chabot Space and Science Center is to host its 5th Tinkerfest this Saturday, May 20, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The all-day event brings together the tinkering community to celebrate the creative, the curious and the innovative spirit in everyone. The Center is located at 10000 Skyline Blvd, in the Oakland hills. Joining the assortment of stations will be the Airplane Engine Take-Apart station with the Aviation Institute of Maintenance. The Car Take-Apart station returns as a classic Tinkerfest staple, along with Cardboardia. Participants of all ages are encouraged to see, touch, and learn about the workings of machinery through hands-on tinkering. Tickets may be purchased at the door or online in advance at chabotspace.org. Members are free. Adults $20, Children (2-12) $15, and Seniors (65+) $10. About Chabot Space & Science Center Chabot Space & Science Center is a non-profit institution and community resource located on 13 trail-laced acres in Redwood Regional Park in Oakland amid the largest stand of coastal redwoods in the East Bay. Chabot features a 241-seat full dome planetarium, interactive and hands-on exhibits, space artifacts, a giant screen theater, NASA Ames Visitor Center, and the only research-level telescopes regularly available to the public for weekly live viewing in the Western United States. Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the Universe and Planet Earth. Chabot Space & Science Center is open Wed.-Sun. 10 am-5 pm with First Fridays the first Friday of every month 6-10 pm. Admission is Adults: $24 • Children 2-12 $19 (under 2 free) • Students/Seniors $19 • Memberships available.

articles.text: Essay writing contest director Jake Lipman (left), with Piedmont winners: Levi Arbit, Susannah Cantrill, Phoebe Kim and Eleanor Hathorn. Essays written by Piedmont fifth graders Phoebe Kim, Susannah Cantrill, Eleanor Hathorn, and Levi Arbit won them top ten bragging rights in the Northern Californian region at the 21st Annual Celebrate America Creative Writing Contest on Wednesday, May 3, at the Chinese American Citizens Alliance in San Francisco. Phoebe Kim won first place for her essay in the “Celebrate America” essay writing competition sponsored by the American Immigration Council (AIC). Her essay was a poem based on an interview with her grandmother who immigrated from Korea. Kim has qualified for the national competition. As the young Piedmont scholars arrived with their proud parents, they were unaware of what they had accomplished until they opened their programs. “When I saw my face on the front page, I was very surprised, and kind of shocked. I didn’t know how to respond and then people were congratulating me all of a sudden,” said Kim. AIC started the contest in 1996; the prompts this year were “Why I’m Glad America Is a Nation of Immigrants” or “What Does It Mean to Be a Welcoming Nation.” At the ceremony the 10 regional finalists read their essays from the podium and received medals and trophies. Cantrill’s essay asked what it means to be a welcoming nation. Her submission asked readers to consider what impact even small choices have on an immigrant trying to find their footing in a foreign place. Arbit’s essay shared an account of his great-grandfather’s harrowing flight from Auschwitz and then his participation in the liberation of the prisoners. Hathorn submitted a poem that created a vivid picture of one immigrant’s journey as a microcosm of the many journeys that have created the United States. The judging panel included San Francisco County Supervisors Catherine Stefani, Aaron Peskin and Hillary Ronen, along with San Francisco Chronicle Education Reporter Nanette Asimov.
articles.title: 4 Piedmont 5th graders in top 10 of NorCal writing contest

articles.text: A Spring Swing for Spring Fling golf and tennis fundraising tournament will take place at Claremont Country Club on Monday, May 22. A fundraiser for Piedmont elementary schools, it is organized by the Piedmont Education Foundation. It begins at 11:30 a.m. with registration and a light Barbecue lunch, Golf, tennis and pickleball games will follow. The event concludes with a combined tennis and golf cocktail reception from approximately 4:00-6:30 p.m. with prizes and awards. Open to all levels of golf, this will be an enjoyable day on Claremont’s wonderful golf course. There will be prizes and games, and someone may end up with a brand new 2023 Kia as winner of the Hole-in-One contest on the 8th hole. “As a parent and community volunteer, this event is such a rewarding experience to be a part of,” said Val Reilly, Co-Chair of tennis at the Spring Swing. “Courtside will be a fun gathering, loaded with friendly competition in a social setting. Whether you’re working on your technique or are a seasoned player in tennis or pickleball, all levels of experience are welcome.” Space is limited, so sign up soon and continue to support Piedmont elementary schools. You can sign up as a foursome or single player. For more information on tickets and participating, visit SpringFlingGolfClassic. com. Tennis players receive some tips from a tennis pro before the start of last year’s Golf & Tennis Classic.

The Life of a Prodigy Juliette keeps her parents busy. With all her activities and ambitions, they are always on the road. They just got back from a trip to Carnegie Hall in New York City where Juliette performed. “She’s the youngest solo violinist to ever play at Carnegie Hall,” Jonathan said. “So, she basically runs us, right?” Willa added. “She wants to do so many things. When she was very, very young she told us she wants to sing. She wanted to sing the national anthem. And by three she was singing the national anthem.” Juliette wanted to perform on a very big stage. “So, we put a video online and then we did get contacted by Reno Aces and the Oakland A’s. She sang at the Coliseum,” said Willa. articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra, the oldest youth orchestra in California and the oldest independent youth orchestra in the nation, is now accepting new members. Auditions are being conducted for trumpet, trombone, bass trombone, tuba, bassoon, oboe, violin, viola, and double bass. Founded in 1936 in Berkeley, YPSO is led by conductor and Music Director David Ramadanoff for 35 years, with an orchestra of more than 100 musicians from schools through the greater Bay Area. YPSO will tour and perform in Japan next year, and will perform in the Bay Area Youth Orchestra Festival at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco. Submission of screening videos are due by June 1. For details and registration: www.ypsomusic. org/how-to-join, YPSO rehearses most Monday evenings at First Congregational Church of Oakland, 2501 Harrison Street from 6:00-9:30 p.m. There is also an annual weekend retreat in the Fall in Carmel Valley and several Saturday afternoon intensives during the year. articles.text: Students and teachers displayed their talents at Piedmont High School’s talent show, “Phantasmagoria,” organized by the Piedmont High School Advanced Acting class and directed by senior Milani Juarbe. The show, filled with outstanding acts and memorable moments, was presented in the Alan Harvey Theater on Friday, May 12. With singing, dancing, and juggling, Phantasmagoria had it all. Audience members were humming along with one act and then jumping out of their seats laughing during the next. Competing acts were intertwined by skits performed by the Advanced Acting class, which added a theatrical touch to the standard talent show format. The skits poked fun at AP tests, sophomores and college essays. Acts included senior Kiralyn Ma, who showed off her dancing skills, freshmen Nate McKenzie and Theo Ferguson singing “Travel Song” from Shrek the Musical, and winners of the school’s World Language Classes Singing competition, Period 6 Spanish 4 Honors Class, with a prize-winning performance of “Ahora Te Puedes Marchar” by Luis Miguel. The Talent Show included students and teachers alike. Science teacher Andy Willats had audience members waving their arms to “Don’t think Twice” by Bob Dylan. Freshman Chaz AmitGuite, who showed off his amazing juggling skills, was briefly accompanied by acting teacher Kim Taylor. Math teachers Auben Willats and John Hayden got the audience to sing the quadratic formula to the tune, “Pop Goes the Weasel.” Three acts received awards presented by Spanish teacher Deysi Sahagen, P.E. teacher Jeff Peters, and Administrative Assistant Darlene Low. Sophomore Daneille Zaroukian’s stunning vocals in a performance of “Quiet” by Jonathan Reid Gealt won an award from the three judges. “The entire experience was so fun, I loved it. The whole production was really great, and all the other acts were really amazing,” Sophomore Daneille Zaroukian’s vocal performance of “Quiet” by Jonathan Reid Gealt won her an award from the three judges. The Advanced Acting Class organized a Talent Show at Piedmont High that included skits and performances. An act put on by one ofSpanish teacher Deysi Sahagen’s classes Senior Micheala Bini’s performance of “Candy” by Paolo Nutini received an award. said Zaroukian. “An added bonus was winning a catered lunch in the park. The whole show was just amazing and I loved performing in it.” The Advance Acting class awarded senior Micheala Bini, who performed “Candy” by Paolo Nutini, a fast pass at the upcoming “Day on the Green.” Bini’s act displayed her remarkable voice, and acoustic guitar skills. She was accompanied by English Teacher Eduardo Wolbert on electric guitar. “Mr. Wolbert keeps three guitars in his classroom, so at the very beginning of the year I asked if I could play the guitar with him and we just started jamming together,” said Bini. The audience awarded a $100 cash prize to senior Ben Kim, who astounded the audience with his violin. Juarbe found that directing a talent show is strenuous, but equally rewarding. “I was very happy with the show. Seeing it all come together with the lighting and sound was wonderful. I keep getting feedback from audience members saying that they loved it.” Senior Jonas Kra-Caskey at the front of the line of Spanish 3 students on stage. Senior Milani Juarbe directed the talent show Phantasmagoria.
