articles.text: An upset was nearly in the making in Mill Valley on Thursday, May 11 at Tamalpais High near the shores of Richardson Bay. But the Highlanders, seeded No. 3, couldn’t thwart the No. 1 Tamalpais Hawks in a sweat-inducing, heart bursting 9-8 loss in sudden death double-overtime. The loss came just two days after Piedmont upset No. 2 Acalanes 9-8, also in double-overtime. With a depleted roster, fatigue increased and Piedmont’s chances began to slip away. “It was a terrific game. We took Acalanes to double-overtime and were able to pull it off,” said coach Al Yu. “This game was a great one all around. The size of our squad and Tam’s was extremely different. To rely on the starters like we do, we have a lot of players who don’t come off the field.” “We went to double-overtime and really didn’t want to do that again. We don’t have a lot of players, so it’s hard to play back-toback long games like that. But it’s always fun to go to Golden Goal, when any shot you take might be the game-winner. These types of games are why you play. You can’t win ‘em all,” said senior leader Soren Dixon, who led Piedmont with four goals. Piedmont took a 5-2 lead by halftime, but the Hawks ate away at the lead to make it 7-5 starting the fourth quarter and eventually went ahead 8-7 with 9:22 remaining in the game. At that point some heroics were required from the Highlanders. “The best and worst part about it was the game was so close,” said Fredericks. I have friends on Acalanes and one of them was guarding me. When we went into the second overtime, I told him that I wouldn’t want this to go down any other way. We talked at practice how we didn’t want another game to go into overtime, Staff Photos Soren Dixon celebrates after scoring a goal in the first quarter. He finished with four goals against Tamalpais. Nate Fredericks scored three goals against Tamalpais.
articles.title: Piedmont falls to Tam in double overtime in NCS championship

articles.text: Taylor, Long place 1-2 in 800; Sorensen-Wald qualifies in 3 events In a highly successful North Coast Section Bayshore Championship meet for Piedmont’s track team on Saturday, May 13 at Hayward High. The Highlanders had 12 athletes qualify for the prestigious NCS Meet of Champions this Friday and Saturday, May 19-20 at Dublin High School. Senior Christian Taylor led the way, winning the 800 meters with a time of 1:56.27 in a field of 23 runners. Teammate and classmate Parker Long was second with a time of 1:57.42, one second back. Mateo Malko-Allen of St. Mary’s was first in the 800 but was disqualified. Spencer Sorensen-Wald (right), a junior, qualified for Meet of Champions in three events; the 100 meter hurdles, 300 hurdles, and pole vault. Jamie Schwarz (middle), a junior, placed fourth in the 800 and also helped the 4x400 relay team qualify for the Meet of Champions. Staff Photos Christian Taylor (middle, right), won the 800 meters at the League Champio0nship track meet and was 4th in the 1600. He qualified for the NCS Meet of Champions in both events plus the 4x400 relay. Earlier in the day, Taylor completed his primary event, the 1600 meters, placing fourth among 24 runners with a time of 4:20.77. He was 10 seconds behind the leader, Malko-Allen, but kept a strategic pace given that he would run in the 800 and 4x800 relay later in the day. Although he came away as the 800 winner, Taylor’s focus at the Meet of Champions will be the 1600 meters (the metric mile). “Today was my last 800, so I wanted to conserve a little bit in the 1600,” he said. “I was with the top boys through 800 meters and then they started to push the pace a little bit more, so I decided to pull back and conserve for the 800. I just wanted to qualify and I finished fourth, I’m hoping to take the 1600 to State.” “I feel like I’m in really good shape. This heat definitely takes a toll, but I know I’m in shape for some pretty crazy times. The heat just means I need to stay hydrated, I made sure to get a lot of water in and stay hydrated quite a bit today,” said Taylor. Piedmont’s mile relay team of Taylor, Long, Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai, and Sam Shelby finished second of 18 teams in the 4x400 with a time of 3:28.47, coming .43 behind Bishop O’Dowd. Spencer Sorensen-Wald had Photo by Steve Zirkelbach Sophomore Ella Yasar qualified for the Meet of Champions in the 300 hurdles and 4x400 relay.

The loss came just two days after Piedmont upset No. 2 Acalanes 9-8, also in double-overtime. With a depleted roster, fatigue increased and Piedmont’s chances began to slip away. “It was a terrific game. We took Acalanes to double-overtime and were able to pull it off,” said coach Al Yu. “This game was a great one all around. The size of our squad and Tam’s was extremely different. To rely on the starters like we do, we have a lot of players who don’t come off the field.” “We went to double-overtime and really didn’t want to do that again. We don’t have a lot of players, so it’s hard to play back-toback long games like that. But it’s always fun to go to Golden Goal, when any shot you take might be the game-winner. These types of games are why you play. You can’t win ‘em all,” said senior leader Soren Dixon, who led Piedmont with four goals. Piedmont took a 5-2 lead by halftime, but the Hawks ate away at the lead to make it 7-5 starting the fourth quarter and eventually went ahead 8-7 with 9:22 remaining in the game. At that point some heroics were required from the Highlanders. “The best and worst part about it was the game was so close,” said Fredericks. I have friends on Acalanes and one of them was guarding me. When we went into the second overtime, I told him that I wouldn’t want this to go down any other way. We talked at practice how we didn’t want another game to go into overtime, See Boys’ Lacrosse on page 29 Spencer Sorensen-Wald (right), a junior, qualified for Meet of Champions in three events; the 100 meter hurdles, 300 hurdles, and pole vault. Jamie Schwarz (middle), a junior, placed fourth in the 800 and also helped the 4x400 relay team qualify for the Meet of Champions. Staff Photos Christian Taylor (middle, right), won the 800 meters at the League Champio0nship track meet and was 4th in the 1600. He qualified for the NCS Meet of Champions in both events plus the 4x400 relay. Earlier in the day, Taylor completed his primary event, the 1600 meters, placing fourth among 24 runners with a time of 4:20.77. He was 10 seconds behind the leader, Malko-Allen, but kept a strategic pace given that he would run in the 800 and 4x800 relay later in the day. Although he came away as the 800 winner, Taylor’s focus at the Meet of Champions will be the 1600 meters (the metric mile). “Today was my last 800, so I wanted to conserve a little bit in the 1600,” he said. “I was with the top boys through 800 meters and then they started to push the pace a little bit more, so I decided to pull back and conserve for the 800. I just wanted to qualify and I finished fourth, I’m hoping to take the 1600 to State.” “I feel like I’m in really good shape. This heat definitely takes a toll, but I know I’m in shape for some pretty crazy times. The heat just means I need to stay hydrated, I made sure to get a lot of water in and stay hydrated quite a bit today,” said Taylor. Piedmont’s mile relay team of Taylor, Long, Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai, and Sam Shelby finished second of 18 teams in the 4x400 with a time of 3:28.47, coming .43 behind Bishop O’Dowd. Nate Fredericks scored three goals against Tamalpais. Photo by Steve Zirkelbach Sophomore Ella Yasar qualified for the Meet of Champions in the 300 hurdles and 4x400 relay. For the first time, this program will offer a 4-week Summer Running program for boys and girls in the 4th and 5th grade in Piedmont schools. It starts July 10 and ends August 2, and meets on Mondays and Wednesdays from 4:00 to 5:15 p.m. at Becker Field at Havens School. Activities besides running include agility drills, active games, relay races, and runs to some of the parks in Piedmont. Every runner new to the program receives a running club t-shirt. articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team gets its Division 4 North Coast Section playoffs journey started today, May 17, as the No. 8 seeded school will host a game with No. 9 Branson at Humphries Diamond at 5:00 p.m. Piedmont enters the postseason tournament with a 12-10 overall record, though it didn’t qualify for the Western Alameda County Conference’s Foothill Division tournament with a 4-6 league record. Piedmont finished fifth in its first season since being promoted from the Shoreline Division after winning the 2022 banner. The Highlanders battled despite having just three seniors on the roster and a batch of players getting their first opportunity on the pitching mound. Branson carries a similar 12-11 record. Branson and Piedmont had just one common opponent this season, Justin-Siena, the No. 5 seed in the D4 NCS playoffs. The Highlanders defeated the Braves 12-8 in their second game of the year on March 2. Justin-Siena battled back to a 9-8 deficit after the bottom of the sixth, but Piedmont scored three times in the top of the seventh. Branson, however, succumbed to the 10-run rule to Justin-Siena early in its season as well on February 22. The Bulls trailed the Braves 5-4 following the first two innings and progressed the lead to 9-5 before adding six runs in the bottom of the sixth to activate the 10-run rule. Branson’s leading hitter is senior William Ashley, who is carrying a stellar .418 batting average with 33 hits, 29 RBIs, six doubles, two triples, and five home runs. Noam AuYeung, meanwhile, is hitting .370 with six triples, and Liam Parrot has five triples and a .353 average. Similar to Piedmont, the Bulls have used a mixed bag of pitchers so far this season with three players with over 10 appearances and two more with nine. The starting pitcher will likely be Wilson Wendt, who has accumulated 45 innings pitched, 34 strikeouts, and carry’s an ERA of 3.89. The Highlanders are led by Michael Aikawa, Ryan McConathy, Will Parker, Markos Lagios, Peter Krumins, and Dimitri Papahadjopoulos. Aikawa has committed to play college ball at Lewis & Clark college in Portland. He leads the team in hitting with a .368 batting average, 10 doubles, while his one home run Piedmont senior Michael Aikawa is the team’s leading hitter and leading pitcher going into the North Coast Section playoffs. Sophomore Markos Lagios carries a .303 batting average with nine doubles, three triples, two home runs, 18 RBIs, and 22 runs scored.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team saw its season come to an end in the semifinals of the Division 2 North Coast Section Team Championship, losing to No. 1 ranked Branson 5-2 on Saturday, May 13 at the College of Marin in Kentfield. The Bulls went on to win the title over University. To reach the finals, Piedmont defeated No. 13 Justin-Siena 6-1 in the first round on Tuesday, May 9, and followed up with a 4-3 victory over Lick Wilmerding on Thursday, May 11. Both matches were played in Piedmont. “Branson was very strong from top to bottom and wound up winning the championship, defeating University 4-3,” explained PHS coach Jim Landes.”Corey [Reich] and I enjoyed coaching the boys this season. We played a lot of tennis, despite a lot of rain in March. We did very well and finished with a 13-5 record, placing second in the WACC League, and reaching semifinals of the team tournament.” Freshman Lucas Smolko, the team’s No. 1 singles player, won all three of his matches. He’s been an impressive addition to the varsity, and reached the finals of the Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament on April 29. Junior Ben Breber also had a strong performance in the team tournament at No. 2 singles, defeating his opponents from Branson and Justin-Siena. “Lucas and Ben played tremendously all season, we’re really proud of them,” said Landes. 5-2 loss to Branson In singles, Smolko defeated Branson’s No. 1 player in straight sets, 7-5, 6-3. At No. 2 Breber won in three sets 6-2, 1-6, 10-6. However, they were the only winners for Piedmont. Cris Li at No. 3 singles lost at No. 3 in straight sets, 6-0, 6-0, and Xiaowei Elias lost 6-1, 6-1 at No. 4. In doubles, Arun Brahma and Monte Imburg lost at No. 1 by scores of 6-1, 6-1. Nick King and Graham Alban lost 6-1, 6-1 at No. 2 doubles and Nate Welch and Will Tenney fell in No. 3 doubles, 6-0, 6-2. 6-1 win vs. Justin-Siena Smol ko defeated Will Bollinger at the No. 1 spot in double-bagel fashion, 6-0, 6-0. Breber also had a strong 6-0, 6-2 win at No. 2. Pham featured at No. 3, winning 6-0, 6-1. Alex Zalewski played at No. 4, losing in three sets, 4-6, 6-1, 4-6. Imburg and Brahma won 6-3, 6-1 at No. 1 doubles; King and Alban won at No. 2 doubles, 6-1, Staff Photos Lucas Smolko won all three of his NCS Team Tournament matches. Ben Breber had a big win in three sets (6-2, 1-6, 10-6) at No. 2 singles against Branson. Arun Brahma paired with Monte Imburg (not pictured), won two of their three NCS Team Tournament matches. 6-1, and Tenney and Welch won the No. 3 doubles match, 6-0, 6-2. 4-3 over Lick Wilmerding In a much closer victory, Piedmont edged out Lick Wilmerding, 4-3. Smolko got things rolling for the Highlanders with a 6-1, 6-0 win over Este Liu. Breber lost 6-4, 6-1 to Soahail Mishra at No. 2 singles, and Pham fell to Joel Collier at No. 3 in three sets, 2-6, 7-6 (7-5), 6-2. Playing No. 4 singles, Li lost in straight sets, 6-3, 6-2. Piedmont won all three doubles matches to claim a team victory. Imburg and Brahma won 6-2, 6-1 at No. 1. King and Alban won 6-4, 7-6 (7-5) at No. 2, and Welch and Tenney outlasted their opponents in three sets to secure the match, 6-4, 4-6, 6-2. NCS Individual Tournament Piedmont sent four athletes to compete in the 2023 North Coast Section Division 2 Individual Tournament on Monday and Tuesday this week, May 15-16, at Arcata and McKinleyville High Schools. Smolko battled his way to the finals, where he lost to Gus Grumet of University. Look for full coverage in next week’s Post.

Piedmont’s continued dominance over Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team continued its dominance over Bishop O’Dowd this season, scoring the most one-sided win over the rival team in school history at 18-1 on March 17 and won its sixth-consecutive league title over the Dragons 14-6 on April 27. The impact of Lucas Smolko It’s always fun to cover a freshman making a quick mark at the school. This year, Lucas Smolko stepped into the No. 1 singles role on the tennis team and battled his way to the WACC Singles Finals and recent Division 2 NCS Singles Finals. He helped lead the Highlanders to a 13-5 record and has a bright three years ahead of him. He’ll be in the running for the Post’s Freshman of the Year award. Parker Long close to 33-year old school record Middle distance runner Parker Long has two more chances to eclipse the school’s record in the 800-meter run. His time marks the third fastest time in school history behind Gordon Johnson (1:51.10 in 1989), and Reece Proctor (1:52.64 in 2018), Cooper Downing ran a 1:53.40 last year. articles.text: Piedmont Middle School’s ultimate frisbee team, Purple Reign, competed last weekend in the Spaghetti Western, a two-day youth ultimate tournament hosted by Bay Area Disc Association in Tracy. It is the largest and most competitive competition in the state, bringing teams from Napa, Sacramento, Santa Cruz, San Francisco, Alameda, Oakland, Berkeley, Mountain View, and even Mexico. Competing in Division 1 for the first time on Saturday, Piedmont played through intermittent rain and finished with an 0-2 record. Seeded No. 6 the team bounced back and won the 5th place bracket game against Baja Sunset 6-5, Purple Rain received exceptional zone defense play from Aidan Stewart, Drew DeVries, Noah Hildebrand, Ben McMurtry, Ari Lopez, Danilo Titterton and Matias Seelenberger. Purple Reign returned on Sunday to compete in Division 2. Wins over Alameda Taurus, 11-8, and Davis Sprockets,11-3, put Piedmont the team in the championship bracket. Am 11-3 semifinal win over the Stanley Middle School Wildcats advanced Purple Reign to the championship game with the Eagles from Mountain View. Solid play from 8th graders Leyton Poole and Ryan Wendel, along with stellar defense from 7th graders Ariel Grossberg and Shane McNulty, helped guide Purple Reign to the win. It is the first tournament win for a team on which no player has more than 1-1/2 seasons of playing experience. “We’re incredibly proud of our team,” said coach Carolyn Stewart. “There was gritty play all weekend and it was a full team effort. They supported one another no matter the score, and they earned this championship,” Photos by Cisco DeVries Danilo Titterton scoring the winning goal in the championship game versus the Eagles. Purple Reign at the Spaghetti Western tournament. Pictured are [Back row] Ariel Grossberg (left), Leyton Poole, Ryan Wendel, Ben Fisher, Coach Don McBirney, Shane McNulty, Ari Lopez, Coach Carolyn Stewart. [Front row] Captain Matias Seelenberger (left), Captain Aidan Stewart, Ben McMurtry, Kai Lopez, Danilo Titterton, Drew DeVries

articles.text: Photo by Chris Hardy Smuin artists Ricardo Dyer (left), Alison Ramoran, Brennan Wall, Marc LaPierre, and Mengjun Chen with the company in Amy Seiwert’s world premiere of French Kiss, unveiled in Smuin’s “Dance Series 2” touring the Bay Area through May 28. We stumble through life and taxes, and then we meet the compact Smuin Ballet which has emerged from the pandemic seemingly unscathed. Its newest Bay Area run showed off 17 beautifully coordinated and trained dancers in pieces new and old, bursting with precision and energy. Purists may carp about the troupe’s leanings toward the commercial, but this group under Celia Fushille offers both sides, serving up contemporary with a capital C, abetted by the new associate director and adroit choreographer Amy Seiwert. The engrossing opening-night program offered the wake-up call via a twin-barrel blast of culture: Val Caniparoli’s earth-shaking foray into a stormy percussive world, and Seiwert’s light-hearted world premiere to French songs so much in the spirit of founder Michael Smuin. (Smuin in early years had actually performed as a nightclub show duo with partner-spouse Paula Tracy – not exactly your typical dancer’s CV.) Seiwert’s piece “French Kiss” showed itself as airy as a sunny Sunday on the Champs-Élysées, with skirts in alluring sherbet-pastel colors, whirled about by cosmopolitan sophisticates. The dozen players flowed on and off stage as smooth as silk, mostly in pairs. No, no kisses, but a lot of youthful exuberance to French songs from the Pink Martini ensemble. Perhaps with a bow to Magritte, a group of dancers hit the stage flourishing black umbrellas, evolving into part of the whimsical décor. Another Seiwert-only touch was the mannequin pas de deux, so appropriate for these AI days, with life-size plastic figures wheeled around by flesh-andblood partners. This sure-fire crowd-pleaser capped the first night at the Lesher Center. And yet what bowled me most over was Caniparoli’s rugged ritual Swipe (2011), as jostling as driving with four flat tires. The bold shoulder swivel-thrusts and bobbing necks had me instinctively flexing muscles dormant for ages. The performers provocatively raised and worked hands on high – I couldn’t tell whether they were waving to Aunt Matilda in the 12th row or simply satirizing empty political speeches, which already anticipate 2024. The high point April 28 was a pairing of Cassidy Isaacson and João Sampaio, nimble and athletic to the core. Among Caniparoli’s quirky enigmas came a woman’s extended leg (Isaacson again) doing a breath-taking full-360 like a sweep-second hand of a clock, in a display of flexibility par excellence, one that’s very rarely done on stage. The program opened with Katarzyna Skarpetowska’s Sextette for four women and two men dancing to Bach, memorable for the skyward leaps of Ricardo Dyer, a dabbler in lofty elevation. In between, Smuin’s duet “Dream” was a vehicle for ballerina Tessa Barbour in a long voluptuous formal, later partnered by the Brazilian flash Sampaio. Of note in this program was the meticulous preparation of the ensemble, with letter-perfect formations, pliable bodies, and ballet moves to remember. Casts change nightly. All the music is prerecorded. Seiwert, just promoted to associate artistic director, turned up at intermission to meet patrons, along with Fushille, in a refreshing turnabout from those troupes that rarely show their directors offstage. SMUIN CONTEMPORARY BALLET opened its 29th season April 28-29 at Walnut Creek’s Lesher Center, then San Francisco’s Yerba Buena Center May 5-14, and Mountain View’s CPA May 25-28. Details online, www. smuinballet.org.

articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre (ACT) will produce Wizard of Oz from June 1-25 at the Toni Rembe Theatre in downtown San Francisco. The classic tale by L. Frank Baum is transformed for the ACT stage by Tony Award–nominated director and choreographer Sam Pinkleton and Tony Award-winning designer David Zinn. “The myth of Dorothy and her friends, and their big adventure, means something different to every single person you ask—whether it’s childhood nostalgia, queer survival, or an unhealthy obsession with flying monkeys,” said Pinkleton. “I’m giddy and honored to enlist the brains, heart, and courage of the Bay Area—in collaboration with mega-genius David Zinn—to create an intimate, intergenerational, human-powered Wizard of Oz that is bursting with contradictions and big beating hearts.” The play is family-friendly and appropriate for young audiences. The cast includes El Beh, Keiko Shimosato, Darryl Jones, Katrina McGraw, Kunal Prasad, Ezra Reaves, Cathleen Riddley and Travis Rowland. For more infor mation, and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/202223-season/wizard-of-oz/. ACT will produce Wizard of Oz starting on June 1.
articles.title: ACT premieres Wizard of Oz June 1

articles.text: Review by Paul Hertelendy With his audacious programming, credit veteran Director Robert Geary for pushing his Volti Chamber Singers a hair beyond. While Volti is not the most accomplished of our many chamber choruses, it is arguably the most adventurous. In their current concert set of five a capella works, the oldest one was two years old. Many a chorus (perhaps like one you’ve been in) manages four-part harmony, perhaps with keyboard accompaniment. But here there are eight-part unaccompanied harmonies, along with precarious melismas, offbeat chords and chaos, shouts and stretches of one’s range. It’s like being parachuted into a trackless jungle with just hunting knives and matches. If there were common themes in the current concert lineup, they were the composers’ greater interest in the sounds than specific texts, as well as in immersive issues of our day, whether the environment or concern about warfare abroad. Among the five works came a world premiere by Mark Winges, a U.S. premiere by Zibuokle Martinaityte, a previous Volti commission from Eric Tuan, plus pieces by Trevor Weston and Pulitzer-Prize winner Caroline Shaw, who had achieved that distinction while still in graduate school. Winges and Ms. Martinaityte were both in attendance May 13 for post-concert commentary. using less comforting intervals like seconds. In Hermatite, the ever-inventive Ms. Shaw played with the letters of F, E, O, bringing to mind the chemical composition of hermatite. And then out of the blue she tosses in lines out of the Columbus-contemporary composer Josquin des Pres, “A Thousand Regrets,” to voice thoughts on climate policy and an absence thereof, emerging in a muddy French that made you wish that someone had given Josquin English lessons. In a similar environmental vein came Eric Tuan’s In the Rain Shadow with the excerpt “Creosote Fractal,” alluding to a plant in the Mohave said to be many millennia old. Trevor Weston’s Given Sound was full of melismas and small clumps of words, showing off Volti’s well-focused soprano section. In the end however, the San Francisco-based group Volti needs to tailor its repertoire to the talents of the singers at hand, otherwise it’s just firing off illshaped rockets that miss the stars. Volti’s latest set was at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Walnut Creek, an attractive, modern structure with a large parking lot nearby. SOUNDS AND SHADOWS, a contemporary program by the chorus Volti, May 13 at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church, Walnut Creek. Repeated Mother’s Day at Kanbar PAC, San Francisco. Reachable via (415) 771-3352, or online, www.VoltiSF.org Volti Chamber Singers are led by Bob Geary, founder of Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. If you expected a concert like a stroll in the park, you got instead a rapid-fire awakening with Martinaityte’s opus Aletheia. Written during the onset of the Ukrainian war, this is all vocalise devoid of consonants and devoid of language, with shout-outs, falling figures and growing chaos, ever more intense, perhaps portraying the horrors of warfare. An unusual technique brings hand to mouth intermittently, like a rapidly repeated organ key. On a theme of discovery of truth, Aletheia proved to be a highly effective outpouring by the Lithuanian-born composer – overtly political, yet without a single incriminating word. articles.text: Berkeley Symphony will host its annual fundraising gala, Symphony Soirée, this Saturday, May 20 at 6 p.m. at the historic Claremont Hotel, 41 Tunnel Road. Guests will first enjoy a reception featuring the music of Berkeley High Jazz Band, hors d’oeuvres, drinks and a silent auction, before dinner by Claremont Hotel Executive Chef Joseph Paire. There will be a special featured performance by Jazz Mafia and Cosa Nostra Strings, followed by an exciting live action hosted by emcee Michael Tate. Proceeds from Symphony Soirée provide vital funding for Berkeley Symphony’s innovative performances and its award-winning Music in the Schools program. Tickets and sponsorships are available online at berkeleysymphony.org or by calling 510.841.2800. “This year’s gala celebrates Berkeley Symphony’s commitment to our long-standing legacy of innovation and inclusion in music, and to help provide a comprehensive music curriculum to Berkeley public elementary students,” said Executive Director Kate Kammeyer. “The Soirée brings together the best Berkeley has to offer, and will enable us to create unique and diverse live performances, while extending our reach to thousands of students each year with Music in the Schools”. “We are thrilled to welcome the community to an unforgettable evening that celebrates Berkeley Symphony’s integral role in the arts and culture of the Bay Area,” said Berkeley City councilmember Rigel Robinson, a Symphony Board Member and Event Chair. Auction items include private culinary experiences, sound healing, and more! Soirée attendees can participate in the live auction, which will feature experiences such as a North Bay “foodie outing” with Berkeley Symphony’s Education Director Ming Luke, a trip to New York City to see Music Director Joseph Young in a performance at Carnegie Hall, and an all-inclusive stay at a charming German country estate. Jazz Mafia will perform its distinctly Bay Area hybrid of musical mayhem, marching band madness, soulful singing, and soaring strings, with a foundation of futuristic beats. Co-founded by trombonist, bassist, composer, arranger, and producer Adam Theis in 2000, the Jazz Mafia collective includes an eclectic group of forward-thinking and accomplished players in Electro, Hip-Hop, World, Classical, and Jazz. Twenty years in the making, Jazz Mafia is a prolific staple of the quintessential San Francisco sound, uniting creative and accomplished Bay Area instrumentalists, vocalists, MCs, composers, and arrangers. An offshoot of the Jazz Mafia collective, Cosa Nostra Strings is a five-piece powerhouse crew that features conservatory-trained classical and jazz musicians who find a common language in their passion for the music that is found in-between the lines. A unique instrumentation of cello, viola, violin, trombone, bass, vocals and percussion provides the perfect vehicle to explore the edges of the perceived musical universe. About Berkeley Symphony Berkeley Symphony is unique among Bay Area and American orchestras for its commitment to innovation, community, and excellence. Founded in 1971 in the intellectual and artistic nexus of Berkeley, California, the Orchestra is committed to performing, premiering, and commissioning new music that reflects the culturally diverse people and the heady creative climate of its home city. In the 2019-2020 season, Berkeley Symphony entered a new era under the leadership of Joseph Young, the Orchestra’s fourth Music Director in its 50-year history, following a highly successful February 2019 debut that was acclaimed by critics and audiences alike. In addition to building on the Orchestra’s artistic innovation, creativity and adventurous programming, Maestro Young is committed to amplifying the voices of underrepresented composers and artists as well as continuing to tell diverse stories that reflect the local Berkeley community. Berkeley Symphony Gala will be held this Saturday at the Claremont Hotel. ®

articles.text: San Francisco’s Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) celebrates Black beauty and femininity with the exhibit Black Venus, on view now through August 20. The exhibit is curated by Aindrea Emelife and is a reflection of the legacy of Black Women in visual culture, from colonial-era caricatures to the reclamation of Black womanhood by 18 artists of numerous nationalities and ages. Artwork spans from 1793 to the present day. Featured artists include Alberta Whittle, Amber Pinkerton, Ayana V. Jackson, Carrie Mae Weems, Carla Williams, Coreen Simpson, Deana Lawson, Deborah Roberts, Frida Orupabo, Ming Smith, Kara Walker, Maud Sulter, Lorna Simpson, Renee Cox, Sadie Barnette, Shawanda Corbett, Tabita Rezaire, Taiye Idahor, Wangechi Mutu, Yetunde Olagbaju and Zanele Muholi. The museum advises visitors that some artwork contains sensitive and difficult imagery. The exhibition’s thematic foundation is the Hottentot Venus, a visual-culture archetype named for the assigned stage name of Saartje Baartman (born 1789 in South Africa), fetishised by Dutch colonizers and slave traders. To learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/black-venus. Museum visitors view an item in MoAD’s Black Venus exhibition. Creating Community through the Power of Music. Sierra Ensemble does much more than define chamber music ... they breathe life into every note for even the most casual listener. (& ONCE-NEW) Concert includes: The Trio in A minor Op. 188 for Piano, Oboe & Horn by Carl Reinecke, the beloved Brahms Horn Trio , the late midcentury electronic Wave Canon by Joseph Julian and the Stravinsky Sérénade en La (1925) for Piano Solo. Joining Sierra Ensemble: special guest artist – oboist Felisa Simon. Matthew Vincent, violin; Marc Steiner, piano; and Janis Lieberman, horn Sierra Ensemble is an innovative violin, French horn, and piano trio committed to supporting a lively chamber music environment. Performing worldwide and throughout the United States since 1998, Sierra Ensemble’s mission seeks to build community and add to the unique violin, horn, and piano trio repertoire via composer commissions, education projects and accessible performances. 801 Magnolia Avenue, Piedmont doors open at 4:30, Concert at 5 pm :/ // /w ww ww w. .e ev ve en nt tb br ri it te e. .c co om m/ /e e/ / 5 57 74 48 87 76 62 22 29 92 27 77 7

San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum in San Francisco is exhibiting Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in Art now through July. The new exhibition features more than 120 artworks borrowed from 20 of the finest museums and private collections in the world, with a focus on the arts of the Indian cultural sphere. Beyond Bollywood includes artwork from India, Pakistan, Nepal, Tibet, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, and Indonesia. “We hope visitors will come away with a transformed notion of the importance and power of dance,” said exhibition co-curator Forrest McGill. Beyond Bollywood will be on display through July 10. Dance dialogues events that include asian folk dance with expert speaker panels, take place May 25, June 11 and 22, and July 9. These pop-ups will include dance performances and demonstrations in the museum gallery, followed by a question and answer session, recurring monthly on selected Sundays and Thursdays. Admission is included with your ticket to Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in Art. Space is limited and reservations are recommended. For a full list of featured dancers and speakers, visit https://asianart.org/beyond-bollywood-events/. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, May 17, 2023 Asian Art Museum: Beyond Bollywood on view through July MoAD’s Black Venus exhibition on view through August 20 By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco’s Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) celebrates Black beauty and femininity with the exhibit Black Venus, on view now through August 20. The exhibit is curated by Aindrea Emelife and is a reflection of the legacy of Black Women in visual culture, from colonial-era caricatures to the reclamation of Black womanhood by 18 artists of numerous nationalities and ages. Artwork spans from 1793 to the present day. Featured artists include Alberta Whittle, Amber Pinkerton, Ayana V. Jackson, Carrie Mae Weems, Carla Williams, Coreen Simpson, Deana Lawson, Deborah Roberts, Frida Orupabo, Ming Smith, Kara Walker, Maud Sulter, Lorna Simpson, Renee Cox, Sadie Barnette, Shawanda Corbett, Tabita Rezaire, Taiye Idahor, Wangechi Mutu, Yetunde Olagbaju and Zanele Muholi. The museum advises visitors that some artwork contains sensitive and difficult imagery. The exhibition’s thematic foundation is the Hottentot Venus, a visual-culture archetype named for the assigned stage name of Saartje Baartman (born 1789 in South Africa), fetishised by Dutch colonizers and slave traders. To learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/black-venus. “Dance dialogue” pop-ups will include dance performances in the Asian Art Museum gallery on selected Sundays and Thursdays. articles.text: I was glad to close the door on last week. The very thought of self-serving bureaucracies infuriates me, but some things never change. If you agree, send a note to the Piedmont schools. Our kids deserve the best, including music education. I had not heard the Oakland Symphony Youth Orchestra in quite some time. They played their spring concert on Sunday in the San Leandro Performing Arts Center. I could see that the members of the orchestra were all well dressed in tuxedos and formal wear. They looked sharp. I was tired of the sloppy look and was pleased to see the teenage musicians looking sharp. It really makes you play your best. That’s the way it is with the Oakland Symphony Youth Orchestra, led by Omid Zoufonoun. The concert opened with an excellent overture, Starburst, written by Jessie Montgomery. Next came “Solitude“ by Duke Ellington in a superb arrangement by Wladimir Selinsky. Everyone knows Duke Ellington but few of us knew Solinski. He was a Russian-born virtuoso violinist, who operated behind the scenes on radio and television. In “Solitude” we had a perfect example of a great composer, represented by a great arranger. The third movement of Sibelius’ popular violin concerto concluded the first half of the program. The young soloist, Michael Oliveira, wowed us, not only with his brilliant technique, but showed that he is a musician of extraordinary, expressive ability. While all too many of today’s violin virtuosos play with perfection but little soul, I am happy to tell you that young Mr. Oliveira has an exciting, artistic spark and a bright future ahead. The Oakland Symphony Youth Orchestra impressed me in just about every way. They are a disciplined group, and at the same time they are enthusiastic and play with inspiration. Omid Zoufonoun provides that inspiration when he is on the podium. That’s what great teachers do. The orchestra concluded with selections from Prokofiev’s Romeo and Juliet. The interpretation was lithe and agile, and they knew how to turn on the emotion in an instant. This orchestra will embark on a European concert tour in July and is scheduled for performances in the musical capitals of Prague, Vienna, and Budapest. I can predict that they will have great success. I encourage our readers to attend their farewell concert outside Oakland City Hall on July 2. articles.text: Reservations for Stern Grove Festival concerts will be open to the public beginning May 18. The festival begins June 18. All concerts are free, but reservation is required. Headlining the 86th season is The Flaming Lips, with performances by Indigo Girls, Santigold, Lyle Lovett, Bob Moses, and Patti Smith. San Francisco Symphony will perform on July 23. Concerts run from June 18 to August 20. Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization whose mission is “to make live musical experiences accessible to all.” Since its inception in 1938, the organization has presented the Stern Grove Festival as free concerts in Sigmund Stern Grove, an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. The amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites. The festival has brought more than eight decades of performing arts - including opera, theatre, and music - completely free. articles.text: Paula Robles and Laia Artigas star in Summer 1993. Summer 1993 is a quiet, poetic meditation on childhood, focused on a six-year-old girl named Frida (Laia Artigas). Her mother has recently died; her father is deceased as well. She is told by her extended family (grandparents and aunts) that she is to live with her uncle, Esteve (David Verdaquer), his wife, Marga (Bruna Cusi), and their 4-year-old daughter, Anna (Paula Robles). Home for this nuclear family is the Catalan countryside, a good distance from the city of Barcelona, which is the only place she has ever known. From the first frame, the camera is centered on Frida as she struggles to comprehend what is a dramatic change in her life, a circumstance layered with a sense of abandonment as well as confusion regarding what happened to her mother. She understands very little about the sudden changes in her life, overhearing only bits and pieces of adult conversation. The truth is only hinted at, and what is implicit is gradually made explicit – AIDs was involved. Her father is a vague memory but apparently his death is connected to the same illness. With a gentle touch, writer/ director Carla Simon creates what is an autobiographical narrative of a young girl who is coping not only with profound loss, but also with the difficult struggle to adapt to a new family. Although her uncle and aunt are related to Frida, they are, essentially, strangers; however, they are consistently kind as they attempt to make her feel at home. The bucolic setting, the stone house, surrounded by woods, with chickens and sheep as part of the landscape, all represent a change that she finds difficult to fully absorb. Simon offers up these summer days in 1993 as a series of vignettes. For Frida, they are days of bright sunlight and nights of deep, silent darkness, far from the sounds of the city. But then this new world mirrors the resilient silence that she uses as a way of defending against a world she initially feels is intrusive and bewildering. Gently, the camera captures her isolation, her soft rebellion, a rebellion that can seem passive-aggressive. And to her new family, she can seem even sinister. Unexpectedly, Anna has an accident when she breaks her arm. She is no longer a toddler but is still defenseless. She acts out, pushing back in her own way against not only Anna, but against her uncle and aunt. Summer 1993 is beautifully rendered. But it is also a film that requires patience as it slowly reveals its moments of painful insights. It is not a movie intended for children. What is so powerful about this story is its ability to hold a point of view that is solely Frida’s. Think of it. A film that is a character study of a young, still forming young girl who is confronted with a world in which those closest to her are gone, most especially her mother. It’s remarkable. I’m reminded of one moving scene in the film in which Frida, in the dead of night, wanders into the woods with a flashlight. She shines it up, into the treetops, and calls out for her mother. Of course, she hears only the whisper of the wind, which only compounds her sense of having been forsaken. Summer 1993 is simultaneously remote and involving. It is subtle and elusive, sometimes repetitive as the days merge, one to the next. But always it’s about Frida’s search for love and reassurance; these are emotions that make all the difference to a film that finds its very special sweet spot. Summer 1993. Foreign film. Subtitles-language Catalan-Spanish. Starring Leia Artigas, Paula Robles, Bruna Cusi. 1 hr., 36 min. Not rated. Released in 2018. Streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Megan Leavey is a sentimental and heartfelt story about the connection between a young Marine corporal (Kate Mara), and her combat dog, Rex. The year is 2003. The initial setting is upstate New York where we find Megan at loose ends, adrift, feeling her life lacks substance and purpose. She turns to the Marines, endures a demanding boot camp, and ends up, for disciplinary reasons, cleaning the cages of a group of specially trained, bomb-sniffing dogs destined for Iraq. She makes the decision that she, above all else, wants to be one of the handlers and begins the arduous journey of learning how to qualify for and then work with a temperamental German shepherd named Rex. Gradually, they form a bond that Megan nurtures, and eventually are shipped out to Iraq, assigned to Ramadi and Fallujah. They are sent on 100 missions searching for hidden ordinance and roadside I.E.D.s. Of course, there are harrowing battle scenes along the way until eventually Megan and Rex are both injured in an I.E.D. explosion. Megan is sent stateside to recuperate requiring that she and Rex be separated. The film feels genuine, the attachment developed between Megan and Rex profound. Their connection is made manifest by the leather leash that Megan is determined to never release. Their partnership is jeopardized and of course the audience yearns for a right ending. Director Cowperthwaite (Blackfish) doesn’t disappoint. But then the audience knows this going in. It’s the journey that is so interesting as both Rex and Megan suffer PTSD, only to deal with it fully the moment they are reunited. Act three is about the struggle they endure to find one another. Megan Leavey. Directed by Gabriela Cowperthwaite. Starring Kate Mara, Ramon Rodriquez and Brad Whitford. 1 hr., 56 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. A film that is a character study of a young, still forming young girl who is confronted with a world in which those closest to her are gone, most especially her mother. It’s remarkable. I’m reminded of one moving scene in the film in which Frida, in the dead of night, wanders into the woods with a flashlight. She shines it up, into the treetops, and calls out for her mother. Of course, she hears only the whisper of the wind, which only compounds her sense of having been forsaken. Summer 1993 is simultaneously remote and involving. It is subtle and elusive, sometimes repetitive as the days merge, one to the next. But always it’s about Frida’s search for love and reassurance; these are emotions that make all the difference to a film that finds its very special sweet spot. Summer 1993. Foreign film. articles.text: The Secret of NIMH is a wonderful, compelling story, both whimsical and thrilling. Its handdrawn animation is extraordinary, rich in detail and color, and follows the tradition in which animals talk and reason. It was adapted from the 1971 children’s classic, Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH, written by Robert C. O’Brien. From the opening set up, the narrative is flooded with a sense of urgency that fully engages the audience. Mrs. Frisby (Elizabeth Harman), a widowed mouse, lives with her two children in a cinder block located in an open field on the Fitzgibbon farm. She learns that the field is soon to be plowed and she must move her family as quickly as possible to a safe place. But she is confronted with what seems an insurmountable problem: she discovers that her child Timothy is ill. She asks Mr. Ages (Arthur Mallet), a friend of her late husband, Jonathan, to see the small child. He tells Mrs. Frisby that Timothy is very sick with pneumonia, gives her some medicine, and adds that the child cannot be moved for at least three weeks. The following day she learns that Farmer Fitzgibbons is going to start plowing early. Suddenly, time is of the essence, and she realizes that help is needed. With her friend Jeremy (Dom DeLuise), a clumsy but comical crow, The Secret of NIMH is adapted from the children’s classic, Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH, by Robert C. O’Brien. she goes to consult the Great Owl (John Carradine) for advice. He wisely tells her to seek out the rats who live under a large rose bush near the Fitzgibbon farmhouse. It’s at this point that act two of The Secret of NIMH begins. Mrs. Frisby is increasingly frantic to find a way to move her home without risking the life of Timothy. She discovers, on her visit to the rose bush that the rats possess a superior intelligence and have created a community that is beyond anything she has ever seen: it’s a warren of sophisticated technology and they even have electricity, which they steal from the Fitzgibbon house. It’s there that she meets the leader of the rats, Nicodemus (Derek Jacobi). He agrees to help her and gives her an amulet that will help her when she needs it most. Thus begins the adventure of Mrs. Frisby in earnest and the secret of NIMH (the National Institute of Mental Health) is revealed. NIMH is simply great storytelling by a group of ex-pats from Disney who launched a new studio headed by Don Bluth, committed to sustaining animation as an art form and not one ruled by CGI. This feature film was their first effort, and it proved to be warm and filled with thrills. A caveat for parents is that though NIMH has a G rating, it can also be darkly intense. The Secret of NIMH. Animated fantasy – adventure. Directed by Don Bluth. With the voices of Elizabeth Harman, Derek Jacobi, and Dom DeLuise. 1 hr., 22 min. Rated G. Released in 1982. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: The film Chemical Hearts is a sensitive high school melodrama, based on the popular 2016 novel of the same name by Krystal Sutherland. The narrative is told from the point of view of 17-year-old Henry Page, who is just beginning his senior year, and eager to be the school’s quarterly newspaper editor. In voiceover, the film opens with Henry explaining that he has always wanted to be writer, but understands that his life experience has thus far been narrow. He’s introverted, has never had a girl friend, has few friends, his only hobby, strangely, is Japanese Kintsuei (repairing broken vases), and admits that he is waiting, with some frustration, for something to happen which will provide him with something, anything to write about. On the first day of school, sitting in his journalism class, he is told by his teacher that he will co-edit the paper with a recent transfer student, Grace Town (Lili Reinhart), also a senior, who has a previous newspaper background, walks with a cane, and shows, at least initially, no interest in working with Henry or the paper. She’d rather spend her time reading Pablo Neruda. Grace is mysterious, remote, and the ever present cane a metaphor indicating some previous trauma. Though initially standoffish, even hostile, Grace and Henry begin to interact (causing Henry to frequently miss his school bus). And so their relationship grows, and gradually she begins to share small bits of herself. She takes Henry to her favorite spot, they walk often in a nearby park, and he yearns to know more about her, while she withholds parts of her past. Slowly, Henry comes to understand that Grace is haunted by grief and a series of catastrophes; her emotions hang by a thread. Nevertheless, he can feel himself falling in love with her, and she begins, however reluctantly, to reciprocate. Chemical Hearts captures the chaos and confusion of adolescence. In the words of the author, Krystal Sutherland, “You are never more alive than when you are a teenager. Writer/director Richard Tanne gets it just right. Chemical Hearts. Directed by Richard Tanne. Starring Lili Reinhart, Austin Abrams, Coral Pena. 1 hr., 35 min. Rated R. Released in 2020, Now Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. Lili Reinhart and Austin Abrams in Chemical Hearts

articles.text: Who knew, when movie stars Tony Curtis and Janet Leigh married, that their daughter would go on to win an award that eluded both her parents: an acting Oscar – at age 64, no less. But that’s just what Jamie Lee Curtis did this year, for her performance in Everything Everywhere All at Once. Fortunately for Piedmont, this limber, wry, sassy actress visited us last week, in one of her best early roles: Wanda in the fizzy 1988 heist comedy, A Fish Called Wanda. The film was the fifth selection in Piedmont’s new, monthly Second Thursday Film Fest. Adding to its quality, the deft comic actor, Kevin Cline, stars as Curtis’s lover and co-conspirator, and the pair are abetted in the movie’s non-stop mischief by a pair of Monty Python alumni: John Cleese and Michael Palin. Written and directed by Cleese and Charles Crichton, Wanda earned three Oscars, including Best Supporting Actor for Kevin Cline. It got a 96% rating from Rotten Tomatoes and was named by the British Film Institute the 39th best all-time English film. The comedy is littered with lies, betrayals, seductions and mayhem, and rarely has rampant bad behavior been so funny. The machinations of the plot turn on a theft of diamonds. Each of the cast plots to lay hands on them exclusively. Along the way, dogs are assassinated, and the climax of the tale involves a steamroller and wet cement. Where does that titular fish come in? At one point the key to a deposit box containing the diamonds is hidden in a fish tank. In a post-showing discussion, most of the audience said they liked the movie. It contains some profanity and sexual references, but no one seemed to mind, nor was anyone concerned about Otto’s treatment of the stuttering Ken – people saw it as an artifact of its time. One person didn’t like the film’s type of humor, but one enthused that she loved it. Next month’s Second Thursday Film Fest, on June 8th, screens one of the best of MGM’s technicolor musicals: The Band Wagon, starring Fred Astaire and Cyd Charisse. The Film Fest takes place each month in the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with the showtime at 10:30. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration with the Rec Department can be done at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Audiences are welcome to bring snacks or lunch.

articles.text: More than 140 Advisory Board members, officers, and donors attended Salvation Army’s Spring Gala on Sunday evening, April 30. The sold-out event, titled “The Way Out”, was held at the University Club high above UC Berkeley’s Memorial Stadium. The Honorary Chair for this year’s gala was the extraordinary Alice Waters of Chez Panisse. Cal’s a cappella group started the evening wth a lively performance by 11 of its members. The featured speakers included UC Berkeley Head Football Coach Justin Wilcox, Executive Vice Chancellor and Provost Ben Hermalin, and Salvation Army Volunteer of the Year honoree Elijah Hicks, a former Cal football player now with the Chicago Bears. Two other awards were presented during the evening; the Community Partner Award, which was given to Lauren Bockmiller, President of Channel Systems Inc., for her partnership in hiring 43 Adult Recovery Center (ARC) graduates in her company. Half of her staff are ARC grads, many with more than five years with the company. The evening ended with a surprise for the gala chair, Debbie Kelley, who was presented with the Others Award for her commitment to helping others by chairing the last four Gala events for the Army, raising a combined $1.3M. A standing ovation ensued.The Others Award honors an individual or organization exemplifying an extraordinary spirit of service to “others,” not only through the support of The Salvation Army but for the broader community as well. A new record of nearly The “Others” award was presented to Gala chair Debbie Kelley by Salvation Army officers James and Laura Sullivan, and John and Pam Brackenbury. $450,000 was raised at the event through live and silent auctions and Fund-A-Need. All proceeds will help fund The Salvation Army’s efforts to meet human need without discrimination in Alameda County. The nonprofit helps with food, rent, utility assistance, and operates the only shelter in the county that accepts families with boys over the age of 12. It also operates pre-schools, after-school programs, music programs, Christmas assistance, a summer camp near Piedmont’s favorite, Camp Augusta, and workforce development programs in construction and certified nurse’s assistant training. The Salvation Army is in the community daily with homeless outreach programs and is often the first nonprofit on the scene during disasters. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, May 17, 2023 Record-breaking evening at Salvation Army Gala More than 140 Advisory Board members, officers, and donors attended Salvation Army’s Spring Gala on Sunday evening, April 30. articles.text: The Piedmont Garden Club (PGC) welcomed the public to a grand display of natural beauty May 2nd through May 4th at the Claremont Country Club. At least 450 visitors arrived to see what all the cork-popping was about. The Garden Club of America-sanctioned Flower Show gave floral designers, photographers, horticulturalists and gardeners of all skill levels a chance to compete for ribbons and honors. Flower Shows like this are put on by industrious garden clubs to help set standards for artistry in floral design, horticulture, conservation and photography, and to broaden the members’ and the public’s knowledge in these areas. Dedicated to long time Piedmont Garden Club members, Mary Wood and Jo Shuman, who both passed away last year, the PGC show brought out the creativity, artistry and talent of those who participated. Key words including “Splash,” Jean Jarvis, Kathryn Pritchett, and Mary Lou Righellis Patty Reed Julia Burke and husband Bruce “Dazzle,” “Pop,” “Chill,” and of course, “Cheers,” were used as guides to inspire participants to take their creativity to new and exciting heights. Entrants weren’t just Piedmont Garden Club members, but included competitors from other GCA clubs around the country. Floral Designers took on challenges, such as underwater design (“Splash”), some went contemporary (“Dazzle”), and miniatures, (“Pop”) and functional table designs were clever and surprising (“Cheers”). Among the top honorees were Sherri Dumke, for her distinctive floral design, and Patty Siskind and Nancy Cecconi for their imaginative “functional table” design. Horticulture classes asked for Cut Specimens (“Dazzle”) as well as container-grown plants that had been owned and tended by entrants for at least three months. Tami Becker, Lili Bassett, Nancy Bishop and Karen Sullivan walked off with blue ribbons for Lilli Bassett, Sharon Hom and Deb Obendorf Diane Coleman Elise Lomenzo and Lisa Dell’Osso

articles.text: The Wednesday before Mother’s Day, May 10, flowers were on the minds of the walking on Wednesdays group. Their destination was an annual visit to the Morcom Rose Garden on the Oakland border at Jean Street near Grand Avenue. The group first paid a visit to the home of walker Sherry Jacobs who was a recent victim of a mugging and strong-arm burglary. She suffered injuries but said she expects to be back with the group in a few weeks. The walkers crossed Grand Avenue and went a short distance on Jean Street to the rose garden, a natural bowl on a 7.5-acre site that was purchased by the City of Oakland in 1915 and originally named Linda Vista Park. Its conversion to a rose garden was a project of the Oakland Businessmen’s Garden Club in 1930 with the support of the city. Work began on the garden in 1931, and it officially opened in 1934. The name was changed in 1954 to honor Fred Morcom, Oakland’s mayor from 1931 to 1933. The park was most recently refurbished in the 1990s. The garden has over 2,400 rose bushes, winding walkways, a reflecting pool, and a cascading fountain. The design was inspired by the gardens of Italy, and has three sections. The Jean Street entrance has a classical, curved colonnade, backed by stone walls, and a rose-lined walkway. The middle section features a reflecting pool encircled by rose beds and an elegant 14-step cascade down the hillside to the west. Above the cascade is an octagonal wedding terrace made of stone and with more rose beds. Facing the pool and cascade from the east is a Mediterranean style loggia. A large Florentine oval garden at the north end has terraced flower beds rising on all sides. The group walked up the main path to the reflecting pool, and admired the many, different roses that were in full bloom. In the early 2000s “the Mother’s Walk” was created from the reflecting pool to the Florentine garden. There are brass plaques in the ground with the names of women honored each year in an annual ceremony for Mother’s Day. In the early 2000s, a group of volunteers, the “Dedicated Deadheaders,” was organized to keep the garden beautiful. One of them is Jennifer Peltzer, a regular walker with the group on Wednesdays. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Thirty five walkers showed up on May 10 for a tour of the Morcom Rose Garden on the border of Piedmont off Grand Avenue at Jean Street. Among those participating were: Brenda Ferrero, Matt Gerhardt, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Jim Kellogg, Noemi Alvarado and Mark Davis, Martin Levy, Will Adams, Elane Rehr, Lisa Euphrat, Charlene Louie, Mike Henn, Nancy DeRoche, Pat Keller, Helene Farber, Elizabeth Richter, Greg Slatoff and Carolyn George, Meghan Bennett, Lilly Guardia-Labar, Vincent Fisher, Joanne Larson, Angela Tom, Cheryl Coleman Jones, Kathy Rolefson, Melba Yee, Jim Kuo, Ken Moy, Alissa Quan, Nancy and Larry Olsen, Ian Morgan, Ann Quinby, and Dick Carter. 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03

articles.text: Oliver Shafroth (right) faces off against Tamalpais’ Lachlan Hindley, who scored the game-winning goal. but that’s the way it is sometimes. “We all played our hearts out,” said Fredericks. The Highlanders battled their way to the Finals without their top scorer, Henry Brayer. Without him leading the charge, Piedmont relied on Dixon, Fredericks, and Jack Nelson. “It’s tricky without Henry. We got our groove back the last three or four games just trying to figure out how to gel together on the field. I think what killed us was we just committed too many turnovers,” said Dixon. Of equal importance, Brayer is also the team’s starting faceoff specialist. Without him, Piedmont had to battle against Tamalpais junior Lachlan Hindley—who won the opening faceoff of the second overtime period and took the ball in transition all the way to Piedmont’s net for the goal. The strategy is what carried Tamalpais through the second half. Piedmont concludes another highly successful season with a 14-4 record and its sixth consecutive Western Alameda County Conference banner. Their return to the Division 2 NCS Finals marked their first appearance since the 2019 championship year, which resulted in Piedmont being moved up to Division 1 and more rigorous competition. PHS will watch leaders like Brayer, Dixon, Fredericks, and Nelson graduate from the school. They have played together since elementary school on Skyline Lacrosse Club teams. “We’ve played together since the second grade” confirmed Dixon. “I’ve always been friends with Jack and then Henry moved in, then Nate started playing. We’ve all really bonded over playing together the last 10 years. It’s just an amazing experience to play with each other for so long,” said Dixon. “I wouldn’t want to do this with another group of guys,” added Fredericks. Match Recap In the first quarter, Tamalpais scored early but Nelson tied the match with 8:30 to go. But from there, PHS wouldn’t score again until just three seconds were left in the first when goalie Gus von Metzch made a save and hurled the ball up to Dixon who launched in a goal as he fell to the ground and tied the match at 2-2.

Finishing with a 14-7 overall record, Piedmont reached its second consecutive NCS quarterfinals, defeating No. 11 Encinal 3-0 on May 2 as the No. 6 seed, eventually falling 3-0 to 3 Acalanes on May 4. The group was led into existence by Wilson Wong as a freshman in 2020 prior to the pandemic. Helping grow the team were players like James MaNguyen and Brayden Day, and making huge strides was freshman Albert Bellingrath and junior John Champion Oliver Shafroth (right) faces off against Tamalpais’ Lachlan Hindley, who scored the game-winning goal. but that’s the way it is sometimes. “We all played our hearts out,” said Fredericks. The Highlanders battled their way to the Finals without their top scorer, Henry Brayer. Without him leading the charge, Piedmont relied on Dixon, Fredericks, and Jack Nelson. “It’s tricky without Henry. We got our groove back the last three or four games just trying to figure out how to gel together on the field. I think what killed us was we just committed too many turnovers,” said Dixon. Of equal importance, Brayer is also the team’s starting faceoff specialist. Without him, Piedmont had to battle against Tamalpais junior Lachlan Hindley—who won the opening faceoff of the second overtime period and took the ball in transition all the way to Piedmont’s net for the goal. The strategy is what carried Tamalpais through the second half. Piedmont concludes another highly successful season with a 14-4 record and its sixth consecutive Western Alameda County Conference banner. Their return to the Division 2 NCS Finals marked their first appearance since the 2019 championship year, which resulted in Piedmont being moved up to Division 1 and more rigorous competition. PHS will watch leaders like Brayer, Dixon, Fredericks, and Nelson graduate from the school. They have played together since elementary school on Skyline Lacrosse Club teams. “We’ve played together since the second grade” confirmed Dixon. “I’ve always been friends with Jack and then Henry moved in, then Nate started playing. We’ve all really bonded over playing together the last 10 years. It’s just an amazing experience to play with each other for so long,” said Dixon. “I wouldn’t want to do this with another group of guys,” added Fredericks. Match Recap In the first quarter, Tamalpais scored early but Nelson tied the match with 8:30 to go. But from there, PHS wouldn’t score again until just three seconds were left in the first when goalie Gus von Metzch made a save and hurled the ball up to Dixon who launched in a goal as he fell to the ground and tied the match at 2-2. Piedmont went ahead 3-2 after over four minutes ran off in the second quarter when Dixon scored on a wraparound, where he held off a defender to send in a shot from close distance. PHS converted a man-up opportunity with Fredericks for a 4-2 lead with 5:36 left, and then went ahead 5-2 with 2:07 to go when Dixon assisted Fredericks. But Tamalpais came out of halftime hot and began eating away at the lead. The Hawks’ Hindley scored after winning the opening faceoff, but Dixon responded on a wraparound one minute later, 6-3. Tamalpais made it 6-4 with 4:37 left in the third and then scored again with 1:23 on the clock, 6-5 Piedmont. Fredericks gave PHS a little insurance with a goal with 51 seconds left after they gained a man advantage, making it 7-5 entering the fourth. Tam’s Hindley won the opening faceoff of the fourth quarter and marched it down to score in five seconds, 7-6. Tamalpais then tied it 7-7 with 9:29 left and went ahead after Hindley won the subsequent faceoff to another fast break goal just seven seconds later. After back-and-forth possessions, Nelson flicked a pass to Dixon from behind the net, leading to the tying goal at 8-8 with 1:24 left. Von Mestzch made a big save for PHS with one minute left in the game, enabling Piedmont to have the final possession. Fredericks nearly won it for Piedmont with 28 seconds on the clock when a low angled shot from distance collided with the crossbar. In the first four-minute overtime period, Tamalpais won the faceoff but had a shot go wide and eventually turned the ball over. Dixon had a shot trail high, and Nelson’s shot went wide with 40 seconds left. In the second double-overtime period, Hindley won the faceoff and took it straight to Piedmont’s net. Running in on the right side, the Tamalpais senior’s shot in point blank range was too quick for Von Metszch, trickling past his feet. Final stats: Dixon scored four goals, one assist, and recovered six loose balls. Fredericks scored three and had one assist. Nelson had one goal, one assist, and four ground balls. Von Metszch made eight saves. Staff Photo The boys’ volleyball team finished with one of its best seasons in school history at 14-7. READ IT IN THE POST

articles.text: A resident reported a catalytic converter theft in progress on Park View and Palm Drive at 5:47 a.m. on Sunday morning, May 14. Officers responded immediately and found the suspect vehicle, a gray GMC, occupied by two suspects. Their vehicle fled police onto Winsor Avenue where it ends at a parking lot at the lower Wildwood School playground. The GMC rammed through two security gates surrounding the playground and drove onto Witter Field. Realizing they were in a dead-end, two subjects left the car and ran away. An officer engaged in a brief foot pursuit until the suspects disappeared into the wooded area close to the baseball field and Magnolia Avenue. A search of the GMC revealed two freshly cut catalytic converters, at least two reciprocating saws, several blades, and miscellaneous burglary tools. At least one cell phone belonging to one of the suspects was left inside the vehicle and collected as evidence. A short time later one male suspect was located and arrested by Piedmont police. Victor Rojo, 40, of Oakland, had outstanding warrants including for narcotics. He was arrested and taken to Santa Rita Jail.

He was also fourth in the 100 meter hurdles in 16.10, and fifth in the pole vault. Jamie Schwarz qualified for the Meet of Champions, placing fourth in the 800 with a time of 2:23.05 in a field of 24. “I’m feeling really good because this is the first time I’ve PR’ed this season. Going into it, I knew I was top-three of four. They runners who were seeded first and second were in the WACC league, so I know them well. The plan was just to stick with them because I know how they race. The heat really affected some people, so once people started dropping, I just tried to stay in the front and kick as hard as I could,” said Schwarz. “My goal was to PR at Bayshore. I PR’ed by a lot by the end of the season last year, so I knew I wouldn’t get to that place for a while. I’m just glad to be back there and I’m grateful to be back at the meet of Champions again,” said Schwarz. Sophomore Ella Yasar also had a productive day, reaching the Meet of Champions in the 300-meter hurdles in 49.56, placing fourth in a field of 21 hurdlers. Yasar was part of the 4x400 relay team that qualified for the Meet of Champions by placing fourth. The relay team includes Schwarz, Emily Fitzgerald, and Skylar Best whose time was 4:17.04. Xander Schulte-Sasse qualified in the 3200 by placing fifth with a time of 9:54. In the pole vault, Conor Kim was fourth of 14 pole vaulters by clearing a height of 12 feet. Miguel Long was fifth of 23 in the triple jump with a distance of 41 feet, 10.75 inches. Events start at 12:30 on Friday and 12:00 p.m. on Saturday. To qualify for the State Meet runners will have to finish in the top-three at the Meet of Champions this weekend or achieve an At Large result.

Lindsey Meyersieck and Gayle Lambert achieved a blue ribbon and Best in Show award for their delightful miniature garden entry. Photographers came with mounted pictures in four classes, depicting • Floral close ups • Multiple blooms or plants • Flowing water in a nature photograph • A quiet moment in an intimate landscape Winners included Andrea Swensen, who won 1st place and the Best in Show Novice award for her intimate photo of a beautiful blossom, and Cris Heins, who was awarded a blue ribbon for her striking photo of flowers in a garden “conversation.” A preview party held on Tuesday evening attracted more than 200 participants and their spouses and friends – just like bees to flowers. At the two sold-out luncheons, guests were treated to floral design demonstrations by John James Designs of San Francisco. A stunning educational display put “Our Essential Oaks” – and especially the Coastal Live Oak native to this area – in the spotlight. It drew raves from the judges who handed its creators, Julia Burke and her team, the Ann Lyon Crammond Award for an outstanding educational exhibit at a GCA flower show, and the Marion Thompson Fuller Brown Conservation Award for an outstanding Conservation exhibit. Visitors learned that the oak trees provide a primary food source for hundreds of insects and shade and shelter for animals. The beauty of nature captured in this three-day flower show in May will remain etched in the minds of all who saw it for a long time. Special thanks go to the chairs of the event, Lili Bassett, Sharon Hom and Deb Obendorf. articles.text: era, things have come full circle. With traffic, congestion, parking limitations and associated costs, driving somewhere in a private car has become a burden instead of a convenience. This is especially true in countries where signs are in a different language, rules of the road are dissimilar, and where parking has its own mysterious regulations. The alternative is public transportation. In Portugal, as in the rest of Europe that I’ve experienced, public transportation is very different than what we are used to in the U.S. The well-used train, metro, bus, taxi, ride sharing and yes…walking routes are most often well thought out. They are interconnected and coordinated, reliable, affordable, safe, and convenient. Using these alternatives to me is easier and less stressful than driving. Utilizing public transportation combined with walking is also fun—an important part of the travel experience adventure. Next: Architecture in Portugal Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com Nowhere is Portugal’s connection to the sea is as dramatic as in Nazaré. The cliffs and Farol lighthouse overlook draw thousands of spectators each winter to witness up close the monster 80 foot Atlantic waves being surfed by the best big wave surfers in the world.

With traffic, congestion, parking limitations and associated costs, driving somewhere in a private car has become a burden instead of a convenience. articles.text: Editor: I just realized this is the letter where I officially become a “grumpy old man.” Since I’ve lived in Piedmont, I’ve noticed a trend that people stroll, jog, push strollers, walk dogs, and sometimes even take photos but in the street. Are the sidewalks not working properly? Why are so many people in the streets? Maybe it’s a legacy Covid behavior, or has it always been this way? In driving around town especially in early morning and evening one notices 10-15 people in the street at any given time. I wouldn’t care except that I’ve already had two close calls – one with a jogger wearing headphones who darted into the road unannounced narrowly missing my car. The other was with a dog who was being walked in the street and was almost hit by another passing car. My intent here is not to be a grumpy old man but to raise awareness of the issue. No one wants to open the Piedmont Post one week to find out something bad has happened that could have been avoided. articles.text: On Saturday, May 6th, much of the world’s attention was on London where Charles III was coronated as the king of England and his wife, Camilla, was crowned queen of England. Charles is the 41st British monarch since William the Conqueror took control of the land back in 1066. Although the power to rule in England resides in Parliament, the king is far from a primarily ceremonial figure. The British monarch has a great many powers and responsibilities. A recent Reader’s Digest article lists 27 of them: Serve as king of England, Scotland, Northern Ireland, Wales as well as the 14 nations that make up the “Commonwealth realm” • Choose to rule or abdicate • Serve as head of the Commonwealth of Nations • Pick the prime minister • Appoint members to the House of Lords • Appoint Supreme Court justices • Initiate the process of “forming a government” • Open Parliament each year • Kick off parliamentary business • Legitimize laws • Summon the prime minister • End the parliamentary session • Open Welsh lawmaking sessions and ratify its legislation • Open Scotland’s parliamentary session • Ratify the laws of Northern Ireland • Appoint the members of the Privy Council • Approve Privy Council orders and proclamations • Break the law without prosecution • Pardon criminals • Drive without a license • Exceed the speed limit • Travel without a passport • Command the armed forces • Grant knighthoods • Appoint archbishops and bishops to the Church of England (Defender of the Faith), • Own all the dolphins in the United Kingdom. This is an impressive list. It represents much power, simply by right of birth, being bestowed on one person; power given without a vote of parliament or people; authority granted without regard to aptitude, attitude or ability. While Charles’ mother, Queen Elizabeth II, was, at the time of her death, widely respected, the current king has not yet won such a secure place in the hearts of those over whom he rules.
articles.title: Thoughts about a Coronation

articles.text: Congresswoman Barbara Lee shows support for Oakland teachers in front of Oakland City Hall on Thursday, May 4. With 12 days left in the school year, Wednesday, May 10, marks the fifth day of a teacher’s strike in Oakland, with little progress made toward any contract agreement. Congresswoman Barbara Lee – who represents California’s District 12, including Piedmont – rallied a crowd of strikers and supporters in front of Oakland City Hall on Thursday, May 4, after more than 3,000 teachers began picketing due to little progress in settlement negotiations with Oakland Unified School District. Teacher demands included higher wages; more support staff; addressing of gun violence issues; addressing of environmental health issues like lead and asbestos in buildings; and student resources including subsidized transportation, reparations for black students, and district housing for homeless students. While apparently unable to meet all teacher demands, the negotiations include a retroactive 10% raise and a $5,000 one-time bonus for teachers, and a minimum salary raise of at least 13% and as much as 22% for every classroom teacher beginning next year. The offer is expected to cost the school district an historic $70 million more annually. Of the 22 largest California school districts which filed teacher pay data with the state for the 2021-2022 year, Oakland ranked 20th in total pay and 22nd in pay adjusted for cost of living. Among the 55 districts with over 1,000 students in San Francisco and the East Bay, Oakland ranked 54th in pay. The district’s 80 schools remain open for the approximately 35,000 affected students, as Oakland School District taps school staff for teaching and supervision. three days a week. articles.text: Piedmont adults and youth have a wealth of opportunities to explore local volunteer work. Here are just a few. Piedmont Ave. Library The Friends of the Piedmont Avenue Library organization is looking for a treasurer and a social media coordinator. An ideal volunteer for the job of treasurer would have knowledge of accounting and recordkeeping, providing oversight of Friends of PAL finances, taking part in board meetings and presenting financial reports to the library’s board. This volunteer would also pay bills, record bank account activity and analyze cash flow, collect and disburse funds, and prepare data for state and federal filing, and work with the library’s fundraising committee to project cash needs and sources. To apply, email contact@friendsofpal.org with information about your interest and a resume, if available. The social media coordinator will manage digital content on Facebook, Instagram, Twitter for the library’s website, and the library’s monthly newsletter. The library’s social media channel would be updated on a weekly basis with fun, uplifting content, to make sure that the community stays up-to-date about the latest happenings at the library. Harbor House Harbor House is a nonprofit Christian community development organization in Oakland which provides opportunities for children, teens, and families. Volunteer opportunities include virtual tutoring, food distribution, after-school program teachers, and facility maintenance (gardening and handiwork). To apply and learn more, contact the volunteer coordinator (nicole@ hhministries.org), or fill out an application at bit.ly/3YBzu16. Piedmont Center for the Arts Throughout the year, the all-volunteer nonprofit Piedmont Center for the Arts hosts music performances, art exhibits, literary events, public speakers and theater. Volunteers do everything — from production, carpentry, and painting to hosting receptions for events, and handling box office duties. The PCA particularly needs volunteers to staff art exhibits on weekends. To learn more and get involved, email the PCA at info@piedmontcenterforthearts.org, or contact Sue Malick at suemalick@gmail.com. Is there a volunteer effort or organization that you would like to highlight? Interested in expanding this list? Please send your suggestions to Selen Ozturk at ozturkselen@gmail.com.
articles.title: Volunteer opportunities for Piedmonters
