By Selen Ozturk The two large auger drills are being removed from the community pool site as drilling for the retaining wall concludes and trucks begin removing soil. The work will continue for eight weeks through June, although trucks will be on-site only two to three days a week. Drilling for concrete piers for approximately 385 feet of a new retaining wall began on April 2. “The contractors will start to bring steel and concrete on-site while hauling soil off-site,” explained Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. The majority of the fence along the pool site from Millennium High School to Bonita has been pulled out 12 to 14 feet. This will provide 22 feet for trucks to pull over, park and get loaded, and drive down Magnolia. Existing parking is not affected. Community Pool Update To prepare for the soil removal, the contractors began installing caissons last week. Gonzales said “These caissons look like steel beams that contractors put into the soil, pour concrete in the bottom of, and put pieces of wood in between. This is to temporarily shore up the soil to keep it from caving as the workers dig. articles.text: The Wildwood Dads Club will host an all-day golf tournament this Friday, May 12, at Oakmoore Golf Course in Stockton. The school fundraiser includes a party bus to and from Stockton, leaving Piedmont Community Hall at 7:00 a.m. and returning at 6:00 p.m. “Part of the fun is jumping on the party bus, where warmup breakfast, drinks and fun games will be had,” said event organizer Reed Johnson. The tournament format is a best-ball foursome scramble. A scramble entails all four team members to tee off on each hole and then each team member plays their next shot from the best ball of the group. Oakmoore Golf Course is a nine-hole course designed for groups to rent out the entire facility. Although hosted by Wildwood Dads Club, participants do not need to be in the club. Space is limited to 80 (20 foursomes) and all are welcome. Trophies will be awarded for best golf outfit, best drives, closest to the hole, and best score by a 4-person team. articles.text: Piedmont adults and students gathered in the Ambassador Chris Stevens Library at Piedmont High School on April 26 to meet Lucy Jane Bledsoe, the author of the book No Stopping Us Now, which was the 2023 Readmont book selection. English teacher Beth Black introduced the acclaimed, Berkeley-based author Bledsoe who shared that her story is closely tied to her own high school experiences. In high school, Bledsoe tried to join the Lettermen Club but failed, and faced retaliation in the press and physical intimidation and slander from a high school employee. Ultimately, she prevailed in getting her school to offer girls basketball and found the travails were a great lesson for her. Through these experiences she found her own voice, learned to stick to her truth and be steadfast. Bledsoe confirmed that making change happen and achieving justice is hard. She confessed that as a 17-year-old she was quite naïve. At that time, she thought simply pointing out inequities existed would result in corrections. She quickly learned that this was far from enough and that it took action on many fronts to achieve change, including speaking to the school board, finding mentors, writing to the state paper, building allies, and understanding the law. She has found that facts seem to be less impactful than stories that speak to people’s hearts. Black opened the evening discussion by thanking The Title IX Celebration Committee and the League of Women Voters of Piedmont for acquiring books for the district. She shared how she learned of the book; as part of the curriculum this year in a UC Berkeley history of women in sports class, it resonated with many of the college students. Following Bledsoe’s remarks, there was a rich Question and Answer session which led to discussions of Bledsoe’s writing process and choices, her parents’ fears of her advocacy work as well as their support, where society has and hasn’t made progress since the 1970’s, feminist role models, coming of age, race and intersectionality, high school friendships, the importance of allies, the impact of shaming and slander, representation, and gender equity in areas beyond sports in Piedmont today. The culminating event of Readmont 2023 was a talk in the PHS library with author Lucy Jane Bledsoe. In heartfelt remarks, an adult in the room shared that this was the first book that she had read that captured her own high school experiences in coming into her own sexuality. Bledsoe was very complimentary of the insightful, candid and thoughtful questions and responses from the audience, particularly those from the students. For suggestions of future Readmont selections, contact Beth Black at bblack@piedmont. k12.ca.us.
articles.title: Author of Readmont selection discusses book on Title IX in Piedmont

articles.text: The annual Cub Scouts Bicycle Rodeo and Safety Day will be held at Beach School this Saturday, May 13, from 10:00 a.m.- 1:00 p.m. The Piedmont Police Department and the Piedmont Scout Council are co-sponsoring the popular event. It is free and open to all kids from kindergarten through 5th grade. A parent needs to be on site to sign a waiver for the agility course. Piedmont Police and the Scout Explorers unit will host the bike agility course, and members of the Piedmont Community Service Crew will sell snacks. “It’s important for our youth to practice how to be safe on their bikes,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “We want to have this event before summer when we see more cycling activity.” For more information, contact the Piedmont Scout office at 547- 4493 (contact@piedmontbsa.org), or Capt. Chris Monahan at the police department at cmonahan@ piedmont.ca.gov. The playground at Beach Elementary is a great place to learn how to take off those training wheels; Ezra Guyette rides his bike as dad Will Guyette gives him a boost. The Scout Council and the Piedmont Police Department are putting on the Bike Rodeo and Safety Day on Saturday, with activities including the balance race.
articles.title: Bicycle Rodeo and Safety Day at Beach School on Saturday

articles.text: David Gard and Ellen Lee have been co-presidents of the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (formerly the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee) since August 2022. Gard, who grew up primarily in Missouri and Southern California, moved to Piedmont in 2014, He has two children at Piedmont High School. He joined PADC in 2015 as a city liaison working with city, police department, and fire department staff. With a Ph.D. in clinical psychology from UC Berkeley, Gard has worked as a private psychotherapist and as clinical psychology professor at San Francisco State University, and as director of the school’s Psychology Clinic. “Piedmont is a wonderful community of kind, thoughtful people who, I think, know the reputation Piedmont can have. By and large we all want to make it known how welcoming of diversity we really are,” said Gard. Lee moved to Piedmont from San Francisco 10 years ago. She has three children spanning elementary, middle, and high school. Before she joined the PADC board two years ago, she was a liaison for Wildwood School and co-chaired the PADC School Committee with former president Sheila Leunig. “As an Asian-American person growing up in the Bay, it’s wonderfully multicultural here, but there are still marginalized David Gard, PADC co-president communities, and Piedmont is no stranger to that,” said Lee. “When I came here, I thought about the role I wanted to play, and thought this was a good one — to make the city a more inclusive place, not only for my kids but for all.” Lee received her bachelor’s degree in English from UC Berkeley and a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University. As an independent journalist for publications including The New York Times, The Atlantic, and Real Simple, she writes about business and technology, parenting and health, and social justice and education. As part of the Asian-American Journalists Association, she also covers Asian-American community stories. The co-presidents have coordinated ongoing events including the annual MLK Day celebration. speaker series, book groups, and a student Art and Writing Showcase, and This year’s MLK Day PADC co-president Ellen Lee. event was attended by over 400 people and featured speakers including social justice activists and Congresswoman Barbara Lee; hip-hop dancers from the Oakland studio New Style Motherlode; and jazz musicians from Oaktown Jazz Workshop. The Appreciating Diversity Film Series at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse was created by the Appreciating Diversity Committee many years ago. It is now co-sponsored by PADC, the city, Piedmont Adult School, and the Piedmont League of Women Voters. “We’ve been around as a nonprofit since 2002,” said Lee. “The hard part for me is the larger scale of the discourse, knowing that nationally there still is some pushback in terms of why this is important.” “For the most part, however, we’re really encouraged. People here do support our mission as a worthwhile endeavor,” added Gard.
articles.title: PADC co-presidents talk about diversity

Piedmont High School and the PHS Parents Club celebrated its teachers and school employees last week, May 1-5, during its annual Teacher Appreciation Week. The Associated Student Body (ASB) made sure school staff members were celebrated throughout the week. Sophomore class president Genevieve Hiller led the initiative setting up tumblers with tea, classroom gifts, and a pun-themed snack bar. On Wednesday, May 3, the teachers’ lounge was decorated with succulents for staff to take home, and on Friday, ASB members delivered 300 notes high school students had written to their teachers, sharing how much they appreciate them. While the week is mostly centered around teachers, appreciating all school staff was important. “I think students should be kind 100% of the time to all adults, I know sometimes that can be difficult. We are here to make sure students are growing and developing, so being nice and following the Golden Rule is really important,” said special education paraeducator Nour Bouhedda. “A lot of students don’t know who we [the paraeducators] are, unless they’re the student that we are there to help, so it’s really nice to be acknowledged,” said paraeducator Carole Frascati-James Frascati, “There was something new every day for us. articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra, the oldest youth orchestra in California and the oldest independent youth orchestra in the nation, is now accepting new members. Auditions are being conducted for trumpet, trombone, bass trombone, tuba, bassoon, oboe, violin, viola, and double bass. Founded in 1936 in Berkeley, YPSO is led by conductor and Music Director David Ramadanoff for 35 years, with an orchestra of more than 100 musicians from schools through the greater Bay Area. YPSO will tour and perform in Japan next year, and will perform in the Bay Area Youth Orchestra Festival at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco. Submission of screening videos are due by June 1. For details and registration: www.ypsomusic.org/how-to-join, YPSO rehearses most Monday evenings at First Congregational Church of Oakland, 2501 Harrison Street from 6:00-9:30 p.m. There is also an annual weekend retreat in the Fall in Carmel Valley and several Saturday afternoon intensives during the year.
articles.title: YPSO holding auditions for next year’s orchestra

articles.text: Airbands, a middle school lipsynch and dance contest, took over the stage of the Alan Harvey Theater on Friday night, April 28. Seven colorful acts by students and teachers were judged by middle school staff members hilariously dressed as Minions from the animated film Despicable Me. The event was organized by Piedmont Middle School’s Associated Student Body class, with P.E. teacher Tim Wisniewski, and tech coordinator Adam Saville acting as emcees. Wisniewski opened the show with guitar in hand dressed as Bradley Cooper from the musical film A Star is Born. As he played the song “Shallow,” Saville, wearing a wig, emulated Lady Gaga and sang a duet with Wisniewski. “Bernie and the Cadillacs” won first place as a group of Adam Saville (left) dressed as Lady Gaga, and Tim Wisniewski, as Bradley Cooper from the film A Star is Born. Photos by Anne Smith The Minion judges in deep contemplation after an act. Attendance Secretary Mike Wong (left), 7th grade teacher Ted Scherman as Gru, 6th grade teacher Michael Bracamonte, and Principal Karen Shipp dancers including 8th graders Livi Britt, Cora Brozowski, Francesca Ceccarellia, Camille Edesess, Sophia Harris, Zee Orta, Jo Palsa, Lily Riley and Zoe Snyder. “Cali Girls” won second place, and “Super Chinese Class” claimed third place. Te a che r s pa r t icipat i ng included science teacher Camilla Thayer performing with the “Yoga Moms” act, Mandarin teacher Xinjia Xia with the Super Chinese Class, and English teacher Jamie Van Kleeck joing the ASB performance. Other choreographed lipsynching performances were titled “The Circus Queens,” and “We love Ms. Benko.” Drawing the biggest laughs were Minion judges who commented on each act. Mike Wong, Michael Bracamonte, Karen Shipp, were clad in yellow caps and suspenders with goggles, while Ted Scherman played the villain, Gru, with a long nose and a tell-tale scarf. Adam Saville announces “Bernie and the Cadillacs” as the winning act of the Airbands competition. The “Yoga Moms” airbands performance.

articles.text: The high school and middle school bands and orchestras in Piedmont will present their final concerts of this school year May 16-18. All concerts will be in the Alan Harvey Theater on the PHS Campus. The public is invited. A $5.00 donation is suggested for adults, and no admission fee for students. Orchestra concert – Tuesday, May 16, 7:00 p.m. The Piedmont High and Piedmont Middle School orchestras directed by Samantha Wilde will perform a Spring concert. Included on the program is an arrangement of Antonio Vivaldi’s “Inferno” from The Four Seasons, a selection from Tchaikovsky’s music for the ballet, Swan Lake, and Antonin Dvorak’s 4th movement from his New World Symphony. In addition, music by the Beatles will also be performed. Band concert – Wednesday, May 17, 7:00 p.m. The PHS Symphonic and Jazz Bands, directed by Dr. Andria Mullan, take the stage. Included on their program is music from the movie, The Incredibles, and from the musical Jersey Boys The concert also will include jazz standards “Afro Blue”, “Laurie”, and “How High the Moon”, plus a composition by Stevie Wonder. Middle School Band concert – Thursday, May 18, 7:00 p.m. Four Piedmont Middle School bands will perform, two from 6th grade, and one each from seventh and eighth grade. The program includes the music of John Williams from the movie Star Wars Episode IV, the jazz standard “All Dem Leaves”, and arrangements of jazz music by Duke Jorda and Mike Dana. articles.text: Without play, we cannot find joy or happiness. We need play. But, as adults, almost none of us prioritize play. We calendar in time for exercise and work and we might find ourselves mindlessly scrolling through social media or watching the latest streaming content, but play rarely becomes a conscious choice day to day. Look at your calendar right now and see if you can find any evidence of prioritizing play. Are there portions of your day blocked out for meaningless fun? Socialization with no practical purpose? Games and activities that are not for the betterment of anyone or anything? The benefits of play include connecting with your creative self, noticing the world around you and appreciating beauty, finding enthusiasm, hope for the future, laughter, stress reduction, improving mood, connecting with others. Dr. Stuart Brown, founder of the National Institute for Play has identified eight different types of play personalities. Do any of these resonate with you? For most of us, it will likely be more than one. The Joker: Play is about nonsense or foolishness. Clowning around, funny noises and jokes Adults find joy and happiness through play. are this person’s fun. The Kinesthete: The ones who move and push their own physical selves for fun. Hikers, skiers, yogis, acrobats, dancers, basketball players are all kinesthetes. The Explorer: Play is about discovery both in the physical, intellectual and spiritual realms. The Competitor: For the competitor, the fun comes from competition and the battle to WIN! The rules matter because it gives the structure for the competition. The Director: The organizers who throw the best barbecues or plan the group camping trip. The Directors are planners and create exquisite experiences for themselves and others. The Collector: The collector likes to acquire and search for items within a specific category and/or collect specific types of experiences. The Artist/Creator: Play for this person is creating something artistic or functional. From building robots to painting or sculpting, the artist/creator is driven to make. The Storyteller: The storyteller lives in his or her imagination. Either by writing or creating worlds or inhabiting them through watching theatre, movies or reading novels, this person finds their play through the magic of story. It’s quite likely that you find play in a number of these categories. Being aware of them will help you identify what kind of play you can pursue. It’s time to bring play back into our day. Even in small amounts. And play that connects to creativity, has the power to change our mood, change our minds and change our meaningful relationships. Nina Meehan is the founder of GoCreate (https://gocreate.zone/) which offers services in consulting, coaching and workshops in creativity and communication.
articles.title: Making time to play

articles.text: Last week Piedmont school kids enjoyed multiple sessions of P.E. class on the Linda Beach pickleball courts. The Linda Beach courts are currently available for pickleball use by the schools and the public during a several month trial being conducted by the Piedmont Recreation Department. At the end of the trial, the City will decide [on] whether [to] use the Linda Beach courts exclusively for pickleball. Pickleball is the nation’s fastest growing sport. The International Federation of Pickleball currently has at least 70 member nations and is striving for inclusion of pickleball as an Olympic sport, possibly as early as 2028. According to the Sports Fitness Industry Association’s 2022 Pickleball Report, a third of pickleball players are under age 25. Former Piedmont High School and professional tennis player, Brad Gilbert, recently told ABC News, “I do see the sport [pickleball] growing because of the much quicker learning curve to play.” Brad Gilbert coached the former tennis great Andre Agassi, who has now become a pickleball convert. According to a recent article on Parents.com, part of the huge rise in pickleball participation is due to the increased inclusion of pickleball in schools’ athletic curriculums and at summer camps. In another article, soccer star Alex Morgan noted that 70 percent of kids in the U.S. stop playing sports by age 13. Morgan urged the prioritization of funding for municipal infrastructure allowing for low-cost participation by kids in sports that are “fun.” Pickleball meets both criteria. Municipalities across the nation are racing to meet the growing demand for pickleball facilities. The Piedmont Pickleball Committee hopes happy youngsters enjoying pickleball at the Linda Beach courts will become a star on a future Piedmont High School Pickleball Team. See PPD Blue on page 30 Kids learn pickleball during P.E. class By Jeff Trowbridge Last week Piedmont school kids enjoyed multiple sessions of P.E. class on the Linda Beach pickleball courts. The Linda Beach courts are currently available for pickleball use by the schools and the public during a several month trial being conducted by the Piedmont Recreation Department. At the end of the trial, the City will decide [on] whether [to] use the Linda Beach courts exclusively for pickleball. Pickleball is the nation’s fastest growing sport. The International Federation of Pickleball currently has at least 70 member nations and is striving for inclusion of pickleball as an Olympic sport, possibly as early as 2028. According to the Sports Fitness Industry Association’s 2022 Pickleball Report, a third of pickleball players are under age 25. Former Piedmont High School and professional tennis player, Brad Gilbert, recently told ABC News, “I do see the sport [pickleball] growing because of the much quicker learning curve to play.” Brad Gilbert coached the former tennis great Andre Agassi, who has now become a pickleball convert. According to a recent article on Parents.com, part of the huge rise in pickleball participation is due to the increased inclusion of pickleball in schools’ athletic curriculums and at summer camps. In another article, soccer star Alex Morgan noted that 70 percent of kids in the U.S. stop playing sports by age 13. Morgan urged the prioritization of funding for municipal infrastructure allowing for low-cost participation by kids in sports that are “fun.” Pickleball meets both criteria. Municipalities across the nation are racing to meet the growing demand for pickleball facilities. The Piedmont Pickleball Committee hopes happy youngsters enjoying pickleball at the Linda Beach courts will become a star on a future Piedmont High School Pickleball Team. This was the first time it has been held since the beginning of the COVID pandemic nearly three years ago. On hand were chefs serving delicious Mexican food along with Will Beuselinck enjoys a churro with his grandmother, Michelle Winchester. In the school courtyard were carnival games for kids, along with garden activities, arts, and crafts. “I just wanted to say thank you. My children have thrived under your leadership. What stands out to me most is what I have learned from you, your calm-under-pressure, your intelligence, your emotional intelligence, your kindness. I’m a better parent and community member by watching you,” said Oldrin. On hand to celebrate her career was husband Jim Cramer, and sons Pete and Jack. Speakers included former Superintendent Gail Uilkema who hired Cramer in 1988, School Board member Cory Smegal and mayor Jen Cavenaugh. “Carol has been wise and caring to students and dads alike, teaching us the importance of teamwork, perseverance and resilience,” said Wildwood Dads Club President Adam Fishman. “Carol has always been there to lend a listening ear, to offer invaluable advice, and champion Master of Ceremony Tory Roman (left) on stage with Carol Cramer as Carol receives a standing ovation. the initiatives that have brought our school community together.” Parents and contemporaries came to speak and give their thanks, including parents Signe Anderssel Venner and Zack Steinberg and former Beach Principal Michael Corritone and current Havens Principal Anne Dolid. After hearing from colleagues, Cramer thanked everyone in attendance. She called out the many people from her past, including former Beach Principal Nancy McHugh, who mentored her. articles.text: PHS returns to NCS finals; plays No. 1 Tamalpais tomorrow Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team has done it again. Seeded No. 3 in the North Coast Section post-season playoffs, it defeated No. 2 Acalanes in Lafayette last night, May 9, in an exhilarating 9-8 double-overtime win on a goal by Soren Dixon. Piedmont won 12-6 over No. 6 Miramonte in the quarterfinals at Witter Field on Thursday, May 4 to reach the semifinals yesterday. The Highlanders last won the NCS championship in 2019 as the No. 2 seed when they upset No. 1 Novato. Both games were won in comebacks. Piedmont responded from a 5-3 halftime deficit to Acalanes and a 4-2 disadvantage in the second quarter against Miramonte. “We were a bit sloppy in the beginning. But once we found our groove, we played together and played the best lacrosse that we could,” said senior leader Jack Nelson. articles.text: Long wins 800, Sorensen-Wald wins pole vault, boys win 4x400 relay Piedmont High’s track and field team produced impressive results at the 2023 Western Alameda County Conference Championships at Hayward High on Wednesday and Friday, May 3 and 5. PHS qualified in 37 events for the North Coast Section Bayshore Championship on May 13 by attaining top-six finishes or qualifying times. Leading the successful day was senior Parker Long, who won the 800-meter run with a time of 1:55.92 in a field of 45 runners. “I’m feeling good, I’m glad that I can prove I have it still. I was the top seed going into it and it still feels new to have the eyes on me,” said Long. As the favorite, Long feels like there’s been a target on him since running a fast time of 1:53.25 at the Dublin Distance Fiesta on March 18. “I got pretty nervous during the second lap [on Saturday]. I felt super tired and a lot of people were hanging with me. With about 200 [meters] to go, I just launched a kick,” he added. Long is hoping to peak at the right time with the big endof-season meets coming up – Bayshore NCS Meet of Champions on May 19-20 at Dublin HS, and the CIF State Championship on May 26-27 in Clovis. Only seconds behind Long in the 800 was teammate and classmate Christian Taylor, whose time was 1:56.25. Taylor also placed second of 47 runners in the 1600 with a time of 4:20.63 in an exhilarating race with Berkeley’s Mason Mullen, who stayed on Taylor’s back heels until the final corner, kicking his way to the front. “No one really wanted to take the lead, so I took it upon myself to do it. I was ahead for most of it, just trying to get on pace for 4:20. Ultimately, I got outkicked in the last 50 meters,” Taylor said. Taylor recently committed to continue his running career at UC Davis. “It’s nice to have my choice made. It was a bit stressful to wonder if I’m going to run in college. There’s a burden off of my Staff Photos Parker Long won the Western Alameda County Conference 800 meter run title. shoulders knowing that I’m going to be in a great program and have a lot of fun the next four years,” said Taylor. Taylor and Long were also featured in the team’s 4x400 relay team’s victory with teammates Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai and Sam Shelby, winning with a time of 3:26.56 against nine other teams. They defeated 2nd place Bishop O’Dowd by eight seconds. It was a highly productive day for Spencer Sorensen-Wald, who qualified for the NCS Bayshore meet in three events. He won the pole vault with a height of 11 feet even, was third of 13 in the 110- meter hurdles in 16:64 seconds, and was fourth of 22 in the 300 hurdles in 42.12. Piedmont also finished second and third in the pole vault with sophomore Meg Foster placing second of eight in 10 feet, 6 inches. Senior Conor Kim was third in 10 feet. Miguel Long was second in the high jump in 5 feet, 8 inches, and was fifth of 18 in the triple jump in 41 feet, 6 inches. Xander Schulte-Sasse placed third in a field of 36 runners in the 3200 with a time of 9:45.69, and. Competed in the 1600. articles.text: Sophomore Taylor Rolefson reached the finals of the 200-meter freestyle at the North Coast Section championships with a time of 1:59.67. She was Piedmont’s only individual finalist. Piedmont’s swim team had 10 athletes qualify for this year’s North Coast Section Championship at the Concord Community Pool, with events May 4-6. Sophomore Taylor Rolefson reached the finals on Saturday and placed 16th in the 200-meter freestyle with a time of 1:59.67. Junior Josie Oesterer competed in the 100 backstroke, finishing the preliminary round with a time of 58.95 in 18th of 39 athletes. Oesterer also swam the 200 freestyle, finishing in 2:01.29. Oesterer also qualified for the preliminary round for the 100 backstroke by finishing with a time of 59.38 in a swim-off against Kennedy Lee of Maria Carillo. Piedmont’s 400 freestyle relay team of Rolefson, Oesterer, freshman Sydney Olson, and sophomore Sonja ten Grotenhuis placed 18th of 38 teams with a time of 3:47.33 in the preliminary round. The girls’ 200 Medley Relay team of Oesterer, freshman Abigail Jacoby, Rolefson, and Olson finished with a time of 2:01.21. Piedmont’s only diver, junior Nina Schwab, was ninth of 16 with a score of 356.55. Boys results The 200-Medley relay team of Dimitri Secor, Ryan Stokes, Nick Costello, and Tom Rolefson was 29th of 40 teams in the preliminary round with a time of 1:44.28. The boys’ 200 freestyle relay team of Rolefson, Secor, Costello, and Stokes came in with a time of 1:32.74 in the preliminary round. In individual events, Rolefson finished the 50 freestyle prelims with a time of 22.26. Secor was also in the 100 backstroke preliminary round, finishing with a time of 56.74. Piedmont’s only diver, junior Nina Schwab, was ninth of 16 at NCS with a score of 356.55. Piedmont qualified two girls’ relay teams at NCS. Pictured are Sydney Olson (left), Sonja ten Grotenhuis (back), Taylor Rolefson, and Josie Oesterer.

articles.text: Eleanor Lavin was selected to play in the U.S. Lacrosse’s NorCal Senior All Star Game on May 21 at Tamalpais HS in Mill Valley. Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team saw its season come to an end on Tuesday, May 2, losing to No. 4 seed San Marin 15-5 in the opening round of the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs. Piedmont was the No. 13 seed. “The girls are a second-half team, and this time, the hole going into halftime was a little too deep to overcome. We had a lot of trouble gaining possession and controlling the ball,” explained PHS coach Carlton Chan. The match closes the Highlanders’ season with an 8-8 overall record. The Highlanders were able to challenge for the Western Alameda County Conference title once again but fell narrowly 11-9 to Bishop O’Dowd on April 27. “Our goal this year was to challenge in the league tournament. articles.text: Piedmont High’s baseball team closed its regular season on a high note, defeating Arroyo in its final two games. Piedmont won 3-2 in San Lorenzo on Wednesday, May 3, and won at home on Friday, May 5, with a comfortable 11-6 score. PHS closed its regular season on a four-game winning streak and finished with a 12-10 record, including 4-6 in the Foothill Division of the Western Alameda County Conference. The team now awaits its seeding in the Division 4 North Coast Section playoffs. Piedmont honored its three seniors on Senior Day on Friday: infielder Michael Aikawa, outfielder Ryan McConathy, and outfielder Liam Campbell. 11-6 over Arroyo Both teams scored four runs in the first inning, and Piedmont went ahead 5-4 following the bottom of the third, and 10-4 by the fifth inning. The Dons scored twice in the top-of-the-sixth, but the Highlanders scored one more run in the sixth for the 11-6 victory. Trailing 4-0 after the top-first, Piedmont got their bottom half started with Aikawa drawing a walk, followed by Markos Lagios smacking a double to center field. Peter Krumins walked to load the bases, then Dimitri Papahadjopoulos singled in Aikawa, then Will Parker hit a two-run single to score Lagios and Krumins, but Papahadjopoulos was thrown out at third. McConathy then slugged a double to center, and John Olsen tied the ballgame at 4-4 with a sacrifice fly to score Parker. In the third, McConathy hit a oneout single followed by Olsen drawing a walk. With two outs, Aikawa lined a single through the hole at second base to bring in McConathy, 5-4 Piedmont. In the fourth, McConathy hit a one-run single to score Krumins, who led off with a single. Liam Campbell scored the game-winning run in Piedmont’s 3-2 win over Arroyo. Piedmont honored its three seniors on Senior Night on May 5. Pictured are coach Eric Olson (left), Ryan McConathy, Michael Aikawa, Liam Campbell, and assistant coach Evan Haarz. Photos by Mark Aikawa Michael Aikawa had five hits and three doubles in a two-game series with Arroyo. Papahadjopoulos, who walked earlier, then scored on an error by Arroyo’s second baseman after McConathy stole second base. Diego Delventhal then singled in McConathy for an 8-4 lead. Piedmont’s two runs in the fifth came from a double by Krumins to score Aikawa. Aikawa also brought in Piedmont’s last run on a double to center field, scoring Olsen. Final stats: Aikawa was 3-for-3 with two doubles, two RBIs, two runs scored, and a walk. Krumins was 2-for-2 with three runs scored, an RBI, and two walks. Papahadjopoulos was 1-for-3 with a run scored and two RBIs. Parker was 1-for-3 with two RBIs and a run scored. McConathy was 3-for-4 with a double, RBI, and two runs scored. Olsen was 1-for-2 with an RBI and run scored. 3-2 over Arroyo Wednesday’s game was much closer. The Dons led 1-0 until Piedmont tied it in the top of the fourth inning. PHS followed with runs in the fifth and sixth innings. Piedmont opened the fourth inning with three walks from Papahadjopoulos, McConathy, and Delventhal. With one-out, Piedmont executed a successful triple steal. PHS went ahead 2-1 in the fifth after Krumins hit a double to center field, followed by Papahadjopoulos’s two-out single to score Krumins. With the game tied 2-2, Piedmont scored the game-winner with two-outs in the top of the sixth after Campbell hit a single and Aikawa slugged a double to deep center field, enabling Campbell to score all the way from first. Seve Sanchez entered as Piedmont’s closer, retiring three of four hitters by way of a ground out, lineup, and then Sanchez picking off Arroyo’s runner at first to end the game in a pickle. Final stats: Aikawa was 2-for-4 with a double and an RBI. Krumins was 1-for-3 with a double and a run scored. Papahadjopoulos was 3-for-3 with a run scored. Campbell was 1-for-2 with the game-winning run. NEXT UP Piedmont (12-10 overall) waits for their seeding in the Division 4 North Coast Section postseason. The opening round is scheduled for Wednesday, May 17, the quarterfinals are on Saturday, May 20, semifinals on May 24, and championship round on May 26-27.

articles.text: Photo by Erin Callaghan Piedmont’s volleyball season came to an end with loss to Acalanes in the North Coast Section Quarterfinals. Piedmont boys’ volleyball team’s season came to an end on Thursday, May 4 in the quarterfinals of the post-season North Coast Section playoffs. Piedmont lost in three sets to No. 3 seeded Acalanes in a match in Lafayette. Piedmont, the No. 6 seed, fell by scores of 26-24, 25-18, and 25-22. “The boys fought so hard during the game,” said PHS coach Mariah Cardenas. “The first set we kept a lead throughout the set but unfortunately the unforced errors held us back from winning. I always tell the boys it is us versus us, not us versus the – Piedmont volleyball coach Maria Cardenas team across the net. Our serve-receive was fairly strong but our defense was not prepared for the speed of Acalanes. The boys honestly did everything they could, and they should be very proud of themselves.” The match concluded a successful season for the Highlanders with a 14-7 overall record and its second consecutive NCS quarterfinals appearance. “It was bittersweet. This year has exceeded all my expectations. This group of young men is truly the dream team. We worked so hard all season to make it where we did,” Cardenas. For this year’s seniors – WilStaff Photo Outside hitter John Champion will be a senior leader on next year’s volleyball team. Staff Photo Senior Wilson Wong was a major part of the revival and success of Piedmont’s boys’ volleyball program. son Wong, James MaNguyen, Brayden Day, Owen Kelly, Eric Olaru-Hagen, Kai Lambert and Jonas Kra-Caskey – the growth of the program is something they hold near-and-dear. Wong helped revive the program in 2020 prior to the Covid pandemic, helping the team improve from a 3-5 record in the shortened 2021 season. Finishing at 7-8 in 2022, they qualified for the North Coast Section playoffs and upset No. 5 Analy in their first post-season match. “It’s been a massive journey. Three of us were on the B-team in middle school and we always felt like the underdog for seven years. But every single year we improved. We have a really special group,” said Wong. Coach Cardenas took the lead role this season after working as an interim coach in 2022. “Piedmont may never see another senior class like this group,” she said. “These boys truly paved this path from nothing. I’m honored to be closing out another historic season with Piedmont. I hope we can continue to flourish.” Looking ahead to 2024, Piedmont will return significant talent to the lineup. Outside hitter John Champion will lead the group, and junior Shunji Higashi made strides as a setter this season. Freshman Albert Bellingrath entered as a starter during the season and should make a big jump as Piedmont’s main middle hitter.

articles.text: Jasper Schuetz wins Freshman race The Piedmont Mountain Bike team wrapped up its season with the NorCal High School Cycling League Championship on Saturday and Sunday, May 6-7 at Six Sigma Ranch in Lower Lake, sending 17 riders to compete. The NorCal Championship was on a 5.1 mile course with an elevation gain of 750 feet. Jasper Schuetz won the Freshman Division 1 race to finish his season undefeated in five races. He is now the Norcal Freshman champion. Schuetz finished with a time of 41:49.93 over his twolap race. He finished 2.14 seconds ahead of Ryder Williams of Woodcreek High School. In the Varsity boys’ category, Andres Roberts finished 37th of 51 riders on the four-lap course. Also competing was Aleksi Valkonen. In the Junior Division, Max Rivera finished 16th of 84 racers with a three-lap time of 1:08:24.23. Matteo Scanu placed 22nd, Mark Hsia was 30th, Griffin Stein was 62nd and Artun Duransoy was right behind him. In the Sophomore Division, Cary Ward finished 64th, ahead of teammate Ethan Becker. Olive Reining raced in the Freshman girls event, finishing with a time of 1:23:30.11, and Caleb Canada, was 61st in the freshman boys’ race. Andres Roberts finished 37th in the boys’ varsity event. Max Rivera (right) placed 16th in the Sophomore event and Matteo Scanu (left) was 22nd.

articles.text: Reservations for Stern Grove Festival concerts will be open to the public beginning May 18. The festival begins June 18. All concerts are free, but reservation is required. Headlining the 86th season is The Flaming Lips, with performances by Indigo Girls, Santigold, Lyle Lovett, Bob Moses, and Patti Smith. San Francisco Symphony will perform on July 23. Concerts run from June 18 to August 20. Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization whose mission is “to make live musical experiences accessible to all.” Since its inception in 1938, the organization has presented the Stern Grove Festival as free concerts in Sigmund Stern Grove, an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. The amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites. The festival has brought more than eight decades of performing arts - including opera, theatre, and music - completely free. To view the full lineup, visit https://www.sterngrove. org/86th-concert-season.
articles.title: Stern Grove Festival begins June 18

articles.text: San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum in San Francisco is exhibiting Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in Art now through July. The new exhibition features more than 120 artworks borrowed from 20 of the finest museums and private collections in the world, with a focus on the arts of the Indian cultural sphere. Beyond Bollywood includes artwork from India, Pakistan, Nepal, Tibet, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, and Indonesia. “We hope visitors will come away with a transformed notion of the importance and power of dance,” said exhibition co-curator Forrest McGill. Beyond Bollywood will be on display through July 10. Dance dialogues events that include asian folk dance with expert speaker panels, take place May 25, June 11 and 22, and July 9. These pop-ups will include dance performances and demonstrations in the museum gallery, followed by a question and answer session, recurring monthly on selected Sundays and Thursdays. Admission is included with your ticket to Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in Art. Space is limited and reservations are recommended. For a full list of featured dancers and speakers, visit https://asianart.org/beyond-bollywood-events/. For more information, and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://exhibitions.asianart. org/exhibitions/beyond-bollywood-2000-years-of-dance-in-art/.
articles.title: Asian Art Museum: Beyond Bollywood on view through July

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California’s newest exhibition, Into the Brightness: Artists from Creativity Explored, opens on May 19. Into the Brightness features artwork from an artist collective with developmental and learning disabilities. The unique, interactive exhibit presents a wide variety of the artists’ personal experiences of the world. Into the Brightness is the largest museum exhibition at OMCA in over a decade, and features artists from Creativity Explored in San Francisco, Creative Growth in Oakland, and NIAD (Nurturing Independence Through Artistic Development) Art Center in Richmond. Featured artists include Saul Alegria, Peter Cordova, Tranesha Smith-Kilgore, Marlon Mullen, Dorian Reid, William Scott, Dinah Shapiro, Nicole Storm, and Marilyn Wong. The exhibition opens on Friday, May 19, and museum members may preview it one day earlier on May 18.
articles.title: Oakland Museum’s Into the Brightness exhibition opens May 19

articles.text: Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside will begin its “Summer Nights” events on June 1. The historic house is open until 7 p.m. and the Gardens open until 8 p.m. Summer Nights are a tradition at Filoli, and serve as a time to gather with family and friends and enjoy the sunset and summer blooms. Every Thursday night throughout the summer, the Grove Bar is serving wine and beer in the garden, nestled under the shade of the Olive Grove. The Georgian-style terraces around the historic house offer sweeping views of the Santa Cruz Mountains, a contrast to the 16-acre formal English Renaissance-style garden to the south. All admissions, including Summer Nights, require advance reservations. Masks will be required for those who are not vaccinated. Visit https://filoli.org/summer-nights/ for more information.
articles.title: Summer nights events at Filoli begin June 1

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet celebrates Patrick Armand’s final season as School Director and the 90th anniversary of the SF Ballet School with a Spring Festival. Performances will be held Wednesday through Friday, May 24-26. San Francisco Ballet School dancers will perform at the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts for this year’s festival, set to Lew Christensen’s Beauty and the Beast. Audiences will see a world premiere from former student and current Company member Myles Thatcher, alongside premieres from SF Ballet School student choreographers, including Dana Genshaft’s Stereo is King, Viktor Plotnikov’s We…, and Larissa Ponomarenko’s Frescoes. A fundraising dinner will be held on Thursday, May 25, with proceeds benefiting the Ballet School. For a list of performance times and dates and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.sf ballet.org/ productions/2023-spring-festival/. San Francisco Ballet School dancers will perform at the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts on May 24-26.
articles.title: SF Ballet School Spring Festival on May 24-26

articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre (ACT) will produce Wizard of Oz from June 1-25 at the Toni Rembe Theatre in downtown San Francisco. The classic tale by L. Frank Baum is transformed for the ACT stage by Tony Award–nominated director and choreographer Sam Pinkleton and Tony Award-winning designer David Zinn. “The myth of Dorothy and her friends, and their big adventure, means something different to every single person you ask—whether it’s childhood nostalgia, queer survival, or an unhealthy obsession with flying monkeys,” said Pinkleton. “I’m giddy and honored to enlist the brains, heart, and courage of the Bay Area—in collaboration with mega-genius David Zinn—to create an intimate, intergenerational, human-powered Wizard of Oz that is bursting with contradictions and big beating hearts.” The play is family-friendly and appropriate for young audiences. The cast includes El Beh, Keiko Shimosato, Darryl Jones, Katrina McGraw, Kunal Prasad, Ezra Reaves, Cathleen Riddley and Travis Rowland. For more infor mation, and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/202223-season/wizard-of-oz/. ACT will produce Wizard of Oz starting on June 1. ®
articles.title: ACT premieres Wizard of Oz June 1

articles.text: For a full lineup of festival events, dates and times, and to purchase tickets, visit https://valleyofthemoonmusicfestival.org/ event/the-symphony-as-a-triomozart-beethoven/. The highly acclaimed Valley of the Moon Music Festival in Sonoma County will take place this summer from July 15 through 30. Tickets are now available, This is the festival’s ninth season and is entitled “Transformation: Grand Works on an Intimate Scale.” This year will highlight works originally written for large orchestras in chamber music versions. The festival will include a mix of alfresco and indoor concerts, as well as livestream events. The festival will kick off on July 15 with “The Symphony as a Trio,” featuring Mozart’s Piano Quartets as written like concertos, with pianist Axel Trolese as soloist. Pianist Axel Trolese will be the soloist in Mozart’s Piano Quartets at the Valley of the Moon Festival in July.
articles.title: Valley of the Moon Music returns to Sonoma County July 15-30

articles.text: Let’s all say hello to our new friend, Pennywise, the clown When I was 11 years old, my dad took me to see a sci-fi film titled The Thing. I was simultaneously riveted and terrified. There was one scene in which the Thing, an enormous, manlike creature from another world, stood on one side of a door and two scientists stood on the other side, debating about turning the knob. It’s a familiar trope now, but for me, a kid whose imagination could slip into overdrive at even the prospect of walking down the stairs into a dark basement, that moment to this day remains unforgettable. I think of it as the meta-creepy, hair-raising sweet spot. It’s a place where our labyrinth of fears resides – fears that can define part of our childhood. And it is in this sweet spot that Stephen King resides, coming at it from a myriad of angles with a prolific talent that seems without end. Regardless of the novel of the same name, King is able to find that cluster of fears that reside within the reader/filmgoer and provoke them until fear morphs into dread, most times with astonishing quickness. It’s why standing on the top step of a dark basement, the ominous smells wafting up, then turning on the light switch and finding that the lights aren’t working, is such an effective preview of ominous things that lie ahead. Therein is the power and effectiveness of the film It, made in 2017. Using the image of the benign and joyful clown, King takes the expected and transforms it into something most frightful. Part of the brilliance of this film, set in the small town of Derry, Maine, in 1989, is that it opens with seven middle-schoolers, all just released from school with the summer stretching before them. At the outset they are not a crew, though each resides on that outcast edge of the school experience. They slowly come together and tentatively share their individual encounters with a shape-shifting clown called Pennywise (Bill Scarsgard). In fact, the initial set up of the movie begins with Bill Denbrough (Jaeden Lieberher) constructing a small boat made out of heavy paper for his younger brother, Georgie (Jackson Robert Scott), who wants to go outside and play in the rain and float the boat in the water-filled gutters while he chases behind. That is until the boat disappears into a storm drain and, of course, Georgie kneels down and looks into the opening. Guess what? There, holding the boat, is Pennywise. What is also immensely important is that Pennywise begins to represent those moments of disbelief and then terror, eliciting from the kids their personal anxieties and apprehensions and unresolved fears that will remain with them for a lifetime. Realize that you are not watching a horror film per se. Though King is thought of as a master of the genre, it’s a shallow definition. Know that it is not Pennywise who is at the center of the story. It is the kids, as a group and as individuals, that give this film its essence and texture. Each is dealing with a standing-at-the-top-of-the-basement-stairs moment. Summoning up massive amounts of will each takes one step then a second into that space defined by their own imaginations. The novel It is over 1,000 pages long and is divided into two parts. This film adaption focuses on the kids; it’s also subtitled, and while the end credits roll, it is titled Chapter One. In the denouement of Chapter One, the seven stand in a circle and take a blood oath, swearing to return to Derry if ever need be. And return they do. Not to face Pennywise (it was never about Pennywise), but to finally face their unresolved fears. It. Directed by Chase Muschietti. Starring Jaeden Lieberher, Jeremy Ray Taylor, Sophia Lillis. 2 hrs., 15 min. Rated R.
articles.title: It – scary film but exceptionally well-made

articles.text: Earwig and the Witch is a story about a fearless young orphan who was left to grow up in an orphanage called The St. Morward’s Home for Children, nestled in the bucolic English countryside. Earwig, though rambunctious, is content at St. Morward. She has a best friend, Custard (Logan Hannan), and wishes not to be adopted. She is also unaware that her mother had magical powers. Her life changes dramatically when a strange couple arrives, Bella Yaga (Vanessa Marshall) and Mandrake (Richard E. Grant), who decide to take in Earwig. Puzzled and uncertain, she senses that her new guardians are unusual. Bella has told her that she is a witch, so Earwig sets about trying to uncover their secrets, and discovers a world of spells and potions and a mysterious song that may be the key to finding the family she always wanted. She is also told by Bella that the only reason she and Mandrake wanted to adopt her is because they needed an “extra pair of hands” to help with the chores. Earwig agrees to work for them if they will teach her about their magic and spells. As you can imagine, things don’t work out quite as expected. Earwig and the Witch comes from the well-known Studio Ghibli and was directed by Goro Miyazaki, son of the famous Hayao Miyazaki. It is the Studio’s first CG animated feature and a striking departure from Ghibli’s astonishing hand-drawn animé. The story is based on the children’s novel of the same name written by Diana Wynne Jones. A special note to our readers who have followed the Post’s run of the works of Studio Ghibli and have taken pleasure in the rich animation and wonderful story telling of Hayao Miyazaki, et al. Earwig and the Witch, while released in Japan in 2020, is now streaming on Prime/VUDU/ Apple tv. Hayao Miyazaki is also scheduled to soon release his much-anticipated animated feature (handdrawn), How Do We Live. Earwig and the Witch. Directed by Goro Miyazaki. Animé from Studio Ghibli. With the voices of Taylor Paige, Richard E. Grant, Vanessa Marshall. 1 hr., 22 min. Rated PG. Released in 2020. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. A scene from Goro Miyazaki’s Earwig and the Witch

articles.text: Alex Roe and Chloë Grace Moretz in The 5th Wave Tweens and teens will find The Fifth Wave compelling considering that it features 16-year-old high school girl, Cassie Sullivan (Chloe Grace Moretz), who has all of her teenage bona fides in place: lots of friends, non-stop texting, is on the soccer team, and is crushing on a senior football player named Ben (Nick Robinson). Based on a Young Adult trilogy by Rick Yancey, the film might qualify for that moniker known as a “chick flick,” had it not been for the fact that it is an apocalyptic/dystopian/futuristic story not unlike Independence Day with an overlay of The Hunger Games. The setup: An average school day, kids in class, all is normal when chilling reports come in that high above the earth hovers a ship of unknown origins. Not just something akin to the Hindenburg floating overhead, but a massive E.T. fortress, one that signals that events are about to take place that will change the lives forever of all those who survive global power outages, earthquakes, tidal waves, a pandemic and finally an invasion. In other words, the visitors don’t come in peace. As her dad (Ron Livingston) explains, “they’re not here for us, they’re here for earth.” Cassie is one of the survivors and she abruptly finds herself alone and on the run. Her father was killed and her mother died of a worldwide flu epidemic carried by birds. Is Cassie resilient? Absolutely. Is the film formulaic and decidedly lame? To the max. Will kids like it? Definitely. End of the world stuff with a small dash of romance. So, while the adults are choosing to stream films such as Tar, Elvis, The Revenant or The Danish Girl, the kids will be eager to see the first installment of The Fifth Wave. The Fifth Wave. Directed by J.Blakeson. Starring Chloe Grace Moretz, Alex Roe, Nick Robinson. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2016, Now streaming on Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: The Fifth Wave – teen survival in a dystopian world

Carnival of life By Joseph Gold The past weekend was a grand musical carnival, beginning with a spectacular SpringFest in Woodside on Saturday. The festivities started with an orchestra concert played by the Fest Orchestra conducted by Geoffrey Gallegos. We heard the theme from the Standard Hour radio program “this hour is yours” written by Julius Haug. Clarinetist Peter Weinberg lent his artistry to the brilliant concertino by Carl Maria von Weber. The All of the amplified music was outdoors. The variety of music included country and western and rock ‘n’ roll…to name but a few. It was a pleasure to experience events like this and made me think of what is possible in Piedmont. Sunday in Piedmont Back home on Sunday, a concert by the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra brought this thought to reality. As readers of this column know, the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra is a community inspired group. Sunday’s concert, conducted by Martha Stoddard, included a well thought out program before a large audience. Members of the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra with conductor Martha Stoddard and young soloist, violinist Madison Lee. A special thanks needs to be given to the orchestra manager Stuart Gronningen, a horn player formerly with Oakland Symphony and Berkeley Symphony orchestras. The concert included a solo of a piece by Vivaldi by guest violinist, Madison Lee, a 7th grade at Thornton Junior High School in Fremont, and the student of Wendy Reid at Holy Names University Preparatory Department. Music education in public schools That brings to mind another subject – Education – a much discussed subject that is rather like the weather as described by Mark Twain: “Everybody talks about the weather but nobody does anything about it.” About two years ago, I learned that the Piedmont schools were looking for teachers. I contacted the personnel department to volunteer my services. They asked me to do a number of things. First I submitted a letter of application. Then they asked me to submit my numerous teaching credentials. I did this. Ditto for letters of recommendation from some of the world’s most famous musicians. Then they asked for proof of vaccinations. They even asked for some bank information, all of which was provided. I even hand-delivered some of the papers to the office. When I arrived, it was obvious that they couldn’t wait to get rid of me fast enough. Two years passed. I sent timely emails and personal hand-written letters to the school. On occasion they responded, but mice on a treadmill make more progress than I did. After two years of getting the runaround, I gave up. They say education is important. Ask the bureaucrats. articles.text: Paul McCartney (left) and John Lennon The origin of the word skiffle is unknown. In the west of England since the late nineteenth century ”to make a skiffle” means to make a mess of any business. In early 20th century America a “skiffle” was a rent party, designed to pay rent on a house. “Skiffle” was first used on a record in 1925 with Jimmy O’Bryant and his Chicago Skifflers. It was used to describe country blues, including “Hometown Skiffle” (1929) and “Skiffle Blues” (1946) by Dan Burley & His Skiffle Boys. Ma Rainey used it to describe her repertoire to rural audiences. The term “skiffle” disappeared from American music in the 1940s. In the 1950’s, a British skiffle revival developed out of the postwar jazz scene, moving toward traditional jazz. It was acoustic music played by working class people. Notable artists were Lonnie Donnegan, Bill Bailey Skiffle Group and Ken Colyer’s Jazzmen. Donegan’s fast-tempo version of Lead Belly’s “Rock Island Line” was a hit in 1956, selling over a million copies. The root players of British rock were skiffle players, including Van Morrison, Mick Jagger, Roger Daltry, Jimmy Page, Keith Richards, Brian May, Robin Trower, David Gilmour, Graham Nash and a working class bloke from the seaport of Liverpool, John Lennon. John started the skiffle group The Quarrymen in 1957. In addition to skiffle music, they also played a lot of American rock and roll. Within months, Paul McCartney was added, then George Harrison in 1958. Paul replaced Stuart Sutcliffe on bass in 1961. Richard Starkey, better known as Ringo Starr, was added in 1962. John Lennon, Stuart Sutcliffe and Cynthia Powell, then Lennon’s girlfriend, came up with a name variation of The Crickets, Buddy Holly’s band, Initially the band was called The Beatlals, then The Silver Beatles, then finally The Beatles. McCartney grew up in a rich exposure to jazz and popular music. His father James led Jim Mac’s Jazz Band in the 1920’s and played piano at family holiday gatherings. Paul didn’t read music like his dad, and learned by ear and by watching his dad play. Eventually, Paul would take over playing at the family gatherings. “[Paul] provided a lightness, an optimism, while I would always go for the sadness, the discords, the bluesy notes,” explained John Lennon some years later. “There was a period when I thought I didn’t write melodies, that Paul wrote those and I just wrote straight, shouting rock ‘n’ roll. But, of course, when I think of some of my own songs- ’In My Life’, ‘This Boy’-I was writing melody with the best of them.” Listen to and read my 17 Lennon-McCartney Beatles solo examples for this column and music for my previous columns at: http://www.guitarimprov.com/ PostColumns.pdf. Jim Gleason is a Piedmont-based author and guitar instructor. Call (510) 923-9522, text (510) 435-3997 or email jim@ guitarencyclopdeia.com for videoconference or in-person lessons. The course is available for free online at www.guitarimprov.com.

articles.text: Piedmont and Millennium High School families arrived at the Alan Harvey Theater foyer on April 27 to see an exhibit of art work produced by students in the Advanced Placement (AP) art class. More than 100 pieces from Piedmont’s top 18 junior and senior artists were on display. This work highlighted the AP 2D and 3D students’ work during the school year. Students were challenged to create an artistic inquiry called a “Sustained Investigation for the College Board” and produce 10 works of art throughout the year. “It is a challenge for a 16- or 17-year-old to design an aesthetic inquiry question that they explore for the entire academic year. There are ebbs and flows of interest in their exploration. It does emphasize intentionality with concept, imagery, and medium which pushes the student artist to work at a conceptual level with their ideas,” explained PHS art teacher Gillian Bailey. Bailey added that after two to three years in PHS art courses, students are prepared “with the technical ability to render well and use a variety of artistic techniques to express their original ideas at a college level, which is what the AP curriculum requires.” Photos by Hannah Bjork and Piedmont Post Beck Peterson, Maissy Richardson, and student artists in the Alan Harvey Theater foyer for the AP Art reception. articles.text: Perhaps no room in the home evokes stronger feelings in homeowners than the bathroom. Whether a primary suite or otherwise, most desire sanctuary, comfort and functionality. If you have a bathroom that isn’t what you want, it’s a great time to explore updating this key space in your home. While primary suites may be foremost, don’t ignore that guest bath and powder room. Floorplan changes, converting tubs to walk in showers and adding extra footage are typical and should only be undertaken with a licensed General Contractor. For all but the most simplest upgrades, your project will require a permit, which can take several weeks to obtain, and you’ll need drawings. California is subject to regulations such as Title 24, which is designed to ensure that building design and construction maximizes energy and water efficiency. Examples include LED lighting and lowflow water fixtures. If your bathroom layout works for you, a less expensive or invasive option is to do a refresh, rather than a remodel. Updated plumbing fixtures, lighting, paint and a new vanity top may be all you need. There are limitless options for countertops, tile and fixtures so you may need a design professional to help guide you. You’ll need to decide not only what you want but most importantly, what you can afford. It’s safe to say every project will have surprises and change orders so your budget should allow for increases. Contractors with lowball pricing and promises of fast completion may seem like the way to go in the beginning, but in the end may not be the best value. You’re likely to experience project delays and unexpected upcharges, Clean lines of a walk-in shower and modern furnishings complement the classic architecture of this main bathroom. The existing layout of a family bathroom was maintained with this stylish and bold renovation. which are difficult to dispute when your bathroom is torn apart. Engaging with and selecting a qualified General Contractor from the beginning is key. They can provide detailed budgets and schedules, setting realistic expectations before your project starts. Seek out an experienced company who will undoubtedly have connections with other qualified professionals. Ask your friends and neighbors for recommendations. Look at jobsites in your neighborhood – are they tidy and respectful of neighbors? It’s never too soon to begin planning. Explore websites and social media for designs and products that appeal to you. You can create a “look book” with wallcoverings, tile, lighting and color schemes on sites such as Pinterest. articles.text: Sabrina Santoyo takes over as owner of Art Loft Framing Many Piedmonters are familiar with Art Loft Framing, the second-oldest business in Montclair Village. Now owned by Sabrina Santoyo, she sat down with the Piedmont Post to discuss her history with the business and her own experience in the picture-framing industry. Art Loft was founded by Tom and Celeste Brodehl 50 years ago, in 1973. Santoyo has worked with the Brodehls for the past 15 years and became the sole owner this year, 2023. The Brodehls first established Art Loft across the street from the current location. “The old location was upstairs and in an actual loft, hence the name,” Santoyo explained. Even after the Brodehls moved the business to its current groundfloor location on Antioch Court in 1984, they kept the name. While Celeste is fully retired, Tom still comes in on Fridays and Saturdays to help facilitate Art Loft’s customer rewards program and “to help me with larger projects,” said Santoyo. “We stay busy here, getting large projects like that about once a week lately. Tom’s the wingspan man.” Working at Art Loft Monday through Friday, Santoyo has had ample time to enjoy and nurture Art Loft’s community of neighboring shops and devoted customers. “Art Loft has been very involved in this community for all of its 50 years,” she said, “and it’s been a joy to continue that tradition where many shops in Montclair Village are clustered. We always put up flyers when our neighbors are having events and promotions.” “The community of our customers, new and longtime, are very invested in the arts — not just framing art. It shows in their care for the pieces they bring and their attentiveness to the work we do.” “There is no typical week,” Santoyo emphasized. Over the course of a few days, framing projects can range from a clasThe exterior of Art Loft. articles.text: If you have a family member with special needs, you might face emotional and physical issues, but you also may be concerned about maximizing the financial support your loved one requires. Consequently, you may want to consider establishing a special needs trust. This type of trust can help maintain the financial security and lifestyle of an individual with special needs. Furthermore, a special needs trust can allow the trust’s beneficiary to receive financial support for supplemental needs without losing public benefits, such as Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and Medicaid. Here’s how it works: You, as the trust’s grantor, establish the trust and name a trustee who is responsible for managing the trust. You can fund the trust with gifts throughout your lifetime or from other sources, such as inheritances or court settlements. But another popular funding mechanism is life insurance, which the trust can purchase on the life of one or both parents of a special-needs child. And as long as the trust is also named the beneficiary of the policy, government benefits will be protected. In a special needs trust, the role of trustee is important. A trustee must manage the funds within the trust and ensure those funds are used only to supplement SSI and Medicaid, the government programs that typically pay for food, housing and medicine. Instead, a special needs trust can be used for most other expenses, including transportation and travel, education, entertainment, professional services and personal items. You could serve as trustee yourself or choose a relative or a trusted friend. Ideally, you want someone who’s familiar with your wishes and the needs of your family member with disabilities and who is also competent at managing finances and staying current on SSI and Medicaid regulations. As an alternative, you could hire a professional trust company to manage your special needs trust. This type of company has expertise in asset management and government regulations and can provide you with strict recordkeeping of all the financial transactions associated with your trust. If you go this route, you’ll want to compare different trust companies’ costs and services. For such a personal matter as administering a trust for your special-needs family member, you’ll want to be sure you’re comfortable with whatever company you select. Also, you’ll want to be familiar with some of the possible areas of concern regarding special needs trusts. For one thing, because the trustee totally controls when and how funds are distributed, beneficiaries can get frustrated if their requests for money are denied. Additionally, while third-party special needs trusts are funded by someone other than the beneficiary, first-party special needs trusts are funded by the beneficiary’s own assets — and for these first-party special needs trusts, the trust must typically pay back Medicaid for money it has spent on the beneficiary’s behalf after the death of the beneficiary. This repayment could deplete the trust, depriving secondary beneficiaries of any assets they might otherwise receive. Third-party special needs trusts do not require Medicaid repayment. Consult with a legal professional before establishing a special needs trust to ensure this arrangement is appropriate for your family’s situation. But if it is, and if it’s managed properly, it can relieve you of some of the stress you may feel over the future of your loved one with special needs. Sabrina Santoyo takes over as owner of Art Loft Framing By Selen Ozturk Many Piedmonters are familiar with Art Loft Framing, the second-oldest business in Montclair Village. Now owned by Sabrina Santoyo, she sat down with the Piedmont Post to discuss her history with the business and her own experience in the picture-framing industry. Art Loft was founded by Tom and Celeste Brodehl 50 years ago, in 1973. Santoyo has worked with the Brodehls for the past 15 years and became the sole owner this year, 2023. The Brodehls first established Art Loft across the street from the current location. “The old location was upstairs and in an actual loft, hence the name,” Santoyo explained. Even after the Brodehls moved the business to its current groundfloor location on Antioch Court in 1984, they kept the name. While Celeste is fully retired, Tom still comes in on Fridays and Saturdays to help facilitate Art Loft’s customer rewards program and “to help me with larger projects,” said Santoyo. “We stay busy here, getting large projects like that about once a week lately. Tom’s the wingspan man.” Working at Art Loft Monday through Friday, Santoyo has had ample time to enjoy and nurture Art Loft’s community of neighboring shops and devoted customers. “Art Loft has been very involved in this community for all of its 50 years,” she said, “and it’s been a joy to continue that tradition where many shops in Montclair Village are clustered. We always put up flyers when our neighbors are having events and promotions.” “The community of our customers, new and longtime, are very invested in the arts — not just framing art. It shows in their care for the pieces they bring and their attentiveness to the work we do.” “There is no typical week,” Santoyo emphasized. articles.text: A solid turnout of 27 walkers and three K-9 best friends showed up at the Exedra last week on May 3 for some exercise with the Walking on Wednesdays group. The group’s submission of the mulberry trees in front of the Piedmont Play School in Hampton Park had been selected as Heritage Trees by the Piedmont Park Commission on Arbor Day. Mulberry trees had been planted in Piedmont during the 1870s in an effort to produce silk at a “Silk Farm” in the area that is now Littlewood Drive. Mulberry leaves are the only source of food for silk worms. Jennifer Jones provided some background information on the subject for the walkers, with some help from the pre-school students at the Play School. At the Arbor Day celebration, the Play School and Walking on Wednesdays received Heritage Tree pins as awards, so the group wanted to pay a visit to Ritchie and the Play School. The walkers headed off following a usual route, going up Highland Avenue to Sheridan, Wildwood and Crocker Avenues. The group enjoyed seeing the beautiful spring flowers, including rhododendrons, azaleas, California poppies, wisterias, and dogwood. The walkers went up Crocker to Hampton Avenue and past Crocker Park. There was a tree covered with messages of appreciation as part of the City’s annual Michelle Ritchie with Piedmont Play School students Jolene Groboske, Parker Giammona, Sophia Fedor, and Grant Ng-Wilson. invitation to share messages of gratitude on trees throughout the city. The group continued up Hampton to Hampton Park, where they could hear children behind the Play School. Michelle Ritchie and other teachers were supervising play activity, and she and four students agreed to visit with the walkers. After presenting another Heritage Trees pin to Ritchie, it was time for students to get back to play and the walkers to get back to their weekly walk. Before leaving Hampton Park, the group checked out the two tennis courts and the Guy Saperstein Basketball Court with Tyson Lake hidden above it up the hill. The pace on the return to the city center was different, and a long line of them arrived at different times around noon at the Community Hall parking lot. A couple of raindrops fell, but the walkers’ charmed weather lives continued. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Wednesday Walkers pose in front of Piedmont Play School: Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Nany Henn, Jim Kellogg, Bill Ahern, Joyce Ahern, Alissa Quan, Jennifer Peltzer, Peggy Schultz, Gloria DaSilva, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Helen Dong, Ken Moy, Quincy Dong, Joanne Larson, Lilly Guardia-Labar, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Sherry Jacobs, Dave DeRoche, Ian Morgan, Ann Quinby, Matt Gerhardt, Mike Nachtwey with K-9 best friend Clooney, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Greg Slatoff, Carolyn George, Chuck Hoffman, and John Engemann who were walking with the group for the first time.
