articles.text: Last month on April 26, the Piedmont Police Department launched its new “Safety 4 Seniors” program. Coordinated by Officer Tyler Petit, the program provides resources to seniors including everyday safety advice, education about phone and online scams, and home security update support. “The program kicked off last October,” explained Petit. “Around that time we started getting more cold calls about seniors facing scams and security problems; at least 60-70% of these issues were preventable given the right safety education. I submitted a memorandum to Chief Jeremy Bowers wanting to create a program providing advice to seniors to prevent them from being victims to these preventable problems, and it was soon approved.” Alongside home security and scam safety presentations during senior meetings at the Community Hall, the program is a new way to provide personalized contact between seniors in Piedmont and the officers serving them and their city. Petit gave a 90-minute presentation and question-and-answer session on April 6 at a meeting with 30 seniors. “I designed the program wanting seniors to know that they can contact PPD and request a one-on-one meeting with other officers or myself to address any safety vulnerabilities they may be facing personally or in their own home,” said Petit. One major resource that the program offers is direct access to the Alameda County Adult Protective Services system. “For seniors in need of home safety or medical assistance – like installing a handicap ramp or establishing easily accessible emergency contacts – who don’t know where to start or are struggling to find help through their own health provider, we can connect them with these services quickly through the county,” said Petit. “Our community policing is strong here in Piedmont, and a lot of our attention focuses on resources for children and younger groups,” he added. “Seniors have had such rich experiences that I think many people assume they have a thorough knowledge of the safety issues they’re vulnerable to, but they didn’t grow up in a time of cryptocurrency assets and gift card scams.” To learn more about the Safety 4 Seniors program or to utilize its resources, contact Officer Tyler Petit at 420-3005 x3241, or by email at tpetit@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: PPD launches Safety For Seniors program

articles.text: The First Mondays Reading Group met in the Community Hall on May 1 with a turnout of 15 readers for the discussion. An update was provided on a new reading group Bob Hall has created that will focus on short literary works. It had a nice toein-the-water start last week in a Zoom call, with seven people sharing ideas about works by Raymond Carver, Nora Ephron, and Emily Dickinson. The new group will meet on the third Monday of the month, May 15, at 1:30 p.m. Those interested should contact Bob Hall at bmkjhall@comcast.net. The discussion on May 1 centered on The Killer Angels, a 1974 historical novel by Michael Shaara that won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1975. The book depicts the three-day Battle of Gettysburg during the American Civil War in July 1863, and the days leading up to it, as the Union and the Confederacy troops moved into battle position around the town of Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. The novel is character-driven and is told from the perspective of different individuals in both the Confederacy and the Union. A film adaptation of the novel, titled Gettysburg, was released in 1993. The book’s title comes from Union Col. Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain, one of the novel’s major characters. He remembers reciting to his father a speech from Hamlet: “What a piece of work is man ... in action how like an angel!” But his sergeant replies, “Well, if he’s an angel, all right then...But he damn well must be a killer angel.” Confederate General Robert E. Lee is leading his army into Pennsylvania. He hopes by threatening Washington, DC he will draw the Union army into battle, crush it, and bring the war to an end. However, his most important general, James Longstreet, is gravely concerned. The Union forces are strongly entrenched, and he tries to persuade Lee twice that the Union’s position is too strong. He urges Lee to march away and fight later on more favorable ground. But Lee orders two different attacks on the Union positions. Longstreet follows orders. General George Pickett leads a charge, but is turned back with heavy losses, and the Confederate attacks are repulsed. A shaken Lee orders retreat. Most members of the reading group liked The Killer Angels. They enjoyed the descriptions of the characters and how Shaara developed them. The book is fiction but reads like non-fiction. Readers said they could feel how tired and hungry the soldiers were. The huge death toll – over 50,000 men in three days – and how it was gruesomely described saddened some readers. Equally sad was the fact that these were Americans fighting other Americans, and often friends fighting each other. Some readers found the battle maps Shaara provided to be helpful to follow the military action, but others found them hard to read and confusing. Another issue for some was that it was hard to follow the many different characters Shaara presented. The question of historical accuracy was raised, but unanswered. Shaara did significant research for the book, and considerable amounts of first-person Civil War documents exist. It was noted that Shaara wrote two other Civil War novels. The readers considered the mindset of soldiers needing to follow orders, even when they knew the direction was flawed. The group felt The Killer Angels was a worthwhile read, and a book most readers would not have read were it not for the First Mondays Reading Group. Future discussions The readers had previously selected The Hare with Amber Eyes by Edmund de Waal for June, How Beautiful We Were by Cameroonian-American novelist Imbolo Mbue for July, and Four Fish: The Future of the Last Wild Food by Paul Greenberg for August. The group’s next discussion will be on Monday, June 6 at 1:30 p.m. at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Parl. New readers are welcome to join the group and there is no fee to participate. articles.text: Oakland Museum to host first NINS event No Immigrants No Spice (NINS), a Bay Area nonprofit focused on awareness of immigrant contributions through food, culture and economy, will hold its second BBQ without Borders event on Saturday, May 13 at Oakland Museum from 5:00-9:00 p.m. The event will feature Chef Ron Dumra of Wah Jee Wah, Chef Lilly Duran of Clandestina Cafe, and Chef Tadayuki of the former Family Cafe, who will celebrate their regional specialties of Lechon, Tandoori and Yakitori. Tickets are on sale now. General entry includes dinner, dessert, one beverage, as well as a full stage show with Taiko drummers, Bhangra, Flamenco, a Cuban salsa band and even an opera performance. Guests will be invited to explore the theme of “cultivating home” through physical mini marts constructed in the museum’s gardens. There will also be an area for kids’ activities with a continuous game of “found object soccer”, a basmati rice bag race, an immersive collaborative art piece and a silent auction of premier prizes. Craft cocktails, mocktails, wine, and beer will also be available, and additional food and drink will be available for purchase. Guests may purchase a VIP ticket and donate directly to the Resilience Fund. A sliding scale option will make tickets more accessible to the public. NINS’ newly established Resilience Fund has been designed to distribute micro grants to vulnerable Bay Area residents: recent arrivals, and those with varying levels of documentation and DACA status. “BBQ without Borders is a space to celebrate and honor our most vulnerable communities,” said NINS founder and Piedmont resident Dr. Vibha Gupta.. “We hope you can come eat something delicious, witness a spectacular performance, meet someone new, and walk away with a new experience.” To learn more about BBQ without Borders, contact noimmigrantsnospice@gmail.com. Tickets and event details can be found at www.noimmigrantsnospice.org and eventbrite (https://www.eventbrite.com/e/ bb q -w it h o u t- b o r d e r s - t ickets-68562557455).

Coordinated by Officer Tyler Petit, the program provides resources to seniors including everyday safety advice, education about phone and online scams, and home security update support. “The program kicked off last October,” explained Petit. “Around that time we started getting more cold calls about seniors facing scams and security problems; at least 60-70% of these issues were preventable given the right safety education. I submitted a memorandum to Chief Jeremy Bowers wanting to create a program providing advice to seniors to prevent them from being victims to these preventable problems, and it was soon approved.” Alongside home security and scam safety presentations during senior meetings at the Community Hall, the program is a new way to provide personalized contact between seniors in Piedmont and the officers serving them and their city. Petit gave a 90-minute presentation and question-and-answer session on April 6 at a meeting with 30 seniors. “I designed the program wanting seniors to know that they can contact PPD and request a one-on-one meeting with other officers or myself to address any safety vulnerabilities they may be facing personally or in their own home,” said Petit. One major resource that the program offers is direct access to the Alameda County Adult Protective Services system. “For seniors in need of home safety or medical assistance – like installing a handicap ramp or establishing easily accessible emergency contacts – who don’t know where to start or are struggling to find help through their own health provider, we can connect them with these services quickly through the county,” said Petit. “Our community policing is strong here in Piedmont, and a lot of our attention focuses on resources for children and younger groups,” he added. “Seniors have had such rich experiences that I think many people assume they have a thorough knowledge of the safety issues they’re vulnerable to, but they didn’t grow up in a time of cryptocurrency assets and gift card scams.” To learn more about the Safety 4 Seniors program or to utilize its resources, contact Officer Tyler Petit at 420-3005 x3241, or by email at tpetit@piedmont.ca.gov. BBQ without Borders Food Festival on May 13 Oakland Museum to host first NINS event No Immigrants No Spice (NINS), a Bay Area nonprofit focused on awareness of immigrant contributions through food, culture and economy, will hold its second BBQ without Borders event on Saturday, May 13 at Oakland Museum from 5:00-9:00 p.m. The event will feature Chef Ron Dumra of Wah Jee Wah, Chef Lilly Duran of Clandestina Cafe, and Chef Tadayuki of the former Family Cafe, who will celebrate their regional specialties of Lechon, Tandoori and Yakitori. Tickets are on sale now. General entry includes dinner, dessert, one beverage, as well as a full stage show with Taiko drummers, Bhangra, Flamenco, a Cuban salsa band and even an opera performance. Guests will be invited to explore the theme of “cultivating home” through physical mini marts constructed in the museum’s gardens. There will also be an area for kids’ activities with a continuous game of “found object soccer”, a basmati rice bag race, an immersive collaborative art piece and a silent auction of premier prizes. Craft cocktails, mocktails, wine, and beer will also be available, and additional food and drink will be available for purchase. Guests may purchase a VIP ticket and donate directly to the Resilience Fund. A sliding scale option will make tickets more accessible to the public. NINS’ newly established Resilience Fund has been designed to distribute micro grants to vulnerable Bay Area residents: recent arrivals, and those with varying levels of documentation and DACA status. “BBQ without Borders is a space to celebrate and honor our most vulnerable communities,” said NINS founder and Piedmont resident Dr. Vibha Gupta.. “We hope you can come eat something delicious, witness a spectacular performance, meet someone new, and walk away with a new experience.” To learn more about BBQ without Borders, contact noimmigrantsnospice@gmail.com. He endured a long journey, with Early-Onset Alzheimer’s Disease. He was nearly 72. Born Steven John Book in North Carolina, he was the son of Dr. Don Book and Jill Book, and spent most of his formative years in West Hartford, CT, attending Loomis Chaffee in high school and MIT in college. Steve could be found with a calculator in his hands at age 3 and learning Eritrean and French as his first languages while living in Ethiopia from age 1-1/2 to 4-1/2. He met his soulmate, Maureen, while she was attending nursing school in Cambridge. Their marriage and love lasted 52 years. After college, they moved to San Francisco with two suitcases and a Martin guitar, with plans to explore the beautiful and innovative city which they savored and enjoyed. They learned Transcendental Meditation through which they developed a rich interior life that lasted a lifetime. They moved from San Francisco to Upper Rockridge in 1987 and then to Piedmont five years later following the loss of their home in the Oakland Hills Fire of 1991. Steve and Maureen ing him to also enjoy being with his family. Steve was a consultant and employee of large firms like Charles Schwab and Visa. However, he enjoyed small, start-up companies most, where he took on various positions at once. His greatest accomplishment was developing software for the New York Stock Exchange. Steve played sports his entire life, including ice hockey, biking, swimming, lacrosse and soccer. Later in life he helped organize an international soccer team in Piedmont and started a men’s support group following the Oakland Fire of 1991. He loved his role as a father, and guided his children, Ben and Annie, to not only use their full potential but to become loving and thoughtful individuals capable of providing service to their communities. Steve will be deeply missed by his wife Maureen, son Ben (wife Daniela, children Natalie, Jackson and Nicholas) and daughter Annie (husband Pete, children Kalber and Otis). He is predeceased by his parents, brother Chris, and sister Lisa. articles.text: Viki Cebers passed away on April 30, 2023, in Walnut Creek after courageously battling a lifetime of health issues. Viki was born December 8, 1947, in San Francisco to Donna Donald and was adopted and raised by Irma Sue and Wilfred Schlieman in Piedmont. She attended Piedmont schools, where she met and later married her high-school sweetheart and love of her life, Hank Cebers, Jr. They enjoyed 32 happy years together before Hank’s passing in 2000. Viki lived for her family and was always looking forward to the next vacation to Graeagle, where she loved seeing everyone together – reading on the porch, working on puzzles and playing cards. Her love for her family fueled her fierce determination and will to live despite her extraordinary health challenges. Her no-nonsense attitude and unique sense of humor helped her fight through incredible physical pain and beat medical odds countless times. Viki is remembered for her selfless contributions to the community. Together with Hank, they were very involved in the Piedmont community, volunteering their time and talents to Piedmont schools, the Piedmont Community Church, the Campfire Girls, and Camp Augusta. Viki was also very active with the fundraising Viki Cebers, a native Piedmonter, died on April 30 at age 75. branches at Children’s Hospital Oakland, both as a member of the Teak Branch for more than 40 years and as the office manager at the branch headquarters until she retired in 2017. Through her service and years growing up and then raising her family in Piedmont, Viki built life-long friendships that kept her energized and inspired her wit. Viki is survived by her three devoted daughters, Mindy Smyth and Michael, Suzy Sims and Josh, and Samantha Cebers and fiancé Aaron. She is also survived by five loving grandchildren, Braden, Parker, Andrew, Jenna, and Carly; her beloved brother Robert Schlieman and wife Bonnie, and her new-found sister, Moire Donald and husband Jeff. Additionally she is survived by two faithful sisters-in-law, Ilze Birznieks (Janis), and Sandra Forderer (Curt), and many nieces, nephews, great nieces and great-nephews. Friends and family are invited to celebrate Viki’s life at a memorial service on Monday, May 15, at 11 am at Piedmont Community Church. In remembrance of Viki’s life, the family suggests making a charitable donation to: Children’s Hospital Branches, Inc., 5700 Martin Luther King Jr. Way T-2, Oakland, CA 94609, with the memo “in honor of Viki” on the check.

articles.text: Members of Girl Scout Troop 33587, sixth graders from Piedmont Middle School, headed out on their most challenging backpacking trip yet. The group hiked three miles to Morgan Territory Backpack Camp near Mt. Diablo on March 11-12, passing through oak groves and grass-covered hills and climbed over and under numerous trees that had fallen during recent storms. Wildflowers were blooming in abundance, including California poppies, larkspur, purple sanicle, Chinese houses, and Mount Diablo sunflowers (endemic to the Bay Area). As they approached the campsite, they saw many cows grazing in the fields. The campsite itself was an idyllic spot with beautiful views of Mount Diablo in the foreground. Once at camp, the girls set up their tents, hammocks, and a kitchen area. They had planned their meals ahead of time, making sure to carry lightweight food. They learned how to filter water and took turns cooking. Meals included a cheese and salami platter for an afternoon snack, tuna and parmesan pasta and Caesar salad for dinner, and omelettes and dried fruit with oatmeal for breakfast on their Piedmont Girl Scouts Adelina Mbise, Devon Porter, Victoria Mbise, Juliette Edesses and Charlotte Phung hike the lush green hills in Morgan Territory in the East Bay. articles.text: tenth of your flocks, and you shall be his slaves. 18 And on that day you will cry out because of your king, whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the Lord will not answer you on that day.” (I Samuel 9, NRSVUE) The Bible is much happier to say that God alone is king. Indeed, some would say that the form of government the Bible advocates is a theocracy. Others note that the problem with a theocracy is that, without God (theos) physically present, there are many who are far too ready to step in and act like God on God’s behalf. Our Baptist forbearers were cautious about the idea of monarchs and they were resolute in their belief that they should not be given religious or spiritual authority. The concept of king as “defender of the faith” with the authority to appoint archbishops and bishops was morally repugnant to them. It is one of the reasons they became Baptist in the first place. The bottom line is that our religious tradition is very much against giving too much power to any single person or institution. It has long resisted giving political authority to religious leaders as well as giving religious authority to political leaders. King Charles III would like to be known as the “defender of all faiths.” I appreciate his concern. However, history shows that the faiths of the world generally need to be defended from falling into the hands of political leaders more than they need to be defended by them. articles.text: The Piedmont School District has announced that Melissa Daymond has been hired as the new principal of Wildwood Elementary. She takes over upon the retirement of Carol Cramer on July 1. Daymond most recently was a 2nd grade teacher in Tiburon at Reed Union School District. During her seven years there, she spent time as Teachers Union President, Summer School Principal, and Grade Level Team Leader. Daymond began her career in education in 1998 in Escondido where she taught for 17 years. “‘I’ve been teaching for 20 plus years, and I still passionately love what I’m doing. But I’m really excited by the challenge of leading a school and a whole community that values excellent education, just as Piedmont does,” said Daymond. Daymond says the population and academic achievement scores at Reed Union are comparable to Piedmont. The Reed Union School District (RUSD) has three schools, two grade schools and a middle school, with a district enrollment of 1,150 students. Daymond attended California Poly as an undergraduate and earned a Masters degree in Educational Administration from San Francisco State University in 2021. “Education is not just about imparting knowledge; it is also about inspiring and empowering students to become the best versions of themselves. I am overwhelmed by the warm welcome I have received and am ready to hit the ground running,” she said. “During the application and interview process, Ms. Daymond stood out as a communicator, collaborator and problem-solver, with the experience and vision to lead Wildwood into its next chapter. I believe she will be a great addition to Wildwood and to PUSD as a whole,” said Piedmont Interim Superintendent, Dr. Donald Evans. 4 Firemen of Piedmont. ...... 1 Letters.......................... 2 Pool update.................... 3 Senior Prom................... 6 Diversity Day.................. 7 Beach School mural.......... 8 PPD Blue....................... 9 4th grade field trip .......... 10 Sports. ......................... 12 Museums ..................... 16 Music.......................... 17 Movies ........................ 18 PCA events.................... 20 Ballet. .......................... 21 Spring Soiree................. 22 Piedmont Pantry............. 24 BBQ Without Border......... 25 Real Estate. ................... 26 Wed. articles.text: Piedmont High and Millennium High students attending this year’s Senior Prom took a trip back in time 100 years to the Roaring 20s. The extravagant dance, organized by Piedmont parents was held Saturday, April 29, at The Speakeasy in the Palace Hotel in San Francisco. Students arrived at the high school at 5:30 p.m. wearing 20s attire, paperboy caps, and formal wear before being transported by bus to the dance. Students entered through the speakeasy’s street alias, “Joe’s Clock Shop,” and were welcomed by a pasta and lasagna buffet dinner catered by Tony’s, a restaurant nearby in North Beach. While enjoying dinner, students were entertained by magicians, comics and a dancer performing on an aerial hoop. Mocktails (non-alcoholic drinks) were served at the various bars, students gambled with play money with their friends in the casino room, and danced the night away on a sunken dance floor. Actors portraying flapper dancers lined every corner, leading students through the mysterious history of the speakeasy. Students took advantage of the prop boxes, overflowing with pocket watches, rings and shawls, to pose with in the photo booth. The Speakeasy truly emulated the 20s atmosphere. English teacher, Eduardo Wolbert, helped chaperone the event and enjoyed getting to explore the exciting venue with his students. “The venue was amazing. It had so many rooms and I thought that having the actors all around was really interesting,” said Prom goers dance the night away at The Speakeasy in San Francisco. Photos by Jane Volich
articles.title: Senior Prom reinvigorates the roaring 20s

articles.text: Editor: I am a regular pickleball player and a Piedmont resident. I was disappointed to hear that support for permanent courts is waning as a result of some residents near Beach complaining about noise. My husband and I live on Jerome Ave. by Witter Field. We hear the noise of baseball, football, track, etc. on a daily basis. We also hear the sound of pickleball from the middle school, and experience it as much less invasive than the fan cheering, rock and roll music and the PA system from the school. Although there are times when I wish it were quieter (and that the city had kept their promise of no organized play on Sundays), we bought our house near the school and consider athletic play a critical part of a healthy life. If you start trying to make decisions based on sound, you are opening a can of worms. The people who live near Beach, like us, bought their homes knowing there was a school and outdoor activities there. Pickleball may have its own sounds, but they are no more than other sports, and they don’t include loud music and raucous fan cheering. I beseech you to resolve this conflict in favor of permanent courts. The pickleball community is a huge asset to the city but won’t continue to be willing to put up with temporary courts that are inadequate in so many ways. –Paula Flamm Newsstand copies of the Piedmont Post are available at Mulberry’s Market, and Piedmont Shell at Grand & Wildwood Ave. Copies of the paper may be purchased for $1 at all locations during business hours. articles.text: April 2023 was the 60th Anniversary of the writing of the “Letter From Birmingham Jail” by the Reverend Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. He wrote the letter in 1963 after being arrested, and subsequently jailed, at a Good Friday protest in Birmingham, Alabama. While in jail Dr. King read a full page advertisement in a local paper signed by eight prominent white clergyman (Protestant, Catholic and Jewish) decrying his presence in their city and labeling him an unwanted, unnecessary and inflammatory outsider. This letter hurt and distressed him. Over the period of his incarceration, he wrote his response in the margins of the paper and on whatever scraps of paper he could find and gave what he wrote to his attorney, Clarence B. Jones, to smuggle out. Jones delivered what King had written to King’s chief of staff, Wyatt Tee Walker, who, along with King’s personal secretary, Dora McDonald, put together the manuscript that was first published shortly thereafter by a Quaker publication. It was later published on June 12, 1963 by a national religious publication, The Christian Century, where King was a contributing editor. articles.text: Work at the Piedmont Community Pool site is continuing on schedule, with contractors now building a retaining wall for the new pool. Since April 21 the contractors from Wickman Development & Construction have been drilling concrete piers for the wall with a large auger and placing steel cages in the holes for reinforcement. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that the contractors currently have completed about 385 feet of retaining wall along Bonita Avenue near the tennis courts, with “interior, site retaining walls that will be constructed later.” The process of drilling piers for the wall is expected to last through mid-May, after which the contractors will start to bring steel and concrete on-site, while off-hauling soil off-site. “By mid-May, there will be more trucking activity,” Gonzales said. “The off-haul won’t be every day, but it’ll be about an eight-week period, going through June. The grading and retaining wall work overall should take up at least the next two months, also through June.” As construction continues, the GEOCON Consultants will perform geotechnical testing for the retaining wall. Through this process, engineers which specialize in soil will make design recommendations as to how the wall can be constructed on existing soil types at the site. Gonzales said that GEOCON consultants will also inspect materials involved in the retaining wall construction, “making sure that the steel used is strong enough and welded correctly, also testing concrete samples to make sure that it’s the right strength.” He added that the company was “one of the first to start on this [pool project] on-site; they took soil samples to look at existing site conditions two years ago, in 2021.” Griffin Structures, the project manager, will oversee work performed by GEOCON. Community members can stay informed about pool construction and get direct updates about traffic, noise, and other impacts by subscribing to the City’s Community Pool Construction Updates email list at bit.ly/3SAmveF. For more information on the Piedmont Community Pool project, visit piedmont.ca.gov/newpool. Those with questions or comments about the pool project can contact Construction Manager George Sanen of Griffin Structures by email at gsanen@griffinstructures.com, or by phone at 415-858-8582. A retaining wall is currently under construction at the Community Pool site.
articles.title: Retaining wall construction continues

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is soliciting suggestions from community members willing to serve on a task force that would help develop a plan for how to electrify Piedmont’s residences. The Building Electrification Strategy Task Force, to be appointed by City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, will work with staff to better understand existing barriers to home electrification and create a strategic framework for equitably moving Piedmont’s building stock off of natural gas. Letters of interest due May 16 The city staff has approached several community members who have previously engaged with the City on electrification and sustainability initiatives about their potential interest in serving on the task force. To ensure that the task force incorporates diverse perspectives and wide-ranging expertise, we are also soliciting interest from the community at large. If you think you can help, send an email to ElectrificationTaskForce@piedmont.ca.gov by Tuesday, May 16 describing why you’re interested in serving on the task force, and what skills, experience, or perspective you would bring. Residential electrification Transitioning Piedmont’s existing residences from natural gas to clean electricity is crucial for meeting the city’s emission reduction targets established in the City’s Climate Action Plan. Despite substantial investment in climate action work – which has earned a Beacon Spotlight Award for Sustainability Best Practices from the Institute for Local Government for two consecutive years – Piedmont is not presently on track to meet its greenhouse gas emissions reduction goals. The gap is largely due to natural gas use in residential buildings, which accounts for roughly half of Piedmont’s in-territory emissions. Because much of Piedmont’s housing stock is old and large, heating and cooling these homes requires greater than average energy use. For each year between 2017 and 2020, annual emissions just from residential buildings exceeded Climate Action Plan targets for total emissions in Piedmont by 2050. Most of these emissions came from natural gas furnaces and water heaters. The City is now seeking to draw on the wealth of expertise within our community to create a strategic plan for expediting this transition. The Task Force will be charged with developing an Existing Building Electrification Strategy that will guide future policies and programs related to residential building electrification. For questions about letters of interest or the Electrification Task Force, contact City Clerk John Tulloch at jtulloch@piedmont. ca.gov or 420-3041. “We can’t beat ‘em, and they won’t let us join ‘em.”
articles.title: City seeks ideas for electrifying residences

articles.text: The city is implementing additional safety measures around the community pool construction site due to increased truck traffic in the coming weeks. Starting next Monday, May 8: • The construction fence on Magnolia Avenue will be extended farther into the street, creating a separate travel lane for trucks inside the fence • The lane will remain open to cars for through-travel • The school pick-up and dropoff area will remain in place These measures will separate trucks from pedestrian activity on Magnolia Avenue. The increased truck traffic is due to excavation and soil removal activity at the pool construction site, and is expected to last eight weeks, through early June. pages.text: Wednesday, May 3, 2023 3 Pool update Retaining wall construction continues By Selen Ozturk Work at the Piedmont Community Pool site is continuing on schedule, with contractors now building a retaining wall for the new pool. Since April 21 the contractors from Wickman Development & Construction have been drilling concrete piers for the wall with a large auger and placing steel cages in the holes for reinforcement. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that the contractors currently have completed about 385 feet of retaining wall along Bonita Avenue near the tennis courts, with “interior, site retaining walls that will be constructed later.” The process of drilling piers for the wall is expected to last through mid-May, after which the contractors will start to bring steel and concrete on-site, while off-hauling soil off-site. “By mid-May, there will be more trucking activity,” Gonzales said. “The off-haul won’t be every day, but it’ll be about an eight-week period, going through June. The grading and retaining wall work overall should take up at least the next two months, also through June.” As construction continues, the GEOCON Consultants will perform geotechnical testing for the retaining wall. Through this process, engineers which specialize in soil will make design recommendations as to how the wall can be constructed on existing soil types at the site. Gonzales said that GEOCON consultants will also inspect materials involved in the retaining wall construction, “making sure that the steel used is strong enough and welded correctly, also testing concrete samples to make sure that it’s the right strength.” He added that the company was “one of the first to start on this [pool project] on-site; they took soil samples to look at existing site conditions two years ago, in 2021.” Griffin Structures, the project manager, will oversee work performed by GEOCON. Community members can stay informed about pool construction and get direct updates about traffic, noise, and other impacts by subscribing to the City’s Community Pool Construction Updates email list at bit.ly/3SAmveF. For more information on the Piedmont Community Pool project, visit piedmont.ca.gov/newpool. Those with questions or comments about the pool project can contact Construction Manager George Sanen of Griffin Structures by email at gsanen@griffinstructures.com, or by phone at 415-858-8582. A retaining wall is currently under construction at the Community Pool site. New safety measures at pool site begin May 8 The city is implementing additional safety measures around the community pool construction site due to increased truck traffic in the coming weeks. Starting next Monday, May 8: • The construction fence on Magnolia Avenue will be extended farther into the street, creating a separate travel lane for trucks inside the fence • The lane will remain open to cars for through-travel • The school pick-up and dropoff area will remain in place These measures will separate trucks from pedestrian activity on Magnolia Avenue. The increased truck traffic is due to excavation and soil removal activity at the pool construction site, and is expected to last eight weeks, through early June. Trucks will enter the construction site at Hillside and Magnolia, be loaded inside the site, then exit directly onto Bonita Avenue. To minimize traffic disruption, truck activity will take place outside of school drop-off and pick-up periods (8-9 a.m., 2-3:30 p.m.). For questions about the traffic changes on Magnolia Avenue, contact Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales by email at dgonzales@piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3061. The Building Electrification Strategy Task Force, to be appointed by City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, will work with staff to better understand existing barriers to home electrification and create a strategic framework for equitably moving Piedmont’s building stock off of natural gas. Letters of interest due May 16 The city staff has approached several community members who have previously engaged with the City on electrification and sustainability initiatives about their potential interest in serving on the task force. To ensure that the task force incorporates diverse perspectives and wide-ranging expertise, we are also soliciting interest from the community at large. If you think you can help, send an email to ElectrificationTaskForce@piedmont.ca.gov by Tuesday, May 16 describing why you’re interested in serving on the task force, and what skills, experience, or perspective you would bring. Residential electrification Transitioning Piedmont’s existing residences from natural gas to clean electricity is crucial for meeting the city’s emission reduction targets established in the City’s Climate Action Plan. Despite substantial investment in climate action work – which has earned a Beacon Spotlight Award for Sustainability Best Practices from the Institute for Local Government for two consecutive years – Piedmont is not presently on track to meet its greenhouse gas emissions reduction goals. The gap is largely due to natural gas use in residential buildings, which accounts for roughly half of Piedmont’s in-territory emissions. Because much of Piedmont’s housing stock is old and large, heating and cooling these homes requires greater than average energy use. For each year between 2017 and 2020, annual emissions just from residential buildings exceeded Climate Action Plan targets for total emissions in Piedmont by 2050. Most of these emissions came from natural gas furnaces and water heaters. The City is now seeking to draw on the wealth of expertise within our community to create a strategic plan for expediting this transition. The Task Force will be charged with developing an Existing Building Electrification Strategy that will guide future policies and programs related to residential building electrification. articles.text: The Mended Hearts, Inc. (MHI) is the largest cardiovascular support organization in the world and a national and community-based non-profit organization. It has been offering the gift of hope to heart disease patients, their families and caregivers. and will host a Zoom seminar this Saturday, May 6, at 10:00 a.m. Saturday’s program will include Mended Hearts and the American Society for Preventive Cardiology for Part 1 of Mended Hearts’ Risk Reduction Webinar Series. In this session they look at controlling your cholesterol and modifying your diet to reduce your risk of heart disease, and associated diseases. Cholesterol has a central role in atherosclerosis, which is the build-up of cholesterol in our arteries. Treating this build up is central to lowering heart disease. There are several methods of LDL Cholesterol reduction, including statins, Ezetimibe, and the PCSK-9 inhibitors. In this first of six Risk Reduction webinars, they review the message that dieting for weight loss is NOT the same as dieting for your heart’s health. As we learned in last month’s webinar on the Connection Between Alzheimer’s Disease and the Heart, several recent studies show that your diet and exercise are factors under your control that also reduce your risk of Alzheimer’s Disease. Founded by Dr. Dwight E. Harken, MHI was started with four of Dr. Harken’s open heart surgery patients. In January 1951 Dr. Harken asked one of the first 50 patients to ever have heart surgery, and three other post-surgery heart patients to meet at the hospital. They spoke of their new feeling of well-being, their plans and hopes for the future — and with renewed happiness they spoke of their “mended hearts.” They realized how wonderful it would be to provide support and help others facing the same experience. In the 70 years since then, Mended Hearts has expanded to provide support and education across the country and around the world. Today there are over 100,000 members, 260 chapters and 350 participating hospitals in the US. The local Oakland chapter has been in existence for over 30 years. In addition to visiting patients at Oakland’s Summit Hospital, the chapter has monthly meetings focused on education related to heart health. Moderator: Andrea Baer, MS, Director of Patient Advocacy and Program Management for Mended Hearts Panelist: Dr. Amit Khera, Professor of Medicine at the University of Texas, Southwestern Medical School in Dallas, Texas. articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra has announced that its annual Spring Concert will be performed on Saturday, May 13, at 7:30 p.m. at First Congregational Church of Berkeley, 2345 Channing Way. David Ramadanoff, now in his 34th season with the 101-piece youth orchestra, will conduct a performance of Brahms’ Academic Festival Overture, Symphonic Metamorphosis of Themes of Carl Maria von Weber by Paul Hindemith, and Maurice Ravel’s LaValse. It will also feature two Concerto Competition winners, violinist Noa Marvit performing the First movement of Symphonie Espagnole by Édouard Lalo, and Ethan Chen in von Weber’s Concertino for Clarinet in E-flat. Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO is the oldest youth orchestra in California and the first independent youth orchestra in the nation. Tickets are $20 and are available online at http:// www.ypsomusic.org/tickets and at the door. For more information call (510) 849-9776 or visit http:// www.ypsomusic.org. ®

articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra, the oldest youth orchestra in California and the oldest independent youth orchestra in the nation, is now accepting new members. Auditions are being conducted for trumpet, trombone, bass trombone, tuba, bassoon, oboe, violin, viola, and double bass. Founded in 1936 in Berkeley, YPSO is led by conductor and Music Director David Ramadanoff for 35 years, with an orchestra of more than 100 musicians from schools through the greater Bay Area. YPSO will tour and perform in Japan next year, and will perform in the Bay Area Youth Orchestra Festival at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco. Submission of screening videos are due by June 1. YPSO rehearses most Monday evenings at First Congregational Church of Oakland, 2501 Harrison Street from 6:00-9:30 p.m. There is also an annual weekend retreat in the Fall in Carmel Valley and several Saturday afternoon intensives during the year.

articles.text: Diversity Day, one of Piedmont Middle School’s most popular events, returned on Monday, April 24 after a three-year absence due to the COVID pandemic. Yearbook teacher Anne Smith, who has helped organize it for many years, revived the event which brings speakers to the school to share their various stories and demonstrate their talents. It encompasses a wide breadth of topics relevant to ethnic, social and cultural diversity. The morning started off with two groups of assemblies in the MPR, with the middle school Jazz Band performing. 6th grader Francesca Clark, a member of the school’s Green Team, and 8th grader Zoe Snyder each gave a Land Acknowledgement. In their classes, before attending speaker workshops, teachers familiarized their students with the speakers’ biographies. “What is Diversity?” classes brainstormed and came up with responses including: ethnicity, gender, personality, religion, age, likes and dislikes, learning styles, and physical traits. Each class attended two of the Lance McGee a.k.a. “Unique Derique” demonstrates “Hambone” body percussion and tells of its origins from times of slavery. 6th grade teacher Hillary Voigt (left) playing Goal Ball blindfolded in the Buzz Redford gym. The “How to play like a paralympic” taught by PMS Adaptive PE teacher Raul Jorcino (standing), with Madeleine Ewen diving for the basketball that has jingle bells inside. Mina Herrgott (left) with Raquel Jetè in Jetè’s demonstration on “Headwraps: A Black Woman’s History.” PMS 6th grade teacher Lea Lotia invited her father, Aquil Lotia, to talk to students on Diversity Fay about his experience growing up in Pakistan. Students learn the intricacies of Cuban dance and Raggaton music from Leyder Chapman. Michael Bracamonte’s 6th grade Core students Jordan Morris-Price (left), Gael Fierro, Emily Hu, Sharlize Sahagon, and Kayleigh Anderson hang up Wish and Action Tags. 14 different workshops offered. Some of the speakers included: • Eliezer Cohn: “History of Anti-Semitism” • Grace Patterson and Morgan Lewis: “Representation and Equity in Film” • Bri Blue: “Spoken Word Artist” • Ali Cannon and Thomas Kennard: “Transgender Journeys: Stories of Becoming Men” • Raquel Jetè: “Headwraps: A Black Woman’s History” • Oluyemi and Ijeoma Thomas: “Jazz Music Workshop” • Unique Derique McGee: “Hambone Body Percussion” Unique Derique (Lance McGee), gave a powerful demonstration to 8th graders about the origins and importance of Hambone body percussion. McGee explained how using the body as a percussive instrument surfaced in the times of slavery after the Djembe Drum was taken away from slaves. African slaves in America were often only given the bone of a ham to eat; from that, they made soup. Hence the body percussion embodies the hambone “making something out of nothing.”

articles.text: Fifth graders at Beach School, its graduating class, have donated a “legacy gift” of an outdoor Teachers’ Lounge complete with new furniture and a brand new, colorful mural. This project, which was finished last weekend, turned what used to be an unused area behind the school into an outdoor oasis fit for the Beach school staff. Over a period of two weekends in April, a total of 75 parents and 5th grade students created the mural under the guidance of artist David Vickers. He began the project by designing a scale model of the mural on graph paper, and then stencils for the design were created. Tonight, Wednesday, May 3, from 5:30-6:30 p.m., the community is invited to attend the unveiling of the mural at the outdoor teachers’ lounge, with tasty tidbits from La Farine Bakery on Piedmont Avenue, and 5 Spiced Kitchen of Montclair. The outdoor lounge is behind the school. (100 Lake Avenue, Piedmont). For more information, see: pp.events/a8o5ZbAZ The state-required implementation of a universal free school lunch program took over the indoor teachers’ lounge space, leaving the teachers with no communal place to have lunch. While volunteering as the organizer of student lunches in November The finished mural and the new outdoor teachers’ lounge behind Beach School 2022, parent and Beach alum Liz Tuuri-Mosbaugh noticed teachers eating lunch on child-sized furniture in the outdoor area behind the school. In January 2023, parent and Beach alum Etienne Fang helped initiate a makeover project with the help of her father-in-law, artist David Vickers. The outdoor space was furnished with dining tables and chairs, lounge seating, and a canopy; funds were raised from the 5th grade classes involved. Potted plants and a landscaped hillside were added to further the ambiance. “My main goals as an artist with this project were first of all to make it an engaging collaboration and secondly to make the process accessible to ‘non-artists.’ The design is meant to be uplifting and playful, providing the teachers with a relaxed background for those precious breaks in their busy days,” said Vickers. Materials for the mural project were donated by Ace Hardware and Nursery on Grand Avenue. Vickers and Fang made a presentation about the creative process of creating an outdoor teachers’ lounge to the 5th grade classes of Jessica Sprague and Tammy Medress. Students learned how to measure to scale, color theory, overall design and the meaning behind their legacy project – to leave behind a positive impact. A new mural at Beach School was finished on Saturday April 29. Pictured are Gigi Estavillo (front), Sloan Estavillo, and Jose Zamorano. articles.text: There is a wonderful artist, Amber Share, who takes the onestar ratings of National Parks and turns them into beautiful, handdrawn and lettered postcards. Yosemite features the caption, “Trees block the view and there are too many gray rocks.” Joshua Tree is, “The only thing to do here is walk around the desert.” And a personal favorite, Pinnacles: “A bunch of rocks. Big deal.” Alarmingly, these reviews were written by adults, but they strike a stark resemblance to the complaints of a child who’s been dragged on a walk. “This is boring.” “There’s nothing to do.” “My feet hurt.” Not everyone has an inherent appreciation of the outdoors and if the family nature hikes feel like an uphill battle, here is some reassurance that you are doing the right thing, Time outside is good for us. The simple act of getting outside reduces stress, regulates emotions, and improves overall health. While most adults enjoy a hearty trail walk, many children are so used to being entertained that nature, by just existing, is boring. To get children outside and with joy the framing and set-up matters. Nature needs to be more than something to play in, but something to play with. Assuming there is groundwork Building appreciation for nature through play for safety and no destruction to protected spaces, playing with nature might look like the following: • Throwing rocks into a creek • Digging a hole in the sand • Climbing on top of a fallen tree or large rock • Picking up a HUGE stick • Picking up another HUGE stick and starting to build a fort While these activities may cause a knee-jerk “stop that!”, they all build a level of freedom and exploration that puts nature at the center of a child’s adventure. Unlike a video game or TV show with a predetermined plot, children are foraging a path on their own when they play outside. Their brains are seeing possibility in a rock and using creativity to overcome the challenges of getting up high or making a fort. The benefits of being in nature don’t change if you’re climbing a tree or taking a walk - all that matters is getting out there. Randall Grayson, Ph.D. is Director at Camp Augusta, a residential camp nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills since 1931 and beloved by many Piedmont families. Information about its summer program and family camps may be found at www. campaugusta.org. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Smolko places 2nd in singles, Breber 4th Piedmont brought seven players to this year’s WACC Tournament: Will Tenney (left), Arun Brahma, Nick King, Ben Breber, Lucas Smolko, Nate Welch, and Ethan Pham. After finishing the regular season in 2nd place, Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team competed in the 2023 Western Alameda County Conference on Friday and Saturday, April 28-29 at Chabot College in Hayward. Freshman Lucas Smolko reached the finals in the singles bracket, junior Carson Breber reached the semifinals in singles, and Arun Brahma and Nate Welch placed fifth in the doubles bracket. Smolko earned the No. 2 seed and a first-round bye. He defeated Bishop O’Dowd’s Lucas Tanaka 6-1, 6-1 in the second-round and followed up with a 6-1, 6-1 victory over Colin Sweeney of O’Dowd to close the first day of action. In the semifinals on Saturday, Smolko defeated Berkeley’s Leighton Sproul in three sets, 6-2, 2-6, 6-4. “It was an interesting match for me because I’ve practiced against Leighton a lot. We’ve almost always had close matches and I knew it could go either way. There were a lot of emotions running through my mind. In the first set, I was a bit more aggressive, then I started to get a bit tentative in the second,” said Smolko following the semifinals. Advancing to the finals, he faced top-seeded Elijah Cho of San Leandro, and took the Pirates’ senior to three sets before falling in a heated final, 7-5, 2-6, 7-5. In the first set, Smolko rallied from being down 4-1 to tie the match set at 5-5. Cho won the next two games to claim victory in the first set. Smolko played a strong second set, winning his fifth point as the returner with a winning forehand, and then won the final game as the server. The third set was nearly identical to the first. Trailing 4-1, battled back to tie the match at before Cho closed out the match by winning Staff Photo Lucas Smolko nearly stole the League singles title from top-seed Elijah Cho of San Leandro.

articles.text: Highlanders seeded #3 in NCS playoffs When it comes to guarantees in life, there are just a few things: death, taxes, and Piedmont High’s boys’ lacrosse team winning the Western Alameda County Conference championship title. On Friday, April 28, playing its usual finals opponent, rival Bishop O’Dowd, Piedmont finally had something of a breather with a 14-6 victory. Championship games in the recent past have been won by a single goal, including twice in overtime. Playing at O’Dowd, Piedmont went into the half clinging to a 5-3 lead. The Highlanders’ defense then turned up the intensity to keep O’Dowd off the scoreboard until the fourth quarter, scoring seven unanswered goals in the second half with the Dragons’ worn down. “This was a good game overall. The message was basically Soren Dixon scored six goals against the Dragons. to play Piedmont lacrosse,” said PHS coach Al Yu. “We were very sloppy in the second quarter and committed a lot of unnecessary turnovers. Once we got back to what we’ve been doing all season, you saw our real team out there. The third and fourth quarters were who we are as a team.” Senior Henry Brayer, coming back from a shoulder injury after missing the last few games, was still feeling some lingering effects but persevered with toughness to appear in the third quarter. “I definitely didn’t play like I usually do; I only played for a small portion of the third quarter,” said Brayer. Jack Nelson, Soren Dixon, and Nate Fredericks helped the school claim three straight league titles. The 2020 season was wiped out due to the pandemic. “We win back-to-back because we have the grit. Last year, we lost to O’Dowd at the start of the season and grinded all season long to win league. This year, we lost a big player (Henry Brayer), but we came together to possess the ball more and play a bit smoother without a key player to carry the offense,” explained Dixon, who led the team with six goals. “Henry is a key player for us, so to take him out of our arsenal has an effect on the team. Once he was back out there, it was like tic-tac-toe and we were back in business,” added Nelson. articles.text: Piedmont’s softball team won an exciting 16-15 game against Berkeley at home in on Wednesday, April 26. It was the team’s first win in the Western Alameda County Conference’s Foothill Division. Two days later, April 28, they lost 7-1 to Castro Valley at the Trojans’ home field Piedmont will honor its six seniors this Friday: Ginger Gardner, Gretchen Gerhardy, Hailey Ronen, Leah Bell, Morgan Hunt, and Mia Leggett. 16-15 over Berkeley Piedmont scored twice in the bottom of the second inning, but Berkeley exploded on offense and took a 8-2 lead by the next inning. Never to be denied, PHS stormed back with five runs, then went ahead 9-8 following the bottom of the fourth. Berkeley then put up six runs in the top-fifth to lead 14-9. PHS scored twice in the bottom-fifth, 14-11, but allowed one in the top-seventh. In the bottom-ofthe-seventh, Piedmont scored four runs to win it 16-15, including a game-winning double by Miya Fujimoto. In the two-run first inning, Fujimoto led off with a walk and stole both second and third base. With two outs, Fujimoto came home on a double-steal with Morgan Hunt taking second base. Gerhardy then brought in Hunt with a single. Piedmont’s five-run bottom of the third started with Ronen singling in Gerhardy with one-out. Ronen made her way to third on an error then scored on a wild pitch. With two-outs, Fujimoto brought in Leggett on a single. Fujimoto and Caitlin Boothby then scored after a groundball from Bell forced an error, 8-7 Berkeley. Trailing 15-12 entering the last inning – the bottom of the seventh – Piedmont drew five consecutive walks to make it a 15-14 game. With one-out, Fujimoto lined a double to left field, to score bringing in Leggett and Boothby with the winning run. Final stats: Fujimoto went 2-for-2 with a double, three RBIs, four runs scored, and drew four walks. Bell went 2-for-5 with two RBIs and a run scored. Sa’mara Levi went 2-got-5 with an RBI. articles.text: Piedmont’s track and field team completed its regular season with meets in Santa Rosa, Hayward, and at home. They hosted a league meet on Thursday, April 20, and participated in another league meet on Thursday, April 27 at Hayward HS. Senior Christian Taylor ran at the Vikings Track Classic at Montgomery High School in Santa Rosa on Saturday, April 22. Piedmont’s boys’ team finished the season undefeated in five league meets to claim the regular season first-place banner, while the girls’ team was 4-1 and finished second to Berkeley. The school honored its 15 members of the Class of 2023 on Senior Night, April 20: Drew Dacanay, Charles White, Shelby Cavenaugh, Tara Kothari, Emily Fitzgerald, Callan Mitchell, Marcos Filho, Parker Long, Alex Aubrecht, Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai, Matthew Riordan, Conor Kim, Jack Gross-Whitaker, and Taylor. “It’s been pretty great to see that we have the depth to score in all 15 events for both the boys and girls, I think that’s why the boys beat up on so many teams [this season], and the girls we were able to go toe to toe even with dominant programs like Berkeley and San Leandro,” said first-year head coach Pouyan Assadi. Piedmont now prepares for the 2023 Western Alameda County Conference Championship meet at Hayward High today, Wednesday, May 3, and Friday, May 5. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team pushed favored Bishop O’Dowd to the limit before falling 11-9 in the league championship game ay O’Dowd on Friday, April 28. In a double header between both schools. Piedmont’s boys team beat the Dragons 14-6 for its 6th consecutive league championship. O’Dowd jumped out to a 5-1 lead, but the Highlanders rallied to tie the game at 7-7 in the early minutes of the second half. However, BOD scored three consecutive goals in a span of two minutes to give the Dragons the edge. It was a strong performance from Piedmont after losing to Bishop O’Dowd 14-7 on March 17. “It was a tough game. We had to climb a mountain. I’m super proud of the girls to keep their heads in the game and then tie it 7-7,” said Piedmont coach Carlton Chan. “The last time we played them, we walked out of the first half down 2-8. This time we had a plan. It ended up being a few possessions’ difference at the end of the game.” Molly Ashton scored two goals and had one assist against O’Dowd. Ruby Guzdar had four goals and an assist versus the Dragons. Staff Photos Coach Carlton Chan with Piedmont lacrosse players during their narrow 11-9 loss to Bishop O’Dowd in the league championship game. “We had it… we had it,” said Chan, shaking his head. “It’s rough. Last year was the first year we lost to them after having a six-year streak against them,” explained senior leader Molly Ashton. “We came out strong like we were already in mid-game form. We’ve had trouble with that, but this time we came out really fast, and I don’t think they were expecting that,” mentioned Ashton. Piedmont has received a No. 13 seed in the post-season North Coast Section playoffs, and faced No. 4 San Marin last night, Tuesday, May 2. results. Match recap O’Dowd jumped out to an early 2-0 lead before freshman Peyton Watson scored six minutes into the first half. But O’Dowd tacked on three goals for a comfortable 5-1 lead with 16:25 left in the half. Ruby Guzdar scored on a feed from Ashton with 9:36 left to narrow the score to 5-3. O’Dowd’s Lucy Yu, the daughter of Piedmont boys’ lacrosse coach Al Yu, scored following a shooting space penalty, and BOD’s Mariah Branscomb netted her third goal of the match to make it 7-3 with 7:59 left in the first half. However, Guzdar scored with a wraparound goal with 5:39 to play, followed Watson recovering a ground ball in front of O’Dowd’s net to score with 3:44 to play. With 1:01 left, Guzdar found Ashton for a goal to bring PHS within one goal, down 7-6. In the second half, the teams traded possession back and forth through the opening 10 minutes until Guzdar scored with 15:20 left, tying the game for the first time at 7-7. However, Yu scored on another shooting space opportunity. But Piedmont’s Chloe Graham then scored to tie the match at 8-8 with 13:14 remaining. O’Dowd then went on a scoring run with a shooting space goal, a wraparound goal by Yu, and another shooting space conversion to make it 11-8. From there, Ashton had a shooting space opportunity stopped by O’Dowd’s goalie, and PHS goalie Friedie Schickedanz returned the favor by blocking a shot soon after. Ashton had a shot trail wide with 5:05 left and had one more shooting space opportunity clang off of the side post. With 2:55 left, Guzdar scored on a low-sidearm shot to make it 11-9, but O’Dowd’s defense prevailed for a tow-goal win. Final stats: Guzdar scored four goals and one assist. Ashton scored twice with one assist. Watson scored twice and recovered two ground balls. Tuesday vs. San Marin Piedmont traveled to No. 4 San Marin in Novato for the first round of the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs, losing by a score of 15-5. See next week’s Post for game details and a season recap.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ volleyball team got its North Coast Section journey started with a 3-0 win against Encinal and advancing to the second round of the playoffs. Playing on Tuesday, May 2 as the No. 6 seed (last year it was seeded No. 11), the Highlanders defeated No. 11 Encinal 3-0 by scores of 25-15, 25-19, 25-22 in a game played in the middle school gym due to testing occupying Piedmont’s high school gym. “I’m excited. We worked really hard the past couple of days. We’ve never played in this gym. We played Encinal before but they were able to beat us last time we played them. We had a game plan and brought great energy,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. It is the team’s second consecutive season to win a game in NCS after upsetting No. 6 Analy last year. “We came in a lot stronger this year. Last year was my first year being the head coach. This year, I knew what we were capable of. We have seven great seniors and I’ve been with them since they were sophomores,” said Cardenas. “It’s feeling amazing. Year 2 in NCS. It’s been a massive journey. Some of us were on the B-team back in middle school and we were always the underdogs. Now, we almost doubled our wins total from last season. We have a really special group,” said senior leader Wilson Wong. It was a productive opening round for freshman Albert Bellingrath, who recorded two kills and three consecutive aces in the second game and made a difference as middle blocker. “Seeing him walk into tryouts was a big confidence booster because we all saw the potential in him,” said Wong. Having a freshman be the tallest player on the team got everyone hyped.” Match recap Piedmont won the first game 25-15 with John Champion slamming down a spike for the winning point. In the second game, Encinal opened with a 3-1 lead but Piedmont went on to score six unanswered points to lead 7-3. The Jets eventually took the lead at 13-12, but Piedmont regained their advantage at 15-14. Encinal tied the match at 15-15 and 18-18 but never went ahead. From there, PHS scored seven of the last eight points, including a spike by Eric Olaru-Hagen, three straight aces by Bellingrath, and a kill by Champion. Encinal got out to a 5-1 lead to start the third game, but Piedmont scored eight of the next 11 points and regain the lead at 8-7. The Jets eventually got back to the front at 19-18 until Piedmont tied the match at 22-22. An interesting turning point awarded PHS’ 22nd point when coach Cardenas challenged a ruling when Encinal’s back row player illegal hit a ball. PHS went ahead 23-22 on an offensive error by Encinal, then Owen Kelly scored on a sneaky push to an open area on the floor. With match point, Brayden Ellis sent a looping serve to the middle of the Jets court, landing for the match-winner. Final stats were not provided. NEXT UP Piedmont (13-6 overall) will face the winner of No. 3 Acalanes and No. 14 Marin Catholic on Thursday, May 4. Freshman Albert Bellingrath had a productive game against Encinal, recording three consecutive aces in the third set.

It was a productive opening round for freshman Albert Bellingrath, who recorded two kills and three consecutive aces in the second game and made a difference as middle blocker. “Seeing him walk into tryouts was a big confidence booster because we all saw the potential in him,” said Wong. Having a freshman be the tallest player on the team got everyone hyped.” Match recap Piedmont won the first game 25-15 with John Champion slamming down a spike for the winning point. In the second game, Encinal opened with a 3-1 lead but Piedmont went on to score six unanswered points to lead 7-3. The Jets eventually took the lead at 13-12, but Piedmont regained their advantage at 15-14. Encinal tied the match at 15-15 and 18-18 but never went ahead. From there, PHS scored seven of the last eight points, including a spike by Eric Olaru-Hagen, three straight aces by Bellingrath, and a kill by Champion. Encinal got out to a 5-1 lead to start the third game, but Piedmont scored eight of the next 11 points and regain the lead at 8-7. The Jets eventually got back to the front at 19-18 until Piedmont tied the match at 22-22. An interesting turning point awarded PHS’ 22nd point when coach Cardenas challenged a ruling when Encinal’s back row player illegal hit a ball. PHS went ahead 23-22 on an offensive error by Encinal, then Owen Kelly scored on a sneaky push to an open area on the floor. With match point, Brayden Ellis sent a looping serve to the middle of the Jets court, landing for the match-winner. Final stats were not provided. NEXT UP Piedmont (13-6 overall) will face the winner of No. 3 Acalanes and No. 14 Marin Catholic on Thursday, May 4. Freshman Albert Bellingrath had a productive game against Encinal, recording three consecutive aces in the third set.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ relay teams won league titles and finished their season undefeated. Pictured are coach Colby Price (left), Abigail Jacoby, Josie Oesterer, Taylor Rolefson, Sonja ten Grotenhuis and Sydney Olson. The Piedmont High swim team – the team with no hometown pool – traveled to Chabot College in Hayward for the Western Alameda County Conference Championship on Friday, April 28. The girls’ team won three events on the day. Piedmont’s girls’ 200 Medley Relay and 400 Freestyle Relay team completed an undefeated season and continued by winning three events at the league championship. Their 200 medley includes junior Josie Oesterer on the backstroke, freshman Abigail Jacoby on the breaststroke, junior Taylor Rolefson on butterfly and sophomore Sonja ten Grotenhuis as the final leg for the freestyle, defeating eight teams with a time of 1:54.74. “It was crazy. I knew I got out to a lead when I was in the pool. When I finished my leg all my teammates behind the block were going crazy,” said ten Grotenhuis. The race came down to the wire with Piedmont defeating Berkeley by .71 of a second. Oesterer finished her leg of the race with a time of 30.50, followed by Jacoby clocking a 31.98. Rolefson entered the water with PHS two seconds behind Berkeley, but her time of 26.58 but her team less than a second back. Ten Grotenhuis blazed through her freestyle in 25.68, beating Berkeley’s Lillian Welsh by nearly two seconds. In the 400 freestyle relay, freshman Sydney Olson replaced Jacoby while ten Grotenhuis raced the second leg, resulting in Piedmont finishing with a time of 3:44.42, beating Castro Valley by .78 of a second and three other schools. “I was the second leg and we got a little lead during my swim. It was really close and we were all really nervous right until the end. Castro Valley is a good team but we beat them during season, so it was really nerve wracking,” said ten Grotenhuis of her run. articles.text: Piedmont High’s baseball team wrapped up a busy week by splitting four games. They lost both a home and away game to Castro Valley on Wednesday, April 26 and Friday, April 28 by respective scores of 12-5 and 4-0. Piedmont followed up with a strong 6-1 win against Oakland Tech on Saturday, April 29, and beating Hayward on the road 7-2 on Monday, May 1 in four extra innings. Piedmont plays a final series against Arroyo today, May 3 in San Lorenzo and at home on Friday, May 5. PHS will honor its three seniors on the roster for Senior Night on Friday: Ryan McConathy, Michael Aikawa, and Liam Campbell. Piedmont’s record is 10-10 overall and 2-6 in the Western Alameda County Conference’s Foothill Division, fifth out of six teams. With the Foothill’s topfour teams all holding a 5-3 league record, PHS is locked out of qualifying for the league tournament. 7-2 over Hayward On May 1, Piedmont and Hayward were tied 1-1 following the second inning. Piedmont jumped ahead 2-1 in the top of the fifth, but the Farmers tied the game at 2-2 in the bottom of the sixth, setting up extra innings. The two sides waged in a 2-2 battle through 11 innings until PHS blasted the game wide open with five runs in the top-of-the-eleventh. In the top of the second, Dimitri Papahadajopoulos smacked a solo home run over the left field fence with one out. Then in the fifth, Aikawa led off with a fourpitch walk, stole second, and advanced to third on a sacrifice fly by Markos Lagios. Peter Krumins was hit by a pitch and then Will Parker brought in Aikawa with a groundout to shortstop. On the mound Ellis Moss threw six innings and had six strikeouts with one earned run. Ryan McConathy entered in relief in the bottom of the seventh. PHS nearly scored the go-ahead in the top of the ninth after Aikawa hit a one-out single followed by a Lagios double. However, Krumins’ sacrifice fly to center field led to Aikawa being thrown out at home trying to score. In the bottom of the ninth, Hayward had two runners on base with one out and Piedmont’s George Bishop making his pitching debut. Bishop was able to force a ground out and then got a strikeout to get out the inning unscarred. Piedmont had a 1-2-3 inning in the bottom of the inning. The Highlanders came to life in the 11th inning with five runs started by Bishop drawing a walk. Diego Delventhal reached first on a bunt, Campbell hit a sacrifice fly to right field, advancing Bishop to third, followed by a single by Aikawa to load the bases. Lagios then smacked a 2-run double to center, and Krumins powered a triple to the left field fence. Parker scored Krumins from third with a single. In relief, Seve Sanchez closed out the game with two straight ground outs, allowed a single, then threw a four-pitch strikeout. Final stats: Papahadjpoulos went 1-for-1 with a double and three RBIs. Krumins had a run and RBI. Lagios drew two walks and scored a run. PHS will host Arroyo this Friday, May 5, at 4 p.m. It will be Senior Night for the Highlanders. Ellis Moss pitched six innings in Piedmont’s 7-2 win over Hayward, striking out six.

articles.text: Museum visitors view an item in MoAD’s Black Venus exhibition. San Francisco’s Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) celebrates Black beauty and femininity with the exhibit Black Venus, on view now through August 20. The exhibit is curated by Aindrea Emelife and is a reflection of the legacy of Black Women in visual culture, from colonial-era caricatures to the reclamation of Black womanhood by 18 artists of numerous nationalities and ages. Artwork spans from 1793 to the present day. Featured artists include Alberta Whittle, Amber Pinkerton, Ayana V. Jackson, Carrie Mae Weems, Carla Williams, Coreen Simpson, Deana Lawson, Deborah Roberts, Frida Orupabo, Ming Smith, Kara Walker, Maud Sulter, Lorna Simpson, Renee Cox, Sadie Barnette, Shawanda Corbett, Tabita Rezaire, Taiye Idahor, Wangechi Mutu, Yetunde Olagbaju and Zanele Muholi. The museum advises visitors that some artwork contains sensitive and difficult imagery. The exhibition’s thematic foundation is the Hottentot Venus, a visual-culture archetype named for the assigned stage name of Saartje Baartman (born 1789 in South Africa), fetishised by Dutch colonizers and slave traders. To learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/black-venus. General Dentistry & Advanced Prosthodontics
articles.title: MoAD’s Black Venus exhibition on view through August 20

articles.text: Paper Bag Thoughts & Conversations, a mixed media art exhibit with the work of Oakland native Marvin McMillian, opens Friday, May 5, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts with a reception at 6 p.m. A former student at both CCAC and the Academy of Art in SF, his work consists of a retrospective of conversations, childhood memories, family traditions, food, music, historical events, and sports. Gallery hours will be from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays for the next four weekends. Harriet T, mixed media, 24x48. In 2016, it was publicly announced that Harriet Tubman would be featured on the $20 bill. Tubman would be the first woman and Black American to be on a U.S. denomination. The production was halted. To pay homage to her, Marvin McMillian created a rendition of what the future bill could look like.
articles.title: Marvin McMillian art exhibit opens May 5 at PCA

articles.text: Artwork by John Singer Sargent is currently on view at the de Young Museum in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park through May 14. Sargent (1856 -1925) is regarded as the premiere portraitist of his era and is also known for his paintings of churches, coastlines, gardens and royal venues. This exhibition highlights his love of Spanish culture and the time he spent in Spain. The exhibit includes Sargent’s oils, watercolors, and drawings, as well as never-before-exhibited photographs showcasing the Mediterranean people, architecture, and urban and rural landscapes. The exhibit is displayed in the museum’s Rosekrans Court. For tickets and for more information, visit https://www.famsf. org. John Singer Sargent (American, 1856–1925). La Carmencita, 1890. Oil on canvas, 90 3/16 × 55 1/8”.
articles.title: Sargent and Spain exhibit at deYoung ends on May 14

articles.text: Dianne Reeves is the host of this year’s SF Jazz Gala on Thursday, May 4. SF Jazz will host its annual gala tomorrow evening, Thursday, May 4. This year’s gala will celebrate SF Jazz Founder and Executive Artistic Director Randall Kline, The gala will feature performances by Ambrose Akinmusire, Regina Carter, Rosanne Cash and John Leventhal, Ravi Coltrane, Herbie Hancock, Eric Harland, Branford Marsalis, Cécile McLorin Salvant and Sullivan Fortner. Dianne Reeves will serve as host, with after party performances by Trombone Shorty and Red Baraat. There will be a live free broadcast of the after-party concert at 8:30 p.m. on May 4. Trombone Shorty (Troy Andrews) is a native of New Orleans’ Treme, a neighborhood seeped in Jazz-rich history and tradition. He is best known as a trombone and trumpet player, but also plays drums, the organ and tuba. He started playing brass instruments on the streets of New Orleans since the age of 4. Ticket purchases support the SF Jazz Fund, with 100% of the proceeds going to SF Jazz’s artistic and education programs. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ tickets/events/2023-gala/ to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Tickets still available for SF Jazz Gala tomorrow

articles.text: Play ends this Sunday, May 7 American Conservatory Theatre’s newest play Poor Yella Rednecks: Vietgone 2 is being performed through May 7. Written by Qui Nguyen, it is a sequel to the popular Vietgone which premiered at the Strand Theater five years ago. Poor Yella Rednecks is part two in a trilogy by Nguyen. The story follows a Vietnamese family who left war-torn Saigon for rural Arkansas in the 1970’s. Married couple Tong and Quang encounter challenges in their new home: namely, their low-wage jobs don’t afford many luxuries, and their son is struggling to keep up with his peers as he tries to learn a new language. “This story goes deep while soaring high,” said ACT Artistic Director Pam MacKinnon. “It’s a personal exploration of the American Dream specific to a Vietnamese immigrant family and first-gen American experience, full of compromise, joy, hardscrabble setback, and love.” “I’m thrilled to be back in San Francisco at one of my favorite theaters in the country. This sequel to Vietgone promises to be just as exciting. Qui’s words will make you want to laugh and dance at the same time,” said director Jaime Castañeda. Cast members inlude Will Dao, Christine Jamlig, Hyunmin Rhee, Jomar Tagatac and Jenny Nguyen Nelson. To learn more and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.act-sf. org/whats-on/202223-season/ poor-yella-rednecks-vietgone-2/. Qui Nguyen, playwright of Poor Yella Rednecks: Vietgone 2, playing through Sunday at ACT Bryan Keane

articles.text: Thomas Wilkins will conduct the San Francisco Symphony for three performances at Davies Symphony Hall Thursday through Saturday, May 4-6, with saxophonist Brandon Marsalis as a guest musician. The story follows a Vietnamese family who left war-torn Saigon for rural Arkansas in the 1970’s.
