articles.text: Steven Spielberg’s The Fablemans, a semi-autobiographical, coming-of-age story, was nominated for seven Oscars, including Best Picture, at this year’s 2023 Academy Awards. Consider it a memoir of sorts that attempts to share with the audience how this extraordinarily talented and prolific filmmaker came to love cinema as a form of storytelling. Regarding the title, I wondered if Spielberg chose the family’s last name “Fableman,” as a way of signaling to the audience that he has devoted his life to entertaining audiences worldwide using the medium of film. Collaborating with screenwriter and Pulitzer Prize award-winning playwright Tony Kushner of Berkeley Rep fame, they create a series of vignettes focusing on the early years of one Sammy Fableman (later the 16-year-old Gabriel LaBelle). The movie opens with young Sammy (Mateo Zoryan Francis DeFord) going with his parents, Mitzi and Burt (Michelle Williams and Paul Dano), to see The Greatest Show on Earth, a larger than life, circus-themed tale released by Cecil B. DeMille in 1952. Wideeyed, Sammy watches a spectacular, jaw-dropping train crash that completely enthralls him and proves unforgettable. How was that done, he wonders? And could he recreate that eye-popping moment? And thus began Sammy’s love affair with cameras, celluloid, and those magical images that can be captured on what was then known as “the silver screen.” As well, Spielberg shares with the audience his anxiety about his parents (who eventually split up), encounters blatant anti-Semitism in high school, and recruits his family (parents and sisters) and peers to make what are in essence grainy, rough-cut home movies. He also includes his first adolescent romance with an enthusiastic girl who is devoted to Jesus (her room is covered with Christ’s image), yet is fascinated by the fact that Sammy is Jewish. While his dad’s work takes the family west, from New Jersey to Arizona to California, Sammy’s camera is always close by. And it’s while learning to edit his films, he comes to realize that not only can movies entertain, but they can reveal. And it’s while editing and splicing recently shot footage that he inadvertently discovers, to his chagrin, that his mother is enamored with Burt’s best friend “Uncle” Benny (Seth Rogen), who is all but a member of the family. While I have always been part of that cohort referred to as Spielberg’s fandom, beginning with Jaws, and the countless films that followed such as E.T., Indiana Jones, Empire of the Sun, Always, etc, I found The Fablemans a bit flat and restrained. Something is missing, perhaps a certain “let er rip” energy that has always defined Spielberg’s work. It’s as if The Fablemans is a home movie and we are guests in his living room. Why it was nominated for seven Oscars is a puzzle. The Fablemans. Written and directed by Steven Spielberg. Starring Michelle Williams, Paul Dano, Seth Rogen. 2 hrs., 31 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2022. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv. Gabriel LaBelle in a scene from The Fabelmans
articles.title: The Fablemans a Spielberg memoir

articles.text: In I’ll See You in My Dreams, writer and director Bret Haley gets just right the essence of Carol, a 72-year-old retired school teacher and widow, played with charming insight by Blythe Danner. To Haley’s credit, he avoids clichés such as “senior citizen” or “the golden years.” And no one is cranky or a hard case curmudgeon. In every respect, Dreams is a sweet and touching film about discovering that life can still be unexpectedly renewed and on occasion a surprise. Carol lost her husband some 20 years ago in a plane crash and has lived an orderly, if somewhat insular life ever since. She takes genuine pleasure in her L.A. home with a pool and garden and never feels weighted by the solitude that frames each day. She wakes at exactly six, makes coffee, and plans her day: time in the garden, a salad for lunch, perhaps a game of cards with her three friends (Rhea Pearlman, Mary Kay Place and June Squibb), all residents of a nearby active retirement community. Her only daily companion is Hazel, a much loved and aging dog. Above all, this is a subtle character study of a lovely if cautious woman surrounded by a quiet routine that, after all these years, she now welcomes. The opening set up finds her waking in the early hours of the morning, realizing that Hazel is not sleeping on the bed. Concerned, she searches the house. Smash cut to the vet hospital where Hazel is close to death. In a moving and heartfelt scene, Carol leans over the stainless steel table and places her hand on Hazel’s forehead as her cherished dog slowly slips away. Hazel’s death pushes Carol out of her comfort zone, and as a result things begin to happen in her life. She befriends Lloyd, the pool guy, a young man who describes how he feels decidedly unmoored. She meets Bill (Sam Elliot), long ago divorced, and also a resident of the retirement community. Their mutual fondness for one another, which evolves in small increments, ultimately leads to a brief romantic interlude that clearly surprises Carol. In a nice way. As it does Bill. If there is a sense of sadness to Dreams – more like a mild melancholy – it resides with the growing realization, voiced by Carol to her daughter, Kat (Malin Ackerman), that life is increasingly finite and far closer to its conclusion that not. The years ahead grow fewer. Behind her are countless incandescent images, memories of her past to be savored and perhaps wept over. She understands that in youth our years are spent like so much loose change, unthinking. Until we don’t, finally understanding that time is all we have and how we spend it comprises the sum total of our lives. Carol and her friends know this and you can almost hear them say, “Carpe diem!” as they plan in the final scene a grand and glorious adventure, just the four of them. So many of our movies are youth-driven. Romantic comedies can seem manic, frenetic, as young people search for what is missing in their lives. Someone else. Something else. Both. Often with abandon and excess. What marks Dreams is its grace, its carefully crafted and beautifully written sensitivity. It’s a film to be savored and enjoyed and contemplated. Between the lines and scenes there is wisdom and intelligence without even one patronizing, overly sentimentalized moment. It’s gently honest and replete with wonderful performances. I’ll See You in My Dreams. Directed by Brett Haley. Starring Blythe Danner, Sam Elliot, Malin Akerman. 1 hr., 25 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2018. Now streaming on WUDU/Prime/HBO MAX/Apple tv.
articles.title: I’ll See You in My Dreams a film possessing grace

articles.text: I’m way beyond the demographic that Marvel Comics is aiming for with Spider-Man: Homecoming. However, I think the stable of writers who worked on the script (six in all) missed a great opportunity to make a spot-on film. What the Marvel superhero creators (aka Marvel Cinematic Universe) have done, at least in the case of Spider-Man, is box themselves in with what they assume is the demand for overthe-top CGI action stuff. Here’s the deal: Spider-Man (he’s never been a man) is and always has been a kid. Young Peter Parker (in this incarnation played by Tom Holland) is a superhero, but a kid superhero. And it’s being an adolescent that makes him unique and special. With Homecoming they come close to keeping the story focused on Peter Parker’s high school issues, until they introduce Adrian Toomes, aka the Vulture (Michael Keaton). He’s totally unnecessary. This is a movie that doesn’t need a nasty villain. And it didn’t need an act three-wham!/ bam!/kaboom! event. When you’re 15-years-old and a sophomore in high school you spend most of your time figuring out all the changes you’re going through. And if you’re discovering that on top of dealing with superhero abilities, well, that means you have a full plate. Peter is a nerd, a geek. He’s on the debate team and was a member of the band. He loves chess. He’s smart. Teachers love smart kids who are free of attitude, so naturally he’s ripe to be picked on by the hard-case crowd. But, alas, Homecoming has a pretty bogus plot, one that is totally beside the point. As well, Peter doesn’t need mentoring by Iron Man. What does he know about kids? Homecoming is the sixth film in the Spiderman series and was ready for a new direction. Instead the tween/newbie teen crowd got more of the same. Coulda, shoulda been about Peter going to Queen’s Midtown High School of Science and all that entails, mixed with Spider-Man as your neighborhood crime stopper. That’s it. Full stop. Spider-Man: Homecoming. Directed by Jon Watts. Starring Tom Holland, Michael Keaton and Jacob Batalon. 2 hrs., 13 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv. Tom Holland as Spider-Man in Spider-Man: Homecoming
articles.title: Spider-Man: Homecoming a big disappointment

articles.text: Apparently Universal Studios has launched a panoply franchise of sorts, the goal being to resurrect those iconic monsters that chilled audiences in the 20s, 30s and well into the 50s. The Mummy is the first of what Universal calls the Dark Universe. If this picture is an example of what lies ahead, I’d judge the yet to be realized franchise is off to a limp start. I confess that I would welcome the chance to see how they update one of my boyhood favorites, The Creature From the Black Lagoon. I will never forget raising goosebumps on top of goosebumps as a group of unsuspecting scientists remains topside in a research boat, floating in an ominous jungle lagoon, while a man/fish, covered in scales with large webbed hands, swims just beneath the surface, waiting. Unfortunately, the recent incarnation of The Mummy is a mess, and the narrative incoherency chronic. No matter that the idea of a resurrected mummy, trailing bandages while staggering after archeologists who never ever should have opened its sarcophagus, dates back to Boris Karloff in the first 1932 version, then brought back in the 1999 Brendan Fraser trilogy, featuring Egyptian tombs and curses and Fraser as a swash-buckling, Indiana Jones type. Same gauzy bandages, indeed, but just a bit more elaborate regarding special effects and artifacts and if memory serves lots of black beetles and sandstorms. Which brings us to 2017 and the durable and protean Tom Cruise who portrays Nick Morton, a mercenary artifact hunter who is also happens to be in the army, and is accompanied by his sidekick Chris Vail (Jake Johnson). The setting is Iraq. A drone missile blows a deep hole in the village square exposing an enormous Egyptian stone mien that curiously happens to be in Mesopotamia. Cue Jenny Halsey (Annabelle Wallis), archeologist, who appears and recognizes that what has been exposed is a tomb or sorts and must immediately be Sofia Boutella as Ahmanet in The Mummy investigated. And so begins a barely intelligible story about an ancient Egyptian princess, Ahmanet (Sofia Boutella), who commits patricide and is wrapped and buried alive in an evil looking sarcophagus filled with mercury (don’t ask). Clearly the hieroglyphics covering the casket make clear that it would be best to not open same. Standard trope. Jenny tries to explain this to Nick, but his eyes glaze over wondering only what such an artifact might bring on the black market. His favorite hieroglyphic is “show me the money,” which is a line we’ve heard before. There is a plane ride that is the best part of the movie – that would be where Nick, Chris and Jenny accompany the sarcophagus back to England and the large military plane goes down, overwhelmed by a flock of crows. It’s quite a gravity-defying ride. The rest of the movie challenges you to suspend your disbelief and try not to say, “as if.” Nick and Jenny are chased, they run, again they chase, and run some more. Who’s chasing them? How about 12th century Crusaders released from their tombs. And there’s a dagger, a missing red stone that Ahmanet really, really wants to get a hold of. If she kills Nick with the dagger, that will release Set, Egyptian god of death. Follow? No? Me neither. There are more crows and rats and even a Dr. Jekyll (Russell Crowe) appears who is taking regular injections to ward off becoming a grim Mr. Hyde. Seriously. Suffice it to say that the sarcophagus is no ark and Cruise is no Indy. When in doubt, add more bandages, unless said mummy is a shapely princess, then less is definitely more. If there is eternal life then it rests with Tom Cruise’s abs which are on display and don’t look 54-years-old. I can’t recall if said abs appeared in the most recent Mission Impossible. Now that’s a franchise that has yet to disappoint. The Mummy. Directed by Alex Kurtzman. Starring Tom Cruise, Russell Crowe, Annabelle Wallis. 1 hr., 47 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2017. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: The Mummy – some scary stuff for kids

No matter that the idea of a resurrected mummy, trailing bandages while staggering after archeologists who never ever should have opened its sarcophagus, dates back to Boris Karloff in the first 1932 version, then brought back in the 1999 Brendan Fraser trilogy, featuring Egyptian tombs and curses and Fraser as a swash-buckling, Indiana Jones type. Same gauzy bandages, indeed, but just a bit more elaborate regarding special effects and artifacts and if memory serves lots of black beetles and sandstorms. Which brings us to 2017 and the durable and protean Tom Cruise who portrays Nick Morton, a mercenary artifact hunter who is also happens to be in the army, and is accompanied by his sidekick Chris Vail (Jake Johnson). The setting is Iraq. A drone missile blows a deep hole in the village square exposing an enormous Egyptian stone mien that curiously happens to be in Mesopotamia. Cue Jenny Halsey (Annabelle Wallis), archeologist, who appears and recognizes that what has been exposed is a tomb or sorts and must immediately be Sofia Boutella as Ahmanet in The Mummy investigated. And so begins a barely intelligible story about an ancient Egyptian princess, Ahmanet (Sofia Boutella), who commits patricide and is wrapped and buried alive in an evil looking sarcophagus filled with mercury (don’t ask). Clearly the hieroglyphics covering the casket make clear that it would be best to not open same. Standard trope. Jenny tries to explain this to Nick, but his eyes glaze over wondering only what such an artifact might bring on the black market. His favorite hieroglyphic is “show me the money,” which is a line we’ve heard before. There is a plane ride that is the best part of the movie – that would be where Nick, Chris and Jenny accompany the sarcophagus back to England and the large military plane goes down, overwhelmed by a flock of crows. It’s quite a gravity-defying ride. The rest of the movie challenges you to suspend your disbelief and try not to say, “as if.” Nick and Jenny are chased, they run, again they chase, and run some more. Who’s chasing them? How about 12th century Crusaders released from their tombs. And there’s a dagger, a missing red stone that Ahmanet really, really wants to get a hold of. If she kills Nick with the dagger, that will release Set, Egyptian god of death. Follow? No? Me neither. There are more crows and rats and even a Dr. Jekyll (Russell Crowe) appears who is taking regular injections to ward off becoming a grim Mr. Hyde. Seriously. Suffice it to say that the sarcophagus is no ark and Cruise is no Indy. When in doubt, add more bandages, unless said mummy is a shapely princess, then less is definitely more. If there is eternal life then it rests with Tom Cruise’s abs which are on display and don’t look 54-years-old. I can’t recall if said abs appeared in the most recent Mission Impossible. Now that’s a franchise that has yet to disappoint. The Mummy. Directed by Alex Kurtzman. Starring Tom Cruise, Russell Crowe, Annabelle Wallis. 1 hr., 47 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2017. articles.text: Come enjoy a range of exhibits and performances at Piedmont Center for the Arts this Spring. Friday, May 5, 6:00 p.m. Marvin McMillian II Fine Art Paper Bag Thoughts & Conversations: a mixed media solo show featuring the work of an Oakland native and student at both CCAC and the Academy of Art in SF, consists of a retrospective of conversations, childhood memories, family traditions, food, music, historical events, and sports. Light refreshments will be available following the concert. Sunday, May 7, 7:00 p.m. In the Tradition Piano Trio In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Rich Trevor, and Anthony Pegram – will perform a Cinco de Mayo Tribute to Mexican Composers. This concert will be loaded with music written by composers from south of our border as well as jazz and blues favorites and other classics. Advance tickets are $23 at https://bpt.me/5691334, or $25 at the door. Seating is limited to the first 70 attendees. Sunday, May 21, 4:00 p.m. Berkeley Symphony & Friends The final chamber concert in this year’s season, Between Worlds, includes music of Carlos Simon, Amy Beach, and Alexander Borodin, performed by Berkeley Symphony allstars Stephanie Bibbo and Emanuela Nikiforova, violins; Ivo Bokulic, viola; and Stacey Pelinka, flute. Tickets are available at https://bit.ly/3lNJ3g4. Saturday, June 3, 2023, 5:00 p.m. Sierra Ensemble Concert Sierra Ensemble is an innovative trio consisting of Matthew Vincent, violin; Marc Steiner, piano; and Janis Lieberman, French horn. Committed to supporting a lively chamber music environment, the ensemble will perform duos by Saint-Saëns and Mozart, as well as two horn trios: the exciting and evocative trio portrait of modern Istanbul, “Chaopolis,” by Turkish composer Tolga Özdemir, and the beloved Brahms Horn Trio. Advance tickets discounted only at https://www.eventbrite.com/e/574876229277. All public events at Piedmont Center for the Arts require photo ID and valid proof of full vaccination for entry, as well as proper masking while inside. Support the programming of Piedmont Center for the Arts by donating generously to the Tip Jar at these events.

articles.text: We stumble through life and taxes, and then we meet the compact Smuin Ballet which has emerged from the pandemic seemingly unscathed. Its newest Bay Area run showed off 17 beautifully coordinated and trained dancers in pieces new and old, bursting with precision and energy. Purists may carp about the troupe’s leanings toward the commercial, but this group under Celia Fushille offers both sides, serving up contemporary with a capital C, abetted by the new associate director and adroit choreographer Amy Seiwert. The engrossing opening-night program offered the wake-up call via a twin-barrel blast of culture: Val Caniparoli’s earth-shaking foray into a stormy percussive world, and Seiwert’s light-hearted world premiere to French songs so much in the spirit of founder Michael Smuin. (Smuin in early years had actually performed as a nightclub show duo with partner-spouse Paula Tracy – not exactly your typical dancer’s CV.) Seiwert’s piece “French Kiss” showed itself as airy as a sunny Sunday on the Champs-Élysées, with skirts in alluring sherbet-pastel colors, whirled about by cosmopolitan sophisticates. The dozen players flowed on and off stage as smooth as silk, mostly in pairs. No, no kisses, but a lot of youthful exuberance to French songs from the Pink Martini ensemble. Perhaps with a bow to Magritte, a group of dancers hit the stage flourishing black umbrellas, evolving into part of the whimsical décor. Another Seiwert-only touch was the mannequin pas de deux, so appropriate for these AI days, with life-size plastic figures wheeled around by flesh-andblood partners. This sure-fire crowd-pleaser Photo by Chris Hardy Smuin artists Ricardo Dyer (left), Alison Ramoran, Brennan Wall, Marc LaPierre, and Mengjun Chen with the company in Amy Seiwert’s world premiere of French Kiss, unveiled in Smuin’s “Dance Series 2” touring the Bay Area through May 28. capped the first night at the Lesher Center. And yet what bowled me most over was Caniparoli’s rugged ritual Swipe (2011), as jostling as driving with four flat tires. The bold shoulder swivel-thrusts and bobbing necks had me instinctively flexing muscles dormant for ages. The performers provocatively raised and worked hands on high – I couldn’t tell whether they were waving to Aunt Matilda in the 12th row or simply satirizing empty political speeches, which already anticipate 2024. The high point April 28 was a pairing of Cassidy Isaacson and João Sampaio, nimble and athletic to the core. Among Caniparoli’s quirky enigmas came a woman’s extended leg (Isaacson again) doing a breath-taking full-360 like a sweep-second hand of a clock, in a display of flexibility par excellence, one that’s very rarely done on stage. The program opened with Katarzyna Skarpetowska’s Sextette for four women and two men dancing to Bach, memorable for the skyward leaps of Ricardo Dyer, a dabbler in lofty elevation. In between, Smuin’s duet “Dream” was a vehicle for ballerina Tessa Barbour in a long voluptuous formal, later partnered by the Brazilian flash Sampaio. Of note in this program was the meticulous preparation of the ensemble, with letter-perfect formations, pliable bodies, and ballet moves to remember. Casts change nightly. All the music is prerecorded. Seiwert, just promoted to associate artistic director, turned up at intermission to meet patrons, along with Fushille, in a refreshing turnabout from those troupes that rarely show their directors offstage. SMUIN CONTEMPORARY BALLET opened its 29th season April 28-29 at Walnut Creek’s Lesher Center, then San Francisco’s Yerba Buena Center May 5-14, and Mountain View’s CPA May 25-28. Details online, www. smuinballet.org. www. something humorous .com

articles.text: If you’ve done any estate planning, or even if you’re just familiar with it, you probably know the basics — that is, a comprehensive estate plan can help you pass on assets to your family while also achieving other goals, such as designating someone to take care of your affairs if you become unable to do so. But you may not know about some other estate-planning issues that could prove important in your life: • Power of attorney for students Children heading off to college may be considered legal adults in many states. Consequently, you, as a parent, may not have any control over medical treatment if your child faces a sudden, serious illness or is involved in an accident. Instead, a doctor who doesn’t know your child or your family may decide on a course of action of which you might not approve. To help prevent this, you may want to have your college student sign a medical power of attorney form, which will allow you to make decisions on your child’s behalf if doctors don’t think your child can make those choices. You might also want to combine the medical power of attorney with an advance health care directive or living will, which lets you specify actions you do or don’t want to happen. In any case, consult with your legal advisor before taking any of these steps. • Community property versus common law Not all states treat married couples’ possessions equally. articles.text: A treat awaits in time for Mother’s Day • Is this fudgy pudding cake on your radar? As the cake bakes, a thick, rich sauce forms on the bottom of the pan, leaving a light, brownie-like cake atop. It’s a marvel to watch as it bakes, and always a crowd pleaser. The recipe scores bonus points as an easy-peasy dessert to fill the bill for newer bakers to prepare for Mother’s Day. This recipe likely dates back to the late- ‘70’s from a fine food shop in Philadelphia. Since then, countless recipes have appeared, and I’ve tweaked my own version over the years. This one has less sugar but still retains a very deep, rich chocolate-y indulgence using a handful of few ingredients, many of which you likely have on hand most of the time! Take note: this cake has a unique process. The pudding layer is achieved by adding the ingredients in a very unconventional way. The thick cake batter forms the base, but then you add the “pudding” on top, which consists of brown sugar, more cocoa powder and hot coffee or water. The liquid=y pudding ingredients begin sinking once in the oven, and the resulting cake is atop the fudge-y pudding. It’s chemistry, or magic. You decide. • 4 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted then cooled slightly 3/4 cup chocolate chips For the pudding: • 2/3 cup light brown sugar • 1/4 cup unsweetened cocoa, processed with alkali (“Dutch” process) • 1-1/2 cups brewed coffee or very hot water INSTRUCTIONS Chocolate Pudding Cake Adapted from King Arthur Baking INGREDIENTS For the cake: • 1-1/4 cups all-purpose flour • 1/2 cup granulated sugar • 2 teaspoons baking powder • 1/2 teaspoon salt • 1/2 cup unsweetened cocoa, processed with alkali (“Dutch” process) • 3/4 cup whole milk, room temperature • 1 large egg, room temperature • 2 teaspoons vanilla extract Position an oven rack to the lower third position. Set a rimmed baking sheet on the rack to catch any drips and/or bake individual ramekins. Preheat the oven to 350°F. Butter an 8ʺ square pan, or eight 8-ounce ramekins. For the cake: In a medium-sized bowl, whisk together the flour, granulated sugar, baking powder, salt, and cocoa powder. Make sure there are no large clumps of cocoa powder, which you can pinch between your fingers to separate. Stir in the milk, egg, vanilla, and melted butter, mixing until smooth. Stir in the chocolate chips. Pour the batter into the prepared 8ʺ pan and spread evenly. If using eight ramekins portion a heaping 1/4-cup of batter into each. For the pudding: Mix the brown sugar with the cocoa powder in a small bowl then sprinkle this mixture evenly over the batter in the pan (or ramekins). Gently drizzle the hot coffer or water over the mixture. It is OK to fill the pan/ramekins pretty full as the cakes do not rise much. Bake for 45 minutes for an 8ʺ pan, or about 30 minutes for ramekins. Remove the cake when it looks set, and the pudding is bubbling around the edges of the pan. Remove from the oven and let cool for 15 minutes before serving. The pudding will thicken as it cools and is ideally served warm with ice cream.

Post your ad in the Call (510) 626-2468 nancy@cmc-ads.com Some “did-you-knows” about estate plans If you’ve done any estate planning, or even if you’re just familiar with it, you probably know the basics — that is, a comprehensive estate plan can help you pass on assets to your family while also achieving other goals, such as designating someone to take care of your affairs if you become unable to do so. But you may not know about some other estate-planning issues that could prove important in your life: • Power of attorney for students Children heading off to college may be considered legal adults in many states. Consequently, you, as a parent, may not have any control over medical treatment if your child faces a sudden, serious illness or is involved in an accident. Instead, a doctor who doesn’t know your child or your family may decide on a course of action of which you might not approve. To help prevent this, you may want to have your college student sign a medical power of attorney form, which will allow you to make decisions on your child’s behalf if doctors don’t think your child can make those choices. You might also want to combine the medical power of attorney with an advance health care directive or living will, which lets you specify actions you do or don’t want to happen. In any case, consult with your legal advisor before taking any of these steps. • Community property versus common law Not all states treat married couples’ possessions equally. If you live in a community property state, the property you acquire during your marriage is generally considered to be owned in equal halves by each spouse, with some exceptions. But if you live in a common law state, the property you obtain while you’re married is not automatically owned by both spouses. In these states, if you buy some property, you own it, unless you decide to put it in the name of yourself and your spouse. This doesn’t necessarily mean that your spouse has no rights, because common law states typically have rules that guard surviving spouses from being disinherited. But here’s the key point: If you move from a community property state to a common law state, or vice versa, you might not want to assume that your and your spouse’s property ownership situations will remain the same. Consequently, if you do move, you may want to consult an estate-planning attorney in your new state to determine where you stand. • Pet trusts You always strive to take good care of your pets. But what might happen to them if you become incapacitated in some way? Unless you have a close family member or friend who’s willing to take over care for your pet, you might want to consider setting up a pet trust, which can take effect either during your lifetime or after you pass away. A trustee typically will make payments to the caregiver you’ve designated for your pet, with payments continuing for the pet’s lifetime or a set number of years. Again, an estate-planning attorney can help you with this arrangement. Estate planning certainly involves the big-picture issue of leaving a legacy to the next generation. But the issues we’ve discussed can also be meaningful to you, so you’ll want to address them properly. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. articles.text: No Immigrants No Spice (NINS), a Bay Area nonprofit focused on awareness of immigrant contributions through food, culture and economy, will hold its second BBQ without Borders event on Saturday, May 13, at Oakland Museum from 5:00-9:00 p.m. The event will feature Chef Ron Dumra of Wah Jee Wah, Chef Lilly Duran of Clandestina Cafe, and Chef Tadayuki of the former Family Cafe, who will celebrate their regional specialties of Lechon, Tandoori and Yakitori. Tickets are on sale now. General entry includes dinner, dessert, one beverage, as well as a full stage show with Taiko drummers, Bhangra, Flamenco, a Cuban salsa band and even an opera performance. Guests will be invited to explore the theme of “cultivating home” through physical mini marts constructed in the museum’s gardens. There will also be an area for kids’ activities with a continuous game of “found object soccer”, a basmati rice bag race, an immersive collaborative art piece and a silent auction of premier prizes. Craft cocktails, mocktails, wine, and beer will also be available, and additional food and drink will be available for purchase. Attendees also have the option of purchasing a VIP ticket and donating directly to the Resilience Fund. There is also a sliding scale option to make the tickets more accessible to all of the public. NINS’ newly established Resilience Fund has been designed to distribute micro grants to vulnerable Bay Area residents: recent arrivals, and those with varying levels of documentation and DACA status. “BBQ without Borders is a space to celebrate and honor our most vulnerable communities,” said NINS founder Dr. Vibha Gupta, a Piedmont resident. “We hope you can come eat something delicious, witness a spectacular performance, meet someone new, and walk away with a new experience.” To learn more about BBQ without Borders, contact noimmigrantsnospice@gmail.com. Tickets and event details can be found at www.noimmigrantsnospice.org and eventbrite (https://www.eventbrite.com/e/ bb q -w it h o u t- b o r d e r s - t ickets-68562557455).

articles.text: Wildwood Dads Club will host an all-day golf tournament to help raise money for the school. The inaugural charity event includes a party bus to and from Oakmoore Golf Course in Stockton, green fees, drinks and food. The tournament takes place on Friday, May 12. A bus will pick up golfers and volunteers at 7:00 a.m. in front of Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, and will return at 6:00 p.m. “Part of the fun is jumping on the party bus, where warmup breakfast, drinks and fun games will be had,” said event organizer Reed Johnson. “It’s a great opportunity to strengthen bonds, share summer plans and just enjoy a dad’s club event without the work associated with running a pumpkin patch.” The tournament format will be a best-ball foursome scramble. A scramble entails all four team members to tee off on each hole and then each team member plays their next shot from the best ball of the group. This is repeated for all shots & putts. Oakmoore Golf Course (3737 North Wilson Way in Stockton) was chosen because it is designed for groups to rent out the entire facility. It is a ninehole course which golfers play twice. Although hosted by Wildwood Dads Club, participants do not need to be in the club. Space is limited to 80 (20 foursomes) and all are welcome. Moms, co-workers and college friends are welcome. Trophies will be awarded for best golf outfit, best drives, closest to the hole, and best score by a 4-man team. This event is structured for fun, even for people who don’t regularly play golf. He has written two books about the cemetery as well as books about Alameda and Oakland’s Laurel District. The walkers were told about the cemetery’s history, including his “three girlfriends” at the main mausoleum. They are statues of three women in its façade, and represent life, and how long it is measured. Dennis has a special interest in the renowned landscape architect Fredrick Law Olmsted, who designed the cemetery in 1863. He also planned New York’s Central Park, as well as much of the UC Berkeley and Stanford University campuses. Olmsted was managing gold mines in Bear Valley, California, when he was asked to design the cemetery. The cemetery is home to renowned 19th and 20th century individuals Charles Crocker, one of the founders of the Central Pacific Railroad, and architect Julia Morgan, among many. After the initial historical background, the group was led to a fountain on the cemetery’s main road. He pointed out the burial place of architect Bernard Maybeck, whose Piedmont-designed homes the group has enjoyed on their walks, is buried. The difference between types of cemeteries was explained. Some have large monuments and tombs, others have smaller headstones, and others have flat-to-the-ground burial markers, which make mowing the grass far easier. The group saw an oak tree that is about 350 years old and a dawn redwood that was brought here from China in the early 1900s. An estimated 170,000 people are buried in the cemetery. The many Washington Monument-style obelisks mark graves from the late 19th Century when the monument was built in Washington DC. At that time the cemetery was also being created, Egyptian archeological discoveries were first being made by the western world, and everything Egyptian was the rage. A humble grave marls the resting place of famed California architect Julia Morgan, who designed Hearst Castle and many Piedmont homes the walkers have enjoyed on their walks. Her grave is part of a Morgan family plot. Further up the hill is “Millionaires’ Row,” a section where the most grand, elaborate crypts are located, housing some of the cemetery’s most famous and wealthy residents. It is located on a hill with an expansive view of Oakland and San Francisco Bay. The group was told about the history of Charles Crocker, Domingo Ghirardelli, and others. One additional stop along the way was the plot for the Grand Army of the Republic soldiers, which Dennis helped restore. The plot is for Civil War Union veterans who died in California, or whose bodies were moved to Oakland. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: and quads hurt, we feel really good about what we did and the cause we did it for,” said McNulty. Since registering for the Big Climb last December, the team has trained continually in Piedmont. “We ran the stairs at Witter Field and Blair, constantly running laps, laps, laps,” said McNulty. “At the firehouse, we did step training every shift, at least three to four times a week. We have a gym stair-stepping machine in our fitness center in the basement, and I put in about 25 minutes every night, and it certainly paid off.” “The Leukemia and Lymphoma Society made a plaque which will be awarded to the team with the fastest three members’ times. We’ve been training especially hard, wanting to earn the plaque.” “It’s also about promoting the importance of fitness for our firefighters,” McNulty added. “No matter how light the equipment gets, no matter how much the technology advances, physical fitness is still at the center of how well we can perform. The fact that everything we fundraised for in this competition is going to such a good cause was a great motivator.” To learn more about the Big Climb, visit bit.ly/3LKBr8r.

The two sides traded possessions until the fourth quarter started with PHS holding a 7-3 lead. Then Piedmont’s offense exploded, scoring five straight goals in less than two minutes. Jack Nelson scored with 8:42 left in the third, followed by Fredericks just 15 seconds later, then he scored again after another 14 seconds. Fredericks then flicked a pass to Dixon for a goal with 7:35 left, then Fredericks netted another after 30 seconds, 12-3. O’Dowd finally got on the board with 4:41 on the clock. Dixon and Jack Nelson scored back-to-back goals to make it 14-4 with 2:37 left in the game, while O’Dowd scored the game’s last two goals. articles.text: Community members came to the Community Hall for the city’s annual Arbor Day on Thursday afternoon, April 27, celebrating the nearly 12,000 public trees in Piedmont. During the event Park Commission chair Tom Smegal announced the city’s new Heritage Trees and presented commemorative Heritage Tree lapel pins to the winning nominators. The five trees selected for recognition were: • Ceanothus trees at the Linda-Kingston Triangle, nominated by Patty Dunlap and Jamie Totsubo. • Copper Beech in Crocker Park, nominated by Alicia Bacon • Palm tree at the Piedmont Recreation Department building, nominated by the students of Hillside Pre-school. • Coast Live Oaks at the Tot Lot in Piedmont Park, nominated by Piedmont Connect and Connie Herrick • Mulberry trees in Hampton Park, nominated by the students of Piedmont Play School and the Walking on Wednesday group. Chad Olcott, owner of Mulberry’s Market, joked about the nomination of the Mulberry Tree, Cameron Wilhelmy explores a bulldozer during the Public Works Department vehicle demonstration. which is currently pruned and bare. “Can we get a better photo when it’s in bloom?” he asked. In addition to the Heritage Tree program, the event featured an “Ask an Arborist” booth answering questions that attendees had about tree maintenance; demonstration of healthy garden maintenance tools like “gator bags” which wrap around a tree’s base to slowly release water; a demonstration of the Public Works Department’s “Treekeeper” database cataloging detailed information about the nearly 12,000 public trees in Piedmont; and promotional materials for the free garden compost available to residents at the Corporation Yard. Representatives from SavAtree raffled off a Japanese Maple tree and $500 in landscaping services; firefighters from the Piedmont Fire Department offered information about fire-proofing landscaping and homes; and Davey Tree Resource Group gave away free key chains. Outside the Community Hall, the Public Works Department held a “meet the staff” demonstration, with four vehicles for children to sit in: a truck connected to a sewer camera; a street sweeper; a vacuum truck; and a bulldozer. articles.text: In an update on pickleball use at the Linda-Beach courts, Recreation Department Director Chelle Putzer announced at a Recreation Commission meeting on April 19 that the department created a QR code with four questions when players check in: how many people are in your group playing, what type of transportation did you use, how long are you going to play, and the number of residents in your group. From March 1 to April 19, Putzer said, the courts had 2,883 check-ins, 60% of which were Piedmont residents. Slightly more than half of the users planned to play for one to two hours. Commissioner Amir Virani noted that the QR survey did not distinguish between participants who dropped in for organized drop-in play and informal drop-in play. He recommended that in the future the QR survey provide such a distinction for arriving players. The Beach courts are open for pickleball play from 9 a.m. to dusk, Monday through Friday. Putzer confirmed that the Recreation Department has “received consistent noise complaint[s] since the start of the [five-month] trial.” To address the complaints, the department will work to find “an acoustical consulting firm to perform some noise measurements.” Pickleball players were encouraged to use noise-dampening paddles provided by the department. Defending the noise complaints, Amy Vallerie said she is “still…disappointed about this Commission’s decision to go forward with this trial, despite having a petition of 250 neighbors about how this trial was arranged, conducted and communicated. For the past six weeks the tone, volume, and popping of pickleball paddles has permeated our homes despite doors and windows mostly being closed.” She recommended that the commission schedule pickleball on courts throughout the city “so that it does not negatively impact one neighborhood.” Another neighbor, Pierre Garrigues, said, “I’ll take kids playing any day before pickleball paddle noise, and I think it changes the feel of the neighborhood when we hear the constant pickleball paddles.” He agreed with Vallerie’s suggestion of “spreading the usage of pickleball across the town.” The Recreation Commission will invite community feedback on pickleball play at the Beach courts again at its meeting on Wednesday, June 21. Community members can send questions and comments about the pickleball trial to BeachPickleballTrial@ piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: Pickleball trial update: user demographics, noise complaints

articles.text: Piedmont’s community reading project, Readmont, now in its 13th year, has selected No Stopping Us Now by Lucy Jane Bledsoe as this year’s collective read. Led by Piedmont High School English Department Chair Beth Black, Readmont will host a community discussion with the author tonight, Wednesday, April 26 at 7:00 p.m. in the Ambassador Chris Stevens Library. The book was chosen to help celebrate the 50th anniversary of Title IX, the federal legislation requiring equal funding for women’s and men’s sports. It is a book about the love of sports, finding one’s own voice, and activism. Based on the author’s true story, the book follows the story of Louisa who fought to bring her hometown into compliance with the new Title IX law so she could play basketball at her high school in Oregon. Those interested in discussing the book and learning more about the author are encouraged to attend the evening event. English department chairperson Black will also lead discussions during lunchtime on April 25 and 26. For more information, contact Kathryn Levenson, Teacher Librarian at Piedmont High School at klevenson@piedmont.k12.ca.us (510-594-2781), or Beth Black, PHS English Department chairperson, at bblack@piedmont.k12.ca.us. No Stopping Us Now by Lucy Jane Bledsoe was named a Finalist for both the Golden Poppy Award and the Rainbow Award. articles.text: Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), a coed Venturing unit with Piedmont Scouts, has served local youth ages 14-20 for two decades, providing much more than an easy way to find service opportunities. As a part of Piedmont Council BSA it follows principles of youth empowerment and actively encourages teens to take on responsibility and give them creative license with guidance so that they gain practical life skills. It hosts service trips, including a plan to build tiny houses in Medford, Oregon this June. The Crew’s largest annual project, renovating a low-income Oakland resident’s house in conjunction with the non-profit Rebuilding Together Oakland (RTO) is now underway. This year’s ambitious project involves rebuilding an entry deck needed for access to the home; replacement of a large window that has been broken for many years; renovation of a bedroom and bathroom damaged by rats and water leaks; and repair of a leaking tub drain. Crew members and parents work together with parents on the RTO project, enjoying teamwork, learning new practical skills, and meeting the homeowners who are grateful and constantly in awe of the work done by the teen members of the Piedmont Community Service Crew. The home restoration project is funded entirely by the crew. Maddy Tran and Stephanie Lee learn drywall patching skills. Mark Modera (left), a long-standing adult contributor and advisor with the RTO projects, discusses plans with Tolganai and Simon March Cunningham during the early phase of the deck rebuilding project. Amelia Carter, all suited up, helps clean up a very dirty bedroom and bathroom. Invitation to new members Teens and adults are encouraged to join now and take part in this once-a-year event. Work days have been scheduled every Saturday and Sunday through mid-May. Middle school families PCSC has a middle school companion club, Piedmont Service Club. Middle schoolers register annually and come to events with their parents. Most of the activities for PCSC youth (age 14 or 8th grade graduates) are open to middle school members, but not the RTO project. Community adults are also encouraged to become involved in PCSC. The crew is youth led, but the teens benefit from adults who mentor them. Some adults engage by being regular crew volunteers at a particular activity of their choosing. For example, cooking meals for the food insecure at College Ave. Presbyterian Church allows crew members to plan a menu, shop for the food, and lead their peers in cooking. Adult volunteers help the youth leaders to plan in advance and help solve problems when they occur. articles.text: Piedmont Education Foundation is pleased to welcome 11 individuals to the Board of Directors for the 2023-24 fiscal year. After a thorough process of nominations and interviews, the board voted to approve Jade Cameron, Marco Gonzalez-Navarro, Michael Gross, Kim Hunter, Judy Lin, Dana Murray, Ashish Patel, Max Roman, Julia Ruthven, and Jennie Stomberg. Sara Davison DeVries has returned to the board after a two-year hiatus to lead the middle and high school parents clubs and Sara Davison DeVries returns to help lead the grantmaking process “We are thrilled to introduce our incoming slate of board members — a group of accomplished individuals who bring a wealth of expertise and a shared passion for our mission,” said Board Chair Amelie Kappes. Jade Cameron, an expert in employment law, joins PEF because of shared values of community, engagement, and connection. Professor Marco Gonzalez-Navarro wants to help Piedmont schools continue to thrive. Michael Gross is an active member of Beach Dad’s Club, and Kim Hunter, while working as an assistant district attorney, has volunteered toward the success of the Giving Campaign, Harvest Festival, Spring Fling, and other PEF fundraisers. Judy Lin currently leads operations for the largest non-profit educational partner of the National Parks Service and looks forward to building resources for PUSD. Dana Murray and Julia Ruthven co-chaired this year’s successful Giving Campaign and both bring exceptional marketing, analytical and communications skills to the board. Dr. Ashish Patel has significant executive-level board experience and will bring that expertise to PEF, and Max Roman, a Piedmont native, wants to use his skill with investments and negotiations to ensure his children have an even better educational experience than he did. Jennie Stomberg, a forensic accountant, brings important audit and governance skills to PEF. “As we welcome new board members, we also bid farewell to some of our long-standing members whose unwavering commitment and valuable contributions have helped shape our organization,” said Kappes. Leaving the board are Cortney Allen, Francis Hoang, John Orta, Sarah Puckett, Rick Smith, Linda Smith Munyan, and Rebecca Thornborrow. “That was the year Dude stopped to smell the roses.”
articles.title: Education Foundation new board announced

This year’s ambitious project involves rebuilding an entry deck needed for access to the home; replacement of a large window that has been broken for many years; renovation of a bedroom and bathroom damaged by rats and water leaks; and repair of a leaking tub drain. Crew members and parents work together with parents on the RTO project, enjoying teamwork, learning new practical skills, and meeting the homeowners who are grateful and constantly in awe of the work done by the teen members of the Piedmont Community Service Crew. The home restoration project is funded entirely by the crew. Maddy Tran and Stephanie Lee learn drywall patching skills. Mark Modera (left), a long-standing adult contributor and advisor with the RTO projects, discusses plans with Tolganai and Simon March Cunningham during the early phase of the deck rebuilding project. Amelia Carter, all suited up, helps clean up a very dirty bedroom and bathroom. Invitation to new members Teens and adults are encouraged to join now and take part in this once-a-year event. Work days have been scheduled every Saturday and Sunday through mid-May. Middle school families PCSC has a middle school companion club, Piedmont Service Club. Middle schoolers register annually and come to events with their parents. Most of the activities for PCSC youth (age 14 or 8th grade graduates) are open to middle school members, but not the RTO project. Community adults are also encouraged to become involved in PCSC. The crew is youth led, but the teens benefit from adults who mentor them. Some adults engage by being regular crew volunteers at a particular activity of their choosing. For example, cooking meals for the food insecure at College Ave. Presbyterian Church allows crew members to plan a menu, shop for the food, and lead their peers in cooking. Adult volunteers help the youth leaders to plan in advance and help solve problems when they occur. articles.text: As the Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO) enters the final stage of fundraising for the new Piedmont pool facility, it thanks the community for coming together to raise the funds necessary to complete the project. Every dollar raised will go directly to completing the pool complex, ensuring that it meets the needs of the community for decades to come. “The dream of creating a world-class aquatic facility is nearing a reality,” said PRFO President Steve Collins. “Over 250 community members have committed from $50 to $500,000 to help reshape central Piedmont. The passion and generosity of Piedmont residents have surpassed all expectations.” In addition to individual community member support, the campaign has received substantial commitments from groups such as Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF), Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF), Piedmont High School Athletic Boosters, and the Piedmont Scouts as well as local sports clubs. Significant progress has been made towards fully matching the $500,000 anonymous gift announced in January, and there is still time to double your impact. There is also one naming opportunity remaining within the pool facility. Those interested should contact Eric Havian PRFO Fundraising Chair. The campaign, which began in September 2022, will end on June 1, 2023. Contributions of any amount are welcome and all gifts $500 or more made prior to June 1 will receive prominent recognition at the new facility. To keep residents informed about the progress of the project, the City has installed a camera for construction updates that can be viewed at https://piedmont. ca.gov/government/projects/piedmont_community_pool. For more information or to make a donation, visit PRFO.org.
articles.title: PRFO in final fundraising stage for new Piedmont Pool

articles.text: Last week 619 teams and over 35,000 people from 18 countries attended the 4-day FIRST Robotics Competition World Championship in Houston. Piedmont’s Team 8033, the Highlander Robotics, finished 3rd in their division, placing them in the top 1.5 percent of all competitors internationally with their robot. Paddo the Frog. The FIRST Robotics Competition, which frames high school robotics as a full contact sport complete with mascots and cheering sections, announces a new game in January of each year to be played by two alliances of three robots in an arena about the size of a basketball court. An entirely new robot must be constructed for each season and competitions start in the sixth week. In this year’s game, Charged Up, robots up to 125 pounds and 6-feet-6-inches tall score points by collecting and placing 9.5- inch inflatable cubes and 1-foot high rubber cones in a grid of poles and pedestals as well as by balancing robots on a see-sawlike platform called a “charging station.” Teams who qualified for the World Championship at regional tournaments in seven countries were placed into eight divisions. Each team plays 10 qualifying rounds with randomly selected partners, after which the highest ranked eight teams become alliance captains and draft three others to work with throughout Mechanical Lead and pit crew member Chloe Kessinger does last minute checks before Paddo’s next match. the double-elimination playoff brackets. Draft selections are key to success in the playoffs and all teams at the elite level dedicate time to track every robot’s performance across 125 qualifying rounds in a process called “scouting.” The Highlanders ended the first day of qualifications on Thursday ranked 36th of 77 in their division. On Friday they continued to perform well with 3 wins and 2 losses and moved up to 19th place while maintaining a rank of 3rd in overall scoring. The Highlanders were picked in the first round of the draft by the 8th seed alliance captained by the Mountie Megabots from Jackson, Michigan and joined by two Israeli teams. In the first round of the double elimination playoffs, the Highlanders lost 208-189 to the 1st seeded alliance, citrus Circuits from Davis. After a first-round loss the Highlanders won three straight matches in the lower bracket to reach the semifinals where they faced faced Citrus Circuits, seeded 1st. Citrus Circuits led for the entirety of the match but in the last 25 seconds the Highlanders whittled a 25--point lead down to 4, 185 to 181 in favor of Citrus Circuits. Citrus Circuits and their alliance went on to win the Galileo division and were eliminated in the final field by an alliance from Madera. A team from Guelph, Canada went on to win the Championship. Paddo the Frog was operated by Vaughn Khouri and Matteo Scanu, supported by drive coach Alex Ware, technician Nate Hart, and human player Paddo, the Highlanders’ robot, features a 3-stage elevator with a wheel-based intake on a wrist that is used for picking up and placing cones and cubes. Ava Grochowski. Helena Young and Peter Stokes led the pit crew which kept the robot running smoothly through 15 full contact matches. Jasper Tripp led scouting and strategy operations with 13 scouts and a software team led by Cassie Colby, Jessica Liu, Caetano de Figueiredo, and Tiago de Figueiredo acted as ambassadors who fielded questions and built connections. Highlander Robotics was founded in 2019 by brothers Henry and Charlie Lambert and now has 54 members from Piedmont High, Millennium, College Prep, Las Lomas, Stanford Online High, Lick Wilmerding, Maybeck, Monte Vista, Head Royce, and Bentley. They work out of the Mary G. Ross Engineering Lab at Piedmont High School. For more information contact Kevin Clark at kevin.clark@ gmail.com or visit https://frc8033. com/. The Highlanders’ Drive Team: Alex Ware (left), Matteo Scanu, Vaughn Khouri, Nate Hart, and Ava Grochowski with robot Paddo the Frog.
articles.title: Highlander Robotics places 3rd at World Championship

articles.text: Advanced Placement (AP) art students will showcase their art in the foyer of the Alan Harvey Theater. Over 100 pieces from Piedmont’s top 20 junior and senior artists will be on display from 6:00-8:00 p.m. The reception will highlight the work of AP art students throughout the school year. Students designed an artistic inquiry called a “Sustained Investigation for the College Board” and follow that concept through artistic inquiry in the creation of 10 works of art throughout the year. Students in Gillian Bailey’s AP 2-Dimensional Design and AP Drawing classes and Hannah Bjork’s AP 3-Dimensional Ceramics class will be represented in the exhibit. Student pieces, including works being submitted to art college art programs and art school, span multiple mediums including: print making, ceramics, acrylic, digital, diorama, watercolor, collage, pencil and photography. articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra has announced that its annual Spring Concert will be performed on Saturday, May 13, at 7:30 p.m. at First Congregational Church of Berkeley, 2345 Channing Way. David Ramadanoff, now in his 34th season with the 101- piece youth orchestra, will conduct a performance of Brahms’ Academic Festival Overture, Symphonic Metamorphosis of Themes of Carl Maria von Weber by Paul Hindemith, and Maurice Ravel’s LaValse. It will also feature two Concerto Competition winners, violinist Noa Marvit performing the First movement of Symphonie Espagnole by Édouard Lalo, and Ethan Chen in von Weber’s Concertino for Clarinet in E-flat. Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO is the oldest youth orchestra in California and the first independent youth orchestra in the nation. Tickets are $20 and are available online at http:// www.ypsomusic.org/tickets and at the door. For more information call (510) 849-9776 or visit http:// www.ypsomusic.org.

articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra, the oldest youth orchestra in California and the oldest independent youth orchestra in the nation, is now accepting new members. Auditions are being conducted for trumpet, trombone, bass trombone, tuba, bassoon, oboe, violin, viola, and double bass. Founded in 1936 in Berkeley, YPSO is led by conductor and Music Director David Ramadanoff for 35 years, with an orchestra of more than 100 musicians from schools through the greater Bay Area. YPSO will tour and perform in Japan next year, and will perform in the Bay Area Youth Orchestra Festival at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco. Submission of screening videos are due by June 1. For details and registration: www.ypsomusic.org/how-to-join. YPSO rehearses most Monday evenings at First Congregational Church of Oakland, 2501 Harrison Street from 6:00-9:30 p.m. There is also an annual weekend retreat in the Fall in Carmel Valley and several Saturday afternoon intensives during the year.

articles.text: What does a focus coach do? I hear this question a lot when I tell people what I do for a living and for good reason. Though ADHD is well known, focus coaching for ADHD is still a relatively new concept. I am a former student of Piedmont schools and I recently started an ADHD focus coaching business, MindsGlowing. I decided to leave my career in tech sales and become a focus coach when I came to realize the unique set of challenges that people with ADHD face when tackling the world around them. I understand these challenges and have faced them in my own life. Before I was diagnosed, I struggled with procrastination, lack of organization, and other ADHD symptoms and it wasn’t until I was diagnosed after college that I began to find relief through medicine and developing systems for myself. After I was diagnosed, I decided to complete a program in Positive Psychology to better understand how the mind works and I now use my certification in Applied Positive Psychology to help people with ADHD achieve their goals. One of my clients is a premedical student at Columbia University who has recently been diagnosed with ADHD. We meet a few times a week for targeted focus sessions where we work on goal setting, craft her to-do lists, and tackling her more difficult projects. My coaching takes many different forms depending on the client, day, and a multitude of factors. I customize each session based on my client’s unique goals and challenges because there is no one size fits all way to coach people with ADHD. I want to introduce one concept, intentional relaxation, which I work on with my clients who struggle with procrastination. The idea behind intentional relaxation is: when you’re watching tv or scrolling through Tik Tok when you’re supposed to do something, it doesn’t feel very good. It becomes hard to enjoy the thing you’re doing when you’re worried about the things that need to get done. To try intentional relaxation, you want to set aside time where you are aware that you’re relaxing and can enjoy it more fully. The best time for this would be when you don’t have too much to do, but you can also use it as a break between two tough tasks or in between school and doing homework. Set a timer for 30 minutes and let yourself watch the show or go on Instagram and really enjoy the time. Once it’s over, you’ll have more energy to complete the task at hand. Check back next month for more on ADHD, focus coaching, and positive psychology tips! Erica Monical is the founder and focus coach at MindsGlowing. This year, seven awards were presented: two for Excellence in Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) Design; Excellence in Home Renovation and Expansion; Excellence in a Comprehensive Stylistic Update; Excellence in Landscaping and Outdoor Living; Excellence in Deck Design; and Excellence in Window Replacement. articles.text: Piedmont’s tennis team returned from Spring Break in good form, defeating El Cerrito 6-1 at home on Wednesday, April 19 and sweeping Mt. Eden 7-0 in Hayward the following day. The pair of wins extends the team’s winning streak to eight matches since March 15. “El Cerrito was a good match. We won 6-1 with the only loss at No. 2 singles; Ben Breber played some good tennis but was a little rusty from hammering nails in Mexico,” said coach Jim Landes with a laugh. “Lucas Smolko played beautifully and defeated a good player quite handily with a good mix of offense and defense. Ethan Pham also played well, hitting some powerful forehands that set him up well at the net. Nick King, a sophomore at No. 4 singles, surprised all of us with his speed; he’s been hiding it. He played great and won handily in straight sets. Against Mt. Eden, we only played four matches and lost just one game in all of our matches. Mt. Eden has a good bunch of Staff Photos Arun Brahma and Monte Imburg (not pictured) had a 6-0, 6-0 win over El Cerrito’s best doubles team. Freshman Lucas Smolko continued his strong run of form, beating El Cerrito’s top player, 6-2, 6-3. kids there and I am glad they are working on their tennis,” added Landes. Piedmont now has one match left in its regular season, April 26 against Berkeley to determine the winner of the 2023 Western Alameda County Conference banner. Later this week, the team will send two singles and two doubles players to the WACC Individual Tournament at Chabot College in Hayward on Friday and Saturday, April 28-29. 6-1 over El Cerrito Smolko won his singles match at No. 1 in straight sets 6-3, 6-2 over Daniel Seo. At No. 2 singles, Breber lost a heated three-set match versus Jayden Baumacega by scores of 7-5, 1-6, 10-8. At No. 3, Pham won in straight sets but had a close first-set that went to a tiebreaker and a narrow second set, winning 7-6 (7-5), 6-4. At No. 4, King won easily, 6-1, 6-3. In doubles, Monte Imburg and Arun Brahma had a clean-sweep 6-0, 6-0 of the Gauchos top doubles duo. At No. 2 was Graham Alban and Willie Tenney, winning 6-4, 6-4. articles.text: Staff Photos Oliver Shafroth had two goals, four assists, and won 11 face-offs against Washington. It’s playoff season at Piedmont High, and the boys’ lacrosse team is leading the charge. The Highlanders will look to capture their sixth consecutive 2023 Western Alameda County Conference championship title after defeating Washington 16-7 on the road in Fremont on Monday, April 24. Piedmont will face rival Bishop O’Dowd in the championship game on Thursday, April 27. The game will be played at O’Dowd, which is hosting both the boys’ and girls’ title games. Earlier last month on March 17, Piedmont won 18-1. For Piedmont coach Al Yu, defeating Bishop O’Dowd is extra sweet. The Oakland school overlooked Yu for its head coaching job prior to his arrival at PHS as an assistant in 2021.Yu’s wife, Monica, coaches BOD’s girls’ team, which is the No. 1 seed, and both of his daughters are on the team. His son, Theo, plays for O’Dowd and is an assistant coach. The Highlanders will walk into the championship game as a heavy favorite. Piedmont may have its best opportunity to claim its second Division 2 North Coast Section title since 2019. NCS playoffs start on Tuesday, May 2 with the championship game scheduled for Thursday, May 11. 16-7 over Washington Piedmont led 7-1 by the end of the first quarter and didn’t allow a single goal in the second quarter to extend the deficit to 13-1 by halftime. The Highlanders were then able to kill clock and rotate bench players into the match. PHS added two goals in the third quarter and one more in the final going. Final stats: Nate Fredericks led the way with five goals. Rylan Nelson had three goals and two assists. Oliver Shafroth had two goals, four assists, and won 11 face-offs. Soren Dixon scored two goals, two assists, and recovered three loose balls. Timmy Kalamas scored twice. Jack Nelson had an individual goal, assist, and ground ball recovery. Andrew McLaughlin Soren Dixon scored two goals, made two assists, and recovered two ground balls in Piedmont’s 16-7 victory. had one goal, two loose balls, and won eight face-offs. Curtis Hohener had one assist and a ground ball. Quintin Shafroth scooped two loose balls. Goalie Gus Von Metzsch recorded seven saves. NEXT UP Piedmont (10-3 overall, 4-0 league) travels to Bishop O’Dowd for the WACC Championship game tomorrow, April 27, at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: Staff Photos Pitcher Miya Fujimoto had 11 strikeouts against St. Joseph. The PHS softball team team ended a seven-game skid on Wednesday, April 19, with a 9-3 defeat of St. Joseph at Witter Field. Nit the team continued to struggle after losing 23-4 to Castro Valley on Monday, April 24 in a game played In Piedmont. It was an impressive group of games for Leah Bell, recording five hits over the two-game span including a three-run homer over St. Joseph. It was also one of Miya Fujimoto’s best games on the mound with 11 strikeouts in a complete game victory over the Pilots. Fujimoto, the team’s former shortstop, has stepped in to fill the pitching void created by the graduation last year of Izzzy Epstein. 9-3 over St. Joseph Piedmont came out hot with five runs in the first inning and added one more in the bottom of the second. St. Joseph broke the shutout in the top of the fourth, but the Highlanders tacked on two more in the bottom half. The Pilots scored twice in the fifth inning, and the Highlanders scored once more in the sixth. In the bottom of the first Fujimoto led off by reaching first on a well-placed bunt. Mia Leggett then smacked a ground ball and reached first base on an error by the second baseman. With two runners on, Bell cracked a home run to center field. Morgan Hunt then drew a four-pitch walk, while Sa’mara Levi and Hailey Ronen also drew walks to load the bases. Caitlin Boothby then hit a high fly ball to right field, but the outfielder botched the catch, allowing Hunt and Levi to score at 5-0. In the second inning, Hunt hit a one-out single, followed by Levi reaching first on an error by the shortstop, sending Hunt to third. Gretchen Gerhardy then hit into a fielder’s choice to score Hunt for an RBI. In the fourth, Leggett led off by getting hit by a pitch and Hunt reached first on a bunt. With one-out, Levi hit into a fielder’s choice to bring in Leggett from third. Gerhardy then hit a double to score Levi, 8-1. PHS scored one more in the bottom of the sixth, starting with a single by Bell, who stole second and advanced to third on a wild throw into the outfield. Hunt then brought in Bell on a groundout to third. Final stats: Bell went 3-for-4 Leah Bell hit a three-run homer against St. Joseph and also was 2-for-3 with two RBIs against Castro Valley. with a home run, three RBIs and two runs scored. Hunt went 1-for-3 with an RBI and two runs scored. Levi went 1-for-3 with two runs scored, one walk, and an RBI. Gerhardy went 2-for-4 with two RBIs. Fujimoto went 1-for-3 with a run scored and a walk. On the mound Fujimoto pitched all seven innings with 11 strikeouts and two earned runs. 23-4 loss to Castro Valley Castro Valley put up 11 runs in the top of the second inning and eight in the third. Piedmont scored twice in the bottom-fourth, allowed four in the top-fifth, and scored twice in the bottom-of-the-fifth to end it by the 10-run rule. Final stats: Bell went 2-for-3 with a double, two RBIs, and one run scored. Levi went 1-for-2 with two RBIs. Fujimoto went 1-for-2 with two runs scored and a walk. Boothby went 1-for-2 with a run scored. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-8-1 overall, 0-6 league) hosts Berkeley today, April 26 at 4:00 p.m. and travels to Castro Valley on Friday, April 28. Freshman Sa’mara Levi scored two runs and an RBI against St. Joseph and had two RBIs in the win over Castro Valley.
articles.title: Piedmont bounces back with win over Pilots

articles.text: =Highlanders defeat Berkeley in semifinals at home Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team will return to the Western Alameda County Conference championship game after defeating Berkeley 11-9 in the semifinals at Witter Field on Tuesday, April 25. Piedmont did well to match up to a physical Yellowjackets team, tiring out the visiting side as the game wore on. “Our game plan was when we get the ball, we’re going to run through our plays. We know Berkeley is not a deep team and they got more tired as the game went on,” said PHS coach Carlton Chan. “In the second half the plays started to open up more.” Piedmont lost 13-12 to the Yellowjackets in last year’s league semifinals 13-12. “We decided in the second half to hold the ball and use our time. We know how physical Berkeley plays and you just have to get back up when you get fouled… That was so difficult last year to lose on our home field. It feels so much better this time around to earn our shot in the finals,” added senior Molly Ashton. The goal all along has been to reach the WACC Finals and square off with Bishop O’Dowd for the league crown, That rematch will take place this Friday, April 28 at the Dragons’ home field. Piedmont went into the league tournament as the No. 2 seed, and O’Dowd enters as the No. 1 seed. “We’re just going to press them. We want to come out quickly and with the same intensity like it was halftime. O’Dowd will be tricky, but I think we can come out with some new plays and catch them off guard. It’s a different game every time against O’Dowd,” said Ashton. PHS now holds an 8-5 overall record and is 5-1 in league. They are assured of being in the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs regardless of Friday’s result. 11-9 win vs. Berkeley Piedmont led 6-5 at halftime, and boosted it to 11-6 with 4:21 left in the game, but Berkeley finished with three unanswered goals to close it out 11-9. Berkeley opened with the game’s first two goals, but Chloe Graham got Piedmont on the board three minutes in, but the Yellowjackets went up 3-1 one minute later. Graham then scored with 17 minutes left in the first half, followed by Ashton with a wraparound goal 30 seconds later to knot it at 3-3. Piedmont then gained the lead with another goal by Ashton with 8:49 left. She scored one more with 6:56 left in the half. Berkeley tied the game with 5:55 left in the half with back-to-back goals, but Friedie Schickedanz fed Ashton for a goal with 7.9 seconds left to make it 6-5. In the second half after a few back-and-forth possessions, Berkeley scored on a shooting space opportunity with17:34 remaining to tie it at 6-6. But Piedmont then marched back to the front with five straight goals by Ashton with 15:02 left, Ruby Guzdar on a wraparound with 10:39 to go, Ashton fed Eleanor Lavin four minutes later, another Staff Photo Hailey Marshburn runs the ball upfield against Berkeley. Staff Photo Molly Ashton scored six goals against Berkeley and four on the win vs. Newark Memorial. wraparound by Ashton, and Guzdar with a low shot with 4:21 left. Berkeley scored with 3:01 left in the game and again with 2:17. Although the Yellowjackets won possession, Piedmont did well to force tough shots and kept BHS off of the board until 33.9 seconds were left to make it 11-9. No one scored from there. Final stats: Ashton scored six goals with one assist, one ground ball, and won one draw. Graham and Guzdar scored twice. Lavin scored once, recovered one loose ball, and won four loose balls. Schickedanz had three assists. Cole Luisa and Peyton Watson had one assist. Senior Night Piedmont hosted Senior Night on Wednesday, April 19 in a game with Newark Memorial, which resulted in a 19-2 win. PHS honored its five seniors: Ashton, Lavin. Lindsay Kottle, Sofia Johnson, and Holland Feinberg. Final stats: Ashton scored four goals, one assist, recovered two loose balls, and won one draw. Graham and Guzdar had two goals and one assist. Laurel Bentley also scored twice. Schickedanz had two goals and two assists. Johnson had a goal and two assists. Hailey Marshburn, Luisa, and Lavin scored once. NEXT UP Piedmont (8-5 overall, 5-1 league) heads to Bishop O’Dowd for the 2023 WACC Championship game this Friday, April 29 at 5:00 p.m. It will be a double-header game with Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team playing O’Dowd for the championship.
