Lindsay Kottle, Sofia Johnson, and Holland Feinberg. Final stats: Ashton scored four goals, one assist, recovered two loose balls, and won one draw. Graham and Guzdar had two goals and one assist. Laurel Bentley also scored twice. Schickedanz had two goals and two assists. Johnson had a goal and two assists. Hailey Marshburn, Luisa, and Lavin scored once. NEXT UP Piedmont (8-5 overall, 5-1 league) heads to Bishop O’Dowd for the 2023 WACC Championship game this Friday, April 29 at 5:00 p.m. It will be a double-header game with Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team playing O’Dowd for the championship. Piedmont bounces back with win over Pilots Staff Photos Pitcher Miya Fujimoto had 11 strikeouts against St. Joseph. By Jonathan Comeaux The PHS softball team team ended a seven-game skid on Wednesday, April 19, with a 9-3 defeat of St. Joseph at Witter Field. Nit the team continued to struggle after losing 23-4 to Castro Valley on Monday, April 24 in a game played In Piedmont. It was an impressive group of games for Leah Bell, recording five hits over the two-game span including a three-run homer over St. Joseph. It was also one of Miya Fujimoto’s best games on the mound with 11 strikeouts in a complete game victory over the Pilots. Fujimoto, the team’s former shortstop, has stepped in to fill the pitching void created by the graduation last year of Izzzy Epstein. 9-3 over St. Joseph Piedmont came out hot with five runs in the first inning and added one more in the bottom of the second. St. Joseph broke the shutout in the top of the fourth, but the Highlanders tacked on two more in the bottom half. The Pilots scored twice in the fifth inning, and the Highlanders scored once more in the sixth. In the bottom of the first Fujimoto led off by reaching first on a well-placed bunt. Mia Leggett then smacked a ground ball and reached first base on an error by the second baseman. With two runners on, Bell cracked a home run to center field. Morgan Hunt then drew a four-pitch walk, while Sa’mara Levi and Hailey Ronen also drew walks to load the bases. Caitlin Boothby then hit a high fly ball to right field, but the outfielder botched the catch, allowing Hunt and Levi to score at 5-0. In the second inning, Hunt hit a one-out single, followed by Levi reaching first on an error by the shortstop, sending Hunt to third. Gretchen Gerhardy then hit into a fielder’s choice to score Hunt for an RBI. In the fourth, Leggett led off by getting hit by a pitch and Hunt reached first on a bunt. With one-out, Levi hit into a fielder’s choice to bring in Leggett from third. Gerhardy then hit a double to score Levi, 8-1. PHS scored one more in the bottom of the sixth, starting with a single by Bell, who stole second and advanced to third on a wild throw into the outfield. Hunt then brought in Bell on a groundout to third. Final stats: Bell went 3-for-4 Leah Bell hit a three-run homer against St. Joseph and also was 2-for-3 with two RBIs against Castro Valley. with a home run, three RBIs and two runs scored. Hunt went 1-for-3 with an RBI and two runs scored. Levi went 1-for-3 with two runs scored, one walk, and an RBI. Gerhardy went 2-for-4 with two RBIs. Fujimoto went 1-for-3 with a run scored and a walk. On the mound Fujimoto pitched all seven innings with 11 strikeouts and two earned runs. 23-4 loss to Castro Valley Castro Valley put up 11 runs in the top of the second inning and eight in the third. Piedmont scored twice in the bottom-fourth, allowed four in the top-fifth, and scored twice in the bottom-of-the-fifth to end it by the 10-run rule. Final stats: Bell went 2-for-3 with a double, two RBIs, and one run scored. Levi went 1-for-2 with two RBIs. Fujimoto went 1-for-2 with two runs scored and a walk. Boothby went 1-for-2 with a run scored. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-8-1 overall, 0-6 league) hosts Berkeley today, April 26 at 4:00 p.m. and travels to Castro Valley on Friday, April 28. Freshman Sa’mara Levi scored two runs and an RBI against St. Joseph and had two RBIs in the win over Castro Valley.

articles.text: Piedmont honored its seven seniors on Senior Night: Owen Kelly (left), Eric Olaru-Hagen, James MaNguyen, Wilson Wong, Brayden Day, Jonas Kra-Caskey, and Kai Lambert. Piedmont High’s boys’ volleyball team split its last two league matches since its return from Spring Break, sweeping Alameda 3-0 on Thursday, April 20 at Binks Rawlings Gym, but losing 3-0 the following day to eventual Western Alameda County Conference champion Bishop O’Dowd, also at home. Thursday’s win was a perfect response to their previous appearance against Alameda, which the Hornets won 3-0 by scores of 25-17, 25-23, and 25-22. “It was a great performance, we had three days of practice to prepare for this game specifically. We played Alameda a couple of weeks ago and they beat us 3-0, so we worked on a lot of strategic things in practice and they applied it. We took away angles for specific players and the line from specific players,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. The pair of matches brings the school’s record to 12-6 overall and 8-5 in league. With just one match left in the regular season, today at Berkeley, Piedmont is getting set for its second consecutive appearance in the North Coast Section playoffs. “We love playing at home. We possibly get another game here with NCS and we want to just ball-out… I think we need more trick plays; we love ours ones-and-twos, but sometimes defenses can read them. We have to work on more things that keeps teams off guard,” added senior Brayden Day. Junior outside hitter John Champion had a strong game against Alameda, gaining the match-winning kill in the third game. He’s been on the mend from a lingering ankle injury and feels more capable of reaching his peak. “I’m feeling good, I really got to rest my ankle over spring break. Specifically for this game, we were working on communication drills and out-of-system plays, and that came in clutch. But I’m feeling so much better; I can jump as high as I want. Once I’m up there, I can swing to wherever I want and hit my targets,” said Champion. PHS honored its seven seniors on the roster prior to Friday’s match against O’Dowd: Owen Kelly, Eric Olaru-Hagen, James MaNguyen, Wilson Wong, Brayden Day, Jonas Kra-Caskey, and Kai Lambert. 3-0 over Alameda Piedmont swept the Hornets with the final two games going to 26 points, winning by scores of 25-21, 26-24 and 26-24. It was an exciting second and third game with multiple lead changes all the way to the finish. In the second game, Alameda gained the lead and went ahead 11-8, but PHS scored seven straight points to lead 15-11. The two teams traded points until Alameda eventually held gamepoint at 24-21. But from there, Champion spiked a pair of kills and then a defensive error by AHS tied it at 24-24. #4 put the Highlanders ahead with an ace, followed by MaNguyen finishing the game with a winning spike. Piedmont opened the third game with a 9-3 lead, but the Hornets rallied to take an 11-10 lead and continued its advantage to 18-14. The Highlanders eventually tied the match three times before going ahead 21-20, but the Hornets got back to the front to gain game-point, once again, at 24-23. However, MaNguyen slammed down another powerful kill and an Alameda offensive error gave PHS the 25-24 lead. Champion had the winning kill for the 26-24 victory. Final stats were not provided. 3-0 loss to Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont lost in three straight games, falling by scores of 25-13, 25-16, 25-17. The Dragons have a strong team this year and are undefeated in league at 12-0 (26-2 overall), They are the defending WACC champions. Final stats were not provided. NEXT UP Piedmont (12-6 overall, 8-5 league) plays its regular season finale at Berkeley today, April 26, at 5:30 p.m. The first round of the Division 3 NCS playoffs is set for Tuesday, May 2 with the rankings and draw released on Sunday, April 30.

articles.text: Jasper Schuetz wins Freshman Div. 1 race Photo by Jane Lin Jasper Schuetz (middle) won his fourth Freshman D1 race of the spring mountain bike season. The Piedmont Mountain Bike team recently competed at the Six Sigma Slinger in Lower Lake on Sunday, April 16. It marked the last race of the team’s regular season before the NorCal Championship on Saturday and Sunday, May 6-7 at the same location. The Six Sigma Slinger featured a 4.5 miles course with an elevation gain of 575 feet. It was another big day for Piedmont High freshman Jasper Schuetz, who won the Div. 1 Freshman race with a two-lap time of 36:02.81, edging the nextbest rider, Alexander Tudor of Salinas, by 0.28 of a second. He has now won all four of his appearances this season and is likely going into the NorCal Championship as a favorite among freshman riders. In the varsity boys’ category, Andres Roberts finished 15th of 29 riders in the four-lap race. Aleksi Valkonen was 27th in 1:24:09. In the Junior Varsity Boys’ Div. 1 category, Mark Hsia was 14th of 74 riders with a three-lap time of 59:01.21. Close behind was Max Rivera in 17th, Matteo Scanu in 19th, and Schuyler Sawicki, 21st, Artun Duransoy was 43rd. In the Sophomore Boys’’ D1 event, Cary Ward finished 32nd. Caleb Canada was 34th and Asher Villareal was 37th. NEXT UP The Piedmont Mountain Bike team will compete in the NorCal Championship on Saturday and Sunday, May 6-7 at Stix Sigma Ranch in Lower Lake. Photo by Jane Lin Mark Hsia was 14th of 74 in the junior varsity D1 race.

articles.text: PHS honored its seniors on Senior Night against Berkeley: Simon Lins, Charlie White, Ryan Stokes, Odessa Dando, and Annika Nilsson, Not pictured: Farris Saffouri and Hamza Mahmood. Piedmont High’s swim team raced its final regular season meet on Friday, April 21 at Berkeley, where the Highlanders honored the seven seniors on the roster. PHS now prepares for the Western Alameda County Conference Championship Meet at Chabot College in Hayward on Friday, April 28. In its dual meet with Berkeley, Piedmont’s boys’ team tied Berkeley 85-85 while the girls’ team suffered its only loss of the season, falling 94-76. The girls close the spring 6-1 overall. Piedmont’s only diver, junior Nina Schwab, also competed in a league meet on Tuesday, April 18, winning her event with a score of 227 over the course of six dive attempts. Piedmont’s boys’ and girls’ relay teams finished their season undefeated in all three their events, the 200 Individual Medley, 200 Freestyle, and 400 Freestyle. The varsity girls’ relay team is led by juniors Taylor Rolefson and Josie Oesterer, sophomore Sonja ten Grotehnuis, and freshmen Abigail Jacoby and Sydney Olson rotated spots. Against Berkeley, Jacoby raced with Rolefson, Oesterer, and ten Grotenhuis to win the 200 IM with an North Coast Section consideration time of 1:56.73. They also won the 200 Free relay in 1:47.01 for another NCS consideration time. Rolefson won two individual events, the 50 freestyle with a NCS consideration time of 25.35, and the 100 Free in 56.65, which was another NCS consideration time. Oesterer won the 100 backstroke with an NCS consideration time of 1:01.46, and placed second in 100 Free in 57.84. Ten Grotenhuis also won the 200 Free with a time of 2:09.41. Freshman Sydney Olson finishing second in the 100 butterfly in 1:09.89; classPiedmont’s girls relay team finished the season undefeated. Pictured are Sydney Olson (left), Sonja ten Grotenguis, Taylor Rolefson, and Josie Oesterer. mate Abigail Jacoby was second in the 100 Breast in 1:17.96, and third in the 200 Individual Medley in 2:23.68. Sophomore Tyler Dacanay was third in the 100 Fly with a time of 1:10. The boys’ relay team of Dimitri Secor, Ryan Stokes, Nick Costello and Tom Rolefson won the 200 IM relay in 1:48.09, an NCS consideration time. They also won the 200 Free in 1:37.77 for another NCS consideration time. Tom Rolefson won two individual events, the 50 Free with a time of 23.33, and the 100 Free with a time of 52.70. Nik Costello also won two events, claiming the 100 Fly in 58.79, and the exhaustive 500 Free with a time of 5:15.56. Secor won the 200 Individual Medley in 2:10.68, and was second in 100 Back in 58.56. Sophomore Evan Byun won the 100 breaststroke, clocking a time of 1:05.75. He was also second in the 200 Free, 2:01.11. Ryan Stokes finished second in 100 Breast in 1:08.31 and third in the 100 Fly in 1:02.63, and sophomore Simon March-Cunningham finished third in the 500 Free in 5:50.25 to gain valuable points for his team. Girls vs. Alameda & Encinal On April 6, Piedmont’s girls’ team was victorious in a its meets with Alameda and Encinal at the Encinal pool. The girls’ relay team of Rolefson, Oesterer, ten Grotenhuis and Olson continued their perfect record. They won the 200 freestyle relay with an NCS consideration time of 1:46.36, and won the 400 Free relay in 3:55.24, picking up another NCS consideration time. Rolefson achieved two NCS consideration times, winning the 200 Free in 2:03.24 and 100 Free in 56.67. Oesterer also won two events, the 200 IM in 2:20.77, and 100 Back with an NCS consideration time of 1:00.42. NEXT UP Piedmont heads to Chabot College in Hayward this weekend for the 2023 WACC Championship Meet on Friday, April 28. Races start at 10:00 a.m.

articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team lost two games to Bishop O’Dowd last week, losing 5-1 on Wednesday, April 19, and 5-0 in a home game at Humphries Diamond on Friday, April 21. PHS also took a 7-2 loss to non-league St. Mary’s on Saturday, April 22 at home. In the 5-1 loss to O’Dowd, the Highlanders went an extra inning into the bottom-of-the-eighth in a 1-1 deadlock, but the Dragons smacked a grand slam to end it. During the game, infielder/ pitcher Michael Aikawa suffered an ankle injury when sliding into base, and he was unable to play the following game. He’s expected to be fine going forward, but his injury left the Highlanders without a key player on Friday. During the game, senior Ryan McConathy was controversially ejected after the umpire ruled the senior purposely made contact with O’Dowd’s first baseman on a run to first. It altered the game with McConathy preparing to enter as a reliever in the bottom of the seventh. Piedmont quickly appealed the ejection with video evidence showing no wrong-doing by McConathy. Nonetheless, he was forced to miss Friday’s rematch due to the North Coast Section office being closed. “Losing Mike and Ryan is a tough blow, but Brandon Dicke played great and Ellis Moss pitched great. It was just one of those days that went their way. Their pitcher did a great job,” said PHS coach Eric Olson. The loss marked Piedmont’s fourth in a row going back to a loss to Alameda prior to spring break on April 6. The batch of games brings Piedmont’s record to 8-8 overall and 2-4 against Foothill Division opponents in the Western Alameda County Conference. articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre’s newest play, Poor Yella Rednecks: Vietgone 2, will be performed on stage through May 7. Written by Qui Nguyen, is a sequel to the popular Vietgone which premiered at San Francisco’s Strand Theater five years ago. The current show is is part two in Nguyen’s trilogy. The play follows a Vietnamese family that left war-torn Saigon for rural Arkansas, set in the 1970’s. Married couple Tong and Quang encounter challenges in their new home: namely the reality that their low-wage jobs don’t allow many luxuries, and their son is struggling to keep up with his peers as he tries to learn a new language. “This story goes deep while soaring high,” said ACT Artistic Director Pam MacKinnon. “It’s a personal exploration of the American Dream specific to a Vietnamese immigrant family and first-generation American experience, full of compromise, joy, hardscrabble setback, and love.” “I’m thrilled to be back in San Francisco at one of my favorite theaters in the country,” said director Jaime Castañeda. “This sequel to Vietgone promises to be just as exciting. Qui’s words will make you want to laugh and dance at the same time,”. The cast includes Will Dao, Christine Jamlig, Hyunmin Rhee, Jomar Tagatac and Jenny Nguyen Nelson. To purchase tickets or for more information, visit https://www. act-sf.org/whats-on/202223-season/poor-yella-rednecks-vietgone-2/. articles.text: Oversize Renaissance palaces, over some dozen, danced scenes played out on dual tiers. An oversize pit orchestra for the eloquent Prokofieff music, the most majestic ballet score of the 20th century, stamping this as the preeminent evening-length achievement of the post-Tchaikovsky era. All this and a massive cast set opulently in Shakespeare’s Verona. Can anything top this ballet for sheer performance power resonating with romanticism? And the feel of a lavish city state from half a millennium ago, with enough period costumes for half a dozen Italian masked balls. In the end, it comes down to the touching tragedy of Juliet who – sorry, Romeo –plays through three distinct phases of life. She ends up dead on her bier, fans crying in their beer, and she breaks every heart in the house. This is a “Romeo and Juliet” ballet to die for, a three-act spectacle and farewell message from the departed Helgi Tomasson and the late designer Jens-Jacob Worsaae in his final masterpiece, created at SF Ballet in 1994. The San Francisco Ballet put it all together for the April 21 opening, with a heroine from the lower ranks emerging, like some forgotten waif, to save the day in the role of Juliet. Tapped for the opener’s cast was a mere soloist, Jasmine Jimison of Palo Alto, with a colossal assignment given the competition of international artists on the SF Ballet roster. If Jasmine is not promoted to principal before the day is out, I’ll eat my Renaissance chapeau. On this very stage where Margot Fonteyn once ruled, this novice tackled the most baffling of all solo challenges in her long Indecision Scene, where acting must triumph over mere dancing. Like the proverbial cat on a hot tin roof, she vacillates, despairs, gravitates and zigzags with her quandary, close to madness: Face the parental orders to marry the bland suitor Paris, or risk possible death by taking the risky draught given her by the benevolent friar turned medicine-man Laurence. (Aficionados will recognize her telltale transition of letting down the long hair, usually verging on some mad scene, as Jimison had already demonstrated Photo by Lindsay Thomas Jasmine Jimison and Angelo Greco in Helgi Tomasson’s Romeo & Juliet in San Francisco Ballet’s current production. playing Giselle this winter.) Tearing around the stage like a trapped wild animal, she shows a rare ferocity, stamping her rare and too-long-overlooked talent. The young artist paired beautifully with the Romeo of Angelo Greco, a good-looking Italian-born matinee-idol type who on any other night might have stolen the show with his skyward leaps, whipping turns, and ferocious fencing to boot. He stands heroic among the five cadavers littering this drama, descending into an unforgettable love-death of a beloved doomed couple, deeply etched in memory after the last curtain. The stunning cast this night featured Luke Ingram as the murderous Tybalt, Esteban Hernández as the ill-fated cutup Mercutio, and the veteran Jim Sohm as the mortar-and-pestle Laurence. Casts change nightly. The oversize orchestra under Martin West was formidable, with the drama of unbridled French horns as well as an alto saxophone so popular in the East. And the lady next to us was ecstatic over the bright multicolor costumes for the huge cast. Last but not least, the most heated or elaborate of sword-fighting scenes were realistically done by Marco Pistone. BALLET NOTES Past performances of “R&J” on this very stage include the fabled mid-1960s pairing of Margot Fonteyn and Rudolf Nureyev, stars apprehended by the S.F. police after a show for attending a pot party, thereby upstaging their on-stage proficiency. In the 1970s Michael Smuin choreographed the world’s only Romeo and Juliet without the mandatory Balcony Scene, which contains one of the most romantic duos in all ballet, all because of production delays at the SFB. Later performances made up for it. A dispute over a possible happy ending, among other things, forced the original “R&J” ballet premiere to be shunting off to the capital of Moravia in 1938 before becoming a mainstay of Soviet ballet companies/ Sunday we learned of the shocking departure, after only one year, of SF Ballet exec director Danielle St. Germain, which 24 hours later the troupe was still unable to confirm. HELGI TOMASSON’S ROMEO AND JULIET with the S.F. Ballet, after Shakespeare, April 21-30, Opera House, San Francisco. articles.text: Piedmont Center for the Arts will display a rare exhibit of the photos of the late Bay Area photographer James Mayer taken in Prague, Czechoslovakia the day the country was invaded by the Soviet Union in 1968. Mayer was a student traveling in Europe in 1968 and was in Prague on August 21, 1968. when Soviet tanks entered the streets of the country’s capital. He managed to document the action and get himself and his pictures out of the country. This is the first public exhibition of these stunning photos, strikingly familiar to the war in Ukraine today. His widow, Jane Flint, invites community members to a reception at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue, on Friday, April 28 from 6:00 to 8:00 p.m. The exhibit will also be open to the public on Saturday and Sunday, April 29-30 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Background of Jim Mayer Jim Mayer graduated from Antioch College in Ohio, where his interest in photography (and motorcycles) grew and expanded to include proficiency in video and film. In his senior year abroad he happened to be in Prague, Czechoslovakia when the USSR invaded. He managed to get himself and the photographs of that event out to the Liberation News Service and the Los Angeles Free Press, which were the first to have footage of the invasion. After graduating, he moved to San Francisco and participated in Project One anchored by a organizations, including Optic Nerve, a photography collective co-founded by Mayer. Jim and Bill Bradbury introduced the group to the SONY Portapak, the first generation of portable video recorders that was instrumental in what came to be known as the Guerrilla Television Movement. Optic Nerve created several early documentaries that were among the first independently produced video documentaries to be broadcast on Public Television. In the late 60’s and early 70’s he studied Shaolin Kung-Fu and Lien-Ying style t’ai chi ch’uan at 5 a.m. in Portsmouth Square Park in San Francisco Chinatown. During the 70’s, he was employed at Xerox PARC in Palo Alto as a video specialist, documenting the many innovations developed at that time. In 1979, Jim, with Steve Christiansen and Lynn Adler, co-produced and directed Salmon On the Run, a documentary on competition between First People, sport fishers, and commercial fishers for the right to fish for Pacific salmon. The show was aired on the PBS science series NOVA. In 1980, Jim, with Optic Nerve A Soviet tank is surrounded by Czech citizens after Prague was invaded on August 21, 1968. Bay Area photographer Jim Mayer at Sutro Heights in San Francisco in 1988 members John Rogers and Lynn Adler, formed Ideas In Motion, continuing the ideals of Optic Nerve within a sustainable financial structure. For 40 years, Jim and his partners created documentaries, sponsored video, and commissioned work, addressing social issues and celebrating the creative spirit. In recent years he also spearheaded a series of videos on the intricacies of complicated watchmaking in Switzerland. He was fully in his element in a breakneck production schedule, doing the work he loved, whether in the ateliers of Le Brassus, or under the streets of Queens. Since its founding, Ideas In Motion provided pro bono video services for Bay Area arts organizations, including the Pickle Family Circus and the San Francisco Mime Troupe. Amazingly, he still found time to restore a MK II 3.8 Jaguar, study Russian Constructivist art and experimental cinema, read extensively on WW2 espionage, develop a good knowledge of French wine and Scotch whiskey, cook, garden, and in later life even took up the clarinet, playing with the Musicians’ Action Group of Berkeley and marching with them in the May Day Parade in Paris in 2016 with a host of other international political action bands. articles.title: Exclusive photos of 1968 invasion of Prague at Piedmont Center for the Arts this weekend

articles.text: Paper Bag Thoughts & Conversations, a mixed media art exhibit with the work of Oakland native Marvin McMillian, opens Friday, May 5 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts with a reception at 6 p.m. A former student at both CCAC and the Academy of Art in SF, his work consists of a retrospective of conversations, childhood memories, family traditions, food, music, historical events, and sports. Gallery hours will be from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays for the next four weekends. Harriet T, mixed media, 24x48. In 2016, it was publicly announced that Harriet Tubman would be featured on the $20 bill. Tubman would be the first woman and Black American to be on a U.S. denomination. The production was halted. To pay homage to her, Marvin McMillian created a rendition of what the future bill could look like.
articles.title: Marvin McMillian art exhibit opens May 5 at PCA

articles.text: Angela Davis: Seize the Time, an exhibition celebrating the political activist, is on display at the Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) now through June 11. Born In Birmingham, Alabama in 1944, Davis is best known as an African American activist and educator who championed civil rights and other social issues, from racial equity to women’s rights and lesbian, gay and transgender rights. She has written Women and Race & Class, Are Prisons Obsolete?, Abolition Democracy, and The Meaning of Freedom. Davis was a professor at the UC Santa Cruz, where she taught courses on the history of consciousness. She retired in 2008. Political activist Angela Davis The exhibition was organized by OMCA in partnership with the Zimmerli Art Museum at Rutgers University, and features photographs and personal entries from the Angela Davis Archive in Oakland. To learn more and purchase museum tickets, visit https:// museumca.org/on-view/angeladavis-seize-the-time/. articles.text: Aurora Theatre is now showing Cyrano onstage through May 7. Based upon the story of Cyrano de Bergerac, written by Edmond Rostand in 1897, the current adaptation is directed by Aurora Theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello. It is a classic tale of Cyrano, who is fearless in battle and swordplay but shy in confronting Roxanne, the woman he loves. Ashamed of his appearance (an oversize nose), he enlists the help of Christian, who has a pretty face but lacks the gift of gab. Costello turns the odd love triangle into an intimate play of life and love. The cast includes William Thomas Hodgson as Cyrano, Leontyne Mbele-Mbong as Roxanne, and Ron Campbell, Adrian Roberts and Steven Flores. Post-show discussions will be held on April 26 and May 4, moderated by Associate Artistic Director Dawn Monique Williams. Visit https://www.auroratheatre.org for showtimes and to purchase tickets. A unanimous decision is not required. • Formula number one: Technique+ personality = artistry • Formula number two: Technique+torque = success My wife’s birthday celebration gave us the perfect excuse to take in a concert of the Monterey Symphony over the weekend. articles.text: Treasure Island Museum welcomes organist Jerry Nagano for an afternoon concert of Hammond organ music on May 13. The lobby of the museum’s historic Building One will host the event, which showcases music that was popular during the 1950’s - 1970’s when the Treasure Island Naval Station was active. During that period, the Island’s Officers’ Club featured a family-friendly, Sunday dinner with organ music, often performed by local performer “Kay” Catherine Rooney. The organ which will be played by Nagano is the same organ that Rooney would play. The organ was donated for the event by Rooney’s niece Chris Weicher. The concert begins at 2 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https:// www.treasureislandmuseum.org/ event-details/organ-concert-withjerry-nagano-at-treasure-islandmuseum.

articles.text: Free concerts in Stern Grove return to San Francisco in June for the 86th season. Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization whose mission is “to make live musical experiences accessible to all.” Since its inception in 1938, the organization has presented the free concert series “Stern Grove Festival” in Sigmund Stern Grove, an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. To view the full lineup, visit https://www.sterngrove. org/86th-concert-season.

In addition to being a fine conductor, he also is a very good public speaker. His musical demeanor on the stage is vigorous and convincing. We are lucky to have so many orchestras in our area. I encourage all music lovers to attend these regional orchestras and receive great musical gratification in return. Returning to my musical equations. You can decide if batting 1000 is the way to go or if you prefer the refinement of the game. It’s fun being the judge and the jury. Aurora Theatre’s Cyrano playing now through May 7 By Allyson Aleksey Aurora Theatre is now showing Cyrano onstage through May 7. Based upon the story of Cyrano de Bergerac, written by Edmond Rostand in 1897, the current adaptation is directed by Aurora Theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello. It is a classic tale of Cyrano, who is fearless in battle and swordplay but shy in confronting Roxanne, the woman he loves. Ashamed of his appearance (an oversize nose), he enlists the help of Christian, who has a pretty face but lacks the gift of gab. articles.text: The Piedmont Chamber Orchestra returns to the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, May 7 to celebrate spring and youth, with 13-yearold soloist Madison Lee featured performing a movement from Antonio Vivaldi’s Concert in G No. 3, composed for the female students under Vivaldi’s tutelage at a Venetian orphanage. Also on the program is Haydn’s Symphony No. 22, written by the young composer early in his service to the Esterhazy family of Hungary, and Franz Schubert’s Symphony No. 5, composed when he was 19. The Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, the city’s homegrown classical music organization, has thrilled local audiences at every performance in its five-year existence. As always, admission is free, and the concert is followed by an open reception. Doors open at 2:30 p.m. with the concert to begin at 3:00 p.m.

articles.text: Come enjoy a range of exhibits and performances at Piedmont Center for the Arts this Spring. Friday, April 28, 6:00 p.m. James Mayer Photo Exhibit Before the days of I-Phones and YouTube, photographer Jim Mayer was a student travelling in Europe in 1968. He found himself in Prague the day the Russians invaded. He managed to document the action and get himself and his pictures out of the country. This is the first exhibition of these stunning photos, strikingly familiar given the war in Ukraine today. Jim’s widow, Jane Flint, invites the public to a community reception in memory of her late husband, who passed away last year. The photo exhibit will also be open Saturday and Sunday from 11 am to 2 pm. Free and open to all. Friday, May 5, 6:00 p.m. Marvin McMillian II Fine Art Paper Bag Thoughts & Conversations: a mixed media solo show featuring the work of an Oakland native and student at both CCAC and the Academy of Art in SF, consists of a retrospective of conversations, childhood memories, family traditions, food, music, historical events, and sports. This collection of original works opens with a reception from 6 to 8 pm Friday evening and will continue with Gallery Hours from 11 am to 2 pm Saturdays and Sundays for the next four weekends. Saturday, May 6, 7:30 p.m. Barry Fischer Comedy Revue Something Humorous in Piedmont, an unexpectedly funny comedy variety show, will include stand-up comics Barry Fischer, Ashley Monique, Marcus Williams, & Jackie Keliiaa joined by The Right Now Improv Trio; David Steinberg, multi-instrumentalist musician; and Claire Neumann, a PHS grad and Broadway actress, doing musical comedy. The event opens with a brief reception at 7 p.m. and the laughter starts at 7:30. Discounted advance tickets at https:// bit.ly/3FXfDTA. Almost sold out. Sunday, May 7, 3:00 p.m. Piedmont Chamber Orchestra The twenty-three musicians of the homegrown Piedmont Chamber Orchestra return to PCA to present a concert titled Celebrating Spring with the Music of Youth. Light refreshments will be available following the concert. The orchestra will perform music composed at young ages by Franz Haydn, Antonio Vivaldi, and Franz Schubert, and will feature a teenaged violin soloist Madison Lee. Free concert – open to all. Sunday, May 7, 7:00 p.m. In the Tradition Piano Trio In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Rich Trevor, and Anthony Pegram – will perform a Cinco de Mayo Tribute to Mexican Composers. This concert will be loaded with music written by composers from south of our border as well as jazz and blues favorites and other classics. Advance tickets are $23 at https://bpt.me/5691334, or $25 at the door. Seating is limited to the first 70 attendees. articles.text: An assortment of Bay Area comedians and diverse comedy formats will be converging on Saturday, May 6 at Piedmont Center for the Arts for the inaugural production of “Something Humorous,” a variety show organized and hosted by Piedmont-based comedian Barry Fischer. Headlining the night will be “The Right Now,” an acclaimed three-woman group of free-form improv blending highly physical short vignettes with longer character-driven scenes. Group members Claire Slattery, Fontana Butterfield, and Mariah Howard play across gender, genre, and form, and are known for their fast-paced wit and seamless transitions. The trio has delighted crowds across a range of prestigious stages, including the San Francisco Improv Festival, SF Sketchfest, Out of Bounds Comedy Festival in Austin, and Blast Theater Festival in Berkeley. Piedmont High alumna and actress Claire Neumann will offer a high-energy dose of comedic musical theater. While at PHS in the early 2000s, Claire twice won the Bird Calling Contest. After graduating from Northwestern University, she became a professional actress and starred in a number of major productions. She’s taken on notable roles in the National Tour of Charlie and The Chocolate Factory, Baghdaddy (a NYTimes’ Critic’s pick and musical about the Iraq War), and the acclaimed Off-Broadway musical Triassic Parq (in which Claire played a dinosaur exploring their gender identity). She was also nominated for Best Actress for her portrayal of Annie Oakley in Annie Get Your Gun and Nellie in Floyd Collins at the Weathervane Theatre. Three other local stand-up comedians and Bay Area music veteran David Steinberg will round out the show. Performance time is 7:30 p.m. on Saturday, May 6, preceded by an outdoor reception on the lawn at 7 p.m. A limited number of tickets remain and are available at www.somethinghumorous.com.
articles.title: Improv trio to headline May 6 comedy show at PCA

articles.text: Tickets for Festival Napa Valley are on sale now. Now in its 17th season, the highly regarded music festival takes place in iconic Napa Valley locations and kicks off July 8 with a gourmet chef-inspired dinner and performance by Jennifer Grim. Grim has performed as a flutist with Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center, St. Luke’s Chamber Ensemble, Zéphyros Winds, and the New York Chamber Soloists. She also serves as principal flute of the Mostly Mozart Orchestra of New York. Proceeds from the evening benefit scholarships for women and girls in the arts and arts education. The festival will be headlined by Grammy-award winning country singer Carrie Underwood and will includes a variety of chamber music ensembles and soloists. “Whatever we put on stage, we want to make sure it’s the best of the best,” said Festival Napa Valley co-founder Charles Letourneau. “We try to balance a variety of genres, artists and programs so that we put together an experience that people will remember forever.” For a list of all programs and performances and to purchase tickets, visit https://festivalnapavalley.org/2023-summer-season/ quick-look/ Festival Napa Valley

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, Aprl 26, 2023 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Plenty to think about in Clouds of Sils Maria By Chris Honore’ The title, Clouds of Sils Maria, is a metaphor. Sils Maria is a mountain range surrounding the Engadine Valley in the Swiss Alps, known for its ethereal cloud formations that slide out of the mountains like a long snake and move inextricably closer to a glacial lake and village. It portends the coming of bad weather. The film opens with Maria Enders (Juliette Binoche), renowned actress, and her assistant, Valentine (Kristen Stewart), on a train heading toward Zurich for a celebratory dinner to be held in honor of her mentor, famous playwright and filmmaker, Wilhelm Melchior. While en route, Maria learns that Melchior has died of a heart attack and suddenly the dinner and anticipated award becomes a eulogy. She also meets in Zurich a highly regarded young director who wants her to agree to do a play, Majola Snake, written and produced by Mechior some 20 tears earlier, and one in which Maria starred as a young unknown actor. The role launched her career. Instead of playing the youthful ingénue (her original role), she will play the older woman, a role about which she feels great uncertainty. An American starlet, Jo-Ann Ellis, (Chloe Grace Juliet Binoche and Kristen Stewart in Clouds of Sils Maria Moretz), who relishes scandal, has been cast as the seductive, manipulating young woman. Maria, for all of her fame, is a woman in midlife crisis, going through a divorce. She is reluctant to fully acknowledge that her youth, and all its allure, is now part of her past. She is, after countless films, someone else. And so she and Valentine retreat to Melchior’s Swiss chalet near Sils Maria where they will rehearse the lines to the play while discussing the characters, especially the older woman that Maria will try to inhabit. Clouds is a film carried by dialogue – lots of dialogue. Val and Maria discuss, spar, argue, drink too much and talk some more. Their relationship bluntly mirrors the play and often it is difficult to know if the encounters they are having are part of the play or simply a harsh and confrontational conversation. While the film has moments that are interesting, and Binoche is clearly a an enormously gifted performer, the narrative seems stilted and even uninteresting. It can feel inaccessible and obscure. As Maria and Val slip from scene to scene, dinner, breakfast, rehearsal, lunch, it can all seem flat, making it difficult to care about the characters. Yes, the point made over and over is that art and life can merge as boundaries fall away. What is fact and what is fiction? But for “Clouds” to touch the audience it must reach for more, for an intimacy, for clarity, for depth as well as breadth, which it fails to do. Binoche is courageous and the camera often lingers on her mature, stunning beauty. Stewart, though reaping much praise for her portrayal as Maria’s bright factotum, seems to have only one gear and that is Stewart doing Stewart. She fidgets, smokes, and debates pop culture and pop movies with Maria and still sounds like a quasi-rebellious teenager whose life experiences remain truncated. But then so much of this movie feels the same way: still unformed, even purposely ambiguous. Clouds of Sils Maria . Directed by Oliver Assayas. Starring Juliet Binoche, Kristen Stewart and Chloe Grace Moretz. 2 hrs., 3 min. Rated R. Released 2015. Streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv. articles.text: The character Astro Boy was created in 1951 by the celebrated animator of Japanese manga (comic books), Osamu Tezuka. In the 1960s, Astro, originally known as Tetsuwan Atomu (Mighty Atom), appeared in a popular television show, viewed in more than 40 countries, and now Astro makes his debut in a feature film. For children today, Astro Boy will be new and fresh. They will be captivated by the story and the nonstop action. This first installment explains how a young boy, Toby (Freddy Highmore), is killed in an experiment conducted by his scientist father, Dr. Tenma (Nicolas Cage). Wracked with grief and guilt, Tenma creates an exact replica of his son, a small android, giving him all of Toby’s memories and a heart of “blue power” which makes the boy (soon to be called Astro) superhuman. He can fly, has machine guns in his butt, x-ray vision, amazing strength, and rockets in his shoes and hands. articles.text: The arrival of extra-terrestrials on earth has been a staple of science fiction filmmaking since celluloid clicked through a theater camera, casting grainy images on a large white screen. More often than not, the intentions of the visitors are malevolent and things generally do not end well for mankind or the E.T.s. It’s a well-established and popular genre. But know – and this is really important – that Arrival is far more thoughtful and cerebral than what the title implies. This is not your standard issue War of the Worlds sci-fi film. Instead, it’s a remarkable puzzle that bends time and situations and relationships in a series of carefully crafted reveals. Know also that writing about this film is dicey. To allow the filmgoer to screen this film with no preconceptions while reviewing it is challenging at best. What can be disclosed – and I believe this appeared not only on the movie’s posters but also in the trailer – is that 12 enormous ships appear around the world, each hovering mere feet off the ground. One is in Montana. The existential questions posed by this dark shape’s ominous presence are: Why is it here? What are its intentions? How do we communicate with those inside? Okay, here’s a bit more. The military (uncertain as to whether the visitors pose a threat or come in peace) reaches out to professor Louise Banks (Amy Adams), a renowned linguist, who is joined by theoretical physicist, Ian Donnelly (Jeremy Renner). They are tasked with decoding their language (strange circles and unusual sounds) and establishing contact. What Arrival is about is language. Can Banks and Donnelly construct a bridge of common understanding that will allow them (and those waiting) to know why the visitors are here? The stakes are high as paranoia begins to creep into the analysis by multiple countries. Meanwhile, in f lashing images, shown via news stations, the world’s population is either deeply fearful, in the grips of a rising panic, or on the verge of mass riots. But this is not a story about finding out we are not alone in the universe. It is instead about overcoming a seemingly impenetrable code. The film is also intercut with images of Banks with her daughter, at first an infant and then growing into a young woman. These are touching scenes that set the stage for an overwhelming grief. How her relationship to her daughter is relevant to the superordinate narrative remains opaque throughout until the final reveal which will likely cause much discussion. The sense of disorientation and ambiguity lasts well beyond the final credits. There is also the possibility that the film is an allegory suggesting that language is fundamental to our humanness. When we stop believing in the magic of language, we can feel a sense of isolation and loneliness. Language shapes us, defines us, and it is something we struggle with each waking moment as we strive to understand and be genuinely heard. That is the communication dilemma posed by this amazing film, based on the sci-fi short story by Ted Chiang and now directed by the gifted French-Canadian Denis Villeneuve (Sicario). Science Fiction has recently experienced a surprising renaissance with films such as Gravity, Interstellar, Ex-Machina and The Martian. Add Arrival to that list – less linear and even confounding, it is worth every moment. Arrival. Directed by Dennis Villeneuv. Starring Amy Adams, Jeremy Renner, Forest Whitaker. 1 hr., 56 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2016, Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: The Piedmont Adult School held its first-ever Expo spanning three days of events last weekend, April 21-23, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. An opening reception on Friday presented community members with the opportunity to view student and instructor artwork, learn about Adult School classes, and sample food prepared by the school’s cooking instructors. Friday’s reception was a smashing success by all measures, with more than 150 people attending. Veteran bagpipe instructor Lynne Miller and one of his students serenaded the guests on the front steps of the Center as they arrived. A popular feature of the Expo were demonstrations and food samples from Adult School cooking instructors including a sushi-making demonstration by veteran Adult School instructor Chat Mingkwan. The walls of the Center for the Arts were decorated with more than 70 pieces of art created by students and instructors. Art instructor Wendy Sorenson was on hand to describe and discuss the art pieces on display. Sorenson teaches Watercolor and a Fine Arts Media class. O ngoi ng Adult School classes include memoir writing, cooking, foreign languages, computers, and art. One-time, weekly and daily class offered by talented instructors are available to fit anyone’s schedule. The spring session runs through May 31. Learn more at Piedmontadultschool.org or by calling Michelle Lucas at 594-2655. Victoria Manley (left) and Denise Bostrom were among the instructors at the event. Manley teaches Cultivating Joy: A Floral Workshop, and Bostrom teaches Family Stories and Memoir Writing. Long-time bagpipe instructor Lynne Miller (right) and one of his students welcomed visitors to the Expo reception. Liz Klute teaches guitar and ukulele, as well as the free Needlework Drop-In class for the Creative Retirement program. Eleanor Walker (left) provided pretzel bites and decorated mini cupcakes. Carmen Chan (center) made a summer salad and gouda-filled meatballs. Visitors enjoyed the opportunity to chat with instructors of different classes. Instructor Wendy Soneson (right) and art student A.J. RobinsonSimikić posed with their paintings.

articles.text: Many of the clients we work with have never engaged an architect and therefore come into the process of remodeling or building a new home knowing very little of the steps of developing a design and bringing it into construction. We have become accustomed to educating our clients about this process and guiding them through it step-by-step until the project is done. Whether the project is small and simple to very complex, many of the steps are the same. For the purposes of this article, we will concentrate on remodel projects rather than new home projects. At the start of a remodel project, we try to understand and help clarify the client’s Program for the project. The Program in the simplest terms is what you are trying to accomplish: more space, bigger spaces for some areas of the house, new kitchen, bathroom remodel, extra bedrooms, developing a basement, etc. The Program may also relate information about how spaces connect to one another, as well as incorporate a description of the desired look and feel. The first step is to develop As-Built Drawings of the existing house or portion of the house. If it is a major remodel, we may do a site analysis to determine how to situate the spaces of the house to maximize access to natural light and views. The next step is to develop a Preliminary Design. Depending on the project, we will develop sketches of possible solutions to the layout and flow issues we are trying to solve. We like to develop multiple ideas to offer alternative approaches. Once an approach to the layout is selected, we do a Design Development process. Here we like to do some 3D modeling to flesh out the design character of the spaces or exterior work. More detailed drawings are developed with notations. These drawings are used to informally discuss with agency staff of the local Building and Planning Departments. Depending on the project, one may need to go through a formal Design Review process. A ballpark pricing exercise with a contractor is also often developed at this time. After any necessary Planning Department approvals are achieved and the preliminary ballpark pricing is in alignment with the client’s budget, we develop the more detailed Permit Drawings and subsequent Construction Drawings. Then we can do the final pricing or bidding with contractors. The advantages of negotiation with a single pre-qualified contractor early in the process vs. having multiple contractors bid only after construction drawings have been completed is the subject of another article. Edward Kaplan AIA, NCARB, is principal of Kaplan Architects, based in Oakland and San Francisco since 1985. Kaplan Architects creates spaces with clients’ needs and desires foremost in mind. For information contact info@kaplanarchitects.com. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, Aprl 26, 2023 Walking on Wednesday Big turnout for 5th anniversary of Wed. Walkers By Dick Carter A great turnout of 53 walkers and four K-9 best friends showed up on April 19 for the fifth anniversary of the Walking on Wednesday group. A lot has happened since the group’s first walk on April 18, 2018 with 17 people. Covid shut most things in 2020, but the group came back in 2021 and has grown even stronger. It currently has 184 members. Thanks were given to architect Jim Kellogg who the week before took the group on an architectural tour of homes designed by noted early 20th Century architects. There was another thank you, too. On the group’s first walk Gail Lombardi, president of the Piedmont Historical Society, provided a tour of buildings in the center of Piedmont. Gail wasn’t able to be with the walkers last Wednesday, but her research in Piedmont Post articles has provided information for many walks. Five of Gail’s articles about Piedmont Park provided historical content for the day’s tour. It started with recalling that Walter Blair, the first European settler in the area, bought 600 acres in what is now Piedmont in 1852 for $750, and that Isaac Holmes discovered mineral springs in the Park’s Bushy Dell Creek about this time. The entrepreneurial Blair built horse trolley lines from Oakland to the Piedmont Springs Hotel that he and investors built in 1872 on an additional 350 acres. They selected the name “Piedmont,” meaning “foot of the hills.” Blair died in 1888 at the young age of 57, which spared him seeing his hotel burn to the ground four years later. Land developer Frank C. Havens entered the scene about this time and decided the mineral springs would be a great attraction for potential land buyers, and he began developing Piedmont Park. The walkers were told that Piedmont Park across from Wells Fargo Bank was where Havens built a firstclass dining room in 1898. He also cleared the vegetation in the ravine below and created a Victorian strolling park with a Japanese Tea House, built as replica of a 15th Century tea house in Kyoto. The current Japanese tea house in Piedmont Park came from a residence on Hillside Avenue when Piedmont Middle School was being built in 1976. The group learned that the location of the current tennis courts in Piedmont Park behind the Community Hall was the location where Havens built his Piedmont Art Gallery with a collection of 375 paintings. It was one of the finest collections in the country. Continuing on the park’s lower trail along Bushy Dell Creek, they passed Havens’ “Cascades” and a grotto where Mark Twain once sampled the mineral springs in the 1860s. They emerged at Witter Field, a natural bowl where Havens created a large circular hedge maze attraction in 1904. Havens got into financial difficulties, and by 1916 he was planning on developing the park for residential sites. However, the land went into foreclosure and the park was to be sold. The school board wanted to buy 13 acres for a new high school and Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander purchased 14 acres for a park, for which the City later reimbursed him. With their park tour complete it was time to return to the Tea House for lunch. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. A group of 53 walkers and four K-9 best friends helped celebrate the 5th anniversary of Walking on Wednesdays. On hand were: Pat Keller, Greg Keller, Joanne Larson, Helena Farber, Carol Lyons, Mike Henn, Renee Goldhammer, Elizabeth Richter, Alan Goldhammer, Sarah Johnson, Jim Kuo, Quincy Dong, Albert Chen, Fang Lai, Christine Calliste, Jennifer Peltzer, Woody Bailey, Dave DeRoche, Helen Dong, Carol Braves, Eric Behrens, Larry Olsen, Garrett Clifford, Leigh Sorensen with K-9 best friend McDuff, Lilly Guardia-Labar, Nancy Henn, Brenda Ferrero, Edith Lee, Nancy Olsen, Joyce Hicks with K-9 best friend Mocha, Harriette Louie, Martin Levy, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Joyce Bailey, Peggy Schultz, Tina Shum, Alicia Rivera, Ian Morgan, Sherry Jacobs, Stella Houston, Laura Goldman with K-9 best friend Vivie, Ann Quinby, Dena Belinkoff, Alissa Quan, Ken Moy, Priscilla Wanerus, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Charlene Louie, Meghan Bennett, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Michael Gardner was back, and Mike Hagerty and Chuck Oraftik came for the first time. articles.text: The Rev. Tom Trutner was called home peacefully on February 1, 2023 surrounded by family and dear friends. He was 87. Tom shall be remembered for many gifts, but none more memorable than happy hugs and his “cheerful easy smile.” He greeted both friend and stranger alike with a sense of genuine warmth and acceptance, and though he was known to his parishioners as “Father Tom,” he would have been just as pleased with “Brother” - Saint Francis was his patron saint, and The Blessing of The Animals was one of his favorite Holy blessings. Born Thomas Kirk Trutner on May 25, 1935, he was the son of Herman and Evelyn Trutner and the younger brother of Tony (Anton) and Fritzi (Frederika). Their grandfather, Herman Cameron Trutner II, was a noted Bay Area conductor and music teacher. His father played the French horn for the San Francisco Symphony and the San Francisco Opera Company. Having grown up with two professional musicians in the family influenced Tom’s preferred listening choice and that was classical – always classical. After graduating from Piedmont High School in 1953, where played quarterback for the football team with his best friend Monte Upshaw, and many others who also became lifelong friends, he completed his undergraduate studies at UC Berkeley and graduated in 1958. He joined the Beta Theta Pi fraternity and began to play the “gentleman’s sport” of rugby. After Cal his decision to attend Princeton Seminary was life-changing. One of his favorite professors was the Scottish minister Ernest Gordon, the author of Miracle on the Kwai. Gordon’s experience as a World War II prisoner in a Japanese camp was transformative for Tom, who learned how men, who left to die, were aided by fellow prisoners encouraging them to live. They “put their feet to their faith” and saved even the sickest. That message of faith set Tom on a life-long path. While at Princeton, he played rugby for three more years and became a “Rugger” for life. Years later, Tom became one of the co-founders of the Old Blues Rugby Club, a team that competed Rev. Tom Trutner in prayer at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland. nationally and internationally, winning the first United States National Club Championship in 1979. After seminary, Tom traveled to Hamburg, Germany with his young family and worked as an associate pastor in a local church. The experience of living abroad led to a lifetime of Tom taking students, parishioners, and friends touring throughout Europe. His philosophy regarding travel was: Visit the cities for their cultural richness found in museums, churches, art galleries, and architecture. Then drive to the towns and villages, sampling their food and local customs. And finally, check out the festivals, for “therein lies the spirit of the people.” Tom loved the family he came from and cherished the family he created with his first wife, Shirlee Jones Sampsel, and their son, Kirk, who became his father’s closest companion and golf partner. Years later, with his subsequent marriage to Jackie Milton O’Connor, he became a stepfather to four boys, Max, Bill and Jim Milton, and Matt O’Connor. Sadly, after 21 years of a wonderful marriage, his beloved Jackie succumbed to ALS, surrounded by all of her children and grandchildren. I n 2001, Tom became acquainted with Roxanna Smith Wing while tossing a football at Bishop’s Ranch Episcopal Retreat in Healdsburg. They were married the following year at the Ranch with Tom becoming once again a stepfather, this time to Roxanna’s daughter, Bria, and her two half-brothers, Rich and Jon Wing. Tom chose to balance his career between the secular community and the church. Of his 55 years in the ministry, 20 were served in the Presbyterian Church and 35 as an Episcopal priest. His career spanned Piedmont Community Church: Youth Director and Camp Director at Lodestar, 1967-70; University of California Berkeley Associate Dean of Students, Student Orientation program (CalSO), Fundraising Chair, School of Optometry, 1970-1987; St. Paul’s Episcopal Church, Oakland, 1978-1987; Associate Priest, Stephens Episcopal Church, Orinda, 1987- 2020. He also shared a Marriage, Family, and Child counseling practice with his good friend Sharon Gillan, and a travel business with Guyla Cashel. Father Tom became the person so many families turned to in times of both sorrow and joy. When he retired he was marrying the children of the couples he previously married over a span of 61 years. Tom recently commented, “I am 87 years old, and I’ve had a good life”. Indeed, he did - he had an extraordinary one. Those meeting Tom for the first time were impressed by his kindness and curiosity, and those who knew him best were touched by his sincere caring and keen interest in their lives. It is we who are left behind who feel that deep sense of loss, yet we are so grateful for the joy he so generously shared with us, and the delightful memories made together. Tom is survived by his wife Roxanne, son Kirk, seven stepchildren, 13 grandchildren, and 10 great-grandchildren. “All shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.” A memorial service for Tom Trutner will be held at the Lafayette-Orinda Presbyterian Church on Saturday, April 29 at 11:00 a.m., with a reception to follow.

articles.text: Helen Steers, a longtime Piedmont resident, passed away peacefully on Monday, April 10, 2023. Born in 1943 in Northern Wales to Evan and Margaret, she moved to the U.S. in 1971 after meeting and marrying Jim Steers of Piedmont. She was hired by Tulloch Construction in 1971 and continued working there for nearly 50 years. She was an active member of Piedmont Community Church for over 45 years, sand served as a Deacon and in many other capacities. She loved to knit with the church Needles and Hooks Club. Her retirement years were spent travelling, spending time with her grandchildren, walking around town, gardening, engaging in public service, and indulging in British crime dramas. While she was very proud of obtaining her U.S. Citizenship, she also loved humor, quiet strength, and selfless generosity of her time. She is deeply missed by her many family members and friends. Helen is survived by her daughter Carys and son-in-law Ben of Alameda, and by son Andrew and daughter-in-law Amanda Steers in South Carolina. She is additionally survived by grandchildren Jamie and Sawyer, Anderson and Alice, her sister Phyllis, brother David, and many cousins, nephews, nieces, grandnephews and grandnieces in both Wales and California. A memorial gathering of family and friends, to honor Helen will be held on May 6, 2023, at Piedmont Community Church at 2 p.m. The family suggests that in lieu of flowers, consider making donations in her name to a local food bank, the SPCA, or a charity of your choice. Helen Steers died on April 10 at age 79. to travel back to Wales as often as possible. She was very involved in the local Welsh Club, and instilled a sense of pride in Welsh heritage with her children and grandchildren (who called her Nain). Helen left a lasting impression of kindness, politeness, British

articles.text: REAL ESTATE AND PIEDMONT TAXES Along with spring’s beautiful flowers comes tax season. Let’s delve into a conversation about two types of taxes that are associated with our homes: property taxes and city transfer taxes. We’ll do our best not to create tax-related anxiety or lull you to sleep with our research! Piedmont’s 2022-2023 Fiscal Year Budget estimates its property tax funds budget at nearly $17M and city transfer tax funds at an estimated $3.2M. PROPERTY TAXES According to the California Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO), “a typical California property tax bill consists of many taxes and charges including the “1 percent rate” (part of the “Ad Valorem Tax” on each bill that goes to the County), voter-approved debt rates, parcel taxes, Mello-Roos taxes, and assessments.” Our homebuyer clients often ask us “How much should I expect to pay in property taxes each year?” The answer is “it depends.” For new homeowners, the majority of their property tax bill comes from taxes and charges that are calculated based on their assessed value. However, charges can also be based on the square footage of your home or parcel. Consequently, there is no fixed property tax rate. Taxes vary by house, city, neighborhood, and parcel. Our new homeowners can usually expect to pay around 1.4 - 1.6 % of their home’s assessed value in the first year. RECENT HISTORY OF PIEDMONT TRANSFER TAXES 2004-2021 Source: City of Piedmont Budget for Fiscal Year 2022-2023 CITY TRANSFER TAXES In Piedmont, every time a home is sold there is a city transfer tax paid by the buyers and sellers in the transaction (typically split 50%/50%). The city transfer tax is $13 per 1,000 of the property’s purchase price, or $13,000 per $1 million in home sales. Is the City on track to meet its FY 2022-2023 transfer tax estimate of $3.2M? It is! We looked at Piedmont home sales from July 1, 2022 to the most recent sales recorded at the County of Alameda and found that the City of Piedmont has already received nearly $3.5M in city transfer taxes with more than two months left before the end of the fiscal year. JUST FOR FUN: SALES TAX BONUS DATA When you buy items for your home, you pay sales tax too. Cities in Alameda County have the highest sales taxes in the state. Los Angeles County comes in a close second. Most CA counties sales tax rates range between 7 - 9%. We believe that the biggest problems are solved long before they happen, one person at a time. Scouting programs are designed to help youth build character, fitness, citizenship, and leadership skills. We help youth to grow into adults who make ethical choices, and who have the skills to carry those choices out. Scout programs have a generational impact today, with skills and leadership training available for youth and the adults who volunteer to lead them. Scout programs have a generational impact down the road, as today’s youth grow into our future citizens, leaders, and parents. CAMP ADVENTURES Top 5 Merit badges earned in Piedmont were: Day Camp, Twilight Camp, and Webeloree provided local adventures for Cub Scouts in grades K-5. Youth in Scouts BSA attended camps ranging from Catalina Island to the northern coast of Oregon. They enjoyed giant canoes, horseback riding, climbing, games at the campsite, the chance to earn merit badges, and so much more. articles.text: These Eagle Scouts led teams of youth and adults through projects totaling 3,210 service hours to the community. Many projects focused on rebuilding or repurposing an area. They include restoration of the Firestorm Memorial Garden, building a shelter at the beginning of a trail, and refurbishing bikes to be given to youth in need. These scouts embody the principals of leading others in service to the community. Outside of Eagle projects, Scouts BSA troops helped clean Kirby Cove and Sausal Creek, assisted with the Turkey Trot and other local events, and supported camps in and out of Scouting. Reported service hours totaled 1,795 hours. Piedmont Community Service Crew is well known for their annual house renovation project done in collaboration with Rebuilding Together Oakland: this is a crew-funded, youth-planned and executed project that takes months of planning. During 2022, the crew also spent many days helping to renovate the CityTeam building in downtown Oakland, donated countless hours planning and cooking food, built a few “tiny bathroom/showers” for a homeless village, and built several beautiful redwood planter boxes for Clausen House and Altenheim Senior Living. All together, the Venturers of PCSC contributed 1,631 service hours to the community. articles.text: “We are Ambassadors,” was the theme of Piedmont Community Church’s house-building mission trip in Mexico during Spring Break this year from April 9-14. For 220 students, 35 adult team leaders and 15 kitchen staff the annual trip emphasized hard work, community and compassion. They built more than houses; the annual mission trip built character, humanity and homes for impoverished people who had never known a shelter with a locking door. “You mean I can stay here now? I mean, this is my house?” said a recipient of a home to Scott Kail, the church’s Youth Minister and trip leader. This year’s trip had 15 teams, each with 15 students and two parent leaders. Each team started building a house by pouring a concrete floor slab on Monday, April 10, and handed keys over to new homeowners on Thursday, April 13. articles.text: With record amounts of rain this winter in the Bay Area and throughout the state, California is predicting a “super bloom” of wildflowers this spring. articles.text: Editor: In May 2018 the Tennis Pickleball sub-committee was formed. They worked diligently over seven months. Their report was adopted by the Recreation Commission on January 16, 2019 and City Council on March 4, 2019. The critical recommendations ….were: (1) an open play system for pickleball, (2) City staff should work with PUSD to explore the creation of permanent pickleball courts at the Middle School sport courts. Subsequently the City paid $50,000 for court repaving. The wisdom of adopting open play is evident with the rapid growth of pickleball: a new vibrant community has been created. There have been no comments or complaints concerning the open play system until the start of the trial to dedicate the Linda tennis courts to pickleball. Now opponents of pickleball in Piedmont wish to negate important previous community work by imposing a reservation system. [The] attempt to remove the long-established open play system is an unneeded distraction from the real issues of what best serves our community. Pickleball opponents wish to eliminate out of town players by imposing a reservation system. Pickleball in Piedmont welcomes all demographics. As City Planner Kevin Jackson stated concerning the housing element: “I am proud to say that this community has embraced the State’s call to welcome more people of all backgrounds in Piedmont.” Piedmont pickleball has been doing that since 2018. As preeminent tennis writer Joel Drucker states: “Pickleball features something frequently missing from tennis: laughter.” Sores of residents now have new friends. Piedmont pickleball checks off all boxes of good public policy: a far more efficient use of limited racquet court space, significantly enhanced older adult programming, integrating neighborhoods and ages which builds community. Piedmont pickleball counters… bad press that Piedmont endures. Imposing a reservation system will significantly reduce player numbers and achieve the goal of Linda Beach opponents: we will not need the space. Deplorably pickleball reservations will destroy what has organically blossomed into an essential part of life in Piedmont for many. –Rick Schiller For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. articles.text: I was up early on Sunday morning, September 11th. A busy day was ahead. The lead television news stories of the morning were of the motorcade carrying the coffin of Queen Elizabeth II through Scotland and somber observances in New York, Washington DC and Pennsylvania commemorating the 21st anniversary of the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. Both stories served as reminders that grief and gratitude are frequent traveling companions. There was an outpouring of grief from people around the globe upon the death of the 96-year-old Queen of England. In Scotland, people lined the roadways as her coffin passed. With the grief there were also many expressions of gratitude for her fidelity to her work, her years as a global leader, her humor and her delight in her four-legged friends. As the motorcade carrying her coffin traversed the Scottish countryside, it was clear that grief and gratitude traveled together. At the sites of the September 11 attacks the dead were remembered, the first responders were honored, hymns were sung, prayers were offered, and speeches were made. All were fitting expressions of the profound grief of that day, the persistent grief that is with us still. Yet, with the grief, there was gratitude. There was gratitude for the courage, the compassion, the connecting which the tragedies evoked. There was gratitude for the rebuilding that has taken place. There was gratitude for the restoration that continues.
articles.title: Grief and gratitude: Traveling companions

It was clear that grief and gratitude traveled together. In the biblical narrative, grief and gratitude frequently travel together. In the Psalms, expressions of grief often give way to songs of gratitude. Psalm 74 is an excellent example. This communal prayer originated with the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of its temple in 586 BCE. The first section (1-11) of complaint and grief is represented by words like “They set fire to your sanctuary, burned it to the ground” (7a). It is followed by a second section (12-17) of gratitude and confidence represented by words like “Yet God has been my king from ancient days” (12a). In the parables of Jesus, grief and gratitude are intermingled. An example is the Parable of the Lost Sheep. In this parable Jesus tells of a shepherd who must leave his flock in order to find one sheep who has wondered away. A lost sheep would have been an occasion for both fear and grief. A caring shepherd would not take such a loss easily or lightly. articles.text: The City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division invites community members to celebrate Earth Day by offering free compost at the City’s Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue at Red Rock Road this Saturday, April 22. Residents may pick up one cubic yard of free compost per household between 9 a.m. and 12 p.m. while supplies last. Residents will need to bring a shovel, gloves, and container for their compost. Volunteers and Public Works staff will be on hand to help with bagging and loading. Optional pre-registration is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ CompostGiveaway. The compost originally came from yard trimmings and food waste that Piedmonters and other communities serviced by Republic Services put in their green waste bins. Republic Services takes this waste to a large-scale facility where it is transformed into compost. This process helps to keep organic materials from emitting greenhouse gasses in the landfill and creates opportunities to use these nutrient-rich resources to regenerate our soils. In addition to the Earth Day event, free self-haul compost is available to residents every Friday outside the Corporation Yard. For more information see piedmont.ca.gov/CompostProgram. For questions contact Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman at adykman@piedmont. ca.gov. Free compost will be available at the Piedmont Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue on Earth Day, April 22. articles.text: – Dr. Mark Jacobson Guest lecturer, Climate Speaker Series On April 5th, the Piedmont League of Women Voters and Piedmont Connect presented the sixth and final event in their joint 2022-23 Climate Speaker Series. This month’s lecture and discussion was given by award-winning scientist, author and Stanford professor Dr. Mark Jacobson. He spoke on the technologies and actions needed to provide 100% of the world’s energy with clean, stable, renewable energy. sensus developed by the United Nations’ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (UN IPCC), a reduction of our emissions by 80% by 2030 and 100% by 2050 is needed to prevent a global average temperature rise of more than 1.5 degree Centigrade. Electric appliances – both heating/ cooling appliances as well as electric vehicles (EVs) – are much more energy efficient than their fossil-or-biofuel-burning equivalents. For example, electric heat pumps use 25% of the energy of natural gas furnaces or water heaters. Similarly, EVs are 4 times more efficient than internal-combustion engines. This is important given that 11.3% of all global energy use is expended to mine, refine, and transport fossil fuels and uranium. Jacobson also described the various available existing technologies to power heavy industry, provide long-haul transportation, and store power. Fuel cells can be used for air travel, shipping, long-haul trucking and military transports when battery EVs (BEVs) become less viable. There are several colors used to classify how hydrogen is developed into a fuel. Jacobsen demystified this hydrogen color spectr um, explaining that only green hydrogen is a positive and efficient solution to the climate crisis and that so-called “blue,” “pink,” “turquoise,” “gray,” “brown” or “black” hydrogen are not. Only green hydrogen, or hydrogen produced from clean, fossil-free, renewable energy sources, is a fuel compatible with retaining stable global climate conditions. Asked about nuclear power as a clean energy option, Jacobson explained that the capital costs are 15x higher and the lead-time 15 years longer to bring nuclear plants into operation in contrast to the capital costs and lead times Dr. Jacobson described his perspective on the problem: Air pollution from burning fossil and biofuels causes 7 million deaths every year at an annual cost of $30 trillion. In addition, the costs of global warming impacts – from wildfires, extreme heat and storms, ocean acidification, vector borne diseases, agricultural shifts and rising sea levels – are expected to rise each year, incurring another $30 trillion by 2050. As fossil fuels become less plentiful, more expensive and difficult to extract and process, price increases coupled with the concentrated control of the resource will lead to increasing levels of social and economic instability and geopolitical conflicts. He presented data that showed using fossil fuels for energy needs is costly, destabilizing, and ecologically ruinous. According to the global scientific conDr. Mark Jacobson was guest speaker at the April 5 Climate Speaker Series event in Piedmont. to bring an equal amount of new solar and wind power generation into operation. This results in nuclear power being eight times more expensive over time than the equivalent wind or solar and, he cautioned, “this doesn’t account for the issues of weapons proliferation, nuclear waste, underground uranium mining, and meltdown risk which nuclear power entails.” As for solar geoengineering as a possible solution – any technique used to reduce the amount of solar radiative energy reaching the earth’s atmosphere – Dr. Jacobsen served a blunt warning: “The problem is burning things. We need to stop the burning; we need to stop the problem, not mask it. That’s the key.” Re-runs available Videos of all 6 events in the Piedmont League’s and Piedmont Connect’s Climate Speaker Series are available on the LWVP YouTube Channel at bit.ly/41fDero. Hope Salzer is a board member of Piedmont Connect, a collaborative community organization supporting resident initiatives and city efforts to build a sustainable future. For more information, visit piedmontconnect.org.

Jacobsen demystified this hydrogen color spectr um, explaining that only green hydrogen is a positive and efficient solution to the climate crisis and that so-called “blue,” “pink,” “turquoise,” “gray,” “brown” or “black” hydrogen are not. Only green hydrogen, or hydrogen produced from clean, fossil-free, renewable energy sources, is a fuel compatible with retaining stable global climate conditions. Asked about nuclear power as a clean energy option, Jacobson explained that the capital costs are 15x higher and the lead-time 15 years longer to bring nuclear plants into operation in contrast to the capital costs and lead times Dr. Jacobson described his perspective on the problem: Air pollution from burning fossil and biofuels causes 7 million deaths every year at an annual cost of $30 trillion. In addition, the costs of global warming impacts – from wildfires, extreme heat and storms, ocean acidification, vector borne diseases, agricultural shifts and rising sea levels – are expected to rise each year, incurring another $30 trillion by 2050. As fossil fuels become less plentiful, more expensive and difficult to extract and process, price increases coupled with the concentrated control of the resource will lead to increasing levels of social and economic instability and geopolitical conflicts. He presented data that showed using fossil fuels for energy needs is costly, destabilizing, and ecologically ruinous. According to the global scientific conDr. Mark Jacobson was guest speaker at the April 5 Climate Speaker Series event in Piedmont. to bring an equal amount of new solar and wind power generation into operation. This results in nuclear power being eight times more expensive over time than the equivalent wind or solar and, he cautioned, “this doesn’t account for the issues of weapons proliferation, nuclear waste, underground uranium mining, and meltdown risk which nuclear power entails.” As for solar geoengineering as a possible solution – any technique used to reduce the amount of solar radiative energy reaching the earth’s atmosphere – Dr. Jacobsen served a blunt warning: “The problem is burning things. We need to stop the burning; we need to stop the problem, not mask it.
