articles.text: In advance of its participation in the Big Climb event at Oracle Park in San Francisco on Friday, April 29, the Piedmont Fire Department is helping raise donations for the nonprofit Leukemia and Lymphoma Society. PFD is registered for the event in the First Responders category along with other law enforcement, emergency medical workers, and other firefighting teams. Piedmont’s 4-man team will climb approximately 2,000 steps in Oracle Stadium, from the bottom of right field to the top and end of left field, to raise awareness and critical funds for blood cancer research and patient support. As of April 17, the Piedmont firefighters had raised $625 of its goal of $2,000. Last year’s Big Climb teams raised an average of $600 each. Led by Fire Captain Justin McNulty, Piedmont’s team includes firefighters Nicholas Christ, Anthony Renteria, and Brian Protheroe, Since registering for the event last December, the team has been training continually. “We run the stairs at Witter Field and Blair, constantly running laps, laps, laps,” explained McNulty. “At the firehouse, we’ve been doing step training every shift, at least three to four times a week. We have a gym stair-stepping machine in our fitness center in the basement, and I put in about 25 minutes every night.” Although this is the first year that the PFD has participated in the Big Climb, he and others in the department have taken part in many similar fitness competitions over the course of his 21 years with the department. “We often do CrossFit challenges; three of us did one in Rocklin recently. We’re encouraged by the fact that much of the physical fitness equipment in our basement is already the kind used to train for these competitions,” he added. “It’s all about the camaraderie and teambuilding for us.” Often participating in the federally funded, internationally touring [annual] Firefighter Combat Challenge, McNulty himself won two world titles with the Northern California team in 2008 and 2009. “For the First Responder teams, the Leukemia Society made a plaque which will be awarded to the team with the fastest three members’ times put together. We’ve been training especially hard, wanting to earn the plaque.” “For me it’s also about promoting the importance of fitness for our firefighters,” McNulty added. “No matter how light the equipment gets, no matter how much the technology advances, physical fitness is still at the center of how well we can perform. The fact that everything we fundraise for this competition is going to such a good cause is a great motivator.” Describing the nonprofit’s efforts to change the face of blood cancer, Christ wrote on his fundraising webpage that “LLS’ continued advancements over the years are responsible for the blood cancer survival rate doubling and tripling; in some cases, the survival rate has even quadrupled. And many LLS supported therapies not only help blood cancer patients but are now used to treat patients with rare forms of stomach and skin cancers. They’re even being tested in clinical trials for patients with a range of cancers including lung, brain, breast, pancreatic and prostate cancers.” All donations are tax deductible, and may be made by clicking on bit.ly/3UIefdH.

articles.text: Renovation of the steps at the eastern edge of Piedmont Park by Highland Avenue and Guilford Road is expected to conclude by the first week of May. The project, which began on January 23, was originally expected to conclude in midMarch; however, rainstorms created delays of more than one month. The $155,000 renovation project was approved by City Council on September 6, 2021, with $55,000 of the cost being paid by Piedmont Beautification Foundation and Piedmont Garden Club. “The main priority of this project is safety,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “The contractor will replace the current steps – wooden railroad ties of varying sizes – with colored concrete steps and landings and add metal handrails on both sides of the steps and landings.” Further additions to the site include benches, trees, and a small plaza with a permeable-pavement floor to accommodate for groundwater runoff. The park entrance at the corner of Highland and Guilford is fenced off until work is completed. Details and a design of the steps is available online at bit.ly/ 3jlK65z. For Questions, contact Daniel Gonzales at dgonzales@ piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3061. Contractors renovate the steps at Piedmont Park by Highland Avenue and Gilford Road. Staff photo
articles.title: Highland/Guilford Steps project nears completion

articles.text: Girls ages 2-18 from across the Bay Area are invited to participate in the 2nd annual Play Like a Girl event in Piedmont on Sunday, April 23, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Witter Field. This fun day of demonstrations and hands-on activities is free to all and offers opportunities to practice pitching, hitting, shooting hoops and even rowing with the guidance of skilled athletes and coaches. The main stage will feature live demonstrations at half-hour intervals. Attendees can try sports ranging from baseball to boxing to ultimate frisbee at 20 stations. The event also includes a Q&A session, photo ops, and meet-and-greet opportunities with professional women athletes and female Olympians, including 7-time Olympic medalist Dana Vollmer, professional soccer player Miranda Nild, professional volleyball player Mandy Bible, and former Olympic rower Liz Behrens of Piedmont. Last year’s event attracted over 400 participants. To register or to sign up as a volunteer, visit piedmont.ca.gov/playlikeagirl. Lifelong benefits Participation in sports builds skills that support girls throughout their lives, teaching leadership, discipline, and teamwork. Girls who participate in sports experience lower rates of depresThe second annual Play Like a Girl event will be on Sunday, April 23 sion and higher self-esteem than their non-athlete peers. • Girls who participate in sports are significantly more likely to graduate high school compared to non-athletes. The correlation is particularly strong for African American and Latinx girls. • Young girls who play sports have higher grades and score higher on standardized tests than non-athletes. • Girls who participate in high school sports earn higher wages than non-athlete peers. Play Like a Girl is a Recreation Department initiative to empower young women through athletics. The Department’s “Try (it) Out Tuesdays” event series gives girls of all skill levels the opportunities to try new sports, meet coaches, ask questions, and learn about opportunities within the community throughout the year. Piedmont Recreation’s Title IX basketball jersey initiative was recently recognized by the California Park & Recreation Society as “Outstanding JEDI Program or Event” of the year. Each jersey for the 450 youth participants in the Department’s citywide elementary and middle school basketball league was numbered after a woman who pushed the boundaries of what is possible in basketball, from early pioneers to outstanding players and coaches of today. When they received their jerseys, the students also got a printed card explaining the significance of their number and the player who wore it. For questions about Play Like a Girl+ Piedmont, contact Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen at ephalen@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: 2nd year of Play Like a Girl event

PHS science teacher, Shelley Seto-Rosen, like many PHS teachers, uses the following “equity-based grading policies,” in her 9th grade Biology classroom: 1) Offer retakes for major assessments 2) Homework is low stakes and only worth a small percentage of the overall grade 3) Extra credit is not offered for non-academic work 4) Participation/ Effort is not a graded category Seto-Rosen clarified that some teachers use a Standards Based Grading (SBG), which falls under the umbrella of Equitable Grading. Seto-Rosen does not use SBG currently. “The major premise of SBG is that a grade should be based solely on assessments of specific, well-defined standards. Students are generally given more than one opportunity to demonstrate their proficiency at these standards,” said Seto-Rosen. In addition to teaching Biology, Seto-Rosen is also a TOSA (Teacher on Special Assignment) working on MTSS (Multi-Tiered System of Support). articles.text: Piedmont’s School Board issued a resolution on April 4 declaring gun violence a public health crisis. The resolution states “gun violence is a public health crisis that adversely impacts our students, our teachers, our families, and our communities.” The resolution directs the Superintendent to disseminate material on an annual basis stressing the importance of secure storage of firearms. This material will be included in the registration packet at the student walk through and will require parent or guardian acknowledgment of receipt. The resolution also instructs the Superintendent to periodically communicate the importance of safe firearm storage and other firearm safety and violence prevention measures to the district during gun violence awareness month (June) and at other appropriate times. Presentations at the board meeting were given by Police Chief Jeremy Bowers and representatives of Brady United Against Gun Violence, Eric Havian, and Steve Roland. Havian’s talk presented alarming facts, such as: the U.S. has 71 times more gun homicides than the UK. “This is really the beginning of a critical conversation related to this issue. We see, unfortunately time after time, where this issue is refreshed in our consciousness. It shouldn’t need to be, but it is,” said Bowers. Piedmont students, in conjunction with the national group “Students Demand Action” staged a walkout and assembly in Piedmont Park in protest last May following the school shooting in Uvalde, Texas. articles.text: WHEREAS, The safety and well-being of our students, teachers, staff, and community is a top priority of Piedmont Unified School District; WHEREAS, in the United States, an estimated 3 MILLION children are exposed to shootings each year, an estimated 15,000 children and teens are shot and injured each year, and an estimated 3,500 children and teens are shot and killed each year. WHEREAS, Rates of death from firearms among ages 14 to 17 are now 22.5% higher than motor vehicle-related deaths. In the U.S., middle and high school age children are now more likely to die as a result of a firearm injury than from any other single cause of death. WHEREAS, Black youth are four times more likely to be killed than their white peers and Hispanic and Indigenous people are more than twice as likely to die by gun violence than white people; WHEREAS, According to a report from the US Secret Service, in incidents of gun violence on school grounds, 76% of attackers acquired a firearm from the home of a parent or another close relative. WHEREAS, Nearly 22,000 Americans die by firearm suicide every year – including over 950 children and teens. WHEREAS, Evidence strongly suggests that secure firearm storage is an essential component to any effective strategy to keep our community safe; WHEREAS, Keeping students, teachers and staff safe from the threat of gun violence is the responsibility of all adult stakeholders within our school district; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Board of Education directs that: 1. The Board hereby declares that gun violence is a public health crisis that adversely impacts our students, our teachers, our families, and our communities. 2. The Board directs the Superintendent to periodically disseminate material on an annual basis stressing the importance of secure storage of firearms and by including this material on an annual basis in the registration packet requiring parent or guardian acknowledgment of receipt with those other annual notifications that are distributed to all school district students; 3. The Board directs the Superintendent to periodically communicate the importance of safe firearm storage and other firearm safety and violence prevention measures to the district during gun violence awareness month and at other appropriate times.

articles.text: Volunteers at Chabot Space & Science Center do incredible things. They assist educators in workshops to inspire students, run scientific demonstrations to educate visitors and donate their time every Friday and Saturday night to offer free telescope viewing to the public. One rockstar, a Chabot Observation Deck volunteer and UC Berkeley student, is Gabrielle Stewart, who has discovered more than 450 supernovae since February 2022. Finding Supernova SN Swicky In the constellation Ophiuchus (the Serpent Bearer), a Type 1a supernova awaited its discovery. With a magnitude of around 19, it wasn’t visible to the naked eye. You’d need a powerful telescope to see it, like the 36-inch reflector on Chabot’s Observatory Deck. For Stewart, this exploding star jumped off the page in photos from the 48-inch telescope at Chabot volunteer Gabrielle Stewart makes a rare discovery. Palomar Observatory near San Diego. What makes this discovery so unique is the fact that this supernova’s brightness is enhanced by gravitational lensing – where a massive object, like a galaxy, has bent the light on its long-distance journey to Earth. Similar to what a lens would do, this effect has made the supernova appear brighter than it normally would. This is only the third such object ever discovered, and the first in six years. Annie McShane is Volunteer Manager at Chabot Space & Science Center, a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth.
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom Volunteer at Chabot Space Center makes rare discovery

articles.text: On an overcast and blustery weekend, Troop 11 recently headed to Dillon Beach for an overnight campout. Famous for its huge sand dunes, Dillon Beach on the Sonoma Coast has long been a favorite destination for Scouts for sand surfing and firing off small rockets. “Playing on the dunes was my favorite!” shared many Scouts, who had come prepared with saucer sleds. As always, the rockets were popular, with adult volunteers on hand to help show Scouts how to set up rockets for a safe launch. Scouts had the opportunity to choose from three categories of engine, from “A” with less power to “C” with considerably more. “A” and “B” engines had the advantage of not going as high – and making it less of a trek to retrieve the rocket. “C” engines had more power and sent the rockets higher into the sky. “They always pick a C engine!” commented Bart Myers. Sunmi Yoo and Cassidy Carter high five after successfully lighting a fire. Piedmont Troop 11 Scout dad Bart Myers shares insight with Mason Myers as he prepares to launch his rocket. Anna Benson (left) and Annabelle Malione practice their fire-building skills under the guidance of Scoutmaster Rob Kobal. Jim Crawford-Jakubiak talks Fred Leonard through the process of connecting his rocket to the launchpad. Seonho Lee chops up an onion for the Fred Patrol’s tacos. The Sour Bacon Patrol of Nick Steimle (left), Senan Brodie, Theo Ferguson, Zach Osborn, and Drew Kobal begins preparing their Golden Spatula meal. “It’s an acquired taste,” explained Drew Kobal in a measured tone. The weekend was the first campout for Scouts who joined Troop 11 during open house season earlier this year. In addition to participating in other activities, the newest Scouts had a chance to earn their Totin’ Chip and Firem’n Chit, which gives new Scouts a foundation in how to safely use knives and axes, and how to safely start and put out a campfire. After a windy night that kept many Scouts awake, they were happy to make breakfast and break camp – but not before a long-held Scout tradition of cleaning the beach before heading home. Colin Amen (left) and Eric Venner put the finishing touches on burying Theo Ferguson in the sand. After setting up camp, the Scouts prepared for the troop’s Golden Spatula competition. They were evaluated on budget, taste, presentation, nutrition, teamwork, and cleanliness. A trio of adult volunteers served as judges and provided feedback at the evening campfire. The Sour Bacon Patrol took top honors this time with a delicious dish of homemade mac ‘n cheese that included broccoli, bacon, and a breadcrumb topping. It was cooked in a Dutch oven and dished up for the enthusiastic Scouts. The dinner was accompanied by a dessert that defied category but included Jello and sprite. “It’s actually pretty good!” said Theo Ferguson. The evening mist caught the light as Troop 11 Scouts perform a skit during the campfire program. Drew Kobal sleds down a steep sand dune. Scouts clamber along the beachside dunes during a litter pickup before leaving Dillon Beach.

articles.text: Frequent readers of the Post’s PPD Blue may have noticed a trend in which cars set off the Automatic License Plate Readers (ALPR) when entering the city. Hyundais and Kias account for nearly half of all stolen cars entering the city and triggering an ALPR. The ALPR devices scan cars with stolen or lost license plates, cars wanted for crimes, and cars without license plates. This is not a Piedmont phenomenon, it is linked to security defects which cause Kia and Hyundais to be easily hotwired and stolen. Viral TikTok videos, made in May of 2022 have increased the trend, by showing just how easily one of these cars can be stolen. Some thieves can steal such a vehicle with only a screwdriver and a USB chord. Between March 10 and March 24, the Piedmont Police log identified 42 ALPR triggers. Thirty-three of the cars were identified by make, and of those, 17 were activated by Kia or Hyundai vehicles. In the same two-week period three of the six vehicles stolen from Piedmont were Kia or Hyundai. The statistics are not an anomaly; a disproportionate number of Kia and Hyundai vehicles are being stolen. A report from Berkeley in March 2023 showed 38% of all stolen cars in that city were Kias or Hyundais. Both auto manufacturing companies are in South Korea; Hyundai is the parent company of Kia. Many of their cars use the same parts and some models are almost identical, like the Hyundai Elantra and the Kia Forte. Kia and Hyundai vehicles made in 2010-2021 were built without engine immobilizers. The common electronic security devices is standard with most other cars made since 2010, and ensures that a car can be started only when the driver’s keyless fob is present. While the Piedmont Police Department does not track ALPR hits by car make, the police have seen more stolen cars entering the city, more stolen vehicle recoveries and more ALPR related arrests in general. Statistics of stolen vehicle recoveries, the value of the recovered vehicles and arrests related to License Plate Readers. “The number [of ALPR hits] is climbing each year,” confirmed Police Captain Chris Monahan. Two years ago in 2021 the police recovered 59 stolen vehicles, and made 30 arrests related to ALPR triggers. Last year, in 2022, the numbers increased to 69 recovered stolen vehicles and 48 ALPR related arrests. Two weeks ago on April 2, an attempted catalytic converter theft by suspects in a silver Kia sedan was interrupted by a Piedmont resident on Florada Avenue. The suspect pointed a Glock handgun at the resident before speeding off into Oakland. This event has prompted the police to urge residents to avoid altercations during crimes in progress. In explaining the current police protocol for pursuit of a stolen vehicle, Capt. Monahan said, “We will not pursue a car if ‘all it is’ is stolen.” said Monahan. “There needs to be a much higher-level crime to warrant a pursuit. The potential for danger during pursuit is high and car thieves can be highly unpredictable.” Owners of Kia or Hyundai can check with the dealership to see if a free fix can be performed as part of a software update rollout in response to the increase in thefts. The update lengthens the time the alarm goes off, from 30 seconds to one minute, and makes it necessary for the key to be in the ignition switch for the vehicle to start. Many Kia and Hyundai dealerships are overwhelmed with demand for this service. Other options include buying an aftermarket alarm or a battery disconnect item with a kill-switch, something that can be purchased for around $15. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team continued its strong pace on the final stage of the regular season. It defeated North Coast Section foe University 22-7 in San Francisco on Saturday, April 1, and beat Amador Valley 19-5 at Witter Field on Saturday, April 15. Its one loss came on April 6 to De La Salle in Concord, 15-6. Piedmont’s record improves to 8-2 with one match left in its regular season, a non-conference game with Serra of the Central Coast Section on Saturday, April 22. The Western Alameda County Conference playoffs will start on Tuesday, April 25, with Piedmont as the No. 1 seed. The league championship game will be on Thursday, April 27, at Bishop O’Dowd. The opening round of the North Coast Section playoffs is set for Tuesday, May 2. Piedmont is expected to receive a high seeding. “We just have to keep our composure in each game. We take it one game at a time and focus on the next one,” said Nathan Fredericks. 22-7 rout of University Piedmont opened the match with a 4-2 lead at the end of the first quarter and boosted its lead to 12-3 by halftime. PHS then scored nine goals in the third and conceded none to the Red Devils, entering the final quarter ahead 21-3. Final stats: Fredericks scored six goals, two assists, and recovered three loose balls. Henry Brayer scored five goals and recovered three ground balls. Rylan Nelson scored four goals and gathered three loose balls. Soren Dixon had three goals and one assist. Jack Nelson had two goals, six assists, and three loose balls. Oliver Shafroth had an individual goal, assist, and ground ball. Curtis Hohener scored once. 15-6 loss to De La Salle De La Salle, winner of last year’s NCS Division 1 title, came out hot with a 6-1 lead at the end of the first quarter and led 11-3 Staff Photos Piedmont lacrosse coach Alex Yu (right) and assistant coach Dave Haffner. Nate Fredericks scored six goals against University. Jack Nelson had three goals against De La Salle, and four in a 19-5 victory over Amador Valley. at the half. The Spartans scored three in the third and held Piedmont scoreless for a 14-3 lead. The Highlanders got on the scoreboard late with three goals in the fourth, finishing 15-6. Sophomore Gus Von Metszch was busy in goal, recording 19 saves. Final stats: Jack Nelson had three goals and two assists. Fredericks and Brayer both had one goal and assist. Dixon scored once and gathered two ground balls. Rylan Nelson had one assist and one loose ball recovery. 19-5 win at home vs. Amador The Highlanders left no doubt early, taking a 10-1 lead by the end of the first quarter and 18-2 at halftime. With PHS rotating in its non-starters, Amador scored twice in the third. Final stats: Brayer led with six goals, one assist, and two ground balls. Dixon had four goals, two assists, and five ground balls. Jack Nelson had four goals, one assist, and recovered two loose balls. Fredericks scored twice and had one assist. Shafroth had one goal and four ground balls. Tuesday vs. Acalanes Piedmont hosted Division 2 opponent Acalanes last night, Tuesday, April 18, in what could be a potential North Coast Section matchup. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP Piedmont (8-2) hosts Central Coast Section school Serra this Saturday, April 22, at 6:00 p.m. It moves to the first-round of the WACC playoffs as the No. 1 seed on Tuesday, April 25, in a game at Witter Field, most likely against Berkeley. The game time is to be determined.

articles.text: Prior to spring break, Piedmont High’s baseball team split a pair of games with Western Alameda County Conference opponent Alameda. The Highlanders defeated the Hornets at Alameda 3-2 on Tuesday, April 4 but lost 7-3 two days later at home at Humphries Diamond. PHS coach Eric Olson called the loss to Alameda unusual and felt his players may have been looking to their weeklong Spring Break the following week. “We’re going to call this an aberration; I don’t think I’ve seen us play like that all season. We need to tighten things up, because it was the same thing against Berkeley where we win the first game and get beaten the second time,” said Olson. Piedmont returns from break with a game tonight, April 19, at Bishop O’Dowd. Two days later it returns home against the Dragons to close out the series. 3-2 over Alameda Piedmont scored once in the top of the first inning and one more in the top of the third, but Alameda tied the game at 2-2 in the bottom of the third. The game remained deadlocked until Piedmont scored the game-winning run in the top of the sixth. Michael Aikawa pitched a complete game with four strikeouts and no earned runs. With one out in the first inning, sophomore Markos Lagios smacked a triple on the second pitch of his at bat to the left field fence. After Peter Krumins drew a walk, Will Parker Staff Photos Ryan McConathy smacked a onerun home run against Alameda. hit a single to left field to bring in Lagios. However, Piedmont ended the inning stranding Krumins at third. In the top of the third, Lagios led off with a double. With two outs, Lagios made his way to third on a mishandled pitch by the catcher, who subsequently threw the ball into the outfield when trying to throw Lagios out at third—allowing him to come home. With the game tied 2-2 going into the top of the sixth, Krumins led off with a single to right field while Parker reached first after smacking a hard ground ball to the second baseman, forcing an error. Krumins then scored in a fielder’s choice after Dimitri Papahadajopolous hit a ground ball to second. Aikawa put them down 1-2-3 in the bottom-of-the-sixth, but the bottom of the seventh was tense. With two outs and the bases Markos Lagios had a double and triple in Piedmont’s 3-2 win over Alameda. Michael Aikawa throws the ball to first base for an out. He pitched a complete game in Piedmont’s 3-2 win over Alameda.

articles.text: Playing in Vallejo on Monday, April 17, Piedmont was overwhelmed by St. Patrick on its first day back from Spring Break, 20-10. The high-scoring game looked more like a football result than softball. It marked the team’s seventh consecutive loss. In what generously is described as a rebuilding season, the team is trying to fill the vacancies of last year’s starting pitcher, Izzy Epstein, catcher Chiarra Lundin, Ginger Gardner and backup pitcher Annabelle Castronovo. Without pitchers, coach Gene Dennard has been forced to use players with no previous experience on the mound. Miya Fujimoto, for example, is this year’s starting pitcher after being the starting shortstop last year as a freshman. She was the Post’s 2022 Freshman of the Year for her contributions at shortstop, a position typically reserved for the team’s best glove. “When Miya is on the mound, it takes away one of our best infielders. She was our starting shortstop last year, we’d much rather have her in the field,” confirmed Dennard. Piedmont’s record now dips to 2-7-1 after making the jump to the Western Alameda County Conference’s Foothill Division, where they are 0-5 versus league teams. Leah Bell went 3-for-4 with four runs scored, one RBI, and four stolen bases against St. Patrick. Angelina Wu gets ready to launch a ball to first. Staff Photos Miya Fujimoto went 1-for-4 with a triple, two runs scored, and an RBI against St. Patrick. She is filling in a pitcher after playing shortstop last year. Game Recap Piedmont opened with a 3-0 lead in the top of the first but St. Patrick answered with three runs of its own in the bottom half. PHS scored one more in the top-second but allowed five runs in the bottom-of-the-second. St. Patrick made it 12-5 after the third, 16-8 after the fourth, and then made it 20-10 in the bottom-of-the-sixth to force the 10-run rule. In the top of the first inning Piedmont came out hot with three runs. Angelina Wu led off with a seven-pitch walk, followed by Fujimoto smacking a triple to center field to drive in Wu. Leah Bell followed with a single to score Fujimoto, and Bell scored after Morgan Hunt hit a hard ground ball that forced an error. However, Piedmont couldn’t score any more runs. In the second, Caitlin Boothby led off with a double to right field and Mia Leggett brought her in with a double, but from there, Piedmont fell in 1-2-3 order. articles.text: Piedmont senior Parker Long has announced he intends to continue his track career in the fall at California Polytechnic State University in San Luis Obispo. Long’s winning time of 1:53.25 in the 800-meter run at the Dublin Distance Fiesta on March 18 was enough to catch the attention of coaches at the Division 1 school. “It’s a good school academically; I think that’s what made me want to go there more than the other schools I was considering,” Long said. “This is a school that has a really good running program and educational system. I really didn’t think I would get in, honestly. I reached out after [the run at] Dublin. They said they were really impressed and wanted me on the team,” said Long. Long is currently No. 3 among Piedmont High’s all-time 800- meter runners. He is narrowly behind The Post’s 2018 Athlete of the Year, Reece Proctor, and Piedmont Sports Hall of Famer, Gordon Johnson. Top-five 800-meter runners: 1. Gordon Johnson, 1:51.10 (1989) 2. Reece Proctor, 1:52.64 (2018) 3. Parker Long, 1:53.25 (2023) 4. Cooper Downing, 1:53.40 (2022) 5. John Weber, 1:55.26 (2010) Long considered attending the University of Oregon as a student, but now found a school where he can competed while also enjoying his college experience at a deeper level than some other candidates. “I was considering a lot of the UC’s and my main one for a while was Oregon, not necessarily as a runner, but just because I liked the campus. Once I got into contact with Cal Poly, they made it sound really good. Then I went to check out the school and it really checked all of the boxes. It’s a little bit warmer {than Eugene] and it’s a unique city,” said Long. Parker plans on majoring in math, but knows he has time to figure out his academic future. Parker and the Piedmont High track team still have a lot of running left. The Western Alameda County Conference championship is on May 5, followed by the North Coast Section Bayshore Finals on May 13, NCS Meet of Champions on May 19-20, and CIF State Championship on May 26-27. Heading into the latter stage of the season, Long is hopeful to hit his peak at the right time and Parker Long, Class of 2023, is set to continue his running career with Cal Poly in San Luis Obispo. avoid fizzling out ahead of the state meet in Fresno. “The big sequence is league championships to the NCS region meet, then to NCS Finals, then to State. As we get closer to those races, I have to think about when I peak with my training. What happens with a lot of runners is they are super ambitious and over-train too early, and they end up dying out before the end of the season. Sometimes runners peak too late as well. I’m trying to find the sweet spot of those two things and peak exactly at the right time,” said Long. Parker Long is currently Piedmont High School’s third fastest all-time 800-meter runner with a time of 1:53.25. Parker Long describes what drew him to Cal Poly and his mindset for the rest of his track season.

Long’s winning time of 1:53.25 in the 800-meter run at the Dublin Distance Fiesta on March 18 was enough to catch the attention of coaches at the Division 1 school. “It’s a good school academically; I think that’s what made me want to go there more than the other schools I was considering,” Long said. “This is a school that has a really good running program and educational system. I really didn’t think I would get in, honestly. I reached out after [the run at] Dublin. They said they were really impressed and wanted me on the team,” said Long. Long is currently No. 3 among Piedmont High’s all-time 800- meter runners. He is narrowly behind The Post’s 2018 Athlete of the Year, Reece Proctor, and Piedmont Sports Hall of Famer, Gordon Johnson. Top-five 800-meter runners: 1. Gordon Johnson, 1:51.10 (1989) 2. Reece Proctor, 1:52.64 (2018) 3. Parker Long, 1:53.25 (2023) 4. Cooper Downing, 1:53.40 (2022) 5. John Weber, 1:55.26 (2010) Long considered attending the University of Oregon as a student, but now found a school where he can competed while also enjoying his college experience at a deeper level than some other candidates. “I was considering a lot of the UC’s and my main one for a while was Oregon, not necessarily as a runner, but just because I liked the campus. Once I got into contact with Cal Poly, they made it sound really good. Then I went to check out the school and it really checked all of the boxes. It’s a little bit warmer {than Eugene] and it’s a unique city,” said Long. Parker plans on majoring in math, but knows he has time to figure out his academic future. Parker and the Piedmont High track team still have a lot of running left. The Western Alameda County Conference championship is on May 5, followed by the North Coast Section Bayshore Finals on May 13, NCS Meet of Champions on May 19-20, and CIF State Championship on May 26-27. Heading into the latter stage of the season, Long is hopeful to hit his peak at the right time and Parker Long, Class of 2023, is set to continue his running career with Cal Poly in San Luis Obispo. avoid fizzling out ahead of the state meet in Fresno. “The big sequence is league championships to the NCS region meet, then to NCS Finals, then to State. As we get closer to those races, I have to think about when I peak with my training. What happens with a lot of runners is they are super ambitious and over-train too early, and they end up dying out before the end of the season. Sometimes runners peak too late as well. I’m trying to find the sweet spot of those two things and peak exactly at the right time,” said Long. Parker Long is currently Piedmont High School’s third fastest all-time 800-meter runner with a time of 1:53.25. articles.text: In mentioning the current athletic accomplishments of student-athletes at Piedmont High, the performances by PHS grads in college can sometimes be overlooked. With Piedmont High senior Parker Long having announced his intention to compete next year for Cal Poly, this article takes a look at three of his former Piedmont teammate who are currently active at the collegiate level, including Parker Terrill with the University of California, Jack Stein at Pomona-Pitzer, and Luke Alban at Connecticut College. Jack Stein, PHS Class of 2022, is competing as a freshman at Pomona-Pitzer. 4:27.29 in the 1-mile event on February 18, and 15:00.42 in a 5K event on March 11. Stein graduated from Piedmont High as its All-Time record holder in the 1600 and 3200 with respective times of 4:14.77 and 9:12.62. He also won the WACC Cross Country championship with a time of 15:34.76, was second of 144 in the NCS Championship in 15:29.4 and placed 12th of 209 at the CIF Championship, clocking a 15:43.4. Stein was named Co-Athlete of the Year by the Post last year. Parker Terrill, PHS Class of 2022, is currently competing as a pole vaulter and hurdler with the University of California in Berkeley. Parker Terrill, UC Berkeley Parker Terrill, PHS Class of 2022, is currently competing in his freshman track and field season at the University of California. Terrill has continued his focus as a decathlete so far this season at Cal. He’s clocked a 100 meter dash time of 11.44, a 400 meter time of 52.41, clocked a 16.77 in the 110 hurdles, 1.75 meters in the high jump, 6.55 meters in the long jump, 36.98 meters in the discus, 37.02 meters in the javelin, 10.98 meters for the shot put, and 15 feet, 7 inches in the pole vault. Terrill departed from Piedmont High as the school’s alltime record holder in the pole vault with a height of 16 feet, 1 inch—which was 2 feet, 1 inch taller than the next best, Marshall Wentworth in 2011. In the 4x400, Terrill made more history with a time of 3:21.77 as the last leg alongside Alban, Cooper Downing, and Long. They topped a 33-year old record which was headlined by Piedmont Hall of Fame member Gordon Johnson. The Post named Terrill the 2022 Co-Athlete of the Year along with classmate Jack Stein Jack Stein, Pomona-Pitzer Jack Stein, PHS Class of 2022, is a freshman on Pomona-Pitzer’s track and field team and also competed in cross country back in the fall. Most recently this track season, Stein clocked a 9:38.24 in the 3K Steeplechase to finished second of 20 in the Pomona-Pitzer Track and Field Invitational on April 8. He’s also ran times of 4:08.34 in the 1500 on March 4, Luke Alban, PHS Class of 2022, helped set a new 4x400 relay record ay Piedmont. Luke Alban, Connecticut College Luke Alban, PHS Class of 2022, is a freshman at Connecticut College after departing Piedmont as a member of the record-setting 4x400 relay team as a senior. The sprinter has been active in recent weeks. At the CGA Invitational on April 8, Alban finished 10th of 45 in the 100 meter dash with a time of 11.37 seconds. He was also 12th of 39 in the 200, 23.18. His 4x100 relay team also was third of six in 44.02. Alban also competed on Connecticut College’s indoor track team over the winter. He clocked a 23.49 in the 200 meter dash at Middlebury’s New England Small College Invitational on January 29, finished 23rd of 51. In the 4x400, Alban’s team finished sixth of seven with a time of 3:32.15. At PHS, Alban helped set the school record in the 4x400 when they finished with a time of 3:21.77 set at the NCS Meet of Champions, beating the previous 33-year old record by 1.2 seconds set in 1989.

articles.text: Piedmont/s girls’ lacrosse team returned from spring break on Monday, April 18 and immediately faced a formidable obstacle, losing 18-4 to North Coast Section foe Tamalpais. Tam is riding high with a 15-2 record. Led y Northwestern-bound middie Madi Smith, it looks like the odds-on favorite to capture the Section title this spring. PHS coach Carlton Chan thinks it was a good matchup for Piedmont to get prepared for the Western Alameda County Conference playoffs. Piedmont has just one game left in its regular season, and will play Newark Memorial tonight, April 19. “We [schedule] Tam because we know they are going to be really good; they are probably going to vie for NCS,” said Chan. “This is the best team we’ve played this season, so it took us Molly Ashton (right) defends Tamalpais’ Madi Smith, a Northwestern bound prospect. a bit to get into the game coming off of spring break. We’re telling them this is a good game for them, we haven’t seen a team that can move the ball this quickly.” The Highlanders’ goal is to compete for the WACC title against top-seed Bishop O’Dowd Ruby Guzdar scored twice against Tamalpais. with the league semifinals set for Tuesday, April 25 and championship game on Thursday, April 27 – both hosted by O’Dowd. “Our focus is going to be on the WACC. Playing a team like Tam will help us prepare for playoffs so they can play hard and come out with fire, like they did in the second half tonight,” said Chan. Piedmont will likely enter as the WACC Playoffs as the No. 2 seeded team and face No. 3 Berkeley, which PHS defeated 13-8 on March 24. Defeating the Jackets will avenge last year’s semifinals 13-12 loss. “In the last two weeks of the season, we’re telling them that they have to come out with fire to every practice. You have to practice at game speed, a team like tonight wakes us up really quickly. We have one more league game and we just want the team to stay at a high level,” said Chan. Piedmont will honor its five seniors prior to the game with Newark: Molly Ashton, Eleanor Lavin, Holland Feinberg, Sofia Johnson, and Lindsay Kottle. Game Recap Tamalpais led 11-0 by halftime and 15-1 when Piedmont got its first goal by Molly Ashton with 15:30 left in the second half. Peyton Watson got Piedmont’s second goal by way of a shooting space attempt with 8:30 left in the game, while Ruby Guzdar scored on athletic runs towards the net with 4:20 and 3:15 left on the game. Final stats: Guzdar had two goals and won two draws. Ashton and Watson had individual goals, while Ashton recovered one loose ball. Chloe Graham, Hailey Marshburn, and Lavin both gathered three ground balls. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-5 overall, 2-1 league) hosts Newark Memorial for Senior Night tonight, April 19, at 7:00 p.m. ay Witter Field.

articles.text: It’s springtime in the Bay Area and blooms of wildflowers abound throughout the entire state. It makes the sun-swept hills of Sibley Volcanic Regional Preserve in the Oakland Hills the perfect place to take in the scenery of the colorful plants and flowers. Sibley is most known for its stone labyrinths, but sunny days following the recent rain has allowed vegetation to grow and keep the hills green. Throughout Sibley Regional, the sharp contrasting orange of California Poppies and purple of Silver Lupine bushes sweep through the hills. Cows have been allowed to graze throughout the park in recent months, resulting in fewer poppies than previous years, but there are still many thickets of orange flowers. Sibley’s Round Top Loop trail is about 2.5 miles and connects to the Quarry and Volcanic trails, where you can find the labyrinths The Mazzariello Labyrinth is the most famous attraction at Sibley Regional Preserve, which was created in 1989. The rolling hills towards Round Top, an extinct volcano that provides the volcanic rock throughout the park Starting your day at Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve adds some shade to your hike and is a bit more hidden than Sibley. Follow the signs toward Sibley Regional from Huckleberry.

pages.text: Wednesday, Aprl 19, 2023 15 HIKING WITH JON Sibley Regional’s springtime splendor By Jonathan Comeaux It’s springtime in the Bay Area and blooms of wildflowers abound throughout the entire state. It makes the sun-swept hills of Sibley Volcanic Regional Preserve in the Oakland Hills the perfect place to take in the scenery of the colorful plants and flowers. Sibley is most known for its stone labyrinths, but sunny days following the recent rain has allowed vegetation to grow and keep the hills green. Throughout Sibley Regional, the sharp contrasting orange of California Poppies and purple of Silver Lupine bushes sweep through the hills. Cows have been allowed to graze throughout the park in recent months, resulting in fewer poppies than previous years, but there are still many thickets of orange flowers. Sibley’s Round Top Loop trail is about 2.5 miles and connects to the Quarry and Volcanic trails, where you can find the labyrinths Photos by Jonathan Comeaux A California Poppy nestled in between Silver Lupine at Sibley Regional Volcanic Preserve The Mazzariello Labyrinth is the most famous attraction at Sibley Regional Preserve, which was created in 1989. Another labyrinth with more purple Silver Lupine bushes and poppies springing up on the The rolling hills towards Round Top, an extinct volcano that provides the volcanic rock throughout the park hillside and other geological features. The park is a popular area for dog walkers and is child friendly. After the loop trail connects to the Volcanic Trail, veer to the right to find the first quarry pit. It will be trail marker No. 2 on the park information pamphlet’s selfguided tour. Old quar r y operations removed massive basalt lava and exposed the interior of the Round Top volcano. The base of the pit consists of bedded tuff-breccias, which is volcanic ash and sedimentary rock fragments. The labyrinth featured at the base of the pit was originally created by Montclair sculptor Helena Mazzariello in 1989. It is the largest of the four stone mazes and is the most photographed spot in the entire park. Continuing on the Quarry Trail just 0.2 from the Mazzariello Labyrinth overlook is another labyrinth. Trail marker No. 5 on the tour is the second-largest labyrinth off of Volcanic Trail. When you reach a fork in the road with the Quarry Trail on the left, head to the right and take a slight uphill walk towards the pit. This one has a smaller heart shaped labyrinth but also a nearly vertical chunk of lava sticking out of the north end of the quarry. This pit was also created by the removal of massive basalt lava. In addition to dog walking, it is a great place to spark your child’s interest in geology. It also won’t be too taxing on their legs given the trail contains minor uphill portions. There is a large parking lot with free parking and a visitor’s center that displays various types of volcanic rocks and clean restrooms. Park at Huckleberry Botanical Sibley Regional is among the most popular parks in the Oakland Hills, often resulting in a crowded parking lot cars parked on Skyline Boulevard. If you’re willing to add 1.8 miles to the day with 600 feet in elevation gain, park at Huckleberry Botanical Regional Preserve. Hiking along the Huckleberry Loop trail until it merges with the Skyline Trail takes visitors to Sibley’s Round Top Loop trail. Taking a right turn adds another .18 of a mile to the hike and adds another 100 feet in elevation gain. Hugging Skyline Boulevard on our custom loop back to the car from Huckleberry to each of the hill-peaks at Sibley creates a 4.79-mile loop with 1,033 feet in elevation gain, and can be done in slightly less than two hours. Here is the map of The Posts’ 4.79 mile loop from Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve to Sibley Regional and back. Starting your day at Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve adds some shade to your hike and is a bit more hidden than Sibley. Follow the signs toward Sibley Regional from Huckleberry. The view from the highest portion of Sibley Regional, where you can get a look of San Francisco Bay on a clear day

articles.text: The de Young Museum in San Francisco is now exhibiting a large, important exhibit of some of the most famous photographs of San Francisco native Ansel Adams. The show, In Our Time, is a retrospective of more than 100 works by the late artist. Adams (1902 - 1984) was a revered American photographer and environmentalist known for his black and white images of Yosemite Valley and the American West. Monolith, The Face of Half Dome, Yosemite Valley, captured in 1927, is considered his most well-known image, and his first photograph that gathered the attention of the public and the art world. The exhibition is Laid out in seven sections that trace Adams’s artistic development, and features some of his most-loved Photographer Ansel Adams was a San Francisco native who lived and worked in Carmel for much of his career. photographs including images of Yosemite, San Francisco, and the American Southwest. The exhibition will be on view at de Young through July 23. To learn more, visit https://www. famsf.org/exhibitions/ansel-adams-in-our-time. Clearing Winter Storm, 1937. Ansel Adams brought Yosemite Valley to life for people throughout the world with his iconic black and white images. Presented by

articles.text: One of San Francisco’s largest independent art and flea markets opens at Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture tomorrow, April 20, and will be open to the public until Sunday, April 23. Fort Mason’s indie market is the city’s longest running art fair, with the participation of 85 top galleries from around the world, including important regional partnerships and a program of public art projects curated by the festival’s Creative Director, Nato Thompson. This year’s art market will be “a powerful platform for the vibrant, experimental, and inclusive strength that defines the Bay Area’s thriving arts community,” said Thompson. Opening day is tomorrow, Thursday, at 6 p.m. The art market will be open through Sunday, April 23, from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. each day. Tickets are required. Visit https://artmarketsf.com/ visit/ to purchase tickets. A photo from last year’s Art Market at Fort Mason. General Dentistry & Advanced Prosthodontics

articles.text: SF Jazz will host its annual gala on Thursday, May 3, when it celebrates SF Jazz Founder and Executive Artistic Director Randall Kline. The gala will feature performances by Ambrose Akinmusire, Regina Carter, Rosanne Cash and John Leventhal, Ravi Coltrane, Herbie Hancock, Eric Harland, Branford Marsalis, Cécile McLorin Salvant and Sullivan Fortner. Dianne Reeves will serve as host, with after-party performances by Trombone Shorty and Red Baraat. There will be a live free broadcast of the after-party concert at 8:30 p.m. on May 4. articles.text: The self-driving orchestra, with vacant podium, has arrived at center stage. Credit composer Brian Baumbusch, 35, from Alameda – along with a Covid quarantine, electronics and a touch of Indonesia. Yes, finally, one tiny benefit we gained from that scourge of a Covid virus, leads to some invention and dispersion of musical ideas. Marooned in a Djakarta quarantine last year, Baumbusch composed his Polytempo Music which was premiered in San Francisco on April 13 by the elite S.F. Contemporary Music Players. His inspiration relegated conductor Eric Dudley to a front-row seat looking on while the dozen musicians played their parts guided by electronic click tracks in earphones, set to such a variety of energetic beats and tempos as to be impossible to conduct. It may sound like total chaos. But no, Baumbusch took his lead from Indonesian gamelan music, where slow and fast tempos are overlaid (a bit like Bach’s “Sleepers Awake” or “Jesu, Joy of Man’s Desiring”), and maintained some harmonic control. This adroit derringdo led to an engrossing world premiere at the Taube Atrium, full of dense overlay and ear-caressing music. The work was fast paced, with striking harmonic shifts, all a coherent dazzle of sound we need to hear again, then ending on a dime. The impetus for revivals remains there, as the 18 minutes The concert opened with a live-instrument arrangement of the late expat Conlon Nancarrow’s Study No. 3a for sextet, with clarinetist Jeff Anderle at the forefront. The arrangement counters Nancarrow’s original musical thrust and method, wherein he had been totally mechanical – all inscribed on hand-cut player-piano rolls, usually intent on defying human capabilities of play. A rare aspect of the stellar conductor Esa-Pekka Salonen was on view with his septet, Catch and Release (2006). Focusing on this 25-minute work was challenged by the distracting, near-bare-chested attire on one player. Please, less distraction and tedium, more decorum! Salonen’s audacity led him to use an unsettling, unorthodox ensemble, whose trumpet, trombone and drumming overwhelmed the strings and woodwinds. Nimble percussionist Haruka Fujii had to fast-step between the drums and a more ingratiating vibraphone. Its finale offered an exercise in staccato, ever more intense. Artistic director Dudley is an amiable conductor with a nonstop smile, frequently bending his knees, seemingly irresistibly impelled by rhythms. NOTES S.F. Contemporary Music Players in its 52nd season with Baumbusch premiere, Nancarrow and Salonen, at the Taube Atrium Theater, San Francisco April 13. Online: info@sfcmp.org. Composer Brian Baumbusch presented here comprised only about one-third of the entire opus, according to one participant. Dudley got up to lead a codicil section with an evolved waltz looming in the mist wafting over – a calm after a windstorm, akin to the storm-scene effect in Beethoven’s Sixth Symphony. Tranquility restored. The evolution of “Polytempo Music” was not the sole fruit of the quarantine. Covid actually encouraged the isolation of the musicians, who learned their parts separately at home, then assembled less for rehearsals and more for sound checks and click audibility. Again, Covid forced musical innovation. During the performance the guidance came from an upstage laptop, with the composer herding all the electronics like sheep. Unplug the laptop and the premiere would be lost – we live and die by PG&E. Some prerecorded tracks also filtered in via loudspeakers overhead. The Cancer League, Inc. thecancerleague
articles.title: What next – even self-driving orchestras?

articles.text: Summer vacation is rapidly arriving. Have you made summer plans for your musical kids? Music camps are taking reservations, and some deadlines have already passed. This article is a reminder to make your reservations. Tempus fugit, as the Romans used to say. Music camps in U.S. One of the greatest experiences I ever had was at the Idyllwild Music Camp when I was in the eighth grade. Idyllwild, which is high above Palm Spring, seems to have fallen by the wayside, but there are other camps that will be of interest. Interlochen Music Camp in Michigan is probably the biggest and the most famous in the United States. It offers sessions in all art categories and has a huge enrollment of international scope. Berklee School of Music is another enterprise of international scope. They have campuses in the eastern United States and also in Europe. The Aspen Music Festival in Colorado has operated since 1949 and has a very good reputation. There are also two fine music camps in our area. Cazadero is the more famous. It is located at Russian River, and for many years has maintained its high standards. Everyone I know has spoken well of the experience. La Honda Music Camp is about an hour away from Piedmont in the Santa Cruz Mountains. I was an instructor there some years ago. It was lots of fun for me, and the kids had a good time. Activities include ensembles both large and small, with intensive instrumental instruction. Jazz is a featured element in addition to classical music. The food is good and there are lots of activities. International music camps Two international music camps come to mind. The fine violinist Emil Altschuler has a summer music camp, Altschuler Summer Music Institute, in Rimini, a resort city in Italy. Emil has patterned his music camp around the ideals of Jascha Heifetz. ASMI emphasizes string instruments. Cristiana Pegoraro, who is well known to Piedmont audiences, continues her excellent Narnia Music Festival in Narnia, Italy. To me, the Narnia program encompasses just about everything that I look for. In the first place, it is an all-encompassing music festival. There is a Festival Orchestra and concerts of all kinds. Some of the concerts feature notable concert performers and the students get many opportunities to perform. While music is featured, everyone has the opportunity to study foreign languages, learn about the local history and go on tours. This barely scratches the surface. Narnia is located about an hour north of Rome. It is a beautiful area and also a famous culinary center. Please take my advice: Make your plans and do it soon. Meanwhile back home at the PCA Fine concerts continue apace in our Piedmont Center for the Arts. Last Saturday, the Diluvian Quartet played. They might even be considered the “in House Quartet“ in the Center since they play there so often. The program was rather brief; Mozart’s famous Quartet in D Minor opened the program and Gliere’s String Quartet No. 2 closed the program. Even though my son is a member of the quartet, I feel that I can be objective in my opinions. Diluvian plays with great discipline and attention to musical balance. It is obvious that they enjoy making music. At the conclusion of the concert, the large and faithful audience burst into vociferous applause. That spoke volumes. Cazadero Music Camp on the Russian River
articles.title: Time to sign up for a summer music camp

articles.text: Piedmont Center for the Arts will display a rare exhibit of the photos of the late Bay Area photographer James Mayer taken in Prague, Czechoslovakia the day the country was invaded by the Soviet Union in 1968 Mayer was a student traveling in Europe in 1968 and was in Prague on August 21, 1968, when Soviet tanks entered the streets of the country’s capital. He managed to document the action and get himself and his pictures out of the country. This is the first exhibition of these stunning photos, strikingly familiar to the war in Ukraine today. His widow, Jane Flint, invites community members to a reception at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue, on Friday, April 28 from 6:00 to 8:00 p.m. The exhibit will also be open Saturday and Sunday, April 29-30 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Bay Area photographer Jim Mayer at Sutro Heights in San Francisco in 1988. A Soviet tank is surrounded by Czech citizens after Prague was invaded on August 21, 1968. Czech citizens marching in protest of Soviet invasion August 21, 1968.

articles.text: Kiersey Clemons and Nick Offerman star in Hearts Beat Loud Movies too often barely dip below the surface, satisfied with a superficial patina of affluence or Disneyesque fantasy, the writing resulting in a coarsening failure of language and imagination. Others are replete with pulp cinema action (read violence and a high body count) that can seem a betrayal of film as a possible art form. But there are those small gems that quietly slip into theaters and, remarkably, find that sweet spot while exploring the human condition, such as it is, in a way that resonates. Hearts Beat Loud is exactly such a film, tenderly told, a narrative that focuses on a father-daughter relationship that feels honest and perfectly imperfect. Frank Offerman portrays Frank Fisher, a crusty, single parent, middle-aged, who has had a record store in Red Hook Brooklyn for 17 years. His daughter, Sam (Kiersey Clemmons), is about to leave for UCLA in California with the goal of becoming a doctor. Frank is already feeling like an empty nester, a certain loneliness closing in as he prepares to shut the doors of his record shop for good. But suddenly change is inserting itself into his life – the life of a once rocker, now a dad to a gifted, precocious teen who can act more adult-like than Frank. Sam is also exploring a new relationship with a young artist and gallerista, Rose (Sasha Lane), who is deeply connected to New York. Since she was 12, they have spent evenings jamming. During one such session they create a single record, Hearts Beat Loud, that unexpectedly takes off on Spotify. It proves to be an intoxicating collaboration, a song filled with emotion, with lyrics and music written and sung by Sam, whose lovely voice soars. Frank is captivated and those long ignored feelings that he missed the train some two decades back return and a nudging hope returns: perhaps he will have a second chance. He gives their 2-person music combo the name We’re Not a Band. What is so moving about this film is that every moment that Sam and Frank have together on screen feels true. Authentic. It’s no small thing. Relationships between parents and teens can be both dynamic and a puzzle within a puzzle, In a sense, the music listened to and created by Frank and Sam becomes part of the story’s dialogue and is a metaphor that repeatedly defines their connection. There is also another layer to Hearts Beat Loud, and that is the friendship Frank has with Dave (Ted Danson), a Brooklyn bar owner. Leaning forward, elbows resting on that long plank of oak, Dave behind the bar, Frank on a stool, they talk about the world. And it’s Dave who looks at Frank for a long moment and says, “When life hands you conundrums, you turn them into art.” That small morsel of wisdom reaches Frank who feels a bit buffeted by life and suddenly at loose ends. It’s a nice moment. As are those moments he spends with Leslie (Toni Collette), his landlord, who reaches out to him and realizes, after an unfortunate encounter, that his rough edges might need a bit of sanding. Hearts Beat Loud is a stirring affirmation, and the music is surprising and uplifting. Hearts Beat Loud. Directed by Brett Haley. Starring Nick Offerman, Kiersey Clemons, Ted Danson. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2018. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Spotlight is not a lament for that moment in journalistic history when ink on paper reporting was still the tip of the spear and valued above all else as a way to inform the public about community life and its institutions. There is nothing about this film that is mournful or melodramatic, which, given its subject matter, it could have been. Rather, it is a celebration of the role fine journalism has played in the health of our democracy, in this case the Boston Globe newspaper. Spotlight is also a newspaper procedural in which a shocking and wrenching story is first investigated and then, finally, going to press after some eight months of “shoe leather” research and interviews and tenacious digging and then waiting until all the pieces fit and the paper concludes unequivocally it had it right. Note that the recent film Truth was a story about the CBS investigation into George W. Bush’s military record. But it was rushed and ultimately the center could not hold and finally unraveled, ending careers. What the Globe did right was demonstrate a careful and granular deliberateness that eventually resulted in the journalists and the paper receiving a Pulitzer Prize. To its credit, the film avoids righteous indignation, histrionics, and all tantalizing speechifying. Rather it almost stoically conveys a tension defined by reluctance and anxiety and restraint as the reporters pursue a story that no one really wants to tell, yet for all those involved know must be told. It’s the very essence of the craft of journalism and defines the moral center of what it means to be a newspaper and newspaper reporter. The year is 2002. In the first set piece of the film, an editor is retiring from The Boston Globe, and staff and editors are waiting for the newly hired Editor-in-Chief, Marty Baron (Liev Shreiber), to arrive from the Miami Herald. One of the first stories that Baron wants the investigative team to revisit is an incident between a child and a local Catholic priest. The reporting team – Spotlight) – consists of Walter “Robbie” Robinson (Michael Keaton), Sacha Pfieffer (Rachel McAdams), Michael Rezendes (Mark Ruffalo) and Matt Carrol (Brian d’Arcy). With some initial reluctance, the team, led by Robinson, begins to peel, ever so painstakingly, an onion that unexpectedly becomes a massive story. It is an archival dig, involving interviews and clippings and city hall records. It means going to court, asking for the release of documents, and, above all, it means overcoming the community’s hostility and the Church’s stonewalling silence. Slowly, however, the team begins to realize that the initial event – one priest, one child – was not a one-off but represented the tip of an iceberg of behavior that reached from the Bishop’s office to the farthest corners of the archdiocese. In the aggregate, the story proves to be a seismic scandal involving the sexual abuse of countless children of Boston by priests. Gradually the reporters come to understand that it occurred because of the collusive response by the Catholic Church as priest after priest was moved from parish to parish, some placed on sick leave, others listed as simply on leave, while the Church used its power and influence to expunge the records and wrap itself in a cloak of conspiratorial secrecy. Spotlight is an astonishingly well-made film, and an example of what fine ensemble acting can achieve. There is no one actor who carries the film. There is only a solid group of actors, each creating a portrayal that is idiosyncratic, flawed and very human. As well, the film has a washedout feel to it, one created by claustrophobic newsrooms with dropped ceilings and fluorescent lighting as the camera holds consistent wide shots, rarely singling out any one individual. It might be hard to imagine that a procedural film, set in basements and stark rooms, could generate atmospherics akin to a murder mystery. And yet, that is exactly what Spotlight achieves. It’s a remarkable film. Spotlight. Directed by Tom McCarthy. Starring Mark Ruffalo, Michael Keaton, Rachel McAdam. 2 hrs., 7 min. Rated R. Released 2015. Now streaming on VUUDU/Prime/HBO MAX,

articles.text: A scene from Happy Feet Happy Feet is charming and playful, making this rollicking tale of a unique penguin named Mumble (Elijah Wood) seem decidedly fresh. Apparently, every Emperor penguin sings a unique song called a “heartsong,” used to attract a mate. If the males’ song matches the females’ song, well, they mate, which is what occurred with Mumble’s parents, Norma Jean (Nicole Kidman) and Memphis (Hugh Jackman). As a result, Norma Jean lays an egg, which she leaves in the care of Memphis while she and the other females go off to fish. It’s a harsh winter, and Memphis accidentally drops the egg. When the new chick, Mumble, is finally born, the parents discover that he can’t sing, but can tap dance. Mumble soon becomes a young adult whose feet never stop moving. The elders, led by Noah (Hugo Weaving), grumpily take exception to Mumble’s dancing and ridicule him for being different. Meanwhile, we learn that he has a secret crush on the talented Gloria (Brittany Murphy), but doesn’t have the “heartsong” that is so necessary to find a companion. Meanwhile, Mumble meets a group of mini-Mexican Adelie penguins, called “the Amigos,” whose leader is Ramon Lovelace (Robin Williams) who is willing to help Mumble court Gloria (Ramon sings “My Way” while Mumble lip-synchs). Naturally, Gloria falls for him. Soon all the young penguins are singing and tap dancing to “Boogie Wonderland.” The elders, of course, are appalled. Mumble is ordered to stop, but refuses, and is exiled from the flock, blamed for what has been a lean fishing season. And so Mumble’s adventure begins. It takes him all the way to Australia where he ends up in a marine sanctuary where kids, one girl in particular, can stand and watch him swimming behind massive glass panes. The girl taps on the glass and Mumble, with his beak, taps back, hoping to communicate with the humans. Event ually, Mumble is released from the sanctuary and finds his way home to his flock. Upon his return he challenges the elders and prevails, and soon everyone is dancing and celebrating, most especially Mumble and Gloria and Ramon. Happy Feet. Directed by George Miller. Voices of Elijah Wood, Robin Williams, Brittany Murphy. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG. Released in 2006. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/HBO MAX/ Apple tv.
articles.title: Happy Feet – a penguin who can’t sing, but can tap dance

articles.text: On ancient maps, when cartographers came to a part of the world that had yet to be explored, they would write, “Here Be Dragons.” What they could have written is “Here Be Beasts.” And it’s around such unknown places a mythology grew of intrepid seafarers who hunted these beasts, which is the sweet spot of Netflix’s brilliantly animated, photo-realistic The Sea Beast, nominated for an Oscar this year. At the center of this imaginative tale is an adventure-seeking, fierce, and delightful protagonist, 11-year-old Maisie Brumble (Zaris-Angel Hator) who runs away from an orphanage, determined to stow away on a magnificent square-rigger, one that is known to place itself in harm’s way as it searches the seas for monsters/ One monster in particular is known as the Red Buster. Maisie sneaks on board a ship with enormous red sails and helmed by the notorious one-eyed captain Crow (Jared Harris) who lost his eye in a battle with Red, Jacob Holland (voiced by Karl Urban) and Maisie Brumble (voiced by Zaris-Angel Hator) in The Sea Beast the fearsome dragon-like monster. Think of him as Ahab and Red Buster as the white whale. His first mate is Sarah Sharpe (Marianne Jean Baptiste). Of course, Maisie is soon discovered on board by the heroic Jacob Holland (Karl Urban), the future heir to captain Crow. And so the two set out on an exciting journey, finding an unexpected kinship, We soon learn that Jacob is also an orphan. The two are shipwrecked on a tropical island, they encounter a rival ship, the Imperator, captained by admiral Hornagold (Don Stevens), and encounter a bevy of perilous situations with a myriad of sea creatures. The Sea Beast is a rousing good yarn, set in the early 1700s, with remarkable visuals – constantly roiling seas, tentacled monsters that take umbrage at the intrusion of the likes of Crow or Hornagold. Kids will love this enthralling story, and they will take delight in the chutzapah of the adorable and vibrant Maisie. The Sea Beast. Animated. Directed by Chris Williams. With voices of Karl Urban, Zaris-Angel Hator, and Jared Harris. 1 hr., 55 min. Rated PG. Released 2022. Now streaming on Netflix
articles.title: The Sea Beast a wonderful children’s tale of adventure

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, Aprl 19, 2023 Features The Wine Corner Wines of the Northern Rhone – Part 2 By Pierre DuMont In my previous article I wrote about a recent visit to the Northern Rhone Valley in France. The Northern Rhone is considered the part of the river that stretches from Vienne south to just before Valence – some 40 miles. Last week I wrote about the northern part of the region focusing on the AVA’s of Cote Rotie and Condrieu home to some of the greatest Syrahs and Viogniers in the world. As we shift to the southern part of the region, Syrah remains the only red grape that is allowed, while the white wines shift from Viognier to Marsanne and RousThe M. Chapoutier tasting room in Tain l’Hermitage. The chapel on top of Hermitage hill sanne. These two powerhouse white grapes are used separately or sometimes blended to create intense long-lived succulent wines. Hermitage One of France’s most famous vineyard sites is Hermitage hill on the east bank of the Rhone across from the town of Tain. The river turns here and the hill, a granitic outcrop, and an extension of the Massif Central, faces south giving perfect exposure to ripen the grapes. Standing on the top of the hill next to the old stone chapel once home to a hermit, you sense that you are in a spiritual place – the spiritual home of the Syrah grape. It is believed that winemaking here goes back to the Roman times but there are no clear records before the 17th century. Hermitage was an official wine in the French courts of King Louis XIII and Louis XIV, and Thomas Jefferson stopped for a visit on his wine tour of France and praised the white wines made here. He even had some shipped back to his home in Virginia. M. Chapoutier A book I was handed simply said “M. Chapoutier Universe.” It is a catalogue of all the wines produced by Michel Chapoutier and his partners around the world. In addition to his massive work in the Rhone Valley, he has partnerships in Australia, Spain, Portugal, Germany and many non-Rhone parts of France, with hundreds and hundreds of wines. I have often heard Michel Chapoutier described as “energetic” but it’s hard to imagine how he can keep track of all of his ventures. Entering the stylish tasting room on a small street in Tain is like entering a temple devoted to wine. We were treated to a private tasting hosted by Michel’s son Maxime (who has developed his own line of beer called One Shot). The tasting began with a 15 euro Viognier that was refreshing and light. Ten wines later it ended with the Le Pavillion Ermitage, a 436 euro ($478) masterpiece of Syrah. After the tasting Maxine took us for lunch at the Ferraton winery overlooking the river. Ferraton is owned by Chapoutier but is managed separately and the house has its own style. After a lunch of grilled sardines, we had the opportunity to taste the Ferraton range of wines. I had never tasted their wines and was pleasantly surprised to discover they were an outstanding lineup. I was also glad to find out they are widely available in the US thanks to K&L Wines in San Francisco. See Wine Corner on page 30 Maxime Chapoutier conducts our tasting. The quaint village of Cornas. articles.text: Community members are invited to join the Walking on Wednesdays group on April 26 for a special docent-led tour of historic Mountain View Cemetery. The tour will be led by long-time Mountain View docent Dennis Evanosky, who has written two books about Oakland’s history, Oakland’s Mountain View Cemetery, and Oakland’s Laurel District. He has also written books about Alameda and San Francisco. The tour of the cemetery will include details of its section devoted to veterans of the Civil War. Besides its flowers and historic monuments, the cemetery has expansive views of Oakland, the Bay, and San Francisco, which the walkers always also enjoy. Participants should plan to meet in front of Mountain View’s main mausoleum on Wednesday, April 26 at 10:30 a.m. The cemetery is located at 5000 Piedmont Avenue at the end of Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. There is parking inside the cemetery. The tour will last for about 1 hour and 45 minutes. For more information, please contact Dick Carter at camktgrp@comcast.net. A large group of walkers received a guided tour of Millionaires’ Row at Mountain View Cemetery on Wednessday, October 27, 2021.
articles.title: Walking Tour of Mt. View Cemetery on April 26

articles.text: The Piedmont Adult School is hosting a three-day Expo this weekend, Friday-Sunday, April 21-23 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia. The Adult School has dozens of affordable class options during its spring session, portions and aspects of the course offerings which will be on display during the Expo for the first time. A reception on Friday, April 21, from 5:00-8:00 p.m. will feature live demonstrations, complimentary food and an art exhibit of student work. It will provide an opportunity for the community to meet the instructors and learn more about the wide variety of classes offered by the Adult School. On Saturday and Sunday, April 22-23, from 11:00 a.m.-2:00 p.m., there will be open gallery hours to view the art exhibit. The expo is free and open to all. The open gallery runs concurrently with the Piedmont FoodFest on Sunday, which will be right around the corner at Piedmont Park. “The PCA is delighted to be working with the Adult School. We see this as a very logical collaboration to display the wide range of classes and activities they have. We hope this is beginning of a very wonderful relationship,” said Center for the Arts president Sue Malick. articles.text: There’s a montage of helpless families being evicted, before Tom joins his long-suffering mother, played by Jane Darwell, who won a Best Supporting Oscar for her role. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a treat last week when architect Jim Kellogg led the group in the absence of Dick Carter. His topic was the introduction of Berkeley Arts and Crafts architecture to Piedmont between 1910 and 1926. He explained that Berkeley Arts and Crafts started with teaching, mentoring, and development of the Arts and Crafts movement by Bernard Maybeck in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He collaborated with and mentored three leading architects on whom the walk focused: John Galen Howard, Julia Morgan, and John Hudson Thomas. Morgan and Thomas met in the office of Howard. Morgan and Thomas became well recognized by the Berkeley School of Architecture. They adopted and built their practices around the Arts and Crafts movement, and each designed numerous notable single-family homes in Piedmont. Although Howard did not design any projects in Piedmont, his influence on Morgan and Thomas was important. Another architect Kellogg included in the tour was Albert Farr. He played a key role in master planning and building Piedmont during this period. His works included: the Piedmont Community Center, City Hall, the Christian Science Church (now The Piedmont Center for the Arts), the Exedra, Piedmont Community Church, and many single-family homes. All three of the famous architects practiced at the same time and designed projects in Piedmont. They had their own styles, and also client bases and political connections that influenced their careers. Morgan embraced arts and crafts and integrated it with classical design popular at that time. She was the first woman to receive a degree from the Beaux Arts School of Architecture in Paris, and the first women to become a registered architect in California. She became famous because of her employment by William Randolph Hearst to design Heart Castle. Thomas also embraced the arts and crafts movement and developed his own “exuberant style” of design and craftsman detailing. His career was focused on luxury single-family homes in the East Bay and San Francisco, but he did not have connections with people such as Hearst. Farr is well respected for his talent, but his style would be described as “eclectic.” The Piedmont Community Church masterpiece is pure California Mission style, but Farr also produced English Tudor, French Classical, as well as Arts and Crafts buildings depending on what his clients wanted. He lived in Piedmont for a while and became well connected with City government including Frank C. Havens which led to many important commissions. A large group of 37 walkers and three K-9 best friends participated in Walking on Wednesdays’ walk on March 12.
