articles.text: Lillian Rubenstein, a woman of style and grace, died at the age of 100 years and 8 months on April 4, 2023 in her home with her three children by her side. She passed away peacefully following a brief period of declining health with a large, smiling picture of her late husband Bob immediately next to her. Lillian was born on July 15, 1922 in Philadelphia. She was the only child of Ukrainian immigrants, Abe and Anna Cohen and was raised as an only child by her mother after her father passed away when she was only three months old. In the late 1920’s, Anna and Lillian came to California at the beginning of the Great Depression, ultimately finding their way to Stockton where Lillian was raised and schooled. She graduated from Stockton High at age 16. In the defining moment of her life, Lillian went to a youth gathering in Petaluma in May 1939 where by chance she met a shy, blond haired, blue-eyed 18-yearold boy from Oakland, Bob Rubenstein. She was as immediately and powerfully attracted to Bob as he was to her. They began a 2 1/2-year long-distance courtship between Stockton and Oakland that culminated on December 14, 1941, when the young couple was married. That day was the beginning of an idyllic, extraordinary almost fairytale relationship that ended only in 2018 when, after 76 1/2 years of a perfect, loving marriage, Bob passed away. Those many years were filled with as much joy, pleasure, happiness, fulfillment and love as any two people could possibly have enjoyed. During that time, the couple had three children, built a home in Piedmont in 1950 that they occupied until Lillian’s passing. They were fortunate enough to enjoy good health and life treated them very well. During their many years together, they created a large and loving family, formed countless extraordinarily close and enduring friendships and enjoyed many, many exciting, varied and wonderful life experiences together. Bob and Lillian complemented each other perfectly with Lillian’s active, outgoing, energetic and strong-willed personality contrasting perfectly and, as recently as last month, took a keen interest in the trials and tribulations of the Warriors. She was known for both her skill and competitiveness as a tennis player. Well into her 100th year, she remained an accomplished mahjong player who thoroughly enjoyed the company of the ladies with whom she played. Lillian and Bob were members of Temple Sinai continuously since 1956 and Claremont Country Club for over 25 years. In her younger years, she was an active member of her socially conscious sorority, Theta Delta Xi. In later years she devoted substantial time and energy to The Cancer League and Hoe and Hope community garden club. Lillian enjoyed the happiest and most fulfilling life one could ever hope to lead. She overcame the adversity of a difficult childhood and devoted her life to being the best, most dedicated and loving wife, mother and friend that she could possibly be. She lived a full and wonderful life. Lillian is predeceased by her ever-adoring husband Bob who passed away in 2018. She is survived by her three loving children, Ron (Erica), Craig (Terri) and Barbee, and by nine grandchildren, Jeff Rubenstein (Amie), Tracy Weis (Brett), Greg Rubenstein (Whitney), Lisa Sommer (Justin), Kim Radtke, Brian Rubenstein (Haleh), Morgan Nelson (Charlie), Mallory Johnston (John) and Tim Johnston (Courtney). She also leaves behind 15 precious great-grandchildren. The family particularly acknowledges and thank Dr. Dean Nickles for his extraordinary and attentive care, and caregivers Dhel Sanchez and Bambi Lao for the warm and compassionate care they gave Lillian during her final days. The family will be forever grateful. The family will host a gathering celebrating Lillian’s welllived 100 plus years on April 25. pages.text: 26 Wednesday, Aprl 19, 2023 Obituary Lillian Rubenstein dies at 100 Lillian Rubenstein, a woman of style and grace, died at the age of 100 years and 8 months on April 4, 2023 in her home with her three children by her side. She passed away peacefully following a brief period of declining health with a large, smiling picture of her late husband Bob immediately next to her. Lillian was born on July 15, 1922 in Philadelphia. She was the only child of Ukrainian immigrants, Abe and Anna Cohen and was raised as an only child by her mother after her father passed away when she was only three months old. In the late 1920’s, Anna and Lillian came to California at the beginning of the Great Depression, ultimately finding their way to Stockton where Lillian was raised and schooled. She graduated from Stockton High at age 16. In the defining moment of her life, Lillian went to a youth gathering in Petaluma in May 1939 where by chance she met a shy, blond haired, blue-eyed 18-yearold boy from Oakland, Bob Rubenstein. She was as immediately and powerfully attracted to Bob as he was to her. They began a 2 1/2-year long-distance courtship between Stockton and Oakland that culminated on December 14, 1941, when the young couple was married. That day was the beginning of an idyllic, extraordinary almost fairytale relationship that ended only in 2018 when, after 76 1/2 years of a perfect, loving marriage, Bob passed away. Those many years were filled with as much joy, pleasure, happiness, fulfillment and love as any two people could possibly have enjoyed. During that time, the couple had three children, built a home in Piedmont in 1950 that they occupied until Lillian’s passing. They were fortunate enough to enjoy good health and life treated them very well. During their many years together, they created a large and loving family, formed countless extraordinarily close and enduring friendships and enjoyed many, many exciting, varied and wonderful life experiences together. Bob and Lillian complemented each other perfectly with Lillian’s active, outgoing, energetic and strong-willed personality contrasting perfectly and, as recently as last month, took a keen interest in the trials and tribulations of the Warriors. She was known for both her skill and competitiveness as a tennis player. Well into her 100th year, she remained an accomplished mahjong player who thoroughly enjoyed the company of the ladies with whom she played. Lillian and Bob were members of Temple Sinai continuously since 1956 and Claremont Country Club for over 25 years. In her younger years, she was an active member of her socially conscious sorority, Theta Delta Xi. In later years she devoted substantial time and energy to The Cancer League and Hoe and Hope community garden club. Lillian enjoyed the happiest and most fulfilling life one could ever hope to lead. She overcame the adversity of a difficult childhood and devoted her life to being the best, most dedicated and loving wife, mother and friend that she could possibly be. She lived a full and wonderful life. Lillian is predeceased by her ever-adoring husband Bob who passed away in 2018. She is survived by her three loving children, Ron (Erica), Craig (Terri) and Barbee, and by nine grandchildren, Jeff Rubenstein (Amie), Tracy Weis (Brett), Greg Rubenstein (Whitney), Lisa Sommer (Justin), Kim Radtke, Brian Rubenstein (Haleh), Morgan Nelson (Charlie), Mallory Johnston (John) and Tim Johnston (Courtney). She also leaves behind 15 precious great-grandchildren. The family particularly acknowledges and thank Dr. Dean Nickles for his extraordinary and attentive care, and caregivers Dhel Sanchez and Bambi Lao for the warm and compassionate care they gave Lillian during her final days. The family will be forever grateful. The family will host a gathering celebrating Lillian’s welllived 100 plus years on April 25. Those interested in attending may send an email to Barbeerube@ gmail.com. articles.text: On Wednesday, March 8, eighteen Piedmont Seniors ventured to KQED’s new facility on Mariposa Street in San Francisco, where the group was able to see both the television and the radio studios. KQED’s new building now incorporates state of the art technology, as almost everything now is computerized and is managed in the control booths. Even the camera movements are done remotely. The Piedmont Seniors also were able to see the studio where Leslie Sbrocco hosts the popular show “Check Please Bay Area”. The building is ADA accessible, allowing people with limited mobility to enjoy the studios. The elevators take visitors to the fourth floor for a breathtaking view of San Francisco. Two knowledgeable volunteer docents met with the Piedmont Seniors to provide an intimate tour. While there, the Seniors met the KQED CEO and President Michael Isip, who said “an informed, inspired and involved citizenry is the foundation of a healthy democracy.” KQED wants to spark curiosity and build bridges across people’s curiosity as they encourage diversity, creativity and trust. KQED’s mission is public service by providing the community with an alternative to commercial media so the public can make more informed decisions regarding politics and other differing opinions. KQED first went on the air in 1954 and was predominantly used for quality children’s programs. It is a non-profit, non-commercial entity that relies on public donations in the form of grants, endowments and bequests. Federal funding through the Corporation for Public Broadcasting makes up less than 10% of its budget. KQED encourages students to explore the facility so they can be exposed to new people, places, and ideas. The station also includes regular free podcasts in addition to their radio and television broadcasts. After the tour, the Piedmont Seniors headed to the Embarcadero for a tasty luncheon at Atwater Tavern. This was the first time the group has been welcomed at the entrance to a restaurant by its owner. Parking is always difficult in San Francisco, but the owner had reserved some spots for the Seniors. The upstairs provides a lovely view of the waterfront and is often used for parties, special events and wedding receptions. The Seniors’ driver, Jim Ayotte, who happens to also be a member of the Piedmont Seniors, is very knowledgeable about the terrain of San Francisco. So, as an extra highlight of the day he acted as a tour guide, and was eager to point out the newer buildings, and give the group some history of the area. Piedmont Seniors pose for a photo on the set of “Check Please Bay Area” at KQED Public television station in San Francisco. Pictured are (front) Yorkman Lowe (left), Arlene Garfinkle, Sue Getreuer, Merilee Hoffman, Marianne Friedman, Tanya and Larry Hu; (back) Jim Ayotte, Piedmont Seniors’ Coordinator Janet Epstein, Ann Morales, Irene Westler, Fred Pemberton, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Mona Jamieson, Carole Jones, Gregory Jurin, and Patti and Larry Singer. Piedmont police officer Tyler Petit will provide Piedmont Seniors with detailed information on remaining safe and avoiding being victims of crime. His talk, titled Safety For Seniors, will take place at the Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, at 11 a.m. a.m. on Wednesday, April 26 as part of the Piedmont Seniors’ regular monthly meeting. By Cookie Segelstein Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I am going to be traveling. My neighbor just came back from being overseas and her phone was hacked. What kind of precautions can I take to prevent that from happening to me? Bert C., Oakland Dear Bert: Your timing on that question is excellent because the FBI just put out a statement last week for travelers and the public to avoid using free charging stations in airports, hotels, restaurants and shopping centers. They said in their announcement that hackers have found a way to use public USB ports to introduce malware, and even monitoring software onto devices. Devices like iPhones, and iPads, with compromised USB cables can be hijacked through software that can access usernames and passwords. When we travel by air, it seems like a welcome convenience that we can just plug our phones and iPads into USB ports that are often in the waiting area of the gate. It’s nice not to have to carry the charger, and just carry the USB cable. And, of course, more and more airlines, have these ports available right at your seat, even in economy. But according to the FBI, and cyber security experts, this is not safe. So, what are you to do when you must travel for many hours and your devices run out of juice? Just carry your own charger and plug it into an available electrical outlet instead. Yes, it’s bulkier, but it’s nothing compared to the nightmare of having your device hacked and even in some cases your identity stolen. This warning by the FBI is not new, the FCC has warned about “juice jacking” (as the malware and hacking scheme is called) since 2021. More and more, bad actors are finding a way to get into our devices. So, as we load more sensitive information onto our devices, we have to be more vigilant. The same caution applies to using public Wi-Fi, whether it’s in a hotel or airport, or coffee shop. If you must use public Wi-Fi, make sure you do not log into any sites that require a password, because hackers could be using software to capture sensitive information, like credit card numbers, and of course usernames and passwords. So, for example, sitting in an airport on the public Wi-Fi is not a good time to log into your bank, or to log into a retail site and use your credit card to buy something. If you must do work or have access to a site where you need to put in sensitive information, it’s vital that you subscribe to a VPN, which is a Virtual Private Network. This type of service encrypts your activity on the web and keeps your identity hidden while surfing. Some of the top reviewed VPNs are CyberGhost, Private Internet Access, NordVPN, and there are several more. Also, make sure your device is not set to automatically connect to available Wi-Fi networks. If you don’t need it, turn Bluetooth off also. Change your passwords to sites you may visit online before you travel, and then change them again when you get home. When you are on the website, make sure it says “https” instead of just “http” (the “s” stands for “secure”). And, of course, when you get back home, check your credit card statements for any unrecognized charges. Enjoy your trip but be careful out there. articles.text: Presumably everyone wants to be healthy on each birthday, but the focus of healthy aging is often on those who are middle aged and beyond. articles.text: When we read about Grandparenting today, how likely is it that we are really referring to Grandmothering? How often does the professional advice and guidance actually support the experience of the grandfathers in the family? Chances are, not often. To be fair, in most families where grandparents play a significant caregiving role, the majority of the care is likely to be provided by grandmothers. But perhaps it’s time to think more broadly about gender stereotyping for grandfathers. Many grandfathers today played a much more active role in the raising of their children than their own fathers did. A grandfather today who raised children in the 80’s and 90’s is likely to have changed diapers and read bedtime stories, have been active in Dad’s clubs, school boards, Scouts, and coached their children in all kinds of sports. They probably attended school parent events, knew who the pediatrician was, and filled out forms for camps. Many of these activities would have been unknown to their own fathers. But even if a dad wasn’t a hands-on parent of little ones when he was young, the role of grandfather may be just what he has been waiting for his whole life. Some men may see this period in their life as a time to redeem themselves if they were less than present when his children were small. Maybe Grandpa regrets how much he was away on business, or how often he had to work nights and weekends, or maybe he just feels that the women in the family subtly nudged him out of a caregiving role he might have enjoyed. If the role of grandfather comes at a time when a man may have fewer professional pressures and obligations, if he is fit and healthy, and desires a meaningful role with his grandchildren, the possibilities for him are endless. The first step for a family is actually recognizing a grandfather’s hopes and dreams for his role. New parents may minimize the kinds of things they can expect from a new grandfather, and overemphasize a grandmother’s role. But whereas a grandmother may feel delighted to be able to use some of her skills and experience from years ago, a grandfather may be feeling a sense that he can now offer a young child something he didn’t manage to offer when he was a young father. Men are grandparents, too. They delight in their grandchildren, want to see them safe and healthy, and want to teach them many things that they feel are important for success in life. Some grandfathers may worry that the family doesn’t trust them with the care of small children, or maybe they are only thought of as financial supporters. But many have a deep desire to be close to grandchildren and to have a significant and meaningful role in their lives. If you are a grandfather, speak your truth to your family and let them know what you are hoping for as the years go on. If you want to be more involved with caregiving but feel unsure of yourself, find out how to get more education about childcare today. Seek support from other grandfathers if you can find it in your area or online. Make sure that your family knows what legacy you’d like to leave after you’re gone. If your children have a grandfather, open your mind to what he may have to offer your children. Ask him to share his feelings about being a grandfather. You might be very surprised by what you learn. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Grandparent Meet-Ups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn. com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@itstheirturn.com. articles.text: According to the National Institute on Aging, more than one-third of people age 65 years and older fall each year. The fear of falling becomes more common as people age. When an in-person “Matter of Balance” class became available, this program seemed relevant for Piedmont Seniors and proved to be very worthwhile. For eight weeks a dedicated group of 12 seniors have met in two-hour sessions to learn ways to prevent falls by learning about improved balance. The key to the program is learning the proper exercises to strengthen arms, legs, and ankles and to increase flexibility. During one session a physical therapist spoke about how to avoid falls, and the group learned the best ways to get up after falling while minimizing injury. This community service presentation was sponsored by the Alameda County of Emergency Services through its Injury Prevention Program. To learn more about the Piedmont Seniors activities, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: Domaine Guy Farge The appellation of Saint Joseph used to be a small region based just north of the city of Tournon in villages like Saint-Jean-deMuzols. About 30 years ago they expanded the appellation to include the entire west bank of the Rhone from Tournon up to Condrieu – about 20 miles. A lot of that territory is not the greatest for growing grapes, so it’s best to stick with the original villages. When we got out of the car at Domaine Guy Farge, we stared up at an impossibly steep hill with narrow terraces of one or two rows of grapes. It was hard to imagine physically working on a nearly 45-degree slope, yet many of the vines are over 100 years old. We were greeted by Thomas Farge who has now taken over the winemaking tasks from his father Thomas Farge takes the reins at Domaine Guy Farge. In the top of the sixth, Bell hit a one-out single and Hunt sent her home to score with a triple to the left field fence. Gerhardy then hit a single past the third baseman to score Hunt. However, the Bruins tacked on four runs in the bottom half to enact the 10-run rule. Final stats: Bell went 3-for-4 with four runs scored, one RBI, the Hornets tacked on three tuns in the top-of-the-third and another three in the top of the fifth. Piedmont rallied for two runs in the bottom of the seventh inning, but had to settle for a 7-3 loss. Final stats: McConathy went 1-for-2 with a home run, two runs scored, one RBI, and one walk. Papahadajopolous went 1-for-3 with one run. Aikawa went 1-for- 4. Lagios had one RBI and drew two walks. NEXT UP Piedmont (8-5 overall, 2-2 league) travels to Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland tonight, April 19, for a 6:30 p.m. game. PHS then hosts O’Dowd at Witter Field on Friday, April 21 at 4:00 p.m. and four stolen bases. Hunt went 2-for-4 with a triple, two RBIs, and one run scored. Gerhardy went 2-for-4 with three RBIs. Fujimoto went 1-for-4 with a triple, two runs scored, and an RBI. Wu went 1-for-2 with two runs scored, one walk, and two stolen bases. Leggett went 1-for-3 with an RBI. articles.text: At their Monday, April 3, meeting, the City Council directed city staff to move forward with the commemoration of Sidney and Irene Dearing, Piedmont’s first Black homeowners, at the triangle park in the median of Wildwood Drive at Nova Avenue. In 1924, soon after the Dearings bought their home near the intersection, the couple was targeted by hundreds of white residents who demanded that the couple move out of Piedmont. After three bombs were planted on their lawn, the Dearings sold the house in 1925. Recently retired City Administrator Sara Lillevand said that since May 2022 a Park Commission subcommittee has been working with city staff, Dearing family descendants, a consultant named Cornelia Sylvester, and community members to explore options to create a commemoration near the home the Dearings occupied. Sylvester said she worked with Dearing family members “to establish guiding principles” for the project: “It should be visible from the street, not just from inside the park. It should teach a little something about Sydney Sidney and Irene Dearing 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com REVIEWERS

articles.text: As I write it is Maundy Thursday 2023. Tonight, many Christians will hold communion services recalling Jesus’ last supper with his disciples. Some of the services will include ceremonial foot washings recognizing that Jesus, modeling servanthood, washed the feet of his disciples. Tomorrow, there will be Good Friday services aplenty. Some of them will last three hours and include sermons on the “Seven Last Words” of Jesus, a compilation of the seven sayings the four gospels record Jesus speaking from the cross. Woven into almost all the services will be the refrain “Jesus died for our sins.” Accompanying these words will be the very widespread interpretation of the crucifixion as some sort of atoning sacrifice, of Jesus laying down his life to make payment for our sins. Almost reluctantly – for to question the theology of substitutionary atonement is heretical to many – I find it necessary to note that this is not the only possible way to interpret the crucifixion. Indeed, from very early times there has been, and continues to be, lively debate about how best to interpret and how best to understand the death of Jesus. In our churches we often hear it said, “The ground is level at the foot of the cross.” I would add “On the level ground at the foot of the cross, there has never been only one officially approved theology of the cross.” In an article titled, “What For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. In 1924, soon after the Dearings bought their home near the intersection, the couple was targeted by hundreds of white residents who demanded that the couple move out of Piedmont. After three bombs were planted on their lawn, the Dearings sold the house in 1925. Recently retired City Administrator Sara Lillevand said that since May 2022 a Park Commission subcommittee has been working with city staff, Dearing family descendants, a consultant named Cornelia Sylvester, and community members to explore options to create a commemoration near the home the Dearings occupied. Sylvester said she worked with Dearing family members “to establish guiding principles” for the project: “It should be visible from the street, not just from inside the park. Tonight, many Christians will hold communion services recalling Jesus’ last supper with his disciples. Some of the services will include ceremonial foot washings recognizing that Jesus, modeling servanthood, washed the feet of his disciples. Tomorrow, there will be Good Friday services aplenty. Some of them will last three hours and include sermons on the “Seven Last Words” of Jesus, a compilation of the seven sayings the four gospels record Jesus speaking from the cross. Woven into almost all the services will be the refrain “Jesus died for our sins.” Accompanying these words will be the very widespread interpretation of the crucifixion as some sort of atoning sacrifice, of Jesus laying down his life to make payment for our sins. Almost reluctantly – for to question the theology of substitutionary atonement is heretical to many – I find it necessary to note that this is not the only possible way to interpret the crucifixion. Indeed, from very early times there has been, and continues to be, lively debate about how best to interpret and how best to understand the death of Jesus. In our churches we often hear it said, “The ground is level at the foot of the cross.” I would add “On the level ground at the foot of the cross, there has never been only one officially approved theology of the cross.” In an article titled, “What Collecting photos for Where in the World For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. De La Torre, Professor of Social Ethics and Latinx Studies at Illiff School of Theology in Denver, suggests an alternative interpretation: Jesus’ death neither pays a ransom nor is a substitution for us. Crucifixion is an act of radical solidarity, specifically, Jesus’ choice to accompany in solidarity those dying on the crosses of religious and political oppression… To pick up our crosses and follow Jesus is an invitation not to suffer but to stand in solidarity with the oppressed of the world, a solidarity which might cost us everything. In this theology of the cross, the emphasis falls on Jesus’ refusal to turn a blind eye to the suffering of the world, his refusal to ignore those that die because someone else wants their land, his refusal to pretend that people are not crushed because they threaten the comfortable lifestyles of the powerful. articles.text: Dr. James Allison (front, left) with California Colorectal Cancer Coalition board members. Last February, longtime Piedmont resident Dr. James Allison received a 2023 Visionary Award from the California Colorectal Cancer Coalition (C4) for championing low-cost colorectal cancer screening options. The award is among many lifetime achievements for Allison. He is also a C4 Board Member; a retired gastroenterologist from Kaiser Oakland Medical Center; a Fellow of the American College of Physicians and of the American Gastroenterological Association; a Clinical Professor of Medicine Emeritus at UCSF; and a member of the Division of Gastroenterology at UCSF and the San Francisco General Hospital. Other notable professional awards he has received include the Lowell Beal, MD Award from Kaiser Oakland Medical Center “in appreciation of his example of academic excellence combined with warm humanity” (1996); the Premier Physician Award from the Bay Area Chapter of the Crohn’s and Colitis Foundation (2003); and the Distinguished Clinician Award from the American Gastroenterological Association (2004). Since 2000, Dr. Allison has worked as an ad hoc consultant to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the National Cancer Institute (NCI), and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) on issues concerned with screening for colorectal cancer. Over the course of his career Allison has become a national and international expert on colorectal cancer screening. He was the first person in the U.S. to show, in a publication in The New England Journal of Medicine in 1996, that a certain kind of fecal immunochemical test (FIT) was superior to the standard guaiac fecal occult blood test being used for screening for colorectal cancer. Speaking on the FIT test, he said, “Many countries in the rest of the world have been using stool tests for years; the U.S. is an outlier. Until around 2012, all that people were told they could have for colon cancer prevention was a colonoscopy. It’s very important to test for colon cancer, but you don’t have to spend that money or go through that hassle” as opposed to a FIT test. Currently, Allison works with C4 and the California and San Francisco Departments of Public Health to increase colorectal cancer screening rates in underserved populations by instituting a FIT-based screening program in clinics served by safety net hospitals. Dr. Allison’s screening and IBD research has been published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, The New England Journal of Medicine, Gastroenterology, Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology, the Journal of the National Cancer Institute and other peer-reviewed journals. He has been quoted in Prevention Magazine, the Ladies’ Home Journal, the Wall Street Journal, the San Francisco Chronicle and the New York Times.

articles.text: Piedmont City Council approved a new traffic and safety design plan at Nova Drive and Magnolia Avenue at its meeting on April 3. The current painted-stripe “bollard island”, approved by Council in April 2019 and installed that year in July, will be replaced by a permanent, curb-defined traffic island with a pedestrian crosswalk through it. The island will provide direction to westbound drivers on Magnolia. The plan also includes an eastbound left turn pocket to allow sight distance for vehicles turning left from Magnolia onto Nova. The traffic island will be treated with mulch to allow for easy landscaping, and will be shaped to allow driveway access for all neighboring residents. A bulb-out will also be added to the 101 corner of Magnolia for traffic making the turn downhill and right onto Nova. The plan will not restrict or eliminate any currently available street parking. The total estimated construction cost is $100,000. Bids will open in late spring and construction is expected to begin soon afterward this summer. At the meeting, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that the project “goes back at least 10 years,” and was included in the Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan adopted in 2015. However, the bollards have been met with constructive criticism from neighbors who contend that bollard configuration is both unsightly and confusing to drivers, doing little to protect pedestrians. In May 2022, 120 residents signed a petition asking the city to make permanent improvements to the 3-way intersection. The “bollard island” at Nova Drive and Magnolia Avenue is expected to be replaced this summer by a permanent traffic island.
articles.title: Bollards to be removed at Nova and Magnolia

articles.text: The cit y of Piedmont re-opened its Linda off-leash dog park last Wednesday, April 5. The city temporarily closed the area in December 2022 due to hazardous conditions created by the first in a series of heavy rains. Slippery conditions, soil erosion, and unstable walking surfaces were exacerbated during the weeks of severe storms in January 2023, forcing an extended closure. The dog area re-opened briefly on February 20, only to close again due to rain four days later. For the last several weeks, the Public Works staff has regularly inspected the site to determine how and when the dog area could re-open. Community members are invited to celebrate Arbor Day at Piedmont Community Hall on Thursday, April 27, from 5-7 p.m. The annual event, hosted by the Park Commission, will feature an announcement of the 2023 Heritage Trees, with tree lapel pins presented to those who nominated winning trees. This year, there will be up to five new additions joining the city’s existing roster of 23 Heritage Trees. The event will also feature an “Ask an Arborist” booth, where guests can ask any questions about tree maintenance. It will include a Public Works Department showcase of tree maintenance trucks and tools used by staff; demonstration of garden maintenance tools like “gator bags” which wrap around a tree’s base to slowly release water; and promotion of the free garden compost available to residents at the Corporation Yard. Park Commission chair Patty Dunlap confirmed that light snacks, pizza, lemonade, beer, and wine will be served, and music will be provided by the Piedmont High School jazz band. articles.text: The Salvation Army will hold its eighth annual gala on Sunday, April 30 at 5 p.m. at the University Club in UC Berkeley’s Memorial Stadium. Chaired by Debbie Kelley of Piedmont, the event will feature live music from the UC Berkeley a cappella group DeCadence, live and silent auctions, testimonials from inspiring Salvation Army beneficiaries, and dinner. The Volunteer of the Year honoree Elijah Hicks, will be introduced. A former UC Berkeley football player, he was drafted by the Chicago Bears last year and has chosen the Salvation Army for philanthropy through his foundation, Intercept Poverty. The organization provides financial assistance to low-income students. All proceeds will help fund The Salvation Army’s efforts to meet human need in Alameda County. The non-profit helps with food, rent, and utility assistance, operates a homeless shelter and homeless outreach programs, preschools, after-school programs, a summer camp in the Sierra foothills, music programs, Christmas assistance, and workforce development programs in construction and certified nurse’s assistant training. Kelley, who is chairing the event for her fourth year, has been on the Salvation Army advisory board since 2016. She confirmed that last year’s gala raised over $420,000 with 150 people in attendance. A similar crowd is expected this year. “The people involved before me said they were lucky to clear $100,000,” said Kelley. “Now we clear $300,000-$400,000, much due Corki Recht, the co-chair for three years.” When Kelley was unavailable last year due to an emergency, Recht ran the event, the first time the gala was held at Memorial Stadium, In prior years it had been held at the Claremont Country Club. Wanting a change of venue, Kelley, who works in ColEvent co-chairs Corki Recht and Debbie Kelley. lege Relations at UC Berkeley, approached the school’s Athletics Director, Jim Knowlton, who encouraged the move. “It was then that we decided to honor a Cal student volunteer,” said Kelley. In 2022 the honoree was professional baseball player Tyson Ross, a pitcher who has created a “Loyal to my Soil” program providing baseball lessons to inner-city children. Highlights at this year’s live auction includes a dinner for 10 cooked by Salvation Army Culinary Director Tim Tucker, and a testimonial by Thomas Wolf, a former homeless man and drug addict who has since reinvented his life due to his work with the Salvation Army. “People think of the Salvation Army as red kettles and thrift stores,” said Kelley, “but they provide such important rehabilitation and emergency service work. They help and employ people in need, and do not discriminate as to who they help. The gala is a wonderful opportunity for Piedmonters to celebrate this spirit of charity.” Individual tickets start at $250. To register for the gala and to learn more about the auction, visit bit.ly/3GihqD2. Salvation Army officers with Corki Recht, Debbie Kelley, Tyson Ross and auctioneer Ellen Toscano at the 2022 Gala.
articles.title: Salvation Army gala at UC Berkeley on April 30

articles.text: Piedmont Food Fest 2 is coming to town Sunday, April 23, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. in Piedmont Park with its signature mix of multicultural food, drink, and entertainment ready to showcase the best of the Bay. Thirty food and drink vendors will be serving, so attendees are encouraged to come hungry and sample often. Event registration is free, with all pre-registrants qualifying for prizes from sponsors Mulberry’s Market and Marielle Hayes Photography. To round out the experience, attendees can also purchase: • Unlimited beer & wine tastings from local breweries, wineries, and ciderhouses, including Buck Wild Brewing, Deer Hill Vineyards, Dokkaebier, Federation Brewing, Maker Wines, Oakland United Beerworks, and Two Broads Ciderworks • KidZone passes for all-day access to 13 carnival games and sno-cone station • Gourmet boba and mochi snack packs from Tea on Piedmont & Bake Sum (very limited supplies) • Collectible Food Fest water bottle, insulated to keep your drinks cold all day A broad array of performers will be on stage throughout the day, including: • 11:15 a.m. Emeryville Taiko has entertained audiences throughout the Bay Area for • • • • • over 25 years with its modern, electrifying “kumi-daiko” style art form, which has its roots in religious and folk festivals of Japan. 11:45 a.m. Han Martial Arts Taekwondo Showcase featuring its youth demo team, trained under the internationally accomplished leadership of Master Han, which blends Korean taekwondo, supplemented with judo and youngmudo/hapkido techniques. 12:15 p.m. Renegade Opera’s Jewelz Moya has brought her operatic arias as a Lyric Soprano to high profile events such as the Edwardian Ball SF and the Lightning in a Bottle Festival. 1:00 p.m. Hiiiwav Showcase, featuring Meaghan Maples and Tyler Reese. Hiiiwav helps Black musician-entrepreneurs build lasting businesses and uplift their communities. 2:00 p.m. LIKHA Pilipino Folk Ensemble helps preserve indigenous Philippine art forms as expressed in music, literature, dance, arts, crafts, and attire through performance, community outreach, and youth development. 2:30 p.m. Oakland Samba Revue brings its unique blend of “little big band” sounds of Brazilian samba de gafieira which blends acoustic samba, jazz, and funk. Registration, packages, and volunteer slots are now available on the website: www.piedmontfoodfest.org

articles.text: Piedmont’s community reading project, Readmont, now in its 13th year, has selected No Stopping Us Now by Lucy Jane Bledsoe as this year’s collective read. It was chosen to help celebrate the 50th anniversary of Title IX, the federal legislation requiring equal funding for women’s and men’s sports. It is a book about the love of sports, finding one’s own voice, and activism. Led by Piedmont High School English Department Chair Beth Black, Readmont will host a community discussion with the author on Wednesday, April 26, at 7:00 p.m. in the Piedmont High School library. Based on the author’s true story, it is a compelling examination of standing up for what is right. The book follows the story of Louisa who fought to bring her hometown into compliance with the new Title IX law so she could play basketball at her high school in Oregon. articles.text: Piedmont and Millennium High School students gathered in the Alan Harvey theater and Binks Rawlings gym on Friday, April 7, for a Diversity Assembly, “I am Here,” in which students presented stories of facing microaggressions, misinformation, and bullying. Organized by PHS junior Valentina Prieto Black, with the help of PHS Theater teacher Kimberly Taylor, the assembly amplified the voices of students with diverse experiences and perspectives. The gathering highlighted Black, Asian, Latinx, gay and transgender identities, and hardships including struggles with racism, eating disorders, and depression. Students presented their own stories and the stories of classmates who submitted their stories anonymously. The assembly came at the end of ‘Diversity Week,’ during which different affinity clubs and student unions were given a platform at lunchtime to educate students about the various backgrounds, cultures, and histories that make up the student body. Prieto Black is the president elect of the school’s “Diversity Committee,” a club that began in 2017 that unites many affinity groups and student leaders. The club has hosted diversity assemblies in 2018 and 2019 and continued its work during the COVID pandemic. articles.text: On Thursday, April 6, the Piedmont Community Church parking lot was filled with eager teens, parents, and adult volunteers loading vans and trucks with supplies and packed bags ahead of the church’s annual Spring Break trip. More than 200 students in the church youth group left for Mexico Sunday morning, April 9, for five days outside Tijuana, Mexico, where they will build 12 houses for impoverished Mexican families. The church’s annual Treasures Sale last month raised $27,000 toward the cost of building materials, food, and travel costs. For more than 24 years, the church has sent volunteers south of the border to build homes for families who often have never had a real roof or a front door that locks. For the community of Piedmont, the Mexico trip has become a rite of passage for Piedmont teens, and often their first direct contact with poverty. When Scott Kail, the church youth minister and leader of the Mission Trip, first went to Mexico in 2004, the crew consisted of 25 to 30 students and adults in total. They built two homes. This week they will build 15 homes. Kail explained that over the years attendance has grown to its “current count of 220 students, 15 teams and 35 adult leaders — two adults for each team — plus 15 adult kitchen crew members, probably the hardest worker of all. Kitchen crews commonly have 12-hour days.” Each of the 15 teams will have its own van. The teams are color coded, and each member wears a distinctive t-shirt with the team color (Peach, Orange, Maroon, Navy). The volunteers will work Monday through Thursday, April 10-13. The houses are 11-feet by 22-feet, each with two rooms, two windows, and a locking front door. Each crew begins by hand-mixing concrete to pour for the foundation slab. On following days they build and erect the house frames, and cover the roofs with tar paper. bailing wire, tar paper, and chicken wire so the homes can be completed with stucco on the fourth day. For Yellow Team Leader Garrett Kail, son of Scott, this will be his ninth Mexico trip. His first four years were as a high school student. “Hands down, this is my favorite week of the year,” Garrett said. “The trip’s impact is almost unexplainable if you don’t experience it yourself. The combination of kindness, fun, hard work, and compassion is at an intensity that I think is nearly impossible to find in everyday life.” “I do it for the love of it, and to serve,” he added. “I’ve seen how the Mission Trip has grown since my father took over the leadership, and he’s always been doing his best work with it. It’s so obvious that this is where his heart is.” Feeding an army of over 200 volunteers is a task on its own. The mess hall tent is constantly in use, with dedicated cooks prepping, cooking, and serving food from morning to evening. Paul Schroeder, a kitchen crew member who is on his 15th Mexico trip since he first started Photos by Selen Ozturk Piedmont Community youth pastor Scott Kail looks on as loading begins for this year’s Mexico Mission Trip. attending in 2003, said, “The cooks arrive one day early, leaving for the 525-mile drive on Friday so we can get in on Saturday and get the camp all set for when everyone else arrives by plane on Sunday.” Scott Willis, now in his 11th year as part of the kitchen team, said, “It’s been a joy to watch the Mexico group grow bigger over the years, although it’s become a little smaller since the COVID pandemic.” In 2019, the last trip before the pandemic, 320 student volunteers built 20 houses. Many of the logistics of the trip are handled by the non-Amor Ministries based in San Diego. It Garrett Kail takes an “Ambassadors Mexico 2023” shirt from a table headed by PHS junior Isabella Wire. Hana Thomas (left) loads her suitcase with the help of Piedmont Middle School teacher Ted Scherman (right), as Zookie Todd (back) watches. works with local Mexican church clergy to identify the poorest of the poor families who are selected to receive homes. Amor also stores the church’s camping gear and house-building tools near Tijuana so they don’t have to be hauled back and forth from Piedmont every year. Amor then coordinates with local building material distributors to have the wood, concrete, and other construction materials delivered to the building sites. As he watched his son Ravi, a Piedmont High School sophomore, load his duffel bag into a waiting van, parent Michael Silverberg expressed his excitement: “It’s Ravi’s first time going, and I’m sure he’ll have a great time. It’s really admirable work.” Isabella Wire, a junior who handed out shirts for the teen and adult volunteers on Thursday, added, “We’re expected to have two huge tents for the groups of boys’ and girls’ teams, so I hope the weather is not too sunny. I don’t think many people can work well when it’s super hot. I’m excited and a little nervous.” “Overall I’m really looking forward to the work in Mexico and I know my friends are, too,” added junior Hana Thomas. Kitchen crew member Paul Schroeder takes a break from loading a van. Wayne Marzolf (left), Ravi Silverberg (center), and Michael Silverberg (right) strike a pose while loading bags.

This week they will build 15 homes. Kail explained that over the years attendance has grown to its “current count of 220 students, 15 teams and 35 adult leaders — two adults for each team — plus 15 adult kitchen crew members, probably the hardest worker of all. Kitchen crews commonly have 12-hour days.” Each of the 15 teams will have its own van. The teams are color coded, and each member wears a distinctive Piedmont teens leave for Mexico Mission Trip t-shirt with the team color (Peach, Orange, Maroon, Navy). The volunteers will work Monday through Thursday, April 10-13. The houses are 11-feet by 22-feet, each with two rooms, two windows, and a locking front door. Each crew begins by hand-mixing concrete to pour for the foundation slab. On following days they build and erect the house frames, and cover the roofs with tar paper. By the third day, teams apply bailing wire, tar paper, and chicken wire so the homes can be completed with stucco on the fourth day. For Yellow Team Leader Garrett Kail, son of Scott, this will be his ninth Mexico trip. His first four years were as a high school student. “Hands down, this is my favorite week of the year,” Garrett said. “The trip’s impact is almost unexplainable if you don’t experience it yourself. The combination of kindness, fun, hard work, and compassion is at an intensity that I think is nearly impossible to find in everyday life.” “I do it for the love of it, and to serve,” he added. “I’ve seen how the Mission Trip has grown since my father took over the leadership, and he’s always been doing his best work with it. It’s so obvious that this is where his heart is.” Feeding an army of over 200 volunteers is a task on its own. The mess hall tent is constantly in use, with dedicated cooks prepping, cooking, and serving food from morning to evening. Paul Schroeder, a kitchen crew member who is on his 15th Mexico trip since he first started Photos by Selen Ozturk Piedmont Community youth pastor Scott Kail looks on as loading begins for this year’s Mexico Mission Trip. attending in 2003, said, “The cooks arrive one day early, leaving for the 525-mile drive on Friday so we can get in on Saturday and get the camp all set for when everyone else arrives by plane on Sunday.” Scott Willis, now in his 11th year as part of the kitchen team, said, “It’s been a joy to watch the Mexico group grow bigger over the years, although it’s become a little smaller since the COVID pandemic.” In 2019, the last trip before the pandemic, 320 student volunteers built 20 houses. Many of the logistics of the trip are handled by the non-Amor Ministries based in San Diego. It Garrett Kail takes an “Ambassadors Mexico 2023” shirt from a table headed by PHS junior Isabella Wire. Hana Thomas (left) loads her suitcase with the help of Piedmont Middle School teacher Ted Scherman (right), as Zookie Todd (back) watches. works with local Mexican church clergy to identify the poorest of the poor families who are selected to receive homes. Amor also stores the church’s camping gear and house-building tools near Tijuana so they don’t have to be hauled back and forth from Piedmont every year. Amor then coordinates with local building material distributors to have the wood, concrete, and other construction materials delivered to the building sites. As he watched his son Ravi, a Piedmont High School sophomore, load his duffel bag into a waiting van, parent Michael Silverberg expressed his excitement: “It’s Ravi’s first time going, and I’m sure he’ll have a great time. It’s really admirable work.” Isabella Wire, a junior who handed out shirts for the teen and adult volunteers on Thursday, added, “We’re expected to have two huge tents for the groups of boys’ and girls’ teams, so I hope the weather is not too sunny. I don’t think many people can work well when it’s super hot. I’m excited and a little nervous.” “Overall I’m really looking forward to the work in Mexico and I know my friends are, too,” added junior Hana Thomas. Kitchen crew member Paul Schroeder takes a break from loading a van. Wayne Marzolf (left), Ravi Silverberg (center), and Michael Silverberg (right) strike a pose while loading bags.

articles.text: Recently, my eleven-year-old decided to start journaling. He had never journaled before, but he was chatting with me about all the thoughts that he had in his head and how they sometimes can get stuck. I suggested that he could write them all down and that might feel good. I have not been a regular journal-er for a while, but in the interest of supporting him, I told him that I would journal as well. So, a few weeks ago, I picked him up from school and went to find the right journal. Since then, we have both been journaling daily. He has chosen to do five minutes before bed and five minutes when he first wakes up and I am writing before bed every night for about 10 minutes. When I think about living a creative life, one of the challenges that I find and that I hear from others is the concept of time pressure. I don’t have time to add more things into my day, but I wonder how much of that time scarcity is less about actual time and is more about Creative Capacity. After all, most of us find time to scroll Instagram or watch the latest episode of “Love is Blind”. our ability to have new ideas, identify original thoughts, come up with novel activities. That time scarcity might be our way of protecting ourselves because our Creative Capacity is low, so we are scared that it will just tax our minds too much to have to come up with one more new idea. And that’s where journaling has really drawn my attention, The more that I have journaled daily, the easier it is to put pen to paper and write. The first few nights I had that hurdle of the “blank page” to overcome. I thought it mattered what I wrote down and I stressed myself out trying to make it “meaningful.” It took cognitive power to come up with an idea or search my brain for what wanted to come out. The more I did it, the easier that barrier to entry became. The words flowed more smoothly. The ideas were just there; I didn’t have to search to find them. My Creat ive Capacit y increased because of Creative Consistency. Creative Consistency means that we embark on a creative process with regularity. The same way that when we go to the gym three days a week, lifting weights feels achievable. When we only go sporadically, every time feels hard. If we choose to do something small every day with our creative superpowers – a mini painting, a doodle board, singing along to one song, dancing for three minutes, doing a journal before bed – that Creative Consistency gives us the lubrication to increase our Creative Capacity because our minds and bodies are primed and ready to go! Nina Meehan is the founder of GoCreate (https://gocreate.zone/) which offers services in consulting, coaching and workshops in creativity and communication. articles.text: Nearly 100 members and friends of Piedmont Community Church celebrated Associate Pastor Don Ashburn’s 20 years of outstanding service to the congregation at a ceremony on Sunday, April 2, With the cooperation of the weather (finally), people gathered in the church Courtyard after worship for cake and heartfelt recollections about how much Don has meant to so many. Don’s wife, Margaret Ovenden, and his two adult children, Griffin and Madeline, were present for the milestone event. Immediate Past President of the Board of Trustees Jan Wolfe emphasized Don’s pastoral skills, which she experienced profoundly when her husband died unexpectedly. “When my healthy, long-distance runner husband died suddenly far from home three years ago, one of my first thoughts was of Don,” Jan said. “I needed that warm, pastoral hug that I associate so much with him. He is so compassionate and wise. Don will always be treasured”. Trustee Kara Baysinger, knowing Don’s love of baseball, regaled the audience by comparing Don’s many skills to team players, utility players (he can handle any role he’s asked to do), and pinch hitters. Emphasizing Don’s intellectual prowess, she added Yogi Berra’s famous quote, “Baseball is 90% mental, and the other half is physical.” Longtime church member Steven Thorne praised Don. “Don has been the spiritual and operational backbone for continuity and stability in this church,” Steven said. Church Trustee Steve Senter and Youth Pastor Scott Kail also showed their gratitude with personal observations. The final speaker, Senior Pastor Steve Schibsted, summarized Don’s excellence as a pastor. “To be a great pastor, you have to have both head and heart,” Steve said. “Don has both. He has a keen intellect. We have definitely experienced it in both his teaching and preaching. And, he has a big heart. He cares deeply Photos by Michael Barber Associate Pastor Don Ashburn, right, receives accolades from Senior Pastor Steve Schibsted during a celebration on Sunday, April 2, when he was honored for 20 years of service to Piedmont Community Church. Board of Trustees member Jan Wolfe and Don enjoy light banter Church member Steve Senter explains the many ways Don has helped him and his family over the years. With palm frond in hand, church member Joyce Hicks stands with husband Eric Behrens in the Courtyard. Nearly 100 people stayed after Sunday worship to acknowledge Don’s service to the church. about people. We have all experienced his love through his pastoral care. He has walked with many of us through some of our most difficult moments.” After these encomiums, Don shared what his 20 years of service and this celebration meant to him. “Twenty years has sure flown by,” he said. “My daughter, Maddy, was born the day I started working at the church and my son Griffin was only three. My family has sort of grown up in the Piedmont community. It’s been a great experience for us – especially now, with a real sense of revitalization at the church.” Days later, Don reflected on the gathering. “The celebration was great,” he said. “We managed to have a clear day, so it was nice to be outside with folks I’ve known and loved and served with for years.” Writer’s Note: Speaking from personal experience, my own family has been involved with Piedmont Community Church for as long as Don has, and he has been a very special part of our lives. His classes and Bible studies have deepened Joyce’s and my faith and after he presided over our daughter Michelle’s wedding, she commented on how insightful and helpful his premarital counseling was for her relationship with her husband, Geoff. Don Ashburn with family, son Griffin, daughter Madeline and wife Margaret Ovenden. Youth Pastor Scott Kail explains how Don led the church successfully during a recent time of transition.
articles.title: Don Ashburn celebrated for 20 years at Piedmont Community Church

They opened the second act with powerful choreography in glow in the dark costumes, proving that they truly are “Unstoppable.” New this year was the tiny TK class of four and five year olds that had everyone smiling as they showed up in fuzzy eared costumes singing “Hey Hey We’re the Monkees.” The TK class was followed by the Kindergarten class making waves with their heartwarming performance of “How Far I’ll Go.” The show is Beach’s second largest money maker, and producers Becky Ackerman, Dana Murray and Heidianne Pillsbury knew that the pressure was on to deliver this year. In partnership with the school district’s facilities team, they were able to move the show from the high school amphitheater to the new Alan Harvey Theater. “The theater was instrumental in allowing us to sell more tickets and make more money. It also opened it up to the community and alumni. At Beach we could barely accommodate students’ immediate families,” said Ackerman, a Beach alum. 4th graders driving “Shotgun” in cut out cars on a hot sunny day. Thirds graders prove they have rhythm in their rendition of “Cups.” The extra capacity paid off, as the 2023 Beach Revue sold over 1,000 tickets and made $26,000 in net profit, the highest in the show’s history. Volunteers and participants put in the work this year to get all the lines and choreography down perfect. Leading up to the event there were six one-hour rehearsals starting February 4th, and two rehearsals before the three performances before the lively audiences. This year’s finale was led by former Padre Grande Arash Ghassemi on ukulele, accompanying his son and the 5th grade cast in “Somewhere Over the Rainbow.” The revue unfolded its denouement with the traditional Photos by Alice Hayashi Ben Spencer’s 4th graders came out with a bang performing “Firework.” slideshow of the kids through the years played in the background, bringing everyone to tears. articles.text: Staff Photos Jim Stehr, a member of the Hall of Fame, was the host speaker for this year’s Hall of Fame induction ceremony. Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame hosted its 20-year anniversary event at the high school’s new Alan Harvey Theater. The Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame inducted six former athletes on Saturday, April 8 at the new Alan Harvey Theater, marking the first time in recent years for the ceremony at a venue other than the Claremont Country Club. “This induction ceremony marks the 20th year of the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame. It’s become an endearing tradition that recognizes, not only great teams and athletes, but coaches from Piedmont’s storied history as well… We’re very excited to start a new tradition here on the high school campus where those memories were made,” said Jim Stehr, the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame host and a member of the first class of inductees. Inductees included Lauren Barbieri from the Class of 2001 (cross country, track), Devin Brown of the Class of 2009 (basketball, football), James Danielson from the Class of 1981 (football, soccer, track), Georgia Hill from the Class of 2013 (basketball, softball), Jon Minor from the Class of 1983 (basketball), and Kerri Roemer of the Class of 1999 (basketball, softball, tennis, track). Founded in 2003 by the late Ken Rawlings and Pete Anderson, and led for many years by former PHS and current Miramonte basketball coach Chris Lavdiotis, the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame honors athletes, coaches, administrators, and community members for outstanding contributions to Piedmont High School athletics. Lavdiotis was honored prior to the start of the ceremony for his efforts to help create the Hall of Fame. He was planning only on a speech for the induction of Brown, a former player he coached. “This is a complete surprise… I had no idea this was happening, I came here to honor Devin Brown. It was really simple [how the Hall of Fame got started]; I walked into the principal’s office and said we need a Hall of Fame. He said, ‘Great idea . He called Bebe Rawlings, because he was thinking about the same thing.’ And now it’s 20 years later. This is awesome,” said Lavdiotis. Lauren Barbieri, Class of 2001 Honors for Barbieri started the induction ceremony. A member of the Class of 2001, Barbieri was a running star at Piedmont High on the cross country and track teams, winning Most Valuable Player honors for all four years of her high school career. Barbieri’s former distance running coach at Piedmont High, Doyle O’Regan, introduced her, reminiscing about when he first heard about her. “I first learned about Lauren when she was in grade school. articles.text: Staff Photos Freshman Lucas Smolko picked up easy wins against Alameda and Arroyo at No. 1 singles. Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team wrapped up a highly productive week by sweeping three matches against league competition, defeating Alameda 7-0 on Tuesday April 4 on the road, beating Alameda again 6-1 on Wednesday, April 5 at home, and shutting out Arroyo 7-0 in San Lorenzo. The batch of wins brings Piedmont’s overall record to 10-4 and 7-1 against league opponents. The match to likely determine the fate of the Western Alameda County Conference title will be on April 26 when the Highlanders host league rivals, Berkeley. “We’re getting the job done against league competition. We have seven dual matches remaining for our regular season, and we know the big one is Berkeley,” said coach Jim Landes. 7-0 over Alameda Piedmont won all seven matches in straight sets against the Alameda Hornets. In singles, Lucas Smolko won at the No. 1 spot with a double-bagel win, 6-0, 6-0. At No. 2, Ben Breber also won 6-0, 6-0. At No. 3, Ethan Pham won 6-1, 6-0, while Alex Zalewski won at No. 4 in straight sets, 6-1, 6-1. In doubles, Monte Imburg and Nate Welch won 6-2, 6-1 at the No. 1 spot. Arun Brahma and Nick King won 6-0, 6-0 at No. 2, while Will Tenney and Graham Alban won 6-2, 6-1 at No. 3. 6-1 over Alameda The following day, Breber played No. 1 singles to win 6-0, 6-1. At No. 2 singles, Pham won 6-2, 6-4. Brady Colbert won 6-2, 6-2 at No. 4. The only loss on the day was Brahma at No. 3 in three sets, 0-6, 6-4, 10-2. Monte Imburg sends in a serve. In doubles, Imburg and Welch won 6-0, 6-1 at No. 1. Alban and King paired at No. 2 and won 6-1, 6-1. At No. 3 was Tenney and Chris Li, winning 6-4, 6-1. 7-0 over Arroyo Smolko returned to the No. 1 singles spot and won easily 6-1, 6-0. Brahma featured at No. 2, winning 6-2, 6-4. Welch played at No. 3 to a shutout 6-0, 6-0 win, while Colbert won 6-2, 6-2 at No. 4. In doubles, Alban and King won 6-1, 6-0 at No. 1. Li and Tenney won 6-0, 6-0 at No. 2, while Zalewski and Xiaowei Elias won 6-2, 6-2 at No. 3. NEXT UP Piedmont (10-4 overall, 7-1 league) hosts Arroyo when they return from spring break on Tuesday, April 18 at 3:30 p.m. They also play the following day, April 19, when hosting El Cerrito at 3:30 p.m. Ben Breber had wins at No. 2 singles and No. 1 singles in two matches versus Alameda.

She served as the ball-girl for Bryan Gardere’s girls’ basketball team during its State title runs in 2004 and 2005. “Bryan’s presence in my athletic journey go well beyond the one year I played varsity basketball. I actually started back in 2003 when coach Gardere asked if I wanted to be the ball-girl for his team. I was 8-years-old and in third grade, but I remember walking down every day to the gym where I would help with practice and games. That team won backto-back state championships – the first in any sport at the school. I didn’t know it at the time, but the influence those years had on me as an athlete was monumental,” said Hill. A standout softball player, Georgia earned first-team AllLeague honors for four years and was named the West Alameda County Conference’s Most Valuable Player in 2013. Hill also earned third-team All-East Bay selection from the East Bay Times and first-team All-State selection by Cal-Hi Sports as a senior. Georgia continued her softball career at the collegiate level, playing two years at The College of Wooster—where she finished with nine home runs, 68 hits, 57 RBIs, and 31 runs scored. Her six homers in her freshman year set a single-season school record. Jon Minor, Class of 1983 Jon Minor, Class of 1983, was a three-year varsity letterman in basketball as a dominant 6-foot- 6-inch center. Minor was introduced by his brother, Jason, who recalled a specific performance in a game with Bishop O’Dowd. “Growing up in Piedmont was special, I remember Jon dunking the ball three-times in a row against Bishop O’Dowd and I’ll always remember our grandmother jumping up-and-down in the stands with her white gloves on cheering for Jon. I remember thinking to myself when I was just 5- or 6-years-old, ‘Only professionals can dunk the ball, so Jon must be a professional’,” said Jason Minor. He earned first-team AllLeague honors and Alameda County Athletic Conference Player of the Year as a junior and senior. He also received the Optimo Award his senior season as the team’s Most Valuable Player. Minor continued playing basketball collegiately at UC Davis under legendary former Aggies coach Bob Hamilton. Kerri Roemer, Class of 1999 Roemer, Class of 1999, earned 11 varsity letters throughout her four years at Piedmont High. Though best known for tennis, her primary sport, she also excelled in basketball, track and field, and softball. She was introduced by her father, Mark Roemer. “I’m really honored to be asked to be here for my daughter. I want to give recognition today to Kerri’s mom, who is no longer here. Her mom did the driving, made the snacks and washed the uniforms. Back then, it was unheard of for girls to earn varsity letters, and Kerri did it in three sports,” said Mark. Roemer made her largest headlines on the tennis courts, PHS grads and athletes Jane Martz (left) and Catey McCreary spoke about the importance of Title IX and women’s sports.

articles.text: Piedmont High sent four athletes to compete in five events at the Arcadia Invitational on Friday and Saturday, April 7-8. The event is considered one of the most prestigious annual events for high school runners with some of the top athletes in the country making their way to the Arcadia HS track, marking the second-consecutive year for PHS be invited. “Parker Long, Christian Taylor, Xander Schulte-Sasse, and Sam Shelby qualified for and raced in arguably the most prestigious high school competition of the year. For reference, multiple U.S. Olympians have raced at the Arcadia Invitational while they were in high school. During the weekend, we saw one Parker Long (left) placed third of 52 at the prestigious Arcadia Invitational. all-time U.S. high school record fall, multiple top-10 all-time marks get hit, and a handful of Xander Schulte-Sasse (left), Parker Long, Christian Taylor, and Sam Shelby competed in the distance medley relay. No. 1 marks in the country for this season. “Simply put, this meet is the best of the best,” said Piedmont head coach Pouyan Assadi. It was a strong day for Parker Long, who placed third in a super fast 800-meters with a time of 1:53.35. He was .03 behind Caleb Levy from Gurnee, Illinois, and 1.17 seconds behind the winner, Colby Jenks of Big Piney, Wyoming. Assadi thinks Long was “boxed in” early on in his race, but the Piedmont runner was able to push through the crowded field. “Parker got boxed in but once an opening appeared, he took off and moved from ninth to seventh, and then finished third. He has incredible top-end speed. Once he adds a little aggressiveness to his race, he’ll take the next leap,” explained Assadi. “I knew I had a good chance to be one of the top finishers,” Long said after the race. “My plan was to go out near the front. I wanted to get a spot in Lane 1 until it was time to kick. There were guys in another section who went out a little faster than I did and they boxed me behind them. I came through the first lap in a not very good position. I wanted to wait for a straight section, and with 300 to go I made a big move. articles.text: The mountain bike team from Piedmont High raced at Fort Ord in Monterey during the Fun At the Fort races on Saturday, March 25, where racers competed on a 5.14 mile course. “It was a fantastic sunny day with the trails riding very well,” said coach Sally Aldridge. ”Fort Ord’s largely single track trails are in sandy terrain, so they drain quickly and are in good shape despite the huge amounts of rain we have experienced this winter. The Fort Ord race start is on a hill and is notorious for creating bottlenecks as riders jostle for position.” Jasper Schuetz won the Freshman Division 1 race with a twolap time of 40:42, clocking times of 20:28 and 20:13, impressively notching a faster time on his second lap. He currently leads the Interscholastic NorCal Cycling League’s D1 Freshman category after three races. Andres Robert placed 18th in the varsity boys’ race with a time of 1:01:47. Jasper Schuetz won the Freshman Div. 1 race at the Fun At the Fort event on Saturday, March 25. In the varsity boys’ category, Andres Robert placed 18th of 32 with a time of 1:01:47 in a threelap race, clocking times of 20:09, 21:17, and 20:20. Aleksi Valkonen placed 28th in 1:06:43. Junior Schuyler Sawicki placed seventh out of 74 riders in the JV boys’ Division 1 category, which puts him in fifth place overall this season after three races. Junior Mark Hsia also was 12th with a time of 43:20, and right behind were teammates Matteo Scanu (14th, 43:32) and Max Rivera (15th, 43:33). In the sophomore Div. 1 race, Cary Ward finished 12th of 42 racers in 46:33, and Ethan Becker was 36th in 1:00:09. Heather Stoneman finished 27th of 38 riders in the JV girls’ race, finishing with a time of 1:11:08 in the two-lap race. Anne Marie Gibbs was 34th in 1:19:07. Schuyler Sawicki placed seventh out of 74 riders in the junior varsity boys’ Division 1 category.

articles.text: Piedmont Swim Team, Piedmont’s independent year-round youth aquatics team, sent a record number of swimmers to compete in the Pacific Swimming Far Western Championships in late March. The 11 qualifiers were: Ryan Stokes (18), Simon Lins (18), Paige Arnold (17), Josie Oesterer (17), Sydney Olson (14), Evan Byun (15), Gabriel Reader (15), Nathan Judy (15), Asher Takazawa (14), Cole Carnazzo (14) and Connor Carnazzo (12). Far Westerns is a high level competition hosted by Pacific Swimming, the third largest region in USA Swimming. The meet, which took place over four days in Morgan Hill from March 30 to April 2, had 119 teams from throughout California, Nevada, Arizona, Oregon, and Utah with more than 1,100 swimmers. “To qualify, swimmers had to meet time standards ahead of time,” explained head coach Stefan Bill. “Those time standards are very fast and only a small percentage of swimmers in the USA get to that level.” The competition featured multiple national age group record holders and many senior high school swimmers that have been recruited to some of the top colCole Carnazzo (left), Head Coach Stefan Bill, Connor Carnazzo, Simon Lins & Paige Arnold leges in the country. “We had a fantastic meet,” said coach Bill. “Almost everyone made finals at least once.” Meet highlights included: • Team Captain Josie Oesterer achieved her first ever sectional cut. • Simon Lins won the 50 freestyle for ages 15-18. • Connor Carnazzo placed 2nd in the 100 backstroke (11-12 category). • Cole Carnazzo got his first sectional cut in the 200 fly and made multiple finals in the 13-14 category. • Asher Takazawa made finals in the 100 and 200 backstroke (13-14 category). • Gabe Reader, Evan Byun and Sydney Olson swam new personal best times. • Ryan Stokes, Paige Arnold and Nathan Judy had some amazing preliminary and finals swims. Though it was a long four days, coach Bill said, “To me as head coach, the most amazing thing was the positive attitude the swimmers and parents had during the meet –the cheerfulness, camaraderie and support the swimmers gave each other and the professionalism everyone displayed during the four days. Our athletes were just a pleasure to be around and to coach during this meet.” Paige Arnold (left), Josie Oesterer, Simon Lins, Connor Carnazzo, Cole Carnazzo, Asher Takazawa, Evan Byun, and Gabe Reader Josie Oesterer (left) and Paige Arnold.

articles.text: The Piedmont Junior Running Club, a Rec Department program for 4th and 5th graders, completed its winter season with a challenge race of one mile at Witter Field on March 8. Under sunny skies and with families looking on, 54 boys and girls from Piedmont elementary schools, in three different heats, ran four laps around the track (one mile) with the goal of trying to do better than their PR (personal record) time during the year for the “PE Mile.” Charley Harnett, a 5th grader Running coach Len Goldman is the founder of both the middle school cross-country program and the 4th and 5th grade Junior Running Club. Fourth and fifth grade members of the Piedmont Junior Running Club show their numbers at Witter Field. at Aurora School in Oakland won Heat 1 with a time of Seven minutes, 10 seconds (7:10). The winner of Heat 2 was Ben Centeno, a 4th grader at Wildwood, whose time was 6:48.3. In the final race of the day, Heat 3, Kenji Holt, a 5th grader at Wildwood, led from start to finish with a very good time of 6:06.4. The first girl overall was Henley Azad, a 5th grader at Havens, who comes from a high-achieving athletic family. Her mother, the former Courtney Gault, was a star basketball and softball player at Piedmont High School, and her uncle, Scott Gault, competed as a rower in two Olympic Games. Henley’s winning time was 6:26.8. Thanks to a grant from the Piedmont Turkey Trot, each runner wore a brand-new Piedmont Junior Running Club t-shirt at the event. The Winter session had one of the largest groups ever to participate in the program with a total of 62 students. What now? The Spring session began on March 27 and there may be some openings at Havens and Beach Schools. The Wildwood program is filled with 25 students registered. Registration is through the Piedmont Rec Department at 420-3070. For the first time, the Junior Running Club will offer a 4-week summer program, which will meet twice a week from July 10 to August 2 on Mondays and Wednesdays from 3:00 to 5:15 p.m. at Witter Field. For more information contact Len Goldman at lgoldman@ pacbell.net. (See more photos at: https://photos.app.goo.gl/gaBM- 2r8RgxDXaxd26)

articles.text: Treasure Island Museum welcomes organist Jerry Nagano for an afternoon concert on May 13. The lobby of the museum’s historic Building One will host the event, which showcases music that was popular during the 1950’s to 1970’s when the Treasure Island Naval Station was active. During that period, the Island’s Officers’ Club featured a family-friendly, Sunday dinner with organ music, often performed by local performer “Kay” Catherine Rooney. The organ which will be played by Nagano, a Los Angeles-based pianist, is the same Hammond organ that Rooney played. The organ has been donated to the Treasure Island Museum by Rooney’s niece, Chris Weicher, for the event. The concert begins at 2 p.m. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.treasureislandmuseum. org/event-details/organ-concertwith-jerry-nagano-at-treasureisland-museum.
articles.title: Jerry Nagano organ concert at Treasure Island

articles.text: The Diluvian Quartet will perform a Spring recital, Great Dedications, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 7 p.m. this Saturday, April 15. Elizabeth Castro Abrams and Jessica Scrimale, violins; Raphael Gold, viola; and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello will perform quartets by W.A. Mozart and Reinhold Gliere, celebrating two prolific composers and the works they dedicated to their most influential colleagues and teachers. Doors open at 6:45 p.m., and the concert begins at 7 p.m. A dessert reception and drinks will follow. Advance tickets are available at www.eventbrite.com/ e/582873007857. Tickets may also be purchased at the door. Highlights Mozart’s Quartet No. 15 is one of his greatest masterpieces. The second of a group of six quartets dedicated to the great Josef Haydn, his friend and mentor, it was the most profound quartet written at the time of its publication. It stands today as one of the most expressive works in the genre. It is marked by a dark and somber melody, at once giving way to a bright and cheerful theme over and over, always with Mozart’s genius ability at musical conversation. Born in Kiev, Ukraine, Reinhold Glière went on to be one of the most important Soviet composers of his generation. The piece on this program, his 2nd quartet, was written in 1905, and was dedicated to the great Russian composer Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov. It is jampacked with themes of Imperial Czarist Russia, lush romantic chords, unabashed emotional expression, and toe-tapping rhythmic gestures. This program features some of the most beautiful music ever written for string quartets. The Diluvian Quartet has been playing together for two years and prides itself on diverse programs that combine standards of the repertoire with lesser-known masterpieces.
articles.title: Diluvian Quartet to perform at PCA this Saturday

articles.text: Performances at Zellerbach Hall Fri-Sun. this weekend Cal Performances at UC Berkeley welcomes the renowned Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater for its annual visit to the Cal campus with performances Friday through Sunday, April 14-16 at Zellerbach Hall. Led by Artistic Director Robert Battle, the dance company’s annual campus residency began yesterday. The program consists of three unique programs, which include repertory works and Ailey classics, as well as premieres of two new dances. Are You in Your Feelings? is choreographed by Kyle Abraham to soul, hip-hop, and R&B music, and the premiere of In a Sentimental Mood showcases an intimate duet choreographed by Jamar Roberts. It is jampacked with themes of Imperial Czarist Russia, lush romantic chords, unabashed emotional expression, and toe-tapping rhythmic gestures. This program features some of the most beautiful music ever written for string quartets. The Diluvian Quartet has been playing together for two years and prides itself on diverse programs that combine standards of the repertoire with lesser-known masterpieces.
