articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SF MOMA) is now showing the works of sculptor Alexander Calder, famous for his intricate mobiles. The exhibit, Dissonant Harmony, will be on view through May. Calder was an American sculpture best known for his whimsical, colorful and geometric mobiles. His first solo exhibition in 1926 at the Gallery of Jacques Seligmann in Paris brought critical success. He later exhibited in top art galleries and museums around the world. His work is now included in permanent collections at the Museum of Modern Art and the Guggenheim in New York, as well as the Centre Georges Pompidou in Paris. The Whitney Museum in New York City currently holds the largest permanent collection of Calder’s sculptures. Visit San Francisco Museum of Modern Art to see well-known Calder pieces like Lone Yellow (1961), Maquette for The Cello Player (1958), and Double Gong (1953). To learn more, and to purchase tickets to SF MOMA, visit https:// www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/ alexander-calder-dissonant-harmony/. Sculptor and mobile creator Alexander Calder.

articles.text: San Francisco’s Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) celebrates Black beauty and femininity with its current exhibit, Black Venus, on view now through August 20. The exhibition is curated by Aindrea Emelife and is a reflection of the legacy of Black Women in visual culture, from colonial-era caricatures to the reclamation of Black womanhood by 18 artists of numerous nationalities and ages. Artwork spans from 1793 to the present day. Featured artists include Alberta Whittle, Amber Pinkerton, Ayana V. The exhibition’s thematic foundation is the Hottentot Venus, a visual-culture archetype named for the assigned stage name of Saartje Baartman (born 1789 in South Africa. To learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/black-venus. The exhibition’s thematic foundation is the Hottentot Venus.

articles.text: Asian Art Museum in San Francisco is currently exhibiting Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in Art beginning March 31. The new exhibition features more than 120 artworks borrowed from 20 of the finest museums and private collections in the world, with a focus on the arts of the Indian cultural sphere. Beyond Bollywood includes artwork from India, Pakistan, Nepal, Tibet, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, and Indonesia. “We hope visitors will come away with a transformed notion of the importance and power of dance,” said exhibition co-curator Forrest McGill. “[Both] what it has meant in the past, and what it can mean in their own lives today.” Burmese artifact c. 1857; wood with lacquer, gold leaf and inlaid glass Beyond Bollywood will be on display through July 10. For more information, and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://exhibitions.asianart. org/exhibitions/beyond-bollywood-2000-years-of-dance-inart/.

articles.text: The Rider, written and directed by Academy Award-winning director Chloé Zhao, is a beautifully made film, so close to its stoic truth that it easily qualifies as cinema verité. The actors essentially played themselves with a naturalness that astonishes. The film is also a Western, wrapped in certain familiar tropes while at the same time being devoid of anything not realistic, which so often defines the Hollywood stories of the early west. The Rider is set on the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota where director Chloé Zhao met Brady Jandreau, who is at the center of the film. He essentially plays himself; his character’s name is Brady Blackburn. His father, in the film, Tim Blackburn, is played by his real father, Tim Jandreau. Brady’s sister, Lilly Blackburn, is his actual sister, Lilly Jandreau, who is on the autism spectrum. His friends are his friends. All are untrained actors, yet they possess an unexpected verisimilitude that lends a remarkable authenticity to the narrative. The film opens with Brady dreaming of horses. Waking, he walks into the bathroom where we see a bandage covering the right side of his head. Slowly he removes the bandage, revealing a stapled half-moon scar. It is ugly in its seriousness, a foreshadowing of what lies ahead for Brady. In bits and pieces, we learn that the injury is from being stepped on by a rodeo bronco after being bucked off, resulting in a plate being inserted just beneath the wound. The implications for Brady are life changing, and he is confronted painfully with the reality that he likely will never be able to do what he deeply loves: rodeoing, riding horses, and training semi-wild horses. It is a gift which is his seemingly magical ability to communicate with these large animals. This is a gorgeously shot film, steeped in an expansive geography, creating a prose-like, metaphorical backdrop for a people who live on the far margins of the American dream. The double-wide mobile homes are surrounded by a landscape of tallgrass prairie, as silent and spare as the people who inhabit it. It’s a place where Brady is completely at home, but also caught in his self-imposed distance that speaks volumes as the camera holds on his sharply constructed young face (he’s 22). The Rider inhabits a middle ground between fiction and real life, and yet it avoids even a moment of gratuitous drama. It is harsh yet sensitive, beautiful and gritty as Brady resists and struggles with the truth of a life he had never planned for. The Rider. Directed by Chloé Zhao. Starring Brady Jandreau, Tim Jandreau, Scott Lane. 1 hr., 44 min. Rated R. Released in 2018. Now streaming on Prime/ Hulu/Vudu/Apple tv. Brady Jandreau in The Rider

articles.text: Know first that Embrace of the Serpent was nominated for an Oscar for Best Foreign Language film from Colombia. Written and directed by David Gallego and photographed in black and white by Gallego, it is set in the heart of Colombia’s Amazon rainforest. Its images are luminous, the scale of its expansive beauty breathtaking. As well, it possesses a depth of melancholy that is unrelenting, for above all it is an allegory as well as a tribute to the indigenous people of the Amazon whose voices are now silent and whose cultures have vanished. The film opens in 1909 as a German ethnographer, Theo (based on the diaries of real life explorer Theodor Koch-Grunberg), portrayed by Jan Bijovet, is deathly ill. He convinces a young shaman, Karamakate (Nibio Torres), to take him up river in search of a plant, the yakruna, which is thought to have healing properties. Karamakate is initially reluctant; he rages at the rubber barons who have decimated his tribe and the ecosystem of the forest. Theo convinces him that if he will act as their guide he will show him where his people, called the Cohiuano, are, insisting they still exist. Karamakate reluctantly agrees. And so, along with Theo’s river Sherpa, the three men begin their journey in a dugout canoe in search of the sacred plant. It is a trip that takes them into Joseph Conrad’s Heart of Darkness. One of the most unsettling moments of the film occurs at a mission where a priest has taken in a group of orphan boys, their parents killed in the rubber wars. Theo finds that the priest is physically abusive and regards his charges as pagans and beats them remorselessly. Running parallel to the story of Theo is that of Evan (Brionne Davis), a character based on the American botanist, Richard Evans Schultes, who, using Theo’s diary and sketches, is also in search of the elusive plant, and its medicinal properties. Forty years later, the guide is once again a now aged Karamakate who agrees to take Evan (as he’s called). Like Theo, they stop at the decaying mission, only now it’s inhabited by a cult that worships a madman who believes he is Jesus. Embedded in the film is one overriding question: what does it mean to be civilized? Can those who called the indigenous people “savages” or “pagans” the carriers of truth? Can they call themselves civilized? What followed in their wake amounted to the genocide of groups of people, decimated by disease and forced labor for the profit of the rubber barons who were unconscionably rapacious. But know that the film is not heavy-handed or overbearing. There is instead an inherent sadness to the story; it is elegiac in its composition, the images startling, evocative, and often unexpected. It is unlike any film you will have seen before. Do not expect a story that relies on lengthy exposition; there is no coherent narrative arc. It is as much a visual experience with almost a documentary feel that borders on the mythical and the surreal, framed by the emotions of grief and loss. Embrace of the Serpent. Directed by Ciro Guerra. In Spanish with subtitles. Starring Jan Bijvoet, Brionne Davis, Nilbio Torres. 2 hrs., 3 min, Not rated. Released in 2016. Nominated for Academy Award for Best Foreign feature length film.
articles.title: Embrace of the Serpent a look at the loss of indigenous cultures in the Amazon

Though it takes Sean a bit longer than Eibhlin to warm up to the girl, it’s with this couple she experiences a kindness and generosity of attention and concern that she has never felt before. Cait comes to realize, slowly, tentatively, that there is a world, and a way of being in that world, which is far different from the one she has known growing up. Expecting indifference or cruelty, she discovers the opposite, and so her silence, her reflexive response to life, is slowly abandoned. Cait, in effect, comes out of hiding and begins to blossom. The Quiet Girl is a beautiful film, gentle and moving, subtle yet deeply emotive. It is a narrative about the power of kindness that is all too often underrated if not absent; yet, when encountered, it can heal, even delight, and be transformative. As it does with Cait. This is a film not to be missed. The Quiet Girl. Written and directed by Colm Bairead, Filmed in Gaelic with subtitles. Starring Catherine Clinch, Carrie Crowley, Andrew Bennett. 1 hr., 34 min. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv/ A scene from Disney’s 1940 animated feature film Pinocchio When Pinocchio was released by Disney on February 23, 1940, it was the company’s second feature-length animated film (it followed Snow White) and won two Oscars at the 13th Academy Awards ceremony. Using ink and brush, drawn by hand, it was considered at the time a technical marvel and lauded as marvelous entertainment for people of all ages, especially the little guys. Based on the 1883 children’s book by Carlo Collodi, it was magical and contained humor, drama, with a bevy of endearing and rogue characters. Hence, it wasn’t long before Pinocchio became an iconic figure, and audiences soon regarded the fairy tale about a small wooden puppet that was turned into a real boy as a classic The story opens with Jiminy Cricket (Cliff Edwards) explaining how an elderly Italian woodcarver, Geppetto (Christian Rub), creates a small wooden puppet. The old man, who lives alone, is so taken with the marionette, who he calls Pinocchio, before falling asleep, he gazes into the night sky and wishes upon a star that his wooden creation be turned into a real boy. This is Disney and so that night the puppet is visited by the Blue Fairy (Evelyn Venable) who promises to grant Geppetto his wish; however, there are conditions. If Pinocchio truly wants to be fully human, he must be brave, truthful and unselfish. And so begins the puppet’s journey, filled with moments that test his character. Will he tell the truth? Will he risk everything inside a monstrous whale and rescue Geppetto? Will he resist the temptations of some unsavory characters such as a con artist fox named Honest John (Walter Catlett). It is at such moments that Jiminy Cricket steps forward and takes on the role of Pinocchio’s conscience and guide, reminding him of his promise to the Blue Fairy. The guild of animators who faithfully brought Collodi’s story to the screen were artists in the truest sense of the word, and that is why this beautiful film will never lose its compelling magic. Pinocchio. Directed by Ben Sharpsteen and Hamilton Luske. Released in 1940. With the voices of Dickie Jones, Cliff Edwards, Walter Catlett. Mel Blanc, Christian Rub. 1 hr., 27 min. Rated G. articles.text: The Quiet Girl has been referred to as a whisper of a film, and it is that and so much more. Based on the 2010 novella by Claire Keegan, and nominated in 2023 for an Oscar in the Best International Feature Film category, it is an unassuming, beautifully acted and photographed coming-of-age drama about a nine-year-old girl named Cait (Catherine Clinch). The film opens with Cait lying in a lush field, hidden, looking up at a blue sky. A voice in the distance is calling her name. We soon discover that she lives with an impoverished farm family. She is harshly ignored by both her parents (Kate Nic Chonaonaigh and Michael Patric) and many siblings. To her shame on occasion she wets her bed. School is also a struggle, something to be endured, a place where she is often ridiculed by her schoolmates. Cait’s father, Da, is shiftless, preferring to spend time in a local pub drinking his pint than preparing for the seasonal harvest. Finding it difficult to feed all the children (Cait’s mother, Mam, is once again pregnant), the parents decide to send Cait to spend the summer with a distant cousin, Eibhlin (Carey Crowley), and her husband Sean (Andrew Bennett), who are rural dairy farmers. Da drives Catherine Clinch stars in The Quiet Girl.
articles.title: The Quiet Girl an Irish film not be missed

pages.text: Wednesday, Aprl 12, 2023 19 MOVIES FOR KIDS The Quiet Girl an Irish film not be missed By Chris Honoré The Quiet Girl has been referred to as a whisper of a film, and it is that and so much more. Based on the 2010 novella by Claire Keegan, and nominated in 2023 for an Oscar in the Best International Feature Film category, it is an unassuming, beautifully acted and photographed coming-of-age drama about a nine-year-old girl named Cait (Catherine Clinch). The film opens with Cait lying in a lush field, hidden, looking up at a blue sky. A voice in the distance is calling her name. We soon discover that she lives with an impoverished farm family. She is harshly ignored by both her parents (Kate Nic Chonaonaigh and Michael Patric) and many siblings. To her shame on occasion she wets her bed. School is also a struggle, something to be endured, a place where she is often ridiculed by her schoolmates. Cait’s father, Da, is shiftless, preferring to spend time in a local pub drinking his pint than preparing for the seasonal harvest. Finding it difficult to feed all the children (Cait’s mother, Mam, is once again pregnant), the parents decide to send Cait to spend the summer with a distant cousin, Eibhlin (Carey Crowley), and her husband Sean (Andrew Bennett), who are rural dairy farmers. Da drives her to the distant farm, saying little, and is so disengaged that when he leaves Cait with the couple, absent even a goodbye, he drives off with her suitcase still in the trunk of the car. Though it takes Sean a bit longer than Eibhlin to warm up to the girl, it’s with this couple she experiences a kindness and generosity of attention and concern that she has never felt before. Cait comes to realize, slowly, tentatively, that there is a world, and a way of being in that world, which is far different from the one she has known growing up. Expecting indifference or cruelty, she discovers the opposite, and so her silence, her reflexive response to life, is slowly abandoned. Cait, in effect, comes out of hiding and begins to blossom. The Quiet Girl is a beautiful film, gentle and moving, subtle yet deeply emotive. It is a narrative about the power of kindness that is all too often underrated if not absent; yet, when encountered, it can heal, even delight, and be transformative. As it does with Cait. This is a film not to be missed. The Quiet Girl. Written and directed by Colm Bairead, Filmed in Gaelic with subtitles. Starring Catherine Clinch, Carrie Crowley, Andrew Bennett. 1 hr., 34 min. PG-13. Released in 2022. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv/ Why the original Pinocchio (1940) lasts forever Catherine Clinch stars in The Quiet Girl. A scene from Disney’s 1940 animated feature film Pinocchio By Chris Honoré When Pinocchio was released by Disney on February 23, 1940, it was the company’s second feature-length animated film (it followed Snow White) and won two Oscars at the 13th Academy Awards ceremony. Using ink and brush, drawn by hand, it was considered at the time a technical marvel and lauded as marvelous entertainment for people of all ages, especially the little guys. Based on the 1883 children’s book by Carlo Collodi, it was magical and contained humor, drama, with a bevy of endearing and rogue characters. Hence, it wasn’t long before Pinocchio became an iconic figure, and audiences soon regarded the fairy tale about a small wooden puppet that was turned into a real boy as a classic The story opens with Jiminy Cricket (Cliff Edwards) explaining how an elderly Italian woodcarver, Geppetto (Christian Rub), creates a small wooden puppet. The old man, who lives alone, is so taken with the marionette, who he calls Pinocchio, before falling asleep, he gazes into the night sky and wishes upon a star that his wooden creation be turned into a real boy. This is Disney and so that night the puppet is visited by the Blue Fairy (Evelyn Venable) who promises to grant Geppetto his wish; however, there are conditions. If Pinocchio truly wants to be fully human, he must be brave, truthful and unselfish. And so begins the puppet’s journey, filled with moments that test his character. Will he tell the truth? Will he risk everything inside a monstrous whale and rescue Geppetto? Will he resist the temptations of some unsavory characters such as a con artist fox named Honest John (Walter Catlett). It is at such moments that Jiminy Cricket steps forward and takes on the role of Pinocchio’s conscience and guide, reminding him of his promise to the Blue Fairy. The guild of animators who faithfully brought Collodi’s story to the screen were artists in the truest sense of the word, and that is why this beautiful film will never lose its compelling magic. Pinocchio. Directed by Ben Sharpsteen and Hamilton Luske. Released in 1940. With the voices of Dickie Jones, Cliff Edwards, Walter Catlett. Mel Blanc, Christian Rub. 1 hr., 27 min. Rated G. Now streaming on VUDU/Disney+/Prime/Apple tv. articles.text: Come enjoy a range of performances and events this spring. Saturday, April 15, 7:00 p.m. Diluvian Quartet Concert The quartet’s Spring recital, Great Dedications, will feature Elizabeth Castro Abrams and Jessica Scrimale, violins; Raphael Gold, viola; and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello, performing quartets by W.A. Mozart and Reinhold Glière. The concert celebrates these two prolific composers and the works they dedicated to their most influential colleagues and teachers. The reception on Friday, April 21, 5 to 8 p.m. will feature live demonstrations, complimentary food, and an exhibit of student and instructor artwork. This will be a chance to meet the instructors and learn more about the wide variety of classes offered by the Adult School. Open gallery hours are April 22 and 23, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Free and open to all. Friday, April 28, 6:00 p.m. Exclusive photo exhibit of Prague 1968 Before the days of I-Phones and YouTube, photographer Jim Mayer was a student travelling in Europe in 1968. He was in Prague the day the Russians invaded Czechoslovakia, and managed to document the action and get himself and his pictures safely out of the country. This is the first exhibition of these stunning photos, strikingly familiar given the war in Ukraine today. Jim’s widow, Jane Flint, invites the public to a community reception in memory of the photographer who passed away last year. The exhibit will also be open Saturday and Sunday, April 29-30 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Free and open to all! The creativity and transforming styles of Marvin’s art will continue to evolve while presenting exciting, dramatic and provocative works of art to the art lovers of the world. articles.text: At age six, Wynton Marsalis was seated at a table with the great trumpeters Al Hirt, Miles Davis and Clark Terry. His father, a pianist, joked that he should get Wynton a trumpet, too. Al Hirt gave him one. When eight, he played with the Fairview Baptist Church band led by legendary banjoist Danny Barker, and at 14 was with the New Orleans Philharmonic. During high school, he performed with the New Orleans Symphony Brass Quintet, New Orleans Community Concert Band, New Orleans Youth Orchestra, New Orleans Symphony, local jazz bands and the funk band The Creators. Wynton began classical training at 12, and at 17 was studying at Julliard Conservatory in New York and playing with The Jazz Messengers and Art Blakey. Wynton and his saxophonist brother Branford are credited with championing overlooked jazz musicians, prompting a jazz renaissance in the early 1980’s. His band performed over 120 Trumpeter Wynton Marsalis concerts each year from 1981 to 1996. Wynton has performed with a diversity of artists and styles. In jazz, he’s performed with Sarah Vaughan, Dizzy Gillespie, Clark Terry, John Lewis, Sonny Rollins, Christian McBride, Ron Carter, Herbie Hancock and Tony Williams. In classical music, he has appeared with the New York Philharmonic, Los Angeles Philharmonic, Boston Pops, Cleveland Orchestra, English Chamber Orchestra, London Royal Philharmonic and many others. In 2008, Wynton recorded Two Men with the Blues with Willie Nelson. In the 2019 Ken Burns documentary Country Music, Wynton explored the shared roots found through American music. In 2011, Eric Clapton and Wynton performed Play the Blues: Live from Jazz at Lincoln Center and released it on an album. Wynton was the first to be awarded a Grammy for jazz and classical in the same year (1983) and has received a total of nine Grammy awards. He has recorded many classical albums and performed with notable orchestras around the world. In 1987, he founded the Jazz At Lincoln Center series. A crowning achievement was winning the Pulitzer Prize for Music in 1997. Always swinging, Wynton plays with a clear tone, depth of emotion and a rich tonal palette of melodic and trumpet techniques, including vocal effects (slides, growls, smears, halfvalve effects, tremolo, shakes, plunger), rhythmic displacement and tension resolution (melodic, harmonic and rhythmic). pages.text: 20 Wednesday, Aprl 12, 2023 The Musical Gourmet places are often very good. Any The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet restaurant with a sign stating “we have good food“ usually does. And that’s the case at Alems coffee shop. My wife and I arrived at lunchtime and were the only non-Ethiopians in the restaurant. I could tell that the woman in the kitchen Good home cookin’ – was the owner. She was friendly and efficient. Ethiopian style I looked into the small kitchen and saw that everything was made to order. This was a very good sign. Another was that all of the customers were Ethiopian. My wife ordered a sandwich and I got the vegetarian stew. In a few minutes, the owner brought our food. The portions were huge. My traditional Ethiopian stew was made of fava beans, tomatoes, onion, and Eritrean spices. It was served with two large French rolls, which were just about the best I’ve had outside of France. The crust was light and flaky, and the inside light and tender. Alems has a diverse menu, which includes American style sandwiches, and traditional Ethiopian/Eritrean cuisine. While you are enjoying the food there you will enjoy chatting with the customers and the owner…if she has a moment to chat. For homework, read the history of Ethiopia/Eritrea. for musical inspiration listen to Verdi‘s opera Aida. Geographically, Ethiopia is half a world away and has a history going back to the beginning of time. If you are interested in military history, you will be interested to know that the Ethiopians used animals as their allies. By using bees, wasps, lions and elephants, they were invaded but never conquered. It was also the site of the greatest evacuation in the history of the world, with 14,325 Ethiopian Jews airlifted from Ethiopia to Israel in a mere 36 hours. The date was May 24-35, 1991. Enjoy the food. But try to remember to have a cup of coffee. Piedmont Center for the Arts Come enjoy a range of performances and events this spring. articles.text: Any homeowner (or handyman) in the East Bay would agree that Spring is a crucial time for home maintenance. Now is the time to take stock after those long winter months in preparation for warmer weather. Here are some essential spring maintenance tasks that every homeowner in Piedmont should consider: Inspect your roof. Multiple atmospheric rivers can be tough on your roof, so it’s important to check for any damage or leaks that may have occurred. Clean those gutters & downspouts. Check your gutters for any leaves, sticks, and other debris. You may be surprised how much you’ll find. Check your HVAC system. Warm weather is on the horizon. Schedule a maintenance check for your heating and cooling system now so it’s ready when you need it most. Inspect your windows and doors. Gaps and cracks can form around frames. Use weather stripping or caulk to prevent airflow and improve energy efficiency for a comfortable home. Straighten up outdoor living spaces. Power-wash your deck, patio, and outdoor furniture so you’ll actually want to use them. It’s time to prune. Trim back overgrown branches and bushes away from your home to prevent damage to your roof or siding. Check your outdoor lighting. Replace burnt-out bulbs or damaged fixtures for better visibility (and safety) at night. Test your sprinklers. Make sure your sprinkler system still works. Check for leaks or damage before the dry season begins. Test smoke and carbon monoxide detectors. Check batteries and replace units as needed. Clean your chimney. Did you use your fireplace or wood-burning stove? Clean if you did or inspect if you didn’t. Need some help getting ready for Spring? Regular maintenance helps prevent costly repairs and keeps your home running efficiently. Contact www.honeyhomes.com for reliable handyman service in the East Bay. You can have your own dedicated Honey Homes service technician year-round with all work included. Don’t gamble with your home. An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

articles.text: Walking through town it is impossible not to notice the aesthetic impact of different ancillary structures that are an integral part of the design of many homes. Falling somewhere between architecture and landscape architecture, fences, walls, and their associated gates are chief among these. They can enhance (or unfortunately sometimes compromise) the building, landscape and/or site design. So…what constitutes nice retaining walls, appealing fences or beautiful gates? Like all of the discussions in this column, I point out different ideas or considerations that hopefully help to answer this ongoing question. But there are usually many good answers as well as exceptions to every general rule. What is ultimately important is just what looks and feels right – what appeals to us. That being said, here are some thoughts. The first thing that comes to mind is that these secondary structures need as much study and consideration as the main building(s) or landscape treatment of which they are a part. It is unfortunately obvious when they are designed as simply an afterthought. Fences, walls and gates certainly must be in the same architectural “family” as the home, though this doesn’t mean they have to be exactly the same form, color or even the same material. They do need to relate most appropriately. They are indeed an opportunity to aesthetically deviate to some degree and add interest to both the building(s) and property. Fences or walls can be used to provide privacy, add security, or merely to demarcate the edge of private or semi-private spaces between adjacent properties, or between a property and the street. Photos and sketch by Will Adams Photos above and below: Two well designed variations of the traditional white picket fence, both stepping to nicely accommodate the slope of the sidewalk and site, as well as adding interest and texture to the street. After adherence to the architectural style of the buildings, the intended use or function of the barrier will be the primary consideration in determining its type, shape and character, i.e., solid (wall) vs, airy (spaced boards), height, extent, and access or gate placements. Gates are, of course, a prominent part of fences and walls, almost automatically seen as a punctuation point because they usually break the horizontal character of the enclosure to which they are attached. Gates are the first thing people use and pass-through in the “entry experience”, as we mentioned in a Photos above: Two elegantly designed gates of completely different architectural styles. Both are perfectly suited to the walled enclosures of which they are a part and enhance and complement their associated building architecture.

pages.text: Wednesday, Aprl 12, 2023 23 The Wine Corner The Wines of the Northern Rhone By Pierre DuMont After a two-year hiatus because of the COVID pandemic. I was able to resume my annual European wine trip with my colleagues Richard Wing and Terry Hershey. This year we decided to head to the Northern Rhone Valley in Southern France, the original home to two of the greatest grape varietals on earth, Syrah and Viognier. We split our time between the northern part of the area centered on Cote Rotie and Condrieu, and the southern part of Hermitage, St. Joseph and Cornas (to be reviewed in the next article.) Cote Rotie The main wine growing area of the Rhone Valley begins about 10 miles south of the ancient Roman city of Vienne. The northernmost appellation is Cote Rotie (the Roasted Slope). It is a high, slanted hillside that is tilted to face the sun and gather the most warmth. The slope is one of the steepest places in the world where wine is grown, making the growing of these grapes incredibly arduous and time consuming. Most places are far too steep for machinery to be used, so everything must be done by hand or by horse. The only red grape allowed in the Northern Rhone is Syrah, and in Cote Rotie it is allowed to mix in some Viognier which can add some interesting floral notes to the wine. The wines of Cote Rotie have been described as “an iron fist in a velvet glove.” They are full and powerful but also elegant and stylish. Pierre Gaillard Our first visit in Cote Rotie was with Pierre Gaillard and his family. Both of his daughters are winemakers with their own brands. Gaillard is based in the ancient town of Malleval founded in the 11th century and still looking like it. Just making your way through the narrow, winding streets is a challenge, to say nothing of when a car comes from the other direction. The Gaillard winery is modern and perched on the edge of town. Pierre was originally from Lyon and did not grow up in the wine business, He decided to make it his life after moving to Francois Villard Christine Vernay, master of Condrieu Lunch with the Gaillard family this area about 40 years ago. He now owns land in Cote Rotie, St. Joseph, Crozes Hermitage and Condrieu. Most of the current vintage of his wines were sold out – a good problem to have. We spent the morning barrel tasting the wines that will be bottled soon. The 2021 vintage was a difficult one in the Rhone; cold and wet weather, even hail, made it tough to mature the grapes. It is hard to complain though, as the Rhone has had a string of great vintages going back to 2014. The tasting by the Gaillard family was incredibly generous, and we ended up trying 23 different wines from the three family properties. If the only Syrahs and Viogniers you have had are from California, you are in for a change of pace. The climate of the Northern Rhone is much colder than California. That results in the wines having more acid and structure. When Viognier is grown in a warm climate it often becomes dull and f labby and Syrah becomes too fruity and sweet. The Rhone versions have incredible balance between fruit and acid and have an earthiness and minerality you don’t find elsewhere. What followed the tasting was one of the highlights of the entire trip. Pierre invited us to join his wife Pascale and daughter Jeanne for lunch at his house. Pascale whipped up an amazing meal of shaved truffles and mushrooms, roast pork and some vegetable I had never seen that was delicious. Pierre dove deep in the cellar and we drank Cote Rotie going back to 2000 finishing with a beautiful Banyuls dessert wine from his estate. We had two more tastings scheduled for the afternoon, but thankfully they were small and uneventful unlike the gargantuan culinary and wine experience at Gaillard. Francois Villard Francois Villard is one of the up-and-coming bright lights in the Rhone Valley. After previous careers as a chef and sommelier, he ventured into wine growing in 1991 with a small parcel of vines in Condrieu which he has expanded into holdings in Cote Rotie. Villard’s style has evolved from the big, heavy oak-laden style of wines that were popular in the 90’s (and still are with Guigal) to more elegant finesse-style wines attained by short fermentations with mostly full clusters. The wines have tremendous perfume and are exquisitely balanced and refreshing. I also appreciate that in a world where wine prices have gotten absolutely crazy, Villard has held the line and his wines represent great values. We tasted 20 wines at Villard and the highlights were the four Condrieu he produces. Each was intense and floral with a huge bouquet of peaches and melon with notes of honeysuckle and a big round mouthfeel but with balance and a stylish, non-cloying finish. He also makes an outstanding Cornas called Jouvet that is a monster wine with huge blackberry fruit and enough tannin and structure to last three decades. After the tasting Francois took us to a restaurant in the center of Ampuis called Bistro de Serrines. Francois is one of the owners, so we had no problem getting a table. The food was delicious, and this unassuming place had a wine list of over 700 wines including many of the most famous names of the Rhone Valley. Highly recommended if you are ever in the area. Georges Vernay Vernay is the most legendary name in Condrieu with an amazing backstory. The Condrieu appellation is the home of the Viognier grape and originally the only place in the world where it was planted. During the 1950’s and 60’s production it had declined to the point when there were only a few hectares left of the grape varietal in the world. George Vernay saw that the disappearance of Viognier would be a tragedy and began to convince other farmers to replant the varietal and even increase acres under vines. The magnificence of the wines began to be rediscovered and Condrieu appellation once more gained its stature as a gem of the Rhone Valley. Viognier vines were exported from Condrieu and planted in California, Australia, Chile, Argentina and many other locations, and is now a popular international varietal that is alive and well – thanks to George Vernay. This flagship estate is now run by daughter Christine Vernay and her husband Paul. Walking through the doors I felt I was entering the holy grail of Viognier. Christine herself poured the wines and talked about the minimalist methods she uses to make them. The flagship is called the Coteau du Vernon from the best located vineyard on the steep Condrieu slope. Equally good I thought was the Les Chaillees de L’Enfer (Steps of Hell) from a place on the hill that gets extremely hot hence the name. Both wines exude honeysuckle and gardenia aromas with luscious peach and apricot fruit with just the right amount of acid for balance. They were full and mouth-filling yet refreshing. To start your tasting journey into the Northern Rhone, the wines listed below are recommended as a beginning. The wines of Pierre Gaillard and Francois Villard are imported by Napa-based Jack Edwards Collection (jackedwardscollection. com) an outstanding source for European boutique wineries. Tasting your way through the Northern Rhone: • 2021 Pierre Gaillard St. Joseph Clos de Cuminalle • 2022 Pierre Gaillard Condrieu • 2020 Francois Villard Condrieu Le Grand Vallon • 2020 Francois Villard Cornas Jouvet • 2021 Georges Vernay Condrieu Coteau du Vernon • 2021 Georges Vernay Chaillees de L’Enfer A steep terraced vineyard in the Rhone

articles.text: World War II ended too soon for Terry Rollin Haws to earn his Army Air Corp wings. So when, on March 19, 2023, he donned his well-deserved and glorious Angelic Wings, he was able to fly upward and onward to his next great adventure. Born in Piedmont on February 24, 1926, he was the only child of Magnolia Cosgrove Haws and Alpheus Haws and lived to be 97. He graduated from Piedmont High School in 1943, and earned a Bachelor’s degree from the University of California in Berkeley, where he was a track star. Some of Terry’s favorite childhood memories were the times he spent at Russian River with his family. He always looked back on his college years fondly. In his senior year at Berkeley, he began dating and subsequently married the love of his life for 71 years, Jacqueline Nino Haws. Terry began working full time for Haws Drinking Faucet Company in Berkeley in 1949, devoting his knowledge and expertise to the family company that was started in 1906 by his grandfather, Luther Ensign Haws, after he invented and patented the first drinking fountain. Under Terry’s leadership, Haws Drinking Faucet Company grew from a small local company into an internationally renowned manufacturer of drinking fountains and emergency equipment with locations in Switzerland, Singapore and Brazil. Terry and Jackie’s first child was a son, Timothy John Haws, whose short life prompted them to keep trying. Their first daughter, Nina Dori Haws, arrived in 1955. Her subsequent Downs Syndrome diagnosis introduced Terry and Jackie to a life of charitable community work. They committed themselves to a lifetime of supporting, developing and funding Las Trampas School for the developmentally disabled. Terry’s leadership on the Las Trampas Board of Directors for over 50 years allowed the organization to flourish and adapt to the changing needs of their clients and the community. In addition to his commitment to his business and philanthropy, Terry was also a devoted and loving father to his three daughters, Nina, Amy and Sallie. He provided and supported endless opportunities for them to participate in swimming, waterskiing, tennis, golf, dance, and music. Terry loved boating on the Delta. A member of Little Venice Yacht Club for over 30 years, he and Jackie made fabulous lasting memories with other members Born and raised in Piedmont, Terry Haws passed away in Lafayette on March 29 at age 97. who became lifelong friends. For almost 20 years after Little Venice closed, Terry and Jackie would spend as much time as they could on their houseboat at Bethel Harbor enjoying a libation on the back deck. After discovering the Big Island of Hawaii when he was nine years old, the Kohala Coast became one of Terry and Jackie’s favorite destination vacations as adults. For five decades they returned year after year to Mauna Kea and Kona Village Resort, and then enjoyed a family home in Kailua-Kona until 2019. A long-time member of the Orinda Country Club, Terry enjoyed golfing into his early nineties. Watching football and reading novels were two of his favorite pastimes he enjoyed until his very last days. Terry’s love, generosity, kindness and wonderful sense of humor created a legacy that will last forever. He was an exceptional father, husband, friend and businessman, who was greatly loved and admired by so many whose lives he touched. Terry Haws is survived by his beloved wife, Jacqueline, his two daughters and sons-in-law, Amy and Dennis Peck of Escondido, California and Sallie Haws and Jim Bowers of Henderson, Nevada; and his two grandchildren, Marquise and Terry Van Tassel of Henderson, Nevada. A memorial and Celebration of Life was held on Saturday, April 8, 2023. In lieu of flowers, the family requests memorial contributions be made to Las Trampas, P.O. Box 515, Lafayette, CA 94549. lastrampas.org/waysto-donate, or a restricted donation to the Bruns House Hospice East Bay, 3470 Buskirk Ave., Pleasant Hill, CA 94523. hospiceeastbay. org/campaign-for-bruns.
articles.title: Terry Haws dies in Lafayette at age 97

articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group got some lovely, spring weather last Wednesday. As some passed the top of Piedmont Park, they were taken back by the beauty of cherry trees in full blossom. An excellent turnout of 32 walkers were at the Exedra for a fun, special walk. The walkers had heard about pickleball, so Helen and Quincy Dong were asked to take the Wednesday Walkers to Linda/ Beach to see pickleball in action. Helen took the group down Magnolia Avenue past the high school. Work on the new aquatics center was fully underway. A very large Deere backhoe was scooping large amounts of earth out of a very large hole where the old pool once was and dumping them into a very large truck with another one waiting. Helen stopped in front of the middle school and told the walkers about the pickleball courts behind the school. The large group continued down Oakland and regrouped for a mass crossing of Grand Avenue, and up to the playfield next to Beach School. The walkers above the field on Howard Avenue made their way down and around the turf playfield that was being used by young Beach students in a P.E. class. The group came out on Linda Avenue and went up to the court entrance. The walkers went behind three sets of four pickleballers to an open area where they could watch the action. Lucy Chiang thoughtfully provided some rackets and encouraged the walkers to try the game. Pickleballer Rick Schiller came over and talked about the benefits of the sport. It was fun, but soon time for the walkers to make their way back up Oakland Avenue. The Dongs stayed to play, so the leader baton was handed off by Helen to Jim Kellogg for the return to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. On hand for last week’s Walk on Wednesday were Marion Lim Yankowitz, Lisa Euphrat, Stella Houston, Gloria DaSilva, Tina Shun, Edith Lee, Kat Lang, Peggy Schultz, Vincent Fisher, Helen Dong, Ken Moy, Quincy Dong, Alissa Quan, Adrienne Hamlin, John Lenahan, Brenda Ferrero, Phil Witte, Mark Davis, Jim Kellogg, Garrett Clifford, Jim Kuo, Christine Calliste, Noemi Alvarado, Cheryl Coleman Jones, Priscilla Wanerus, Harriette Louie, Alan Goldhammer, Swee Ling Chen, Albert Chen, and Dick Carter.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group met on April 3rd once again inside the Community Hall. There was a large, but manageable turnout of 21 readers for the discussion. Before the group started their discussion, Bob Hall proposed a new reading group focused on short literary works. At each gathering members would discuss a short story, a short work of non-fiction and perhaps a poem, all of which he would choose and provide via email. The purpose is both literary and social: to enjoy one another’s company by sharing thoughts and feelings about the art of writing. The group was there to discuss Born a Crime by South African comedian Trevor Noah. It was published in 2016, favorably received, and became a No. 1 New York Times Bestseller. It was also named one of the best books of the year by the Times. The book tells of Noah growing up in his native South Africa during the apartheid era. He is the mixed-race son of a white Swiss-German father and a black mother. Noah was classified as a “coloured” in accordance with the country’s apartheid system of racial classification at that time. He writes that under apartheid it was hard for him to fit into this racist society because it was a crime “for to be born as a mixedrace baby.” Born a Crime tells Noah’s stories, but also pays homage to his mother who grew up in a hut with fourteen occupants. She is stubborn, fearless, and a fiercely religious woman who took her son to three churches every Sunday, a prayer meeting on Tuesday, Bible study on Wednesday, and youth church on Thursday. This is happening when black South Africans were rioting in the streets, and most people were staying inside the safety of their homes. Despite growing up in poverty in a racist society and having a part-time biological father and later an abusive stepfather, Noah navigates through this world. He uses his intelligence, social and mental agility, as well as his fluency in languages and ability to mimic others, to be accepted as a mixed race child and become an amazing performer. His mother provides tough love and “oldschool, Old Testament discipline” as he goes. This was one of those unique books where all the readers enjoyed it with little to criticize. Some readers didn’t know much about Noah except that he is a comic. The “stories from a South African childhood” were revelatory about Noah and life then in South Africa. Noah is able to deal with a dark time in a light tone. He is cleaver and humorous, but the book is not funny. He doesn’t preach, so everyone including readers just looking to be entertained find the book acceptable. Those members of the group who listened to the book’s audio version found it especially enjoyable. Noah is a gifted performer and mimic. His reading made the different situations and people with different styles of speech all the more fun. Some readers questioned how factually accurate the different stories were, but it was accepted they might be “family stories” where precise accuracy is not that important. The group previously selected The Killer Angels by Michael Shaara for May, The Hare with Amber Eyes by Edmund de Waal for June, and How Beautiful We Were by Cameroonian-American novelist Imbolo Mbue for July. The next book discussion will be on May 1at 1:30 p.m. at the Community Hall. New readers are welcome to join the group. Register at https://bit.ly/3R86PP4. There is no fee to participate. A total ot 21 people showed up for the First Mondays Reading Group on April 3 at Piedmont Community Hall: Mike Bandrowski, Phil Witte, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Dale Benveniste, Richard Sigel, Ken Young, Pat McMahon, Bob Hall, Mike Henn, Nancy Henn, Sarah Johnson, Martin Levy, Lisa Euphrat, Adrienne Hamlin, Albert Chen, Laura Goldman, Lois Price, Barbara Eisenbach, Carol Long, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03

pages.text: Wednesday, Aprl 12, 2023 25 First Monday Readers discuss Trevor Noah’s Born a Crime By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group met on April 3rd once again inside the Community Hall. There was a large, but manageable turnout of 21 readers for the discussion. Before the group started their discussion, Bob Hall proposed a new reading group focused on short literary works. At each gathering members would discuss a short story, a short work of non-fiction and perhaps a poem, all of which he would choose and provide via email. The purpose is both literary and social: to enjoy one another’s company by sharing thoughts and feelings about the art of writing. The group was there to discuss Born a Crime by South African comedian Trevor Noah. It was published in 2016, favorably received, and became a No. 1 New York Times Bestseller. It was also named one of the best books of the year by the Times. The book tells of Noah growing up in his native South Africa during the apartheid era. He is the mixed-race son of a white Swiss-German father and a black mother. Noah was classified as a “coloured” in accordance with the country’s apartheid system of racial classification at that time. He writes that under apartheid it was hard for him to fit into this racist society because it was a crime “for to be born as a mixedrace baby.” Born a Crime tells Noah’s stories, but also pays homage to his mother who grew up in a hut with fourteen occupants. She is stubborn, fearless, and a fiercely religious woman who took her son to three churches every Sunday, a prayer meeting on Tuesday, Bible study on Wednesday, and youth church on Thursday. This is happening when black South Africans were rioting in the streets, and most people were staying inside the safety of their homes. Despite growing up in poverty in a racist society and having a part-time biological father and later an abusive stepfather, Noah navigates through this world. He uses his intelligence, social and mental agility, as well as his fluency in languages and ability to mimic others, to be accepted as a mixed race child and become an amazing performer. His mother provides tough love and “oldschool, Old Testament discipline” as he goes. This was one of those unique books where all the readers enjoyed it with little to criticize. Some readers didn’t know much about Noah except that he is a comic. The “stories from a South African childhood” were revelatory about Noah and life then in South Africa. Noah is able to deal with a dark time in a light tone. He is cleaver and humorous, but the book is not funny. He doesn’t preach, so everyone including readers just looking to be entertained find the book acceptable. Those members of the group who listened to the book’s audio version found it especially enjoyable. Noah is a gifted performer and mimic. His reading made the different situations and people with different styles of speech all the more fun. Some readers questioned how factually accurate the different stories were, but it was accepted they might be “family stories” where precise accuracy is not that important. The group previously selected The Killer Angels by Michael Shaara for May, The Hare with Amber Eyes by Edmund de Waal for June, and How Beautiful We Were by Cameroonian-American novelist Imbolo Mbue for July. The next book discussion will be on May 1at 1:30 p.m. at the Community Hall. New readers are welcome to join the group. Register at https://bit.ly/3R86PP4. There is no fee to participate. A total ot 21 people showed up for the First Mondays Reading Group on April 3 at Piedmont Community Hall: Mike Bandrowski, Phil Witte, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Dale Benveniste, Richard Sigel, Ken Young, Pat McMahon, Bob Hall, Mike Henn, Nancy Henn, Sarah Johnson, Martin Levy, Lisa Euphrat, Adrienne Hamlin, Albert Chen, Laura Goldman, Lois Price, Barbara Eisenbach, Carol Long, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. articles.text: On Sunday morning, April 2, a resident interrupted catalytic converter thieves as they tried to steal the emission device from his Toyota parked on Florada Avenue. The resident woke up at 6:30 a.m. after hearing sawing noises and approached the suspects who were in a silver Kia sedan with the engine running. After being spotted, one suspect pointed a black Glock handgun at the resident. He said something in Spanish to the resident, who put his hands up and retreated to his home. No shots were fired, and there were no injuries. The suspects then fled on Florada towards La Salle. Catalytic converters are coveted for the precious metals within and nationwide crime rings facilitate the extraction and sale of the metals. The resident’s converter was damaged, but not removed. The Police Department strongly urge residents not to interfere with crimes in progress. “For your own safety, when you witness a crime, please call 9-1-1 immediately and stay on the phone with dispatchers until officers arrive. The best way to help our officers protect you is to stay inside your home and provide the dispatcher with a thorough description of the suspects and the vehicle associated with them,” the police stated. A crime in progress requires a 9-1-1 call. The non-emergency dispatch line for the Piedmont Police is 420-3000.

articles.text: Gonzales said that, since then, Public Works has held “at least three public meetings, and then a number of follow up meetings with individuals who are impacted by the project, both one on one and then in small neighborhood working groups.” The meetings focused on traffic impact, pedestrian counts, maintaining access to driveways, and maintaining adequate sight distance for drivers turning left onto Nova from Magnolia. Gonzales said that the new plan was “generally … very well received.” Jane Lim and Mary Wells, two residents who live by the intersection of Magnolia and Nova and who spoke at the meeting, echoed Gonzales’ statement. Although minor changes could have been made, they said — Lim emphasized more traffic-calming measures for speeding vehicles and Wells emphasized drought-tolerant planting on the island — they both commended the city for arriving at a plan which addressed major resident concerns. More details about the traffic and safety redesign plan at Nova and Magnolia are available in the City Council staff report, at bit. ly/43e45pb. For questions about the plan, contact Daniel Gonzales by email at dgonzales@piedmont. ca.gov or phone at 420-3061.

articles.text: gressions. “The main thing I really dealt with at this school was being called the name of the only other Asian girl in class. People do that a lot and don’t understand that it’s more impactful than they think. It’s really hurtful,” said Kong. “We are all different people. We may have similar features, but no one is clearly the same. You have to just try, and you can’t just brush it off.” While Piedmont is a relatively homogeneous community, highlighting diversity within it and its schools is necessary to combat ignorance and to celebrate all students. “It is important to show people that there are a lot of different personalities and identities at the schools. Piedmont is majority white, but we can’t ignore or not see the people who don’t identify as that,” Kong added. “It’s good for students to know and recognize that not everybody is the same and there are differences within our community.” the Duke Ellington song Rubber Bottom. You have to just try, and you can’t just brush it off.” While Piedmont is a relatively homogeneous community, highlighting diversity within it and its schools is necessary to combat ignorance and to celebrate all students. “It is important to show people that there are a lot of different personalities and identities at the schools. Piedmont is majority white, but we can’t ignore or not see the people who don’t identify as that,” Kong added. “It’s good for students to know and recognize that not everybody is the same and there are differences within our community.” Guitar Improv Continued from page 20 key of music,” has prompted Wynton to make free and expressive use of all the keys and modes. articles.text: Returning to the neighborhood location where she learned to play basketball, baseball, softball, and soccer, Piedmont City Administrator Sara Lillevand was celebrated at an outdoor party on Sunday, April 2, at Hampton Park (formerly Hampton Field) on the occasion of her retirement. Standing near second base, she addressed family, friends, and coworkers in an afternoon farewell event ahead of her official retirement this Thursday, April 6. Snacks and beverages were provided, and predictably some games for kids to play. Distinct from traditional retirements events, Lillevand chose to be the only speaker – and she covered it all, providing details and some highlights of her impressive athletic career prior to joining the city government. It was a trip down memory lane for her. She grew up on Sotelo Avenue, one block from the field, and described how she, her father, Dave, and her brother David would spend every available sliver of time at the field playing sports. She was often the only girl on boys’ teams because no girls’ teams existed. A gifted athlete from a young age, she Photos by Piedmont Post and Dave Brannigan City Administrator Sara Lillevand speaks before family, friends, and coworkers at a farewell party held for her at Hampton Field on Sunday, April 2, ahead of her official retirement date on April 6. went on to star in basketball at Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland and UC Davis. Following college she coached women’s collegiate basketball, and ultimately became the Athletic Director at Hayward State. Many observers of city politics were unaware of her athletic background, and with her father in attendance, she praised him for his steadfast support and encouragement over many years. “Hampton Field holds a very special place in my heart, so having such a fun day at the park was a perfect farewell for me. To share the day with my dad and brother was particularly meaningful,” commented Sara, who said she particularly looked forward to spending more family-focused time after her retirement. At the farewell, Lillevand decided to have only one speaker: herself. She spoke at length about her experience growing up in Piedmont just one block from Hampton Field and was touched
articles.title: Farewell party for Sara Lillevand at Hampton Field where she learned to play sports

articles.text: During a City Council meeting on Monday, April 3, Council members honored City Administrator Sara Lillevand who will retired from city government this week on Thursday, April 6. Acknowledging that it is her birthday, the council will issue a proclamation stating April 5, 2023 to be Sara Lillevand Day in Piedmont. Speaking on Lillevand’s time working with the city, Councilmember Betsy Andersen said that anyone who has “worked with Sara on city initiatives or is employed by the city of Piedmont knows how hard Sara has worked on behalf of our community. Sara’s optimism and foresight is reflected in her personal mantra, which is not only to do the right thing at any given moment in time, but to look ahead and always try to do the next right thing.” Andersen particularly praised the “city management dream team” to bring together a full-time staff which kept the city “running smoothly during the ultimate test of a global pandemic.” Elaborating on “the tangible things Sara has done for our town,” Andersen mentioned the renovation of Hampton Park, the renovation and endowment of the Corey Reich Tennis Center, and the Piedmont Community Pool project. “I would be remiss if I did not mention how hard Sara has worked to collaborate with the school district and with our many civic volunteer organizations,” Andersen added. articles.title: City Council honors Sara Lillevand on Monday night

articles.text: Ahead of her first day as Piedmont’s new City Administrator this Thursday, April 6, Rosanna Bayon Moore spoke with the Piedmont Post about her background, experience, and intentions for her work with the city. Originally from Southern California, Moore was born in Los Angeles and primarily raised in Monterey Park in the San Gabriel Valley. She spent her summers from earliest childhood through early adulthood with her father in rural Imperial Valley by the city of El Centro, near the Mexican border; both of her parents were born and raised there. After graduating in 1991 from Mayfield Senior School, an allgirls Catholic high school in Pasadena, she studied at UC Berkeley, where she earned a Bachelor of Arts in English and political science in 1995 and met her husband. For five years onward, she did nonprofit work in the Bay Area. In 1997, she was accepted into the San Francisco-based Northern California Coro Fellows Program in Public Affairs. In 2020, Piedmont Unified School District passed a Racial Equity board policy that made Assistant Superintendent of Educational Services Dr. Cheryl Wozniak responsible for its implementation. Dr. Wozniak thought the course grading formula should be standardized keeping a goal of racial equity in mind. Since roughly 2020, some PMS and PHS teachers voluntarily began experimenting with a grading system based on a book called “Grading for Equity” by Joe Feldman. Do racial differences in grade distributions prove a biased education? As school board president, Veronica Andersen Thigpen agendized this topic for action by the board at a public meeting on March 22, 2023, but did not appear at the meeting to defend her position. Thigpen, who is a Fellow at Just Equations, a nonprofit that reconceptualizes the role of math in ensuring educational equity, ran for school board in 2020 on the premise that there should be equity in educational outcomes for all races. At the public meeting on March 22, 2023, Wozniak led a presentation on “Equitable Grading Practices” to update the school board on her efforts with support from PMS and PHS school principals. Wozniak argued: “Teachers sincerely want their students’ grades to be objective, but our grading systems historically have systemically perpetuated opportunity gaps and biases. For example: providing extra credit, penalizing for lateness, punishing cheating in the grade, evaluating student behavior (like how often a student raises their hand and participates), and including homework. These are all biased grading practices and dependent on a student’s life circumstances, culture, and for all kinds of reasons.” Feldman’s grading is solely based on a student’s mastery of the content based on assessments, nothing behavioral. Feldman prohibits grading credit for homework completion, class participation, extra credit, or grade punishment for cheating because it disproportionately impacts low-income and minority students. Instead, he promotes giving students the option to be retested or resubmit work in subject areas the student did not master (a.k.a. Mastery-Based Grading), and instead of a failing grade below 50%, he would give students an incomplete that would not count against their GPA.

articles.text: A time-lapse camera was installed on Monday, April 3, on the roof of the Piedmont Recreation Center to record progress at the Piedmont Community Pool site, with a photo feed available on the city website. Photos will be uploaded to the city website every 15 minutes from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. at piedmont. ca.gov/newpool. Piedmont Communications Manager Echa Schneider confirmed that the cost of camera and installation was $13,500. The online host service is webcam provider EarthCam. Pool excavation continues, but at a slower pace due to the rain between December and March. The contractors have been busy preventing on-site flooding by pumping out water which accumulated in the holes cut in bedrock for the new main and medium-sized pools. However, the biggest storm-related challenge and the main reason for delays has been PG&E. Its utility workers were originally expected to come as soon as Friday, March 10, but they still haven’t arrived to pull meters and disconnect the power from the sites of former pool facility buildings. Construction manager George Sanen reached out to PG&E three times in the last week, but “we still haven’t received a confirmed day,” said Gonzales. “They must be backlogged with more urgent storm damage response tasks and in the meantime the contractors are working to minimize schedule impacts.“ “The biggest impact is because there are still live gas lines, identifying where they are, largely keeping things in place there, and digging slowly elsewhere. Since it’s more about a change in sequence they’re still able to do much of the work. They’re finishing up on moving out concrete and steel; soon it’ll just be soil,” said Gonzales. Community members can stay informed about pool construction and get direct updates about traffic, noise, and other impacts by subscribing to the City’s Community Pool Construction Updates email list at bit.ly/3SAmveF. For questions or comments about parking and traffic, contact Gonzales by email at dgonzales@ piedmont.ca.gov. For more information on the Piedmont Community Pool project, visit piedmont. ca.gov/newpool. A time-lapse camera recently installed at the Community Pool construction site will provide ongoing images of the progress of the city’s new swimming pools.
articles.title: Live-feed camera installed for pool project

The bulk of the costs are for third-party contractors assisting in cleanup and additional internal personnel costs (overtime After being pounded by heavy rain and wind on March 21, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that the storm one week later on March 28 “paled in comparison to the previous ones. The rain intensity was so spread out, more like a Seattle drizzle than a New Mexico flash flood,” he said. Although Piedmont faced no downed trees or power lines like it did earlier, “Even small amounts of rain at this point create issues that we don’t typically see because the ground is so saturated,” Gonzales added. Workers with the Public Works Department have been patching the sinkhole temporarily with cold patch asphalt. “It’s a fast fix — you open the bag, dump it in, but since it’s not hot, it breaks up faster … [requiring replacement] after a few days if water is involved.” Residents with questions about storm costs can contact Michael Szczech by phone at 420-3045 or by email at mszczech@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: The Salvation Army will hold its eighth annual gala on Sunday, April 30 at 5 p.m. at the University Club in UC Berkeley’s Memorial Stadium. Chaired by Debbie Kelley of Piedmont, the event will feature live music from the UC Berkeley a cappella group DeCadence, live and silent auctions, testimonials from inspiring Salvation Army beneficiaries, and dinner. The Volunteer of the Year honoree Elijah Hicks, will be introduced. A former UC Berkeley football player, he was drafted by the Chicago Bears last year and has chosen the Salvation Army for philanthropy through his foundation, Intercept Poverty. The organization provides financial assistance to low-income students. All proceeds will help fund The Salvation Army’s efforts to meet human need in Alameda County. The non-profit helps with food, rent, and utility assistance, operates a homeless shelter and homeless outreach programs, preschools, after-school programs, a summer camp in the Sierra foothills, music programs, Christmas assistance, and workforce development programs in construction and certified nurse’s assistant training. Kelley, who is chairing the event for her fourth year, has been on the Salvation Army advisory board since 2016. She confirmed that last year’s gala raised over $420,000 with 150 people in attendance. A similar crowd is expected this year. “The people involved before me said they were lucky to clear $100,000,” said Kelley. “Now we clear $300,000-$400,000, much due Corki Recht, the co-chair for three years.” When Kelley was unavailable last year due to an emergency, Recht ran the event, the first time the gala was held at Memorial Stadium, In prior years it had been held at the Claremont Country Club. Wanting a change of venue, Kelley, who works in College Relations at UC Berkeley, approached the school’s Athletics Director, Jim Knowlton, who encouraged the move. “It was then that we decided to honor a Cal student volunteer,” said Kelley. In 2022 the honoree was professional baseball player Tyson Ross, a pitcher who has created a “Loyal to my Soil” program providing baseball lessons to inner-city children. Highlights at this year’s live auction includes a dinner for 10 cooked by Salvation Army Culinary Director Tim Tucker, and a testimonial by Thomas Wolf, a former homeless man and drug addict who has since reinvented his life due to his work with the Salvation Army. “People think of the Salvation Army as red kettles and thrift stores,” said Kelley, “but they provide such important rehabilitation and emergency service work. articles.text: If you own real property in California, you must pay property taxes twice a year. The second installment of property taxes is due by Monday, April 10. Missing the deadline is a very expensive mistake, since the penalty is 10% plus a $10 fee. If you don’t pay by June 30, things start to get worse You can send a check, along with your 2nd payment voucher, or pay by phone. However, most people find it more convenient to pay online. The Alameda County Tax Collector’s URL for making payments is: http://co.alameda.ca.us/propertytax/ If you want to use a credit card and get those frequent flyer miles, you can do so, but you will pay a 2.5% processing fee, money that does not go to the county. A direct debit to your bank account does not incur any additional charges.

articles.text: The Appreciating Diversity Film Series will present an evening of Short Films on April 20 at 7:00 p.m. at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse on the Havens School campus at 325 Highland Avenue Help the Appreciating Diversity Film Series enrich the Piedmont Food Fest’s celebration of Bay Area diversity with five family friendly films that will explore the many flavors of families. Bring your family and friends and experience the range of family diversity through themes such as adoption, homelessness, women’s issues, education, and gender identity. The films are appropriate for children ages 10 and up. As always, Diversity films are free. The films which will be screened starting at 7:00 p.m. are listed below in the order in which they will be seen. The total running time for all five films is about one hour. • Absolutely No Spitting A Jewish mother and her multiracial 4-year-old adopted daughter explore their DNA profiles and what it means to have many identities and cultures in your genetic heritage. • A Concerto Is a Conversation A virtuoso jazz pianist and film composer traces his family’s lineage through his 91-year-old grandfather from Jim Crow laws in Florida to the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles. The grandfather describes the development of his love for music as well as his ingenious methods of getting ahead that made it possible for his family to thrive then and for coming generations. • Almost Famous: The Silent Pulse of the Universe In 1967, a young astronomer, Jocelyn Bell, made a breakthrough discovery in astronomy, but as a woman in the sciences her role was overlooked and unfairly ignored. While Jocelyn was belittled and sexually harassed by the media, the Nobel Prize was awarded to her professor and his boss. • What You’ll Remember The story of young Bay Area parents determined to give their four children a good life despite moving in and out of homelessness over a period of fifteen years. While the family waited for stable, affordable housing, they nurtured and educated their children in resourceful, inspiring ways, creating a feeling of “home” even when there was no house. • Texas Strong Kai Shappley, a 6-year old trans child in Texas, fights to be recognized and accepted by her devout Christian family. Kai’s mother, Shirley, must deal with her church, while Kai navigates life at school, where she is banned from the girls’ bathroom. Winner of the 2018 Emmy for Outstanding Short Documentary. The Appreciating Diversity Film Series is co-sponsored by Piedmont School District, the City of Piedmont, the Oakland and Piedmont Leagues of Women Voters, and the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee.
articles.title: Diversity Film series joins Piedmont Food Fest

articles.text: Photos by Selen Ozturk. Off-season and holiday clothing in a Dress Best for Less storage room. On Tuesday morning, March 21, Dress Best for Less volunteers returned to their marking room at First Congregational Church in Oakland to see that their storage bins, and everything inside them had been destroyed by an arson fire the night before. Some DBFL staff say that the event feels like the tipping point of six months of insecurity since the non-profit thrift business was forced last October from the now-demolished Carriage House, by the Piedmont Pool. DBFL has raised over $1 million dollars for Piedmont School District since its founding in 1982, through sales of donated items to its retail shop on Piedmont Avenue. However, neither the school district nor the city have provided suitable space for a marking room – a location where donated items can be sorted and priced before being put on sale at the retail shop. Karen Eppler, who has been involved with DBFL since its inception said the organization moved to the Carriage House around 1993. Before that it operated out of a vacant classroom in Havens School, Elementary, and then from an unused classroom at Piedmont High. “After that we hauled it all back and used another room at Havens,” she recalled. “I was on the committee to find us a space in Piedmont after the Carriage House,” said Huldah Hodgkinson, who has been the vice president of DBFL for four years. “Conna McCarthy from City Council and Hillary Cooper from the School Board were reps. The school district did offer us spaces, but not the amount we needed. One was a tiny side alley between Driscoll [Playhouse] and Havens.” Dress Best has donated about $100,000 a year to the Piedmont Education Foundation. Since moving to the church at 2501 Harrison St., this has no longer been possible as Piedmonters no longer have a convenient space to donate clothes, shoes, accessories, and household items. “It was disillusioning that the district had the money to construct two new buildings”–. the Alan Harvey Theater and the STEAM Building at Piedmont High – “but had no space for us. Our mission is to support the schools, and this made us feel devalued,” said Hodgkinson. Piedmont School District’s budget for 2022-2023 is over $52 million. Since last week’s arson at the new location (across the street from Whole Foods at 27th & Harrison in Oakland), Hodgkinson said that DBFL’s about 20 volunteers have been even more demoralized. “We don’t have the police support in Oakland that we had in Piedmont. We file a report and that’s all; no one comes. Not to mention the usual urban issues, like people urinating and defecating on our building. The volunteers we rely on don’t feel totally safe working under these conditions, and I believe it’s just a matter of time until someone breaks into the actual building,” she added. The fire completely scorched a 10-foot square storage shed, and charred a donation bin half that size to the point of unusability. Eppler said DBFL board members could not yet provide an estimate for replacement, as they are still discussing cost setbacks with insurance providers. DBFL staff member Beverly Bucci, who has been involved with the organization for 15-20 years, said “when we were at the Carriage House, the donation bin was always full. We’d easily get 10 donators a day. Now it’s more like three to four.” “I’d like to emphasize how close we still are to Piedmont, only two miles,” added staff member Sharon Sanford, who has been involved with DBFL for 20-30 years. “This space sure isn’t an advantage to us,” she said, “especially since we have to make even more room for the bags that would have gone in the burned bins. However, our very large parking lot and dropoff space can be an advantage to Piedmonters.” While DBFL has considered downsizing to only keep their retail store on Piedmont Avenue next door to Piedmont Grocery, this store alone does not have adequate space to store donations, nor a place for dropping off items. For DBFL staff, the future is uncertain. “We’re seriously rethinking whether our business is viable; we can’t continue like this,” said Hodgkinson. “Sustainability – reusing, recycling – is Piedmont’s mission, and it’s crucial to us. We’re asking the community to support us in our mission to help Piedmont schools.” Those interested in donating to DBFL may find a list of acceptable items and make an appointment at dressbestforless.org.
articles.title: DBFL strained after Piedmont eviction, arson at new site

articles.text: Piedmont Food Fest 2 is coming to town Sunday, April 23, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. in Piedmont Park, and will be a super-sized multicultural festival with many aspects for visitors to experience. Piedmont Food Fest will feature 30 Bay Area food vendors, breweries, and wineries including several Piedmonter-run businesses, including Robert Dorsey Catering, Tea on Piedmont, Bakesum, Mo’s Bakeshop, and Yumbini. This year’s live performances will include Hiiwav music showcase featuring Meaghan Maples and Tyler Reese, Emeryville Taiko, Renegade Opera, LIKHA Pilipino Folk Ensemble, Oakland Samba Revue, and the Han Martial Arts Demo Exhibition. Volunteer slots are now available to assist with check-In, the KidZone carnival, as well as vendor and artist setups. Guests may register for free at www.piedmontfoodfest.org as well as pre-order drink packages, carnival passes, and snackpacks. All registrants who sign up before the event will be eligible to win gift certificates from sponsors Mulberry’s Market and Marielle Hayes Photography.
articles.title: Food Fest is coming to town Sunday, April 23
