articles.text: Alison Montes and daughter Julia, a sophomore at Piedmont High School, will travel to Malawi this summer to help build rabbit fences with a volunteer committee and buy computers and videography equipment for a film school at Dzaleka Refugee Camp in Malawi, Africa’s poorest country. The project is coordinated by Vijana Africa, a 501(3)c non-profit. It is a community-based organization operating in the refugee camp. For more information and to donate, contact amontes@ otismcallister.com. All donations are tax deductible. For online donations, please click on the Facebook fundraiser page: ht t ps://w w w.facebook.com / donate/1398293844329517/ Vijana Africa’s Videography School has training programs in videography and computer basics, and currently has over 20 people sharing three computers. The beneficiaries are refugees ages 13-20 who are learning how to use Microsoft Windows, Word, and Excel, and shoot and edit videos. At the end of their training, they present a documentary. Participants in the program are developing skills they can use to improve life in Dzaleka and when they are able to resettle in their home country. Alison Montes and daughter Julia with students in the Videography School at Dzaleka Refugee Camp in Malawi
articles.title: Mother, daughter plan fundraising effort in Malawi this summer

articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is pleased to announce its fourth annual essay contest open to all high school juniors and seniors who are either currently enrolled at Piedmont or Millennium High School or are residents of Piedmont. This year’s essay, to be 250-500 words, is due by May 7. The topic is: “In the last decade, the US Supreme Court has severely weakened the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (VRA), which was widely agreed to be the most effective civil rights law in our history. What action can the League of Women Voters take to counteract the negative effects of the Supreme Court’s decisions regarding voting rights, specifically those that place hurdles upon voting?” A $500 prize will be awarded to the first place entry. For more information and to submit an essay, visit lwvpiedmont.org/ essay-contest.
articles.title: High School essay contest offered by League of Women Voters

articles.text: Becker Dashing through a downpour, more than 100 students and parents flooded into Alan Harvey Theatre eager to further uncover one of America’s greatest mysteries – the college admissions process. On Tuesday, March 21, during a heavy rain and windstorm, the Regional Admissions Counselors of California (RACC) hosted a mock admission night for Piedmont students to learn what makes a strong college application. “I’m sure most kids would agree, the whole process of doing your applications can be really hard to understand. I think attending this can help take some of that mystery away,” said Axel Saldanha, a junior at Piedmont High. The attendees were first presented with information about “Lake Washington University”, a fictional college meant to simulate a school that students might apply to. The students then split into groups and reviewed mock applications, deciding which would be accepted, waitlisted, or rejected. “Looking through the applications was really interesting; we got to see the process from the other side, which I think will be helpful,” George Stein. Afterwards tables were displayed with information about colleges for students to look into, including Texas Christian University, University of Arizona, and University of Oregon. “I’m glad I attended. I think the whole event helped bring me closer to the finish line with my college apps,” said Cole Nash. Among the event’s organizers was Arizona College Admissions Counselor Molly Ingram. “I absolutely think the event went well tonight. I was impressed with how many people braved the wind and rain and came out to see how the application process works,” Ingram said. Micah Temple and William Becker are Piedmont High School students and interns with the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: In spite of storm, big turnout for Mock Admission Night

articles.text: I was listening to a podcast featuring Dr. Saundra Dalton-Smith in which she was discussing the seven different kinds of rest that we need. One really stood out to me: Creative Rest. Her definition of creativity is any time we need to solve a problem. moment of parenting is an act of creativity. How do we get the kids out of the house in the morning when they are moving as slow as turtles? How can we get the siblings to stop arguing over who gets to choose the show to watch during screen time? How do we convince an unwilling child to engage in homework that is hard? All of these problems require creativity in order to solve them, and as parents we are in a constant state of creative thinking. Dr. Dalton-Smith recommends that those of us who are in creative thinking mode all day every day need a rest from that kind of work and that we can find that rest through viewing beauty. That could be through seeing art in an art gallery, going to see live theatre, listening to music or spending time in nature. I realized that, in my life, pre-pandemic, I engaged in a lot of these activities – exploring a new exhibit at a museum, watching musicals and plays, going to live concerts – but all of these activities came to an abrupt halt when the Covid shutdown started. Instead, I drastically increased my time in nature. Like so many others, taking walks, going on hikes, camping, cross country skiing all became a lifeline for me. It wasn’t until I heard this podcast that I realized that being outdoors – in the mountains, at the beach, observing wildflowers – had taken on a critical new dimension, both physical and spiritual. Now that the arts and culture sector has opened again, I am seeing shows again – and it feels amazing. But I am still in nature whenever possible, and I have a newfound appreciation for the creativity and beauty of nature. • The wind in the trees is a symphony. • The sunset is a glorious painting. • Two squirrels arguing over an acorn is theater. • The movement of the waves as they crash on the shore is modern dance. As we move into the spring and summer, I want to encourage all parents to take the Creative Rest we need. Find the beautiful things that inspire you. Go see the shows and enjoy the exquisite nature all around us. It might just give your depleted system the rest it needs. Nina Meehan is a Creativity Consultant and Speaker and founder of Bay Area Children’s Theater. Find out more information about her work at gocreate. zone.
articles.title: Finding Creative Rest in a busy world

For more information and to donate, contact amontes@ otismcallister.com. All donations are tax deductible. For online donations, please click on the Facebook fundraiser page: ht t ps://w w w.facebook.com / donate/1398293844329517/ Vijana Africa’s Videography School has training programs in videography and computer basics, and currently has over 20 people sharing three computers. The beneficiaries are refugees ages 13-20 who are learning how to use Microsoft Windows, Word, and Excel, and shoot and edit videos. At the end of their training, they present a documentary. Participants in the program are developing skills they can use to improve life in Dzaleka and when they are able to resettle in their home country. Alison Montes and daughter Julia with students in the Videography School at Dzaleka Refugee Camp in Malawi Thinking Outside the Classroom Finding Creative Rest in a busy world By Nina Meehan I was listening to a podcast featuring Dr. Saundra Dalton-Smith in which she was discussing the seven different kinds of rest that we need. One really stood out to me: Creative Rest. Her definition of creativity is any time we need to solve a problem. By that definition, basically every moment of parenting is an act of creativity. How do we get the kids out of the house in the morning when they are moving as slow as turtles? How can we get the siblings to stop arguing over who gets to choose the show to watch during screen time? How do we convince an unwilling child to engage in homework that is hard? All of these problems require creativity in order to solve them, and as parents we are in a constant state of creative thinking. Dr. Dalton-Smith recommends that those of us who are in creative thinking mode all day every day need a rest from that kind of work and that we can find that rest through viewing beauty. That could be through seeing art in an art gallery, going to see live theatre, listening to music or spending time in nature. I realized that, in my life, pre-pandemic, I engaged in a lot of these activities – exploring a new exhibit at a museum, watching musicals and plays, going to live concerts – but all of these activities came to an abrupt halt when the Covid shutdown started. Instead, I drastically increased my time in nature. Like so many others, taking walks, going on hikes, camping, cross country skiing all became a lifeline for me. It wasn’t until I heard this podcast that I realized that being outdoors – in the mountains, at the beach, observing wildflowers – had taken on a critical new dimension, both physical and spiritual. Now that the arts and culture sector has opened again, I am seeing shows again – and it feels amazing. But I am still in nature whenever possible, and I have a newfound appreciation for the creativity and beauty of nature. • The wind in the trees is a symphony. • The sunset is a glorious painting. • Two squirrels arguing over an acorn is theater. • The movement of the waves as they crash on the shore is modern dance. As we move into the spring and summer, I want to encourage all parents to take the Creative Rest we need. Find the beautiful things that inspire you. Go see the shows and enjoy the exquisite nature all around us. It might just give your depleted system the rest it needs. Nina Meehan is a Creativity Consultant and Speaker and founder of Bay Area Children’s Theater. Find out more information about her work at gocreate. zone. READ IT IN THE POST High School essay contest offered by League of Women Voters The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is pleased to announce its fourth annual essay contest open to all high school juniors and seniors who are either currently enrolled at Piedmont or Millennium High School or are residents of Piedmont. This year’s essay, to be 250-500 words, is due by May 7. The topic is: “In the last decade, the US Supreme Court has severely weakened the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (VRA), which was widely agreed to be the most effective civil rights law in our history. What action can the League of Women Voters take to counteract the negative effects of the Supreme Court’s decisions regarding voting rights, specifically those that place hurdles upon voting?” A $500 prize will be awarded to the first place entry. For more information and to submit an essay, visit lwvpiedmont.org/ essay-contest. In spite of storm, big turnout for Mock Admission Night By Micah Temple and William Becker Dashing through a downpour, more than 100 students and parents flooded into Alan Harvey Theatre eager to further uncover one of America’s greatest mysteries – the college admissions process. On Tuesday, March 21, during a heavy rain and windstorm, the Regional Admissions Counselors of California (RACC) hosted a mock admission night for Piedmont students to learn what makes a strong college application. “I’m sure most kids would agree, the whole process of doing your applications can be really hard to understand. I think attending this can help take some of that mystery away,” said Axel Saldanha, a junior at Piedmont High. The attendees were first presented with information about “Lake Washington University”, a fictional college meant to simulate a school that students might apply to. The students then split into groups and reviewed mock applications, deciding which would be accepted, waitlisted, or rejected. “Looking through the applications was really interesting; we got to see the process from the other side, which I think will be helpful,” George Stein. Afterwards tables were displayed with information about colleges for students to look into, including Texas Christian University, University of Arizona, and University of Oregon. “I’m glad I attended. I think the whole event helped bring me closer to the finish line with my college apps,” said Cole Nash. Among the event’s organizers was Arizona College Admissions Counselor Molly Ingram. “I absolutely think the event went well tonight. I was impressed with how many people braved the wind and rain and came out to see how the application process works,” Ingram said. Micah Temple and William Becker are Piedmont High School students and interns with the Piedmont Post. ADVERTISE IN THE POST Join us for Carol Cramer Day! articles.text: “Empathy. It’s really rooted in empathy” nods 8th grader Sophia Harris. Sophia, along with Lily Riley, Zoe Snyder, Camille Edesess and Nora Taggart have organized and planned a ceremony called the Council of All Beings for five 6th grade Green Team wheel rotations. But wait. What is the council of all beings anyway? Developed in 1985 by Joanna Macy, the council is a communal gathering where participants dress up as animals and have a conversation with humans as if they were the animals. The goal of this ritual is to feel what animals go through and to recognize our impact on the ecosystem. This school year Piedmont Middle School has adapted the council for its 6th graders, teaching them the importance of empathy and seeing how humans are not superior and that all animals – including humans – are all connected. The council consists of 8th graders who play humans asking the animals three questions: Who are you and what do you contribute to the ecosystem? What message do you want to give the humans? What gift would you give the humans? After all the questions were answered the students took off their masks and threw them into the middle of the circle. After the ceremony, I had the wonderful opportunity to speak to some 6th graders about why they felt the Council was an important and impactful experience. Elly Mak, who represented a Siberian tiger said, “To me, the council is all about noticing what is wrong and what we can do to change.” On the other hand, Aava Lokre, who represented a panda, noted that it was more about “feeling interconnected and giving animals a voice”. Naiomi Jerez stated, “We need to see things from a different perspective and overall, feel a sense of empathy”. Empathy. Empathy is the theme, and the purpose of the council – and what it all comes back to. Samantha Pell is a seventh grade intern with the Piedmont Post.

articles.text: Playing lacrosse in a hurricane is no joke During the afternoon of Tuesday March 21, one of the worst rainstorms on record hit the state of California. It was so intense that trees fell, the power went out, and flooding was widespread. Any rational person would look outside and come to the conclusion that any planned outdoor activity could wait. Any activity that required leaving the house should have been put on hold. Yet for reasons still unknown the Bentley girls’ lacrosse team chose not to reschedule or forfeit. Having an all-weather field means to some that you play regardless of weather, unless there is lighting. That Tuesday there was everything: hurricane-strength wind gusts, near-freezing temperatures, rain pouring as if from a bucket, but no lightning. Our team was scheduled to play International High School from San Francisco, who were driving to Lafayette. While players were changing into uniforms, there wasn’t one person who didn’t utter the words, “I don’t want to play right now.” And rightfully so. The rain picked up and so did the wind. Most of the players had some sort of extra layer on – sweatshirt, sweatpants or both. it was the one day I didn’t have my sweats at a game, so I slipped a jacket underneath my uniform for some semblance of warmth. As we ran onto the field, the rain picked up once more. The players were more than happy to start warm-ups – anything to get our blood pumping. my fingers started to freeze, and my lacrosse stick became extremely slippery and passes became harder. Our team wanted to get a win and get off the field and into the warm comfort of our homes, but the game hadn’t even started yet. Our coach gathered us for a team huddle, but the morale was rock bottom. When the coach assured us this was better weather than in Scotland (where he once coached), no one laughed. When the game began the wind hadn’t picked up, and the rain seemed to be calming down. At the time I thought, Oh nice, it’s not so bad; this game will be easy. Famous last words. It was at that moment that the wind decided to go full force and the rain was coming down in sheets. I don’t remember much of the game; I was too cold and wet. Did you ever try tying your shoelaces with frozen fingers? At h a l f t i me eve r yone sprinted to the tents that were set up for shelter from pelting rain. We were up by four goals and really wanted to just get off the field. The other coaches proposed the idea of a forfeit, and the wild cheering from both teams suggested we would stop the game. But after a quick huddle, the visiting team decided to keep playing. Even with a running clock (no delays) the game seemed to go on forever. I noticed that the other team’s goalie was sitting in the goal with her head down and with her goalie stick up. Something just didn’t seem right. Two minutes later a ref came running over and declared the game over. It turned out that the goalkeeper’s helmet was too tight, and she couldn’t play. Finally, we got off the field and into the locker room. The group consensus was that the game never should have been played. But there was more. The scariest part was driving home. My mother had her hazard lights on and was driving in the slowest lane on the highway. The usual freeway exits were closed because of fallen trees or flooding, so we had to take several detours. That was the day that Bentley’s girls’ lacrosse team became the strongest bonded team on the planet. Piedmont resident Larissa Edel is a sophomore at Bentley School. Sophia, along with Lily Riley, Zoe Snyder, Camille Edesess and Nora Taggart have organized and planned a ceremony called the Council of All Beings for five 6th grade Green Team wheel rotations. But wait. What is the council of all beings anyway? Developed in 1985 by Joanna Macy, the council is a communal gathering where participants dress up as animals and have a conversation with humans as if they were the animals. The goal of this ritual is to feel what animals go through and to recognize our impact on the ecosystem. This school year Piedmont Middle School has adapted the council for its 6th graders, teaching them the importance of empathy and seeing how humans are not superior and that all animals – including humans – are all connected. The council consists of 8th graders who play humans asking the animals three questions: Who are you and what do you contribute to the ecosystem? What message do you want to give the humans? What gift would you give the humans? After all the questions were answered the students took off their masks and threw them into the middle of the circle. After the ceremony, I had the wonderful opportunity to speak to some 6th graders about why they felt the Council was an important and impactful experience. Elly Mak, who represented a Siberian tiger said, “To me, the council is all about noticing what is wrong and what we can do to change.” On the other hand, Aava Lokre, who represented a panda, noted that it was more about “feeling interconnected and giving animals a voice”. Naiomi Jerez stated, “We need to see things from a different perspective and overall, feel a sense of empathy”. Empathy. Empathy is the theme, and the purpose of the council – and what it all comes back to. Samantha Pell is a seventh grade intern with the Piedmont Post. articles.text: Last weekend a total of 37 students from Highlander Robotics traveled to the FIRST Robotics Competition’s Monterey Bay Regional Tournament with their robot “Paddo the Frog”. They placed second and earned a place at the World Championship in two weeks in Houston. The FIRST Robotics Competition announces a new game each January to be played by two alliances of three robots, built by 9th to 12th grade students, in an arena about the size of a basketball court. A new robot must be built for each season and competitions begin 6 weeks after kickoff. In this year’s game, Charged Up, robots up to 125 pounds and 6-feet-6-inches tall scored points by collecting and placing 9.5- inch inflatable cubes and 1-foot high rubber cones in a grid of poles and pedestals, as well as balancing robots on a see-sawlike platform called a “charging station”. During regional competitions, teams play up to 12 qualifying rounds with randomly selected partners. The highest individually ranked eight teams then become alliance captains and draft two others to work with throughout the double-elimination playoffs and best-of-three finals. After the first day of qualifying rounds in Monterey, the Highlanders had a 6-2 record and in fifth place of 36 behind 2019 World Champion MadTown Robotics from Madera, last year’s World Championship Roebling Division Finalist BREAD Robotics from Redwood City, 2009 World Champion Spartan Robotics from Mountain View, and Duncan Dynamics from Fresno. Highlander Robotics had shown they could keep up. They ranked third in points overall and in one round had won nearly unassisted after one alliance partners was carried off the field before the match began. They were guaranteed to have the option to be an alliance captain if they stayed in fifth through their last three quals, but their best path to Worlds would be as a first pick. Invitations to the World Championship are earned by the winning alliance of a regional tournament as well as by winners of FIRST’s two most prestigious judged awards, Engineering, Inspiration, and Impact. “[Top ranked] MadTown qualified in Fresno and was favored to win at Monterey, likely in an alliance with the #2 team, BREAD. If that happened they would generate a wildcard” said Rui de Figueiredo, the Highlander’s Ava Grochowski passes a cone to the Highlanders Robot Paddo the Frog. Scouting and Strategy mentor. “Spartan, who we expected to be the captain of the second seed alliance, had won the San Francisco Regional so any wildcard would skip them.” This meant that Rookie All Star, if awarded, was the only thing standing in the way of sending the Spartan’s first pick to Worlds should they make Pit crew members (left to right) Helena Young, Beck Peterson, and Reece Beck wait for a robot inspector to qualify Paddo as ready to compete. Paddo scores by placing a cone on the Charged Up grid. Paddo (8033) scores by climbing the see-saw-like Charging Station. finals. “So we waited and hoped everything went right”, said de Figueiredo. Things started well the next morning as the Highlanders decisively won their last three qualification rounds. In the second round of the series, they found themselves on an alliance with Spartan Robotics and had an opportunity to audition the partnership. The result, 170-92, left the team hopeful. “We just work really well together” said Captain Alex Ware. Shortly after, Spartan confirmed their intention to draft the Highlanders. The second seed alliance of Spartan Robotics, Highlander Robotics, and The Apes of Wrath from San Jose went 3-1 in the double elimination playoffs, only losing to the first seed alliance of MadTown, BREAD, and Unipards from Taipei. In the best of three finals, the MadTown lead alliance won in two high intensity rounds 184- 152 and 158-150. As finalists, the only thing that would prevent MadTown’s wildcard going to the Highlanders would be a Rookie All Star. “Then I saw the award on the presenter’s table” said Ware. Rookie team The Mechanical Magicians from Newark had earned the wildcard to Houston. “It was clearly well deserved, but hard not to feel disappointed” he added. Very few paths to Worlds remained. The Highlanders could win Engineering Inspiration or Impact themselves and qualify directly or an additional wildcard could be generated if BREAD or Unipards won. So the team waited and hoped as the awards were announced. Teams can win only one judged award per competition, so any other award would eliminate a possibility. The Highlanders won the Imagery Award, which celebrates attractiveness in engineering and outstanding visual aesthetic integration of machine and team appearance. In particular, the judges recognized the Highlanders rebrand, led by Ava Grochowski, Chloe Kessinger, and Jessica Liu, which sought to maintain a connection to Piedmont while being more inclusive to non-PHS students. BREAD won the Engineering Excellence award. Unipards won Engineering Inspiration, triggering a second wildcard and sending Highlander Robotics back to Houston. “[It was a] rush of emotions. All the hard work had finally paid off.” said Ware. Fundraiser before Worlds The Highlanders are now fundraising to pay the $5000 registration fee, costs to ship the robot and pit, and financial aid for students. Community members can help by making a donation at: frc8033.com. Paddo the Frog was operated by Vaughn Khouri and Matteo Scanu and supported by drive coach Alex Ware, technician Nate Hart, and human player Ava Grochowski. Helena Young and Peter Stokes led the pit crew which kept the robot running smoothly through 17 full contact matches with turnarounds as quick as 30 minutes. Jasper Tripp led scouting and strategy operations. Lewy Seiden led a team of 5 ambassadors who fielded questions, built connections with other teams, and represented the team to FIRST Judges. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse team had a big 11-10 overtime win over Las Lomas in Walnut Creek on Tuesday, March 28, and dominated Moreau Catholic 18-2 on Monday, April 3. Two days earlier, Saturday, April 1, they lost 16-6 to San Marin at Witter Field. “In every single game, the girls get better and better,” said veteran coach and. Piedmont native Carlton Chan. “In the San Marin game, even though we lost, we played them really hard – we just didn’t have enough wheels at the end.” In the victory against Las Lomas, Piedmont mounted a terrific second-half comeback after trailing 9-5 at the half. PHS scored six unanswered goals to force overtime, when Ruby Guzdar scored the game-winner with 40 seconds remaining. “Our defense adjusted and closed the gaps. We fouled Las Lomas with just 50 seconds left and gave them a free position shot to win the game but Lindsay made an incredible left foot save to send the game to overtime. In OT, we told the girls that at this point in the game, it’s all about who wants it more,” said Chan. Guzdar finished the night with six goals. “I looked at the scoreboard and saw there was only so much time left. I thought I just have to go. I saw an opening and went for it. They basically cleared out the left side for me to get a shot,” recalled Guzdar of the winning moment. 11-10 OT win over Las Lomas Piedmont led 2-1 after five minutes with a pair of goals by Guzdar, but they didn’t score again for 12 minutes, and the Knights pulled ahead, 7-2. Molly Ashton and Guzdar scored to cut it to 7-4, while both teams traded goals in the final minute for a 10-5 score at halftime. In the second half, Las Lomas scored 50 seconds in, but it was Photos by Todd Marshburn and Ken DeCrosta Ruby Guzdar scored Piedmont’s game-winner in overtime against Las Lomas. the last time they got on the board. Ashton scored with 17 minutes left, followed by one from Guzdar and two more by Ashton to push the score to 10-9 with eight minutes left. Guzdar then scored with 2:40 left in regulation to tie the game. Goalie Lindsay Kottle made the huge save with 50 seconds left to thwart a shooting-space opportunity and force the game into overtime. After back-and-forth possessions in the three-minute overtime period, Guzdar scored the game-winner after beating her defender around the edge. Final stats: Guzdar had six goals and won one draw. Ashton scored four goals. Kottle made seven saves on the night. 16-6 loss to San Marin San Marin led 9-4 at the half, and added seven more goals in the second half. Final stats: Ashton had two goals. Peyton Watson had two goals and recovered two loose balls. Eleanor Lavin had one assist and won seven draws. 18-2 win vs. Moreau Catholic The Highlanders beat Moreau, a weaker Division 2 NCS foe, and led 12-2 at halftime. They added six more goals in the second half without conceding any, allowing Molly Ashton scored four goals in the big win over Las Lomas. the team to rotate in many JV and reserve players. Final stats: Friedie Schickendanz had six goals and two assists. Watson had three goals and won five draws. Chloe Graham scored three goals, one assist, and won six draws. Guzdar had two assists. Laurel Bentley and Hailey Marshburn scored once. Alicia Bernales had one goal and assist. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-4 overall, 2-1 league) hosts Washington at Witter Field tomorrow, Thursday, April 6, at 7:00 p.m. Goalie Lindsay Kottle recorded seven saves against Las Lomas, including a critical stop with 50 seconds left.

articles.text: Piedmont High won its only tennis match of the week, shutting out league opponent Castro Valley 7-0 on March 30. PHS also had matches scheduled against Berkeley (March 28), St. Mary’s (March 29), and Bishop O’Dowd (March 31), but the St. Mary’s match was canceled due to rain, and both Berkeley and O’Dowd were rescheduled to later dates. The win improves the Highlanders’ record to 4-1 in league. Its only league loss was to rival Berkeley on March 2 when it played without No. 2 singles starter Ben Breber. “We had to move things around because of rain and Bishop O’Dowd on its spring break. It was a perfect day against Castro Valley with nearly everyone winning in straight sets. We have a full lineup now that Ben is back and we’re hoping to get some revenge on Berkeley,” said PHS coach Jim Landes. Against the Trojans, it was a quick day for the singles lineup with all four players winning in straight sets. At No. 1, Lucas Smolko won handily 6-1, 6-0, while Ben Breber won 6-3, 6-1 at No. 2. Breber, who missed time at the beginning of the season with an illness, said, “It’s great to be back. I’ve been really eager to play, I’ve been feeling great out there.” At No. 3 singles, Ethan Pham on 6-1, 6-3 while Alex Zalewski closed out the day with a double-bagel at No. 4, winning 6-0, 6-0. “Ethan has been playing really well, He helps make up a strong singles lineup for us,” said Landes of the senior. PHS girls beat Las Lomas in overtime By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse team had a big 11-10 overtime win over Las Lomas in Walnut Creek on Tuesday, March 28, and dominated Moreau Catholic 18-2 on Monday, April 3. Two days earlier, Saturday, April 1, they lost 16-6 to San Marin at Witter Field. “In every single game, the girls get better and better,” said veteran coach and. Piedmont native Carlton Chan. “In the San Marin game, even though we lost, we played them really hard – we just didn’t have enough wheels at the end.” In the victory against Las Lomas, Piedmont mounted a terrific second-half comeback after trailing 9-5 at the half. PHS scored six unanswered goals to force overtime, when Ruby Guzdar scored the game-winner with 40 seconds remaining. “Our defense adjusted and closed the gaps. We fouled Las Lomas with just 50 seconds left and gave them a free position shot to win the game but Lindsay made an incredible left foot save to send the game to overtime. In OT, we told the girls that at this point in the game, it’s all about who wants it more,” said Chan. Guzdar finished the night with six goals. “I looked at the scoreboard and saw there was only so much time left. I thought I just have to go. I saw an opening and went for it. They basically cleared out the left side for me to get a shot,” recalled Guzdar of the winning moment. 11-10 OT win over Las Lomas Piedmont led 2-1 after five minutes with a pair of goals by Guzdar, but they didn’t score again for 12 minutes, and the Knights pulled ahead, 7-2. Molly Ashton and Guzdar scored to cut it to 7-4, while both teams traded goals in the final minute for a 10-5 score at halftime. In the second half, Las Lomas scored 50 seconds in, but it was Photos by Todd Marshburn and Ken DeCrosta Ruby Guzdar scored Piedmont’s game-winner in overtime against Las Lomas. the last time they got on the board. Ashton scored with 17 minutes left, followed by one from Guzdar and two more by Ashton to push the score to 10-9 with eight minutes left. Guzdar then scored with 2:40 left in regulation to tie the game. Goalie Lindsay Kottle made the huge save with 50 seconds left to thwart a shooting-space opportunity and force the game into overtime. After back-and-forth possessions in the three-minute overtime period, Guzdar scored the game-winner after beating her defender around the edge. Final stats: Guzdar had six goals and won one draw. Eleanor Lavin had one assist and won seven draws. 18-2 win vs. Moreau Catholic The Highlanders beat Moreau, a weaker Division 2 NCS foe, and led 12-2 at halftime. They added six more goals in the second half without conceding any, allowing Molly Ashton scored four goals in the big win over Las Lomas. the team to rotate in many JV and reserve players. Final stats: Friedie Schickendanz had six goals and two assists. Watson had three goals and won five draws. Chloe Graham scored three goals, one assist, and won six draws. Guzdar had two assists. Laurel Bentley and Hailey Marshburn scored once. Alicia Bernales had one goal and assist. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ volleyball team defeated St. Joseph 3-1 on March 30 at Binks Rawlings Gym but lost its other two games last week. The pair of losses at Alameda on Friday, March 31, and Foothill on Wednesday, March 29, were both shutouts with 3-0 scores. Following the 3-1 win over St. Joseph, PHS coach Mariah Cardenas said, “Normally we’re slow at first and then build into the game. This time, we started really strong, and it was a cohesive unit in the beginning. I think we got a bit comfortable in the third game,” Thursday’s game with the Plots marked a return for junior outside hitter John Champion, who aggravated an ankle injury prior to playing Arroyo on March 15. He’s been battling back from a fracture he suffered during the offseason. “It’s feeling pretty good. It was Staff Photos John Champion returned to the lineup after missing two weeks due to an ankle injury. really difficult because I came back immediately and it never got better. This time, I talked to Torge Kraft, an exchange student from Lüneburg, Germany, recorded 16 kills against St. Joseph. Wilson Wong had 15 kills against the Pilots. doctors, put a boot on it and put more focus on my recovery,” said Champion. It’s been a big season for outside hitter Torge Kraft, a junior exchange student from Germany. He recorded 16 kills in the win against St. Joseph. “I think we have way more potential than we are showing right now, so there are some things we still have to work on. Against St. Joseph, we had a really good serve-receiver, but we didn’t connect on some big hits. If the set isn’t perfect, we have to find ways to hit it,” said Kraft. Coming from Lüneburg in northern Germany, Kraft is glad to be experiencing a warmer California winter, although he didn’t expect so much rain. articles.text: Piedmont’s track and field team traveled to Palo Alto on Saturday, April 1, for the prestigious and highly competitive Stanford Invitational The Highlanders competed in two relays and four individual events this year. “This was particularly fun as competitors from all over the West Coast and beyond drove and flew in to compete in front of college coaches, athletes, and Stanford alumni. We had some great performances,” said first year PHS head coach Pouyan Assadi. In a strong outing for Parker Long, the senior finished third of 26 runners in the 800- meter run with a blazing time of 1:53.77, a half-second from matching his personal best set at the Dublin Distance Fiesta on March 18. “For this meet he got caught up at the beginning but was able to make his way to the front. He has the skills and motivation to continue on this incredible trajectory, and if we do our part as coaches, he’ll take the leap,” said Assadi. It was also a good day for classmate Christian Taylor, who placed 8th in a field of 26 runners in the 1600 with a personal record time of 4:15.07, topping his previous best by 3.6 seconds set at the Dublin Distance event. Taylor was also 21st in the 800 with a time of 2:00.14. Taylor’s time in the 1600 makes him the school’s third fastest runner of all time, .15 behind Tom Phelps’ time of 4:14.92 in 2001 and .30 back of Jack Stein’s 4:14.77 performance last year. “Christian is a true leader,” said Assadi. Also competing was Spencer Sorensen-Wald in the 400 meter hurdles, finishing 11th of 18 in 59.85. Piedmont’s girls’ 4x100 relay team of Miranda Liu, Ella Yasar, Darcy Mckee, and Breah Bell finished with a time of 51.24, and the boys’ 4x400m relay team of Sorenson-Wald, Long, Shelby, and Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai placed 18th with a time of 3:32.54. “The girls 4x100 are already competing against the best, and we’ve only gotten a small glimpse of what they’re truly capable of,’ said Assadi. NEXT UP PHS runners head out next week for Spring Break, and won’t race again until Thursday, April 20 when the host a league meet with Alameda, Bishop O’Dowd, Hayward, and Mt. Eden. Christian Taylor placed 8th of 26 milers in the 1600 meters, posting the third fastest time in PHS history. Freshman Miranda Liu competed in the 4x100 relay. She’s a two-sport athlete with soccer.

articles.text: Piedmont High senior Audrey Lam is set to continue her international soccer career after being invited for the third year to train with the U.S. Women’s Youth National Under 18/19 Team in North Carolina this spring from April 15-22. Lam and the U18/ U19 team will train in an overlapping camp with the U.S. Women’s U-20 team is it prepares for the 2024 U-20 FIFA World Cup. During the camp this month, teams will scrimmage while U-20 head coach Tracey Kevins evaluates all 46 players to decide who will be part of a 21-player roster for the 2023 CONCACAF Women’s U-20 Championship from May 25-June 4 in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic. Lam was initially invited to train with the national youth team in Kansas City in 2019 and most recently played for the U-17 Women’s National Team in friendlies against Spain and Germany last August. She trains with Lamorinda Soccer Club and competes on their Premier League team, Lamorinda United, under head coach Mohamed Mohamed, who describes Lam as a player who “makes everyone better.” “She is extremely talented and a hard worker, not just offensively but defensively as well. She’s the type of player who makes everyone around her better and is someone other players look up to. She’s an extremely humble perStaff Photo Audrey Lam, PHS senior Audrey Lam recently was named the WACC’s Player of the Year. She’s an amazing teammate and we are so proud of her to reach this level and also watch her grow,” said Mohamed. Lam is currently committed to play collegiately at Brown University in Rhode Island with the eventual goal of playing professionally and making the senior U.S. Women’s team. articles.text: Dragons set stage for victory with early lead over Spartans An early lead helped the Piedmont Dragons defeat the Piedmont Spartans 11-4 on Sunday, April 2, at Humphries Field in the 2nd annual Piedmont Pony City Baseball Championship. The baseball teams are comprised of local seventh and eighth graders. Base hits by Mateo Quintero and Milo Chipman brought in three runs and keyed a big six-run second inning. Quintero led the Dragons with two hits and three RBIs. Chase Knapp reached base three times. Mateo Long and Knapp each scored twice. Long and Derek Lee each had three stolen bases as the Dragons stole a total of 20 bases. The Spartans racked up nine hits on the day. John Bunje and Griffin Guidi each managed multiple hits. Bunje went 3-for-3 at the plate to lead the Spartans, while Sammy Ragones hit an RBI double to deep left field to score the first run of the game. The big story of the game was the Dragon defense led by a rare complete game from starting pitcher Derek Lee, who was named tournament MVP. He allowed just four runs over seven innings, striking out four while walking only two. Evan Ma caught all seven innings, and the Lee-Ma battery held the Spartans to just two stolen bases. All players contributed to an errorfree performance by the Dragon defense, with key contributions by Theo Barber at shortstop and Russel Pan at first base. Special thanks to Commissioners Dave Ragones and Kim Hunter who conceived the City Championship. The Dragons also won last year’s Championship by defeating the Spartans in the inaugural edition. Both Piedmont Baseball Softball Foundation teams compete in the East Bay Pony Premier League with teams from Moraga, Orinda, and Lafayette. The Spartans are currently in first place with a record of 5-1, while the Dragons evened their season mark to 3-3 with the Championship win. The Piedmont Dragons team won the Piedmont Pony Baseball Championship.

As a senior at Piedmont High this year she won the Western Alameda County Conference’s Player of the Year award and helped lead the school to its first Division 4 North Coast Section title in 20 years. The baseball teams are comprised of local seventh and eighth graders. Base hits by Mateo Quintero and Milo Chipman brought in three runs and keyed a big six-run second inning. Quintero led the Dragons with two hits and three RBIs. Chase Knapp reached base three times. Mateo Long and Knapp each scored twice. Long and Derek Lee each had three stolen bases as the Dragons stole a total of 20 bases. The Spartans racked up nine hits on the day. John Bunje and Griffin Guidi each managed multiple hits. Bunje went 3-for-3 at the plate to lead the Spartans, while Sammy Ragones hit an RBI double to deep left field to score the first run of the game. The big story of the game was the Dragon defense led by a rare complete game from starting pitcher Derek Lee, who was named tournament MVP. He allowed just four runs over seven innings, striking out four while walking only two. Evan Ma caught all seven innings, and the Lee-Ma battery held the Spartans to just two stolen bases. All players contributed to an errorfree performance by the Dragon defense, with key contributions by Theo Barber at shortstop and Russel Pan at first base. Special thanks to Commissioners Dave Ragones and Kim Hunter who conceived the City Championship. The Dragons also won last year’s Championship by defeating the Spartans in the inaugural edition. Both Piedmont Baseball Softball Foundation teams compete in the East Bay Pony Premier League with teams from Moraga, Orinda, and Lafayette. The Spartans are currently in first place with a record of 5-1, while the Dragons evened their season mark to 3-3 with the Championship win. The Piedmont Dragons team won the Piedmont Pony Baseball Championship.

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California celebrates Earth Day this Friday, April 7. The free family-friendly event begins at 5 p.m. in the museum’s courtyard and garden. Guests will discover the unique flora and foliage of the Oak, Chaparral, and Redwood forest regions of California. Young museum goers can create art inspired by California’s native plants and learn about Earth Day events offered in the Bay Area this month. Special guest, Stomper, the Oakland A’s mascot, will be in attendance. From 6 p.m. to 7 p.m., educator Bowen Lyam Lee will read Stories for a Healthy Planet in the garden. Lee is a fifth generation Chinese American born and raised in Oakland, and has been a teacher for 36 years, incorporating storytelling into all aspects of teaching. DJ Benet will be playing in the Amphitheater from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m. This event is part of the museum’s Friday Nights series, where food trucks, live music and art-inspired activities are available. For more information, visit https://museumca.org/event/friday-nights-at-omca-with-off-thegrid-earth-day/.
articles.title: Celebrate Earth Day at Oakland Museum on Friday

articles.text: Botanist-guided classes this week The Filoli Garden House Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside will host botanical bouquet workshops now through April 7 to celebrate its spring blooms. The garden’s veteran staff will guide you through a bouquet-making session featuring the estate’s well-prized flowers. Filoli is home to 16 acres of formal gardening grounds and a vast collection of native and exotic flowers. The most fertile and popular flowers during March are Camellias, Magnolias, Irises, and Wisteria. In April, the historic gardens will welcome a bloom of roses and Lavender. The workshop is from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. Light refreshments and wine are provided with registration purchase. Visit https://filoli.org/events/ flora-party/ or call (650) 364- 8300 to purchase tickets. Filoli is located at 86 Canada Road in Woodside.
articles.title: Mix the perfect bouquet with Filoli staff

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet is currently performing Cinderella onstage through April 8. Choreographer Christopher Wheeldon transforms the classic fairytale set to Sergei Prokofiev’s score with mesmerizing visual effects and stunning costume design by Tony Award-winning designer Julian Crouch. Included in this production is San Francisco-native puppeteer Basil Twist, who creates a tree that grows from the princess’s tears at the end of Act I. Cinderella is a co-production of Dutch National Ballet, and first premiered at the San Francisco War Memorial Opera House in 2013. Educator Appreciation Day: April 7 San Francisco Ballet will host an Educator Appreciation Day this Friday, April 7, welcoming teachers, paraprofessionals, school staff, administrators, and teaching artists from schools across the Bay Area to view the production. Cinderella runs approximately 2 hours and 30 minutes including two intermissions. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sf ballet.org/productions/ cinderella/, or call the box office at 415-865-2000.
articles.title: SF Ballet performing Cinderella through April 8

The San Francisco Playhouse production of Clue will continue through April 22. Based on the popular 1985 film and derived from the popular board game of the same name, the play follows six dinner guests – Miss Scarlet, Professor Plum, Mrs. White, Mr. Green, Mrs. Peacock, Colonel Mustard, and Wadsworth, the butler – in a hilarious whodunnit murder mystery. San Francisco Playhouse’s production of Clue is written by Sandy Rustin and directed by Susi Damilano, with original music composed by Michael Holland. The cast includes Courtney Walsh, Renee Rogoff, Stacy Ross, Michael Sullivan, Greg Ayers, and Michael Wisley. articles.text: Retired brass and vocal teacher Dorothy Moskowitz Falarski will have a record release party this Saturday, April 8, from 1:00 to 3:00 p.m. at Mars Records, 4125 Piedmont Avenue. Her newest album “Under an Endless Sky” will be released by Josh Rosenthal, founder of Tompkins Square Records. Her most recent work with Italian composer Francesco Paladino and his partner, writer Luca Ferrari, attracted the attention of Rosenthal. The album features the music of Moskowitz Falarski and the United States of Alchemy. The public is invited to meet Dorothy and hear some of the details about the new album.

articles.text: The Diluvian Quartet will perform a Spring recital, Great Dedications, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 7 p.m. on Saturday, April 15. Elizabeth Castro Abrams and Jessica Scrimale, violins; Raphael Gold, viola; and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello will perform quartets by W.A. Mozart and Reinhold Gliere, celebrating two prolific composers and the works they dedicated to their most influential colleagues and teachers. Doors open at 6:45 p.m., and the concert begins at 7 p.m. A dessert reception and drinks will follow. Advance tickets are available at w w w.eventbr ite. com/e/582873007857. Tickets may also be purchased at the door. Highlights Mozart’s Quartet No. 15 is one of his greatest masterpieces. The second of a group of six quartets dedicated to the great Josef Haydn, his friend and mentor, it was the most profound quartet written at the time of its publication. It stands today as one of the most expressive works in the genre. It is marked by a dark and somber melody, at once giving way to a bright and cheerful theme over and over, always with Mozart’s genius ability at musical conversation. Born in Kiev, Ukraine, Reinhold Glière went on to be one of the most important Soviet composers of his generation. The piece on this program, his 2nd quartet, was written in 1905, and was dedicated to the great Russian composer Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov. It is jampacked with themes of Imperial Czarist Russia, lush romantic chords, unabashed emotional expression, and toe-tapping rhythmic gestures. This program features some of the most beautiful music ever written for string quartets. The Diluvian Quartet has been playing together for two years and prides itself on diverse programs that combine standards of the repertoire with lesser-known masterpieces. articles.text: How can so much exuberance emanate from one of the most depressing large-scale symphonies ever written? Easy. You put a beloved ex-maestro like Michael Tilson Thomas back on the podium. Upon entry, the revered 78-yearold conductor got a standing ovation from the near-sell-out crowd. And at the end, the fired-up patrons accorded the S.F. Symphony and him an inordinately rare six-minute ovation. Gustav Mahler (1860-1911) himself would never have believed it for the deeply aggrieved Sixth Symphony of 1904, which had left the ultra-emotional composer sobbing uncontrollably on first hearing. Here was the ultimate late romantic, carried away by his own music – so searing in its impact, he could not contain his emotions. Analysis from this (distant) vantage-point seat suggests it all dealt with premonitions of death. His heart was never fully sound, presaging his demise at age 50. The finale’s sledge-hammer blows on a resonant wood box, executed by percussionist Jacob Nissly with a Donner-sized sledge from the balcony a full floor higher than the stage, are unique in music as such premonitions, even more so than the death-rattle bass trill interrupting the melody of the Schubert Piano Sonata in B Flat Major’s opening (that being the speculation by pianist Andras Schiff). We have to thank Mahler’s unquenchable work ethic, and presumably the Almighty, that he was around to write three-plus additional symphonies, along with vocal works. But none of the later ones resonated with such tragedy as the music of the Sixth. Still, it’s a thoroughly engrossing, mammoth-scale opus whose complexity and giant-sized orchestra draws you along with it – passionate despair be damned. The Sixth is a multi-dimensional wonderworld full of trapdoors. The long opening movement is a dour military march toward some lemming-like goal. The Scherzo has another funeral march in minor with big brass gestures and snare drums. Only the appearance of the sweet-tender Ländler (Austrian waltz-predecessor) mitigates among the abrupt gearshifts, some of them on tiptoe. Finally the slow movement arrives with its eight (!) French horns and a woodwind chorale, all a genteel, spacey escape in the midst of this voyage of heavenly length. The multitude of emotions is like itself – only that Mahler suffered the extremes more than perhaps anyone. The boisterous finale offers tumult via the ominous boxsmasher, plus horns playing bells-up in a raw sound mode. The frenzy subsides now and then, enabling cowbells to sound out offstage. Currents and crosscurrents endure until a brassy ending, still with strings bowing away tirelessly, comes as you had never dared possible, with fulfillment and a measure of relief. The performance was inspiring. Most notable is that all the augmented sections, like four clarinets, two harps, six trumpets, etc. – coalesced into a coherent whole without loose ends. This was an achievement of which MTT could be proud into his retirement days – if they ever come. MUSIC NOTES MTT’s return to action has come this season with much cheering, as only optimists could have predicted given his precarious brain-cancer operation (glioblastoma) of a year ago. Three cheers for the unsung tuba: At the end of the March 30 concert, MTT accorded the first of the orchestral bows to Jeffrey Anderson, the tuba principal who too often is taken for granted. San Francisco Symphony with M.D. Laureate MTT in Mahler’s Symphony No. 6, March 30-April 1. Davies Hall. S.F. Piedmont resident Paul Hertelendy was music critic at the San Jose Mercury News for 20 years and currently writes for the Bay Area-based web journal artsSF.com.
articles.title: SF Symphony performs Mahler – Victory through despair

articles.text: Fire of Love, a documentary by Piedmont High School alumnus Sara Dosa, class of 2000, was nominated for an Oscar this year. The film follows the life of husband and wife, Maurice and Katia Krafft, who studied volcanoes throughout the world and captured the most intense interior photos on record. Dosa premiered the film at the 2022 Sundance Film Festival, where it was one of five films selected in the documentary category. Following the festival it was purchased for national distribution in theaters by National Geographic Documentary Films, a worldwide rights deal valued at a mid-seven-figure deal. Dosa is an Indie Spirit Award-nominated director and Peabody Award-winning producer, whose film credits include Audrie & Daisy, available on at-home streaming service Netflix, The Seer and Unseen, and The Last Season. Fire of Love, Dosa’s documentary chronicling the work of Maurice and Katia Krafft, French husband-wife volcanologists, opened the Sundance Film A scene from documentary Fire of Love, which recently was a nominee for an Academy Award Documentary film director and producer Sara Dosa, a Piedmont native Festival on January 20. The film contains over 20 years of archival footage and dramatic shots of active volcanoes and explosions beginning in 1966. The Krafft couple traveled to volcanic locations in Zaire, Iceland, the Americas and Japan, capturing then-unseen footage of seismic, tectonic eruptions. Under Dosa’s direction, the team behind Fire of Love weaved the footage together to tell the couple’s love story, The Kraffts spent decades collecting data mere feet away from danger. In 1991 they were killed capturing an explosion on Japan’s Mount Unzen. Their legacy included some of the most dramatic footage humans may ever be able to capture. “I like to think of it as a love triangle. Maurice and Katia were obviously the love story that drove [the narrative], but you also have the volcanoes they chased. In a way they were both in love with this important work they did,” Dosa said. T he docu ment a r y was reviewed favorably in both the New York Times and the San Francisco Chronicle. A.O. Scott, co-chief film critic for the New York Times, noted the exceptional cinematography of the film. “The sheer existence of these photos is mind-boggling when you think about how close the people with the cameras must have been to the lava and the smoke,” said Scott. As director, Dosa had her hand in every stage of the film, including in the documentary’s clever use of animation and in writing the copy provided to Miranda July, author and independent film screenwriter, who narrates the film. Dosa said she consulted with colleagues of the Kraffts when considering what story she wanted to tell - but that the bulk of the narration comes directly from the footage the couple captured, and the Kraffts’ own notes, speeches and published works. National Geographic Films released Fire of Love on July 6, 2022. Dosa’s documentary is showing at Alamo Drafthouse Cinema, New Mission, and AMC Kabuki 8 theatre in San Francisco. To find a theater near you where the film is playing and to stream online, visit: https://films.nationalgeographic.com/fire-of-love.

articles.text: Guillermo del Toro’s reimagined Pinocchio, based on the classic Carlo Collodi’s children’s book written in 1883, won an Oscar for Best Animated Feature at this year’s 2003 Academy Awards. But parents should know that this stop-motion version, while immensely creative, is not your grandfather’s Pinocchio. Disney or Pixar it’s not. The reframed story opens by introducing the audience to Geppetto (David Bradley), an elderly Italian woodcarver, and his much-adored young son Carlo. The time is the early 1900s and the world is on the cusp of WWI. Geppetto has been hired to carve a massive crucifix for the local church. Of course Carlo is at his side, helping, his favorite pinecone always nearby. While working, Carlo hears the sounds of planes overhead and tells his father who grows concerned. He tells Carlo that they must leave the church and hurry home. Just as they are leaving, Carlo remembers he has forgotten his pinecone and runs back into the church to find it. Meanwhile one of the bombers has dropped a bomb that hits the church, killing Carlo who is still inside. Geppetto, stunned, knocked off his feet by the blast, finds the body of Carlo lying near a pew. Holding the boy in his arms, he is inconsolable, his grief and sense of loss are beyond comprehension. Tearfully, he buries Carlo along with the pinecone, and so years pass. Geppetto’s sadness only increases and he takes to drink, trying to lose himself in the bottle. Italy, now controlled by Il Dulce, has now become a fascist state while supporting Germany as it prepares for WWII. And then, unexpectedly, in a grief-stricken drunken rage, Geppetto goes to Carlo’s grave site and with an ax chops down the pine tree that his grown by Carlo’s tombstone. In a haze of anger and grief, he spends a fevered night carving a wooden puppet from the trunk of the tree. Recall that this is del Toro, and the wooden boy bears little resemblance to Carlo. His legs are long and spindly, his nose too long, his body round and wooden. And, of course, there is no star for Geppetto to wish upon. But there does appear in the early dawn, while Geppetto sleeps, a blue fairy (Tilda Swinton). And while Sebastian J. Cricket (Ewan McGregor), the story’s narrator, watches, life is bestowed on the wooden marionette. And so begins the strange, melancholy journey of Pinocchio, an undisciplined boy who brings only chaos into the old woodcarver’s life while Geppetto feels helpless to control him and the villagers think of the wooden youngster as a demon. The embedded question going forward is will Pinocchio become the boy prescribed by the Blue Fairy (truthful and obedient), or will he fall under the spell of a cohort of unsavory characters? That is the tale that unfolds. Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio. Directed by del Toro and Mark Gustafsen, A stop-motion animation. Voiced by Gregory Mann, Ewan McGregor, David Bradley. 1 hr., 57 min. Rated PG. Released in 2022. Now streaming on Netflix.
articles.title: Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio wins Academy Award

articles.text: Pardee Family Museum in downtown Oakland will host a fashion show, “Wedding Gowns With History” in the museum’s historic garden at 672 11th Street on Sunday, April 30 from 2:00 to The fashion show is presented by Karen Tierney of StudioTrousA champagne reception with sweets and savories will follow. study of historic sewing stems from the need to have historically accurate gowns for performance by Danse Libre. Karen has displayed vintage inspired gowns in Europe, has lectured on the history of 19th century fashion and was a former Board Member of the Museum of Lace and Textiles in Berkeley, California. One of her focuses is working with brides who have family gowns that need to be restored, resized and redesigned so they can be worn again. She also creates custom gowns, veils and head pieces, and repairs delicate laces. Karen will show and discuss many restored family heirloom wedding gowns ranging from 1883 to 1968 and new historically referenced wedding gowns ranging from 1810 to 1930. They will be brought to life by several models, some of whom are the brides who wore them. This elegant fashion show should be a fascinating and memorable occasion. articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Smoked Salmon and Asparagus Mini-Frittatas Springtime means brunch time for many of us. And finally, we are slated for some dry and sunny days to gather with family and friends. I often make a frittata for our Sunday brunch. It’s usually in a 12-inch skillet to savor leftovers the next day. I’ve modified a springtime favorite to bake in muffin tins for individual servings, ideal for entertaining and your brunch spread. Advance notes: It’s important to liberally grease each muffin cup, even if for “nonstick” pans. If well buttered or oiled, the muffins are removed easily. Omit this if using parchment liners. I add the salmon, asparagus pieces (saving the tips for topping), crumbled cheese and chives into the egg mixture; just as I do for a large frittata. For mini-frittatas, carefully fill each cup with about the same amounts of everything in each. If you want to be more precise, layer the fillings before adding the egg mix as follows: asparagus pieces, salmon pieces, crumbled cheese and lastly chives on top. Smoked Salmon and Asparagus Mini-Frittatas Serves 12 INGREDIENTS • 10 large eggs • 1/2 cup whole milk • 4 ounces cold smoked, sliced sockeye salmon • 12 stalks asparagus, about the diameter of a pencil. • 2.5 ounces goat cheese, crumbled (about 1/3 cup) • 1/4 cup fresh chives, cut into 1/4-inch lengths • 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt, or to taste • 2 teaspoons olive oil, extra-virgin • Vegetable oil spray or butter for greasing the muffin tins. Omit if using parchment liners. INSTRUCTIONS Prepare a 12-cup muffin pan by liberally greasing each cup or use parchment liners. Position an oven rack to the lower third position. Preheat the oven to 425°F. Cut a 1-1/2 inch length of the asparagus tips off, then cut the remaining stalks into 1/2-inch pieces to measure a generous one-half cup of pieces. Heat the 2 teaspoons of olive oil in a small skillet over medium heat. Add all the asparagus pieces and sauté until just tender. Remove from heat and set aside. Separate the asparagus tips from the 1/2-inch pieces, the tips will be used to decorate the tops of each frittata. Cut the smoked salmon into 1/2-inch squares by first cutting the entire piece of adhered sliced salmon in half lengthwise. Stack the two pieces atop each other, then cut in 1/2-inch strips lengthwise. Turn the strips 90-degrees and cut these strips crosswise in 1/2-inch increments. Gently separate the slices. It’s OK if there are a few of the thin slices stick together. Whisk together the eggs, milk, salt, and pepper in a large bowl. Add the salmon, asparagus pieces, cheese, and chives and stir to evenly distribute. (Optional: see the advance note above to layer the filling.) Divide evenly among muffin cups, leaving about 1/4-inch from the rim. Bake for 10 minutes, then remove the muffin pan to place an asparagus tip atop each mini frittata. Return to the oven, continue baking until the frittatas are lightly browned, set in the center, and puffed up. Total baking time is about 18 – 20 minutes. (Their puffy splendor is temporary, as they will fall to about even to the rim upon removal from the oven.) Transfer the muffin pan to a wire rack and cool for 10 minutes. Use a small silicone spatula to loosen around the edges and bottoms of each tin. Remove gently and serve warm.

articles.text: Piedmont resident Louis (Lou) Highman, beloved father, brother, uncle, and friend, passed away on March 23, 2023. Born Louis A. Highman, he was the second of three sons born to Arthur and Edith Arkoff Highman. He grew up in the San Fernando Valley and graduated from Birmingham High School in Van Nuys in 1965. While in high school he was student body vice president, the salutatorian of his senior class, and a champion debater. At age 16, Louis was admitted to Stanford University and graduated Phi Beta Kappa in 1969. He obtained a J.D. from Boalt Hall School of Law at the University of California, Berkeley in 1974. Between college and law school, Louis served for two years in the AmeriCorps Volunteers in Service to America (VISTA) program. After law school, he worked as a legal aid attorney for the San Francisco Neighborhood Legal Assistance Foundation before becoming a founding member of Highman, Highman & Ball, an employment and consumer law firm. Louis was a committed and talented advocate, whose legal skills and dedication improved the lives of many individuals. With cases he pursued through the higher courts, Louis helped establish precedents that continue to bolster the rights of employees and consumers. Louis enjoyed sharing his professional knowledge and experience with fellow lawyers, students, and the broader public through teaching and television and radio appearances. In 1988, Louis married Shannon Maloney and within a few years they were a family of four with two daughters, Alice and Molly. As a young family, they shared many happy times traveling, enjoying new adventures, and visiting family and friends. Louis was devoted to Shannon. Her death in 2009 was a hard Louis Highman passed away on March 23. blow, but Louis put his family ahead of his own loss. The happiness, well-being, and education of Alice and Molly became his priority. Being a father was his most treasured job and he excelled at it. Louis eagerly shared with his daughters his experiences, interests, and talents, including music, language, travel, and a lifelong love for France, which he developed during a college semester abroad in Tours, France. He was a patient and encouraging coach for the girls’ soccer and softball teams, and later he lent his considerable experience to their high school mock trial team. Louis’ sense of adventure, intellectual curiosity, and humor were matched only by his profound kindness, gentleness, and idealism. He will be dearly missed by his daughters, brothers Mark (Phyllis) and Bruce (Justine), nieces, nephews, cousins, and many (many) friends. A funeral service was held on March 27, 2023 at Mountain View Cemetery. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that memorial donations be made to the American Civil Liberties Union or another organization that honors Louis’ values and memory.
articles.title: Louis Highman dies on March 23

articles.text: Are you dreaming of taking a trip to Italy and speaking Italian while you are there? Piedmont Adult School is offering a class titled Italian for Travelers starting on April 19. The class will be on Wednesday evenings at 7 p.m. weekly to May 31. The class will be taught by Piedmont resident Rosalie Marshall, who has lived and studied in Italy and France, and holds degrees in Italian, French and Spanish. In this class, students will learn how to communicate in social and travel settings, as well as important information about the country’s culture, cuisine, and its unique lifestyle. The class is designed for travelers, foreign business professionals and those who simply enjoy a new academic adventure. To register for this or other classes, call Piedmont Adult School at 594-2717 or visit piedmontadultschool.org. Wednesdays, 7-9 p.m. April 19 - May 31 (7 sessions) $136 Instructor: Rosalie Marshall

articles.text: 5 birds recovered after fallen tree damages aviary Six exotic birds escaped after a large Eucalyptus tree fell on an aviary at Oakland Zoo during the rain and windstorm on March 21. Storms have caused the Oakland Zoo to close again after a major rain and windstorm on Tuesday, March 21. The storm knocked down a number of trees including one large Eucalyptus which lanced open an aviary. Six of the 20 aviary residents escaped through the opening, but five have since been recovered by the zoo. The tree fell onto the newest aviary at the zoo, the mesh-enclosed Hillside Aviary in the “African Savannah” section of the zoo, which was built two years ago in 2021. Six exotic birds flew out: two pied crows, one African hooded vulture, and three superb starlings. The three starlings, which are native to East Africa, flew back into their habitat on their own two days later, March 23. On Friday, zoo staffers were able to entice Oliver, the African hooded vulture, into the zoo’s flamingo habitat with some “tasty treats,” they said. The highly intelligent pied crows, native to South Africa, took their escape a little further, venturing outside the zoo property. On Saturday, March 25, a pied crow, named Deauville, was seen in a residential area about two miles from the zoo. Zookeepers, aided by a homeowner, were able to cajole Deauville into a house and eventually get him back to the zoo. The successful crow coaxing can be seen on video at: Twitter. com/oakzoo/status/16398142428 10601477?s=46&t=YY32UTCQNlVIEnmcCfuXvg Deauville’s escape partner and fellow pied crow, Diego, has still not been located. Zoo officials are asking Oakland residents to notify them if he is spotted. A black crow with a white chest, he easily stands out from other crows. “If you spot him, please don’t A rare and endangered African hooded vulture escaped from the aviary at Oakland Zoo, but was recovered after two days on the loose. Deauville, a pied crow, was caught on Saturday, March 25 after being lured onto the front porch of a house in Oakland. One pied crow, Diego, remains at large. try to catch him – he’s a very shy bird and startles easily,” advised the zoo. Anyone who sees the bird is asked to call the Zoo’s rescue hotline: 703-8986. Oakland Zoo Marketing Manager Isabella Linares stated that none of the birds posed a threat to the community, other wildlife, or pets. “These are captive bred birds who do not know how to survive on their own in the wild. They are safer at the Zoo. Our staff is working 24 hours a day to monitor and hopefully recover the remaining bird.” Open year-around, Oakland Zoo has had extensive closures due to winter storms this year. The zoo closed at the start of January for a couple of weeks when a sinkhole rendered the entry way impassible. The highly intelligent pied crows, native to South Africa, took their escape a little further, venturing outside the zoo property. On Saturday, March 25, a pied crow, named Deauville, was seen in a residential area about two miles from the zoo. Wanting to use her talents within the same mix of urban and rural government which she’d known all her life, the couple moved to El Centro in Southern California in 2002 a few months after 9/11. For four years, she served as a City Council member and, ultimately, mayor in El Centro. After additional public and private sector community development work, she worked as a Regional Affairs Officer developing housing and city growth policies with the Southern California Association of Governments (the equivalent of ABAG in the Bay Area) from 2009 to 2011. She was named City Manager of nearby Brawley where she worked for nine years, “collaborating with staff to operationalize a new fire station, establishing a new Emergency Operations Center, and renovating multiple high utilization parks, in partnership with community groups and engaged residents.” After being named Assistant City Manager of Antioch in 2020, she and her husband moved there. “Because I hadn’t been in a setting with a very large population before,” she said, “I thought it was important to add to my experience from a different position. It helped me remember that no matter the size of the city, so many issues with regard to delivering public services, maintaining infrastructure, and planning for future growth within certain financial constraints are similar.” After two years with Antioch, where she led “initiatives to design a bridge housing program for unsheltered residents and a 24-hour, 365-day community crisis intervention team,” Bayon Moore “became interested in finding an involved community where I could serve in the lead position and work directly with the Council and city staff.” Upon hearing of the job opening in Piedmont, she was struck by the city’s high level of community engagement and “the commitment of its local leaders to the democratic process. Productive dialogue never ends up the way you expect it to, yet there’s always solid decision-making as an outcome.” “Piedmont is a built-out community of 1.7 square miles … The best part is that the size allows for local government to be so in tune with residents and with opportunities to develop as a community,” she said. As well as my family and my friends for supporting me in my bird calling ventures,” Foster added, “And to Piedmont High School, I thank you for this honor. I’m never going to give this up.” Other par ticipants also stunned the audience with their amazing calls. Senior Stitch Lawrence imitated the anti-social “Go-Away Bird;” freshman Theo Ferguson, made a splash with his blue flippers as the Blue Footed Booby seabird; and the California Gull, by freshman Isabelle Myers, shed a new light on sandwich-stealing seagulls. The winners were chosen by a panel of five judges, including PHS English teacher Jamieson Mockel, Vice Principal Irma Muñoz, PHS alum Joe Fendel, and celebrity judges Rosemary Orozco and Michael Poryes. Orozco is an Emmy AwardWinning meteorologist on KTVU. Poryes, a 1973 PHS alum, produced Disney Channel hits “Hanna Montana,” “That’s so Raven” and “Life with Boys”. The PHS dance team gave a graceful performance to begin the show, Emcee Daniel Banin, a junior, cracked birding jokes in between acts, and the PHS Jazz Quartet played while the judges deliberated. This year’s contest added a new tradition, “The Great Squawk,” with past Bird Calling participants joining the competitors on stage for one final combined call. The Bird Calling Contest originated in 1963, with students attempting bird calls in the classroom of science and biology teacher Leonard Waxdeck. It was instantly popular and had to be moved to the school auditorium the following year. But as the show continues after five decades and a pandemic, the contest has become anything but regular. Past winners were invited on ‘The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson,’ and ‘Late Night with David Letterman.’ In 2022, 2015 Bird Calling winner, Maya Guzdar, showed off her call as an audience member on “The Daily Show with Trever Noah.” “As a ‘new kid,’ the silly spirit of the Bird Calling Contest helped me feel at home in Piedmont,” said Guzdar, “The contest is important, not only for its historical legacy, but in carrying forward that lightness and ‘I can make fun of myself’ attitude for Piedmont. I’m so happy that the contest is back. Let’s work as a community to keep it going.” Sohrab “Seb” Ford is a senior at Piedmont High School and an intern with the Piedmont Post. Emcee Daniel Banin has the bird callers perform their calls one last time for the judges before the winners are announced. Clio Salzer (left) and Charlotte Mascola watch a clip from Alfred Hitchcock’s film The Birds as part of their skit before performing their bird call. Since a yearlong renovation and drainage improvement project which concluded in March 2017, Hampton Field has been used for many of the sports which Sara herself played when she was in elementary and middle school: baseball, softball, soccer, basketball and tennis. Sue and Tom Smegal, who attended the event, were close friends of Sara’s parents even before 1974, when both families moved from Oakland to Piedmont. The commonality did not stop there, as the Smegals’ daughter Betsy, grew, like Sara, to be a public political figure in A view of the crowd at the retirement event at Hampton Park for Sara Lillevand. Sunday afternoon at Hampton Park was a feel-good day for Piedmonters. Lillevand Honored Continued from page 1 for her mental tenacity and physical acumen on baseball fields and basketball courts. … Without a doubt, it takes a particular type of courage to carry the expectations of people who have loved and admired you your whole life, who now look at you during times of controversy, with a deep hope that you don’t disappoint them … I have rarely seen anyone work as hard as Sara has to resolve problems, listen to community voices, guide staff and inform council members, while always working to balance perspectives, and unify community interest.” Councilmember Jennifer Long said “I want to highlight a few of the words about Sara that resonate deeply for me: integrity, respect, calm, warmth, generosity, thoughtfulness. You are all of those things, and so much more … I don’t feel a loss with you leaving, because I feel like you are a friend.” After praising Lillevand as “a trailblazer, breaking barriers in her personal and professional lives, including as Piedmont’s first female City Administrator,” mayor Jen Cavenaugh presented a proclamation that Wednesday, April 5, 2023 would be Sara Lillevand Day. “There’s no crying in baseball,” added Lillevand. “And there’s no crying in the Council chambers.” She then thanked the “leadership team who’s here, but also the 93 individuals who come together every day, and execute very different roles and responsibilities to deliver a sum of service that is much greater than its parts.” “I can say I’ve given this job my all and I’m really, really tired, and I’m ready for a rest,” she added, “But I’m excited also for the future of Piedmont … and the City Administrator coming in on Thursday. I’m thrilled that I get to be a resident of Piedmont still knowing that Rosanna Bayon Moore is going to be a tremendous leader for the best city department head team ever and the best City Council any city could ever wish for.” 2023 Calendar of Events APRIL 10 – APRIL 23 Meetings may be viewed on KCOM (Channel 27) and on the City’s website: piedmont.ca.gov. City Hall Thursday, April 20 7 p.m. .................Diversity Film Series. .....................................................Ellen Driscoll Playhouse Sunday, April 23 11 am–4 pm ........Piedmont Food Fest. ...................................................................Piedmont Park Sara Lillevand with her father, Dave, at her retirement party at Hampton Park on April 2. her hometown. “Sara has been special since the day I met her,” said Sue, the mother of City Council member Betsy Andersen. “Her mother was absolutely one of my best friends, and I feel like we raised all the children together. Betsy has told me time and time again since being on Council that Sara is the best thing that has ever happened. I think we’re really lucky to have had her.” After the farewell event, Sue wrote a message to Sara praising her intelligence and common sense, both as a decision maker and as a listener of varying community perspectives. In response, Sara thanked Sue for her “care and love over the decades,” adding that “working with Betsy has been a highlight” of her time working with the city. City Council honors Lillevand The following day, Monday, April 3, Sue went with a friend to Ole’s Waffle Shop in Alameda – where Sara’s father and Sue grew up – and an eatery they enjoyed. When Sue mentioned this, Betsy said, “‘Now I know what to give to Sara for her birthday” on April 5. “She had me buy a gift certificate to Ole’s so Sara and her dad could go together,” explained Sue. “It really was the perfect present.” The crowning achievement for Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO) has been the fundraising effort to fully renovate Hampton Park. Eric Havian, PRFO’s General Counsel, was one of those involved from start to finish. “There were a lot of damp eyes after [Sara] talked about how special that field was to her, growing up in Piedmont. I’m sure her replacement will be outstanding, but Sara’s really a tough act to follow,” Havian said. “Many people at the farewell expressed their admiration for Sara’s leadership, particularly when it came to the Housing Element, the pool project, and the pandemic. The success we’ve had with Hampton Field itself is due in large part to Sara, as a PRFO liaison, making sure everything was on track,” Havian continued. “I think we’ll all remember this farewell for a long, long time.” Where in the World Are We?
